name: Brown Butter and Sage Butternut Squash Bake
ingredients:
Nonstick cooking spray, for the baking pan
1 1/4 pounds (567 g) butternut squash, cubed
6 tablespoons (85 g) unsalted butter
1 medium onion, finely diced
2 tablespoons (6.9 g) chopped fresh sage
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) freshly ground black pepper
10 to 15 butter crackers, such as Ritz, roughly crushed
directions:
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees F. Spray a baking pan with nonstick cooking spray and place the squash in the pan.

Heat 1 tablespoon of the butter in a medium skillet over medium heat. Add the onion and cook until tender and translucent, 6 to 8 minutes. Transfer the onion to the pan with the squash.

Return the skillet to the heat and add the remaining 5 tablespoons butter. Heat until the butter melts and begins to brown, 3 to 4 minutes. (The butter will begin to separate and sizzle. Take care to let it gently brown rather than burn. If the butter burns, throw it out and try again.) Stir in the sage. Drizzle the butter mixture over the squash and sprinkle with the salt and pepper. Use a wooden spoon to toss the mixture until the squash is evenly coated with the browned butter.

Bake until the squash is tender and beginning to brown around the edges, about 1 hour. Remove from the oven and increase the temperature to 400 degrees F. Top the squash with the crackers and cook until the crackers are nicely golden brown, an additional 20 minutes.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Katie Lee Biegel builds an autumn side around cubed butternut squash baked with butter that has been cooked until it browns, plus fresh sage and softened onion. Browning the butter first drives off water and toasts the milk solids, which is where the nutty depth comes from that plain melted butter cannot give. Crushed butter crackers scattered over the top crisp in the oven and supply the contrast to the soft squash.

Note on the source: no comments or rating on Food Network page

Link confidence: LOW — this URL is a plausible version of the dish but was not verified as the family's exact recipe. Treat the link as a lead, not a citation.

claude_opt.changes: Comparable squash gratins (Cookin' Canuck) cover the pan for the first bake so raw cubes steam tender without drying; this recipe bakes uncovered a full hour. Cover with foil first.

name: Brownie Nut Pie
ingredients:
2 eggs, well beaten
1 c. (200 g) sugar
1/2 c. (114 g) butter or margarine, melted
1/2 c. (60 g) flour
4-5 T. (22-27 g) cocoa
1 T. (13 g)  vanilla [recipe says T but perhaps should be t]
1 c. (117 g) chopped walnuts
fresh strawberries or raspberries to decorate
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.

Lightly grease a 9" pie plate. Mix eggs, sugar, and melted butter or margarine. Mix dry ingredients together and add to egg mixture. Add vanilla and nuts. Pour into pie plate and bake 20-25 minutes or until center is just firm. Do not overbake. Cool slightly before cutting into pie-shaped wedges. Dust with confectioners sugar and decorate with fruit.

claude_opt.changes: 1 Tbsp vanilla (already flagged in the card as possibly a typo) is 3x a typical brownie pie's amount for this batter size; use 1 tsp (4 g) unless the strong vanilla is intentional.

name: Brownies
ingredients:
3 oz. (85 g) unsweetened chocolate
6 T. (85 g) butter
1 1/2 c. (300 g) sugar
3 eggs
1/4 t. (1.5 g) salt
3/4 c. (90 g) flour
3/4 c. (88 g) chopped walnuts
1 1/2 t. (6.3 g) vanilla
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.
Grease 9" square pan. Melt chocolate and butter until smooth. Add sugar, eggs, salt flour, walnuts, and vanilla. (This can all be done in the melting pan.) Combine well. Bake 40 minutes. Cool 15 minutes before cutting.
description: Our standard brownie recipe.
notes:
Web summary (pattyandersonsblog.blogspot.com). Patty Anderson writes this up as the plain, reliable brownie from the Fannie Farmer Cookbook, offered without embellishment because it does not need any. The whole thing is mixed in the pan the chocolate and butter were melted in, so there is one dish to wash and no creaming step, which is what makes it a standing family recipe rather than an occasion bake. Nuts are treated as optional.

What readers report: One reader found the vanilla quantity too high and cut it to two teaspoons with good results. Another had lost their own old Fannie Farmer copy in the Hurricane Harvey flooding and was using this page to recover the recipe — an indication of how closely it tracks the printed original.

Note on the source: Right cookbook (explicitly the Fannie Farmer Cookbook, which is exactly what the collection records) and clearly the same recipe: the blog's version is a scaled-up pan, with chocolate, butter, flour, walnuts and salt all exactly double the family's 3 oz / 6 T / 3/4 c / 3/4 c / 1/4 t. Not provably the identical printing: sugar is 2 3/4 c where double would be 3 c, and eggs are 4 where the family has 3 (double would be 6). Also a personal blog rather than an authoritative Fannie Farmer page, and no official one exists. Note the Seattle Times 'Fannie Merritt Farmer style' result is the 1896 Boston Cooking-School original, a different and much cakier recipe — not this one.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Family calls this their standard; other printed Fannie Farmer versions vary widely in ratio and bake time, so there's no clear consensus fix to chase.

name: Bruschetta
ingredients:
1-2 medium tomatoes (1 c chopped)
1/3 c chopped creen onions
1/2 c chopped black olives
1 tsp (3.0 g) capers (drained)
1 T olive oil
1 T fresh basil
1 T oregano
2 small cloves garlic
2 t Balsamic vinegar
Ground pepper
directions: Mix together, refrigerate. Cut long fresh bread in 1" slices. Sprinkle bread with oil. Toast in 425 F oven about 5 min. Cool. Spoon topping on slices, serve!

claude_opt.changes: If the oregano is dried rather than fresh, 1 Tbsp will overpower the topping; modern bruschetta recipes use dried herbs by the teaspoon. Cut to 1 tsp if it's dried oregano.

name: Brussels Sprouts -- Braised
source: 2004 The New Best Recipe Book, ATK
ingredients:
1 lb. (454 g) Brussels sprouts, stem end trimmed and discolored leaves removed by hand
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
1/2 c. (118 g) water
directions: Bring sprouts, water, and salt to a boil in a 2 qt. saucepan over medium-high heat. Cover and simmer (shaking pan once or twice to redistribute sprouts) until knife tip inserted into center meets no resistance, 8-10 minutes. Drain well and season with pepper, butter, and/or salt.
notes:
Web summary (americastestkitchen.com, 4 out of 5 stars (11 ratings)). The test kitchen landed on braising as the best treatment for sprouts because it draws off bitterness while keeping the colour bright and the texture tender rather than squeaky. Nothing is needed but water and salt in a covered pan, which is the point — the method beat microwaving and other shortcuts in their testing without adding a single extra ingredient. Seasoning is left until after draining so the sprouts are not watered down.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS — rating shown but no reader comments on the page.

Note on the source: Exact match. ATK's ingredient list is 1 lb Brussels sprouts (stem ends and discoloured leaves removed) and 1/2 tsp table salt, with the 1/2 cup water in the method — identical to the family's 1 lb / 1/2 t salt / 1/2 c water, and the family's directions (boil covered, shake the pan, 8-10 min, drain, season with butter/salt/pepper) track the ATK method step for step. Collection records '2004 The New Best Recipe Book, ATK' and this is that recipe in ATK's own archive. Page is subscription-gated for full text but the headnote, ingredients and rating came through.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. This is an exact match to ATK's tested method (water, salt, covered, 8-10 min), and no reviewer comments flag any problem with it.

name: Buckwheat Pancakes
ingredients:
1/2 c. (122 g) milk
2 tb. melted butter
1 egg
1/2 c. (60 g) AP flour
1/2 c. (60 g) buckwheat flour
2 tsp. (8.0 g) baking powder
2 tb. sugar
1/2 tsp. (3.0 g) salt
directions: Put milk, melted butter, and egg in bowl and beat lightly. Add flours, baking powder, sugar, and salt. Mix lightly. Pour onto greased hot skillet. Serve with maple syrup.
notes: Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Method already matches modern buckwheat pancake technique: wet ingredients beaten first, dry folded in lightly to avoid toughening. No doneness, safety, or ingredient issues found.

name: Butter-Braised Asparagus
ingredients:
1 1/2 pounds (680 g) large or medium asparagus
6 tablespoons (85 g) butter
Salt and pepper
2 tablespoons (30 g) lemon juice
1/2 teaspoon (1.0 g) lemon zest
1 tablespoon (3.0 g) snipped chives
1 tablespoon (3.8 g) roughly chopped parsley or chervil
1 teaspoon (1.1 g) chopped tarragon, plus more for garnish
1 tablespoon (2.8 g) chopped dill, plus more for garnish (optional)
directions:
Snap off and discard the tough bottoms of the asparagus spears. If using large, thick asparagus, peel the lower ends with a vegetable peeler.

Put butter in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. Add asparagus in one layer and season with salt and pepper. Add 1/2 cup water, cover, and bring to a simmer. Cook until the asparagus is firm-tender, about 3 minutes. Take care not to overcook them; they should still be bright green. (They will continue to cook a bit once the heat is off.) Remove the asparagus from the pan and place on a serving platter.

Turn heat to high and simmer briskly until most of the liquid has evaporated, a minute or so. Add lemon juice and zest to the buttery juices. Turn off heat and stir in chives, parsley, tarragon and dill, if using. Check seasoning. Spoon the sauce over the asparagus, garnish with a few herb leaves, and serve.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (953)). A deliberately plain treatment for the first asparagus of spring: butter, lemon and delicate herbs, nothing more. The one step the recipe insists on is peeling the stalks, which it says changes the texture substantially. It ran alongside a piece on asparagus being at its sweetest in spring.

What readers report: The top note (101 votes) is about waste: microwave the trimmed-off ends, puree them, enrich with butter and seasoning, and serve that as a buttery sauce beside the spears. The next (79) invokes Julia Child in support of peeling medium and large spears, but disputes the usual prep - do not snap the spears at their natural break point, line them up and cut about half an inch off instead, which wastes far less. A 49-vote note gives a peeling technique: press the spear flat on a board with one hand and shave with the other. A dissenting 40-vote note prefers Patricia Wells's braise - wash but do not dry the spears and braise in 2 to 3 tablespoons of butter per pound and a half, no peeling. One commenter questions trimming the ends at all.

Note on the source: readers disagree on whether to peel and on snapping vs cutting the ends

name: Buttermilk Blue Cheese Dressing
ingredients:
2 ounces (60g) mild blue cheese
1/2 cup (120ml) mayonnaise
1/2 cup (120ml) sour cream
1/2 cup (120ml) buttermilk
1 tablespoon (15ml) fresh juice from 1 lemon
Freshly ground black pepper
Kosher salt (if needed)
directions: 1. In a medium bowl, mash blue cheese with a whisk. Whisk in mayonnaise, sour cream, buttermilk, and lemon juice until a smooth, slightly lumpy dressing forms. Season with pepper. (The blue cheese will likely make the dressing salty enough, but taste and add salt if necessary.) Serve.
description: 8/18 Use more blue cheese!
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.3 (6) / 12 Reviews). Daniel Gritzer offers this as a short case for making blue cheese dressing yourself rather than buying it. He builds it on a mild rather than aggressive blue cheese loosened with sour cream and mayonnaise, with lemon juice to bring the whole thing into balance. The point he stresses is the buttermilk, which might look redundant next to two other dairy ingredients but earns its place twice over: it contributes a lactic tang that cuts the richness of the mayonnaise and cheese, and it thins the dressing just enough to pour cleanly over a wedge of iceberg instead of sitting on it in clots.

What readers report: Two themes dominate this small set of reviews. First, make it ahead: several people report the blue cheese flavor is muted if served right after mixing and that a few hours, or overnight, lets it develop, with one calling it better still on following days. Second, readers consistently want more aromatics than the recipe includes - garlic comes up repeatedly, alongside suggestions of Worcestershire sauce, a dash of cayenne, and using Maytag or gorgonzola in place of a generic mild blue. Consistent with the make-ahead point, the one negative review found the dressing thin, diluted and barely tasting of blue cheese. Greek yogurt was reported as a working substitute for buttermilk where it is unavailable, and it holds a thicker consistency. The dressing is also used as a dip for buffalo wings.

Note on the source: Headnote on this page is very short - only a few sentences plus two 'why it works' bullets, no long article. Page title is 'Best Buttermilk Blue Cheese Dressing Recipe' vs manifest name. Only 12 reviews, several are praise-only.

claude_opt.changes: Double the blue cheese to 4 oz, as your 8/18 note already found necessary. Mix a few hours or overnight ahead — readers report the flavor is muted when served immediately.

name: Buttermilk Roast Chicken
ingredients:
1 4-pound (1.8 kg) chicken
2 cups (484 g) buttermilk
¼ cup (54 g) plus 2 tablespoons vegetable oil
2 cloves garlic, lightly crushed
1 tablespoon (8.7 g) crushed black peppercorns
1 tablespoon (7.5 g) Maldon or other sea salt
2 tablespoons (6.9 g) fresh rosemary leaves, roughly chopped
1 tablespoon (21 g) honey
directions:
Butterfly chicken by placing breast side down and using heavy-duty kitchen shears to cut along both sides of backbone. Discard backbone, turn chicken over and open it like a book. Press gently to flatten it.

Place chicken in a large freezer bag. Add buttermilk, 1/4 cup oil, garlic, peppercorns, salt, rosemary and honey. Seal bag securely and refrigerate overnight or up to two days.

Heat oven to 400 degrees. Remove chicken from marinade and place on a rack so excess can drip off. Line a roasting pan with foil and place chicken in pan. Drizzle with remaining 2 tablespoons oil. Roast for 45 minutes, then reduce heat to 325 degrees. Continue roasting until well browned and until juices run clear when chicken is pierced where leg joins thigh, about another 20 minutes.

Place chicken on a carving board and allow to rest for 10 minutes before cutting into serving pieces. Place a portion on each of four plates, and drizzle each serving with pan juices.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (4,275)). Nigella Lawson's spatchcocked roast chicken, which reads as casual as barbecue without any of the work. Butterflying the bird takes nothing more than kitchen shears. The buttermilk - normally a fried-chicken ingredient - both tenderises the meat and carries the rosemary, pepper and garlic deep into it, so the aromatics register properly. Maple syrup substitutes for the honey if you prefer. The marinating bird will happily sit in the fridge for up to two days, getting more tender, so dinner is just a matter of putting it in the oven.

What readers report: The most-endorsed change (616 votes) is to stop discarding the marinade drippings and instead roast the chicken over sliced potatoes in a cast-iron pan so they soak up the juices, which also removes the need for a rack. A 338-vote note extends this: add carrots and halved Brussels sprouts around the bird about 20 minutes into the roast. A 254-vote question - rack or straight onto foil - goes unresolved by the recipe itself. Thighs work well in place of a whole bird (249 votes), and that commenter used 2 tablespoons of honey and found the rosemary did not dominate. Practical tip at 169 votes: crush the peppercorns between a towel or heavy paper with a mallet, checking often since they pulverise fast. Maple syrup is the common swap.

Note on the source: recipe is ambiguous about rack vs. direct pan - a highly-voted question with no author answer

name: Buttermilk Vanilla Waffles
servings: Two 8-inch square waffles or three 7-inch belgian waffles
ingredients:
6 1/2 ounces all-purpose flour (1 1/3 cup; 185g)
1 1/2 ounces powdered sugar (1/4 cup plus 2 tablespoons; 45g)
1/2 teaspoon (2g) Diamond Crystal kosher salt; for table salt, use half as much by volume or use the same weight
1/2 teaspoon (3g) baking soda
1/2 teaspoon (2g) baking powder
1 vanilla bean, split and scraped (see note)
14 ounces cultured lowfat buttermilk (1 3/4 cup; 395g) (see note)
1 1/2 ounces unsalted butter, melted (3 tablespoons; 40g)
2 large egg whites (about 2 1/2 ounces; 70g)
1 teaspoon (5ml) vanilla extract
Maple syrup, for serving
directions:
1. For the Batter: In a large bowl, combine flour, powdered sugar, salt, baking soda, baking powder, and the scrapings of one large vanilla bean, mixing by hand until the seeds are well dispersed. Add buttermilk, melted butter, egg whites, and vanilla extract and whisk until smooth.

2. For the Waffles: Set waffle iron to medium and preheat until the indicator is ready. For an 8-inch square machine, scrape in roughly half the batter. For a 7-inch Belgian machine, scrape in about one-third. Close lid and cook until waffle is golden brown but still steaming, 4 1/2 to 6 minutes depending on the depth and heat of your machine. Serve immediately, with copious amounts of maple syrup, and griddle remaining batter as before.
description: 5/2019 Will and Lene made. Used setting 5 on waffler.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.7 (18) / 78 Reviews). Stella Parks makes the case for a deliberately lazy one-bowl waffle batter: no separating or whipping eggs, no separate wet and dry bowls, no sifting or folding. Her argument is that whipped whites exist to aerate batters that rise slowly in an oven, whereas a waffle is pressed between hot plates where steam does all the lifting, so hydration matters more than aeration. She builds the batter on buttermilk and egg whites only - moist and high in protein but lean, which gives structure and keeps the waffles crisp rather than cakey - uses powdered sugar because it dissolves smoothly, and adds only a pinch of baking soda, treating it as a seasoning that tempers the buttermilk's tang without cancelling it. Her main warning is not to overfill the iron, since batter that spreads outward cannot rise or vent its steam, and slightly ragged edges are a sign it had room to expand.

What readers report: The single most useful correction addresses limp, flat waffles: one reviewer traced the problem to thin store-bought buttermilk, noting Stella's is thick and creamy and that homemade milk-plus-vinegar substitutes make the batter too loose, and reports that switching to kefir produced crisp, airy results. Flavored kefir also works and doubles as a flavoring - blueberry kefir plus frozen berries adds flavor and, because the batter goes in very cold, slows cooking and browns the waffles better. Granulated sugar can stand in for powdered if it is whisked into the liquid first so it dissolves, and vanilla extract substitutes acceptably for the bean, though several say the bean is noticeably better. The recipe halves cleanly. Some cut the sugar by half. The waffles are reported to freeze and reheat well. One open question, unanswered, is whether any egg substitute works for the whites.

Note on the source: Several comments end in 'Read More' and may be truncated.

claude_opt.changes: If waffles turn out flat, thin store-bought buttermilk is the likely cause; swap in thick buttermilk or plain kefir, which readers found gives crisper, better-risen waffles for no extra time.

name: Cacio E Pepe (Spaghetti with Black Pepper and Pecorino Romano)
ingredients:
4 tablespoons (60ml) extra-virgin olive oil, divided
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) coarsely ground black pepper, to taste
Kosher salt, to taste
1/2 pound (225g) spaghetti
2 tablespoons (30g) unsalted butter
2 ounces Pecorino Romano cheese (about 1 cup; 55g), very finely grated on a Microplane or the smallest holes of a box grater, plus more for serving
directions:
Heat 3 tablespoons olive oil and about a teaspoon of black pepper in a medium skillet over medium-low heat until ingredients are fragrant and pepper is barely starting to sizzle, about 1 minute. Set aside.

Place spaghetti in a large skillet and cover with water. Season with a small pinch of salt, then bring to a boil over high heat, prodding spaghetti occasionally with a fork or wooden spoon to prevent it from clumping. Cook until spaghetti is al dente (typically about 1 minute less than the package recommends). Transfer 2 to 3 tablespoons of pasta cooking water to the skillet with the olive oil/pepper mixture. Stir in butter. Using tongs, lift spaghetti and transfer it to the oil/butter mixture.

Add cheese and remaining tablespoon olive oil to the skillet and stir with a fork until cheese is completely melted. Add a few more tablespoons of pasta water to the skillet to adjust consistency, reheating as necessary until the sauce is creamy and coats each strand of spaghetti. Season to taste with salt and more black pepper. Serve immediately, passing extra grated cheese and black pepper at the table.
description: 11/21 Method worked really well. Used store bought fancy linguine. Did by eye. We ended up with too much pepper and too much salt in the water. But overall very good.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.6 (24) / 85 Reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt treats this three-ingredient Roman pasta as a deceptively hard dish, since the two classic failures - a thin greasy sauce or stubborn clumps of cheese - both come from trying to make something creamy out of a hard, dry, aged cheese. He explains that aged Pecorino is low in moisture and prone to breaking, which starchy pasta water fixes, while its tight protein structure tangles into lumps if heated too fast. His answers are to grate the cheese as finely as possible on a Microplane so it melts evenly, and to use two pans: one to boil the pasta and a second, cooler one in which the sauce is built. The second pan brought an unexpected bonus, since toasting the pepper in oil there mellows and sweetens it, and he cooks the spaghetti in just enough water to cover so the starch stays concentrated, lifting the pasta straight across with tongs instead of draining.

What readers report: The most-endorsed point, echoing the article, is that the cheese must be ground truly fine - one reviewer with two votes says skipping that left a cheese ball the size of a tennis ball. A highly rated comment credits the method as written and reports no clumping. Alternatives appear for cooks who still struggle: one describes a Roman restaurant method of working powdered cheese and pepper into a paste with ice water so no heat touches the sauce until it meets the hot pasta; another returns drained pasta to the pot and stirs the cheese in thirds with the lid on two to three minutes between additions. Dissent exists - one cook who weighed everything and used a Microplane still got an oily result across four attempts, and another warns too much cheese always clumps and that hand-grating rock-hard Pecorino blows past the stated 20 minutes. Popular additions: minced garlic in the pepper oil, plus shrimp or chicken.

Note on the source: Several comments end in 'Read More' and may be truncated.

claude_opt.changes: Cut the pepper to a scant 1/2 teaspoon and salt the pasta water lightly — your 11/21 note found both overdone. The Microplane-fine grated cheese called for is already correct; keep that.

name: Caesar Salad
ingredients:
2½ oil-packed anchovy fillets
1 large clove garlic, grated Kosher salt and pepper
¼ cup (55 g) mayonnaise
1½ tsp (7.8 g) Dijon mustard
½ tsp (1.0 g) lemon zest plus
1 Tbsp (15 g) lemon juice
12 oz (340 g) romaine lettuce hearts (halved, or cut into thirds crosswise if large), leaves separated
2 Tbsp (11 g) grated Parmesan cheese, plus more for servinga
directions:
Place anchovy fillets on cutting board, sprinkle grated garlio and ½ tsp salt on top and finely chop together, smashing with back of knife, until paste forms. Transfer to large bowl and whisk in mayonnaise, mustard, lemon zest and juice and ¼ tsp pepper to combine. Toss with romaine to coat, then grated Parme-san. Serve with additional Parmesan and cracked pepper if desired.
SERVES 4

claude_opt.changes: Already a modern, food-safe Caesar: mayo-based dressing (no raw egg), anchovy-garlic paste, Dijon and lemon match current best-practice versions exactly. Nothing worth changing.

name: Candied Orange Peel
ingredients:
3 large oranges
450g castor sugar
water
directions:
Cut off the ends of the oranges and place them cut side down on a chopping board. Use a knife to peel the oranges from top to bottom, removing the skin with as little white pith as possible.

Slice peel into thin strips, then put in a small saucepan and cover with cold water, then bring to a boil on high heat.

Once boiling, strain off the water, then repeat the process by covering with cold water again and bringing to a boil on high heat.

Once boiling for the second time, strain off the water and cover with 450ml of cold water, and add the sugar. Bring to a boil and then let simmer for half an hour.

Once finished, strain off the sugar solution and let the candied peel cool and dry out for a couple of hours on a cooling rack. Store in a cool, dry place and it will last for a long time.
description: 12/25 Used this recipe and 5 navel oranges for the Massari panettone. Massari calls for a bit more peel than I had. Could do 1-2 more orangea. Also a candied lemon peel recipe from the same author.
notes:
Web summary (maxmakesmunch.com). Max Makes Munch treats candied peel as a way to use up what normally goes in the bin, and points out the result can be eaten plain, tossed in sugar or dipped in chocolate. The key move is boiling the peel in several changes of fresh water before it ever meets the syrup, because that is what strips out the bitterness in the pith. Only then does the peel simmer in sugar syrup long enough for the sugar to replace the water inside it.

name: Caramelized Onion and Fennel Risotto
ingredients:
1 small bulb fennel, sliced thin
1 medium onion, sliced thin
1 tablespoon (14 g) olive oil
3 tablespoons (43 g) butter, divided (use Earth Balance to make it vegan)
¼ teaspoon (1.4 g) sea salt
¼ teaspoon (1.1 g) sugar
2 cloves garlic, minced
2 cups (400 g) Arborio rice
1 ½ cups (356 g) dry white wine
2 tablespoons (6.9 g) fresh rosemary leaves, minced
Handful of fresh parsley, minced
4 cups (960 g) vegetable broth, heated
¾ cup (68 g) grated Parmesan cheese (omit Parmesan to make it vegan)
directions:
In a heavy pot or Dutch oven, heat oil and 2 tablespoons butter over medium-low heat. When butter is melted, add sliced onion and fennel and stir until coated. Cover the pan and cook slowly until tender, about 10 minutes. Stir in salt and sugar. Raise heat to medium-high and cook, stirring frequently until onions are dark brown, about 25-30 minutes.

Simmer broth in a separate pot on the stove.

To the onions and fennel, add garlic, Arborio rice and herbs. Cook, stirring frequently until the rice is translucent around the edges, about 3 minutes. Add wine and cook, stirring frequently, until fully absorbed, 4 to 5 minutes. When the wine is fully absorbed, add 2 cups hot broth and simmer, stirring every 3 to 4 minutes until liquid is absorbed, about 12 minutes. Stir in another 1/2 cup of hot broth and cook, stirring constantly until absorbed. Repeat with additional broth 2 or 3 more times, until rice is al dente. Remove risotto from heat and stir in remaining 1 tablespoon butter and Parmesan. Serve.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (630)). A substantial autumn risotto whose flavour comes from onions and fennel cooked down until caramelised. It was submitted by a reader, Joe DiMaria of Somerville, who wanted a vegetarian holiday main that did not fall back on squash, root vegetables or sweet potatoes - the usual default, and one he does not like. NYT ran it as part of a vegetarian Thanksgiving series.

What readers report: Vote counts here are low (top note 42), so treat the advice as suggestive. That top note warns the fennel comes through only faintly while the herbs, rosemary in particular, are assertive and should be dialled back. A 16-vote note is blunter: the recipe works but only if you ignore parts of it, singling out the 25 to 30 minute caramelisation over medium-high heat as far too aggressive for most pans. Several cooks scale the rice down to one cup while keeping a full onion and fennel bulb, which shifts the ratio toward the vegetables - one specifies 1 tablespoon rosemary, one onion, one bulb, one cup rice, finished with lemon juice to brighten it. Going heavy on onion and fennel with a punchy olive oil is a recurring endorsement.

Note on the source: low vote counts throughout; commenters say the stated caramelisation heat and time are wrong

name: Caribbean Chicken
ingredients:
2 1/2 lbs. (1.1 kg) cut up chicken
2 cloves garlic
2-3 peppercorns
1 t. (1.1 g) oregano
2 t. (12 g) salt
3 T. (41 g) oil
1 T. (15 g) vinegar
juice of 2 limes or lemons
directions: Put chicken in a sturdy zip lock bag with lime/lemon juice. Blend rest of ingredients to a thick paste. Add to chicken. Marinate at least 1 hour (better overnight). Grill or broil for 25 minutes or until done.

ahead: Marinate at least 1 hour (better overnight).

claude_opt.changes: Grilling/broiling 'until done' is vague and risks over- or under-cooking; use a thermometer instead, pulling at 165F for breast or 175F for thigh/leg meat.

name: Carrot Cake
ingredients:
2 1/4 c. (270 g) flour
2 1/2 t. (6.5 g) cinnamon
1 1/2 t. (6.9 g) baking soda
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
4 eggs
2 c. (400 g) sugar
1 1/2 c. (192 g) grated carrots (about 3 large)
3/4 c. (164 g) vegetable oil
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.

Mix flour, cinnamon, soda and salt. Set aside. In bowl of mixer beat eggs and sugar until fluffy and lemon-colored. Add carrots and oil and mix well. Add flour mixture and stir to mix well. Pour into greased pan and bake for about 45 minutes. Cool at room temperature and frost. 

Frosting (optional)
Beat together 3 oz. of softened cream cheese and 1/4 c. softened butter. Add 2 1/4 c. confectioners sugar and 1 t. grated lemon peel; beat until it reaches spreading consistency.
notes: Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Baking by time alone ('about 45 minutes') doesn't account for pan size or oven variance; add a toothpick doneness check (clean or a few moist crumbs) before pulling from the oven.

name: Cauliflower Cheese Pie
ingredients:
Potato Crust:
2 cups (300 g) grated raw potatoes
1/2 teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
1 large egg
1/4 cup (40 g) grated onion
Olive oil
Filling:
4 large eggs
1/2 cup (122 g) milk
3 tablespoons (17 g) grated Parmesan
3/4 to 1 teaspoon (4.5-6.0 g) salt
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) freshly milled black pepper
3 tablespoons (43 g) butter
1 cup (160 g) chopped onions
1 garlic clove, finely chopped
1 medium cauliflower, broken into small florets
2 tablespoons (7.5 g) chopped fresh parsley
1 1/2 teaspoons (0.8 g) chopped fresh basil, or 1/2 teaspoon dried
3/4 teaspoon (0.9 g) chopped fresh thyme, or 1/4 teaspoon dried
1 3/4 cups (198 g) grated Gruyere
Paprika
directions:
Preheat the oven to 400 degrees F. Generously oil a 9-inch pie pan.

Potato Crust: Place 2 firmly packed cups grated raw potatoes in a colander placed over a bowl; toss the potatoes with 1/2 teaspoon salt and set aside for 10 minutes. Squeeze out the excess water. Combine the drained potatoes, 1 large egg, beaten, and 1/4 cup grated onion in a medium bowl. Pat the potato mixture into the oiled pie pan, building up the sides of the crust with lightly floured fingers. Bake for 35 to 40 minutes, until golden brown, brushing the crust with oil after the first 20 minutes to crisp it.

Remove crust from the oven and reduce the temperature to 350 degrees F.

Meanwhile, beat together the eggs, milk, 1/2 teaspoon of the salt, and the pepper in a small bowl; set aside.

Blanch cauliflower. Melt the butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add the cauliflower, onions, garlic, and 1/4 to 1/2 teaspoon of the remaining salt; cook, stirring frequently, until lightly browned, about 5 minutes. Add the parsley, basil, and thyme; cook, covered, for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Remove from the heat.

Layer the baked potato crust with 1/2 of the cheese, then the cauliflower mixture, then the remaining cheese. Pour the milk mixture over the top and lightly dust with paprika. Bake for 35 to 40 minutes, until set. Remove from the oven and serve.
description:
12/08 Good! Takes time! Maybe do crust ahead.
6/13 Fabulous with fresh herbs.
9/17 Made again with great results. Could have used more potatoes than 1 russet.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Credited to Lori Stein, Joanne Lamb Hayes and Maura Webber, this is a vegetarian main built on a crust of grated raw potato rather than pastry, bound with egg and onion and crisped in oil before the filling goes in. Cauliflower florets are cooked down with onion, garlic and herbs, then set in an egg-and-milk custard with a generous amount of Gruyere and Parmesan. The custard is what holds the vegetables together so the pie slices rather than crumbles.

Note on the source: no comments or rating on Food Network page

Link confidence: LOW — this URL is a plausible version of the dish but was not verified as the family's exact recipe. Treat the link as a lead, not a citation.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Notes across three years (12/08, 6/13, 9/17) already cover it: use more than one potato in the crust, and make the crust ahead of time.

name: Cauliflower Gratin with Leeks and White Cheddar--Alison Roman
ingredients:
1 small-ish head cauliflower (about 2 pounds), green leaves removed
Olive oil, for drizzling
1 small leek, white and light green part only, very thinly sliced
Kosher salt and black pepper
¾ cup (178 g) heavy cream
6 ounces (170 g) sharp white Cheddar, grated (about 1 1/2 cups)
directions:
Heat oven to 425 degrees. Slice cauliflower head lengthwise into 1/2-inch thick slices, including the core and leaves. (Some smaller bits will fall away: That’s fine. You’ll use them as well.)

Drizzle some olive oil onto the bottom of a 2-quart baking dish. (An oval, square or rectangular dish will all work.) Layer about a third of the cauliflower along the bottom, and about a third of the leeks. Season with salt and pepper, and repeat until all of the cauliflower and leeks are used. (Don’t worry about perfectly layering them.) Season with salt and pepper and drizzle cream over. Scatter cheese on top, and season again with salt and pepper. Lightly cover with foil and place in the oven.

Bake until cauliflower is nearly tender, 10 to 15 minutes. Remove foil and continue to bake until cream has thickened and reduced nearly completely and the top is golden brown and crisp, 35 to 40 minutes. Remove from oven and let cool slightly before eating.
description:
2/19 Excellent. Made 4x already! Added serrano and extra leeks. Made with florets rather than slices. Bake for 20 minutes covered, then 40 mins uncovered. This helps to reduce the wateriness.
1/21 Great with a bit of bacon. 
10/23 Added roast chicken. Delish. Made a whole meal.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (3,677)). Alison Roman's shortcut gratin: no blanching the cauliflower and no bechamel to make. The cauliflower and leeks go into the dish with cream and bake under foil, which steams them tender without letting them dry out. Pulling the foil off for the rest of the bake browns the top and reduces the cream into a thick, glossy sauce on its own. If you want crunch, scatter olive-oil-tossed, seasoned bread crumbs over it at the point the foil comes off.

What readers report: The most-voted note (249) is a leek-cleaning technique rather than a recipe change: cut an X into the base and stand the leek in a bowl of water for five to ten minutes so the grit falls out. The dominant substantive thread is dairy substitution, which the recipe does not address - a 242-vote question asks for an alternative to heavy cream and whether it freezes, and readers answer from experience: coconut milk changed neither flavour nor texture (205 votes), half-and-half works (134), and plain Greek yogurt works when doubled, though with a looser result (107). Cheese is equally flexible - Gruyere and Parmesan in place of cheddar, and an onion standing in for the leek, drew 175 votes. Bread crumbs on top are near-universally recommended.

Note on the source: top-voted question about cream substitutes goes unanswered by the recipe; readers supply the answers

name: Char Siu
ingredients:
Pork:
3 lbs (1.4 kg) lean pork (boneless ribs or tenderloin). Cut prices 1/2" thick + 6" long
1 tsp (6.0 g) salt 
2 Tbs (25 g) sugar

Marinade:
3 T Hoisin sauce
1 T Ketchup 
2 T Honey
1 T dry sherry
1 T Soy sauce
1/8 t. Spice powder
directions:
Mix salt and sugar. Rub onto pork strips. Let Stanford for 15 minutes.

Pour marinade onto pork strips for 3 hrs or overnight. Place oven rack on top shelf. Use metal paper clips to flay meat strips. Hang on top rack. 

Place pan with water under meat to catch the drippings. Bake 350 F (45-60 minutes)

ahead: Pour marinade onto pork strips for 3 hrs or overnight.

claude_opt.changes: Lean tenderloin/boneless ribs dry out over a 45-60 min hanging bake; pork shoulder or country ribs stay juicier. Baste with reserved marinade every 15 min and pull at 145F internal.

name: Charlie Bird’s Farro Salad
ingredients:
1 cup (200 g) farro
1 cup (240 g) apple cider
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) kosher salt, more as needed
2 bay leaves
8 tablespoons (108 g) extra-virgin olive oil
2 tablespoons (30 g) fresh lemon juice
70 grams Parmesan cheese, shaved with a vegetable peeler (1/2 cup)
70 grams chopped pistachio nuts (1/2 cup)
2 cups (40 g) arugula leaves
1 cup (60 g) parsley or basil leaves, torn
1 cup (45 g) mint leaves
¾ cup (112 g) halved cherry or grape tomatoes
⅓ cup (39 g) thinly sliced radish
Maldon or other flaky sea salt, for finishing
directions:
In a medium saucepan, bring farro, apple cider, salt, bay leaves and 2 cups water to a simmer. Simmer until farro is tender and liquid evaporates, about 30 minutes. If all the liquid evaporates before the farro is done, add a little more water. Let farro cool, then discard bay leaves.

In a salad bowl, whisk together olive oil, lemon juice and a pinch of salt. Add farro, cheese and pistachio nuts and mix well. This salad base will keep for up to 4 hours at room temperature or overnight in the refrigerator (bring to room temperature before serving). Just before serving, fold in arugula, herbs, tomatoes, radish and flaky salt to taste.
description:
4/2022 Made with cranberry juice instead of cider. Still great. No need to chop the pistachios if you prefer larger pieces.

8/2019 Excellent. Omitted mint, used basil and arugula, but both work equally well. Have done it with cider, apple juice, and chicken stock. Cider is best.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (12,066)). A farro salad from the SoHo restaurant Charlie Bird, adapted by Melissa Clark from chef Ryan Hardy. The trick is seasoning the grain itself: the farro simmers in apple cider with bay leaves and a good deal of salt so it tastes good before anything is added. It is then enriched with generous olive oil, pistachios and Parmesan, and finished with tomatoes, radishes, arugula and herbs folded in just before serving.

What readers report: The most-voted note (979) explains the recipe's biggest variable: pearled versus unpearled farro cook at very different rates, so go by texture rather than the stated time. A 692-vote note used Trader Joe's 10-minute farro with 1 cup cider plus 1 cup water and simmered only about 15 minutes. Several cooks (579 votes) improvise the cider with roughly 1/2 to 3/4 cup apple cider vinegar plus 1 to 2 tablespoons honey topped up with water, though another popular note (469) warns readers not to confuse cider with cider vinegar in the cooking liquid itself. A repeated complaint (542 votes) is that the salt in the farro is too much once salty Parmesan goes on top; cut it back. Roasted vegetables are a common addition.

name: Cheese Straws--bread sticks
ingredients:
2 sheets (1 box) frozen puff pastry (preferably Pepperidge Farm), defrosted overnight in the refrigerator
1 extra-large egg
1/2 cup (45 g) freshly grated parmesan cheese
1 cup (113 g) finely grated gruyere cheese
1 teaspoon (1.1 g) minced fresh thyme leaves
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt
Freshly ground black pepper
directions:
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees F.

Roll out each sheet of puff pastry on a lightly floured board until it's 10 by 12 inches. Beat the egg with 1 tablespoon of water and brush the surface of the pastry. Sprinkle each sheet evenly with 1/4 cup of the parmesan, 1/2 cup of the gruyere, 1/2 teaspoon of the thyme, 1/2 teaspoon of the salt, and some pepper. With the rolling pin, lightly press the flavorings into the puff pastry. Cut each sheet crosswise with a floured knife or pizza wheel into 11 or 12 strips. Twist each strip and lay on baking sheets lined with parchment paper.

Bake for 10 to 15 minutes, until lightly browned and puffed. Turn each straw and bake for another 2 minutes. Don't overbake or the cheese will burn. Cool and serve at room temperature.

Let the puff pastry thaw in the refrigerator overnight.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten makes these from thawed frozen puff pastry brushed with egg wash and pressed with grated Parmesan and Gruyere plus minced thyme, then cut into strips and twisted. The egg wash glues the cheese on and the pastry's laminated layers do the rest, puffing and browning while the cheese crisps into the surface. It is an appetiser with almost no hands-on time beyond thawing and cutting.

Note on the source: no comments or rating on Food Network page

claude_opt.changes: Cloudy Kitchen's well-tested puff pastry version freezes twisted straws 15-20 minutes before baking so they hold their twist; this recipe skips that and risks them unwinding in the oven.

name: Chef John's Bacon and Asparagus Dutch Baby
ingredients:
3 large eggs
⅔ cup (163 g) milk
½ cup (45 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese (not packed)
½ cup (60 g) packed all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon (2.0 g) lemon zest
¾ teaspoon (2.1 g) kosher salt
Freshly ground black pepper to taste
1 pinch cayenne pepper
1 tablespoon (14 g) olive oil
6 strips bacon, cut into 1/2-inch pieces
1 cup (134 g) trimmed fresh asparagus, cut into 1/4-inch pieces
directions:
Preheat oven to 475 degrees F (245 degrees C).

Place eggs in mixing bowl. Add milk, grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese, flour, lemon zest, salt, black pepper, and cayenne pepper. Whisk together until completely combined.

Heat 2 teaspoons olive oil in cast-iron skillet over medium heat. Add bacon and cook until fat is rendered out and bacon begins to crisp up. Add asparagus and raise heat to high. Cook and stir about 1 minute.

Pour batter into pan in a circular motion.

Bake in preheated oven until browned and puffed, 12 to 13 minutes.
notes:
This recipe makes 2 large or 4 small portions.

Web summary (Allrecipes, 4.4 (40) / 31 reviews). Chef John (John Mitzewich) gives just a couple of lines: he had been noticing savoury, non-breakfast Dutch babies on restaurant menus and wanted to make one with bacon and asparagus. His only technical steer is that a 12-inch cast iron skillet is the right pan, with a cook's note that the recipe feeds two generously or four modestly. The method itself carries the rest, rendering the bacon and briefly cooking the asparagus in the skillet before the batter goes in and the pan hits a 475F oven.

What readers report: The highest-voted review (12 helpful, Redcaddy97) says to follow it exactly, that 1 cup of asparagus really is enough provided it is sliced thinly, and that broccoli, sausage or diced ham would all substitute; leftovers were good cold the next day. Mushrooms are another reported addition, and a non-cast-iron high-heat skillet worked for one reviewer. Salt is the quantity most often adjusted down: one reduced it to half a teaspoon and would omit it entirely when using bacon, noting the bacon fat is not drained but the result still was not greasy. A couple of reviewers report that it does not puff much and eats like a frittata or thin-crust pizza; one suggests slightly less flour. Whole wheat flour was tried once and blamed for a dull texture. Smoked paprika substitutes for the cayenne if you want no heat.

Note on the source: Headnote is only two sentences on the page; comment volume is small (31 reviews) and only one review carries a helpfulness count.

name: Cherry and Almond Traybake
ingredients:
For the base:
90g unsalted butter, softened
90g caster sugar
1 large free-range egg, beaten
110g plain flour
20g self-raising flour
1/2 tsp (1.3 g) ground cinnamon
Pinch of salt
For the filling:
6-8 tablespoons (120-160 g) of morello cherry jam (I left this out)
40g dried sour cherries, chopped
5 maraschino cherries chopped
90g unsalted butter, softened
80g caster sugar
2 large free-range eggs, beaten
180g ground almonds
30g plain flour
A few drops almond extract
Zest of a lemon
Pinch of salt
Topping:
60g unsalted butter
60g caster sugar
1tbsp (21 g) runny honey
60g flaked almonds (I used macadamias)
40g dried sour cherries, chopped
30g glacé cherries, chopped
directions:
Heat the oven to 180 C degrees or 160 C degrees fan-forced. Line a 18cm x 27cm x 3cm baking tray with baking paper leaving 5cm excess on all sides.

Combine the ingredients for the base in a bowl and mix. Dollop the mixture into the lined tray and using the back of a spoon, smooth out the batter to create an even base.

Combine the ingredients for the filling and spoon across the base.

Combine the ingredients for the frangipane and mix until smooth. Put spoonfuls of the frangipane over the cherry layer and then, with a fork, push the batter across to create a smooth layer. Even the surface with the back of a spoon.

Place in the centre of the oven and bake for 20-23minutes until the top is puffed and golden.

About 15 minutes into the cooking time, put all of the ingredients for the topping into a saucepan. Place over a low heat and stir gently until the butter and sugar has melted. Turn up the heat and simmer for three minutes.

Remove the traybake from the oven and pour the topping over the surface. Using the back of a metal spoon, spread and smooth the topping all over the frangipane.

Return to the oven and bake for 8-10 minutes until the nuts are golden and the honey syrup is bubbling all over.

To get a really neat finish on the portions the traybake needs to be cut upside-down, so that you are cutting the nutty topping against the firm surface of a chopping board.

Remove the traybake from the oven and cool in the tin for 15 minutes. This allows for the topping to cool and set a little so that it does not stick to the board when you turn it out. Place a clean chopping board on top of the bake and, wearing oven gloves, flip it over. Peel away the baking paper and place a wire rack, upside down, on the bake. Flip again and remove the chopping board. Cool completely on the rack.

When cool, replace the chopping board gently on top and flip the bake as above. Using a large, sharp knife trim the edges and then cut into portions.

Delicious straight away and keeps well if you put it into an airtight tin.
description: From Ruby Lai, 2019.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. The source's own ingredient list already marks the jam layer optional, and this cake-style base doesn't need the blind-baking that pastry-shell frangipane tarts require.

name: Cherry Jelly
ingredients:
2 c. (308 g) pitted sour cherries (1 can is ok)
1/2 c. (100 g) sugar
1 T. (9.6 g) gelatin
1 c. (237 g) boiling water (or can juice)
1/2 c. (118 g) cold water
directions: Dissolve gelatin in cold water. Boil other water or juice. Add cherries until liquid boils again. Add sugar and dissolved gelatin. Chill.

claude_opt.changes: Technique is already correct: gelatin blooms in cold water before being fully dissolved into the hot liquid, the standard modern method. No change needed.

name: Chicken and Black Bean Enchiladas
ingredients:
2 T. (27 g) vegetable oil, plus more for the dish
1 or 2 cloves garlic
4 scallions (white and tender green parts)
15 oz. (425 g) can black beans, drained and rinsed
1 chipotle chili pepper in adobo sauce, finely chopped
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
1/2 t. (1.1 g) cumin
Few drops lime juice
1 c. (140 g) diced, cooked chicken
4 to 6 lg. flour tortillas
8 oz. (227 g) shredded Monterey Jack cheese
About 1 c. (260 g) green (tomatillo) salsa
directions:
Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Oil an 8 or 9" square baking dish.
In a large skillet over medium heat, heat the oil. Add the garlic and the scallions and cook, stirring, for about 1 minute. Add the drained black beans and cook until heated through, about 5 minutes. Using a potato masher or the back of a wooden spoon, mash the beans. Add the chipotle,salt, cumin and lime juice and cook, stirring constantly, for 1 minute. Add the chicken and toss to combine; set aside.
Place a skillet over medium-high heat. Heat the tortillas, 1 at a time, until softened and flexible, about 10 seconds per side. 
Working 1 at a time, spoon an even share of the black bean mixture along the center of the tortilla and then sprinkle with 1/4 c. cheese. Roll the sides of the tortilla over the filling and place in the baking dish, seam side down. Repeat.
Sprinkle the rolled tortilla with the remaining cheese and pour the sals over the top. Bake until the salsa is warmed through, about 20 minutes.
description: 1/2021 We made them flat in a casserole, w/o the chiles or salsa. A bit dry, of course, but tasted good.

claude_opt.changes: Cooks' note attributes dryness to skipping the chiles/salsa. Spoon a thin layer of salsa in the dish before rolling and cover with foil for the first 15 minutes of baking to trap steam.

name: Chicken and Orzo Soup with Leeks, Peas and Asparagus
ingredients:
8 cups (1.9 kg) low-sodium chicken broth
1 pound (454 g) boneless chicken breast or thigh meat, visible fat removed
1 bay leaf
3/4 teaspoon (4.5 g) fine sea salt or table salt, divided
1 medium carrot (about 4 ounces), scrubbed and sliced 1/4-inch thick
1 celery rib, sliced 1/4-inch thick
1 pound (454 g) leeks, white and light green parts only, washed well, halved and then thinly sliced
1/2 teaspoon (0.5 g) dried thyme
1/4 teaspoon (0.5 g) crushed red pepper flakes (optional)
3/4 cup (150 g) orzo (about 4 ounces)
12 stalks asparagus (about 4 ounces), trimmed and cut into 1-inch lengths
1/2 cup (72 g) (2 ounces) green peas (fresh or frozen; if frozen, no need to defrost)
2 tablespoons (6.9 g) minced fresh tarragon, plus more for garnish
Freshly ground black pepper
directions:
In a large pot over high heat, heat the chicken broth. Cut the chicken pieces in half or thirds crosswise. Add the chicken, a bay leaf and 1/4 teaspoon of salt. Stir once or twice, cover and bring to a gentle simmer. Reduce the heat to medium or medium-low, cover and gently cook until an instant-read thermometer reads 160 degrees when inserted into the thickest pieces of chicken, 10 to 12 minutes. Do not allow the chicken to boil. (This is a good time to prepare your vegetables.)

Transfer the chicken to a cutting board and let it cool to the touch, then slice and shred with a fork or your fingers, breaking it into bite-size pieces.

Once the chicken is removed from the broth, increase the heat to medium-high and add the carrot, celery, leeks, thyme, red pepper flakes (if using) and the remaining salt and cook until the vegetables have softened, about 10 minutes. Add the chicken, orzo, asparagus and peas and cook until the orzo is tender and the asparagus is crisp-tender, about 7 minutes, stirring two or three times to prevent the orzo from sticking to the bottom of the pot.

Stir in the tarragon. Taste, and add salt and pepper, as needed. Stir well to redistribute some of the orzo that may sink to the bottom, then ladle into bowls. Sprinkle with more fresh tarragon, if desired, and serve hot.
notes:
Web summary (washingtonpost.com). Ann Maloney's spring adaptation of a chicken soup from America's Test Kitchen's The Chicken Bible, written for cold spring days when you still want the season's produce. The broth gets its character from thinly sliced leeks, celery and a little dried thyme; carrots and peas go in for colour and sweetness, and the asparagus goes in near the end so it keeps some bite. Cooked chicken - poached, or leftover, light or dark meat - is shredded in at the finish. She praises it mainly as a way to use up odds and ends of vegetables and cut waste.

Note on the source: Washington Post article page, not NYT; the site shows a comment count (17) but no readable notes/reviews section on the recipe, so no comment digest could be built; no star rating displayed
nutritional_info: Calories: 233; Total Fat: 4 g; Saturated Fat: 1 g; Cholesterol: 46 mg; Sodium: 385 mg; Carbohydrates: 31 g; Dietary Fiber: 3 g; Sugar: 5 g; Protein: 21 g.

claude_opt.changes: Cook orzo separately in salted water, not in the broth pot. Comparable orzo soups (Mediterranean Dish) warn pasta keeps absorbing broth and turns soup to stew/mush on standing.

name: Chicken Breasts with Lemon
ingredients:
1/2 cup (60 g) flour for dredging
Salt and freshly ground pepper to taste
4 skinless boneless chicken breasts, about 6 ounces (170 g) each
2 tablespoons (27 g) olive oil
4 sprigs fresh thyme or 1 teaspoon dried
2 tablespoons (20 g) finely chopped shallots
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) finely chopped garlic
2 teaspoons (4.0 g) grated lemon zest
3 tablespoons (46 g) lemon juice
1/2 cup (120 g) chicken broth, fresh or canned
2 tablespoons (28 g) butter
directions:
Season flour with salt and pepper, and dredge the chicken all over. Remove the excess flour.

Heat the oil in a heavy skillet large enough to hold the chicken pieces in one layer. Add chicken and cook, uncovered, over medium heat for 5 minutes or until lightly browned.

Flip the chicken and cook for 5 minutes more, or until cooked through. Carefully remove the oil from the skillet, leaving the chicken. Discard the oil.

Add the thyme, shallots and garlic, and cook for about a minute. Do not burn the garlic. Add the lemon rind, the lemon juice and the broth.

Scrape the skillet to dissolve the brown particles that cling to the bottom. Add the butter, and cook for 3 minutes longer. Serve immediately.
description: 2/26 Light and bright. We liked it. Butterflied the breasts—good. Maybe try NOT nonstick next time to have more fond. Maybe leave the fat in the pan after the chicken cooked.

name: Chicken Breasts with Mustard Sauce
ingredients:
2 1/2 lbs. (1.1 kg) (4 whole) boneless chicken breasts 
3 T. (43 g) butter
2 T. (20 g) finely chopped shallots
1/2 c. (118 g) dry white wine
1 c. (238 g) heavy cream
3 T. (47 g) imported mustard, preferably whole grain mustard such as Pommery Moutarde de Meaux
3 T. (9.0 g) finely chopped chives, optional
directions:
1. Split the chicken breasts in half lengthwise. Cut away and discard any cartilage and connecting tissue. Sprinkle the breasts with salt and pepper.
2. Heat the butter in a large, heavy skillet and add the breasts in one layer. Cook over moderately low heat 3-4 minutes or until lightly browned. Turn the pieces and continue cooking 7-8 minutes.
3. Transfer the pieces to a warm platter. Add the shallots to the skillet and cook, stirring, about 30 seconds. Add the wine and cook, stirring, about one minute. Ad the cream and cook down until reduced to about 3/4 cup. Stir in the mustard; return the breast halves to the skillet and turn them in the juice. Bring to a boil.
4. Sprinkle with chives and serve. Rice goes well with this dish.

claude_opt.changes: No internal-temp target, only pan minutes; use an instant-read thermometer and pull chicken at 160°F to let carryover reach 165°F, avoiding the dry, overcooked breast this timing risks.

name: Chicken Cordon Bleu
ingredients:
6 medium whole chicken breasts
1 8 oz. (227 g) pkg. swiss cheese
1 8 oz. (227 g) pkg. sliced ham
3 T. (22 g) flour
1 t. (2.3 g) paprika
6 T. (85 g) butter or margarine
1/2 c. (118 g) dry white wine
1 chicken bouillon cube
1 T. (7.1 g) corn starch
1 c. (238 g) heavy cream
directions:
1. Spread breasts flat (or butterfly if using modern large half-breasts). Fold cheese and ham to fit on top. Fold back over filling. Fasten with toothpicks.
2. On wax paper, mix flour and paprika. Use mixture to coat chicken pieces.
3. In 12" skillet over medium heat in hot butter cook chicken until browned on all sides. 
4. Add wine and bouillon. Reduce heat to low. Cover and simmer 30 minutes or until tender. Remove from skillet. Keep in warm oven.
5. In cup, blend starch and heavy cream until smooth. Gradually stir into skillet. Cook stirring constantly until thickened. Serve sauce over chicken.

claude_opt.changes: Braising 'until tender' has no temp check; verify 165°F at the thickest part, avoiding the cheese pocket. Use butter, not margarine, for better flavor in the pan sauce.

name: Chicken Cutlets in Cornmeal Stuffing
ingredients:
2 c. (276 g) Pepperidge Farm Cornmeal Stuffing
3/4 c. (68 g) Parmesan cheese grated
2 garlic cloves
2 sticks (227 g) butter
1/2 t. (1.1 g) pepper
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
1/2 c. (30 g) parsley
8 boneless chicken breasts
directions:
Preheat oven to 375.

1. Mix stuffing (crush a bit) with parmesan. 
2. Press garlic cloves with sticks butter, pepper, salt, parsley.
3. Melt butter mix and soak chicken for 3 minutes.
4. Roll chicken in bread crumbs. Put on a half sheet pan (or a flat casserole). Put remaining butter crumbs on top. 
5. Bake uncovered until temperature reaches 150º F.
description:
RM 10/15: I really like it because it's all pantry staples except for the chicken. I rarely use parsley, and any cornmeal stuffing will do. You can use bread crumbs in a pinch. Do check the temp with a thermometer.
RM 10/15: Bake, uncovered, for 35 minutes or until temperature reaches 150º F (his forwarded copy revises the 2013 original's 45 minutes / 165º F).
RM 9/26: Always cook at 375, on a half sheet pan. The full two sticks of butter is necessary for this much chicken. Pepperidge Farm cornbread stuffing mix is necessary — don't swap for panko or other bread crumbs (this replaces the 10/15 line that any cornmeal stuffing or bread crumbs will do).
notes: Data fix (Oct 2026), at Robert's request: oven 325 changed to 375; "Put in flat casserole" changed to a half sheet pan; "1-2 sticks butter" changed to 2 sticks; step 5 "Bake uncovered for 45 minutes" changed to bake until 150º F, because 45 minutes was the time at 325 and his 10/15 note had already replaced it. Total time re-estimated from about 1 h 5 min to about 45 min.

claude_opt.changes: Your 9/26 note moves this to 375°F on a half sheet pan. No bake time is recorded at that heat: expect 150°F in roughly 20-25 minutes for whole breasts, 12-15 for tenderloins. Start checking early.

name: Chicken Divan
ingredients:
1 1/2 lb. (680 g) fresh broccoli, cut into spears and steamed to tender-crisp
1 1/2 lb. (680 g) or more of leftover chicken or turkey meat
1/4 c. (57 g) butter
6 T. (45 g) flour
2 c. (480 g) chicken broth
1/2 c. (119 g) whipping cream
3 T. (44 g) dry white wine
1/4 c. (22 g) grated parmesan cheese
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
dash pepper
directions:
Preheat oven to 375.

Make white sauce with butter, flour, and chicken broth. Stir in cream and wine. Layer chicken and broccoli in 9x13 inch baking dish. Cover with white sauce. Sprinkle cheese on top. Bake 15-20 minutes.

claude_opt.changes: Omitting curry powder and sherry (common in modern Divan) is a valid simpler tradition, not an error. The roux-based sauce and 15-20 minute bake are technically sound as is.

name: Chicken in Mustard Sauce
ingredients:
8 5-ounce (142 g) chicken breasts, skinless and boneless
½ teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
½ teaspoon (1.1 g) freshly ground black pepper
1 tablespoon (14 g) vegetable oil
1 cup (160 g) onion, finely chopped
2 tablespoons (15 g) flour
2 cups (474 g) water
1 ½ teaspoons (3.3 g) dry mustard
1 tablespoon (16 g) Dijon mustard
directions:
Sprinkle the meat with the salt and pepper.

Heat the oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat. When it is hot, brown the chicken for one-and-a-half minutes on each side.

Mix in the onion and continue cooking for one minute.

Sprinkle the flour on the chicken pieces, turning them so that all the pieces are coated. Cook one minute to lightly brown the flour.

Add the water and stir to dissolve the flour until the mixture comes to a boil. Lower the heat, cover the skillet and boil gently for five minutes.

Remove the meat to a serving platter and keep warm.

Cook the sauce to reduce it to about one-and-a-half cups. Mix the dry mustard with the Dijon mustard and stir until smooth. Stir the mustard mixture into the sauce and heat, but do not allow the sauce to boil after the mustard has been added.

Place the chicken pieces in the sauce and warm over low heat for 10 to 15 minutes to develop the flavor.

Serve the chicken with the sauce.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (3,245)). A Jacques Pepin dish that ran in the Times in 1988 - light but polished, and quick enough for a weeknight at roughly half an hour. Brown the chicken, then build a fast sauce from onions, water and mustard and reduce it until it thickens. Rice is the suggested partner so nothing is wasted, with a sharp green salad alongside. Boneless thighs substitute happily for breast if you add a little extra cooking time.

What readers report: The comments are largely a collective rewrite of the sauce. The top note (667 votes) flours the chicken first, removes it, then cooks the onion with sliced mushrooms and garlic before deglazing. A 352-vote note is openly critical - it says plenty of readers find the dish flat and blames the water, recommending broth, white wine and/or lemon juice in its place. That substitution recurs throughout, often alongside doubling the mustard and using both Dijon and stone-ground (66 votes). Garlic and additional herbs are the other standard additions. A dissenting 98-vote note says skip the flouring step entirely as unnecessary, and suggests honey, apricot jam or cardamom in the sauce. A 130-vote defender likes it as written for its richness without cream.

Note on the source: substantial reader disagreement with the author - many find the water-based sauce bland and swap in stock or wine

name: Chicken Spaghetti
ingredients:
Kosher salt (such as Diamond Crystal)
Black pepper
8 ounces (227 g) spaghetti, broken into thirds
4 tablespoons (57 g) unsalted butter, plus more for greasing 
1 small yellow onion, finely chopped
4 ounces (113 g) white button mushrooms, finely chopped
2 celery stalks, finely chopped
1 medium green bell pepper, finely chopped
2 garlic cloves, minced
1/4 cup (30 g) all-purpose flour
1 cup (244 g) milk
1 cup (240 g) low-sodium chicken stock or broth 
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) onion powder
1/4 teaspoon (0.7 g) garlic powder
2 (10-ounce) cans diced tomatoes with green chiles, drained
1 pound (454 g) cooked chicken, chopped or shredded
2 cups (226 g) (8 ounces) shredded Cheddar
1 cup (90 g) (3 ounces) shredded or grated Parmesan 
Hot sauce, to taste (optional)
directions:
Heat the oven to 350 degrees with the rack in the center position. Butter a 9-by-13-inch casserole dish. Bring a large pot of well salted water to a boil. Add the spaghetti and cook until just shy of al dente, about 9 minutes. Drain and transfer to a large mixing bowl. 

Meanwhile, in a large pan, melt the butter over medium heat. Add the onion, mushrooms, celery and bell pepper. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, 10 to 12 minutes. Add the garlic, season with salt and pepper, and cook, stirring occasionally, for 2 minutes. Stir in 2 tablespoons of the flour until smooth; repeat with the remaining flour, continuously stirring until the flour releases a nutty aroma, about 2 minutes. 

Slowly pour in the milk, 1/4 cup at a time, stirring continuously so there are no lumps. Slowly pour in the chicken stock, stirring continuously. Add the onion powder, garlic powder, 1 teaspoon salt and 1/2 teaspoon black pepper. Stir continuously, until thickened, about 5 minutes. Stir in the tomatoes, taste for seasoning and remove from the heat. 

Add the saucy vegetable mixture, chicken, 1 cup of the Cheddar and the Parmesan to the spaghetti and toss well to combine. Taste, adjust seasoning, and add hot sauce, if you like. Transfer the spaghetti mixture to the prepared casserole dish, spreading it out evenly and topping with the remaining Cheddar. Bake, uncovered, until the cheese melts and the casserole is bubbling, about 40 minutes. Remove from the oven and let cool for 5 minutes before serving.
notes:
To freeze the entire casserole, prepare and assemble in a freezer- and oven-safe casserole dish up to the point of baking. Cool to room temperature, cover with foil and freeze for up to 3 months. Remove cover and bake until warmed through and bubbling, about 45 minutes.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (703)). A Southern potluck and picnic casserole: creamy, cheesy noodles bound with chicken, tomatoes and chiles, buried under more cheese and baked till it bubbles. The dish has drifted a lot over the years - some versions lean on Velveeta and canned cream of mushroom, and Craig Claiborne's own childhood recipe added a quarter pound each of ground beef and pork to a whole chicken. This one drops the canned soup for a roux thickened with milk and stock, and uses Cheddar with Parmesan. Any cooked chicken works, from leftover roast to rotisserie.

What readers report: Vote counts are modest, so nothing is heavily validated. The clear leader (132 votes) is a flavour fix: boil the spaghetti in chicken broth rather than water and use a cup of that cooking liquid where the recipe calls for liquid - the commenter says it transforms the dish. Sour cream stirred in is the next most-endorsed addition (56 votes) for a smoother, creamier result. Others double the garlic and use fresh chopped tomatoes in place of canned. Several note the close kinship to chicken tetrazzini, the difference being the tomatoes and green chiles. One variation swaps the spaghetti entirely for taco-flavoured corn chips. A few remark on how dated the onion and garlic powder feel, and report it freezes well in portions.

Note on the source: low vote counts; no strong corrections to quantities or timings

name: Chicken Tortilla Soup
ingredients:
5 large plum tomatoes (about 1 pound), cored and halved
1 white onion, peeled and quartered
12 ounces (340 g) cherry tomatoes (about 2 heaping cups)
2 jalapeños, stemmed and halved, 1 seeded and de-ribbed
8 garlic cloves (unpeeled)
1/4 cup (54 g) vegetable oil
1 1/2 teaspoons (4.2 g) coarse kosher salt, plus more to taste
2 tablespoons (33 g) tomato paste
2 1/2 teaspoons (5.2 g) ground cumin
2 teaspoons (2.0 g) dried oregano
1 teaspoon (2.4 g) onion powder
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) garlic powder
1½ pounds (680 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs
2 carrots, peeled, halved lengthwise and thinly sliced
6 cups (1.4 kg) chicken broth or stock
1 avocado, peeled, pitted and cubed
1 lime
Tortilla chips
Any combination of hot sauce, cilantro, queso fresco, for topping
directions:
Heat a broiler with a rack 4 to 6 inches from the heat source. Line a sheet pan with foil and arrange the plum tomatoes on it, cut sides up. Add the onion, cherry tomatoes, jalapeños and garlic, distributing them evenly, then broil for 15 minutes, checking and rotating the pan every 5 minutes to ensure the vegetables char evenly. (You want the vegetables to be blackened in many spots, slumped and sizzling. Many of the cherry tomatoes will have burst.) Let the vegetables sit 1 or 2 minutes, until just cool enough to handle.

Warm the vegetable oil in a large pot or Dutch oven over medium-high. Transfer the charred onion to a cutting board, roughly chop it, and add it to the pot, along with the salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, discard the garlic skins then chop the garlic, jalapeños and plum tomatoes. Lift two sides of the foil and tip the cherry tomatoes and any juices into a bowl; set aside for the salsa.

Add the chopped garlic, jalapeño and plum tomatoes to the pot, and cook, stirring often, until slightly reduced and glossy, about 2 minutes. Add the tomato paste, cumin, oregano, onion powder and garlic powder, and cook, stirring constantly, until toasted and fragrant, 1 to 2 minutes. Add the chicken thighs, carrots and broth, and scrape the bottom of the pot to loosen any browned bits.

Increase the heat to high, cover the pot and let the soup come to a boil. Uncover the pot, reduce the heat to medium-high for a medium-brisk simmer, and cook, stirring once or twice, until the chicken and carrots are tender, 15 to 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, gently fold the avocado into the cherry tomatoes; add the juice of half the lime and season to taste with salt.

With a slotted spoon or tongs, transfer the chicken to a bowl. Coarsely shred and break up the meat with a fork, then add it back into the pot. Squeeze in the juice of the remaining half lime, and add more salt if necessary.

Serve the soup in bowls topped with crushed tortilla chips and spoonfuls of the tomato-avocado salsa. Pass hot sauce, queso fresco and/or cilantro at the table, if desired.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (989)). A weeknight take on sopa de tortilla, the central Mexican classic built on a clear chicken broth flavoured with pureed roasted tomatoes, chiles and garlic and finished with fried tortilla strips. Here the tomatoes, onion, garlic and chile go under the broiler on a foil-lined sheet pan, which does the charring with almost no cleanup. It takes well to additions - sliced zucchini or epazote with the chopped tomatoes, or corn kernels stirred in at the end - and swapping cooked black beans for the chicken makes it vegetarian. A slow-cooker version exists separately.

What readers report: The two highest-voted notes (177 and 122) both shortcut the broiling step with canned fire-roasted tomatoes - either one 28-ounce can or two 14-ounce cans - instead of fresh plum tomatoes. The 122-vote note goes further and skips the cherry-tomato salsa garnish altogether, finishing instead with shredded cabbage, sour cream, sliced radish and avocado. Against that, a 29-vote note from someone who has made a lot of tortilla soup says the sheet-pan roasting is the whole point and is worth keeping. Ordinary tomatoes work fine if that is what you have (48 votes), with cilantro blended into the salsa. Smaller suggestions: build the broth yourself from bone-in skin-on thighs and vegetable scraps, add more tomato paste, and use rotisserie chicken.

Note on the source: readers split on whether to broil fresh tomatoes or use canned fire-roasted

claude_opt.changes: Skip broiling fresh tomatoes and use one 28-oz can fire-roasted tomatoes instead, per the two highest-voted notes (177, 122); keep charring the onion, garlic and jalapeños for flavor.

name: Chicken-Tarragon Pot Pie
ingredients:
FOR THE CRUST:
2 cups (240 g) all-purpose flour
14 tablespoons (199 g) (1 3/4 sticks) cold unsalted butter, cut into pieces
1 tablespoon (13 g) cold vegetable shortening
Scant 1/2 teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
Scant 1/2 teaspoon (2.1 g) sugar
1 egg
FOR THE FILLING:
5 tablespoons (71 g) unsalted butter
1 cup (128 g) chopped carrot
1 cup (101 g) chopped celery
1 cup (89 g) thinly sliced leeks
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) chopped fresh tarragon
1 cup (145 g) frozen baby green peas
4 tablespoons (30 g) all-purpose flour
2 ½ cups (600 g) chicken broth
1 cup (238 g) heavy cream
¼ teaspoon (1.5 g) salt
¼ teaspoon (0.6 g) freshly ground pepper
3 cups (420 g) leftover roast chicken, cut into 1/2-inch chunks
directions:
To make the crust, combine flour, butter, shortening, salt and sugar in a food processor. Pulse together just until the mixture is crumbly and butter is broken into small pieces. Pour 1/3 cup ice water into the machine, and pulse 3 or 4 times. Squeeze a little dough in your hand to see whether it clumps together and is evenly moist. If not, add another tablespoon of water, and pulse 1 or 2 times more. Don't overmix so that the dough forms a ball.

Turn out dough on a large sheet of plastic wrap. Lift ends of plastic to gather dough together inside. Press into a large disk, and wrap tightly in plastic wrap. Refrigerate until ready to use, up to 2 days.

To make the filling, melt 2 tablespoons butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add carrot, celery, leeks and tarragon, and cook, stirring, just until slightly softened but not browned (reduce the heat if necessary to prevent browning), about 3 minutes. Transfer cooked vegetables to a bowl, wipe out the skillet, and place it back on the stove.

Add remaining 3 tablespoons butter, and melt over medium heat. Whisk in flour, and cook, whisking, until the mixture bubbles and smells cooked. Do not let it brown. Whisk in 2 cups broth, and cook, whisking, 1 minute. Whisk in cream, and cook 2 or 3 minutes, just until thickened. Add salt and pepper. If the sauce is too thick, whisk in remaining broth.

Heat the oven to 400 degrees. Add cooked vegetables and peas, chicken and sauce to 8-inch deep pie dish or other baking dish, mix gently, and taste for seasoning.

Flour a work surface. Remove dough from refrigerator. Roll out the dough, turning and flouring often, and cut a shape approximately the size of your baking dish plus 1 1/2 inches overlap all around.

Roll dough up onto the rolling pin, and unroll over dish, so it rests evenly on top of filling. Fold the edges under and crimp. Poke tip of knife through crust to create 3 vent holes near the center. Whisk the egg with a teaspoon of cold water. Use a pastry brush to lightly coat the entire crust with egg wash. Place on cookie sheet, and place in oven.

Bake 20 minutes, then reduce temperature to 375 degrees. Bake 25 to 30 minutes more, until crust is golden and filling is bubbling through vents. Let rest 10 minutes before serving.
description:
1/26 Great. Used big Emile Henry quiche dish, worked very well. Used thyme.  Cooked 50 minutes. Steph wasn’t sure the crust was yet fully done. Maybe convection bake for the last 20-30 minutes. Homemade stock. 

1/30/2024 Super! Followed recipe, substituting fresh thyme for tarragon. Add leeks after carrots and celery. Great use for leftover roast chicken and its stock. Delicious crust; flattened disk to 7 inches before refrigeration so less rolling. Flaky pastry. 

Used our deepest 9” glass pie plate. Fit perfectly! Pressed crust disk out on plastic wrap most of the way, last bit rolled. 

Serves six. 

1/25 Fabulous! Tried some thyme from the garden but didn’t have enough. Don’t forget to salt to taste before baking.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (3,124)). Julia Moskin's adaptation of a recipe from Julia and Jacques at Home, which ran with a Times piece on roast chicken. It is designed around leftovers and works just as well with what is left of the Thanksgiving turkey. Rich, but loaded with vegetables. Dried tarragon can stand in for fresh, though use less than a tablespoon and taste as you go.

What readers report: The top note (411 votes) addresses a soggy bottom: use a double crust, and brush the raw bottom crust with egg white before the filling goes in to seal it. A 205-vote note found the crust troublesome, went back to the Child and Pepin original, and reports the source recipe calls for only half a batch of crust and bakes in an oval eight-cup dish - a real discrepancy with the NYT version. Another well-liked tip (289) is to chill poultry stock overnight, lift the solidified fat off and use it in the pastry for deeper flavour. On the filling, 251 votes confirm 2 percent milk substitutes for the cream without problems. A 207-vote note is candid about using store-bought crust and treats the recipe as a template for any pot pie. Season the filling generously.

Note on the source: crust quantity appears to differ from the Child/Pepin original - flagged by a 205-vote commenter
