name: Chili a la Franey
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) very lean coarsely ground pork
1 pound (454 g) very lean coarsely ground beef
1 tablespoon (14 g) oil
2 cups (320 g) finely chopped onions
1 cup (149 g) finely chopped green pepper
1 cup (101 g) finely chopped celery
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) finely minced garlic
1 tablespoon (3.0 g) crumbled dried oregano
2 bay leaves
2 teaspoons (4.2 g) ground cumin
3 tablespoons (23 g) chili powder
3 cups (786 g) tomatoes with tomato paste
1 cup (240 g) beef broth
1 cup (237 g) water
Salt and freshly ground pepper
¼ or ½ teaspoon (0.5-0.9 g) dried hot red pepper flakes, as desired
2 cups (354 g) drained kidney beans, or drained black beans
Sour cream as garnish, optional
Lime wedges as garnish, optional
Chopped cilantro as garnish, optional
directions:
1. If possible, have the pork and beef ground together. If not, mix well with hands in mixing bowl.

2. Heat the oil in a large heavy kettle and add the meat. Cook, chopping down and stirring with the side of a heavy metal kitchen spoon to break up the lumps.

3. Add the onions, green pepper, celery, garlic, oregano, bay leaves, cumin, and chili powder. Stir to blend well.

4. Add the tomatoes, broth, water, and salt and pepper to taste. Add the red pepper flakes. Bring to a boil and cook, stirring often, about 20 minutes. Add the beans and cook 10 minutes longer. Serve in hot bowls with a dollop of sour cream, lime wedges, and sprinkling of cilantro.
notes:
Web summary (pierrefraney.com). Pierre Franey offers a crowd-scale chili using equal parts lean ground pork and beef, and is explicit that the cumin, oregano and chili powder are meant to be dialled up or down to taste rather than treated as fixed. He notes that if you swap fresh tomatoes for canned you should add tomato paste, since fresh tomatoes carry more water and the chili will not thicken properly without it. Kidney beans go in near the end and the bowl is finished at the table with sour cream, lime, cilantro and sharp cheddar.

Note on the source: archival site with no comment or rating system

Link confidence: LOW — this URL is a plausible version of the dish but was not verified as the family's exact recipe. Treat the link as a lead, not a citation.

claude_opt.changes: Brown the 2 lbs of meat in two batches, not one — a single batch overcrowds the pot and steams instead of browning, unlike ATK's crowd chili.

name: Chili Dip (Jalapeño Jack)

Monterey Jack cheese with jalapeño

Corn chips
directions: Spread cream cheese in over spoof pan. Add chili & top with grated cheese. Heat in microwave. Serve with con clips.
notes: Renamed September 2026 from "Chili Dip": another, different recipe in the collection shares that title, so both were given distinguishing names.

name: Chili Verde
ingredients:
2 ½ pounds (1.1 kg) boneless pork loin
3 tablespoons (29 g) corn or safflower oil
2 ½ cups (372 g) cored, seeded green peppers cut into 1-inch cubes
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) finely minced garlic
3 cups (396 g) chopped tomatillos or use 3 cups chopped, peeled, seeded, red ripe tomatoes, or canned imported tomatoes
1 6-ounce (170 g) can chopped green chilies (you may use part chopped fresh or canned jalapeno peppers)
2 tablespoons (13 g) ground cumin
¼ teaspoon (0.5 g) ground cloves
2 tablespoons (11 g) chopped fresh coriander
1 cup (237 g) dry white wine
Salt and pepper to taste
directions:
Cut the meat into one-and-one-half-inch cubes. 2. Heat the oil in a pressure cooker. When it is quite hot, add about one-third of the cubes of meat. Cook, stirring, until nicely browned.

Using a slotted spoon, transfer the cubes to a separate platter. Add another third of the remaining cubes to the pressure cooker and cook until nicely browned. Transfer to the platter. Continue cooking the remaining cubes and transferring them to the platter.

Add the green peppers to the fat remaining in the pressure cooker and cook, stirring, until wilted. Add the garlic and cook about five seconds, stirring.

Return the meat to the cooker. Add the remaining ingredients. Cover the cooker with the lid and pressure regulator. Cook 20 minutes. Remove the lid from the cooker, following the manufacturer's instructions. Cook down, uncovered, about 10 minutes or until the sauce is reduced slightly. Serve with cumin rice (see recipe).
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (251)). No headnote on the page - the recipe is tagged only as having run in Pierre Franey's 60-Minute Gourmet column, so there is no descriptive text to paraphrase. Commenters identify it as a pork chili verde from one of Franey's one-hour cookbooks, written around a pressure cooker to hit the time limit.

What readers report: Only fifteen notes and low vote counts, so the guidance is suggestive rather than settled. The most-voted (25) says the pressure cooker is unnecessary - long, slow cooking gets you the same place. A 17-vote note raises a definitional objection to the recipe itself: if it contains tomatoes it is not chili verde at all but chili rojo, and should be a separate recipe. Practical amendments from lower-voted commenters: use pork shoulder rather than tenderloin, which the recipe's timing tends to dry out; oven-simmer covered for about three hours, break the pork up, add the cilantro, then another 45 minutes uncovered to reduce; or pressure-cook and shred the pork while the sauce reduces. One family compares it to green pozole with hominy added.

Note on the source: no headnote exists; only 15 comments; a commenter disputes that the recipe is chili verde at all

name: Chocolate Chunk Cookies
ingredients:
1 cup (2 sticks/228 grams) unsalted butter, at room temperature
¾ cup (150 grams) granulated sugar
¾ cup (165 grams) firmly packed light brown sugar
2 eggs
½ teaspoon (2.1 g) vanilla extract
1 cup (140 grams) unbleached all-purpose flour
1 cup (150 grams) bread flour
1 teaspoon (4.6 g) baking soda
½ teaspoon (1.4 g) kosher salt
9 ounces (255 grams) semisweet chocolate, chopped (about 1½ cups)
2½ ounces (70 grams) milk
chocolate, chopped (about ½ cup)
directions:
- Using a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment (or a handheld mixer or a wooden spoon), cream together the butter granulated sugar, and brown sugar on medium speed for about 5 minutes, or until the mixture is light and fluffy. (This step will take 10 minutes if using a handheld mixer or a spoon.) Stop the mixer a few times and use a rubber spatula to scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl and the paddle to release any clinging butter or sugar. Beat in the eggs and vanilla on medium speed for 2 to 3 minutes, or until thoroughly combined. Scrape the bowl and the paddle again to make sure the eggs are thoroughly incorporated. 

- In a medium bowl, stir together the all-purpose flour, bread flour, baking soda, and salt until well mixed. Add the semisweet and milk chocolates and toss to combine. On low speed (or with the wooden spoon), slowly add the flour-chocolate mixture to the butter sugar mixture and then mix just until the flour mixture is totally incorporated and the dough is evenly mixed.

- For the best results, scrape the dough into an airtight container and let it rest in the refrigerator overnight (or for at least 3 to 4 hours) before baking. When you are ready to bake, position a rack in the center of the oven, and heat the oven to** 350 degrees F**.

- Drop the dough in ¼-cup balls onto a baking sheet, spacing them about 2 inches apart. Flatten each ball slightly with the palm of your hand. Bake for 15 to 18 minutes, or until the cookies are golden brown on the edges and slightly soft in the center. Don't let them get brown through and through. Part of their appeal is the chewiness of the slightly underbaked centers. Let cool on the baking sheet on a wire rack for 5 to 10 minutes, then transfer the cookies to the rack to cool completely.

The cookies can be stored in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days.
The unbaked dough can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.
notes:
Web summary (masterclass.com, 5 stars, 105 ratings). Joanne Chang builds her chocolate chunk cookie around chocolate hand-chopped off bricks rather than chips, so the pieces are large and irregular and the chocolate flavor is more pronounced. She blends bittersweet with a little milk chocolate for a rounder flavor, and cuts bread flour into the all-purpose for extra structure and chew. The method is fussy on purpose: eggs cracked separately and added one at a time, long creaming to aerate the butter and sugar, and a multi-hour chill before baking, all of which give a lighter, crisper cookie.

Note on the source: Author and recipe name match the collection's source (Flour / Joanne Chang) exactly; this is Chang's own published version of the Flour bakery cookie, hosted on MasterClass rather than the cookbook itself.

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

claude_opt.changes: Use firm baking chocolate (Valrhona, Callebaut, Scharffen Berger), not a softer eating chocolate like Lindt — reviewers found soft chocolate makes the dough spread more during baking.

name: Chocolate Polka Dot Cake
ingredients:
2 1/4 c. (254 g) sifted cake flour
3 t. (12 g) baking powder
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
1/3 c. (68 g) shortening
3/4 c. (150 g) sugar
2 eggs
1 1/2 t. (6.3 g) vanilla
2/3 c. (163 g) milk
7 oz. (198 g) package of chocolate bits
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.

Sift flour, baking powder, and salt. Cream shortening. Add sugar gradually and beat until light and fluffy. Add eggs, one at a time, beating well after each. Add vanilla. Add flour alternately with milk beating after each addition. By hand, stir in 1/3 of bits and turn into 2 greased layer pans. Sprinkle 1/3 of bits on top. Bake 25 minutes.

Put layers together with 7 minute icing flavored with peppermint or vanilla. Sprinkle remaining bits between layers and on top.
notes: Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Toss the reserved chocolate bits in a little flour before folding in and sprinkling on top, the standard fix for chips sinking during baking; check doneness with a toothpick, not just the clock.

name: Chocolate Sauce
ingredients:
1/4 c. (57 g) butter
1/4 c. (42 g) shaved unsweetened chocolate (2 one-ounce squares)
3/4 c. (150 g) sugar
1/4 c. (21 g) cocoa
1/2 c. (119 g) light cream
pinch salt
1 t. (4.2 g) vanilla
directions:
Melt the butter in a saucepan. Add the shaved chocolate and keep over a low flame until smooth, or use a double boiler.

Then add the sugar, cocoa, cream, salt and vanilla. Bring to a boil.

Chill. Reheat as needed. Never sugars.
notes: Data fix (Sept 2026): the method was written inside the ingredients list; moved to Directions, wording unchanged.

claude_opt.changes: Add vanilla off heat after boiling, not before; its aromatics fade under prolonged heat. Modern hot-fudge recipes stir vanilla in at the end for a stronger finish.

name: Chocolate Sheet Cake
ingredients:
For the cake:
2 c. (240 g) flour
2 c. (400 g) sugar
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
2 sticks oleo or 1 stick plus 1/2 c. (102 g) shortening
1 c. (237 g) water
5 T. (27 g) cocoa
2 eggs (beaten well)
1 t. (4.6 g) soda
1/2 c. (121 g) buttermilk
1 t. (4.2 g) vanilla

For the icing:
1 stick oleo
5 T. (27 g) cocoa
6 T. (92 g) milk
1 box confectioners sugar
1/2 c. (54 g) chopped pecans
1 t. (4.2 g) vanilla
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.

For the cake:
Combine flour, sugar and salt. In saucepan put oleo, water and cocoa. Bring to a boil and pour over flour and sugar mixture. In another bowl put eggs, soda, buttermilk, and vanilla. Add to above mixture and mix well. Bake in greased and floured cookie sheet pan with edge (15 1/2 x 10 1/2") for 20 minutes. Start making icing at last 5 minutes of baking.

For the icing:
Mix oleo, cocoa, and milk. Heat over low flame but don't boil. Remove from heat. Add confectioners sugar, nuts, and vanilla. Mix well. Frost cake as soon as removed from oven.
description: Steph makes this often. To fit a regular half-sheet pan, make a 1.5 times recipe. Can make 1/2 of the frosting.
notes: Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Swap oleo/margarine for real butter 1:1 in both cake and icing; modern Texas sheet cake recipes agree butter gives clearly better flavor for the same effort.

name: Chocolate Teepees
ingredients:
1 6-oz. (170 g) pkg. semi-sweet chocolate chips (1 c.)
1 6-oz. (170 g) pkg. butterscotch chips (1 c.)
2.5-oz. (71 g) chow mein noodles - crushed a little (1 1/2 c.)
1 7 1/2-oz. (213 g) can salted peanuts (2 c.)
directions: Melt both chips over hot water. (Alternative: melt chips in microwave at 70% for 4 minutes stirring often to prevent mixture from seizing up.) Mix in nuts and noodles. Drop tsps on waxed paper. Allow to cool and harden.
notes: I usually make a double batch. It is important to monitor the melting process so the chocolate doesn't get overheated. La Choy makes a 5 oz. can of noodles.

claude_opt.changes: No changes needed; melting method (double boiler or 70% microwave) and ratios already match how modern chow-mein-noodle haystacks are still made. A durable, correct family candy.

name: Chocolate Trifle
ingredients:
6 full size Heath bars, or whole bag minis, crushed
2 8-oz. (227 g) Cool Whip
2 instant chocolate pudding mixes
2 round dark chocolate cake layers, cooled and sliced to make 4 layers
directions: Place a cake layer in trifle dish, then spread 1/4 of pudding in a layer, then 1/4 of cool whip. Do outside edge first to preserve smooth even height. Then add layer of 1/4 of Heath bars. Repeat layering.

claude_opt.changes: No fix needed; layering technique matches modern trifle assembly. Optional: chill the assembled trifle several hours or overnight so cake and pudding layers set together.

name: Chocolate Truffles Ina
ingredients:
1/2 pound (227 g) good bittersweet chocolate such as Lindt
1/2 pound (227 g) good semisweet chocolate such as Ghiradelli
1 cup (238 g) heavy cream
2 tablespoons (30 g) Grand Marnier, optional
1 tablespoon (15 g) prepared coffee
1/2 teaspoon (2.1 g) good vanilla extract
Confectioners' sugar
Cocoa powder
directions:
Chop the chocolates finely with a sharp knife. Place them in a heat-proof mixing bowl.

Heat the cream in a small saucepan until it just boils. Turn off the heat and allow the cream to sit for 20 seconds. Pour the cream through a fine-meshed sieve into the bowl with chocolate. With a wire whisk, slowly stir the cream and chocolates together until the chocolate is completely melted. Whisk in the Grand Marnier, if using, coffee, and vanilla. Set aside at room temperature for 1 hour.

With 2 teaspoons, spoon round balls of the chocolate mixture onto a baking sheet lined with parchment paper. Refrigerate for 30 minutes, until firm. Roll each dollop of chocolate in your hands to roughly make a round ball. Roll in confectioners' sugar, cocoa powder, or both. These will keep refrigerated for weeks, but serve at room temperature.
description:
12/2018 Excellent! Valrhona.
12/2020 Valrhona 66 percent. Rolled in chopped walnuts.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Adapted from Ina Garten's Barefoot in Paris, this is a straight ganache: hot cream poured over a mix of chopped bittersweet and semisweet chocolate, flavoured with a little coffee, vanilla and optionally Grand Marnier. The coffee is there to sharpen the chocolate rather than to taste of coffee. The ganache is chilled until firm enough to scoop and hand-roll, then rolled in cocoa or confectioners' sugar; the batch runs to around sixty and keeps for weeks refrigerated.

Note on the source: no comments or rating on Food Network page

Link confidence: LOW — this URL is a plausible version of the dish but was not verified as the family's exact recipe. Treat the link as a lead, not a citation.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Ratio is deliberately richer in chocolate than typical ganache (about 1.9:1 vs King Arthur's 1:1) for firm hand-rolling, and your 12/2018 and 12/2020 notes both call it excellent.

name: Classic Caesar Salad
ingredients:
The Dressing:
6 anchovy fillets packed in oil, drained
1 small garlic clove
Kosher salt
2 large egg yolks
2 tablespoons (30 g) fresh lemon juice, plus more
¾ teaspoon (3.9 g) Dijon mustard
2 tablespoons (27 g) olive oil
½ cup (109 g) vegetable oil
3 tablespoons (17 g) finely grated Parmesan
Freshly ground black pepper
The Croutons:
3 cups (135 g) torn 1" pieces country bread, with crusts
3 tablespoons (40 g) olive oil
The Lettuce:
3 romaine hearts, leaves separated
The Cheese:
Parmesan, for serving
directions:
THE DRESSING:
Chop together anchovy fillets, garlic, and pinch of salt. Use the side of a knife blade to mash into a paste, then scrape into a medium bowl. Whisk in egg yolks, 2 Tbsp. lemon juice, and mustard. Adding drop by drop to start, gradually whisk in olive oil, then vegetable oil; whisk until dressing is thick and glossy. Whisk in Parmesan. Season with salt, pepper, and more lemon juice, if desired.

DO AHEAD: Can be made 1 day ahead.

THE CROUTONS:
Make your own. Tearing, not cutting the bread ensures nooks and crannies that catch the dressing and add texture. Preheat oven to 375°. Toss bread with olive oil on a baking sheet; season with salt and pepper. Bake, tossing occasionally, until golden, 10–15 minutes.

THE LETTUCE:
Use whole leaves; they provide the ideal mix of crispness, surface area, and structure.

THE CHEESE:
Caesars crowned with a mound of grated Parmesan may look impressive, but all that clumpy cheese mutes the dressing. Instead, use a vegetable peeler to thinly shave a modest amount on top for little salty bursts.

THE ASSEMBLY:
Skip the tongs. Use your hands to gently toss the lettuce, croutons, and dressing, then top off with the shaved Parm.
notes: Web summary (bonappetit.com, 4.1 (1559)). Sue Li and Chris Morocco's headnote frames this as a back-to-basics classic Caesar, built on raw egg yolks and anchovies to make a dressing that coats without weighing the leaves down, with a callout that shaved (not grated) Parmesan avoids muting the dressing under clumped cheese. What readers report: the most substantive note (Ale Jacchia, 1 reaction) is a historical correction — inventor Caesar Cardini's original dressing used both anchovies and Worcestershire, not one or the other — and the commenter adds both, plus chills washed romaine wrapped in a towel for extra crispness. Two readers (Kenneth; Eric) report the finished dressing runs thin and light-bodied, with Eric blaming the 1/2 cup vegetable oil specifically and finding most quantities besides anchovies too skimpy. Several push back on the vegetable oil itself, preferring all olive oil (QSKE, 1 reaction) or substitutes like corn oil (Andy P) or avocado oil (Jimbo Slice, 1 reaction). A veteran maker (Sequitur, 2 reactions, ~40 batches) swaps an emulsifier for hand-whisking and pre-marinates the bread cubes in oil and smashed garlic before baking, though a reply questions whether that emulsifier method turns the olive oil bitter. Others substitute mayonnaise for the yolk-and-oil emulsion (DARI, 1 reaction) or use anchovy paste with pre-soaked garlic (Madagascar).

makeahead: DO AHEAD: Can be made 1 day ahead.

claude_opt.changes: Toss the croutons with smashed garlic along with the oil before baking — the most experienced commenter's (40 batches) fix for more flavor. Whisk the dressing by hand; a food processor risks turning the olive oil bitter, per reader caution.

name: Classic Cheese Fondue
ingredients:
1 garlic clove, peeled
2 cups (474 g) dry white wine
1/2 pound (227 g) Emmenthaler
1/2 pound (227 g) Gruyere
3 T flour (we add 1 more T for a thicker preparation)
3 T Kirsch or brandy (optional)
Dash nutmeg
French or Italian bread in 1" cubes
directions: Rub sides and bottom of fondue pot with garlic. Sprinkle cheese with flour. Pour wine in pot and set over low heat. When bubbles rise (DO NOT BOIL) add cheese, and handful at a time, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon until the cheese is smooth and melted. Add seasoning and Kirsch or brandy, stirring until blended. Keep fondue mixture bubbling hot over preheated table burner while serving. Spear bread on fondue forks and swirl in a figure eight motion in cheese mixture.

claude_opt.changes: Add a small squeeze of lemon juice with the wine; the extra acid helps the cheese emulsify and resist turning stringy, a step most modern versions include.

name: Classic Meat Tortellini with Tomato Sauce
servings: 4 servings, plus leftover pasta and sauce
ingredients:
4 tablespoons (54 g) extra-virgin olive oil
1/2 pound (227 g) ground beef
1/2 pound (227 g) ground pork
2 cloves garlic, sliced
2 ounces (57 g) mortadella, finely diced
1/4 cup (22 g) (1/2 ounce) freshly ground Parmesan
3 tablespoons (11 g) very finely chopped parsley
1/8 teaspoon (0.3 g) freshly grated nutmeg
Large pinch ground cloves
Salt
Freshly ground black pepper
2 large eggs
1 28-ounce (794 g) can peeled Roma or San Marzano tomatoes in their juices
1/2 cup (108 g) extra-virgin olive oil
1 medium yellow onion, diced
Salt
2 cloves garlic, sliced
1 teaspoon (1.0 g) dried oregano or 12 basil leaves, torn into large pieces
Freshly grated Parmesan for serving
Fine sea salt or kosher salt, preferably Diamond Crystal
Basic egg pasta dough, cut into sheets (see recipe)
Semolina flour for dusting pasta
directions:
Make the filling: Add 3 tablespoons olive oil to a large cast-iron pan set over medium-high heat. Crumble in ground beef and pork and reduce heat to medium. Using the edge of a metal spoon, break up clumps of meat as they form, stirring regularly. Once the meat is evenly broken up, continue to cook, stirring only occasionally, until all of the water has evaporated and the cooking sounds change from steaming to sizzling, about 7 to 8 minutes.

As the meat begins to brown, clear a spot in the center of the pan and add 1 tablespoon olive oil and the garlic. Cook the garlic until it starts to release an aroma, about 20 seconds, then stir it into the meat and cook another 30 seconds or so. Remove from heat and cool to room temperature.

In the bowl of a food processor, combine meat mixture, mortadella, Parmesan, parsley, nutmeg, cloves, 1 teaspoon salt and pepper. Pulse to combine, then taste and adjust salt and pepper as needed. Add eggs and pulse, stopping to scrape the sides of the bowl with a rubber spatula, until the mixture is smooth and tacky. Cover and refrigerate until you’re ready to assemble ravioli.

Make the tomato sauce: Pour tomatoes and their juices into a medium bowl and use your hands to crush them. Pour 1/4 cup water into the can and swirl, then add to tomatoes. Set aside.

Set a small Dutch oven or similar pot over medium-high heat and add 3 tablespoons olive oil. When it shimmers, add onion and a generous pinch of salt. Reduce heat to medium, and cook, stirring occasionally, until onions are tender and golden brown, about 10 minutes.

Move onions to the edges of the pot and add 1 tablespoon olive oil. Add garlic and allow it to gently sizzle, about 20 seconds. Before the garlic has a chance to start browning, stir it into the onions and add tomatoes. Season with salt and oregano or basil and bring to a hard simmer. Stir, then reduce heat to low and cover pot (to prevent splattering). Cook, stirring occasionally, for 40 minutes or until raw tomato taste is gone. (Tomato sauce can be made up to 2 days in advance and refrigerated.)

Shape the tortellini: Place a sheet of pasta on your workspace and dust off any excess flour. One sheet at a time, cut the pasta into 2 1/2-inch squares, or use a 2 1/2-inch biscuit cutter to cut rounds from the pasta sheets. As you cut or punch, stack and store the pieces under a lightly dampened dish towel or in a plastic bag to keep them from drying out.

On a clean work counter, lay out about 15 pasta rounds or squares at a time, and spoon rounded teaspoonfuls of filling onto the pasta, just off center. Use a spray bottle or wet pastry brush to lightly dampen the edges of the pasta.

One at a time, pick up a piece of pasta and fold in half over the filling, squeezing out air bubbles as you press the dough around the filling with dry fingers to seal the tortellino. If you’re working with circles, you’ll be left with a half-moon shape. If using squares, fold corner-to-corner to form a triangle.

Holding a tortellino in one hand, use your other index finger to gently poke an indent into the center of its base (the bottom of the filling). Folding the tortellino around the indent, draw both of its bottom corners together as if forming a fortune cookie. Overlap the corners and press to seal them together.

Toss lightly with semolina flour, then lay out in a single layer on the second prepared baking sheet. Continue with remaining pasta and filling.

Finish the tomato sauce and cook the pasta: Set a large pot filled with 5 quarts of water over high heat, cover, and bring to a boil. Add 6 tablespoons fine sea salt or 1/2 cup kosher salt. Drop 48 tortellini into the water and stir.

Remove the sauce from heat and stir in 1/4 cup olive oil. Pass sauce through a food mill or use a stick blender to puree. Taste and adjust salt as needed. Set a large frying pan with curved edges on the stove over low heat. Add 1 1/2 cups tomato sauce and bring to a simmer.

When the tortellini are cooked, about 3 to 4 minutes, use a spider or skimmer to lift them out, shake off excess water, and place directly into the pan of sauce. Toss and swirl tortellini in sauce until they are all evenly covered. If the sauce is too thick, add pasta water 1 teaspoon at a time to loosen. The sauce should cling to the pasta without appearing to seize. Serve immediately with grated Parmesan.
description: 4/24 Really good. A bit dry perhaps? Seemed like a little burger inside the pasta. Add some ricotta? Spices were forward.
notes:
Cover and refrigerate any uncooked tortellini for up to 1 day, or freeze in a single layer. When rock hard, transfer to a zipper-sealed plastic bag and freeze for up to 6 weeks. To cook, do not defrost. Drop frozen tortellini into salted boiling water and cook for 4 to 7 minutes until cooked through.

Cover and refrigerate tomato sauce for up to 1 week, or freeze for up to 8 weeks.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (146)). A from-scratch tortellini project based on the version codified by Bologna's Confraternita del Tortellino, with the usual legend about the shape echoing Venus's navel. Traditionally these are served in a light meat broth, but here they are tossed with a simple tomato sauce and a little Parmesan as a main course. The yield is generous, and both pasta and sauce freeze well separately.

What readers report: Only a handful of notes, and the loudest theme is time: the top comment flatly says to budget about three hours rather than the listed hour and fifteen minutes, and a second cook makes the same complaint while calling the method overcomplicated. Both still count the tomato sauce a success. Two separate cooks disliked the filling for the same reason, describing it as crumbly, dry and off-putting in texture; one said the leftover pasta scraps tasted better than the finished tortellini, and another praised the red sauce while conceding the filling may be a matter of personal taste. Nobody offered a fix for the filling.

name: Classic Panzanella Salad (Tuscan-Style Tomato-And-Bread Salad)
ingredients:
2 1/2 pounds (1.1kg) mixed tomatoes, cut into bite-size pieces
2 teaspoons (8g) kosher salt, plus more for seasoning
3/4 pound (340g) ciabatta or rustic sourdough bread, cut into 1 1/2–inch cubes (about 6 cups bread cubes)
10 tablespoons (150ml) extra-virgin olive oil, divided (2T for bread, 8T for tomato dressing)
1 small shallot, minced (about 2 tablespoons)
2 medium cloves garlic, minced (about 2 teaspoons)
1/2 teaspoon (2.6 g) Dijon mustard
2 tablespoons (30 g) white wine vinegar or red wine vinegar
Freshly ground black pepper
1/2 cup (12 g) (1/2 ounce) packed basil leaves, roughly chopped
directions:
1. Place tomatoes in a colander set over a bowl and season with 2 teaspoons (8g) kosher salt. Toss to coat. Set aside at room temperature to drain, tossing occasionally, while you toast the bread. Drain for a minimum of 15 minutes.

2. Meanwhile, preheat oven to 350°F (180°C) and adjust rack to center position. In a large bowl, toss bread cubes with 2 tablespoons (30ml) olive oil. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet. Bake until crisp and firm but not browned, about 15 minutes. Remove from oven and let cool.

3. Remove colander with tomatoes from bowl with tomato juice. Place colander with tomatoes in the sink. Add shallot, garlic, mustard, and vinegar to the bowl with tomato juice. Whisking constantly, drizzle in the remaining 1/2 cup (120ml) olive oil. Season dressing to taste with salt and pepper.

4. Combine toasted bread, tomatoes, and dressing in a large bowl. Add basil leaves. Toss everything to coat and season with salt and pepper. Let rest for 30 minutes before serving, tossing occasionally until dressing is completely absorbed by bread.
description: 7/17 Made with heirloom brandywine tomatoes. Excellent. Didn't add salt after 2 tsp. That was enough. Lighter sourdough better than heavy multigrain bread. Might have done more bread than needed.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.9 (34) / 57 Reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt frames panzanella as a bread salad flavored with vegetables rather than a tomato salad with bread in it, and insists it only works with genuinely good ripe tomatoes. He tested bread four ways - fresh, dried in the oven, stale-but-wrapped, and stale-and-dry - plus the common trick of soaking and squeezing, and concluded that drying is what matters and staling is not: lightly oven-dried fresh bread held its texture best, while wet or merely stale bread turned mushy or leathery. Because drying takes only about 15 minutes in a low oven, the salad needs no day-ahead planning. He also salts and drains the tomatoes for that same 15 minutes to concentrate their flavor, then whisks the drained juice into the vinaigrette with shallot, garlic and a little Dijon, raising the olive oil accordingly so the extra liquid does not break the emulsion.

What readers report: Reviews are overwhelmingly positive and offer variations more than corrections. The most repeated practical point is that whisking the drained tomato juice into the dressing is the step that makes the recipe, with one cook saying it was exactly what earlier attempts had been missing. Herb substitutions work: cilantro was used successfully and parsley in tabouleh-like quantity is recommended by two people, with oregano suggested untested. Additions people report liking include torn mozzarella or burrata to turn it into a main dish, and green onion in place of shallot. Several note the salting-and-draining trick rescues mediocre off-season supermarket tomatoes and use it on other salads. Bread choice is flexible - flavored bakery loaves, garlic cheddar sourdough and already-stale bread all worked. One unanswered question asks whether the salted tomatoes should be rinsed before going into the salad, as some other Serious Eats recipes direct; another asks whether anchovies and capers are a regional variant.

Note on the source: No corrections to quantities or timings appear in the comments; the hausflip question about whether to rinse the salted tomatoes is left unanswered on the page. Several comments end in 'Read More' and may be truncated.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Your 7/17 note confirms Kenji's method as written — 2 tsp salt on the tomatoes was enough, lighter sourdough beat heavy multigrain, and no reader correction to quantities exists.

name: Classic Pasta Alla Norma
ingredients:
Extra-virgin olive oil
1 small onion, diced
Salt and pepper
2 garlic cloves, peeled
Pinch of crushed red pepper
12 basil leaves, plus a few basil sprigs for garnish
4 cups (720 g) peeled, chopped tomatoes with juice, fresh or canned
3 or 4 small eggplants (about 2 pounds), peeled and cut into 1-inch cubes
1 pound (454 g) pasta, such as penne, rigatoncini or spaghetti
1 cup (246 g) coarsely grated ricotta salata
¼ cup (27 g) toasted bread crumbs, preferably homemade
directions:
Make a quick tomato sauce: Put 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large, deep skillet over medium-high heat. Add onions, season with salt and pepper and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, about 10 minutes.

Stir in garlic, red pepper and basil leaves and cook for 1 minute. Add tomatoes, stir and bring to a simmer. Reduce heat to low and let sauce simmer gently for 20 minutes, until slightly thickened. Taste and adjust seasoning. Set aside. (Sauce may be prepared up to 2 days in advance.)

Meanwhile, bring a large pot of well-salted water to a boil. Turn heat to low and cover pot until it’s time to cook the pasta.

Put a wide cast-iron pan over medium-high heat. Add 4 tablespoons olive oil to coat surface of pan. When oil is wavy, test by adding a cube of eggplant. It should begin to sizzle and brown immediately. Fill the pan with a single layer of eggplant cubes. Turn eggplant with a spatula or tongs and brown nicely on all sides. Lower heat as necessary to maintain an even temperature; if the pan is too hot, the eggplant will burn.

Remove cooked eggplant to a plate and continue to fry remaining eggplant in batches, adding more oil as necessary. Season finished eggplant with salt and pepper. (Alternatively, roast the eggplant on a baking sheet at 400 degrees, lightly drizzled with oil, until cooked and nicely browned, about 20 minutes.)

To assemble and serve, boil pasta until al dente, leaving it a little firmer than normal. Bring the tomato sauce to a simmer. Add eggplant to sauce and gently stir to combine. Reserve a cup of pasta cooking water, then drain pasta and add to sauce. Using 2 wooden spoons or tongs, toss pasta and sauce, and let cook 1 minute more. Thin sauce if necessary with a little pasta cooking water.

Transfer to a warmed wide pasta bowl. Sprinkle with grated ricotta salata and bread crumbs. Garnish with torn or whole basil leaves and a drizzle of olive oil, if desired.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (904)). A plain, traditional Sicilian dish built on four cheap staples: olive oil, eggplant, tomato and pasta, finished with grated ricotta salata and toasted bread crumbs. The name is popularly traced to Bellini's opera and the composer's fondness for the dish.

What readers report: The top note (140 votes) argues for an ordering change: toss the pasta with the tomato sauce first and add the eggplant afterward, otherwise the eggplant flavour disappears into the sauce. The next most-voted tip (67) is that the frying oil must be up to temperature before the eggplant goes in, or the cubes soak it up. A large contingent skips frying entirely: broiling or roasting the eggplant comes up repeatedly (49 and 31 votes), with cooks saying they lose no flavour and use far less oil, and one warning that roasted eggplant vanishes off the sheet pan before it reaches the pot. A Sicilian-heritage commenter offers context on the dish's name. Garlic quantity is treated as a floor, not a ceiling.

name: Cold Noodle Salad with Spicy Peanut Sauce
ingredients:
Kosher salt
10 ounces (284 g) soba noodles
1 medium zucchini or cucumber (about 6 ounces)
5 radishes (about 4 ounces)
1 bell pepper (any color)
1 tablespoon (14 g) sesame oil
1/2 cup (73 g) roasted salted peanuts (about 2 ounces), roughly chopped
2 scallions, trimmed and finely chopped
Handful of cilantro leaves
1 lime, cut into wedges for serving
1/2 cup (129 g) smooth peanut butter (not natural)
1/4 cup (64 g) soy sauce
2 tablespoons (40 g) maple syrup
2 tablespoons (30 g) lime juice (from 1 lime)
1 tablespoon (14 g) sesame oil
2 teaspoons (10 g) chile oil or hot sauce, plus more to taste
1 garlic clove, grated
directions:
Bring a pot of salted water to the boil. Add the soba, stir to prevent sticking, and cook according to package instructions until just tender. Rinse under cold water until the noodles are completely cold.

Meanwhile, make the sauce: In a medium bowl, combine the peanut butter, soy sauce, maple syrup, lime juice, sesame oil, chile oil or hot sauce, and garlic. Add 1/4 to 1/2 cup water, 1 tablespoon at a time, and whisk until the sauce is a pourable consistency. Taste and add more chile oil or hot sauce as desired; set aside.

Cut the zucchini or cucumber and radishes into 1/8-inch thick slices, then cut into thin matchsticks. Slice the peppers into 1/8-inch pieces. Place them all in a large bowl.

Loosen the soba noodles by running them under some water, then allow to drain again. Add them to the vegetables, add the remaining 1 tablespoon sesame oil and toss to combine.

When you are ready to serve, drizzle with spicy peanut sauce and top with peanuts, scallions and cilantro. Serve immediately, with lime wedges alongside.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (9,943)). Cold soba noodles tossed with a spicy peanut sauce and a heap of raw crunchy vegetables, with the vegetables treated as fully swappable (cabbage, carrot, fennel, asparagus, broccoli, cauliflower). Any nut or seed butter can stand in for the peanut butter, including tahini. Noodles and sauce can both be made a day ahead but should be combined only at serving, and the sauce needs a spoonful or two of water to loosen after it sits.

What readers report: Peanut butter choice dominates. The highest-voted note (1,238) explains that conventional emulsified peanut butters blend into the sauce more readily than natural ones because of the added oils, and a 797-vote note raises the same natural-versus-processed question; a 638-vote commenter recommends powdered peanut butter reconstituted with water for a lower-fat sauce, warning about added sugar in some brands. On technique, a 555-vote note says to stop whisking by hand and instead use an immersion blender in a deep measuring cup with about 1/4 cup water. A 687-vote tip changes assembly: dress the noodles with sauce first and lay the vegetables on top so they stay crisp and keep their colour. Fresh ginger and cilantro in the sauce, and sriracha for the chile oil, are common additions.

name: Company Pot Roast
ingredients:
1 (4 to 5-pound) prime boneless beef chuck roast, tied
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
All-purpose flour
Good olive oil
2 cups (256 g) chopped carrots (4 carrots)
2 cups (320 g) chopped yellow onions (2 onions)
2 cups (202 g) chopped celery (4 stalks)
2 cups (178 g) chopped leeks, white and light green parts (2 to 4 leeks)
5 large garlic cloves, peeled and crushed
2 cups (474 g) good red wine, such as Burgundy
2 tablespoons (28 g) Cognac or brandy
1 (28-ounce) can whole plum tomatoes in puree
1 cup (240 g) chicken stock, preferably homemade
1 chicken bouillon cube
3 branches fresh thyme
2 branches fresh rosemary
1 tablespoon (14 g) unsalted butter, at room temperature
directions:
Preheat the oven to 325 degrees F.

Pat the beef dry with a paper towel. Season the roast all over with 1 tablespoon salt and 1 1/2 teaspoons pepper. Dredge the whole roast in flour, including the ends. In a large Dutch oven, heat 2 tablespoons olive oil over medium heat. Add the roast and sear for 4 to 5 minutes, until nicely browned. Turn and sear the other side and then turn and sear the ends. This should take 4 to 5 minutes for each side. Remove the roast to a large plate.

Add 2 tablespoons olive oil to the Dutch oven. Add the carrots, onions, celery, leeks, garlic, 1 tablespoon salt, and 1 1/2 teaspoons pepper and cook over medium heat for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until tender but not browned. Add the wine and Cognac and bring to a boil. Add the tomatoes, chicken stock, bouillon cube, 2 teaspoons salt, and 1 teaspoon pepper. Tie the thyme and rosemary together with kitchen string and add to the pot. Put the roast back into the pot, bring to a boil, and cover. Place in the oven for 2 1/2 hours, until the meat is fork tender or about 160 degrees F internally. Turn the heat down to 250 degrees F after about an hour to keep the sauce at a simmer.

Remove the roast to a cutting board. Remove the herb bundle and discard. Skim off as much fat as possible from the sauce. Transfer half the sauce and vegetables to a blender or a food processor fitted with the steel blade and puree until smooth. Pour the puree back into the pot, place on the stovetop over low heat, and return the sauce to a simmer. Place 2 tablespoons flour and the butter in a small bowl and mash them together with a fork. Stir into the sauce and simmer for 2 minutes, stirring until thickened. Taste for seasonings. Remove the strings from the roast, and slice the meat. Serve warm with the sauce spooned over it.
description:
2024 Enjoyed again. Used most of the salt. Cooked choice beef shoulder. Needed 3 hours. Still not super tender, but very tasty. Makes way more gravy than needed. 
2009. Delicious. Plenty for 6-8. Did not use brandy. Steph thought was too salty. 
2010. Used shoulder.
2010. Added parboiled potatoes, but they did not fully cook. Could cut salt by 1 tsp if using table salt rather than Diamond kosher as Ina recommends.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten's pot roast is a chuck roast floured and seared hard, then braised low and slow on a bed of carrot, onion, celery and leek with garlic, red Burgundy, a shot of Cognac, canned plum tomatoes and stock. The long gentle braise is what converts the connective tissue in chuck to gelatin, so the meat shreds while the liquid thickens into a glossy sauce. The vegetables are pureed into the braising liquid at the end, which is what gives it body without a heavy roux.

What readers report: Readers report the recipe takes well to substitution rather than needing correction. Smaller roasts than the four-to-five pound piece called for work fine with the timing scaled down, beef stock stands in for the chicken stock without loss, and the Cognac can simply be left out. The most repeated practical tip is to use an immersion blender directly in the pot to puree the braised vegetables into the sauce, which gives a smoother, more restaurant-like finish than pushing it through a food mill or leaving it chunky. Nobody takes issue with the author's method or timings; the consistent reports are tender meat and a rich sauce, and the recipe is described as working for both an ordinary family dinner and entertaining.

claude_opt.changes: Cut the salt by about 1 teaspoon if using table salt, not Diamond Crystal — your 2009/2010 notes both found it too salty. Budget closer to 3 hours in the oven, as your 2024 note found, not 2.5.

name: Coq Au Vin (Chicken Braised in Red Wine)
ingredients:
2 whole small chickens (about 3 pounds each, see note), each chicken cut into 4 pieces, backbones reserved for stock
2 cups (474 g) dry red wine
8 ounces (227 g) pearl onions (see note)
1/4 pound (113 g) slab bacon or salt pork, cut into 1- by 1/4- by 1/4-inch sticks
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
8 ounces (227 g) button or cremini mushrooms, woody stems trimmed if necessary, quartered
3 medium carrots, diced (about 1 1/2 cups)
4 medium cloves garlic, crushed
2 sprigs thyme
2 bay leaves
2 cups (480 g) gelatinous homemade chicken stock (see note) or low-sodium chicken broth
3 tablespoons (43 g) cold unsalted butter, cubed
1/4 cup (15 g) minced flat-leaf parsley
directions:
Preheat oven to 350°F. Add chicken to a 1-gallon zipper-lock bag. Pour in wine and seal bag, pressing out air. Let stand while you prepare the remaining ingredients.

Using a paring knife, trim off the ends of each onion and score a light "X" into one cut side. Bring a small pot of water to a boil over high heat. Add onions and cook until outer layers are soft, about 1 1/2 minutes. Drain onions and run under cool water until cold enough to handle. Peel onions with your fingers and discard peels.

In a large Dutch oven or rondeau, cook bacon over medium-high heat, stirring and reducing heat as necessary to prevent scorching, until browned and fat has rendered, about 10 minutes. Remove from heat and, using a slotted spoon, transfer bacon to a paper towel-lined plate.

Remove chicken from zipper-lock bag, reserving wine, and pat dry. Season with salt and pepper. Return Dutch oven with rendered bacon fat to medium-high heat and, working in batches, add chicken, skin side down, and cook until browned, about 7 minutes. Turn and brown other side, about 5 minutes. Transfer browned chicken to a wire rack set over a rimmed baking sheet. Reserve at room temperature.

Once all chicken is browned, add mushrooms to Dutch oven and cook over medium-high heat, stirring frequently, until browned, 10 to 12 minutes. Add pearl onions, carrots, and garlic and cook, stirring, until lightly browned, about 5 minutes. Add bacon, wine, thyme, and bay leaves and bring to a simmer, stirring up any browned bits.

Stir in stock. Add chicken legs skin side up, nestling them into the Dutch oven so that they are partially submerged but top of skin is above the liquid. Pour in any accumulated juices from chicken. Transfer to oven at 350° and cook, uncovered, for 1 hour.

Add chicken breasts, nestling them skin side up amongst the legs, and return to the oven. Cook until breasts are just cooked through (they should register 145 to 150°F on an instant read thermometer), about 20 minutes.

Transfer chicken breasts and legs to a clean rack set over a rimmed backing sheet. Set Dutch oven over medium-low heat and simmer until sauce is lightly viscous, about 10 minutes. Whisk in butter, then season with salt (if necessary) and pepper. Stir in half of parsley.

Return chicken to pot, spooning sauce on top. Garnish with remaining parsley. Serve right away with buttered potatoes, pasta, or rice.
description: 1/22 Delicious. Lots of work but intense flavor. Didn’t use gelatin. Really liked the broth. Could have been more. Lots of chicken. Perhaps salt the chicken while browning. Maybe increase the amount of broth or reduce the chicken a bit.
notes:
If you can't find small 3-pound chickens, use one 4-pound chicken plus 1 pound of chicken legs. The chicken stock should have enough gelatin in it that it sets like jello when chilled. If it is thinner than that, you will need to add gelatin. Pour the stock into a large bowl and sprinkle with 2 packets of unflavored gelatin. Let the gelatin fully hydrate. The stock will have a grainy appearance but will smooth out once added to the recipe.

Frozen pearl onions can be used in place of fresh; to use frozen onions, cook direct from frozen, skipping Step 2. This braise can be made ahead and tastes even better the next day: Complete recipe through Step 7, then let cool at room temperature for 1 hour before transferring Dutch oven to refrigerator; reheat gently in 350°F oven before proceeding with Step 8.

Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.6 (8) / 39 Reviews). Daniel Gritzer explains that the dish was built around an old rooster that needed hours of cooking, and that using a modern tender hen the same way just dries out the breast, which he demonstrates with a side-by-side of 20-minute and 45-minute breast meat. His fix is to brown all the chicken, braise only the legs for about an hour, and add the breasts for the last 20 minutes, with a short wine marinade beforehand so the quick-cooking breast still tastes like part of the braise. He tested marinating times and found even 25 minutes, the time it takes to prep everything else, gives most of the benefit, and he argues the specific wine barely matters once stock, pork, mushrooms and aromatics are in the pot. For the sauce he rejects beurre manie in favor of reducing a gelatin-rich stock and finishing with butter, warning that heavy reduction concentrates salt so seasoning should wait until the end.

What readers report: The most substantive criticism concerns the sauce. One detailed reviewer argues the 1:1 wine-to-stock ratio yields too little wine flavor and too pale a sauce, preferring roughly 3:1 or no stock at all, and reports that even with two packets of gelatin and hard reducing it lacked body until thickened with a cornstarch slurry. A second cook also reached for cornstarch, partly because the article says to pour off most of the fat after browning while the recipe steps omit that, leaving the dish too fatty to finish with butter. Against that, another says reducing by two-thirds gave a glossy sauce needing no thickener, so patience may be the variable. Scaling matters: using one 4-pound chicken instead of two small ones leaves too much liquid unless the wine and stock are cut too. Carrots are contested. Two readers raise food-safety unease about the partly cooked breasts resting at room temperature.

Note on the source: The published recipe steps do not include the article's instruction to pour off excess fat after browning the chicken - two reviewers were tripped up by this. Some comments end in 'Read More' and may be cut off.

1 (8 oz.) carton whipped cream cheese, softened
1 cup (150 g) crumbled feta cheese
1/4 cup (25 g) chopped green onions
1 (6 oz.) pkg dried cranberries
4 (10 inch) flour tortillas
directions: Combine cream cheese, feta, and onions. Stir in cranberries. Spread 1/2 c. of the mix over each tortilla and roll. Wrap with plastic wrap and refrigerate at least 1 hour. Cut each roll into 10 pinwheel slices.
notes:
Web summary (tasteofhome.com, 24 reviews; star value not numerically shown). Joy Manning's no-bake party appetizer: whipped cream cheese loosened and blended with crumbled feta, green onion and dried cranberries, spread on large flour tortillas, rolled and sliced. It works on contrast rather than cooking, plush cream cheese against salty feta and chewy sweet cranberry. Rolling the logs and chilling them before slicing both firms the filling and lets the flavors settle, so it is deliberately a make-ahead.

Note on the source: Exact title match and this is the most widely circulated original of the dish, but the collection records the source as 'Susan Symmes - Christmas '22', i.e. passed along within the family. Cannot prove Susan's card came from Taste of Home rather than one of the many blog clones.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Technique (chill before slicing) already matches Taste of Home's well-reviewed original; no consistent complaints found about sogginess or filling firmness across 24 reviews.

name: Cranberry Jelly
ingredients:
1 lb. (454 g) cranberries (5 c.)
2 c. (474 g) boiling water
1 3/4 c. (350 g) sugar
dash salt
directions: Put cranberries in saucepan. Boil for 20 minutes. Rub through a sieve (or a food mill) to remove skins. Cook 3 minutes. Add sugar and salt and return to a boil. Cook 2 minutes. Pour into mold. Chill
description: We haven't had success scaling this recipe. Just stick to 1 lb. of cranberries.

claude_opt.changes: No changes needed; boil-mill-cook technique and sugar ratio already match how modern jellied cranberry sauce is made. A durable, correct method.

name: Cream Sponge Cake
ingredients:
4 egg whites
4 egg yolks
1 c. (200 g) sugar
3 T. (44 g) cold water
1 1/4 t. (5.0 g) baking powder
1 t. (4.2 g) lemon extract
1 1/2 T corn starch
1 c. (113 g) cake flour, less 1 1/2 T.
1/4 t. (1.5 g) salt
directions:
Preheat oven to 375.

Beat whites until stiff but not dry. Beat in half the sugar gradually. Set aside. Beat yolks until thick and lemon-colored. Add water one T. at a time. Then add 1/2 c. sugar gradually and continue beating until very thick. Combine white and yolk mixtures with folding motion. Mix well and add lemon extract and dry ingredients sifted lightly into mixture until completely mixed. Pour into ungreased tube pan and bake 35-40 minutes, or possibly a bit less. Invert until cool.
notes: Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Lower oven to 350°F; 375°F is hotter than modern tube-pan sponge/chiffon recipes use and risks over-browning or toughening this delicate egg-foam cake. Extend baking a few minutes to compensate.

name: Creamed Onions
ingredients:
2 lbs (907 g) boiler onions 
4 T flour
4 T butter 
2 c milk
3/4 t Diamond Crystal Kosher salt
1/4 t freshly ground pepper
1.5 c bread crumbs tossed with melted butter
directions:
Blanch whole onions in boiling water for about 5 minutes. Remove from water. When cool enough to handle, peel off outer layer of skin and trim ends. Return peeled onions to salted water and boil until just tender when pierced with a fork. 

Make white sauce. Melt butter in 2 quart saucepan and stir in flour. Let cook for 3-5 minutes to remove raw flour taste, being careful not to brown. Slowly add warmed milk, using whisk to combine. Heat until thickened. Add salt and freshly ground pepper. 

Put cooked onions in swallow casserole dish and pour whte sauce over. Top with buttered breadcrumbs. Bake at 400 degrees for 40 minutes or until bubbly and bread crumbs brown. Goes well with roast turkey or beef.
notes:
Boiler onions are hard to find. Check Safeway. 
11/2025 Used 2.5 lbs of raw onions. Enough for 9”x13” pyrex casserole dish

claude_opt.changes: Frozen pearl onions (thawed) can replace hard-to-find fresh boiler onions; skip the initial blanch-and-peel and go straight to simmering in salted water, a substitution modern recipes note saves real time.

name: Creamed Spinach Pasta
ingredients:
1 cup (246 g) whole-milk ricotta
Kosher salt and black pepper
1 pound (454 g) long pasta, such as fettuccine or tagliatelle
3 tablespoons (25 g) pine nuts (optional)
4 tablespoons (57 g) unsalted butter
3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1 pound (454 g) fresh baby spinach
1 cup (238 g) heavy cream
¼ teaspoon (0.6 g) grated nutmeg
Grated pecorino or Parmesan, for serving
directions:
Add the ricotta to a large bowl; season well with salt and pepper and set aside.

Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a boil. Add the pasta and cook according to package instructions until al dente. Reserve 1 cup of pasta cooking water and drain.

Prepare your sauce while the pasta cooks: If using, cook the pine nuts in a deep 12-inch skillet over medium heat until toasted, stirring occasionally to make sure they do not burn, 2 to 3 minutes. Transfer to a small bowl.

Wipe skillet clean and melt the butter over medium-low heat. Add the garlic and sauté until pale golden, about 2 minutes. Add the spinach, stirring it in by the handful if needed, and cook until it wilts, adding a few tablespoons of the pasta water to help it along if needed, about 4 minutes. Season with salt.

Add the cream, bring to a simmer over medium heat and cook until sauce begins to thicken slightly, about 2 minutes more. Stir in the nutmeg then season with salt and pepper. Add the cooked pasta directly to the skillet and toss until the noodles are glossy with sauce.

Turn off heat and stir in the prepared ricotta, thinning the sauce with a bit of pasta cooking water if needed. Taste and adjust seasonings as needed. Divide among bowls. Top with pine nuts, if using, and pass grated pecorino or Parmesan at the table.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (2,958)). Colu Henry's weeknight pasta borrows from the steakhouse side dish. A full pound of fresh spinach wilts down in garlicky butter, cream goes in and simmers until thick, and the cooked pasta finishes in the sauce with ricotta stirred through. Long noodles such as fettuccine or tagliatelle hold the sauce best. Nuts on top are optional, and it works either as a side to grilled meat or fish or as a meal on its own.

What readers report: The highest-voted note (263) says ricotta quality decides the texture: good whole-milk ricotta keeps the sauce smooth, yogurt is a passable substitute and cottage cheese was judged a poor one, though a 158-vote commenter disagrees and likes cottage cheese, while also calling the separate bowl for seasoning the ricotta a pointless extra dish. A 216-vote note skips fresh spinach entirely for two 16-ounce bags of frozen chopped spinach, microwaved and squeezed dry. Timing is the common correction (197 votes): a pound of fresh spinach takes well over the four minutes given. Cooks add lemon zest and juice at the end for brightness (168), and a 128-vote note reports the recipe works with any cooking green and with half-and-half in place of heavy cream.

claude_opt.changes: A full pound of fresh spinach needs well over 4 minutes to wilt down, per reader consensus (197 votes) — cook until fully collapsed, not by the clock. Finish with lemon zest and juice; it cuts the cream's richness.

name: Creamy Coleslaw
ingredients:
For the Slaw Mix:
1 large head green cabbage, about 3 1/2 pounds (1.6 kg), finely shredded on a mandoline or by hand (see note)
1 large red onion, finely sliced on a mandoline or by hand
1 large carrot, peeled and grated on the large holes of a box grater (see note)
1/4 cup (15 g) roughly chopped fresh parsley leaves
1 cup (200 g) white sugar
1/2 cup (67 g) kosher salt
For the Dressing:
3/4 cup (165 g) mayonnaise
1/4 cup (60 g) apple cider vinegar
2 tablespoons (31 g) dijon mustard
1 tablespoon (6.9 g) freshly ground black pepper
3 tablespoons (38 g) sugar
directions:
1. For the Slaw Mix: Combine cabbage, onion, carrot, and parsley in a large bowl, leaving plenty of room to toss (you may have to use two large bowls if your bowls are not large enough). Sprinkle with sugar and salt and toss to combine. Let rest five minutes, then transfer to a large colander and rinse thoroughly under cold running water.

2. Transfer rinsed mixture to a salad spinner and spin dry. Alternatively, transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet lined with a triple layer of paper towels or a clean kitchen towel and blot mixture dry with more paper towels. Return to large bowl and set aside.

3. For the Dressing: Combine mayonnaise, vinegar, mustard, black pepper, and sugar in a medium bowl and whisk until homogenous.

4. Pour dressing over cabbage mixture and toss to coat. Taste and adjust seasoning with more salt, pepper, sugar, and/or vinegar if desired.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.4 (31) / 81 Reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt writes that he came to coleslaw late, after a bad KFC encounter and a much better tangy, barely-creamy version at a Boston restaurant, and this is his attempt at that lightly dressed style. He argues green cabbage beats savoy because its crunch and sulfurous bite hold up, and that the cabbage must be pre-treated or the dressed salad turns watery and raw-tasting. His testing showed that a heavy salt-and-sugar coating draws out moisture fast, so a five-minute purge followed by a cold rinse concentrates flavor without wrecking texture, while longer sits make the shreds limp. He also found that blotting or salad-spinning the rinsed vegetables dry, rather than wringing them out, preserves the crunch, and that the concentrated cabbage then needs only a small amount of mayonnaise-cider vinegar-Dijon dressing plus far more black pepper than seems sensible.

What readers report: The dominant complaint is salt. Several cooks found the half-cup of kosher salt overwhelming and blamed volume measurement: one notes Kenji almost certainly used Diamond Crystal and reports using 68.5 g for Morton's with good results; another had to soak the vegetables in water to undo the damage; others ask outright for gram weights, and one long review criticizes the recipe for giving no weights at all. Repeat advice: rinse very thoroughly and taste the vegetables after rinsing to confirm they are bland before dressing, since under-rinsing has ruined batches. Celery seed is a popular addition, mentioned by more than one reviewer. One halved the vegetables (1.5 lb cabbage before coring) and still had dressing left over, suggesting the dressing yield runs generous. Another halves the black pepper. Unanswered questions include whether bagged slaw mix needs the purge and whether 3.5 lb of cabbage is really correct.

Note on the source: Manifest calls this 'Creamy Coleslaw' but the page title is 'Classic Coleslaw' (URL slug is creamy-cole-slaw) - same recipe, different title. Recipe gives no weights for the salt/sugar purge, which multiple reviewers flag as a real problem; Kenji's own reply confirms a 2013 vintage. Several reviewer comments end in 'Read More' and may be truncated.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. The gram weights already resolve the Diamond Crystal vs. Morton salt confusion that caused most complaints, and the purge-rinse-dry steps readers needed are already in the method.

name: Creamy Corn Pasta with Basil
ingredients:
Fine sea salt
12 ounces (340 g) dry orecchiette or farfalle
1 tablespoon (14 g) olive oil, plus more for drizzling
1 bunch scallions (about 8), trimmed and thinly sliced (keep the whites and greens separate)
2 large ears corn, shucked and kernels removed (2 cups kernels)
½ teaspoon (1.1 g) ground black pepper, more for serving
3 tablespoons (43 g) unsalted butter
½ cup (45 g) grated Parmesan cheese, more to taste
⅓ cup (8.0 g) torn basil or mint, more for garnish
¼ teaspoon (0.5 g) red pepper flakes, or to taste
Fresh lemon juice, as needed
directions:
Bring a large pot of well-salted water to a boil. Cook pasta until 1 minute shy of al dente, according to the package directions. Drain, reserving 1/2 cup of pasta water.

Meanwhile, heat oil in large sauté pan over medium heat; add scallion whites and a pinch of salt and cook until soft, 3 minutes. Add 1/4 cup water and all but 1/4 cup corn; simmer until corn is heated through and almost tender, 3 to 5 minutes. Add 1/4 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper, transfer to a blender, and purée mixture until smooth, adding a little extra water if needed to get a thick but pourable texture.

Heat the same skillet over high heat. Add butter and let melt. Add reserved 1/4 cup corn and cook until tender, 1 to 2 minutes. (It’s O.K. if the butter browns; that deepens the flavor.) Add the corn purée and cook for 30 seconds to heat and combine the flavors.

Reduce heat to medium. Add pasta and half the reserved pasta cooking water, tossing to coat. Cook for 1 minute, then add a little more of the pasta cooking water if the mixture seems too thick. Stir in 1/4 cup of the scallion greens, the Parmesan, the herbs, the red pepper flakes, 1/4 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Sprinkle with fresh lemon juice to taste. Transfer to warm pasta bowls and garnish with more scallions, herbs, a drizzle of olive oil and black pepper.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (11,089)). Melissa Clark's summer pasta gets its creaminess from pureed fresh corn and sauteed scallions rather than any dairy cream, with Parmesan for savor and red chile flakes for contrast. Lemon juice and fresh herbs go in at the very end and matter, cutting the richness. Best at peak corn season, but the recipe is forgiving enough for supermarket ears or frozen kernels.

What readers report: The dominant tip by a wide margin (900 votes) is to simmer the stripped cobs in water for 10 to 15 minutes and cook the pasta in that corn stock for deeper flavour, while holding back a larger share of whole kernels for texture. Adding halved or quartered grape tomatoes at the end for acidity is the next most popular change (410 votes), and shrimp with a clove of garlic and mint appears at 202 votes; bacon is a recurring suggestion. The main dissent is about sweetness: a 169-vote commenter who followed the recipe exactly found the corn puree cloying even after cheese, lemon and basil, and a 154-vote note calls the dish underwhelming for the effort. Chile flakes and lemon are the usual correctives.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. The top reader tip — simmering cobs for stock — meaningfully lengthens a 30-minute dish for a modest gain; the built-in chile flakes and lemon already address the sweetness some found cloying.

name: Creamy Dill Sauce for Salmon or Trout
ingredients:
DILL SAUCE
3/4 cup (172 g) sour cream (1)
2 tsp (10 g) Dijon or hot English mustard (2)
1/2 tsp (1.4 g) garlic powder or 1 small garlic clove , minced
2 1/2 tbsp (7.0 g) fresh dill , finely chopped
1 tsp (2.0 g) lemon zest
1 - 2 tbsp (15-30 g) lemon juice
2 tbsp (30 g) milk (or olive oil, for richness)
1/4 - 1/2 tsp (1.5-3.0 g) salt
1/2 tsp (2.1 g) white sugar
FISH
1/2 - 1 tbsp (6.8-14 g) oil
4 salmon or trout fillets (125g / 4oz each)
Salt and pepper
directions:
Mix the Dill Sauce ingredients together (Mix well to loosen the sour cream). Adjust consistency with milk and tartness with lemon juice. Set aside for 10 minutes if you can - if using fresh garlic, set aside for 20 min.

Pat fish dry with paper towel. Sprinkle with salt and pepper.

Heat oil in skillet over medium high heat. Place fish in skillet skin side down. Cook for 2 minutes, then flip and cook the other side for 1 1/2 minutes.

Remove from skillet onto serving plates. Serve with Dill Sauce on the side, garnished with fresh dill and lemon wedges if desired.
description: 8/21 Made it today. Very good, though a large number of ingredients. Used garlic powder rather than garlic.
notes:
Web summary (recipetineats.com, 4.98 stars from 44 votes). Nagi Maehashi pairs pan-cooked salmon or trout with a sauce that needs no cooking at all: sour cream loosened with milk and sharpened with mustard, lemon zest and juice, garlic and a lot of fresh dill. The acidity and the mustard are there to cut through the fat of an oily fish, which is why this reads lighter than a butter or cream reduction. The whole dinner lands in about fifteen minutes and stays under 400 calories a serving.

What readers report: The strongest and most repeated point is that fresh dill is not optional here; readers who reached for dried report the sauce falls flat. Greek yogurt is the substitution people vouch for most often in place of sour cream, giving a tangier and slightly thicker result. Several note the recipe makes more sauce than the four fillets need and treat the surplus as a dip or spoon it over potatoes, roasted vegetables and salads, and a number report it works equally well on other fish including tilapia and snapper. One commenter found it too sharp as written and cut the lemon juice back toward the lower end of the range. No one reported problems with technique or timing.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Your 8/21 note confirms garlic powder works fine, and reviewers report no technique or timing problems — the fresh dill and quick sear are already right.

name: Creamy Horseradish Sauce
ingredients:
prepared horseradish
mayonnaise
salt
whipping cream
directions: In a small bowl mix one 6-oz. jar prepared white horseradish (drained), 1/2 c. mayonnaise, and 1 t. salt. Whip 1/2 c. heavy cream. Fold into horseradish.

claude_opt.changes: No changes needed; whipped-cream-folded-into-horseradish-and-mayo is the same method modern horseradish cream sauces for beef still use. No raw-egg or safety concern.

name: Creamy Hummus—Ina
ingredients:
2 (15.5-ounce) cans chickpeas, rinsed and drained
½ teaspoon (2.0 g) baking powder
4 cloves garlic, finely grated on a rasp
1/3 cup (81 g) freshly squeezed lemon juice, plus extra (2 lemons)
¼ teaspoon (1.2 g) Tabasco
¼ teaspoon (0.6 g) smoked paprika, plus extra for garnish
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ cup (120 g) tahini, stirred well (see note)
Good olive oil
¼ cup (36 g) salted, roasted regular or Marcona almonds (optional)
Toasted pita triangles, for serving (see note)
directions:
Combine the chickpeas, baking powder and 6 cups water in a large saucepan, cover, and bring to a boil over high heat. Uncover, lower the heat, and simmer for 25 minutes, stirring occasionally.

Meanwhile, combine the garlic and 1/3 cup lemon juice in a small bowl and set aside.

Drain the water and the chickpea skins that float to the top, leaving the chickpeas in the pan. Add cold water, stir vigorously to loosen more skins, and drain off the water and skins that float to the top, again leaving the chickpeas in the saucepan. Do this 5 or 6 times, until most of the skins are drained off. Drain the chickpeas, setting aside 2 tablespoons for the garnish and place the rest in the bowl of a food processor fitted with the steel blade. Add the garlic mixture, Tabasco, the ¼ teaspoon paprika, ¼ cup warm water, 1 tablespoon salt, and 1 teaspoon pepper and process until very smooth. Add the tahini and 2 tablespoons of olive oil and puree for one full minute, until creamy. Add 2 to 3 tablespoons of extra lemon juice (to taste), 1 teaspoon salt, and enough warm water (1 tablespoon at a time) to make the hummus the consistency of thick yogurt.

Using a rubber spatula, spread the hummus on a large (12-inch) flat, round serving plate, leaving a 2-inch border. Sprinkle the reserved chickpeas and almonds (if using) evenly on top. Drizzle with extra olive oil, sprinkle lightly with extra paprika, and serve with toasted pita triangles.

Notes: Grate the garlic very finely on a rasp.

Before starting the recipe, I transfer the entire contents of the tahini can to the food processor fitted with the steel blade, puree it, then pour it back into the can.

To toast the pita, place it on a sheet pan and bake for 10 minutes at 350 degrees.
notes:
Web summary (barefootcontessa.com). Ina Garten's route to a genuinely smooth hummus is to simmer canned chickpeas with a little leavening and then rub and rinse the skins off before blending. The alkaline cooking water loosens the skins, and removing them is what separates silky hummus from the slightly gritty version most home cooks get. Tahini, grated garlic, lemon juice, smoked paprika and a dash of Tabasco season it, with olive oil and optional roasted almonds on top.

Note on the source: barefootcontessa.com carries no comments or ratings; note the page lists baking POWDER where the alkaline-softening technique conventionally uses baking soda - worth checking against the printed book

Link confidence: LOW — this URL is a plausible version of the dish but was not verified as the family's exact recipe. Treat the link as a lead, not a citation.

claude_opt.changes: Card lists baking powder for the chickpea simmer; Ina's actual technique and every write-up of this trick (ATK, Yahoo) use baking soda, the stronger alkalizer that loosens skins better.

name: Creamy Winter Squash Soup with Brown Butter Streusel Topping
ingredients:
½ cup (44 g) old-fashioned oats
½ cup (64 g) unsalted pepitas, roughly chopped
½ cup (106 g) brown sugar
½ cup (60 g) all-purpose flour
Kosher salt
6 tablespoons (85 g) unsalted butter
2 quarts (1.9 kg) chicken or vegetable stock
2 whole medium butternut squashes, peeled, seeded and cut into 2-inch cubes
½ cup (119 g) heavy cream
2 tablespoons (40 g) maple syrup
¼ teaspoon (0.5 g) ground ginger
¼ teaspoon (0.6 g) freshly grated nutmeg
Ground white pepper
directions:
Make the streusel topping: Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper. In a medium bowl, combine oats, pepitas, brown sugar, flour and a generous pinch of salt, and mix to combine.

Set a small, heavy pan over medium-low heat and add 4 tablespoons butter. As butter melts and bubbles, watch it carefully: Browned butter blackens and turns acrid quickly. Once butter is golden brown and smells nutty, after 1-2 minutes, drizzle it over oat mixture, and toss to combine. Spread mixture evenly across prepared baking sheet. Bake until mixture turns light brown and crumbly, about 15 minutes. Let streusel cool at least 5 minutes.

As the streusel bakes and cools, make the soup: Pour stock into a wide pot and bring it to a simmer over medium-high heat. Add squash and bring liquid back to a boil. Reduce heat to maintain an active simmer and cook until squash is fully tender and, at the end, submerged by about 1 inch of liquid, about 15 minutes. If necessary, add splashes of water to keep squash submerged in just enough liquid. Use a blender or food processor to purée squash and its cooking liquid until completely smooth. Pass soup through a fine-mesh sieve, back into its pot, so the consistency becomes very silky. Set pot over low heat and stir in cream, maple syrup, 2 tablespoons butter, ginger and nutmeg until thoroughly incorporated. Season with salt and white pepper to taste.

Ladle hot soup into serving bowls and scatter streusel overtop. Serve immediately.
notes:
Web summary (wsj.com). A Wall Street Journal Slow Food Fast column featuring Anne Quatrano, the Atlanta chef behind Bacchanalia and several other restaurants, where the recipe first appeared more than a decade ago. Butternut squash is enriched with a little maple syrup and heavy cream and warmed with ginger and nutmeg. The garnish is a brown-butter streusel of toasted oats and pumpkin seeds, which Quatrano wants for the crunch against the velvety soup. She notes the dish is forgiving because squash is essentially impossible to overcook.

Note on the source: WSJ article, no ratings or reader comments on the page

claude_opt.changes: No onion or aromatic base, unlike nearly every well-reviewed butternut soup (ATK, Ahead of Thyme), which sautes onion before adding stock. Sweat one chopped onion in the butter first for depth.

name: Crisp Gnocchi with Brussels Sprouts and Brown Butter
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) brussels sprouts (or cruciferous vegetables like broccoli, cauliflower or even cabbage)
1 lemon
4 tablespoons (54 g) extra-virgin olive oil
Kosher salt (such as Diamond Crystal) and black pepper
1/2 teaspoon (0.9 g) red-pepper flakes
1 (18-ounce) package shelf-stable or refrigerated potato gnocchi
6 tablespoons (85 g) unsalted butter, sliced into 6 pieces
1/2 teaspoon (3.5 g) honey
Freshly grated Parmesan, for serving
directions:
Trim and halve the brussels sprouts. Using a vegetable peeler, peel thick strips of lemon zest, then coarsely chop. (You should have about 2 teaspoons chopped zest.)

In a large (preferably 12-inch) skillet, heat 3 tablespoons olive oil over medium-high. Add the brussels sprouts, season with 1/2 teaspoon salt and a few grinds of pepper, then arrange the brussels sprouts in an even layer, cut side down. Scatter the lemon zest over the top and cook, undisturbed, until the brussels sprouts are well browned underneath, 3 to 5 minutes. Add the red-pepper flakes, stir and cook until the brussels sprouts are crisp-tender, 2 to 3 minutes. Transfer to a medium bowl.

In the same skillet, heat the remaining 1 tablespoon olive oil over medium-high. Break up any gnocchi that are stuck together, add them to the pan and cook, covered and undisturbed, until golden brown on one side, 2 to 4 minutes. Add the butter and honey, season with salt and a generous amount of black pepper, and cook, stirring, until the butter is golden, nutty smelling and foaming, 1 to 2 minutes. Stir in the brussels sprouts until warmed through. Serve with grated Parmesan.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (27,461)). A 20-minute skillet dish built on one trick: store-bought gnocchi are never boiled, just seared until crisp and golden outside while staying chewy inside, closer to fried dough than to boiled dumplings. They are tossed with sauteed brussels sprouts, lemon zest, red-pepper flakes and brown butter. Both shelf-stable and refrigerated gnocchi work, though the shelf-stable kind crisps better.

What readers report: The single loudest practical complaint concerns the sprouts: a 570-vote note reports they were nowhere near done in the stated five minutes, and the most-endorsed workaround is to roast them separately and fold them in. Several highly rated notes describe this (885, 678 and 597 votes), roasting at 425 to 450 degrees for 15 to 25 minutes while the gnocchi crisp on the stovetop, which keeps the total time close to 20 minutes and produces crispier sprouts; shallot and garlic are often added at the toss. A 1,551-vote note swaps a splash of aged balsamic for the honey, gaining acidity along with sweetness, and a 1,258-vote note confirms Trader Joe's cauliflower gnocchi works. The top comment by votes is an anecdote about the skillet in the photograph, not cooking advice.

name: Crockpot Rosemary Pork and Mushrooms with Shallots
ingredients:
1 tbs. (14 g) oil
1 cup (160 g) shallots, chopped
1 medium onion, sliced (we added to recipe)
2 Ibs. boneless pork shoulder, sliced into ½ inch slices (we used 2 bone-in thick chops)
2 cups (140 g) mushrooms, sliced
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) fresh rosemary
1 tsp. (6.0 g) salt
1 tsp. (2.3 g) black pepper
1 14 oz. (397 g) can diced tomatoes
directions:
Heat the oil in a skillet and brown the pork. Remove. and drain excess oil and place the pork in the Crock-Pot® Slow Cooker. Add the remaining ingredients and stir. Cover and cook on Low for 8 hours or on High for 4 hours.
Recommended Unit Size: 3 - 6 Quarts.
description:
2/24 Quite delicious. Made with two large bone-in pork chops totalling 1½ pounds. Seared pork chops on all sides. Once seared deglazed pan with ½ c white wine. Used a 14 oz. can of petit diced tomatoes. Added a large onion sliced, plus the shallots. Put sliced onions on the bottom of the crock pot, added seared chops, and then other ingredients mixed together. Cooked for 4 hours plus, starting with high for 1 hr, then reduced to low. The meat was tender and not dried out. Could easily double amounts in our crockpot.

11/21 Made with pork chops. Delicious.

1/25 Used bone-in pork chops and onions instead of shallots. Excellent!

used bone-in pork chops
and onions instead of
shallots Excellent!
notes:
Web summary (food.com, 5 reviews; star value not numerically shown). Posted by BeckyF as a family recipe that reminds her of her mother's cooking. Sliced pork shoulder goes into the slow cooker with shallots, mushrooms, rosemary and canned tomatoes and cooks unattended. The long, low heat is what makes it work: it renders the connective tissue in the shoulder so the slices turn tender, while the rosemary and tomato have time to melt into a sauce.

What readers report: Several cooks increased the rosemary well past the listed tablespoon, saying the dish reads bland at the written seasoning level. One substituted a bay leaf plus Worcestershire when out of rosemary. Doubling the mushrooms is a common tweak, and the usual serving suggestion is over rice or egg noodles.

Note on the source: NEEDS HUMAN EYE. I attached the same Food.com page on the assumption the two cards are the same dish entered twice; if the family's cookbook version is genuinely a separate rosemary-free recipe, this link is wrong and should be cleared.
