Web summary (food.com, 5 reviews (no star count displayed)). Posted by food.com member BeckyF as a slow-cooker supper that reminded her of her mother's cooking. Pork shoulder is cut into half-inch slices and browned first, then the fat is drained off before everything goes into the cooker, which is what keeps the finished braise from turning greasy over eight hours. Shallots, mushrooms, rosemary and a can of diced tomatoes supply all the liquid the pot needs.

What readers report: The recurring correction is that the rosemary is underdosed -- several cooks doubled or tripled it, and some used whole sprigs instead of chopped. Other repeat additions are garlic powder, Worcestershire, a bay leaf and extra mushrooms. It is commonly served over rice or egg noodles.

Web summary (food.com, 5 stars, 5 reviews). A plain slow-cooker braise: pork shoulder cut into half-inch slices, browned first in a skillet, then left in the cooker with shallots, sliced mushrooms, fresh rosemary and a can of diced tomatoes. Browning is the only stovetop step and it is worth doing, since nothing else in the pot will produce color or fond. The half-inch slicing of the shoulder matters too - it gives far more surface for the tomato and rosemary to work on than a whole roast would, and it cooks to shreddable in eight hours on low.

What readers report: The single loudest note across the reviews is that the dish as written is under-seasoned: reviewers double or even triple the rosemary, and many add garlic powder, a bay leaf, or Worcestershire. Crushed tomatoes in place of diced works, and extra mushrooms are a common and successful addition. Served over rice, egg noodles or mashed potatoes rather than on its own.

name: Crusty Baked Shells & Cauliflower
ingredients:
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
3/4 pound (340 g) medium shells
Good olive oil
2 1/2 pounds (1.1 kg) cauliflower, cut into small florets (1 large head)
3 tablespoons (10 g) roughly chopped fresh sage leaves
2 tablespoons (18 g) capers, drained
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) minced garlic (3 cloves)
1/2 teaspoon (1.0 g) grated lemon zest
1/4 teaspoon (0.5 g) crushed red pepper flakes
2 cups (226 g) freshly grated Italian Fontina Val d'Aosta cheese, lightly packed (10 ounces with rind)
1 cup (246 g) (8 ounces) fresh ricotta
1/2 cup (25 g) panko (Japanese bread flakes)
6 tablespoons (34 g) freshly grated Italian Pecorino cheese
2 tablespoons (7.5 g) minced fresh parsley leaves
directions:
Preheat the oven to 400 degrees.

Fill a large pot with water, add 2 tablespoons salt, and bring to a boil. Add the pasta and cook al dente, according to the instructions on the package. Since it will be baked later, don't overcook it! Drain and pour into a very large bowl.

Meanwhile, heat 3 tablespoons of olive oil in a large (12-inch) saute pan over medium-high heat, add half the cauliflower in one layer, and saute for 5 to 6 minutes, tossing occasionally, until the florets are lightly browned and tender. Pour the cauliflower, including the small bits, into the bowl with the pasta. Add 3 more tablespoons of oil to the saute pan, add the remaining cauliflower, cook until browned and tender, and add to the bowl.

Add the sage, capers, garlic, lemon zest, red pepper flakes, 2 teaspoons salt, and 1 teaspoon black pepper to the bowl and stir carefully. Stir in the Fontina. Transfer half of the mixture to a 10 x 13 x 2-inch rectangular baking dish. Spoon rounded tablespoons of ricotta on the pasta and spoon the remaining pasta mixture on top. Combine the panko, Pecorino, parsley, and 1 tablespoon of olive oil in a small bowl and sprinkle it evenly on top. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, until browned and crusty on top. Serve hot.
notes:
1/13/21 Made 1/2. Followed recipe closely. Lots of ingredients. Alan thought it was a bit bland. We agreed it was perfectly good.

Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten roasts cauliflower florets until browned before folding them through cooked shells with fried sage, capers, garlic, lemon zest and chilli flakes. Roasting rather than boiling the cauliflower is the point: it concentrates the flavour and keeps the bake from going watery. Fontina and ricotta make it creamy from the inside while a panko and Pecorino topping bakes to the crust the name promises, and the whole thing can be assembled ahead.

Note on the source: no comments or rating on Food Network page

name: Cumin-Baked Pork Chops
ingredients:
4 8-ounce (227 g) pork chops
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt
4 teaspoons (21 g) grainy Dijon mustard
2 tablespoons (13 g) crushed cumin seeds
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) cracked black pepper
1 teaspoon (4.5 g) canola oil
directions:
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees. Sprinkle the pork chops on both sides with salt, then brush each side with mustard. Rub the cumin and pepper into the mustard.

Heat the oil in a large cast-iron skillet over high heat. Add the pork chops and brown for 2 minutes on each side. Put the skillet in the oven and bake until the chops are just cooked through, about 12 minutes. Divide among 4 plates and serve.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (3,503)). A quick pork chop recipe that reached The Times in 1997 through Molly O'Neill's feature on cumin. The chops are coated and baked, and the recipe suggests crushing whole cumin seeds rather than using pre-ground for a bit of fresh texture, while allowing ground cumin as a substitute.

What readers report: Toughness is the recurring problem and brining is the top-voted fix (240 votes): about 45 minutes in roughly 3 tablespoons table salt per quart of water, then rinse, before proceeding. Several of the next most helpful notes rearrange the order of operations, since cooks report the mustard coating makes browning difficult: brown the chops first in a little oil for about 2 minutes a side, let them cool slightly, then apply the Dijon and crushed cumin before the oven (216 and 116 votes). A 216-vote cook used thick 1 1/4-inch bone-in chops and worked about 3/4 teaspoon ground cumin into the mustard. Ground cumin mixed straight into the mustard works fine (93 votes), a nonstick skillet prevents sticking with 10 minutes in the oven right for 8-ounce chops (69), and one cook skipped the searing entirely and still liked it.

name: Currant Scones
ingredients:
3½ cups (420 g) unbleached all-purpose flour
½ teaspoon (2.3 g) baking soda
1 tablespoon (12 g) baking powder
½ teaspoon (1.4 g) kosher salt
¾ cup (150 g) sugar
1 cup (227 g) (2 sticks) cold unsalted butter, cut into 1-inch cubes
1 cup (145 g) dried currants
¾ cup (178 g) heavy cream
¾ cup (182 g) buttermilk

Topping:
¼ cup (50 g) sugar
1 teaspoon (2.6 g) ground cinnamon
directions:
Preheat the oven to 375°F. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper or a baking mat.
Sift the flour, baking soda, and baking powder together into the bowl of a stand mixer or a large bowl.

If using a stand mixer, add the salt and sugar to the bowl and mix with the paddle attachment on low speed until combined. Add the butter and cut it in on low speed for about 4 minutes, or until it is the size of small peas. Mix in the currants. Make a well in the center and add the cream and buttermilk. Mix briefly, just until the ingredients come together; some loose flour should remain at the bottom of the bowl.

If making by hand, add the salt and sugar to the bowl and stir with a wooden spoon until combined. Add the butter and cut it in with a pastry cutter or 2 dinner knives until it is the size of small peas. Using the spoon, mix in the currants. Make a well in the center and add the cream and buttermilk. Mix briefly, just until the ingredients come together; some loose flour should remain at the bottom of the bowl.

Gently shape the dough into balls about 2¼ inches in diameter (they should have a rough, rocky exterior) and place them on the prepared pan about 2 inches apart.

For the topping, mix the sugar and cinnamon together in a small bowl. Sprinkle the mixture on the top of the scones. Bake on the middle rack of the oven for 15 to 17 minutes, or until light golden brown on top. Transfer the scones to a wire rack to cool.
description: Also great with chocolate bits or blueberries instead of currants.
notes:
Web summary (bakingbites.com). Nicole at Baking Bites reprints the currant scone from The Cheese Board: Collective Works, the cookbook of the Berkeley bakery collective, where it was the original bestseller at several hundred a day on a busy Saturday. Her framing is that a scone this rich in butter and cream is worth eating occasionally rather than apologizing for. The high fat and the pairing of heavy cream with buttermilk are what keep the crumb moist and tender while the outside stays slightly crisp.

What readers report: One reader found the dough far too wet to handle as written. Another asked about adjusting for a convection oven, having had them come out dry. No consensus correction offered by the author.

Note on the source: Page explicitly credits The Cheese Board: Collective Works, matching the collection's recorded source.

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

claude_opt.changes: A reader of this same recipe reported dry scones from a convection bake. With your convection ovens, drop the temp ~25F or check at 12-13 min instead of the full 15-17.

name: Curried Chicken Breast with Zucchini
ingredients:
4 boneless, skinless chicken breasts (about 1 1/4 pounds)
2 tablespoons (27 g) olive oil
Salt to taste if desired
Freshly ground pepper to taste
1 zucchini, about 1/2 pound (227 g), ends trimmed
2 teaspoons (4.0 g) curry powder
1 tablespoon (14 g) butter
2 tablespoons (20 g) finely chopped shallots
½ cup (120 g) chicken broth
2 tablespoons (30 g) heavy cream
directions:
Put chicken pieces in a bowl and add 1 tablespoon of the oil, salt and pepper.

Trim off the ends of the zucchini and cut it into 12 rounds, each about 1/2-inch thick. Add zucchini and curry powder to the chicken and blend well with the fingers to coat the pieces evenly.

Heat the remaining 1 tablespoon of oil in a heavy skillet and add the chicken pieces in one layer. Scatter the zucchini rounds between the chicken pieces, preferably in one layer. Cook over moderately high heat until chicken pieces are nicely browned on one side, about 3 minutes. Turn the chicken pieces and the zucchini rounds and cook over moderately low heat about 5 minutes.

Transfer chicken pieces and zucchini rounds to a warm serving dish.

Pour off the fat from the skillet and add the butter. Add shallots and cook, stirring, about 30 seconds. Add broth and cook until reduced to about 1/3 cup. Add cream, stir and bring to a boil. Return chicken and zucchini pieces to the sauce and turn the pieces in the sauce. Cook about 2 minutes.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (1,401)). A Pierre Franey 60-Minute Gourmet weeknight skillet dish. Boneless chicken breasts (thighs work too) and zucchini are tossed with curry powder, oil, salt and pepper and browned, then the pan is emptied and a fast sauce built from shallots, chicken broth, heavy cream, oil and butter; everything goes back in to warm through. Serve over rice, couscous or with mashed potatoes.

What readers report: The top note (295 votes) lists three worthwhile changes: fresh ginger with the shallots, dropping the butter and relying on pan juices, and a substitution for the cream. Doubling the sauce is a short, emphatic recommendation (65 votes) on the grounds that the sauce is what makes the dish. Coconut milk in place of heavy cream comes up more than once, served with couscous and cucumber raita, and a 54-vote cook added sweet potatoes and suggests mushrooms would work. One cook substituted vermouth when broth was not to hand. Cooks are generally heavy-handed with the curry powder and say they would go further; thick breasts need somewhat longer than the stated time. A 184-vote note is a fond reminiscence about Franey rather than a cooking tip.

name: Detroit-Style Pan Pizza
ingredients:
For the Dough:
300g bread flour (10.5 ounces; about 2 generous cups)
5g instant yeast (0.15 ounce; about 1 teaspoon), such as SAF Instant Yeast
9g salt (0.3 ounce; about 1 1/2 teaspoons table salt or 1 tablespoon Diamond Crystal kosher salt)
220g water (7.75 ounces; about 1 cup minus 1 1/2 teaspoons)
Extra-virgin olive oil, as needed
For the Sauce:
2 tablespoons (30ml) extra-virgin olive oil
3 medium cloves garlic, minced
2 teaspoons (about 5g) dried oregano
Dash red pepper flakes
1 (28-ounce; 800g) can high-quality crushed tomatoes
1 teaspoon (about 6g) granulated garlic powder
1 teaspoon (about 6g) granulated onion powder
1 tablespoon (about 15g) sugar
Kosher salt, to taste
To Finish:
12 ounces (340g) Brick cheese, cut into 1/2-inch cubes (see note)
12 ounces (340g) high-quality natural-casing pepperoni, such as Boar's Head or Vermont Smoke & Cure, cut into 1/8-inch slices (optional)
directions:
To Make the Dough in a Stand Mixer: Combine flour, yeast, and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with a dough hook attachment. Stir to combine, then add water. Mix on low speed until dough comes together into a rough ball, then shut off mixer and let rest for 10 minutes. Continue mixing at medium-low speed until dough forms a smooth, silky ball, about 10 minutes longer. (It should stick to the bottom of the bowl as it kneads rather than riding around the edges.) Remove dough hook, form dough into a tight ball, set in the bottom of the mixer bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and set aside in a warm place until dough has roughly doubled in volume, about 2 hours.

To Make the Dough in a Food Processor: Combine flour, yeast, and salt in the bowl of a food processor and pulse to combine. Add water, then turn on processor and process until dough forms a ball that rides around the bowl of the processor, about 30 seconds. Continue processing for 30 seconds longer. Transfer dough to a bowl, form a tight ball, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and set aside in a warm place until dough has roughly doubled in volume, about 2 hours.

To Make the Dough by Hand: Combine flour, yeast, and salt in a large bowl. Whisk to combine, then add water and stir with a wooden spoon until a rough ball of dough has formed. Set aside for 10 minutes. Turn dough out onto a countertop and knead until a smooth, silky ball has formed, about 10 minutes. Transfer dough to a bowl, form a tight ball, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and set aside in a warm place until dough has roughly doubled in volume, about 2 hours.

Pour a couple tablespoons olive oil in the bottom of a Detroit-style anodized aluminum pan or two 8- by 8-inch cake pans. (Split dough in half if using cake pans.) Transfer dough to pan(s) and turn to coat in oil. Press down on dough and spread it toward the edges. You won't be able to get it all the way to the edges; this is okay. Spread it as much as you can without tearing, then cover tightly in plastic and set aside for 30 minutes to allow dough to relax. Return to dough and stretch it out again. It should be able to reach the edges this time. If not, let it rest a little more and try again. To get the dough to stay in the corners, stretch it up beyond the corners so that it pulls back into place. Once dough is stretched, cover again and set aside while you make the sauce.

For the Sauce: Adjust oven rack to lowest position and preheat oven to 550°F (290°C), or as close to it as your oven gets. Heat 2 tablespoons (30ml) olive oil in a medium saucepan over medium heat until shimmering. Add minced garlic, oregano, and pepper flakes and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Add tomatoes, garlic powder, onion powder, and sugar. Bring to a simmer and cook until reduced to about 3 cups, about 30 minutes. Season to taste with salt.

To Form the Pizza: Press down on dough with your fingertips to remove any large air bubbles. Lay half of pepperoni (if using) evenly over face of dough. Top with cheese, spreading it evenly all the way to the very edges of the pan, then add remaining pepperoni. Spoon sauce over surface in 3 even rows. (You will need only about half the sauce—save the rest for another pizza.)

Transfer to oven and bake until edges are black and bubbly and exposed cheese on top is starting to lightly brown, 12 to 15 minutes. Transfer to a trivet or folded kitchen towel on countertop.

Run a thin metal spatula all the way around the edges of the pan to loosen the pizza. Carefully lift it out and slide it onto a cutting board. Cut pizza and serve.
description: 1/22 Made with Robert and Laura and their new purpose-built pans. Delicious. Used low-fat string cheese which ended up hard. We enjoyed the sauce. Steph liked the pepperoni.
notes:
Brick cheese is a high-fat aged cheese from Wisconsin. It has a buttery flavor and browns very well, giving Detroit pizza its distinct flavor. You can order it online from Amazon. If it's unavailable, you can use a combination of Jack or young cheddar and low-moisture mozzarella.

For best results, use a Detroit-style anodized aluminum pan. If you can't get your hands on that kind of pan, you can split the recipe into two square 8- by 8-inch cake pans.

Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.7 (59) / 250 Reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt spent months reverse-engineering the Detroit pie, which he describes as built upside down with cubed cheese laid directly on the dough and thick seasoned sauce striped over the top. He started from his no-knead pan pizza dough but found it produced too rustic and irregular a crumb, so he switched to a kneaded dough with a short autolyse; he settled on bread flour rather than Adam Kuban's all-purpose, which was too tender, at about 73 percent hydration rather than 75, and notes a food processor develops the gluten in about a minute. The signature lacy black cheese edge depends on Wisconsin brick cheese, whose very high butterfat drips down and fries the crust, giving the buttery flavor despite no butter in the recipe, and on a dark-surfaced Detroit pan, with a 50/50 mix of low-moisture mozzarella and Jack as the closest substitute and two 8-inch cake pans as a fallback. The sauce is simmered down and seasoned with both fresh and granulated garlic plus onion powder and sugar, and he lays pepperoni both under and over the cheese to get integrated flavor and crisp cupped edges.

What readers report: Burning is the most common failure. The top-voted note warns against the lowest rack on a first attempt, where 12 minutes at 550F burned the pizza; one cook following the recipe exactly at 500F fused the pizza to the pan. Others succeed on the middle rack at 550F for about 18 minutes, at 500F on the lowest rack for 18 minutes, or just under 12 minutes on a preheated half-inch baking steel, so oven position matters more than the stated time. A detailed reviewer says do not use pre-sliced Boar's Head pepperoni because the thin slices burn, a caveat present in the article but not the recipe; another argues 12 ounces of pepperoni is roughly double what one pie needs and oversalts against the brick cheese. Multiple cooks say the sauce weights are off and measure by volume instead. Jack and young cheddar, cast iron, and doubling across two pans are all reported to work.

Note on the source: 'Load More reviews' present, so only part of the 250 reviews is in the paste; the paste includes a 'Most helpful positive review' block and a 'Featured Tweaks' block with vote counts of 1 on several entries. Several comments end with 'Read More' and may be truncated. Questions about substitute-cheese proportions appear unanswered in the visible text.

directions: Mix sugar, eggs, salt, oil, and lemon extract in bowl with spoon until well blended. Then add dry ingredients and milk alternating, beginning and ending with dry ingredients. The dough will be quite soft. Pour into doughnut maker and drop into fat heated to 360-370 degrees. Turn as quickly as possible and then again to prevent bubbles.

claude_opt.changes: Frying temp (360-370°F) and multi-turn technique already match modern cake-doughnut guidance (King Arthur: 365-375°F, minimal handling, three flips). Nothing to change; clip a thermometer to the pot to hold temp steady.

name: Dry-Brined Turkey
ingredients:
1 12- to 16-pound (5.4-7.3 kg) turkey, preferably a heritage or pasture raised bird
Kosher salt
1 tablespoon (6.9 g) black pepper
10 sprigs fresh thyme
1/2 bunch flat-leaf parsley
2 small onions, halved
2 small apples, cored and halved
1/2 cup (114 g) unsalted butter, softened
2 cups (474 g) white wine (see tip)
directions:
Two days before serving, rinse turkey and pat dry. Rub all over with kosher salt, slipping salt under skin where possible and rubbing some into cavities. Use about 1 tablespoon per 4 pounds of bird.

Wrap bird in a large plastic bag and place in refrigerator. On second night, turn turkey over. A couple of hours before cooking, remove turkey from bag and pat dry. (There is no need to rinse it first.) Place in roasting pan and allow to come to room temperature.

Heat oven to 450 degrees. Sprinkle half the pepper into main cavity of turkey; add thyme, parsley, half the onions and half the apples. Truss legs with kitchen twine. Put remaining apples and onions in neck opening and tuck neck skin under bird.

Rub butter under breast skin and onto thigh meat. Sprinkle bird with remaining pepper.

Roast for 30 minutes. Remove turkey from oven, reduce heat to 350 degrees and cover breast of bird and wing tips with foil. Add 1 1/2 cups white wine (or use water) to bottom of roasting pan and roast bird for another two hours, depending on size; figure 12 minutes a pound for an unstuffed bird. Remove foil in last half-hour so breast browns.

When turkey has roasted for 2 hours, begin to test for doneness by inserting a meat thermometer (digital is best) into two places in thigh, making sure not to touch bone. It should be at about 160 degrees.

When roasting is done, tip turkey so interior juices run back into pan. Remove turkey to a separate baking sheet or serving platter, cover with foil and then a damp kitchen towel and allow to rest for at least 30 minutes before carving.

Pour fat and drippings from pan into a measuring cup. Deglaze pan with 1/2 cup white wine (or use broth) and pour that into same measuring cup. Fat and drippings can then be used to make gravy.
description: 11/24 Used 20 lb. frozen Butterball. Bought Wednesday, put directly in fridge to thaw, and dry brined Tuesday. Best turkey ever, by heneral acclaim. Started Tuesday. Spatchcocked by James after 1 day, and added some more salt especially under the skin. Roasting took over 3 hours. Didn’t bother with the veg. Did not stuff. Cook was excellent. Tender white and dark meat.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (5,843)). A Thanksgiving turkey that applies Judy Rodgers's Zuni Cafe method of salting birds well in advance instead of soaking them in liquid brine, which the recipe argues changes the texture of the meat. The payoff is crisp golden skin over moist meat. The bird needs two days in the refrigerator to season before it is roasted.

What readers report: The most-voted comment by a wide margin (1,692) is a challenge to the method rather than a report: if the point is to dry the skin, why wrap the bird in plastic in the fridge? A 701-vote note raises the same question from the air-drying angle, and many cooks resolve it by leaving the bird uncovered for the final stretch. A 253-vote note answers a common worry: after two days there is no salt left to rinse off because it has dissolved into the meat, so just blot the surface dry with paper towels. A 337-vote question about whether the bird can be stuffed under this method, and how to adjust the 12-minutes-per-pound guideline, goes largely unresolved. Among people reporting results, a 292-vote cook called it the best turkey they had made and confirmed 1/2 cup salt was right. Convection roasting is discussed.

name: Easy Coleslaw Dressing
ingredients:
½ cup (110 g) mayonnaise
2 tablespoons (25 g) white sugar
1 ½ tablespoons (23 g) lemon juice
1 tablespoon (15 g) vinegar (used cider vinegar)
½ teaspoon (1.1 g) ground black pepper (key ingredient)
¼ teaspoon (1.5 g) salt
directions: Whisk mayonnaise, sugar, lemon juice, vinegar, pepper, and salt together in a bowl until smooth and creamy. Toss with shredded cabbage and grated carrots.
description: 7/2021 - Excellent with purple cabbage and grated carrots as an accompaniment to fish tacos
notes:
Web summary (Allrecipes, 4.9 (2,790) / 2,337 reviews). GarlicQueen offers only a line: a creamy dressing built from things already in the cupboard, enough for a 14-ounce bag of slaw mix, usable right away or kept in the fridge. The Allrecipes editors (contributions by Melanie Fincher) expand on why the formula works, explaining that mayonnaise carries the creaminess, sugar balances the acidity of the vinegar and lemon, and the vinegar supplies the tang, with plain salt and pepper being all the seasoning it needs. They note the yield covers about 8 cups of shredded cabbage and carrot, the dressing keeps a week made ahead, and dressed slaw keeps about two days.

What readers report: The most helpful review (815 votes, raysmom) insists the dressing is right exactly as written and that the point is not to complicate it. The most common addition anyway is celery seed, about a quarter teaspoon; dry mustard, horseradish or Dijon for bite, and a spoonful of buttermilk with honey (307 helpful) are the other frequent tweaks. Half a teaspoon of black pepper reads as a lot, and while a few cut it back, those who followed it report it stays balanced. Sweeteners swap freely - honey, agave, coconut sugar - though one found an artificial sweetener would not emulsify and added crema. Apple cider vinegar is favoured. Making the dressing a day ahead is repeatedly said to improve it, and one salts and rinses the cabbage first to stop the slaw going watery. A recurring gripe: the recipe never says how much cabbage and carrot to use.

name: Easy Sole Meuniere
ingredients:
1/2 cup (60 g) all-purpose flour
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
4 fresh sole fillets, 3 to 4 ounces (85-113 g) each
6 tablespoons (85 g) unsalted butter
1 teaspoon (2.0 g) grated lemon zest
6 tablespoons (92 g) freshly squeezed lemon juice (3 lemons)
1 tablespoon (3.8 g) minced fresh parsley
directions:
Preheat the oven to 200 degrees F. Have 2 heat-proof dinner plates ready

Combine the flour, 2 teaspoons salt, and 1 teaspoon pepper in a large shallow plate. Pat the sole fillets dry with paper towels and sprinkle one side with salt.

Heat 3 tablespoons of butter in a large (12-inch) saute pan over medium heat until it starts to brown. Dredge 2 sole fillets in the seasoned flour on both sides and place them in the hot butter. Lower the heat to medium-low and cook for 2 minutes. Turn carefully with a metal spatula and cook for 2 minutes on the other side. While the second side cooks, add 1/2 teaspoon of lemon zest and 3 tablespoons of lemon juice to the pan. Carefully put the fish filets on the ovenproof plates and pour the sauce over them. Keep the cooked fillets warm in the oven while you repeat the process with the remaining 2 fillets. When they're done, add the cooked fillets to the plates in the oven. Sprinkle with the parsley, salt, and pepper and serve immediately.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten's take on the French classic dredges sole fillets in seasoned flour and cooks them fast in butter, then builds the sauce in the same pan by browning fresh butter and hitting it with lemon juice and zest. The flour coating is what gives the fish a thin crust and keeps the delicate fillets from falling apart when turned. Speed matters: sole is thin enough that it is done in a couple of minutes a side.

name: Einkorn Risotto with Fresh Herbs
ingredients:
1 ¼ cups (238 g) einkorn
6 cups (1.4 kg) vegetable or chicken broth
Salt to taste
2 tablespoons (27 g) extra-virgin olive oil
2 shallots, minced
2 garlic cloves, minced (optional)
½ cup (118 g) dry white wine, such as pinot grigio or Sauvignon blanc
2 tablespoons (6.0 g) chopped fresh marjoram
¼ cup (12 g) chopped chives
Black pepper
¼ cup (15 g) chopped fresh parsley
¼ cup (22 g) freshly grated Parmesan, more to taste (optional)
Walnut oil for drizzling, if not using Parmesan
directions:
Rinse einkorn and place in bowl. Cover with boiling water and let sit for 30 minutes, or cover with room-temperature water and leave overnight. Drain and reserve about 1/2 cup soaking water.

Place 1/4 cup soaked einkorn in food processor and pulse about 10 times to crack some of the grains.

Pour broth and reserved soaking water into a saucepan and bring to a simmer over medium heat. It should be lightly seasoned, as it will reduce while you slowly cook the einkorn.

Heat oil in a wide, heavy saucepan over medium heat. Add shallots and, if using, garlic and cook gently until shallots are just tender, 3 to 5 minutes. Add whole and cracked einkorn and stir over medium heat until grains dry out a bit and begin to crackle, a couple of minutes. Add wine and cook, stirring, until it evaporates.

Stir in enough simmering broth to just cover einkorn. The broth should bubble slowly. Cook, stirring often, until it is just about absorbed. Add another ladleful or two of broth and continue to cook in this fashion until einkorn is tender, about 25 minutes. It will still be chewy. Add marjoram, chives and pepper, and more broth if there is none visible in pan. Taste and adjust salt. Continue to simmer, stirring often, another 5 minutes.

Add another ladleful of broth to the pan and remove from heat. Stir in parsley and, if using, Parmesan. Mixture should be creamy. Serve right away in wide soup bowls, and top with walnut oil if desired.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (46)). A straightforward risotto made with einkorn rather than rice, flavoured with shallots, optional garlic and a generous quantity of marjoram, chives and parsley. The herbs carry enough flavour that the Parmesan finish can be left out, making it workable as a vegan main or side.

What readers report: There are only a few notes and none of them report actually cooking the dish, so there is no tested guidance on liquid, timing or texture. The entire discussion is about the grain itself: several readers ask what einkorn is and where to buy it, and the answers identify it as an ancient variety of wheat domesticated roughly 11,000 years ago, sold as einkorn wheat berries, stocked by health food stores and Whole Foods and available fresh at the Union Square Greenmarket in New York. One commenter notes that einkorn does contain gluten despite its reputation as a health grain, and suggests spelt or farro as workable substitutes in this recipe.

name: Farfalle With Salmon
ingredients:
1 lb. (454 g) farfalle
¼ c extra-virgin olive oil
1 t. (2.8 g) finely chopped garlic
¼ t. (0.5 g) red pepper flakes
2 c. (488 g) canned tomatoes, with their juice, roughly chopped
salt
½ lb. (227 g) fresh boned salmon filet, skin removed, cut into ½” dice
1 c. (238 g) heavy cream
2 T. (3.0 g) shredded fresh basil
directions:
1. Put the olive oil, garlic and red pepper flakes in a large skillet over a medium-high heat and cook until the garlic just begins to change color.

2. Add the tomatoes and season with salt. When the tomatoes begin to bubble, turn the heat down to medium-low and cook until the tomatoes have reduced and separated from the oil, about 20 minutes.

You can prepare the sauce ahead of time up to this point and refrigerate or even freeze it. 

3. Bring 4 quarts of water to a boil in a large saucepan or pot, add 1 T. of salt, and drop in the pasta all at once, stirring well.

4. Return the skillet with the tomato sauce to a medium-high heat and add the salmon, cream, and a pinch of salt. Cook over a medium-high heat until the cream has reduced by half. Stir in the basil and remove from the heat. 

5. When the pasta is cooked al dente, drain it and toss it with the sauce. Taste for salt and spiciness and serve at once.
description: Always a hit! We make it with hand rolled garganelli (like penne).
notes:
Web summary (app.ckbk.com). Giuliano Hazan notes that salmon is not a traditional Italian pasta fish, but that its richness takes well to the standard Italian treatment. He builds the sauce the way an Italian cook would if salmon were common there: a fresh tomato base started with garlic and olive oil, with the fish added late so it stays moist. The approach keeps the salmon from drying out while the tomato and chile carry the seasoning.

Note on the source: Correct author (Giuliano Hazan) and a near-identical title, but the page is on ckbk and mostly paywalled, so only a partial ingredient list was visible. It is from Thirty Minute Pasta; the family version may instead come from The Classic Pasta Cookbook. Same author either way.

makeahead: You can prepare the sauce ahead of time up to this point and refrigerate or even freeze it.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Cook's note already calls it a hit; poaching the diced salmon directly in the hot tomato-cream sauce, as Hazan does, is the standard technique for this dish.

name: Farro Salad with Beets, Greens and Feta
ingredients:
2 medium or 3 small beets (any color) with greens, the beets roasted, the greens stemmed and washed in two changes of water
1 cup (200 g) farro, soaked for one hour in water to cover and drained
Salt, preferably kosher salt, to taste
2 tablespoons (30 g) sherry vinegar
1 teaspoon (5.3 g) balsamic vinegar
1 small garlic clove, minced or pureed
1 teaspoon (5.2 g) Dijon mustard
½ cup (108 g) extra virgin olive oil (may substitute 1 to 2 tablespoons walnut oil for 1 to 2 tablespoons olive oil)
½ cup (58 g) broken walnut pieces
2 ounces (57 g) feta or goat cheese, crumbled (more if desired for garnish)
¼ cup (15 g) chopped fresh herbs, such as parsley, tarragon, marjoram, chives, mint
directions:
Bring 2 quarts water to a boil in a medium saucepan. Fill a bowl with ice water. When the water comes to a boil, add salt to taste and the greens. Blanch for two minutes, and transfer to the ice water. Allow to cool for a few minutes, then drain and squeeze out excess water. Chop coarsely and set aside.

Bring the water back to a boil, and add the farro. Reduce the heat, cover and simmer 45 minutes, stirring from time to time, or until the farro is tender. Remove from the heat and allow the grains to swell in the cooking water for 10 minutes, then drain.

While the farro is cooking, make the vinaigrette. Whisk together the vinegars, salt, garlic and mustard. Whisk in the oil(s). Add to the farro. Peel and dice the beets and add, along with the beet greens, feta or goat cheese, herbs and walnuts. Toss together, and serve warm or room temperature with a little more cheese sprinkled over the top if you wish.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (1,663)). Farro is sturdy and nutty enough to carry assertive partners like beets, their greens and salty feta, and the grain turns it into a main course; poached or roasted chicken is suggested if more substance is wanted. The red beets tint the farro pink, and the colour deepens over hours, so the salad can be assembled a day ahead and travels well for picnics. The instruction that matters most is to soak the grain for an hour and cook it until genuinely tender, or the result is chewy.

What readers report: The clearest gap cooks point out (74 votes) is that the headnote refers to roasted beets while the recipe steps never say to roast them, leaving the beet method to the cook. Many answer that themselves by avoiding the oven: a 35-vote note pressure-cooked golden beets for 15 to 30 minutes on high rather than roasting in July, and another popular note used a comparable stovetop shortcut. Goat cheese is confirmed as an equal substitute for feta (82 votes), and a 45-vote cook rebuilt the dish gluten-free with Lentils du Puy in place of farro plus lightly steamed lacinato kale, parsley and chives. A 57-vote note says the oil quantity is too high. Carrots and radishes are common additions.

name: Farro Tabbouleh with Feta
ingredients:
2 1/2 cups (500 g) pearled farro (1 pound)
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 hothouse cucumbers, unpeeled, halved, seeded, and 1/2-inch diced
1 (15-ounce) can chickpeas, drained and rinsed
8 scallions, green and white parts, thinly sliced diagonally

directions:

name: Fast French Onion Soup
ingredients:
1 tablespoon (13 g) sugar
5 pounds (2.3 kg) yellow onions, thinly sliced
2 tablespoons (28 g) unsalted butter
1/4 teaspoon (1.1 g) baking soda
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) kosher salt, plus more as needed
1/2 cup (118 g) water
1/4 cup (59 g) dry sherry
6 cups (1.4 kg) homemade or low-sodium chicken broth
2 bay leaves
6 to 8 sprigs fresh thyme
Freshly ground black pepper
1 baguette, sliced 1-inch thick and toasted
8 ounces (227 g) Gruyère or Swiss cheese, grated
directions:
Pour the sugar into a large Dutch oven and cook over medium-high heat, swirling the pot gently as the sugar melts, until it is completely liquid and a golden-brown caramel. Add the onions and cook, stirring with a wooden spoon and tossing constantly until they are evenly coated in the caramel, about 30 seconds. Add the butter, baking soda and 2 teaspoons salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions are a light golden brown and a brown coating has started to build up on the bottom of the pot, about 10 minutes.

Add 2 tablespoons water and scrape the browned coating from the bottom of the pot. Shake the pot to distribute the onions evenly over the bottom and cook, shaking occasionally, until the liquid evaporates and the browned coating starts to build up again, about 5 minutes. Add 2 more tablespoons water and repeat, allowing the coating to build up and scraping it off, then repeat two more times. (Reduce the heat as needed if the coating is burning and turning black.) By this point, the onions should be deep brown. If not, continue deglazing and stirring until the deep brown color is reached.

Add the sherry, chicken broth, bay leaves and thyme, bring to a boil, and reduce the heat to low, so the soup is at a gentle simmer. Simmer, uncovered, until the liquid is deeply flavored and slightly reduced, about 15 minutes. Season to taste with salt and pepper. Discard the bay leaves and thyme.

To serve, heat the broiler. Ladle the soup into four broiler-proof bowls. Float 1 or 2 bread slices on top of each bowl and cover with the grated cheese. Broil until the cheese is melted, bubbly and golden brown in spots. Serve immediately.
notes:
Web summary (washingtonpost.com). A Washington Post version of the classic that borrows J. Kenji Lopez-Alt's shortcut for caramelizing onions: sugar, baking soda and higher heat to compress what is normally a long process. The Post's testers rated it the richest of the several versions they tried, dark enough to pass for homemade beef broth even though it is built on store-bought chicken broth. If the serving bowls are not broiler-safe, the cheese-topped bread can be broiled separately on a sheet pan and floated on top. A published correction notes the recipe originally called for baking powder; both work, but soda caramelizes faster.

name: Fettuccine Alfredo — Elaine’s
ingredients:

1 t. (5.2 g) Dijon mustard
directions:
Cook fettuccine. Meanwhile peel shrimp. Cut zucchini and carrots in to 1x1/4 inch strips. Heat 2 T. butter in large skillet over medium heat and saute shrimp until no longer transparent. Remove from heat. 

Saute zucchini, carrots, and onions until tender crisp. Add garlic and basil and saute a few minutes more. Add shrimp. When past done add to veggies and shrimp. Add 2 T. butter and parmesan cheese.

claude_opt.changes: Shrimp is cooked fully, removed, then reheated with the pasta and veggies — the classic cause of rubbery shrimp. Pull it slightly underdone, still a touch translucent, so the reheating finishes it gently.

name: Fettuccine with Asparagus and Smoked Salmon
ingredients:
½ pound (227 g) fresh asparagus, medium thickness
Salt
1 tablespoon (14 g) butter
½ tablespoon (5.0 g) minced shallots
1 cup (238 g) heavy cream
4 ounces (113 g) smoked salmon sliced 1/4-inch thick
Freshly ground black pepper
1 teaspoon (5.1 g) fresh lemon juice
9 to 10 ounces (255-284 g) fresh green fettuccine noodles
2 tablespoons (5.6 g) minced fresh dill
directions:
Snap off the ends of the asparagus where they break naturally and peel the stalks. Cut the asparagus on a slant to pieces about an inch long.

Steam the asparagus until they are just barely tender and still bright green, about three minutes. Rinse under cold water, drain well on paper towels and set aside.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil for the pasta.

While the water is coming to a boil, melt the butter in a large heavy skillet. Add the shallots and saute until soft but not brown. Stir in the cream and simmer about five minutes, until the cream has thickened somewhat.

Cut the salmon into slivers, add it to the cream and remove the skillet from the heat. Season with pepper and lemon juice. Add the asparagus.

When the pot of water is boiling, add the fettuccine, stir it once or twice, then cook two to three minutes after the water has returned to a boil. Drain well.

Briefly reheat the sauce. Transfer the fettuccine to a warm serving bowl, pour the sauce over it and toss. Sprinkle with dill and serve.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (2,790)). A quick, slightly dressy pasta from a Times column on vegetables and pasta: fettuccine, asparagus and smoked salmon bound in a shallot cream sauce, done in well under an hour.

What readers report: The top note by a clear margin (408 votes) saves a pan by dropping the asparagus into the pasta water for the last two minutes of cooking rather than boiling it separately, and suggests spring onion alongside or instead of the dill; a 90-vote cook confirms this works and says the cold-water shock can be skipped too. A 320-vote cook instead sautes the asparagus with the butter and shallots and reports success with squid-ink linguine and canned smoked salmon. Another practical tip (57 votes) is to skip peeling the stalks and simply steam the thicker end pieces briefly before adding the tips. A 102-vote note drops the cream entirely for a shallot-and-dill olive oil and still rates it highly. One cook found the sauce thinner than expected.

name: Fettuccine with Sausage and Fried Sage
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) fettuccine
1 pound (454 g) hot Italian sausage
About 24 sage leaves
3 to 4 tablespoons (40-54 g) olive oil
1 clove garlic, minced
About 1 cup (238 g) heavy cream
Coarse sea salt and freshly ground pepper to taste
Freshly grated Reggiano Parmesan
directions:
Bring four quarts of water to a boil for the fettuccine.

Fry the sage leaves in the olive oil in a skillet until they are crisp. Drain them on paper towels, leaving the oil in the skillet.

Chop the sausages in chunks and sauté them in the oil until the pieces are browned, adding the garlic toward the end so that it gets golden but not burned. Remove the sausage from the pan and set aside. Meanwhile, cook fettuccine until al dente.

Pour off the fat from the skillet (preserving the garlic) and add the cream. Bring it to a boil, scrape up cooking juices and return the sausage to heat through. Season with salt and pepper, to taste.

Drain the pasta and put it in a heated serving bowl. Pour the sauce on top. Toss and sprinkle with sage leaves. Serve with Parmesan passed separately at the table.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (617)). From a 1997 Moira Hodgson piece arguing that sage deserves more than a Thanksgiving role. Frying the leaves in oil or butter, as Italians do, softens their strong earthy character to a trace. The crisped leaves come out of the pan, then a pound of hot Italian sausage and garlic brown in the flavoured oil, cream deglazes the pan, and the whole thing is tossed with fettuccine and Parmesan with the sage scattered over. About 30 minutes.

What readers report: A small comment set with modest vote counts. The most-endorsed change (29 votes) is to squeeze the sausage out of its casings and crumble it while frying rather than cutting it into chunks, and a related tip (12 votes) is to slit the casings lengthwise while the sausages are still very cold from thawing, which makes them come away cleanly. Quantity is the other recurring note (14 votes): the sauce as written barely coats a full pound of fettuccine, so either increase the cream or use less pasta. One cook found the dish bland made as written and plans considerably more garlic plus red-pepper flakes next time. Dried sage sprinkled into the oil is reported as an acceptable fallback when fresh is unavailable.

Note on the source: only 45 comments, low vote counts

claude_opt.changes: Squeeze sausage from its casings and crumble while browning instead of cutting chunks — better coverage and sear, the most-endorsed reader fix. Add a splash more cream; readers found the sauce too thin for a full pound of pasta.

name: Financier - Almond Brown Butter Cakes
ingredients:
Cakes:
3 oz. (85 g) almond flour (finely ground)
4 oz. (113 g) granulated sugar
2 T. (15 g) flour (AP)
1/8 t. (0.8 g) salt
5 T. (71 g) unsalted butter
1/3 c. (81 g) of egg whites (~3 eggs)

Toppings:
toasted almonds
sliced fruit
berries
chocolate chunks (1/2")
directions: Preheat oven to 375 degrees. Whisk flours, sugar and salt together in a bowl.  Brown butter in fry pan swirling over medium heat for 1-3 minutes making sure it toasts but does not burn. Milk solids will darken. Transfer to a heat proof bowl to cool. You can leave behind some of the dark bits. Separate egg whites and discard yolks. Add whites to the dry mixture and blend into a paste (getting the lumps out) with a spatula. Add cooled browned butter (including some browned bits is just fine) and mix until smooth. Prepare mini muffin pans (24 count) by spraying with baking spray with flour. Four particles allow cakes to rise slowly and the top will come out flat. Portion batter into prepared muffin pan filling half full. Add special toppings if desired: toasted almonds, 1/2" semi-sweet chocolate chunks, fruit slices, or berries. Plain is fine too! Bake in 375 degree oven for 14 minutes turning pan once for an even bake. Remove from oven and immediately invert over rack and flip right side up by hand. Allow cakes to cool completely. Crust will harden, but inside will remain soft. Great served after dinner with a cup of coffee or tea!
notes:
Web summary (americastestkitchen.com, 4.5 stars (205 ratings)). Lan Lam's take on the French mini cake, aimed at a crisp caramelized shell around a tender, moist centre. Browned butter supplies the nutty depth that defines a financier, while almond flour keeps the crumb soft rather than cakey. She calls for flour-based baking spray in the molds so the batter climbs evenly and the tops bake flat instead of doming.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS - the page carries a 4.5-star average from 205 ratings but no reader comment text was retrievable.

Note on the source: Family card names America's Test Kitchen and the ATK title matches (ATK spells it 'Browned'). ATK also has a small-batch variant at https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/16479-small-batch-financiers-almond-browned-butter-cakes if the family yield is smaller.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Ratio and immediate-unmolding technique already match the most highly-rated versions elsewhere (Mama Gourmand, ATK); browned-butter depth and almond flour crumb are already dialed in.

name: Fish Soup
ingredients:
3 tablespoons (40 g) olive oil
¼ cup (40 g) finely chopped onion
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) finely chopped garlic
½ cup (74 g) chopped green pepper or red
½ cup (44 g) chopped leeks, optional
½ cup (64 g) finely chopped carrots
1 hot red pepper, crumbled 
1 bay leaf
2 teaspoons (2.3 g) fresh thyme sprigs, or
½ teaspoon (0.5 g) dried thyme 
1 cup (237 g) dry white wine
1 cup chopped fresh or canned tomatoes
⅓ pound (151 g) potatoes 
1 cup (237 g) water 
1¼ pounds (567 g) white-fleshed, non-oily fish such as cod, tilefish, or a combination of two or more fish, filleted and cut into one-and-one-half inch cubes
½ pint bay scallops, we omit
1 cup (238 g) heavy cream
¼ cup (15 g) finely chopped fresh parsley
Salt and freshly ground pepper
16 toasted croutons (see recipe).
directions:
1. Heat the oil in a kettle and add the onion, garlic, green or red pepper, leeks, and carrots. Cook, stirring often, until the onions are wilted.
2. Add the crumbled red pepper, bay leaf, thyme, wine, and tomatoes. Bring to the boil.
3. Peel the potatoes and cut them into half-inch cubes. Drop into cold water briefly. Drain. Add the potatoes to the soup.
4. Cover closely and cook 10 minutes.
5. Add the water. Uncover and cook 5 minutes.
6. Add the fish and scallops and simmer 2 or 3 minutes. Do not overcook or the fish will fall apart. Add the cream and bring to the boil. The soup must be piping hot.
7. Gently stir in the parsley and add salt and pepper to taste. Add one or two croutons to each serving and serve the remainder on the side.
Yield: Four servings.
description: Excellent. Our Christmas eve standard. 3X recipe for 7 people is ample. We cook the potatoes separately. Otherwise they stay hard.

claude_opt.changes: Cooks' note already fixes the recipe's real flaw (cook potatoes separately). Franey's timing and method otherwise match modern versions of this dish closely; nothing else here is worth changing.

name: Fish Tacos
ingredients:
2 medium tomatoes, seeded and finely chopped
1 small red onion, peeled and finely chopped
1 clove garlic, minced
½ cup (23 g) roughly chopped cilantro
1 jalapeño, halved lengthwise, seeded and cut crosswise into half moons (optional)
¼ cup (55 g) mayonnaise
½ cup (115 g) sour cream
2 limes, 1 halved and 1 cut into wedges
Kosher salt
Freshly ground black pepper
1 tablespoon (6.9 g) canned chipotle pepper, finely chopped (optional)
½ cup (60 g) flour, preferably Wondra or other fine-milled flour
1 ½ teaspoons (3.9 g) chili powder
½ cup (122 g) milk
¼ cup (54 g) peanut oil, plus a splash more for greasing pan
Pat of butter
1 pound (454 g) flounder or any firm white-fleshed fish, cut across the grain of the flesh into strips about 1/2 inch wide by 3 inches long
12 6-inch fresh corn tortillas
2 cups (178 g) shredded green cabbage
A saucy hot sauce, like Tapatio or Frank’s
directions:
In a medium bowl, combine the tomatoes, onion, garlic, cilantro and jalapeño (if using).

In a small bowl, whisk the mayonnaise and sour cream until combined. Season to taste with the halved lime, salt, pepper and chipotle (if using).

In a medium bowl, mix together the flour, chili powder and 1 1/2 teaspoons each of kosher salt and black pepper. Pour the milk into another medium bowl, and place the fish into it.

Pour 1/4 cup of the peanut oil into a 12-inch frying pan and place over medium-high heat until it shimmers and is about to smoke. Remove the fish pieces from the milk bath and dredge them lightly through the flour mixture, shaking to remove excess. Add the butter to the pan. Place some fish pieces in the oil, without crowding them, and cook until deep golden brown on one side, 3 to 4 minutes. Turn carefully and cook for 1 minute more. Remove to a warmed, paper-towel-lined plate and sprinkle with salt. Repeat with the remaining fish.

Meanwhile, lightly grease a skillet with a drizzle of oil and set over medium heat. Heat the tortillas, one or two at a time, until they are soft and hot. Keep them warm, wrapped in a dish towel.

Fill each tortilla with 3 pieces of fish, browned side up, followed by tomato salsa and a pinch of cabbage. Drizzle with the cream sauce. Serve 2 to 3 tacos per person, with lime wedges and hot sauce on the side.
description:
9/18 Really good with 1/2 lb. of halibut, 1/2 recipe.
Peach salsa 1/2 recipe: 1 peach, diced and sauteed, 1/8 c. red onion chopped. 1/4 jalapeno chopped, 1/8 c. chopped cilantro, 1 juice of one lime, 1/2 tsp sugar, salt.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (9,599)). Sam Sifton's Baja-style fish tacos: fish fried in strips, served on warm corn tortillas with a simple salsa, shredded cabbage, plenty of lime and a cream sauce that can be sharpened with chopped chipotle. The recipe presents itself as no harder than making burgers. Sifton developed it after working with a chef who specialises in fish, and drew on the version at El Siete Mares on Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles, which closed in 2020.

What readers report: The top note by a wide margin (1,063 votes) skips frying altogether: brush the fish strips with oil, roll them lightly in panko and bake at 400 degrees. A 420-vote cook does something similar with tilapia, brushing with olive oil and chipotle and baking about 12 minutes at 350. Greek yogurt in place of sour cream in the chipotle sauce is a popular and well-liked substitution (596 votes), and the sauce draws more praise than any other component. A 337-vote note from Ensenada, Baja California adds a traditional garnish: sliced onion marinated 24 hours in olive oil with a teaspoon of dried oregano. Several cooks (270 votes) treat the recipe as a build-your-own buffet with assorted tortillas and toppings, and multiple notes warn the prep chopping takes real time.
