name: Fish Tacos with Creamy Chipotle Cabbage Slaw
ingredients:
For the slaw:
4 cups (356 g) shredded green cabbage (1 medium to large cabbage)
1 cup (89 g) shredded purple cabbage
2 medium carrots, shredded
1 small red onion, very thinly sliced
3 large scallions (white and light green parts), thinly sliced
1 jalapeño, seeded and minced
1/2 cup (110 g) store-bought or homemade mayonnaise
1/2 cup (122 g) plain Greek yogurt (preferably full fat) or sour cream
1/4 cup (60 g) fresh lime juice, or 1/8 cup fresh lime juice plus 1/8 cup Champagne vinegar, white wine vinegar, or apple cider vinegar
2 tablespoons (25 g) granulated sugar or honey
1 teaspoon (2.1 g) ground cumin (optional)
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) chipotle powder (optional)
Sea salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
For the fish tacos:
1/3 cup (40 g) all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) chipotle powder
1 teaspoon (5.5 g) finely ground sea salt, or to taste
1 pound (454 g) mild white fish (such as cod, halibut, or tilapia), cut into 4 fillets
3 tablespoons (40 g) olive oil
For the assembly:
8 small corn tortillas, warmed (or 16 tortillas if you want to be authentic)
Cilantro leaves for garnish (optional)
directions:
Make the slaw

Combine the cabbages, carrots, onion, scallions, and jalapeño in a large bowl.

In a medium bowl, whisk the mayonnaise, yogurt or sour cream, lime juice or lime juice and vinegar, sugar or honey, and the cumin and chipotle powder, if using, until smooth and creamy.

Pour the dressing over the cabbage mixture and toss to combine. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Cover and refrigerate for at least 20 minutes before serving and up to 2 days. (If refrigerating for more than an hour or so, drain off any liquid that pools at the bottom of the bowl just prior to serving.)

Make the fish tacos

In a shallow bowl, combine the flour, chipotle powder, and 1 teaspoon salt, or to taste. Pat each fish fillet dry and lightly dredge in the flour mixture, shaking off any excess flour.

Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a skillet over medium heat and place 2 fillets at a time in the pan. Gently fry for 3 to 6 minutes, until the underside of the fish turns opaque. Use a spatula to flip the fillets and cook until opaque throughout. Place on a paper towel-lined plate, drain the remaining oil from the pan, and repeat with 1 tablespoon oil and the remaining 2 fillets.

To serve, for each fish fillet, heat tortillas in a clean skillet in batches with the 1 remaining tablespoon oil, flipping them once, then place them on a plate.

Assemble the tacos

Cut each fillet in half and divide the fish evenly among the tortillas. Toss the slaw to recombine and then add a spoonful to each taco along with some cilantro, if desired. (Chances are you will have excess slaw. Just cover it and stash it in the fridge and serve it alongside pulled pork, grilled chicken, or just about anything.)

GLUTEN-FREE FISH TACOS VARIATION

Simply skip the step where you dredge the fish in flour and instead sprinkle the fish with the chipotle powder and salt.
notes:
Web summary (leitesculinaria.com, 4.92 out of 5 stars, 12 votes). David Leite pairs mild white fish, dusted in flour spiked with chipotle powder and pan-fried, with a slaw dressed in mayonnaise and Greek yogurt rather than a vinaigrette. The cool, acidic slaw is doing the work of cutting the fried fish, while the chipotle brings smoke without the heat overwhelming a delicate fillet. Everything is assembled in warmed corn tortillas with cilantro.

What readers report: Testers kept coming back to the slaw rather than the fish: several rate it the best part of the recipe and report using it with roasted pork or simply as a side salad. The most practical correction is that the slaw throws off a lot of liquid once refrigerated, so it needs draining before it goes into a taco or the tortilla goes soggy. On seasoning, readers push back on the recipe treating the cumin and chipotle powder as optional, saying the slaw is bland without them. Two assembly notes recur: warm the corn tortillas properly or they crack, and double them up per taco for structure. One tester missed the sauteed onions and peppers from an earlier version of the recipe. The slaw keeps well as a leftover.

ahead: Cover and refrigerate for at least 20 minutes before serving and up to 2 days.

claude_opt.changes: Don't treat the cumin and chipotle powder in the slaw as optional — readers report it's bland without them. Double the corn tortillas per taco; a single one won't hold without cracking.

name: Flour and Corn Tortillas All in One
ingredients:
1 CUP (120 g) ALL-PURPOSE FLOUR
1 CUP (154 g) MASA HARINA CORN FLOUR
1 TEASPOON (2.8 g) KOSHER SALT
TEASPOON BAKING POWDER
1/3
CUP SHORTENING MELTED
1¼ CUPS (296 g) WARM WATER
KITCHEN ESSENTIALS FOR THIS DISH
A COMAL
A TORTILLA WARMER
directions:
Combine the dry ingredients in a large bowl.

Melt the shortening. Add the warm water to the melted shortening.

Gradually mix the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients until dough forms. Transfer the dough to a flat surface and knead for a few minutes. It should feel moist and slightly tacky. If it feels dry, work in a little more water, 1 tablespoon at a time.

Divide dough into 16 equal dough balls and transfer to a plastic storage bag. Let sit for 20 minutes.

Preheat comal or griddle pan to medium heat for 5 minutes. Before rolling out the dough ball, roll it in the palm of your hands and flatten slightly. Place on a lightly floured flat work surface, and roll out to about 5 inches. Flip and turn as needed using minimal flour to roll out. The more flour you add, the less fluffy the tortilla will be.

Cook on hot surface for 1-2 minutes, turning after tortilla begins to bubble up and inflate. You should have medium to dark brown spots on the tortillas. If they are too black, adjust the heat to a slightly lower temperature.

Transfer cooked tortillas to a tortilla warmer or a covered pot lined with a kitchen towel. The steam created will yield an extra soft tortilla. Cool tortillas completely before storing in a plastic storage bag.

Chef Notes

Freshly made tortillas can be stored at room temperature for 2 days. After that they can be refrigerated for a week. The older the tortillas get, the more dried out they will become.
notes: Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

makeahead: Freshly made tortillas can be stored at room temperature for 2 days.

claude_opt.changes: King Arthur's well-tested 50/50 version rests dough balls 30 minutes before rolling versus this recipe's 20; longer rest relaxes gluten and reduces spring-back so rounds roll thinner without tearing.

name: Fluffy Mashed Potatoes
ingredients:
3 pounds (1.4 kg) russet potatoes
1 cup (244 g) whole milk, plus more as needed
½ cup (114 g) cold salted butter, cut into pats
Salt
Freshly ground white or black pepper
¼ cup (60 g) heavy cream, plus more as needed (optional)
directions:
Prepare a steamer: Arrange an insert or basket (or a large colander, if you have neither) in a large pot, and add enough water to come just below the base of the steamer. Bring water to a boil over medium-high heat.

Rinse potatoes well, then peel. Rinse again, then cut into 1-inch chunks. Spread evenly in the steamer, cover, reduce heat to medium and steam until the potatoes are very tender, 20 to 25 minutes. A fork should slide easily into a piece and break it without effort. Turn off the stove, carefully remove the steamer insert and drain the water from the pot. Pour the potatoes back into the pot and spread evenly.

Let the potatoes stand until their surfaces are dry, about 3 minutes. Meanwhile, heat the milk in a small saucepan over medium-high until steaming, then keep warm over low. Set the potatoes over low heat and mash thoroughly with a dinner fork. Add about one-quarter of the milk and mash until the milk is incorporated.

Scatter the butter evenly over the potatoes and mash in until all traces of butter disappear. Add half of the remaining milk and mash to incorporate, then add the rest of the milk and gently whip until smooth, circling the fork as if beating eggs. If you don’t want your mashed potatoes so thick, beat in more milk. Sprinkle with salt and pepper, taste, and season more if you’d like.

Serve immediately, keep warm over low heat for up to 1 hour, or transfer to airtight containers and refrigerate for up to 2 days. Mashed potatoes thicken as they cool, so they need cream to regain the right consistency. If kept warm, gently mash in heavy cream until smooth and loose again, adding more if you’d like. If cold, heat the cream in a large pot until steaming, then add the potatoes. Gently mash and whip, adding more cream as needed, until heated through and fluffy. Season to taste again before serving.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (1,519)). The method here rests on two choices: Russet Burbank baking potatoes, which mash without turning gluey, and steaming rather than boiling, so the potatoes are not waterlogged and keep their faintly sweet flavour. Seasoning is held to the very end for the same reason. A ricer is recommended for the smoothest texture, pressing the steamed potatoes straight back into the pot before butter and milk are folded in gently.

What readers report: Make-ahead reheating dominates the notes, starting with the most-voted comment (309) asking how to do it. The two best answers follow: a 229-vote note bakes them in the oven after pricking the surface with a fork and dotting with butter, and a 196-vote catering trick spreads them in an ovenproof dish, pours cream over, covers with foil and warms at 300 degrees until hot. A 59-vote cook reheats in a crockpot and says it has never failed over several Thanksgivings. The main challenge to the method is a 147-vote note preferring an Instant Pot, pressure cooking peeled chunks for 4 to 5 minutes on a steamer insert so they never sit in water. Folding finely grated Gruyere into the finished potatoes is a well-liked addition (108).

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Steaming rather than boiling and seasoning at the very end are already the tested method here; the reader notes are about reheating leftovers, not the base recipe.

name: Fluffy Omelet
ingredients:
4 eggs, separated
2 T. (30 g) water
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
dash pepper
2 T. (15 g) flour
1 T. (14 g) butter or oil
1 can Campbell's tomato soup
directions:
Preheat oven to 300.
1. Separate eggs. Beat whites until frothy. Add water and salt. Beat until stiff but not dry. Beat flour, yolks, and pepper until thick and lemon-colored. Fold into whites.
2.  Heat butter in 10" skillet. When fat is hot enough to make a drop of water sizzle, pour in omelet mixture. Level gently, leaving slightly higher around the edge.
3. Cook over low heat till puffy and lightly browned on bottom, about 5 minutes. 
4. Finish in oven for 8-10 minutes. 
5. Fold in half to serve.

claude_opt.changes: 300°F is cooler than the modern puffy-omelet standard (~350°F); raise to 325-350°F so the center fully sets in the same 8-10 minute finish, rather than staying wet under the hot soup topping.

name: Foolproof Pan Pizza
ingredients:
400g bread flour (14 ounces; about 2 1/2 cups), plus more for dusting
10g kosher salt (0.35 ounces; about 2 teaspoons), plus more for sprinkling
4g instant yeast (0.15 ounces; about 1 teaspoon), such as SAF Instant Yeast
300g (kenji says 275g) water (9.5 ounces; about 1 cup plus 3 tablespoons)
8g extra-virgin olive oil (0.25 ounces; about 2 teaspoons), plus more to coat pans and for drizzling
1 1/2 cups (368 g) pizza sauce, such as our New York–style pizza sauce
12 ounces (340 g) grated full-fat, low moisture (dry) mozzarella cheese (see note)
Toppings as desired
Small handful torn fresh basil leaves (optional)
2 ounces (57 g) grated Parmesan or Pecorino Romano cheese (optional)
directions:
Combine flour, salt, yeast, water, and oil in a large bowl. Mix with hands or a wooden spoon until no dry flour remains. (The bowl should be at least 4 to 6 times the volume of the dough to account for rising.)

Cover bowl tightly with plastic wrap, making sure that the edges are well sealed, then let rest at cool room temperature (no warmer than 75°F) for at least 8 hours and up to 24. Dough should rise dramatically and fill bowl. In a hot kitchen, the dough may overproof near the end of that range.

Sprinkle top of dough lightly with flour, then transfer it to a well-floured work surface. Divide dough into 2 pieces and form each into a ball by holding it with well-floured hands and tucking the dough underneath itself, rotating it until it forms a tight ball.

Pour 1 to 2 tablespoons oil in the bottom of two 10-inch cast iron skillets or round cake pans (see note). Place 1 ball of dough in each pan and turn to coat evenly with oil. Using a flat palm, press dough around the pan, flattening it slightly and spreading oil around the entire bottom and edges of the pan. Cover tightly with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature for 2 hours (at room temperatures above 75°F, the dough may require less time to rise; at temperatures below 65°F/18°C deg;F, it may require more time). After the first hour, adjust an oven rack to the middle position and preheat oven to 550°F (290°C).

After 2 hours, dough should be mostly filling the pan up to the edges. Use your fingertips to press it around until it fills in every corner, popping any large bubbles that appear. Lift up one edge of the dough to let any air bubbles underneath escape, then repeat, moving around the dough until there are no air bubbles left underneath and the dough is evenly spread around the pan.

Top each round of dough with 3/4 cup sauce, spreading sauce to the very edge with the back of a spoon. Sprinkle evenly with mozzarella cheese, all the way to the edges. Season with salt. Add other toppings as desired. Drizzle with olive oil and scatter a few basil leaves over the top of each pizza, if desired.

Transfer pan to oven and bake until top is golden brown and bubbly and bottom is golden brown and crisp when you lift it with a thin spatula, 12 to 15 minutes. Immediately sprinkle with grated Parmesan or Pecorino Romano cheese, if using. Using a thin spatula, loosen pizza and peek underneath. If bottom is not as crisp as desired, place pan over a burner and cook on medium heat, moving the pan around to cook evenly until it is crisp, 1 to 3 minutes. Remove the pizzas and transfer to a cutting board. Cut each pizza into 6 slices and serve immediately.
description:
2025 We now use 1/2 recipe for the 12 inch pan. A little extra water. 

1/22 Use 2/3 recipe for 12 inch cast iron fry pan. We used a full recipe and the crust was pretty thick. Great with pre-sauteed sausage. 

11/21 Great! A whole day of rising.

RM 3/13: ~5 oz cheese per pizza is ideal. Microwave pepperoni briefly before it goes on. Use Kenji's sauce recipe rather than a substitute. Baked in Lodge 10.25" and 12" skillets simultaneously, one dough batch split between them. Made regularly with the kids.
notes:
Although mozzarella is standard, any good melting cheese, such as cheddar, Jack, or young provolone, will work for this recipe. This recipe is intended to be made with dry (aged) mozzarella cheese, the yellowish variety that comes in firm blocks. Do not use fresh mozzarella, as it is too moist. If you want to bake only one pizza at a time, you can transfer one ball of dough to a sealed zipper-lock bag or container in step 3 and store it in the refrigerator for up to three days. Continue with step 4 when ready to bake.

Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.9 (112) / 368 Reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt sets out to recreate the thick, fried-bottomed, focaccia-like pan pizza of childhood Pizza Hut memory, and frames the recipe around removing the three things that make home pizza hard: kneading, stretching and transferring. He uses a no-knead dough because flour's own enzymes cut the proteins into shorter pieces overnight while yeast gas jostles them into a gluten network at least as strong as a kneaded dough, with better flavor, provided hydration stays high, around 65 percent. The stretching problem disappears because a wet, oil-coated ball slides out to fill a greased cast iron skillet or cake pan on its own over a couple of hours, needing only fingertip docking to kill the big bubbles that would otherwise balloon and shed their toppings. Building the pie in the pan removes the peel and stone entirely. He pushes the oven to its maximum, 550F, because fast bubble expansion gives both a crunchier exterior and a more open crumb, and he finishes with grated hard cheese after baking.

What readers report: The fix cooks report most often is for a pale, soft bottom: after baking, set the hot pan over a burner on medium or low for a few minutes to crisp the base without overcooking the top, which several say rescued the pie. Ovens topping out at 500F work but need longer, with reports of 18 to 25 minutes, and one cook using a 10-inch pan with only a 7.3-inch cooking surface still got a wet, pale crust at 25 minutes. Pan size is flexible: the full dough works in a single 12-inch skillet, and one cook made 1.5x split between a 12-inch skillet and a 9x13. Active dry yeast substitutes for instant at about 1.25 teaspoons, and pre-shredded part-skim mozzarella works despite the note calling for dry aged. One reader challenges the 400 g to 2.5 cups flour conversion. Others find the dough too soft to ball neatly and simply drop it in the pan.

Note on the source: 'Load More reviews' present, so only part of the 368 reviews is in the paste; the paste includes a 'Featured Tweaks' block above the main review list. Several comments end with 'Read More' and may be truncated. Several questions in the paste have 'View Replies' links whose replies are not included.

ahead: Cover bowl tightly with plastic wrap, making sure that the edges are well sealed, then let rest at cool…

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Your RM 3/13 note already dialed in the ratios — 5 oz cheese per pizza, half recipe for a 12-inch pan — and the bottom-crisping stovetop fix readers recommend is already in the directions.

name: Free-Form Apple or Pear Tart
ingredients:
1 ¼ cups (150 g) all-purpose flour
Pinch salt
3 tablespoons (38 g) sugar
9 tablespoons (128 g) cold butter
1 egg yolk
3 or 4 medium apples, preferably Golden Delicious, or pears, peeled, cored and very thinly sliced
2 tablespoons (26 g) brown sugar
Crème fraîche, sweetened
Whipped cream or vanilla ice cream
directions:
Combine flour, salt and sugar in a food processor; pulse once or twice. Cut 8 tablespoons butter into chunks, and add it and egg yolk to flour mixture. Process until butter and flour are blended, about 10 seconds. Turn mixture into a bowl, and add cold water, a tablespoon at a time, stirring after each addition. After adding 3 or 4 tablespoons you should be able to gather mixture into a ball; wrap ball in plastic, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour (or freeze for about 15 minutes).

Preheat oven to 400 degrees. Roll or pat dough into a 10-inch circle; it can be quite crude in shape. Place it on a cookie or pizza sheet, preferably nonstick. Arrange fruit slices on top, right out to edges; make the pattern attractive, if you like. Sprinkle with brown sugar. Cut remaining butter into bits, and top fruit with it.

Bake until crust is nicely browned and fruit is tender, 20 to 30 minutes. Remove, and serve warm or at room temperature, with crème fraîche, whipped cream or ice cream.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (634)). A Mark Bittman Minimalist recipe from a column on entertaining simply, for a rustic free-form tart made with either apples or pears. The page carries no descriptive headnote beyond the article credit, so the method itself is the whole story.

What readers report: Handling the dough is what cooks talk about. The top note (99 votes) says to roll it directly on parchment and slide the paper onto the baking sheet, removing any transfer anxiety; a 64-vote cook rolls it out on a baking stone instead, and a 32-vote note reports the dough is soft enough to simply pat out on the sheet pan with no rolling pin or parchment at all. Several cooks call the crust the best part, describing it as buttery and shortbread-like. Popular flavour changes (23 votes) are cinnamon, nutmeg and cardamom sprinkled over the fruit and turbinado sugar in place of brown. Ripe pears, including a glut of gift pears, are praised as well as apples, and one cook rested the dough a full 24 hours in the fridge with good results.

Note on the source: page has no real headnote, only a 'Featured in' credit

claude_opt.changes: Roll the dough out on parchment paper, then slide the paper straight onto the sheet pan — the top reader tip, removes the transfer risk of a crude free-form dough at zero added cost.

name: French Onion Soup (Soupe à l'Oignon Gratinée)
ingredients:
6 tablespoons (90g) unsalted butter, plus more for bread
3 pounds (1.4kg) yellow or mixed onions, sliced 1/8 inch thick (see note)
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste, divided
1/2 cup (120ml) dry sherry (such as Amontillado)
2 quarts (1.9 kg) (1.8L) homemade or store-bought low-sodium chicken stock
2 sprigs thyme
1 bay leaf
1 teaspoon (5ml) Asian fish sauce (optional)
1 teaspoon (5ml) cider vinegar
8 bowl-size slices rustic bread, toasted until crisp
1 medium clove garlic
1 pound (450g) Gruyère cheese, grated
2 tablespoons (6.0 g) freshly minced chives, for garnish
directions:
In a large stainless steel saucepan, or in 2 large stainless steel or cast iron skillets, melt butter over medium-high heat until foaming. Add onions and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, about 8 minutes. Lower heat to medium-low and cook, stirring frequently, until onions are very sweet and a rich golden-brown color, 1 to 2 hours. If browned onion juices on bottom of pot threaten to burn, add 1 tablespoon (15ml) water, scrape up browned bits, and continue cooking. Season with salt and pepper.

Add sherry and bring to a simmer, scraping up any browned bits. (If using 2 skillets, divide sherry between them, then scrape onions and liquid from both pans into a pot or Dutch oven to continue.) Cook until alcohol smell is mostly gone, about 3 minutes. Add stock, thyme, and bay leaf; raise heat to medium-high; and bring to a simmer. Lower heat and simmer for 20 minutes.

Add fish sauce, if using, and cider vinegar. Season with salt and pepper. Discard thyme sprigs and bay leaf.

Preheat broiler and adjust oven rack to top position. Butter toasts and rub with garlic clove until fragrant. Spoon a small amount of broth into the bottoms of 4 ovenproof serving bowls, then top with half the toasts. Sprinkle some grated cheese on top of toasts, then spoon more soup and onions on top, nearly filling bowls. Set remaining 4 toasts in bowls, pushing to nearly submerge them. Top with remaining grated cheese and set bowls on a rimmed baking sheet. Broil until cheese is melted and browned in spots. Garnish with chives and serve.
description:
2/26 3+ lb onion (untrimmed) with 4 c stock. A little extra cider vinegar, Worcestershire instead of fish sauce, and bourbon instead of sheery. Onions took about 100 mnutes, with careful tending. Tasted carefully to get enough salt. Its a fair amount. Thick and savory. Perhaps the best yet. 

11/25 5 lbs onions and 5 c stock. Very concentrated and strong. Sweet and oniony. Would have been better with more broth. Could have used more vinegar. Make sure you add enough salt. 

11/24 Used 8 lbs of onions for same stock. Still not too much onion! Delicious. Used bourbon at half strength instead of sherry. Works fine. 

11/23 Doubled the onions. Caramelized for several hours. Way better this way. 
1/22 Great! Used 2 red, one white, 3 yellow, 1 big shallot. Followed recipe. Homemade stock. Used big all clad dutch oven. 2 hours to to caramelize the onions. Perhaps could have turned it up a bit further. Added 4 ½ Tsps of diamond kosher salt. About right. Half of recipe would be plenty for two. Substitute worcestershire for the fish sauce next time?
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.7 (23) / 90 Reviews). Daniel Gritzer argues that this soup lives or dies on two things, the onions and the stock, and that the cheese and croutons should be a bonus rather than cover for a weak base. His central claim, backed by citations to Soltner, Julia Child and Patricia Wells, is that the near-universal instruction to cook the onions to a very dark mahogany is wrong and risky: the sweet, deep flavor arrives well before that point, and pushing further easily introduces the bitterness behind most bad versions, so he aims for a rich golden brown. He is blunt that this takes one to two hours in butter over gentle heat, not the 15 or 25 minutes most recipes claim, and he rejects the common shortcuts, finding baking soda turns onions into greenish mush with an off flavor and added sugar pushes them to candy sweetness. He prefers cast iron, carbon steel or stainless to enameled pots, which brown the pan rather than the onions and force constant deglazing. Since good store-bought beef stock is hard to find, he says homemade chicken stock or even a decent boxed brand beats it, and he finishes with sherry, thyme, bay, a little fish sauce for depth and cider vinegar for balance.

What readers report: The most-flagged issue is yield: a reader points out that 1.8 liters of stock plus the onions is roughly eight cups for four servings, and halved the stock for a heartier, more onion-rich soup; another independently agrees the yield is off. Worcestershire is the usual substitution for fish sauce, and the highest-voted review warns it is strong enough that half a teaspoon would be plenty. Soy sauce with dried thyme also works, as does dried thyme with boxed chicken stock, and several readers boost boxed broth with Better Than Bouillon beef base. Caramelizing times run about an hour to an hour and fifteen minutes with frequent deglazing. One reviewer disputes the author directly, saying the photographed onions are far darker than the golden brown the text prescribes and that chicken broth alone gave a pale result. Gritzer replies in the thread explaining why he rejects baking soda.

Note on the source: 'Load More reviews' present, so only part of the 90 reviews is in the paste; the paste includes a 'Most helpful positive review' block and a 'Featured Tweaks' block with vote counts of 1 on a few entries. Several comments end with 'Read More' and may be truncated.

name: French Toast
ingredients:
1/2 egg slightly beaten
dash of salt
2 slices of bread
1 1/2 tb. of fat
1/4 c. (61 g) milk
directions:
Mix together egg, salt and milk in a shallow pan or plate. Dip the bread into mixture and soak lightly.  Fry over low flame turning to brown both sides. Add more fat if necessary to keep slices from sticking. Place on hot plate and serve with syrup.

Syrup: 1/4 c. brown sugar melted in 1/2 c. water.

claude_opt.changes: Custard is egg-thin (half an egg per 2 slices, no cream) versus richer modern ratios. Use closer to one egg per 2 slices with a splash of cream and slightly stale bread for custardy centers.

name: French Yogurt Cake with Marmalade Glaze
ingredients:
1 cup (120 g) all-purpose flour
½ cup (72 g) ground almonds (or, if you’d prefer, omit the almonds and use another 1/2 cup all-purpose flour)
2 teaspoons (8.0 g) baking powder
Pinch of salt
1 cup (200 g) sugar
Grated zest of 1 lemon
½ cup (122 g) plain yogurt
3 large eggs
¼ teaspoon (1.1 g) pure vanilla extract
½ cup (109 g) flavorless oil, such as canola or safflower
½ cup (160 g) lemon marmalade, strained, for glazing the top (optional)
1 teaspoon (4.9 g) water, for glazing the top (optional)
directions:
Getting ready: Center a rack in the oven and preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Generously butter an 8 1/2-x-4 1/2-inch loaf pan, place the pan on a lined baking sheet and set aside. Whisk together the flour, ground almonds, if you’re using them, baking powder and salt and keep near by as well.

Put the sugar and zest in a medium bowl and, working with your fingertips, rub the zest into the sugar until the sugar is moist and aromatic. Add the yogurt, eggs and vanilla to the bowl and whisk vigorously until the mixture is very well blended. Still whisking, stir in the dry ingredients, then switch to a large rubber spatula and fold in the oil. You’ll have a thick, smooth batter with a slight sheen. Scrape the batter into the pan and smooth the top.

Slide the baking sheet into the oven and bake 35 to 40 minutes for the round cake or 50 to 55 minutes, or until the cake begins to come away from the sides of the pan; it will be golden brown and a knife inserted into the center of the cake will come out clean. Transfer the pan to a rack, cool for 5 minutes, then run a blunt knife between the cake and the sides of the pan. Unmold and cool to room temperature right-side up.

To make the glaze: Put the marmalade in a small pot or a microwave-safe bowl, stir in the teaspoon of water and heat (on the range or in the microwave oven) until the jelly is hot and liquefied. Using a pastry brush, gently brush the cake with the glaze.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (1,183)). Emily Weinstein's note frames this as a deliberately plain, faintly tangy everyday cake, served in France with lightly sweetened creme fraiche. Because it is unassertive it takes almost any accompaniment: sliced peaches or plums, sugared berries, lemon curd or mousse, or chocolate mousse or sauce.

What readers report: The recipe's own wording is the main complaint. A 94-vote note points out that step 3 refers to a round pan without ever giving a size, and a 71-vote note finds the pan and timing instructions contradictory, since one step specifies an 8 1/2-by-4 1/2-inch loaf pan while the times cover both a round cake (35 to 40 minutes) and a loaf (50 to 55). An 8-by-8 square pan is reported to work. The most-voted note (170) comes from a repeat baker who cut the oil to 1/3 cup and swaps sour cream or creme fraiche for the yogurt. A 104-vote request for a butter-for-oil conversion is answered at 70 votes with Amanda Hesser's ratio of about 3/4 cup oil to 1 cup butter. Several cooks reduce the sugar to 1/2 cup.

Note on the source: only 32 comments but well voted

name: Fresh Crab Nachos - Ina
ingredients:
6 ounces (170 g) cream cheese, at room temperature
½ cup (110 g) good mayonnaise, such as Hellmann’s
¼ cup (58 g) sour cream
12 ounces (340 g) fresh jumbo lump crabmeat (see note)
¾ cup (75 g) minced scallions, white and green parts (4 to 5 scallions)
1 (4-ounce) can diced green chiles
Grated zest of 1 lime
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
12 ounces (340 g) sturdy yellow corn chips, such as Garden of Eatin’
6 ounces (170 g) freshly grated extra-sharp white Cheddar
6 ounces (170 g) freshly grated Monterey Jack
4 ounces (113 g) canned pickled jalapeño pepper slices, drained
5 large plum tomatoes, seeded, cored, and small-diced
1 cup (160 g) minced yellow onion
3 tablespoons (21 g) minced fresh jalapeño pepper, seeds removed
2 tablespoons (30 g) freshly squeezed lime juice
1 tablespoon (14 g) good olive oil
1 large ripe Hass avocado, pitted, peeled, and ¹/₃-inch diced
3 tablespoons (11 g) minced fresh parsley or cilantro
Juice of ½ lime, for serving
directions:
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees.

In a medium bowl, stir together the cream cheese, mayonnaise, and sour cream until smooth. Gently stir in the crabmeat, scallions, chiles, lime zest, 2 teaspoons salt, and 1 teaspoon black pepper and set aside.

Distribute half of the corn chips on a large (12 × 18 × 2-inch) ovenproof serving platter (or a sheet pan). Spoon half of the crab mixture over the chips in dollops and then sprinkle with half of the Cheddar, half of the Monterey Jack, and all of the pickled jalapeños. Sprinkle with the remaining chips, then distribute the remaining crab mixture and cheeses on top. Bake for 20 to 30 minutes, until the cheese is melted and bubbling.

Meanwhile, prepare the topping. In a large bowl, combine the tomatoes, onion, jalapeño pepper, lime juice, olive oil, avocado, parsley, and 1 teaspoon salt. Spoon onto the nachos, sprinkle with lime juice, and serve hot.
notes:
I prefer jumbo lump crabmeat instead of shredded because you can really taste the crabmeat.

Pick through the crabmeat to remove any shells.

Be sure to wash your hands after handling the chiles and pickled jalapeños so you don’t get the spicy oils in your eyes.

Web summary (barefootcontessa.com). Ina Garten builds nachos around jumbo lump crabmeat bound in a cream cheese, mayonnaise and sour cream base with scallions, green chiles and lime zest, spread over corn chips and baked under grated white Cheddar and Monterey Jack. The creamy binder keeps the crab from drying out under the oven heat and stops it sliding off the chips. A raw tomato, onion, jalapeno and avocado salsa goes on after baking, so the dish arrives with both hot and cold layers.

Note on the source: barefootcontessa.com carries no comments or ratings

Link confidence: LOW — this URL is a plausible version of the dish but was not verified as the family's exact recipe. Treat the link as a lead, not a citation.

claude_opt.changes: Every well-reviewed crab dip recipe drains and pats the lump crabmeat dry before mixing - this one doesn't, and residual liquid is the top cause of soggy baked crab dishes.

name: Fruit Chili Sauce
ingredients:
30 tomatoes, peeled and quartered 
6 pears, peeled and chopped
6 peaches, peeled and chopped
6 onions chopped
6 green peppers chopped
4 c. (800 g) sugar
2 T. (36 g) salt
¼ c. (24 g) mixed pickling spices tied in cloth
16 oz. (454 g) cider vinegar
directions: Cook slowly for several hours until desired thickness. Remove pouch of spices and bottle.
description: 8/23 Half recipe yielded 13 cups. Seemed good and sweet. Don’t add more sugar. Cooked for 3 hours. Followed canning directions, as with jam, but processed for 12 - 15 minutes.

claude_opt.changes: Only 16 oz vinegar acidifies a huge batch of low-acid pears, peaches, onions and peppers plus tomatoes — an untested ratio for safe water-bath canning. Add bottled lemon juice per jar or check pH first.

name: Fruit Galette
ingredients:
FOR THE DOUGH:
1 ⅓ cups/165 grams all-purpose flour
1 tablespoon/15 grams sugar
½ teaspoon/3 grams fine sea salt
1 large egg
Heavy cream, as needed
1 stick/113 grams unsalted butter, cut into big pieces
2 teaspoons (10 g)/10 milliliters lemon juice
½ teaspoon/4 grams grated lemon zest (optional)
FOR THE FILLING:
3 cups (450 g) summer fruit of your choice (berries, stone fruit, figs), sliced or cubed if necessary
½ cup to 3/4 cup/100 to 150 grams sugar, to taste
Pinch of salt
Juice and grated zest of 1/2 lemon (optional)
3 to 4 tablespoons/25 to 35 grams cornstarch or same quantity of quick cooking tapioca (tapioca leaves a more glistening fruit filling)
directions:
MAKE THE CRUST:

In a food processor fitted with a steel blade, or in a large bowl, pulse or mix together flour, sugar and salt. In a measuring cup, lightly beat the egg, then add just enough cream to get to 1/3 cup. Lightly whisk the egg and cream together.

Add butter to flour mixture and pulse or use a pastry cutter or your fingers to break up the butter. If using a food processor, do not over-process; you need chickpea-size chunks of butter. Drizzle the egg mixture (up to 1/4 cup) over the dough and pulse or stir until it just starts to come together but is still mostly large crumbs. Mix in lemon juice and zest if using.

Put dough on lightly floured counter and pat it together to make one uniform piece. Flatten into a disk, wrap in plastic and chill for 2 hours, or up to 3 days.

Heat the oven to 400 degrees. Roll the dough out to a 12-inch round (it can be ragged). Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet lined with parchment paper and chill while preparing the filling.

MAKE THE FILLING:

Toss together fruit, all but a tablespoon of sugar, the salt, the lemon juice and zest, and the cornstarch. Use more cornstarch for juicy stone fruit and less for blueberries, raspberries and figs. Pile fruit on the dough circle, leaving a 1 1/2-inch border. Gently fold the pastry over the fruit, pleating to hold it in (sloppy is fine). Brush pastry generously with leftover egg and cream mixture. Sprinkle remaining sugar on the crust.

Bake for 35 to 45 minutes, until the filling bubbles up vigorously and the crust is golden. Cool for at least 20 minutes on wire rack. Serve warm or at room temperature.
description: 7/2019 Excellent! Used peaches. Filling can leak out. Parchment lining for the sheet pan is a must!
notes:
I sometimes use preserves (strawbery or apricot jam) spread in a thin layer on the dough before adding the fruit mixture. This adds intensity to the fruit flavor.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (2,109)). Melissa Clark's template galette, written to work with whatever fruit is around; the variable to adjust is the sugar and cornstarch. Tart stone fruit such as apricots, peaches, nectarines, plums and sour cherries needs more of both, while figs, grapes, berries and Bing cherries need less, and she advises adding sugar gradually and tasting. A thin layer of jam under the fruit deepens the flavour, matched or contrasted as you like, and vanilla seeds, ground spices or minced candied ginger can replace the lemon zest. The dough holds three days, but the galette is best the day it is baked.

What readers report: Leaking juice is the problem cooks hit, and the top note (445 votes) describes liquid escaping and burning on the sheet pan; the fix borrowed from the NYT blueberry pie is to drain the macerated fruit and use that liquid separately. An 81-vote note asks for an explicit warning about how much liquid berries release, raspberries especially. The second most-voted tip (215) is a genuine ambiguity in the instructions: do not pour the whole egg-and-cream mixture onto the crust, which the recipe only makes clear too late. A 115-vote note recommends watching the accompanying video for technique, and cooks endorse making the crust in a food processor (98 votes). Popular additions are cardamom or cinnamon with peaches, and lime with mango.

name: Fudge Squares or Brownies
ingredients:
3 T. (38 g) Crisco
1 c. (200 g) sugar
1 egg
2 oz. (57 g) baking chocolate
1/2 t. (2.1 g) vanilla
1/3 c. (81 g) milk
1 c. (120 g) flour
1 t. (4.0 g) baking powder
1/2 c. (58 g) nut meats
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.
Melt shortening and chocolate. Add sugar and unbeaten egg. Mix well with spoon. Add vanilla, milk, and flour sifted with baking powder and salt. Add nuts and mix well. Spread 1/2 inch thick in greased pan. Bake 20-30 minutes.
description: Very inexpensive! Double the recipe for a regular sheet pan.
notes: Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Crisco-and-chocolate method is sound; keep it as-is. "Bake 20-30 minutes" is vague — use a toothpick with a few moist crumbs as the doneness cue instead of time alone, to avoid dry, overbaked squares.

name: Garden Vegetable Soup
ingredients:
2 T. (28 g) butter
2 T. (27 g) vegetable oil
1 c. (128 g) sliced carrots
1 c. (101 g) chopped celery with some leafy tops
1 lg. onion, chopped
1 clove garlic, crushed
2 17-oz. (482 g) cans peeled tomatoes or 9 medium-sized tomatoes
1 t. (1.1 g) oregano
1 t. (0.5 g) basil
2 t. (12 g) salt
1/4 t. (0.6 g) pepper
1 can (13 3/4 oz) beef broth
1/4 lb. (113 g) green beans chopped into 1" pieces
1/2 lb. (227 g) zucchini, sliced
1/4 c. (15 g) chopped parsley
grated Parmesan cheese
directions:
1. Heat butter and oil in Dutch oven. Saute carrots, celery, onion, and garlic for 5 minutes.
2. Peel tomatoes. Cut in half and remove seeds by squeezing. Chop pulp and add to juice in a large bowl.
3. Add tomatoes and juice to Dutch oven. Add oregano, basil, salt and pepper. Cook 15 minutes.
4. Add beef broth and green beans. Cook 30 minutes longer, adding zucchini and parsley after 20 minutes.
5. Serve with Parmesan cheese.
notes: Freezes well.

claude_opt.changes: Canned beef broth is already salted, so the full 2 t. salt risks oversalting; add it in two additions and taste before the last. Otherwise technique (late zucchini, short simmer) matches modern versions well.

name: Garlic-Ginger Chicken Breasts with Cilantro and Mint
ingredients:
8 garlic cloves, minced
2 tablespoons (12 g) minced fresh ginger
1 tablespoon (2.8 g) finely chopped fresh mint leaves, plus more for garnish
1 tablespoon (2.9 g) finely chopped fresh cilantro leaves, plus more for garnish
3 tablespoons (46 g) fresh lemon juice (from 1 lemon)
3 tablespoons (40 g) plus 1 teaspoon olive oil
1 tablespoon (5.4 g) ground coriander
1 teaspoon (3.0 g) ground turmeric
1 teaspoon (2.5 g) amchur (dry mango powder), optional
1/2 teaspoon (1.3 g) red chile powder, like ground cayenne
3/4 teaspoon (2.1 g) kosher salt
4 boneless, skinless chicken breasts (1/2 to 3/4 pound each)
directions:
Make the marinade: Add the garlic, ginger, mint, cilantro, lemon juice and 3 tablespoons oil to a large resealable bag. Seal the bag and massage to combine the ingredients into a paste. Add the coriander, turmeric, amchur (if using), red chile powder and salt, and seal the bag. Shake or massage to combine.

Place the chicken breasts in the marinade and seal the bag tightly. Use your hands to gently massage the marinade onto the chicken breasts until each breast is coated. Refrigerate at least 2 hours and up to overnight.

Warm a large lidded skillet over medium-high heat. Once the pan is quite hot, add the oil, swirling the pan to coat the entire surface. Reduce the heat to medium, remove the chicken from the marinade and shake gently to remove any excess marinade. Add it to the pan. Working in batches if necessary, cook the breasts, undisturbed, until lightly golden underneath, 1 to 2 minutes, then flip them and cook until lightly golden on the second side, 1 to 2 minutes.

Reduce the heat to low, cover, and cook the chicken for 10 minutes (no peeking!). Turn off the heat (if you have an electric stove, take the pan off the heat) and let the chicken sit, covered, for 10 to 15 minutes, depending on the thickness of the breasts. Don’t lift the lid, or you’ll release the hot steam that finishes cooking the chicken.

Check to make sure the breasts are cooked through: There shouldn’t be any pink in the middle. If you have a meat thermometer, the chicken should register at least 165 degrees. Place the chicken on a cutting board, and slice each breast into strips. Garnish with mint and cilantro.
description: 5/24 Delish. Very Indian taste. Got some buning on the initial saute but that seems to be intended in the recipe. Steph felt the scorchy flavor was more than wanted. Steaming method worked well. We left it for 15 minutes. Probably 13 would have been enough.
notes:

name: Garlicky Broccolini
ingredients:
Kosher salt
2 pounds (907 g) Broccolini (about 4 bunches)
1/4 cup (54 g) extra-virgin olive oil
4 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1 teaspoon (1.8 g) crushed red pepper
directions:
Gather the ingredients.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add the Broccolini and cook until bright green and barely crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Drain, reserving 1/2 cup of the cooking water.

In a very large skillet, heat the olive oil with the garlic and crushed red pepper and cook over moderate heat until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Increase the heat to high, add the Broccolini, and toss to coat with the oil. Add the reserved cooking water and toss occasionally, until the Broccolini is crisp-tender, about 2 minutes. Season with salt and transfer to a platter. Serve warm or at room temperature.
description: 10/23 Robert made this for us. He likes it with less broccolini per sauce.
notes: Web summary (foodandwine.com, 4.4 (8)). Jason Travi's headnote frames this as a fast, five-ingredient formula — blanch, then saute in garlic- and chile-infused olive oil, finished with a splash of the reserved cooking water for a light glaze — pitched as adaptable to other mild vegetables like cauliflower or green beans. What readers report: the dominant, repeated fix is that the recipe's 1-3 minute blanch overcooks the broccolini into mush; several independent commenters (MustardPecan1894; StrivingMango9305; AmbitiousRefrigerator8531; CapableOven3352) cut the blanch to about 1 minute or swap it for a brief steam, and the page's flagged 'most helpful positive review' (EffervescentStrawberry2990) skips blanching entirely, sauteing the broccolini directly in the garlic-chile oil, then covering and steaming with a little water. One commenter (JovialFish8040) accidentally omitted the reserved cooking water step and found the dish better for it — less mushy — though they preferred it served hot rather than at the room temperature the recipe suggests. Another (dustylnguyen) recommends an ice bath after blanching to stop the cooking and preserve color when it won't be eaten right away. No numeric helpfulness votes are shown beyond the 'most helpful' label; only small reply counts (0-1) appear on the reviews.

claude_opt.changes: The recipe's 1–3 min blanch reliably overcooks the broccolini into mush — the dominant, repeated complaint among readers. Cut the blanch to about 1 minute, or skip it and sauté directly in the garlic oil, then cover briefly to steam.

name: Gateau Reine De Saba
ingredients:
FOR THE CAKE:
12 tablespoons (170 g) (1 1/2 sticks) butter, more for pan
6 ounces (170 g) bittersweet chocolate, chopped into small pieces
A few drops almond extract
2 tablespoons (30 g) strong coffee
4 large eggs, separated
Pinch of salt
1 cup (200 g) sugar
1 ¾ cups (250 g) finely ground almonds
FOR THE GLAZE:
2 tablespoons (25 g) sugar
1 tablespoon (20 g) corn syrup
4 ounces (113 g) bittersweet chocolate, chopped into small pieces
1 tablespoon (14 g) butter
directions:
PREPARE CAKE:

Heat oven to 325 degrees. Butter a 9-inch springform pan, and line the side wall with parchment paper. In a heavy-bottomed pan, combine 12 tablespoons butter, 6 ounces chopped chocolate, almond extract and coffee. Melt over low heat, then transfer to a bowl and allow to cool.

With an electric mixer, whisk egg whites and salt until soft peaks form. Slowly add 1/2 cup sugar until thick and glossy. Set aside.

In a separate bowl, whisk together egg yolks with remaining 1/2 cup sugar until thick. Fold in the melted chocolate mixture. Add ground almonds and mix well. Whisk in a dollop of egg whites to lighten mixture. Using a rubber spatula, gently fold in the rest of egg whites, keeping batter airy.

Scrape batter into pan and bake until cake is dry on top and a bit gooey in center, 30 to 40 minutes. (After 30 minutes of baking, check center of cake with a tester or toothpick. If center seems very wet, continue baking.) Cool cake on a rack for 20 minutes, then remove side of pan. Allow to continue cooling. Top of cake may crack as it cools, but glaze will cover most cracking.

PREPARE GLAZE:

In a small saucepan, combine 2 tablespoons sugar, the corn syrup and 1/4 cup water. Bring to a boil, then remove from heat. Add 4 ounces chopped chocolate, swirl pan to mix, and allow to stand until melted, about 3 minutes.

Whisk 1 tablespoon butter into icing, then pour evenly over cake. Use a spatula to ease icing out to edges of cake. Allow icing to cool, and set before slicing.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (458)). Nigella Lawson offers her own simplified take on the cake Julia Child described as the first French cake she ever ate. She melts the chocolate with liquid and uses all ground almonds instead of the usual almond-and-flour mix, which also makes it gluten-free. She wants the texture closer to pudding, dense and melting, and notes a small slice goes a long way, so one cake serves about twelve.

What readers report: The most-voted note (81) argues a plain ganache of chocolate and cream beats the recipe's glaze and skips corn syrup entirely; a 30-vote reply defends the corn syrup as what keeps the glaze glossy and suggests keeping a small bottle just for glazing. Another popular commenter substituted raw honey for the corn syrup successfully. On the almonds, a 46-vote note clarifies that ground almonds and almond flour are essentially the same thing, ground almonds simply being the British term, and a baker reports good results with roughly 1 1/4 cups almond flour plus 1/2 cup almond meal. One person's cake rose higher and domed more than the photograph but was still well received. Several non-US readers grumble about butter measured in tablespoons.

name: Gougeres
ingredients:
1/2 cup (122 g) whole milk
1/2 cup (118 g) water
8 tablespoons (114 g) (1 stick) unsalted butter, cut into 4 pieces
1/2 teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
1 cup (120 g) all-purpose flour
5 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/2 cups (170 g) coarsely grated cheese, such as Gruyère or cheddar (about 6 ounces; see above)
directions:
Position the racks to divide the oven into thirds and preheat the oven to 425 degrees F. Line two baking sheets with silicone baking mats or parchment paper.

Bring the milk, water, butter, and salt to a rapid boil in a heavy-bottomed medium saucepan over high heat. Add the flour all at once, lower the heat to medium-low, and immediately start stirring energetically with a wooden spoon or heavy whisk. The dough will come together and a light crust will form on the bottom of the pan. Keep stirring—with vigor—for another minute or two to dry the dough. The dough should now be very smooth.

Turn the dough into the bowl of a mixer fitted with the paddle attachment or into a bowl that you can use for mixing with a hand mixer or a wooden spoon and elbow grease. Let the dough sit for a minute, then add the eggs one by one and beat, beat, beat until the dough is thick and shiny. Make sure that each egg is completely incorporated before you add the next, and don't be concerned if the dough separates—by the time the last egg goes in, the dough will come together again. Beat in the grated cheese. Once the dough is made, it should be spooned out immediately.

Using about 1 tablespoon of dough for each gougère , drop the dough from a spoon onto the lined baking sheets, leaving about 2 inches of puff space between the mounds. Using about 1 tablespoon of dough for each gougère, drop the dough from a spoon onto the lined baking sheets, leaving about 2 inches of puff space between the mounds. Slide the baking sheets into the oven and immediately turn the oven temperature down to 375 degrees F. Bake for 12 minutes, then rotate the pans from front to back and top to bottom. Continue baking until the gougères are golden, firm, and, yes, puffed, another 12 to 15 minutes or so. Serve warm, or transfer the pans to racks to cool.

Gougères are good straight from the oven and at room temperature. I like them both ways, but I think you can appreciate them best when they're still warm. Serve with kir, white wine, or Champagne.

Storing:

The best way to store gougères is to shape the dough, freeze the mounds on a baking sheet, and then, when they're solid, lift them off the sheet and pack them airtight in plastic bags. Bake them straight from the freezer—no need to defrost—just give them a minute or two more in the oven. Leftover puffs can be kept at room temperature over night and reheated in a 350-degree-F oven, or they can be frozen and reheated before serving.
notes: Web summary (epicurious.com, 4.4 (34)). In the visible portion of her headnote, Dorie Greenspan presents these cheese choux puffs as a French classic she's often asked to make by French friends and one of her most-requested recipes; most of her technical framing sits behind Epicurious's paywall. What readers report: the clearest correction is that the recipe's 5 eggs is too many, making the dough too runny and the baked puffs flat unless piped very small (a 14-year-old comment, echoed independently by BavarianCook, who used one fewer egg and less cheese with good results). A related fix, credited to another reviewer, is to bake until deep golden-brown, since underbaked puffs collapse; agasque adds that beating the dough longer than instructed also helps it hold its shape. One reader (Pariscafe) reports a full failure — flat, flavorless discs — and blames the recipe's dough-consistency description ('dry' dough) as too vague to gauge. Technique notes include sifting the flour for smoother dough (SZEIGLER) and mixing by hand rather than machine for better rise (Smaggy66), though abedvm used a stand mixer successfully. Multiple readers confirm both dough and baked puffs freeze well, including baking straight from frozen two months later (christopherbromsey), but leftovers should not go in the microwave, which turns them soft and limp (agasque). No vote or helpfulness counts are shown on the page.

claude_opt.changes: Independent reports 14 years apart find 5 eggs makes the dough too runny, yielding flat puffs — use 4 eggs and slightly less cheese. Bake to deep golden-brown, not just golden; underbaked puffs collapse as they cool.

name: Greek Baked Fish with Tomatoes and Onions
ingredients:
2 pounds (907 g) boneless fish fillets or steaks, halibut (Pacific US), black cod (Alaska and Canada), porgy, striped bass or mahi mahi (United States)
Salt and freshly ground pepper
Juice of 1 large lemon
2 tablespoons (27 g) extra virgin olive oil
1 pound (454 g) onions, cut in half lengthwise and then sliced thinly across the grain
2 large garlic cloves, minced or puréed
1 28-ounce (794 g) can chopped tomatoes with juice (in summer use 2 pounds grated or peeled seeded ripe tomatoes)
⅛ teaspoon (0.5 g) sugar
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) sweet paprika
⅛ teaspoon (0.3 g) cinnamon
1 tablespoon (16 g) tomato paste dissolved in 1/4 cup water
½ cup (118 g) dry white wine or red wine
Leaves from 1 bunch flat-leaf parsley, chopped (about 1/2 cup)
directions:
Pat the fish dry and season to taste with salt and pepper. Oil one or two baking dishes large enough to accommodate the fish in one layer. Lay the fish in the dish and pour on the lemon juice. Refrigerate for 30 to 60 minutes while you prepare the remaining ingredients.

Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Heat the oil over medium heat in a large, heavy skillet and add the onions. Cook, stirring often, until they have softened and begun to color slightly, 8 to 10 minutes. Add a generous pinch of salt and the garlic and cook, stirring, until the garlic is fragrant, 30 seconds to a minute. Stir in the tomatoes, sugar, paprika, cinnamon, dissolved tomato paste, wine, half the parsley and more salt and pepper to taste and bring to a simmer. Simmer uncovered, stirring often, until the sauce has cooked down a bit and is very fragrant, about 15 minutes. Remove from the heat and pour over the fish. Sprinkle on the remaining parsley.

Place in the oven and bake until the fish is opaque and pulls apart easily with a fork, about 30 minutes. Baste the fish every 10 minutes if it is not submerged in the sauce. Serve hot or warm, with rice, bulgur, or potatoes.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (1,306)). Martha Rose Shulman frames this as the baked fish you meet travelling in the Greek islands, a robust tomato-and-onion sauce that needs a firm white fish under it. She points readers to the Monterey Bay Aquarium's sustainability rankings and suggests Pacific cod, halibut, black cod or striped bass, with US mahi mahi as a second-tier choice. It ran with a piece on healthier fish dishes.

What readers report: The strongest practical correction (52 votes) is on timing: cooks say it takes nowhere near the stated two hours, that the first step is unnecessary, and that the fish is done in as little as 20 minutes. On seasoning, a 62-vote note would drop the tomato paste, which makes the sauce heavy, and use tomatoes alone plus a little red pepper. Several skip the sugar without missing it. Popular additions are red bell pepper and pitted olives (37 votes), while a commenter from a Greek village family says raisins, allspice and cinnamon belong in it and cod is the fish of choice there (35). Another suggests swapping the fish for a couple of cans of chickpeas for a vegetarian version. An 84-vote note simply confirms it works exactly as written.

name: Greek Lamb Meatballs (Keftedes Tiganites)
ingredients:
1 large red onion grated
2 lbs (907 g) ground lamb or beef
3 garlic cloves minced
2 tsp (2.0 g) dried oregano
1/4 cup (11 g) fresh mint chopped
1 tsp (2.1 g) ground cumin
1 tsp (1.8 g) ground coriander
1/2 cup (54 g) plain breadcrumbs
1 large egg
1 tbsp (14 g) olive oil
1/4 cup (22 g) grated Parmesan cheese (See Note 1)
1 tsp (2.8 g) kosher salt
1/2 tsp (1.1 g) ground black pepper
1/3 cup (40 g) flour for dredging
olive oil (for frying)
directions:
Grate the red onion over a bowl, transfer to a sieve and press to extract excess water. Discard onion water.

Transfer grated onion to a large bowl along with the lamb, garlic, oregano, mint, cumin, coriander, breadcrumbs, egg, oil, cheese, salt and pepper. Mix using your hands and squeeze mixture until thoroughly mixed.

Set up small bowl with flour. Shape meat mixture into walnut size meatballs (See Note 2) and roll in the flour to coat. Gently shake excess flour off and place on a tray. Repeat and you should end up with 36 meatballs.

FRIED VERSION

Heat 1/2-inch of olive oil in a deep skillet until it just starts to shimmer. Fry the meatballs for 7 minutes and brown all over in several batches. Remove and keep warm on a paper towel lined plate.

BAKED VERSION

Bake in 400°F oven for 20 minutes on parchment lined, rimmed baking sheet.

SERVE

Serve with tzatziki sauce, warm pita for an appetizer on a meze platter or as a main dish with steamed rice and a Greek Feta Salad.
notes:
A traditional Greek kefalotyri cheese is preferred if you can find it.

After rolling the meatballs and before rolling in the flour, I often times save half the batch to freeze. Later, when ready to use, thaw and dredge in flour before frying.

You could also bake these on a tray after dredging in the flour in a 400°F oven for 18-20 minutes if you do not want to fry. They will not be as crispy though.

Web summary (silkroadrecipes.com, 5 stars from 2 votes). Kevin at Silk Road Recipes explains that tiganites means little fried things, and these walnut-sized lamb or beef meatballs are shallow-fried so they crisp outside while staying juicy within. The technique he singles out is grating the red onion rather than chopping it, which lets you squeeze out water that would otherwise make the mix too loose to hold its shape. Oregano, mint, cumin, coriander and grated Parmesan season the mixture, and a light dredge in flour helps the crust form.

Note on the source: comment thread exists but holds only praise plus questions about frying temperature and air-fryer adaptation; no corrections, substitutions or disagreements to digest

name: Greek Lemon Potatoes
ingredients:
½ cup (120 g) chicken broth or water
½ cup (108 g) olive oil
½ cup (122 g) freshly squeezed lemon juice (from 3 to 4 large lemons)
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) kosher salt
3 pounds (1.4 kg) large Yukon Gold potatoes (about 6), peeled then halved lengthwise and crosswise
1 tablespoon (3.0 g) dried oregano (optional)
Flaky salt and black pepper, for serving
directions:
Heat the oven to 450 degrees. On a rimmed sheet pan, combine the chicken broth, olive oil, lemon juice and kosher salt. Toss the potatoes in the liquid to coat, then arrange the potatoes in an even layer, cut-sides down. Sprinkle the oregano over the potatoes, if using.

Roast the potatoes, flipping halfway through, until fork-tender, dark brown and crispy on top, 55 to 60 minutes. (If the potatoes are cooked through but not as crispy as you’d like, run them under the broiler for a few minutes.) Sprinkle with flaky salt and black pepper as desired.
description: 5/21 Half recipe. Smaller potatoes cooked in 25 minutes. Burning on the sheet pan. Too strong lemon flavor.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (9,101)). A classic Greek approach to roast potatoes: peel them and roast in equal parts olive oil, lemon juice and chicken stock so the interiors stay creamy while the high oven heat crisps the outsides. The potatoes drink up the seasoned liquid as they cook. Russets can be used the same way but come out drier than the recommended potato.

What readers report: This one splits sharply. The single most-voted comment (2,175) is a joke at the recipe's expense, renaming it after burnt potatoes and ruined sheet pans, and a 1,041-vote note goes further: skip the stock altogether, just toss the potatoes with lemon juice, oil and seasonings and roast on a sheet pan. Against that, a 1,508-vote comment insists the stock is essential, makes it exactly as written, and notes vegetable stock works for a vegan version. The most useful technique tips are to marinate the potatoes in the liquid for a few hours before baking so the lemon penetrates (832 votes), and to toss everything in a bowl before transferring to the pan, with a tablespoon of flour added for extra crispness (626).

Note on the source: strong disagreement in comments over whether the stock helps or causes scorching

claude_opt.changes: Your 5/21 note already found the burning and over-strong lemon. Drop the chicken broth per the 1,041-vote fix — its sugars likely cause the scorching — and cut lemon juice to 1/3 cup.

name: Greek Orzo Salad, Healthy & Delicious
ingredients:

1 large cucumber, peeled, seeded, and diced
3 plum tomatoes, seeded and diced
1 medium red onion, small diced

name: Greek Salad (Washington Post)
ingredients:
4 tomatoes
1 lg. cucumber
2 green bell peppers
1/2 lb. (227 g) feta cheese, crumbled
4 oz. (113 g) Greek olives, pitted
1/3 c. (20 g) chopped fresh parsley
2 T. (5.6 g) chopped fresh mint
1 T. (3.4 g) chopped fresh oregano
1/4 c. (54 g) olive oil
1 1/2 T. (24 g) balsamic vinegar
2 cloves garlic minced
1/4 t. (1.5 g) salt
1/4 t. (0.6 g) pepper
directions:
Cut tomatoes in half horizontally and squeeze out seeds. Coarsely chop. Coarsely chop cucumber and green peppers and toss with tomatoes, feta, olives, parsley, mint and oregano. 

Whisk together remaining ingredients or combine in a blender. Pour over salad, just before serving, tossing gently.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten's Greek salad is a chopped vegetable salad with no lettuce, dressed in a garlic, oregano, Dijon and red wine vinegar vinaigrette whisked with olive oil. The salad is meant to sit for a short while before serving so the vegetables take on the dressing and the flavours pull together. The feta is diced rather than crumbled so it stays in distinct pieces.

What readers report: Readers treat this as a base recipe rather than something needing correction, and most of the discussion is about extending it. Substituting a different cheese for the feta comes up repeatedly, with havarti named specifically, presumably for people who find feta too salty. Turning it into a main is the other common move: grilled chicken stirred through, or cooked rotini added to make a pasta salad that travels. Additional vegetables people add include artichoke hearts and romaine. It is widely reported as a potluck, dinner-party and barbecue dish, valued for holding up after dressing. No one raised problems with the vinaigrette proportions or the resting step.

name: Green Beans Almondine
ingredients:
1/2 c. (46 g) sliced almonds
2 lb. (907 g) fresh green beans
1/3 c. (76 g) butter
1 T. (15 g) lemon juice
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
1/4 t. (0.6 g) pepper
directions:
1. Bake sliced almonds in shallow pan at 350 for 5-10 minutes or until toasted. Set almonds aside.
2. Split beans lengthwise (optional).
3. Cook beans in boiling water to cover in a Dutch oven 4 minutes or until tender. Drain.
4. Melt butter in Dutch oven. Add almonds, beans, lemon juice, salt and pepper. Toss to coat.
5. Serve immediately.

name: Grilled Herb Shrimp—Ina

name: Grilled or Oven-Roasted Santa Maria Tri-Tip
ingredients:
1 whole tri-tip, about 2 pounds (907 g)
3 tablespoons beef rub of your choice (see recipe)
directions:
Trim silver skin. The meat may have a thick layer of fat, some of which can be sliced off, but keep a good amount to help baste meat.

Sprinkle meat with rub and massage lightly all over. Cover and refrigerate at least an hour or as long as overnight. Remove from refrigerator an hour before cooking.

Prepare charcoal grill or heat a gas grill to high. Place roast on grill and sear one side well, 6 to 8 minutes, checking for flare-ups. Turn the roast and sear other side for about the same time. Then lower gas to medium-high or move the meat to a cooler part of the charcoal grill.

Turn meat again and cook another 8 to 10 minutes. Flip and cook again. A 2-pound roast will require about 20 to 25 minutes total cooking time. The roast is ready when an instant-read thermometer reaches 130 degrees when inserted into the thickest part of the meat.

Rest roast on a cutting board 10 to 20 minutes. Slice against the grain. The roast is shaped like a boomerang, so either cut it in half at the center of the angle, or slice against the grain on one side, turn the roast and slice against the grain on the other side.
description: 5/21 We followed this recipe using a top sirloin, and using the California beef rub also include here. Really enjoyed!
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (3,123)). Sourcing is the first hurdle: you may have to ask a butcher or the store's meat manager to order a tri-tip, and two pounds is the useful size, though a bigger one yields sandwich leftovers. The headnote's main technical point is carving, since the grain changes direction within this cut. Inspect the raw roast to see where the muscle fibres shift, and after a 15-minute rest cut the roast in two at that junction and slice each half separately against its own grain.

What readers report: The most-voted note (380) calls tri-tip the best underused cut and reassures cooks that the rub survives missing ingredients. The main methodological split is oven versus grill: a 344-vote commenter uses a dry rub, wraps in foil and holds it at 250F for about three hours, while a 225-vote cook browns the fat side over direct heat then moves to indirect at high temperature for 10 to 15 minutes, using the oven only in bad weather. Regional authenticity draws sharp comment: a fifth-generation Santa Maria native (193 votes) says the real meal is tri-tip with pinquito beans, green salad, garlic-buttered French bread and salsa, and flags the coffee in this rub as a departure from tradition. Another (116) wants the Times to report the original barbecue properly.

name: Grilled Shrimp with Garlic and Lemon
ingredients:
2 1/2 pounds (1 kg) large shrimp (15–20 per pound), peeled and deveined
1/2 teaspoon (2.3 g) baking soda
1 tablespoon (9 g) Diamond Crystal kosher salt, plus more to taste; for table salt, use half as much by volume or the same weight
1 teaspoon (4 g) sugar
4 medium cloves garlic, minced, divided
1/4 cup (60 ml) extra-virgin olive oil, divided
1 teaspoon (2 g) zest and 4 teaspoons (20 ml) juice from 1 lemon
2 tablespoons (10 g) minced fresh parsley leaves
Freshly ground black pepper
directions:
In a medium bowl, combine shrimp, baking soda, salt, and sugar and toss to coat. Thread shrimp onto sets of 2 skewers, alternating heads to tails and pushing shrimp so that they are nestled snugly together; you should have about 6 shrimp on each set of skewers. Lay skewers on top of a baking dish so that shrimp are suspended above bottom of dish. Transfer to refrigerator and allow to rest for 1 hour. Meanwhile, in a small bowl, combine half of garlic and half of olive oil in a small bowl and set aside. In a large bowl, combine remaining garlic and olive oil, lemon zest and juice, and parsley leaves and set aside.

When shrimp are ready to grill, brush both sides with garlic-oil mixture. Light one chimney full of charcoal. When all charcoal is lit and covered with gray ash, pour out and arrange coals on one side of charcoal grate. Set cooking grate in place, cover grill, and allow to preheat for 5 minutes. Alternatively, set half the burners on a gas grill to the highest heat setting, cover, and preheat for 10 minutes. Clean and oil grilling grate.

Place shrimp directly over hot side of grill and cook, turning occasionally, until shrimp are just cooked through and well charred, 4 to 5 minutes total. Transfer shrimp to a cutting board.

Carefully remove skewers from shrimp and transfer to bowl with garlic-oil-lemon mixture. Toss to coat. Season to taste with salt and pepper and serve immediately.
description: 5/25 I liked it. Good flavor. But Steph tasted a tarry flavor on the shrimp and wasn’t a fan.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.4 (13) / 44 Reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt frames grilled shrimp as a conflict between two goals: browning needs hard, fast heat, but shrimp go from snappy to rubbery within a few degrees, and they are too small to char before the middle overcooks. His fix is a set of pre-treatments rather than a hotter fire alone. Tossing the shrimp with salt, a little sugar and baking soda helps on three fronts, since salt keeps them holding moisture, sugar speeds surface browning, and the alkaline baking soda both firms the texture and raises pH so the Maillard reaction runs faster. He then packs the shrimp tightly against each other on double skewers, a Cook's Illustrated idea, because less exposed surface slows heat reaching the centers and buys grilling time. Finally he air-dries the skewers uncovered in the fridge for an hour, on the logic that surface moisture must evaporate before browning can start, and dresses the shrimp in a garlic-lemon-parsley oil after cooking rather than marinating beforehand.

What readers report: The dominant correction is salt: several reviewers found the finished shrimp too salty, one saying they would leave the salt out entirely next time, another reporting it even while using the specified half teaspoon baking soda and kosher salt. One reader raises a plausible cause, that some shrimp are sold pre-brined and may need soaking first, which suggests salting to taste rather than by the recipe. Cooks working with smaller batches or already-cooked shrimp cut the grilling time sharply, one reporting only one to two minutes per side for jumbo shrimp, while another using 12-per-pound shrimp needed a few minutes more than the stated four to five. Reviewers confirm the salt, sugar and baking soda treatment as the part worth keeping. Reported variations that worked: skipping skewers in favor of a grill rack, substituting lime for lemon, and serving over linguine as a grilled scampi.

Note on the source: 'Load More reviews' present, so only 9 of 44 reviews are in the paste. One comment ends with 'Read More' and may be truncated.

name: Herb-Marinated Pork Tenderloins
ingredients:
1 lemon, zest grated
¾ cup (183 g) freshly squeezed lemon juice (4 to 6 lemons)
½ cup (108 g) good olive oil
2 tablespoons (17 g) minced garlic (6 cloves)
1 ½ tablespoons (5.2 g) minced fresh rosemary leaves
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) chopped fresh thyme leaves
2 teaspoons (10 g) Dijon mustard
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) Kosher salt, plus more for sprinkling 
3 pork tenderloins (about 1 pound each)
Freshly ground black pepper
directions:
Combine the lemon zest, lemon juice, 1/2 cup olive oil, garlic, rosemary, thyme, mustard, and 2 teaspoons salt in a sturdy 1-gallon resealable plastic bag. Add the pork tenderloins and turn to coat with the marinade. Squeeze out the air and seal the bag. Marinate the pork in the refrigerator for at least 3 hours but preferably overnight.

Preheat the oven to 400 degrees F.

Remove the tenderloins from the marinade and discard the marinade but leave the herbs that cling to the meat. Sprinkle the tenderloins generously with salt and pepper. Heat 3 tablespoons olive oil in a large oven-proof saute pan over medium-high heat. Sear the pork tenderloins on all sides until golden brown. Place the saute pan in the oven and roast the tenderloins for 10 to 15 minutes or until the meat registers 137 degrees F at the thickest part. Transfer the tenderloins to a platter and cover tightly with aluminum foil. Allow to rest for 10 minutes. Carve in 1/2-inch-thick diagonal slices. The thickest part of the tenderloin will be quite pink (it's just fine!) and the thinnest part will be well done. Season with salt and pepper and serve warm, or at room temperature with the juices that collect in the platter.
description:
10/2017 Made with bed of apples. Saute 2 apples per tenderloin for about 5 minutes. Then into the oven with pork on the top.
4/2018 Used double herbs--great! Cooked on grill.
6/2023 Roasted to 145 and then tented. Tender and very good
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten leans on a sharply acidic marinade rather than a rub: lemon zest and a large quantity of juice, plus garlic, rosemary, thyme and Dijon in olive oil. Several hours (ideally overnight) of marinating lets the acid and herbs work into the lean tenderloin, which has little fat of its own to carry flavour. The meat is then seared to build colour and finished in the oven so it does not dry out.

What readers report: The most common adjustment is to the lemon: several cooks found three-quarters of a cup of juice aggressive and cut it back, or shortened the marinating time so the acid did not start to cure the surface of the meat. Dried rosemary and thyme are widely reported as an acceptable swap when fresh is not on hand, at roughly a third the volume. Many cooks skip the sear-and-roast entirely and grill the tenderloins over direct heat, or smoke them, and say the marinade suits both. The brightness of the marinade is the feature people return for.

name: Home-Style Pork Carnitas
ingredients:
A 3-pound (1.4 kg) pork shoulder roast, cut in 2-inch slabs (no thinner)
Salt
1/2 cup (124 g) cup orange juice or water
Optional Flavorings
6 garlic cloves, peeled and halved
4 bay leaves
A heaping teaspoon Mexican oregano
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) coarsely ground black pepper
For serving
2 1/2 cups (575 g) Guacamole (you’ll have extra, but you’ll be glad you do)
About 1 1/2 cups (390 g) Salsa Verde OR
About 1 1/2 cups (390 g) Chopped Tomato Salsa
2 or 3 limes, cut into wedges
15 (or a few more) warm corn tortillas
directions:
Bake the pork. Heat the oven to 325 degrees. Lay the pork on a cutting board and sprinkle all sides liberally with salt (you’ll need at least 2 teaspoons). Nestle the meat into a baking dish just big enough to hold it (it usually fits in a baking dish about 7x11 inches) and drizzle the water or orange juice on and around it, lifting to allow liquid to run under the meat. If using the optional flavorings, nestle the garlic and bay leaves around the meat (both should be in moist places), then sprinkle with oregano and black pepper. Cover tightly with foil and slide into the hot oven. Set the timer for 1 1/2 hours.

Brown the pork. Remove the pan from the oven and uncover. Test the pork: it should be almost tender when pierced with a fork. (If the meat is still very firm, re-cover and bake for an additional 20 minutes or so, then re-test.) Raise the oven temperature to 450 degrees. Slide the uncovered pan back in the oven and roast until all the liquid has evaporated and only the rendered fat remains, about 30 minutes. Use a large metal spatula to turn the meat over, break it into large chunks, return to the hot oven and roast for another 20 minutes or so, turning the meat every 7 or 8 minutes, until the carnitas are richly golden all over.

Serve. Arrange the carnitas on a warm serving platter and sprinkle with salt (a good finishing salt is welcome here—I’m particularly fond of Maldon). Serve with the guacamole, salsa, limes and warm tortillas. Encourage your guests to pull apart the golden pieces of deliciousness, fitting several pieces on each tortilla, before topping with guacamole, salsa and lime.

Working ahead: Once the carnitas have been browned, you need to serve them right away. You can, however, braise the pork up to a couple of days ahead, cover and refrigerate it. On the day you’re serving, let the pork come to room temperature, and, an hour before serving, roast it.
notes:
Web summary (rickbayless.com). Rick Bayless walks through the usual carnitas additions - orange, cola, sweetened condensed milk, herbs, spices - and explains what each is actually doing: the rind contributes fragrance while the juice and milk sugars drive browning. His argument is that the high heat of the cooking burns off most delicate aromatics anyway, so pork shoulder cooked with nothing but salt gives a result as good as the elaborate versions. The optional garlic, bay, oregano and pepper are offered as embellishments rather than requirements.

Note on the source: no comments section on page

makeahead: You can, however, braise the pork up to a couple of days ahead, cover and refrigerate it.

claude_opt.changes: Swap the recipe's thin baking dish for your enameled Dutch oven during the final high-heat fat-rendering step for steadier heat and less risk of scorching the fond.

name: Hot Chicken Salad
ingredients:
4-6 whole chicken breasts
2 c. (216 g) slivered almonds

directions:
Stew or bake chicken and but into bite sized pieces. Mix with all other ingredients except chips and stuffing, and refrigerate overnight.

ahead: Mix with all other ingredients except chips and stuffing, and refrigerate overnight.

name: Hot Chocolate
ingredients:
1/2 c. (118 g) water
2 oz. (57 g) semi-sweet chocolate
3 c. (732 g) milk (whole is best)
directions: Combine water and chocolate in medium saucepan. Cook, stirring constantly, until chocolate is melted. Bring mixture to a boil for 2 minutes, then reduce heat to low. Stir in 3 c. of milk and a dash of salt. Warm for 5-7 minutes.

claude_opt.changes: Technique already avoids the classic error of boiling milk (which scorches it and forms a skin) — only the water-chocolate base boils; milk is just warmed. Nothing to change.

name: Hot Crab Dip
ingredients:

directions: Mix & heat. Serve with crackers. May add Worcestershire sauce.

name: How To Properly Cook A Scallop
ingredients:
6 oz (170 g) New England scallops per person, or about 5 scallops
2 Teaspoons (9.0 g) of Olive Oil
2 Teaspoons (9.5 g) of Unsalted Butter
directions:
Rinse and pat scallops dry. Remove side muscle (Fishmonger will be happy to show you if you don't know how

Season scallop with sea salt

When oil starts to smoke put scallops in pan, being careful to not overcrowd (1/2 inch btwn each scallop)

Heat for roughly 1.5 minutes per side. Scallops should have about a nickel thick golden curst on each side and translucent in the center. Serve immediately
description: 2/22 Followed ATK which is very similar. 0.6 pound was more than enough for the two of us. Oil first, then add butter when turning the scallops.
