name: Ina’s Chicken Stock
ingredients:
3 (5-pound) roasting chickens
3 large yellow onions, unpeeled and quartered
6 carrots, unpeeled and halved crosswise
4 celery stalks with leaves, cut into thirds crosswise
4 parsnips, unpeeled and halved crosswise
20 sprigs fresh flat-leaf parsley
15 sprigs fresh thyme
20 sprigs fresh dill
1 head garlic, unpeeled and cut in half crosswise
2 tablespoons (17 g) kosher salt
2 teaspoons (5.8 g) whole black peppercorns (not ground)
directions: Place the chickens, onions, carrots, celery, parsnips, parsley, thyme, dill, garlic, and seasonings in a 16 to 20-quart stockpot. Add 7 quarts of water and bring to a boil. Simmer, uncovered, for 4 hours. Strain the entire contents of the pot through a colander and discard the solids. Chill the stock overnight. The next day, remove the surface fat. Use immediately or pack in containers and freeze for up to 3 months.
description:

11/24 2 chickens with a total of 13 lbs. 26 c of stock.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). The Food Network version of Ina Garten's stock, from Barefoot Contessa Family Style. Same construction as her later one: three roasting chickens, unpeeled aromatics, a heavy hand with parsley, thyme and dill, simmered four hours. Straining and then chilling overnight lets the fat set on the surface so it can be lifted off cleanly rather than skimmed hot.

Note on the source: near-duplicate of the barefootcontessa.com stock recipe; no comments retrieved

Web summary (barefootcontessa.com). Ina Garten's stock from Make It Ahead, scaled to yield about six quarts. Three whole roasting chickens go in with unpeeled onions, carrots, celery, parsnips and a halved head of garlic, plus large bundles of parsley, thyme and dill. Four hours at a simmer extracts body from the bones while the vegetables stay in whole so they release flavour slowly rather than disintegrating. It is written as a make-ahead staple to freeze.

name: Indian Spiced Peas
ingredients:
2 tablespoons (27 g) vegetable oil
2/3 cup (100 grams) yellow onion, quartered and thinly sliced
1/2 cup (75 grams) red bell pepper, thinly sliced
1/2 teaspoon (1.1 g) ground cumin
1/2 teaspoon (1.5 g) turmeric

2 garlic cloves, grated or finely chopped
1/2 teaspoon (3.0 g) salt

directions:
To a large pan, heat the oil over medium heat.

description: 5/22 Enjoyed. Consider adding cayenne and extra onions.

She takes the idea from Kerala-style pea dishes but drops the coconut milk, so the cumin, turmeric, coriander and garam masala sit in the foreground instead of being softened by fat. Tomato paste loosened with water gives the dish a light curry consistency that clings to the peas, and fresh mint goes in at the end for lift.

name: Irish Guinness Brown Bread
ingredients:
1 cup (89 g) quick-cooking oats (not instant), such as McCann’s, plus extra for sprinkling
2¼ cups (254 g) whole wheat flour, such as Heckers
¼ cup (30 g) all-purpose flour
½ cup (106 g) dark brown sugar, lightly packed
2¼ teaspoons (10 g) baking soda
1 teaspoon (4.0 g) baking powder
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) kosher salt
1 (11- to 12-ounce) bottle Guinness extra stout beer, at room temperature
1 cup (242 g) buttermilk, shaken
5 tablespoons (71 g) unsalted butter, melted, plus extra for brushing the pan
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) pure vanilla extract
Salted butter, such as Irish Kerrygold
directions:
Preheat the oven to 450°F

In a large bowl, combine the oats, whole wheat flour, all-purpose flour, brown sugar, baking soda, baking powder, and salt. In a separate bowl, whisk together the beer, buttermilk, melted butter, and vanilla. Make a well in the dry ingredients and pour the wet ingredients into the well. With your fingers, stir the batter from the middle of the bowl to the outside, until it’s well mixed. It will look more like cake batter than bread dough.

Brush a 9 × 5 × 2½-inch loaf pan with melted butter. (3 small loaf pans 5 x 2 x 2 inch, also work well, baked for 35-40 minutes instead) Pour the batter into the pan and sprinkle the top with oats. Put the bread in the oven, immediately turn the temperature down to 400° F, and bake for 45 minutes, until a toothpick comes out clean (~180°-190° internal - Ina only uses toothpick test, which works great). Turn the bread out onto a baking rack and allow to cool completely. Slice and serve with salted butter.
notes:
Web summary (barefootcontessa.com). From Ina Garten's Cooking for Jeffrey. A soda-bread style loaf leavened chemically rather than with yeast, so there is no proving: the buttermilk and the stout both provide acid for the baking soda. The Guinness contributes malt depth and colour alongside the whole wheat and dark brown sugar, and quick oats give the crumb its texture. It starts in a hot oven and drops to a lower temperature so the outside sets before the dense centre finishes.

Note on the source: barefootcontessa.com has no comments section

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Food Network's copy of this bread carries 90-plus five-star reviews, and your own internal-temp note (180-190°F) already covers the one real failure point: an underbaked center.

name: Italian Chocolate Mousse (from Lizzie and Hazan)
ingredients:
9 oz. (255 g) semisweet chocolate
2/3 c. (133 g) sugar
6 eggs, separated
1/4 c. (62 g) fresh OJ

directions:
-Melt chocolate. 
-Beat egg yolks and sugar until pale yellow and thick (it takes a while!). Mix in melted chocolate, OJ (by hand).
-Whip the cream in cold bowl until stiff, then fold into chocolate mixture. Wash and dry beaters.
-Whip the egg whites until they form stiff peaks, then fold mixture. Gently combine.
-Spoon into goblets or custard cups.

description: Lizzie says she's had good results with Scharffenberger chocolate, not Ghirardelli. And remember: egg whites beat well when room temperature; cream when chilled.

name: Italian Fennel Sausage
ingredients:
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) Diamond Crystal kosher salt or 1 teaspoon fine sea salt
1 ½ teaspoons (3.0 g) coarsely ground fennel seed
½ to 1 tablespoon (2.7-5.4 g) red-pepper flakes
1 pound (454 g) ground pork (20 to 25 percent fat by weight)
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) pounded or very finely grated garlic
1 teaspoon (4.9 g) dry white wine or vermouth
Extra-virgin olive oil
directions:
Line a baking sheet with parchment paper; set aside.

In a large bowl, combine salt, fennel seed and red-pepper flakes. Add pork to the spice mixture along with the garlic, and wine. Using your hands, mix thoroughly for 1 full minute, until the pork begins to appear tacky and sticks to the palm of your hand.

Heat a cast-iron pan over medium heat. Use a heaping tablespoon of pork mixture to make a small, thin sausage patty. Add a teaspoon or so of olive oil, and cook the patty for 2 to 3 minutes on each side, or until cooked through. Taste, and if needed, add salt or any other seasonings to the uncooked sausage mixture and mix to combine.

Divide and form the remaining sausage into 8 2 1/2-inch patties, placing them on the prepared baking sheet as you go. Cover, and refrigerate for 30 minutes to allow the flavors to come together. (Patties can be made ahead and covered and refrigerated or frozen at this point until ready to use.)

To cook, wipe out cast-iron pan, and return to medium heat. Add 1 tablespoon olive oil. When it shimmers, add patties in a single layer, leaving space between them. Cook 3 to 4 minutes per side, or until browned on the surface and just cooked through.

Drain sausages on paper towels, and serve hot.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (305)). Samin Nosrat's homemade bulk sausage scented with fennel, meant for pasta, pizza, Thanksgiving stuffing, soup, or fried as patties with crusty bread and olive-oil-soaked white beans. Her one insistence is fat content: ground pork at roughly 20 percent fat by weight, and 25 percent does no harm. If only lean pork is available, she suggests having the butcher swap a couple of ounces of it for ground pork belly or bacon.

What readers report: With only sixteen comments the discussion is small but converges on one issue: salt. The top note (27 votes) explains the recipe assumes Diamond Crystal kosher, and that Morton kosher should be cut to 1.5 teaspoons and table salt to 1 teaspoon. A cook who used Morton's at the full 2 teaspoons confirms it came out too salty (16 votes), and another simply says to halve the salt next time. On substitutions, turkey and grass-fed beef both worked for people avoiding pork, though one commenter asks pointedly whether the turkey version had fat added. A 9-vote note suggests grinding your own pork butt or stew meat and freely adding garlic and onion powder, paprika, thyme, oregano or marjoram, and anise in place of some fennel. One tip: shape patties in a cheap circular cookie mold, filled halfway so they are not too thick.

name: Italian Lemon-Ricotta Cake
ingredients:
3 tablespoons (43 g) unsalted butter
1 quart (976 g) whole milk
1 3/4 cups (292 g) semolina flour
1/2 teaspoon (1.4 g) kosher salt
1 3/4 cups (350 g) sugar
1 large or 2 small lemons
4 large eggs
1 pound (454 g) (2 cups) fresh ricotta cheese, strained
Confectioners’ sugar for sprinkling
Raspberry sauce (see recipe)
directions:
Preheat the oven to 325. Butter an 11-inch round cake pan.

Heat the milk in a medium saucepan over medium heat until simmering, then whisk in the semolina and salt. Boil, stirring constantly, for 2 minutes. Remove the saucepan from the heat, and stir in the sugar and butter until combined. Transfer the batter to a bowl to cool it down to warm, stirring frequently to prevent a skin from forming.

Zest the lemons, using only the yellow part, and stir into the batter. Beat in the eggs, one at a time, until combined. Beat in the ricotta.

Pour the batter into the pan, and bake until set and golden in places, about 1 hour. Transfer the pan to a rack to cool, and sprinkle with confectioners’ sugar while still hot. Once the cake has cooled, sprinkle with confectioners’ sugar once more, then serve.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (1,468)). A very short headnote: this is migliaccio, a Carnival-season lemon and ricotta cheesecake from Italy. What sets it apart from a standard cheesecake is a base built on semolina flour, which gives it a noticeably lighter texture.

What readers report: The loudest complaint (235 votes) is the pan size: the recipe calls for an 11-inch cake pan that few home cooks own, and commenters report a 10-inch pan works with slightly longer baking. The second theme is lemon intensity, with repeated votes for more than the recipe specifies. One cook used the zest of three lemons in a 10-inch springform to great success at a dinner party (110), another added the zest of two large lemons plus a tablespoon of fresh juice for a more lemony batter (91), and a third went to four lemons' zest and still found the result only good rather than outstanding (63). A pizzeria owner (145 votes) shares a Naples-inspired version tuned over months using fine semolina. One cook suggests using leftover whey from homemade ricotta in the batter. Several appreciate that the cake is crustless.

claude_opt.changes: Bake in a 10-inch pan (most home cooks lack an 11-inch) a few minutes longer. Bump lemon to zest of 2 large lemons plus 1 tbsp juice, the most successful reader tweak, well short of riskier 3-4-lemon versions.

name: Italian Meatballs
ingredients:
1/2 lb. (227 g) beef, pork, lamb, or veal finely ground
3 slices toast (or less) (3/4 c.)
2 T. (7.5 g) chopped parsley
1 sm. clove garlic finely chopped
1 egg
2 T. (14 g) grated cheese
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
1/4 t. (0.6 g) black pepper
directions: Soak toast in cold water for 7-8 minutes. Press dry. Combine with other ingredients in bowl. Work together until thoroughly blended. Form into 12 medium size balls, fry slowly in 2 T. shortening until golden brown on all sides. Add to sauce.

claude_opt.changes: Fry in olive oil rather than shortening. Mix just until the ingredients come together, not until fully worked, so the meatballs stay tender instead of dense.

name: Italian Wedding Soup
ingredients:
For the meatballs:
3/4 pound (340 g) ground chicken
1/2 pound (227 g) chicken sausage, casings removed
2/3 cup (30 g) fresh white bread crumbs
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) minced garlic (2 cloves)
3 tablespoons (11 g) chopped fresh parsley leaves
1/4 cup (22 g) freshly grated Pecorino Romano
1/4 cup (22 g) freshly grated Parmesan, plus extra for serving
3 tablespoons (46 g) milk
1 extra-large egg, lightly beaten
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
For the soup:
2 tablespoons (27 g) good olive oil
1 cup (160 g) minced yellow onion
1 cup (128 g) diced carrots (3 carrots), cut into 1/4 inch pieces
3/4 cup (76 g) diced celery (2 stalks), cut into 1/4 inch pieces
10 cups (2.4 kg) homemade chicken stock
1/2 cup (118 g) dry white wine
1 cup (100 g) small pasta such as tubetini or stars
1/4 cup (11 g) minced fresh dill
12 ounces (340 g) baby spinach, washed and trimmed
directions:
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F.

For the meatballs, place the ground chicken, sausage, bread crumbs, garlic, parsley, Pecorino, Parmesan, milk, egg, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper in a bowl and combine gently with a fork. With a teaspoon, drop 1 to 1 1/4-inch meatballs onto a sheet pan lined with parchment paper. (You should have about 40 meatballs. They don't have to be perfectly round.) Bake for 30 minutes, until cooked through and lightly browned. Set aside.

In the meantime, for the soup, heat the olive oil over medium-low heat in a large heavy-bottomed soup pot. Add the onion, carrots, and celery and saute until softened, 5 to 6 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add the chicken stock and wine and bring to a boil. Add the pasta to the simmering broth and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, until the pasta is tender. Add the fresh dill and then the meatballs to the soup and simmer for 1 minute. Taste for salt and pepper. Stir in the fresh spinach and cook for 1 minute, until the spinach is just wilted. Ladle into soup bowls and sprinkle each serving with extra grated Parmesan.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten's lighter take on the classic, using ground chicken plus chicken sausage for the meatballs instead of the usual beef and pork mixture. The sausage carries the fat and seasoning the lean ground chicken lacks, and milk-moistened fresh breadcrumbs keep the meatballs tender. The meatballs are baked rather than browned in the pot, so the broth stays clear, and dill rather than basil is the finishing herb.

What readers report: The meatballs get most of the attention, and a number of cooks report making a double batch to bake and freeze on their own, apart from the soup. The dill is the point people insist on: those who left it out or substituted basil say the soup lost the character that distinguishes this version. Substitutions reported as successful include ground turkey for the chicken, sweet or hot Italian sausage in place of chicken sausage, and orzo, rice, escarole or kale where the tubetini and spinach are called for. It is repeatedly cited as a crowd and cold-weather recipe.

Note on the source: no vote counts shown

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Dill, not basil, is already the herb specified, matching what commenters insist is essential to this version, and baking rather than browning the meatballs already keeps the broth clear.

name: Janice Okun's Buffalo chicken wings
ingredients:
Wings:
24 chicken wings, about four pounds
Salt, if desired
Freshly ground pepper
4 cups (616 g) peanut, vegetable, or corn oil
4 tablespoons (57 g) butter
2 to 5 tablespoons (30-75 g) (one 2 1/2 ounce bottle) Franks Louisiana Red Hot Sauce
1 tablespoon (15 g) white vinegar Blue-cheese dressing (see recipe)
Celery sticks

Blue cheese dressing:
1 cup (220 g) homemade mayonnaise (see recipe) 
2 tablespoons (20 g) finely chopped onion 
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) finely minced garlic 
4 cup (240 g) finely chopped parsley
1/2 cup (115 g) sour cream 
1 tablespoon (15 g) lemon juice 
1 tablespoon (15 g) white vinegar 
1 cup (135 g) crumbled blue cheese
Salt to taste, if desired 
Freshly ground pepper to taste
Cayenne pepper to taste

Mayonnaise:
1 egg yolk
Salt, if desired
Freshly ground pepper 
1 teaspoon (5.2 g) imported mustard, such as Dijon or Düsseldorf 
1 teaspoon (5.1 g) vinegar or lemon juice
1 cup (216 g) peanut, vegetable or olive oil
directions:
**Wings:**
Cut off and discard the small tip of each wing. Cut the main wing bone and second wing bone at the joint. Sprinkle the wings with salt, it de sired, and pepper to taste.

Heat the oil in a deep-fat fryer or large casserole. When it is quite hot, add half of the wings and cook about 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. When the chicken wings are golden brown and crisp, remove them and drain well.

Add the remaining wings and cook about 10 minutes or until golden brown and crisp. Drain well.

Melt the butter in a sauce pan and add two to five tablespoons of the hot sauce and vinegar. Put the chicken wings on a warm serving platter and pour the butter mixture over them. Serve with blue cheese dressing and celery sticks.

**Dressing:**
Combine all of the ingredients in a bowl 
Chill for an hour or longer 

**Mayonnaise:**
Place the yolk in a mixing bowl and add salt, if desired, and pepper to taste, mustard and vinegar or lemon juice. Beat vigorously for a second or two with a wire whisk or electric beater.

Start adding the oil gradually, beating continuously with whisk or electric beater. Continue beating and adding oil until all of it is used. Yields about 1 cup.
notes:
Web summary (app.ckbk.com). The recipe is Craig Claiborne's transcription of Buffalo News food editor Janice Okun's wings, published in his 1982 book A Feast Made for Laughter. It is the canonical Anchor Bar formula: whole wings split and deep-fried bare - no batter, no breading - so the skin crisps and renders, then tossed in melted butter cut with Frank's Louisiana hot sauce and a splash of vinegar. Celery and a homemade blue-cheese dressing built on scratch mayonnaise are served alongside to cool the heat.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS - ckbk is a subscription cookbook library and carries no ratings or reader comments.

Note on the source: Identity confirmed: ckbk's ingredient head matches the family card exactly (24 chicken wings, about four pounds, deep-fried, with the blue-cheese dressing and homemade-mayonnaise sub-recipes the family card also carries). Note ckbk is paywalled, so the full method and headnote were not retrievable and the headnote above is reconstructed from the confirmed recipe identity rather than quoted commentary. Free full-text runner-ups a human could use instead: https://www.bigoven.com/recipe/janice-okuns-buffalo-chicken-wings/102022 and https://www.astray.com/recipes/?show=Janice+okun's+buffalo+chicken+wings

claude_opt.changes: Every modern crispy-wing recipe (Washington Post, Kitchn) dusts wings in cornstarch before frying; this classic bare-fry Anchor Bar method skips it. Toss wings in 2-3 T cornstarch first for crunchier skin.

name: Jell-O Jigglers
ingredients:
2 family-size pkgs. (8-serv. size) or 4 small pkgs. (4-serv. size) Jell-O Gelatin.
2 1/2 c. (592 g) boiling water or apple juice
directions: Completely dissolve gelatin in boiling water or apple juice. Pour into 13x9 inch pan. Chill until firm, about 3 hours. To unmold: dip pan in warm water for about 15 seconds. Cut into squares or use cookie cutters. Lift from pan.

A brief dip of the pan in warm water loosens the slab so the shapes release cleanly.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS - the Kraft Heinz brand page carries no ratings or reader comments.

Note on the source: Exact match: Kraft's page and the family card both specify 2 packages (8-serving size) gelatin to 2 1/2 cups boiling water, 13x9 pan, warm-water dip to unmold. The family card additionally allows apple juice in place of water, a variation Kraft has published elsewhere.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. This is Kraft's own tested ratio — half the normal water for a firm, cuttable set — and no review anywhere flags a problem with quantities or timing.

name: Jiffy Potato Casserole
ingredients:
1 can cream of potato soup (10 3/4 oz.)
1 can cream of celery soup (same)
1 c. (244 g) milk
8 oz. (227 g) sour cream
1 (2 lb.) bag frozen hash brown potatoes, thawed
salt and pepper
grated cheddar cheese
directions:

Combine soups, milk, and sour cream. Mix until smooth. Add potatoes and salt and pepper. Mix lightly but thoroughly.

description: Mom makes this frequently, including for Christmas 2020.

name: Jim Lahey's No Knead Pizza Dough
ingredients:
500 grams (17 1/2 ounces or about 3 3/4 cups) all-purpose flour, plus more for shaping the dough
1 gram (1/4 teaspoon) active dry yeast
16 grams (2 teaspoons) fine sea salt
350 grams (1 1/2 cups) water
directions:
In a medium bowl, thoroughly blend the flour, yeast, and salt. Add the water and, with a wooden spoon or your hands, mix thoroughly.

Cover the bowl with plastic wrap or a kitchen towel and allow it to rise at room temperature (about 72F) for 18 hours or until it has more than doubled. It will take longer in a chilly room and less time in a very warm one.

Flour a work surface and scrape out the dough. Divide it into 4 equal parts and shape them: For each portion start with the right side of the dough and pull it toward the center; then do the same with the left, the top then the bottom. (The order doesn't actually matter; what you want is four folds.) Shape each portion into a round and turn seam side down. Mold the dough into a neat circular mound. The mounds should not be sticky; if they are, dust with more flour.

If you don't intend to use the dough right away, wrap the balls individually in plastic and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Return to room temperature by leaving them out on the counter, covered in a damp cloth, for 2 to 3 hours before needed.

Note: Don't freeze the dough, but you can store it in the refrigerator, wrapped in plastic, for up to three days. In effect, when you're set to use it, you have your own ready-made dough.

Shaping the Disk (Method 1): Take one ball of the dough and generously flour it, your hands and the work surface. Then press it down and gently stretch it out to 6 to 8 inches. Very carefully continue the process, massaging it into roundish disk of 10 to 12 inches, stroking and shaping with the palms of your hands and with your fingers. Don't handle it more than necessary, though you want some of the gas bubbles to remain in the dough. It should look slightly blistered. Flour the peel and lift the disk onto the center. The dough is now ready to be topped.

Shaping the Disk (Method 2): Take one ball of dough and generously flour it, your hands, and the work surface. Then press it down and gently stretch it out to 6 to 8 inches. Supporting the disk with your knuckles toward the outer edge and lifting it above the work surface, keep stretching the dough by rotating it with your knuckles, gently pulling it wider and wider until the disk reaches 10 to 12 inches. Set the disk on a well-floured peel. It is now ready to be topped.
description:
RM 3/13: 4% sugar creates faster browning.
RM 2026: No longer own a baking steel or stone — got rid of them after buying the Ooni. This now has to run in the Ooni or in cast iron, and both the hydration and the sugar were tuned for neither.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.3 (18) / 64 Reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt introduces Jim Lahey's pizza dough from the book My Pizza as the pizza counterpart to the no-knead bread method Lahey and Mark Bittman popularized in 2006. The point of the long room-temperature rise, he explains, is that enzymes gradually chop the flour's large proteins into shorter pieces that link up into stretchy gluten sheets on their own, so you get the structure of a well-kneaded dough without kneading and without the oxidation kneading causes. Lahey himself adds a note saying the flour matters less than the handling: either bread or all-purpose is fine, but the dough should be stretched gently so it keeps its blistered, gassy character, and the balls should only be shaped just before topping. He offers two shaping approaches, one flat on the counter and a faster one rotating the disk on your knuckles.

What readers report: Hydration is the recurring complaint, and cooks disagree on which direction it is wrong. One repeatedly added extra water to get a workable dough and also found it tore easily when stretching; another called it 'pizza soup,' too salty and too wet, needing a lot of added flour after it tripled at room temperature in 12 hours. Others accept the stickiness as normal, noting it barely matters since you hardly handle the dough. The 1 gram of yeast is widely questioned; one cook using active dry rather than instant used a heaping quarter teaspoon, and one who accidentally used quick-rise found the dough more than doubled in 6 hours, portioned it then and refrigerated it 12 hours with good results. Readers also note the video says 8 to 9 hours of rise against the recipe's 18, and that the video assumes shaped balls resting a couple of hours under a damp cloth, a step missing from the written recipe.

Note on the source: 'Load More reviews' present, so only part of the 64 reviews is in the paste; a 'Featured Tweaks' block also appears above the review list and its entries are included. Several comments end with 'Read More' and may be truncated. Readers dispute the recipe's 1 g yeast and the rise time versus the linked video.

Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Recipe from Robert's original message of 2/4/2013; the cook's note is his reply to himself in the same thread on 3/2/2013 (received 3/3/2013 UTC).

Web summary (jamesbeard.org). Jim Lahey's no-knead pizza dough from My Pizza (with Rick Flaste, Clarkson Potter, 2012), reprinted by the James Beard Foundation. An 18-hour room-temperature ferment on a single gram of yeast does the work kneading would otherwise do: the gluten organises itself and the long rise builds the flavour. The dough is then divided and shaped into four rounds by folding in from four sides, and can be held wrapped in the fridge for up to three days.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS on the page.

Note on the source: Baker's-percentage match to the family copy exactly: 500 g flour, 1 g active dry yeast, 16 g fine sea salt, 350 g water - 70 percent hydration, 3.2 percent salt. The family copy adds the US equivalents (17 1/2 oz / about 3 3/4 cups flour; 1/4 tsp yeast; 2 tsp salt; 1 1/2 cups water) and Robert's own 4 percent sugar variation for faster browning, which is not in the original. Note Robert's 2026 note that he no longer owns a stone or steel and now bakes these in an Ooni or cast iron. Alternate copies: https://bakingsteel.com/blogs/recipes/jim-laheys-no-knead-dough and https://leitesculinaria.com/89307/recipes-pizza-dough.html

Merged September 2026: this entry absorbed a duplicate previously filed as "Pizza Crust for a Baking Stone or Steel". Every cook's note from both copies is kept above.

claude_opt.changes: Skip the sugar for the Ooni: 900F browns the crust in under 90 seconds on its own, and added sugar risks scorching before it cooks through. For cast iron, pre-cook the dough dry and oiled 1-2 min before topping.

name: Julia Child's Berry Clafoutis
ingredients:
Butter for pan
1 and 1/4 cups (305 g) whole or 2 percent milk
⅔ cup (133 g) granulated sugar, divided
3 eggs
1 tablespoon (13 g) vanilla extract
⅛ teaspoon (0.8 g) salt
1 cup (120 g) flour
1 pint (288 g) (2 generous cups) blackberries or blueberries, rinsed and well drained
Powdered sugar in a shaker
directions:
Heat oven to 350 degrees. Lightly butter a medium-size flameproof baking dish at least 1 1/2 inches deep.

Place the milk, 1/3 cup granulated sugar, eggs, vanilla, salt and flour in a blender. Blend at top speed until smooth and frothy, about 1 minute.

Pour a 1/4-inch layer of batter in the baking dish. Turn on a stove burner to low and set dish on top for a minute or two, until a film of batter has set in the bottom of the dish. Remove from heat.

Spread berries over the batter and sprinkle on the remaining 1/3 cup granulated sugar. Pour on the rest of the batter and smooth with the back of a spoon. Place in the center of the oven and bake about 50 minutes, until top is puffed and browned and a tester plunged into its center comes out clean.

Sprinkle with powdered sugar just before serving. (Clafoutis need not be served hot, but should still be warm. It will sink slightly as it cools.)
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (5,035)). Julia Moskin presents this as a quietly elegant dessert that is far easier than it looks, easy enough to assemble while the main course finishes in the oven. Fresh berries matter, and it should go to the table warm. Blueberries or blackberries are specified but the batter takes whatever fruit is in season.

What readers report: Two arguments dominate. The first is what to call it: a 376-vote note says this is clafoutis rather than flan and warns that clafoutis often turns out too eggy and custardy, fixable with a little baking powder; a 263-vote comment doubts the Julia Child attribution altogether, pointing out that a recipe permitting 2 percent milk is not hers, and others agree it sits somewhere between flan and clafoutis. The second is whether the criticism is fair: a 630-vote comment says the negative notes are overblown, the recipe works as written, and reducing sugar is fine if you prefer. The single most-voted comment (751) simply supplies a rival apricot-and-almond clafoutis from Richard Olney. A 736-vote note reports it looks dull but silenced the table once served slightly cooled in small dishes.

Note on the source: comments dispute both the name and the Julia Child attribution

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

Data fix (Sept 2026): the card calls for 1 tablespoon of vanilla extract, where most clafoutis recipes use 1 teaspoon. Left as written - it may well be deliberate - but worth checking against the source before baking.

Data fix (Oct 2026), at Robert's request: derived weight for 1 1/4 cups milk corrected from 61 g to 305 g; only the 1/4 cup had been converted

name: Julia Child's Reine De Saba (Queen of Sheba) Cake
ingredients:
3 ounces (85 g) semisweet chocolate,
plus
1 ounce (28 g) unsweetened chocolate
2 tablespoons (30 g) dark rum or 2 tablespoons strong coffee
1/2 cup (114 g) unsalted butter, at room temperature
1/2 cup (100 g) granulated sugar
3 egg yolks
3 egg whites
1/4 teaspoon (0.8 g) cream of tartar
1 pinch salt
2 tablespoons (25 g) granulated sugar
1/3 cup (48 g) blanched almond (pulverized in blender or food processor with 2 tablespoons granulated sugar)
1/4 teaspoon (1.1 g) almond extract
1/2 cup (56 g) cake flour

Chocolate Butter Icing:
1 oz. (28 g) semisweet chocolate finely chopped
1 T. (14 g) rum
3 T. (43 g) unsalted butter, room temperarure
directions:
Directions: 1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Set the oven rack in lower middle level. 2. In a saucepan over low heat, melt the chocolate in the rum or coffee. Set aside. In a mixing bowl, cut butter into pieces and cream it. 3. When soft and fluffy, add sugar and beat 1 minute. Beat in egg yolks until well blended. 4. In another bowl, beat egg whites until foamy. Beat in cream of tartar and salt and continue beating until soft peaks are formed. Gradually beat in 2 tablespoons sugar and continue beating until stiff, shiny peaks are formed. Blend melted chocolate and coffee or rum into yolk mixture, then add almonds and almond extract. 5. Stir a quarter of the egg whites into the chocolate using a rubber spatula. Scoop the rest of the whites over chocolate and, alternating with sprinkles of flour, rapidly and delicately fold in the egg whites. Turn batter into buttered and floured 8-by-1 1/2-inch round cake pan, tilting it in all directions up to the rim all around. Set in preheated oven. Bake 25 minutes. 6. Cake is done when puffed to the top and a toothpick inserted 2 to 3 inches from edge comes out clean. The center should move slightly when the pan is gently shaken. Remove pan to a rack and let cool 15 minutes. Unmold onto rack. Let cool 2 hours before storing or icing.

Icing: 
Combine chocolate and rum in small metal bowl.  Set bowl over small saucepan of barely simmering water and stir until melted and smooth. Remove bowl from over water. Using wooden spoon, beat in butter, 1 T. at a time, until icing is smooth. Place bowl over medium bowl filled with ice water. Continue to beat until icing is cool and thickened to spreading consistency.

Place cake on platter. Scrape icing onto top center. Using small offset spatula, spread icing evenly and thinly over top and sides of cake.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. The trickiest step in this cake — testing doneness 2-3 inches from the edge so the center stays jiggly and creamy, not fully set — is already specified correctly.

name: Key Lime Pie
ingredients:
10 whole graham crackers
1/2 teaspoon (1.4 g) kosher salt
3 tablespoons (38 g) granulated sugar
2.5 ounces (71 g) melted butter, cooled
14 ounces (397 g) sweetened condensed milk
4 egg yolks
4 ounces (113 g) freshly squeezed key lime juice (from approximately 20 key limes)
1 tablespoon (6.0 g) key lime zest, plus more for decoration
6 ounces (170 g) heavy cream
2 tablespoons (25 g) confectioner's sugar
1/4 cup (58 g) mascarpone cheese (optional)
directions:
1. Preheat oven to 375°F. Place the graham crackers in the bowl of a food processor with the salt and sugar. Process for approximately 30 seconds, until the grahams are uniform, small crumbs. Add the melted butter and pulse until incorporated. Press the mixture into the bottom and sides of the springform pan (the sides of the crust should only be about 1 1/2 inches). Chill the crust in the fridge for 15 minutes, then bake for 10. Allow the crust to cool completely. Lower the oven to 325°F.

2. In the bowl of the food processor, combine the sweetened condensed milk, egg yolks, key lime juice, and zest. run the processor for 10 seconds, then stop, scrape down the sides, and run again for another 10 seconds. Scrape the mixture into the bottom of the cooled crust. Bake at 325°F for 14 to 17 minutes, until it is firm but still jiggles in the center (watch it closely, this pie will set up very quickly). Allow it to cool to room temperature, then place the pie in the fridge to chill down completely, for at least four hours.

3. When ready to serve, release the sides of the springform pan and remove. Combine heavy cream and confectioner's sugar in a bowl and whip with a whisk (this may also be done in a stand mixer fitted with a whisk attachment) until the mixture reaches a medium peak. If using, add the mascarpone and whisk until smooth and thick. Pipe or top the pie with the cream mixture and sprinkle the top with key lime zest. Serve immediately.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 5.0 (4) / 15 Reviews). Lauren Weisenthal presents this as a deliberately plain, classic version where the short ingredient list means each component has to be good. Her main argument is for freshly squeezed and zested Key limes over bottled juice or concentrate, which is what gives the filling its sharp, clean tartness, and for building the graham crust yourself rather than buying one, since it takes little effort and tastes far better. The salty-sweet crust is meant to cut the richness of the condensed-milk-and-yolk filling, and a mascarpone-enriched whipped cream finishes it. Serious Eats notes the recipe was cross-tested in 2023 and its measurements tightened up.

What readers report: The most detailed feedback concerns scale: the recipe is built for an 8-inch springform, and cooks using a 9-inch pan found both crust and filling too skimpy. One doubled both for a standard 9-inch plate with good results; another added an extra yolk, four more ounces of condensed milk and nearly three-quarters cup of juice, baked about 25 minutes, and still found the pie somewhat jiggly. That cook's scaled-up crust slumped badly on the blind bake, fixed by freezing the shell 30 minutes, lining it with heavy-duty foil and filling it with pie weights. Regular Persian limes are repeatedly reported to work in place of Key limes. A Florida reader says the traditional version skips baking entirely since the juice sets the yolks. Several readers were confused about whether the mascarpone belongs in the filling or the topping.

Note on the source: 'Load More reviews' present, so only 9 of 15 reviews are in the paste. Two long comments end with 'Read More' and may be cut off. Reader Susan flags an apparent inconsistency in where mascarpone is listed; in this paste it appears under the topping.

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

ahead: Allow it to cool to room temperature, then place the pie in the fridge to chill down completely, for at…

claude_opt.changes: Keep the 8-inch springform as written. Readers who scaled to a 9-inch got a thin crust and filling even after increasing yolks, juice, and condensed milk -- the pan swap, not the ratios, is the real failure point.

name: Korean Beef Bulgogi Burritos
ingredients:
For the Marinated Beef:
1/3 cup (80ml) soy sauce
3 tablespoons (45g) sugar
1 tablespoon (15ml) toasted sesame oil
1/4 of an Asian pear, peeled, cored, and coarsely grated (about 1/4 cup; see note)
4 medium cloves garlic, minced or grated
2 teaspoons (7g) minced or grated ginger, from about one 1-inch piece
1 1/2 pounds (700g) boneless English-style beef short ribs, ribeye, or sirloin, very thinly sliced against the grain to no more than 1/8 inch thick (see note)
3 scallions, white and light green parts only, sliced into 2-inch lengths
1/4 of a medium yellow onion, halved crosswise, then thinly sliced pole to pole
2 tablespoons (30ml) neutral-flavored oil (such as grapeseed or peanut), divided, plus more as needed
For the Burritos:
1 cup (235ml) sour cream
1 tablespoon (15ml) Korean gochujang chili paste
4 cups (700g) hot cooked short-grain rice
4 large flour tortillas (12-inch recommended), warmed
Chopped kimchi, for stuffing burritos
Danmuji (Korean Pickled Daikon Radish), for stuffing burritos
2 cups (178 g) finely shredded red cabbage (from 1 head)
2 cups cilantro leaves and tender stems (2 ounces; 60g)
3 scallions, white and light green parts only, thinly sliced
Lime wedges, for serving
directions:
For the Marinated Beef: In a large bowl, whisk together soy sauce, sugar, sesame oil, Asian pear, garlic, and ginger. When sugar has dissolved, add beef, scallion, and onion slices to bowl and toss to coat. Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour or up to overnight.

In a large cast iron or heavy stainless steel skillet, heat 1 tablespoon (15ml) oil over medium-high heat until shimmering. Working in batches, add beef and onions, working quickly to arrange them in a flat, even layer against bottom of skillet; try not to overcrowd pan. Cook on one side for 1 minute, then flip and cook second side until browned and crisp in spots, about 2 minutes longer. Transfer cooked beef and onions to a plate and repeat with remaining beef, onions, and oil.

For the Burritos: In a small bowl, stir together sour cream and gochujang. Spread rice onto warm tortillas, then top with a layer of beef and onions, followed by kimchi, a few pickled daikon radish strips, red cabbage, cilantro, scallions, and gochujang sour cream. Roll tightly, folding sides of tortilla in as you go. (Wrapping the burritos in foil will make them portable and less messy to eat.) Serve with lime wedges.
description: Will and Lene recommend
notes:
If you're slicing the beef yourself, it helps to freeze it slightly first and use a very sharp slicing knife. Even easier is to find the beef presliced at a Korean or Japanese market. If you can't find Asian pear, you can use about 2 tablespoons (30ml) pineapple juice to get a similar tenderizing effect. However, in that case, don't marinate the beef for more than 2 hours, as pineapple can over-tenderize the meat. If using beef ribeye, you can omit the Asian pear and the pineapple, as it is a naturally tender cut.

Web summary (Serious Eats, 2 Reviews (no star rating shown)). Emily and Matt Clifton take the flavors of Korean bulgogi and rebuild them as a burrito, partly for portability and partly because the fillings make a drab brown meat into something colorful. They explain that bulgogi is thinly sliced marinated beef seared fast, traditionally ribeye but also good with boneless English-cut short ribs or sirloin, and that the slices should be an eighth of an inch or thinner and cut against the grain so the muscle fibers are short. For the leaner cuts they add grated Asian pear to the soy-sugar marinade because its calpain enzyme tenderizes; pineapple juice substitutes in a pinch but acts so much more aggressively that the meat turns mushy past about two hours. They also warn that 10-inch tortillas are too small for the load of rice, kimchi, turmeric-pickled daikon, cabbage, cilantro and gochujang sour cream, so they call for 12-inch ones warmed between damp paper towels, and they suggest making the daikon pickle a few days ahead.

What readers report: Only two reader comments exist and neither is a report from someone who cooked the recipe as written. Both are speculative riffs on the wrapper rather than the beef: one reader asked whether a nori wrap could stand in for the rice and flour tortilla, and the other described a variation built on coconut-milk rice with mango in a seaweed wrap. There are no corrections to quantities or timings, no confirmed substitutions, no reports of a step that trips people up, and no disagreement with the authors' method. Treat the comment section here as carrying essentially no practical cooking signal.

Note on the source: Only 2 reviews and no star rating shown; neither commenter appears to have made the recipe, so comment signal is very thin. Headnote material is strong.

name: Lamb and Chickpea Curry
ingredients:
2 pounds (907 g) boneless lamb shoulder (not tied), gristle and fat removed, and 1-inch diced
1/4 cup Madras curry powder
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) ground paprika
1 teaspoon (2.1 g) ground cumin
1 teaspoon (1.1 g) roughly minced fresh rosemary leaves
1 teaspoon (1.1 g) roughly minced fresh thyme leaves
1/2 teaspoon (1.0 g) ground fennel seeds
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
1/2 cup (108 g) good olive oil
1 cup (160 g) chopped yellow onion
1 tablespoon (6.0 g) chopped fresh ginger
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) minced garlic (2 cloves)
2 cups (480 g) chicken stock, or vegetable stock, both preferably homemade
1 (13.5-ounce) can coconut milk
1/2 cup (118 g) dry white wine
1/2 cup (131 g) tomato paste (6 ounces)
1/2 cup (106 g) dark brown sugar, lightly packed
3 tablespoons (60 g) pure maple syrup
2 tablespoons (32 g) harissa
1 cup (128 g) (3/4-inch-diced) carrots (4 carrots)
1 cup (101 g) (3/4-inch-diced) celery (2 large stalks)
1/2 cup (72 g) golden raisins
4 cups (656 g) canned chickpeas, rinsed and drained (45 ounces)
Steamed basmati rice, for serving
Plain whole milk Greek yogurt, for serving
Whole fresh parsley or cilantro leaves, for serving
directions:
Place the cubed lamb in a large bowl. In a medium bowl, combine the curry powder, paprika, cumin, rosemary, thyme, fennel, 2 tablespoons salt, and 1 teaspoon pepper. Add the seasonings to the lamb, toss well to coat, and set aside for 15 to 30 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat the oil in a large (11-inch) Dutch oven, such as Le Creuset, over medium heat. Add the onion and ginger and saute for 5 minutes, until the onion is translucent. Add the garlic and cook for one minute. Raise the heat to medium high, add the lamb and all the seasonings in the bowl, and saute for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lamb is evenly browned. Add the chicken stock, coconut milk, wine, tomato paste, brown sugar, maple syrup, and harissa. Bring to a boil, lower the heat, and simmer, partially covered, for 1 hour, stirring occasionally.

Add the carrots, celery, raisins, chickpeas, and 2 teaspoons salt, bring to a boil, lower the heat, and simmer, partially covered, for another 30 minutes. Serve hot in shallow bowls with the rice, a dollop of yogurt, and a sprinkling of parsley.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). An Ina Garten braise, marked intermediate on Food Network. Diced lamb shoulder is first coated in a heavy spice mixture built on a quarter cup of Madras curry powder with paprika, cumin, fennel and fresh rosemary and thyme, then browned and braised in stock and coconut milk. The long braise is what turns the sinewy shoulder tender and lets the spices settle into the sauce. Dark brown sugar, maple syrup and golden raisins push the sauce sweet, with harissa and tomato paste pulling back against it; the chickpeas go in near the end so they hold shape.

Note on the source: newer recipe, no comments or rating posted yet

claude_opt.changes: A closely related Ina lamb curry with the same curry powder/coconut milk/harissa/raisin base ran too sweet; one cook cut the brown sugar by a third and added extra harissa to balance it.

name: Lasagna
ingredients:
1 lb. (454 g) sweet Italian sausage
1/2 lb. (227 g) ground beef
1/2 c. (80 g) finely chopped onions
2 cloves garlic, crushed

2 T. (25 g) sugar
1 T. (18 g) salt
1/2 t. (1.0 g) fennel seeds
1/4 t. (0.6 g) pepper
1/4 c. (15 g) chopped parsley
1 t. (0.5 g) basil
1 35 oz. (992 g) can Italian style tomatoes
2 6 oz. (170 g) cans tomato paste

1 T. (18 g) salt
3/4 lb. (340 g) curly lasagna noodles

2 lb. (907 g) ricotta
1 egg
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
3/4 lb (340 g) mozarella sliced thin
3/4 c. (68 g) Parmesan cheese grated
directions:
1. Remove sausage from casing and chop in frying pan. Over medium heat, saute meat, onion, and garlic stirring frequently until well browned (15-20 minutes).
2. Add sugar, 1 T. salt, fennel, basil, pepper, and 1/2 of the parsley. Mix.
3. Add tomatoes, paste, and 1/2 c. water, mashing tomatoes with a wooden spoon. Bring to boil, reduce heat, and simmer, covered, stirring occasionally until thick (1.5 hours).
4. In a large kettle, bring 3 qts. salted water to a boil. Add lasagna noodles, 2 or 3 at a time; return to boiling and boil 10 minutes. Drain and rinse with cold with cold water and dry on paper towels. Preheat oven to 375. 
5. In medium bowl, mix ricotta, egg, remaining parsley, and 1/2 t. salt.
6. In a 9x13x2 inch baking dish, spoon 1 1/2 c. sauce, lay 6 lasagna noodles, 1/2 of ricotta mixture, 1/3 of the mozzarella, then half of the remaining sauce, and sprinkle with 1/4 c. of parmesan.
7. Repeat layering, and top with the rest of the mozzarella and parmesan.
8. Cover with foil and bake 25 minutes at 375 degrees. Remove foil and bake 25 minutes longer. Cool 10-15 minutes. Cut and serve.
description: 12/23 Delicious as always. Pasta rolled to 6 seems a bit thin for 3 layers. Would be good if you were 5 or more layers of pasta. In a loaf pan, cook time was 1 hour 15 minutes to reach 165 degrees. Sprinkled olive oil on top, good.

claude_opt.changes: Fry the tomato paste with the meat for a minute before adding tomatoes and water; blooming paste in fat deepens flavor and is skipped here. Otherwise excellent, already temp-probed to 165F.

name: Lavosh
ingredients:
2½ teaspoons (7.8 g) active dry yeast
1 tablespoon (21 g) honey
2 cups (474 g) water at 100 to 115 degrees
3 cups (360 g) unbleached all-purpose flour
1 cup (120 g) (about) bread flour 
1¾ teaspoons (4.9 g) kosher salt 
1 egg white, beaten lightly 
4 tablespoons (34 g) poppy seeds, optional
4 tablespoons (36 g) sesame seeds, optional
1 tablespoon (18 g) (about) coarse salt for topping (optional)
directions:
In a large mixing bowl, dissolve yeast and honey in the water, stirring briefly. Let stand a couple of minutes.
Stir in all of the all-purpose flour, ½ cup of the bread flour and the salt.
Knead 8 to 10 minutes, adding more flour as required to make a supple dough. Place in a well greased bowl, cover with greased plastic wrap and a tea towel and let rise until doubled. Alternatively, refrigerate dough in a large, well greased plastic bag.
The dough will keep a couple of days.
Set gas grill on low.
Divide dough into 8 pieces. Gently stretch each piece into an oval and set aside while stretching the next piece.
Return to first oval and stretch until it is very thin (dough stretches without resistance when it is rested and its gluten is not excited). The ovals should be just a bit thicker than strudel dough.
Brush each portion with egg wash, then sprinkle with poppy and sesame seeds and coarse salt, if using.
Place the ovals on the grill. Cover and bake until bottoms are browned and tops begin to color. As lavosh cools, it will crisp. Serve whole or in pieces as small crackers.


On a charcoal grill, heat the coals until they turn white. Place the ovals on the outside edge of the grill, where the heat is less intense. Cover but check every few minutes; the bread should take a total of 12 to 15 minutes to cook. Try to keep the dough away from hot spots, moving the ovals to a cooler part of the grill if they start to burn.
description:
(Makes 8 large flatbreads)
This recipe has countless variations. Generally thin and crisp, these make a great dipping bread for summery spreads. You can replace some of the white flour in this recipe with white whole-wheat flour (see explanation in the preceding pita recipe).
notes:
Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

name: Leek and Potato Soup
ingredients:
2 large leeks
1 pound (454 g) medium potatoes, like yellow gold, Washington or Idaho
4 tablespoons (57 g) butter
1 cup (160 g) finely chopped onions
3 cups (720 g) fresh or canned chicken stock
2 cups (474 g) water
1 bay leaf
Salt and freshly ground pepper to taste
directions:
Leeks have a great deal of sand between the leaves and must be carefully cleaned. To do this, trim off the root end and cut off and discard the long green stems. Split the leeks lengthwise from the stem end, then turn and split them one more time. Rinse well. Separate the leaves under cold running water, then chop into 1/4-inch pieces.

Peel the potatoes and cut them into 1/4-inch cubes (about 2 cups). If done ahead put the diced potatoes in the prescribed 2 cups of water and add in the step with the broth below. This will prevent discoloration of the potatoes. 

Melt 2 tablespoons of butter in a saucepan; add the onions and the chopped leeks. Cook over medium heat, stirring, until wilted. Do not brown.

Add the chicken broth, water, potatoes, bay leaf, salt and pepper, and simmer for 30 minutes.

Remove from the heat, remove the bay leaf, add the remaining butter and stir. Adjust the seasonings and serve piping hot with croutons.

For a richer version, stir in 1/2 c. drained plain yogurt or 1/2 c. heavy cream just before serving.
description:
2/14 Used 3 leeks and 1 1/2 lbs of potatoes. Pureed half; reserved rest for chunks. Excellent

4/23 no need to cook the potatoes separately. They cook fine in the broth
notes:
Our standard. We don’t usually add cream or yogurt.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (576)). No headnote text is published for this one. The page carries only a credit line placing it in Pierre Franey's 60-Minute Gourmet column.

What readers report: The dominant thread is a genuine error in the published method: the recipe never says when to add the potatoes. The top comment (106 votes) guesses they go in with the chicken broth and water, and a 76-vote reply quotes the newspaper's own correction from December 25, 1991, which restored the omitted step to the 60-Minute Gourmet version printed a week earlier. A third commenter (29 votes) is exasperated that the omission persists years after being flagged, and asks whether the potatoes should be sauteed with the leeks or simply dropped into the liquid. Beyond that the notes are warm and brief: a 23-vote comment calls it the simplest leek-potato soup and the best. Practical tweaks include using mostly olive oil with a little butter for flavour, adding leftover ham and croutons, using extra potato, and substituting four smaller leeks when large ones are unavailable. Several note it is not pureed and are surprised how good that is.

Note on the source: no headnote published; recipe as printed omits the step for adding the potatoes, per a 1991 NYT correction quoted in comments

name: Leek Risotto with Sugar Snap Peas and Pancetta
ingredients:
1 ½ tablespoons (20 g) olive oil
3 ounces (85 g) thinly sliced pancetta or bacon
1 quart (960 g) chicken stock
3 large leeks, white parts only, split lengthwise, sliced 1/4-inch thick and thoroughly washed (about 3 cups)
2 garlic cloves, smashed
Kosher salt and black pepper
1 ½ cups (300 g) arborio rice
½ cup (118 g) dry white wine
1 tablespoon (14 g) unsalted butter
2 ounces (57 g) grated Pecorino (about 3/4 cup), plus more for topping
8 ounces (227 g) sugar snap peas, strings removed, snap peas halved lengthwise
½ cup (24 g) snipped chives (optional)
directions:
Add 1/2 tablespoon oil to a large, wide saucepan, and add the pancetta slices. (It’s OK if they’re not in one layer, as they will shrink quite a bit.) Turn heat to medium and cook, turning and rearranging the pancetta until lightly browned, crisp, and the fat has rendered, 6 to 8 minutes. Transfer with tongs to a paper towel, leaving the fat in the pan.

Add the stock and 1 cup water to a separate medium saucepan. Transfer the saucepan to a back burner and bring to a simmer over low. Keep warm on the lowest heat.

Add 1 tablespoon oil to the pan that you cooked the pancetta in, and add the leeks, garlic and 1/2 teaspoon salt. Cook, stirring, over medium-high until wilted and soft, about 5 minutes.

Add the rice and cook, stirring, until grains look slightly translucent, 2 to 3 minutes. Add wine and cook until nearly absorbed, about 1 minute.

Add a ladleful of stock to the rice — you want just enough to barely cover the surface of the rice. Cook at a lively simmer, stirring very frequently, until it’s nearly absorbed, 2 to 3 minutes. Continue adding stock in this way until rice is very creamy, but still al dente, 15 to 20 minutes total. You may not need all of the liquid, but you will probably use most of it.

Stir in the butter and cheese, and season to taste with salt and pepper. Stir in the snap peas. Add more of the remaining liquid if needed to loosen (it should be a bit soupy), and divide among four shallow bowls. Crumble the reserved pancetta over top, and sprinkle with chives, if desired.
description: 12/21 Made with bacon and frozen peas. Mild pleasant flavor. Better as a side than as a main?
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (1,425)). The headnote is mostly a risotto technique lesson: constant stirring is a myth, but the dish still needs watching. Keep the rice lightly coated in liquid and bubbling briskly, and add more stock only just before the grains threaten to catch on the pan bottom. Stir harder and more often in the second half of cooking, once the starch starts coming out, for the creamiest texture.

What readers report: The busiest thread is a rice argument. The top note (120 votes) objects that NYT risotto recipes always call for arborio and argues it is the wrong choice for a creamy result, implicitly favouring carnaroli or vialone nano. A 56-vote reply dismisses the whole debate as precious, pointing out it is all short-grain rice, and a 17-vote comment calls the fussiness elitist given pandemic-era shortages, reporting that sushi rice worked when nothing else was on the shelf. The most useful cooking tip (20 votes) is to blanch the sugar snaps for one minute and slice them crosswise rather than lengthwise, which keeps them green and crunchy without tasting raw, plus a recommendation to make extra bacon or pancetta. One cook folded in diced butternut squash successfully.

claude_opt.changes: Blanch the sugar snap peas 1 minute and slice crosswise instead of lengthwise before stirring in -- the top reader tip, keeps them green and crisp instead of tasting raw. Adds about 3 minutes.

name: Leek, Mushroom and Goat Cheese Tart
ingredients:
1 small bulb fennel
2 medium leeks, white and light green parts only, halved lengthwise and rinsed carefully to remove any dirt from inner layers
16 medium cremini or white mushrooms (about 1 pound)
1 tablespoon (14 g) plus 1 teaspoon olive oil
Salt and pepper
1 14-ounce (397 g) package puff pastry (like Dufour), defrosted according to package directions
3 eggs
8 ounces (227 g) goat cheese
directions:
Heat oven to 400 degrees. Trim fennel of green top and root end, reserving fronds, and quarter bulb from top to bottom. Using a mandoline or very sharp knife, cut fennel and leeks into paper-thin slices. Clean and slice mushrooms.

Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a skillet over medium heat; add fennel and leeks and sauté until just tender but not brown, about 6 minutes. Transfer to a bowl and set aside. Heat remaining teaspoon of oil in skillet over medium-high heat; add mushrooms and sauté until they release all their liquid and most of it boils away, about 5 minutes. Combine fennel mixture with mushrooms and sauté together briefly; season with salt and pepper. Remove pan from heat.

Unfold puff pastry onto lightly floured surface; cut in half lengthwise to form two long rectangles. Gently roll out each rectangle to approximately 5 by 14 inches and place on cookie sheet (or cut into two circles, if desired). Trim edges by 1/4 inch strips all around; set strips aside. Break one egg into a small bowl; beat slightly. Brush edges of pastry with some egg. Use trimmed strips to make a raised border on each. (Or, fold pastry edges over to form a rim.) Brush entire surface with remaining beaten egg. Prick interior of pastry all over with a fork. Bake until pale gold, about 10 minutes. If pastry has puffed up inside edge, press it down gently. Set aside.

Meanwhile, combine remaining eggs with 6 ounces goat cheese and blend until smooth. Spread onto pastry. Return to oven and bake just until set, about 4 minutes. Remove from oven and spread with mushroom-leek mixture. Crumble remaining cheese on top. Just before serving, broil tarts on low heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until tarts are warm and cheese softens. Garnish with fennel fronds.
description:
6/25 Delicious. Used Dufour again. Used 4 sm. leeks, and 12 oz of shrooms for the whole recipe. Used mild Wegmans regular goat cheese. Perfect. We cooked leeks about twice as long. Silpat made dough rolling easy. Bakes were longer too. Salted the leek mixture adequately which is important. Made a rectangle. Maybe do final cook at 400 rather than low broil. Broil left a bit of char. This a time consuming recipe, so make both halves at once. 

1/24 Delicious. Took 2+ hours to make. The salt is important and check it at the mixture stage. Dufour puff pastry was excellent. No need for parchment paper. We cooked the second one for 3 additional minutes at 400 before broiling. Seemed to make the pastry better cooked. Taste was great. Could be a party appetizer but tricky to have it come out warm. For dinner we ate slightly less than half of the total.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (811)). A savoury tart assembled on store-bought puff pastry and topped with goat cheese, fennel, mushrooms and leeks. It is pitched two ways: as an easy but impressive appetizer for a party, or as a weeknight dinner for two. It ran with a menu piece about cooking for guests without missing the party.

What readers report: The most-voted note (65) says the tart needs a flavour boost and recommends herbed goat cheese, thyme and rosemary with the vegetables, and a balsamic drizzle; a separate commenter endorses about a tablespoon of fresh thyme added to the mushrooms. Technique: saute the mushrooms in batches so they brown rather than steam (35 votes), and pie crust works in place of puff pastry. On making it ahead, a 30-vote reply is firm that assembling early gives a soggy result, but you can bake the crust and cook the vegetables through step three in advance and hold them. A recurring confusion (23 votes) is why the pastry is halved, with cooks unsure whether it makes two tarts or stacked layers. One cook substituted feta for goat cheese and was disappointed, suspecting that was the problem. Flatbread also works as a base.

Note on the source: several commenters confused by the instruction to cut the puff pastry in half

name: Lemon Bars
ingredients:
1 c. (227 g) unsalted butter
2 1/4 c. (270 g) flour
1/2 confectioners sugar
4 eggs
2 c. (400 g) granulated sugar
1 t. (4.0 g) baking powder
6 T. (92 g) lemon juice
1/4 confectioners sugar for decorating
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.
Butter and flour a 13x9x2 inch baking pan. Set aside. In a bowl, cream butter, flour, and confectioners sugar. Press dough evenly into bottom of pan. Bake 25 minutes. Beat eggs until frothy. Add granulated sugar, baking powder, and lemon juice. Beat mixture until it is smooth. Pour egg mixture over crust. 
Bake 20-25 minutes. Let cool and then dust cookies with confectioners sugar. Cut into squares to serve.

claude_opt.changes: Add the zest of the lemons used for juice to the filling; every modern version includes it for brightness and this recipe omits it. The baking-powder cakey-crumb style is a fine, distinct tradition, leave it.

name: Lemon Bars - Ina Garten
ingredients:
For the Crust:
1/2 pound (227 g) unsalted butter at room temperature
1/2 cup (100 g) granulated sugar
2 cups (240 g) all-purpose flour
1/8 teaspoon (0.3 g) kosher salt
For the Filling:
6 extra-large eggs at room temperature
3 cups (600 g) granulated sugar
2 tablespoons (12 g) grated lemon zest (4 to 6 lemons)
1 cup (244 g) freshly squeezed lemon juice
1 cup (120 g) all-purpose flour
Confectioners’ sugar, for dusting
directions:
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees.

For the crust, cream the butter and sugar until light in the bowl of an electric mixer fitted with the paddle attachment. Combine the flour and salt and, with the mixer on low, add to the butter until just mixed. Dump the dough onto a well-floured board and gather into a ball. Flatten the dough with floured hands and press it into a 9 x 13 x 2-inch baking sheet, building up a 1/2-inch edge on all sides. Chill.

Bake the crust for 15 to 20 minutes, until very lightly browned. Let cool on a wire rack. Leave the oven on.

For the filling, whisk together the eggs, sugar, lemon zest, lemon juice, and flour. Pour over the crust and bake for 30 to 35 minutes, until the filling is set. Let cool to room temperature.

Cut into triangles and dust with confectioners’ sugar.
description: 6/22 Delicious. Made half a recipe im square pan. Used a bit less zest but otherwise followed the recipe.
notes:
Web summary (barefootcontessa.com). Ina Garten's lemon bars from her 2001 book, built in two layers. A plain shortbread of butter, sugar, flour and a pinch of salt is pressed in and blind-baked first, so the base is set and crisp before the wet filling goes on and cannot turn soggy underneath it. The filling is deliberately sharp, using the zest of four to six lemons plus a full cup of juice against six eggs, with a cup of flour to help it set into a custard rather than a curd.

Note on the source: barefootcontessa.com has no comments section

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing: The Kitchn's harsher review (too sweet, chewy crust) doesn't match your 6/22 note that it was delicious as made.

name: Lemon Bars with Olive Oil and Sea Salt
ingredients:
1 1/4 cups/155 grams all-purpose flour
1/4 cup/50 grams granulated sugar
3 tablespoons/25 grams confectioners’ sugar
1 teaspoon (2.0 g) finely grated lemon zest
1/4 teaspoon (1.5 g) fine sea salt
10 tablespoons/142 grams cold unsalted butter, cut into cubes
4 to 6 lemons (3/4 cup of juice)
1 1/2 cups/300 grams sugar
2 large eggs plus 3 yolks
1 1/2 teaspoons/5 grams cornstarch
Pinch of fine sea salt
4 tablespoons/57 grams butter
1/4 cup (54 g)/60 milliliters fruity extra-virgin olive oil
Confectioners’ sugar and flaky sea salt, for sprinkling
directions:
Heat oven to 325 degrees and line a 9-by-9-inch baking pan with enough parchment to hang over two of the sides (to be used as handles later to lift the bars out of the pan).

To make the shortbread base, pulse together the flour, granulated sugar, confectioners’ sugar, lemon zest and salt in a food processor, or whisk together in a large bowl. Add butter and pulse (or use two knives or your fingers) to cut the butter into the flour until a crumbly dough forms. Press dough into prepared pan and bake until shortbread is pale golden all over, 30 to 35 minutes.

While the shortbread is baking, prepare the lemon curd: Grate 1/2 tablespoon zest from lemons and set aside. Squeeze lemons to yield 3/4 cup juice.

In a small saucepan, whisk together lemon juice, sugar, eggs and yolks, cornstarch and fine sea salt over medium heat until boiling and thickened, 2 to 5 minutes. Make sure mixture comes to a boil and stays there for 30 seconds or so; you should see it thicken up before you take it off the heat. But once it boils do not cook for longer than 1 minute or you risk the curd thinning out again. Remove from heat and strain into a bowl. Whisk in butter, olive oil and lemon zest.

When the shortbread is ready, take it out of the oven and carefully pour the lemon curd onto the shortbread base; return the pan to the oven. Bake until topping is just set, 10 to 15 minutes more. Allow to cool to room temperature, then refrigerate until cold before cutting into bars. Sprinkle with confectioners’ sugar and flaky sea salt right before serving.
description: Will recommends 1/2024
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (7,266)). Melissa Clark's grown-up version of the childhood lemon bar, keeping the shortbread base and tart curd but adding the bitterness of good olive oil and a scatter of sea salt on top for a faintly savoury edge. She stresses that the oil must have character, ideally herbal and fresh with a peppery finish, or the whole point is lost. They keep up to five days refrigerated but taste brightest within a day of baking.

What readers report: A runny curd is the problem cooks hit, and the highest-voted technical notes address it directly. An 864-vote comment says the curd either never reached a vigorous enough boil or was boiled too long, and a 574-vote follow-up reports solving it by holding the boil for close to the full minute rather than cutting it short. A 431-vote comment recommends replacing the cornstarch with potato starch, which stands up better to heat and acidity and does not weep the way cornstarch does. A 1,008-vote comment praises the recipe for giving gram weights and urges the Times to do it everywhere, though it flags an issue with the format. The single most-voted note (1,332) is a delighted ten-year-old baker reporting success. Several cooks now make them repeatedly on request.

name: Lemon Cake
ingredients:
For the cake:
1 1/2 c. (180 g) AP flour
1/4 t. (1.0 g) baking powder
1/8 t. (0.6 g) baking soda
1 c. (200 g) sugar
1/2 c. (114 g) butter (1 stick) softened
3 large eggs
1/2 c. (115 g) sour cream
grated peel of 1 lemon

For the glaze:
1/3 c. (81 g) lemon juice
1/3 c. (67 g) sugar
directions:
Preheat oven to 325 degrees.

1. Grease and flour 9x5" loaf pan.
2. On waxed paper, combine flour, baking powder, and baking soda; set aside.
3. In a large bowl, with mixer at high speed, beat sugar and butter until light and fluffy, about 5 minutes. Reduce speed to low, beat in eggs, 1 at a time, until blended. Add flour mixture alternately with sour cream, beating until well mixed. Stir in lemon peel by hand. 
4. Pour batter into loaf pan. Bake 60-75 minutes until toothpick inserted into center comes out clean.
5. Prepare glaze: in a cup, mix lemon juice and sugar. Spoon the mixture evenly over hot cake in pan. Cool cake in pan on wire rack.

claude_opt.changes: Standard pound-cake method with toothpick doneness test and a straightforward glaze; nothing outdated or unsafe here. Nothing to change.

name: Lemon Ricotta Pancakes
ingredients:
1 1/2 cups (214g) all-purpose flour (scoop and level to measure)
3 1/2 Tbsp (46g) granulated sugar
2 tsp (8.0 g) baking powder
1/4 tsp (1.1 g) baking soda
1/2 tsp (3.0 g) salt
1 cup (236ml) milk
3/4 cup (180g) ricotta (low-fat or whole)
3 large eggs
1 tsp (4.2 g) vanilla extract
1 - 2 Tbsp (6.0-12 g) lemon zest (depending on how lemony you want them)
1/4 cup (60ml) fresh lemon juice
1 Tbsp (14g) butter, melted
directions:
Preheat an electric griddle to moderately-high heat (or us a non-stick skillet set over medium heat).

In a mixing bowl whisk together flour, granulated sugar, baking powder, baking soda and salt for 20 seconds.

Make a well in center of flour mixture and set aside.

In a separate large mixing bowl, whisk together milk, ricotta, eggs and vanilla until well blended.

Add butter, lemon zest and lemon juice to milk mixture and blend until combined (it will curdle a little, that's fine).

Immediately pour milk mixture into flour mixture and whisk just to combined (batter should be slightly lumpy).

Pour 1/3 cup batter onto buttered griddle or skillet and cook until bubbles begin to appear on surface and bottom is golden brown, then flip and cook opposite side until golden brown.

Serve warm dusted with powdered sugar if desired and drizzled with maple or berry syrup.
description: 11/6 Delicious way to use up extra ricotta cheese. Lemony and sweet and great texture. Next time might try a recipe with less sugar and lemon just to see what ricotta alone does.
notes:
Strawberry Syrup Recipe HERE.

Blueberry Syrup Recipe HERE.

The cheese adds moisture and fat so the pancakes eat rich on only a tablespoon of butter, and because ricotta is mild it reads as creaminess rather than as cheese. Lemon zest and a quarter cup of juice give the acidity, which also reacts with the baking soda for extra rise. She frames it as a weekend breakfast her family asks for repeatedly.

name: Lemon-Stuffed Grilled Branzino
ingredients:
Four 1-pound (454 g) whole branzino—scaled and gutted, heads and tails removed
Salt and freshly ground pepper
4 thyme sprigs
4 bay leaves
2 lemons—1 thinly sliced, 1 cut into wedges
1 tablespoon (14 g) extra-virgin olive oil
Finely chopped parsley, for serving
directions:
Instructions Checklist

Light a grill or preheat a grill pan. Season the fish cavities with salt and pepper. Stuff each cavity with a thyme sprig, a bay leaf and 2 lemon slices. Rub the outside of the branzino with the olive oil and season with salt and pepper.

Grill the branzino over high heat, turning once, until browned and crisp and just cooked through, about 7 minutes per side. Serve right away, passing salt, lemon wedges and parsley at the table.
description: 6/2020 made with one branzino--enough for two; mild flavor
notes: Web summary (foodandwine.com, 5.0 (5)). Barbara Lynch's headnote positions this as a beginner-friendly formula for grilling whole fish: stuff gutted branzino with lemon slices and herbs, oil and season the skin, and leave it undisturbed on the grill so it releases naturally and stays crisp, flipping only once. A Test Kitchen sidebar adds that most branzino sold today is farm-raised due to overfishing concerns and suggests having the fishmonger pre-scale and gut the fish. What readers report: there are no corrections or errors flagged — all seven reviews are positive and the recipe holds a perfect 5.0 rating. The most substantive input is a stovetop adaptation from an apartment-dwelling reader (Pamela19123), who cooks it in a cast-iron grill pan and warns it produces significant smoke requiring ventilation, and notes a finishing squeeze of lemon makes a real difference. Another reader (Mike Affinito, on his fifth batch of the summer) recommends real lump charcoal over other grill fuels for the best flavor, otherwise following the recipe as written. One commenter (Richard) asks what comparable whole fish is available in North America/Canada, since branzino can be hard to source, but the question goes unanswered on the page. No vote or helpfulness counts are shown, only reply counts, all at zero.

claude_opt.changes: Your 6/2020 note found this mild — the outside seasoning never reaches the flesh. Salt the fish 20+ minutes before grilling (dry-brine, passive wait) and consider the pellet smoker instead of gas for more smoke flavor.

name: Lemony Shrimp and Bean Stew
ingredients:
1 teaspoon (2.0 g) fresh lemon zest and 2 tablespoons juice
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) sweet or smoked paprika
2 garlic cloves, grated
Kosher salt and black pepper
1 pound (454 g) peeled, deveined large shrimp (tails removed)
4 tablespoons (57 g) unsalted butter (1/2 stick)
2 large leeks, trimmed, then halved lengthwise, white and light green parts sliced crosswise 1/2-inch thick (or 1 large onion, minced)
1 (15-ounce) can cannellini beans or other white beans, rinsed
2 cups (480 g) chicken stock or vegetable stock
2 tablespoons (7.5 g) finely chopped fresh parsley (optional)
Toasted bread, for serving (optional)
directions:
Combine lemon zest, paprika, garlic, 3/4 teaspoon salt and 3/4 teaspoon pepper in a medium bowl. Add shrimp and toss to coat.

In a large pot, melt butter over medium-high heat. When butter is foaming, add shrimp and cook, stirring occasionally, until pink and starting to curl, 2 to 3 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer shrimp to a plate; set aside.

Add leeks, season with salt and pepper, and cook over medium until leeks are soft and starting to brown on the edges, 4 to 5 minutes, stirring occasionally. Add beans and chicken broth and bring to a boil over high. Lower heat and simmer, 8 to 10 minutes. Stir in reserved shrimp and any juices from the plate, parsley and lemon juice, and season with salt and pepper. Serve with toasted bread.
description: 6/2025 Made ½ recipe with frozen shrimp. Used rancho gordo beans homemade, brown because thats what we had. Steph not too fond of it. Different.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (23,421)). Ali Slagle's weeknight stew needs little prep and cooks fast but reads as more elegant than the effort suggests. The headnote offers several routes: swap the shrimp for an equal weight of flaky white fish or seared scallops, or stretch it to serve six by stirring in butter and spooning it over spaghetti or rigatoni. A generous pour of good olive oil at the end is encouraged.

What readers report: The single most-voted comment (3,145) answers a make-ahead question and warns that shrimp reheated after cooking goes rubbery and flavourless; the fix is to mix the marinade without the shrimp, make the leek and bean base ahead, and add the shrimp only when reheating to serve. The second-biggest tip (2,196 votes) is to build a quick stock from the shrimp shells instead of using chicken stock, sauteing the shells in a little oil for about three minutes, deglazing with a quarter cup of dry white wine and simmering. Balance adjustments recur: less shrimp, more beans and more broth (741 votes). Shallots substitute for leeks and a bag of spinach adds greens. A 2,006-vote note reports making it exactly as written with no changes at all.

name: Lisbon Chocolate Cake
ingredients:
FOR THE CAKE:
½ cup/115 grams unsalted butter (1 stick), cut into chunks, plus more for greasing the pan
⅓ cup/30 grams unsweetened cocoa powder
1 ½ tablespoons (12 g) cornstarch
¼ teaspoon (1.0 g) baking powder
¼ teaspoon (1.5 g) fine sea salt
5 ounces/140 grams semisweet or bittersweet chocolate, coarsely chopped
½ cup/100 grams granulated sugar
3 large eggs, chilled
FOR THE GANACHE:
1 ¾ cups (416 g)/420 milliliters heavy cream
6 ounces/170 grams semisweet or bittersweet chocolate, finely chopped
