3 tablespoons (16 g) unsweetened cocoa powder
directions:
Make the cake: Center a rack in the oven, and heat oven to 325 degrees. Butter a 9-inch cake pan, line with parchment paper and butter the paper.

Sift together the cocoa powder, cornstarch, baking powder and salt in a medium bowl. Whisk to blend.

Put the 1/2 cup butter in a large heatproof bowl set over a saucepan of simmering water. Scatter the semisweet or bittersweet chocolate on top, and heat, stirring often, until the mixture is smooth and glossy. Remove the bowl from the pan, and stir in the sugar. One by one, energetically stir in the eggs, beating for 1 minute after the last egg is added. The mixture will look like pudding. Stir in the dry ingredients. Scrape the mixture into the cake pan, and give the pan a couple of good raps against the counter to settle the batter.

Bake for 18 to 20 minutes, or until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (or with only a tiny streak of chocolate). Transfer to a rack, cool for 5 minutes, then unmold the cake. Peel off the paper, invert the cake and cool to room temperature. Wash and dry the cake pan.

Make the ganache: Pour 1 1/4 cups cream into a small saucepan; refrigerate the rest. Scald the cream over medium heat, turn off the heat and stir in the semisweet or bittersweet chocolate until fully incorporated. Transfer to a heatproof bowl. Refrigerate the ganache for 10 minutes, whisk it, then refrigerate again for 10 minutes. Repeat chilling and whisking steps until the ganache is thick enough to make tracks when you stir, 50 to 60 minutes.

Cut two 3-by-16-inch pieces of parchment or foil, and crisscross them in the cake pan. Carefully return the cake to the pan. (The mousse layer is too soft to stand on its own until it's chilled. It needs the support of the pan sides.)

Whip the remaining 1/2 cup cream until it holds medium peaks.

Using a whisk, gently beat the ganache until it’s soft and spreadable. With a spatula, fold in the whipped cream. Spread over the cake, and refrigerate for 2 hours (or cover and keep for up to 2 days). The cake is best served cool or at room temperature, so take it out of the fridge about 20 minutes before serving.

To finish, put the cocoa powder in a fine-mesh strainer, and shake it over the top of the cake. Run a table knife along the sides of the pan. Using the parchment or foil handles, carefully lift the cake out of the pan and onto a serving plate. Discard the strips. Cut the cake using a long knife that has been run under hot water and wiped dry between each cut.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (5,139)). Dorie Greenspan tells the story behind it: pickpocketed of all her credit cards on Lisbon's No. 28 tram on her first day, she nearly left the city, but she and her husband Michael worked through their eating list anyway and found this cake at Landeau Chocolate on the last day. Her version is a dense but not heavy brownie-like base under a whipped chocolate ganache with the texture of mousse, finished with a heavy dusting of cocoa. Since the cake is nothing but chocolate, she says to use one you genuinely like.

What readers report: A former pastry chef's note leads at 837 votes, recommending Valrhona cocoa for assertive chocolate flavour without bitterness and good colour. The most repeated practical change is baking in a springform pan (757 and 441 votes), which removes the awkward transfer; one cook also spread a layer of ganache on the serving plate before setting the cake down. A pinch of espresso powder in the batter is a popular addition, and several report the mousse set without trouble when made a day ahead. A 311-vote comment flags that the cake is flourless and therefore gluten-free. A large tangent (755 and 653 votes) debates whether preheating the oven first is wasteful, with the reply explaining that oven thermostats sense one corner and the cavity needs longer to even out than the beep suggests.

claude_opt.changes: Bake and set the mousse layer in a springform pan instead of transferring it back into a standard cake pan — the top reader fix; it removes the fragile pan-swap the current method requires. No added time.

name: Lobster - Steamed
directions:
Steam for 12-15 minutes.
Temp should be 145 in tail.

claude_opt.changes: Pull the lobster at 138-140F in the tail instead of 145; carryover finishes it, and modern guides warn 145 already risks rubbery meat.

name: Luscious Apple Cake
ingredients:
3 eggs
2 c. (400 g) sugar
2/3 c. (145 g) vegetable oil
1 t vanilla
2 1/2 c. (300 g) flour
2 t baking powder
1 t baking soda
1 t salt
1 t cinnamon
3 c. (327 g) coarsely chopped apples (Granny Smiths)
1 c. (117 g) chopped walnuts or pecans
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.
Beat eggs well. Add sugar, oil, and vanilla. Beat for 3 minutes at medium speed. Combine flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, and cinnamon. Add to egg mixture. Blend thoroughly at low speed. Stir in apples and nuts. Pour into one large (10" x 15") or two (8" square) greased pans. Bake for 50 minutes. Serve warm. Delicious with vanilla ice cream.

claude_opt.changes: Add a toothpick-clean doneness check before pulling at 50 minutes; apple moisture varies enough that a fixed time alone risks an underbaked center.

name: Luscious Sponge Cake
ingredients:
3/4 c. (182 g) egg whites (5-6 eggs) at room temp
1/2 c. (122 g) egg yolks at room temp
1 1/3 c. (151 g) sifted cake flour
1/2 t. (2.0 g) baking powder
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
1 1/2 c. (300 g) granulated sugar
1 t. (3.1 g) cream of tartar
1/4 c. (59 g) water
1 t. (4.2 g) vanilla
1 t. (4.2 g) lemon extract
directions:
1. One hour ahead: set out whites and yolks.
2. Preheat oven to 375. Sift flour, baking powder salt, and 1 c. sugar in a small bowl.
3. In mixer bowl, combine egg whites and cream of tartar. Beat high speed until soft mounds form. Then beat in 1/2 c. sugar, 2 T. at a time. Beat until stiff peaks form. 
4. Combine yolks, water and extracts. With a spoon, stir into flour mixture. Beat 1/2 minute.
5. With a spoon, fold yolk mixture into whites until blended. Plop into ungreased 4"x10" tube pan. Cut through batter.
6. Bake 35-40 minutes. Invert until cool.
notes: Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing to change. Hot-oven bake, cream-of-tartar-stabilized whites, ungreased tube pan, and invert-cooling already match current sponge/chiffon technique; the recipe is sound as written.

name: Luxurious Turkey Tetrazzini
ingredients:
6 tablespoons (85 g) butter
1/2 pound (227 g) mushrooms thinly sliced
1 tablespoon (15 g) Madeira
4 tablespoons (30 g) flour
1 1/2 cups (360 g) chicken or vegetable broth
1/2 cup (119 g) heavy cream
2 to 3 cups (280-420 g) leftover cooked turkey, cut into 3/4-inch dice
1/2 pound (227 g) linguine cooked to al dente stage
1/3 cup (30 g) grated Parmesan cheese mixed with 2 tablespoons dry bread crumbs
Salt and freshly ground black pepper
directions:
Heat 2 tablespoons of the butter in a skillet. When the foaming subsides, add the mushrooms and saute, over high heat for 2 to 3 minutes until the mushrooms have absorbed the butter and are tender. Stir in the Madeira and evaporate over high heat.

In another saucepan heat 3 tablespoons of butter. When foaming subsides, stir in the flour and cook for a minute. Whisk in the chicken broth and bring to a boil. Cook, over low heat, for about 5 minutes or until thickened. Remove sauce from heat and stir in the cream. Season to taste with salt and pepper. Fold in the mushrooms and turkey.

Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Butter a 1 1/2 quart casserole. Layer half of pasta, half of mushroom and turkey mixture and repeat with pasta and turkey mushroom mix. Scatter Parmesan and bread crumbs over the top and dot with remaining tablespoon of butter. Heat for 45 minutes or until heated through, sauce is bubbling and top is browning. If you wish, slide casserole under the broiler for a moment to brown the top.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Michele Urvater's version of the classic leftover-turkey bake. Mushrooms are sauteed and deglazed with a spoonful of Madeira before the flour goes in, so the roux picks up the browned mushroom flavour rather than just thickening plain broth. Broth and heavy cream make the sauce, which is folded through diced turkey and al dente linguine. A Parmesan and breadcrumb topping browns under the oven heat and gives the finished dish a crisp contrast to the creamy interior.

name: Mai Tai
ingredients:
2 ounces (57 g) dark rum
3/4 ounce (21 g) orange curaçao
3/4 ounce (21 g) lime juice, freshly squeezed
1/2 ounce (14 g) orgeat
1/4 ounce (7.1 g) simple syrup
Garnish: lime wheel
Garnish: mint sprig
directions:
Add the ingredients into a shaker with ice and shake lightly. 

Pour into a double rocks

Garnish with a lime wheel and mint sprig.
notes: Web summary (liquor.com, 4.0 (627), 16 reviews). Liquor.com's unsigned staff framing traces the Mai Tai's contested origin between Trader Vic Bergeron and Don the Beachcomber in the 1930s-40s, notes its slide into sugary mixer-drink territory before the Tiki revival restored a rum-forward style, and frames this build around blending a white rum base with a dark rum float, dry (not blue) orange curacao, almond-true orgeat and fresh lime. What readers report: several commenters dispute the recipe's authenticity rather than just tweaking it -- one says true Mai Tais don't use white rum at all, another calls it 'terrible,' arguing that color terms (white/dark) say nothing about flavor and that the original Trader Vic drink uses an aged Jamaican rum plus a Martinique rum, all shaken together with no floater. A third makes the same color-terminology point, recommending aged Jamaican rum with agricole instead. Technique note: one reader tried floating Morgan's Spiced as the dark rum and found it wasn't dense/dark enough to actually float, implying the float needs a heavier rum like Smith & Cross Navy Strength (used successfully by another commenter, who also upped the orgeat to 3/4 oz). Common substitution questions, left unanswered by the author: Triple Sec or Cointreau in place of curacao, Malibu for the white rum, and what orgeat even is. No vote or helpfulness counts are shown on any comment.

claude_opt.changes: The recipe's single dark rum already sidesteps the disputed white-rum-base debate. Choose a full-bodied aged rum (commenters favor Jamaican-style) over a light one — the recurring authenticity complaint is that a thin rum flattens the drink.

name: Mango Salsa
ingredients:
1 mango - peeled, seeded, and chopped
¼ cup finely chopped red bell pepper
1 green onion, chopped
1 fresh jalapeño chile pepper, finely chopped
2 tablespoons (5.8 g) chopped cilantro
2 tablespoons (30 g) lime juice
1 tablespoon (15 g) lemon juice
directions:
Gather ingredients.

Place mango, red bell pepper, green onion, jalapeño, cilantro, lime juice, and lemon juice in a medium bowl.

Mix ingredients well to combine. Cover and let sit at least 30 minutes before serving.

Serve with chips.
description: Made in June 2023 with champagne mangos; great salsa option without tomatoes.
notes:
Web summary (Allrecipes, 4.8 (494) / 358 reviews). IYENGAR21's note is short: ripe mango, bell pepper, jalapeno and lime make an easy, refreshing salsa that suits fish tacos or chips. A cook's note adds that it is especially good over fish blackened with Cajun seasoning. The editorial section (contributions by Corey Williams) explains that the flavours meld with time, so the salsa is better made a day ahead and should rest at least 30 minutes before serving, and that it keeps about a week refrigerated in a shallow airtight container.

What readers report: The top review (345 helpful) swaps halved cherry tomatoes for the red pepper, adds avocado, and says to squeeze the juice clinging to the mango pit into the bowl, while stressing that making it early lets the flavours blend. Resting is the step people skip: more than one thought it tasted flat until it had sat, and overnight is better. Salt is the most common missing ingredient, since the recipe includes none; several add it after the salsa sits. Other reported fixes: use a very ripe mango for texture, and cut back to a little over 2 tablespoons of citrus juice total if it turns liquidy or too acidic. The jalapeno divides people, some halving it, others doubling it or using serrano or scotch bonnet. Red onion for green onion is frequent; avocado, tomato, pineapple and mint also work. Canned mango was a poor substitute.

claude_opt.changes: Add salt — the recipe omits it and several readers note the salsa tastes flat without it; salt to taste after the rest. Resting longer, even overnight, further melds the flavors per top reviews. No added time.

name: Maple Pear Upside-Down Cake
ingredients:
11 tablespoons (156 g) butter
3/4 cup (242 g) maple syrup
1/4 cup (53 g) packed brown sugar
3 to 4 pears, peeled, cored and thinly sliced
3/4 cup (150 g) granulated sugar
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) vanilla
2 large eggs
1 1/2 cups (180 g) flour
1 1/2 teaspoons (6.0 g) baking powder
1/4 teaspoon (1.5 g) salt
1/2 cup (122 g) milk
directions:
Heat oven to 350 degrees. Melt 3 tablespoons butter in a small pan over medium heat; add maple syrup and brown sugar and cook, stirring, until sugar dissolves. Bring to a boil and cook for another 2 minutes; remove from heat and set aside. When mixture has cooled a bit, pour it into a 9-inch baking pan and arrange pear slices in an overlapping circle on top.

With a handheld or standing mixer, beat remaining 8 tablespoons butter and the sugar until light and fluffy. Add vanilla and eggs, one egg at a time, continuing to mix until smooth. In a separate bowl, combine flour, baking powder and salt.

Add flour mixture to butter mixture in three batches, alternating with milk; do not overmix. Carefully spread batter over pears, using a spatula to make sure it is evenly distributed. Bake until top of cake is golden brown and edges begin to pull away from sides of pan, about 45 to 50 minutes; a toothpick inserted into center should come out clean. Let cake cool for 5 minutes.

Run a knife around edge of pan; put a plate on top of cake and carefully flip it so plate is on bottom and pan is on top. Serve warm or at room temperature.
description: 1/25 Delicious. Sweet and rich.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (899)). No headnote is published; the page carries only the credit placing it in a Times column on upside-down pear cake.

What readers report: Sweetness of the maple topping is the recurring complaint and the main disagreement. A 48-vote note says the topping comes out soupy and too sweet while the cake itself works as advertised, proposing to cut the maple syrup to about half a cup and reduce the brown sugar. A 77-vote comment simply omits the brown sugar on a repeat bake, and a 47-vote cook did the same and reports it turned out perfectly with a clean flip and no sogginess. Pushing back, a 33-vote commenter says ignore the reviews claiming three-quarters of a cup of syrup is too much and notes cooling the cake closer to 15 minutes before inverting. A 75-vote note recommends reducing the caramel longer than the recipe says. One commenter supplies a vegan adaptation using two tablespoons of ground flaxseed with six tablespoons of warm water in place of the eggs.

Note on the source: no headnote published

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

name: Marcella Hazan’s Bolognese Sauce
ingredients:
1 tablespoon (14 g) vegetable oil
3 tablespoons (43 g) butter plus 1 tablespoon for tossing the pasta
½ cup (80 g) chopped onion
⅔ cup (67 g) chopped celery
⅔ cup (85 g) chopped carrot
¾ pound (340 g) ground beef chuck (or you can use 1 part pork to 2 parts beef)
Salt
Black pepper, ground fresh from the mill
1 cup (244 g) whole milk
Whole nutmeg
1 cup (237 g) dry white wine
1 ½ cups (366 g) canned imported Italian plum tomatoes, cut up, with their juice
1 ¼ to 1 ½ pounds (567-680 g) pasta
Freshly grated parmigiano-reggiano cheese at the table
directions:
Put the oil, butter and chopped onion in the pot and turn the heat on to medium. Cook and stir the onion until it has become translucent, then add the chopped celery and carrot. Cook for about 2 minutes, stirring vegetables to coat them well.

Add ground beef, a large pinch of salt and a few grindings of pepper. Crumble the meat with a fork, stir well and cook until the beef has lost its raw, red color.

Add milk and let it simmer gently, stirring frequently, until it has bubbled away completely. Add a tiny grating -- about 1/8 teaspoon -- of nutmeg, and stir.

Add the wine, let it simmer until it has evaporated, then add the tomatoes and stir thoroughly to coat all ingredients well. When the tomatoes begin to bubble, turn the heat down so that the sauce cooks at the laziest of simmers, with just an intermittent bubble breaking through to the surface. Cook, uncovered, for 3 hours or more, stirring from time to time. While the sauce is cooking, you are likely to find that it begins to dry out and the fat separates from the meat. To keep it from sticking, add 1/2 cup of water whenever necessary. At the end, however, no water at all must be left and the fat must separate from the sauce. Taste and correct for salt.

Toss with cooked drained pasta, adding the tablespoon of butter, and serve with freshly grated Parmesan on the side.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (31,112)). After Marcella Hazan died in 2013 the Times asked readers which of her recipes had entered their regular rotation, and the answer that came back most often was her Bolognese. She wrote several versions; this is the one from Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking, which one reader called the gold standard.

What readers report: With over 3,000 notes the top-voted entry (11,324) is a much-loved anecdote about a Labrador eating the cooling sauce rather than cooking advice. The substantive guidance sits just below. A 4,747-vote question asks whether the separated fat should be skimmed at the end, which is the step newcomers find unclear. A cook of 25 years (2,362 votes) confirms it works with all beef or a beef, pork and veal mix. A 2,076-vote comment insists that disappointing results come from deviating and urges following Hazan exactly, particularly the slow simmer. Importantly, a 1,923-vote commenter working from the 1979 edition reports materially different proportions there, giving three tablespoons each of olive oil and butter for three-quarters of a pound of beef, so the published ratios are not the only authoritative ones.

Note on the source: commenters report the 1979 edition of the book gives different ingredient proportions

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. This is the well-tested Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking version, and reader consensus says follow it exactly; the fat separating out at the end is expected, not a sign to skim.

name: Margarita

1 oz (28 g) Cointreau

name: Marinated Chicken Fingers With Pasta - Franey
ingredients:
1 1/4 pounds (567 g) boneless, skinless chicken breasts, cut into thin strips about 1 1/2 inches long 
1/4 cup (64 g) light soy sauce 
2 tablespoons (30 g) white wine vinegar 
2 tablespoons (17 g) finely chopped garlic
1 teaspoon (2.0 g) freshly grated ginger 
1 tablespoon (15 g) fresh lemon juice 
1 teaspoon (2.1 g) ground cumin 
1 small jalapeno pepper, cored, seeded and chopped fine 
Salt and pepper to taste 
2 tablespoons (27 g) olive oil 
1 large sweet red pepper, cored, seeded and sliced into
1/4-inch-wide strips 
1 yellow pepper, cored and seeded, cut into 1/4-inch-wide strips 
1 green pepper, cored and seeded, cut into 1/4-inch-wide strips 
1 cup (160 g) thinly sliced white onions 
3/4 pound (340 g) fine angel-hair pasta 
1 cup (230 g) sour cream 
3/4 cup (85 g) shredded cheddar cheese 
4 tablespoons (22 g) coarsely chopped coriander.
directions:
1. Place the chicken strips in a bowl and add soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, ginger, lemon juice, cumin, jalapeno pepper, salt and pepper. Blend well. Cover and refrigerate for 15 minutes. Just before using, drain the chicken strips. Discard marinade.

2. In a large nonstick skillet, or 2 smaller ones, heat the olive oil over high heat. Add the drained chicken strips; cook, tossing and stirring, for 1 minute. Add the red, yellow and green peppers, onions, salt and pepper. Cook, tossing and stirring, for 5 to 6 minutes.

3. Meanwhile, place the pasta in two quarts of salted boiling water and cook according to package instructions. Stir often but do not overcook. Drain. Return the pasta to the pot. Add the sour cream, blend well, tossing and stirring. Keep warm.

4. Place the chicken, cheddar cheese and coriander over the pasta, and serve.

Yield: 4 servings.
description: 1992. Our standby! Cook times take longer than indicated.

claude_opt.changes: Check chicken reaches 165F with no pink before tossing with sour cream; thin strips can look cooked outside while raw inside, which matches your own note that timing runs long.

name: Mark Furstenberg's White Bread
ingredients:
FOR THE WHITE SPONGE/STARTER
48 grams white bread flour, preferably King Arthur (1/3 cup)
52 grams cool water (1/4 cup)
1 gram instant yeast, such as Fleischmann's RapidRise (about 1/3 teaspoon)
FOR THE DOUGH:
450 grams white bread flour, preferably King Arthur (about 2 3/4 cups)
350 grams cool water (1 3/4 cups)
White sponge/starter (see above; about 1/2 cup)
5 grams instant yeast, such as Fleischmann's RapidRise (about 1 1/2 teaspoons)
13 grams fine sea salt (2 teaspoons)
Rice flour, for dusting
Rolled oats, for the baking receptacle
directions:
For the white sponge/starter: Combine the flour, water and yeast in a medium mixing bowl; stir just to combine. Cover the bowl tightly with plastic wrap and let it sit at room temperature for 6 to 10 hours, or refrigerate for later use. (If refrigerated, after several days the sponge will sour. But that's okay.)

For the dough: Combine the flour, sponge/starter, water, yeast and salt in a large mixing bowl. Cover and let sit at room temperature for 6 to 12 hours, or refrigerate for up to 1 day. The dough should resemble a thick batter with lots of different-size bubbles. (If refrigerating, it may be necessary to let the chilled dough come to room temperature so its bubbles can emerge.)

If the bubbles become too fat or collapse, the bread will not have a light interior, but the dough can be used to make flatbread, or it can be used instead of a sponge for your next round of baking.

Spray the inside of a large bowl with nonstick oil spray, or dust a bread proofing basket heavily with rice flour.

Spray a work surface with nonstick cooking oil spray and pour the dough onto the prepared surface. Use a wet plastic scraper or wet hands to lift the edges of the dough from the work surface and fold them onto the center of the mass of dough. Repeat 4 to 6 times, slightly rotating the dough as you work to keep it from sticking to the work surface. Wet your hands and the scraper often.

Place the dough in the bowl or basket; cover with a clean dish towel, being careful not to let it touch the dough. Let it sit at room temperature for 90 minutes or until the dough has nearly doubled in size. The dough's texture should look lighter. You will see bubbles beneath the skin of the dough.

About 30 minutes before the dough is finished proofing, preheat the oven to 475 degrees. Ten minutes before the bread is to be baked, heat a medium-size (4-quart) Dutch oven with its lid on. (The dough should fill the Dutch oven about halfway; if the Dutch oven is too large, the loaf will bake flat.)

When ready to bake the bread, work quickly. Transfer the heated Dutch oven to the stovetop (off the heat). Sprinkle rice flour in the bottom of the heated Dutch oven. Turn the dough into the hot pot. Use a lame (special tool used to slash marks in the dough) or a razor blade to make several quick, clean, assertive strokes, about 1/2 inch deep, creating diagonal slashes on the top of the dough. (This may be hard to do because the dough is quite wet.)

Re-cover the pot and place in the oven; immediately reduce the heat to 450 degrees. After 25 to 30 minutes, check the look of the bread; it should begin to pick up color. Remove the lid and bake for 10 minutes, until the loaf looks deep golden brown. The bread will be done when tapping your fingers on the bottom of the loaf produces a clearly hollow sound, as opposed to a dull thud. Transfer the loaf to a wire rack to cool for at least 60 minutes.
notes:
Web summary (washingtonpost.com, 5.0 (2)). A short note from the Washington Post crediting baker Mark Furstenberg, who specifies a bread flour of roughly 12 percent protein for this loaf. Storage advice is to keep the loaf unwrapped, cut side down on a board, and eat it within three days. The recipe builds on a small white sponge or starter and is already given in grams alongside cup measures, making about a pound and a half of bread.

name: Meat Loaf with Parsley and Tomato
ingredients:
1 lb. (454 g) ground beef
1 c. (108 g) bread crumbs
1 egg
1/2 onion chopped fine
3/8 c. (92 g) tomato sauce
3/4 t. (4.5 g) salt
1/2 t. (1.1 g) pepper
1/4 c. (15 g) minced parsley
1/2 t. (0.2 g) basil
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.

Mix ingredients together. Put into loaf pan. Bake 45 minutes.
notes:
Web summary (recipelink.com). A transcription of the Fanny Farmer Cookbook (1986) meat loaf, presented as a base recipe with a set of named variations. The base is a bread-crumb/egg/milk binder with Worcestershire and dry mustard; the 'Parsley and Tomato' variation drops the Worcestershire and mustard, swaps tomato juice for the milk, and folds in minced parsley and crumbled basil, with tomato sauce spooned over the top. The tomato liquid and sauce keep a lean loaf moist while the herbs push it toward an Italian profile. The book suggests turning leftovers into rye-bread sandwiches with pickles.

Note on the source: Confirmed against the family text: 'Meat Loaf with Parsley and Tomato' is the exact name of a variation printed in the Fanny Farmer Cookbook, and the family version is that variation at half scale (1 lb beef, 1 c crumbs, 1 egg, 1/2 onion, 3/8 c tomato sauce, 1/4 c parsley, 1/2 t basil). Source field 'Fannie Farmer' matches. URL is a faithful recipelink.com transcription, not a publisher page; no official Fannie Farmer page exists online.

claude_opt.changes: Shape free-form on a foil-lined sheet pan instead of a loaf pan: thinner shape browns on all sides instead of steaming and cooks faster. Pull at 160°F internal rather than by time alone.

name: Meatballs
ingredients:
2 slices good-quality white sandwich bread, crusts removed and slices torn into small pieces
½ cup (122 g) buttermilk or 6 tablespoons plain yogurt thinned with 2 tablespoons whole milk
1 pound (454 g) ground meat, preferably ¾ pound ground chuck and ¼ pound ground pork
¼ cup (22 g) freshly grated Parmesan cheese
2 tablespoons (7.5 g) minced fresh parsley leaves 
1 large egg yolk
1 small garlic clove, minced fine or pressed
through a garlic press
¾ teaspoon (4.5 g) salt
Ground black pepper
1-1½ cups (218-327 g) vegetable oil for pan-frying
directions:
1. Combine the bread and buttermilk in a small bowl. Let sit for 10 minutes, mashing occasionally with a fork, until a smooth paste forms.
2. Place the ground meat, cheese, parsley, egg yolk, garlic, salt, and pepper to taste in a medium bowl. Add the bread-milk mixture and combine until evenly mixed. Shape 3 tablespoons of the mixture into a 1½-inch round meatball. (When forming meatballs, use a light touch. If you compact the meatballs too much, they can become dense and hard.)
You should be able to form about 14 meatballs.
3. Pour the vegetable oil into a 10- or 11-inch sauté pan to a depth of ¼ inch. Turn the heat to medium-high. After several minutes, test the oil with the edge of a meatball. When the oil sizzles, add the meatballs in a single layer. Fry, turning several times, until nicely browned on all sides, about 10 minutes. Regulate the heat as needed to keep the oil sizzling but not smoking. Transfer the browned meatballs to a plate lined with paper towels and set aside.
ntil the sauce thickens, about 10 minutes.
notes:
Web summary (crumblycookie.net). Blogger Bridget (The Way the Cookie Crumbles) reprints the Cook's Illustrated meatballs, tracing them to the January 1998 issue -- the same recipe collected in The New Best Recipe. The bread-and-buttermilk panade is the point: the soaked paste keeps the meat tender and prevents the dense, bouncy texture that comes from overworking or from dry crumbs. A chuck-and-pork blend plus Parmesan, parsley and an egg yolk supplies fat and flavor, and shallow pan-frying in a quarter-inch of oil browns all sides.

What readers report: Commenters report reliably tender results. One swapped ground Italian sausage for the pork successfully. A recurring point of confusion is the term 'sweet milk' in the yogurt substitution, which simply means ordinary milk as opposed to buttermilk.

Note on the source: Ingredient list matches the family text essentially line for line, including the unusual 2 slices white bread + 1/2 cup buttermilk panade, 1/4 cup Parmesan, 1 egg yolk, 3/4 tsp salt, and 1-1/4 cups oil for pan-frying. Blog names Cook's Illustrated as the origin, which matches the recorded source 'The New Best Recipe Cookbook'. Runner-up a human might prefer: https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/762-classic-spaghetti-and-meatballs (the publisher's own page, but paywalled).

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. This is Cook's Illustrated's tested panade method already; readers report reliably tender results and no better-reviewed alternative technique surfaced worth switching to.

name: Meatballs with Any Meat
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) ground meat (pork, beef, veal, chicken, turkey or a combination)
1/2 cup (54 g) panko bread crumbs
1 egg
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt, more as needed
Black pepper and/or ground cumin, curry powder, chile flakes, garam masala, etc., to taste
Minced garlic, onion, scallions or shallot
Chopped parsley, basil or cilantro
Olive oil, for frying (optional)
directions:
In a large bowl, gently combine all ingredients. Roll into 1 1/2-inch balls. Transfer to a baking sheet.

Broil until golden and firm, 7 to 10 minutes. Or fry in oil until deeply browned all over. Sprinkle with more salt before serving.
notes:
6/22 Made 1 ½ times this recipe for beer meatballs. Used 1 lb 80 percent ground beef and ½ lb ground pork. Also panko, 1 whole egg and 1 yolk. Garlic salt and pepper. Used disher. Fried in canola oil. Froze. Tender but held together well.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (6,051)). Melissa Clark presents this as a ratio to memorise rather than a fixed recipe: one pound of any ground meat, half a cup of breadcrumbs for lightness, a teaspoon of salt and one egg to bind. Everything else, pepper and spices, chopped herbs, minced garlic, onion, scallion or shallot, is adjustable, and even fish works. Broil or fry as you prefer. The page notes she tested at least half a dozen approaches before a professional tester repeated the recipe a minimum of three times.

What readers report: Cooking method divides the comments. The top note (1,273 votes) borrows an Alton Brown approach, rolling the meatballs in fine breadcrumbs and baking them in a greased muffin tin, which builds a crust and keeps them plump. A 1,080-vote comment argues the opposite, insisting you should fry rather than bake, and adds two of its own rules: a tablespoon of ricotta per pound of meat, and a mix of veal, pork and beef. Two further high-voted notes defend baking, one on a rack at 400F so the fat drains and they brown all over, another at 375F on convection. The most broadly useful tip (966 votes) is to soak the panko or breadcrumbs in milk first, which prevents them drying the meatballs out and improves binding. For even sizing, pat the mixture into a rectangle and cut squares before rolling, or use a small scoop.

name: Meera Sodha’s Naan
ingredients:
4 cups all-purpose flour, or 500 grams
2 tablespoons (27 g) neutral oil, like canola, plus a teaspoon more
4 tablespoons (61 g) whole-milk yogurt
1 packet of active dried yeast, or 7 grams
2 teaspoons (8.4 g) sugar
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) kosher salt
1 level teaspoon baking powder
1 cup (244 g) whole milk, warmed
directions:
Put the flour into a large mixing bowl. Make a well in the middle, and add two tablespoons of the oil to it, along with the yogurt, yeast, sugar, salt and baking powder. Use your fingers to combine the ingredients until they resemble crumbs, and then add the warm milk in splashes, mixing until it comes together into a dough.

Put the dough on a clean, well-floured cutting board. It will be very sticky. Flour your hands, and knead the dough for five minutes or so, then scrape off your hands and knead it again, making it into a round ball. Rub a teaspoon of oil over the exterior of the dough, and place it in a clean mixing bowl. Cover with a dish towel, and place in a warm spot to rise for 60 to 90 minutes, or until it has doubled in size.

Using a knife, divide the dough into 12 pieces. Take each piece, roll it into a ball and flatten it between your palms. Dust the dough with flour, and roll each piece out into an oval of about 5 by 8 inches.

Place a large sauté pan over medium-high heat, and allow it to get hot. When it is, cook one naan in it for 30 to 40 seconds on one side, or until it begins to bubble, then use a spatula to flip it over to cook the other side for about the same amount of time, checking regularly to make sure that it does not burn. Flip the naan one more time, and press on it lightly with your spatula for 10 to 15 seconds, then remove to a warm platter. Repeat with the rest of the dough. (Keep the finished naan in a low oven, or wrap in foil until ready to serve.)
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (3,131)). Sam Sifton introduces this as a recipe the British cookbook author learned from her aunt Harsha and published in Made in India in 2015. The flatbreads come out crackly and blistered outside but tender within, with a slight yogurt tang, made for dragging through curry. He advises setting up an assembly line to roll and pan-cook them, and says two or three attempts will end your naan buying.

What readers report: Hydration is the theme. The top note (935 votes) recommends mixing everything except the flour first, because the liquid-to-flour ratio needs adjusting by feel rather than by the stated measure, and a 118-vote reply gives the same advice as a fix for a specific cook's problem: withhold a few tablespoons of flour and judge the dough's consistency. A 600-vote comment describes a stand mixer method, wet ingredients with sugar and yeast first using the paddle, dry sprinkled in after, again holding back some flour. A 596-vote note confirms the dough freezes well wrapped as individual balls. For those without a suitable pan, a 152-vote comment bakes them on a pizza stone or sheet tray at about 470F until they puff, then flips them. Yogurt is essential and has no easy substitute.

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

name: Mexican Street Corn Salad (Esquites)
ingredients:
2 tablespoons (30ml) vegetable oil
4 ears fresh corn, shucked, kernels removed (about 3 cups fresh corn kernels)
Kosher salt
2 ounces (60g) feta or Cotija cheese, finely crumbled
1/2 cup (50 g) finely sliced scallions, green parts only
1/2 cup (23 g) (1/2 ounce) fresh cilantro leaves, finely chopped
1 jalapeño pepper, seeded and stemmed, finely chopped
1 to 2 medium cloves garlic, pressed or minced on a Microplane grater (about 1 to 2 teaspoons)
2 tablespoons (30ml) mayonnaise
1 tablespoon (15ml) fresh lime juice from 1 lime
Chile powder or hot chile flakes, to taste
directions:
Heat oil in a large nonstick skillet or wok over high heat until shimmering. Add corn kernels, season to taste with salt, toss once or twice, and cook without moving until charred on one side, about 2 minutes. Toss corn, stir, and repeat until charred on second side, about 2 minutes longer. Continue tossing and charring until corn is well charred all over, about 10 minutes total. Transfer to a large bowl.

Add cheese, scallions, cilantro, jalapeño, garlic, mayonnaise, lime juice, and chile powder and toss to combine. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and more chile powder to taste. Serve immediately.
description: 7/22 Used wok outside. Had trouble getting corn blackened. Maybe indoors would work better? We might have had less corn so the topping seemed generous. Cheese had a bit of a funky flavor. Hard to know if that is intended. Overall really good.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.9 (45) / 119 reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt offers esquites as the spoonable, less messy alternative to elotes, with the added advantage that it needs no grill. The trick to making it indoors is cutting the kernels off before cooking rather than after, then charring them in a ripping-hot wok or skillet and leaving them undisturbed long enough for the sugars to caramelise and darken before tossing, repeating until they are charred all over; done properly a few kernels pop like popcorn, so a splatter guard is worth having. The hot corn is tossed immediately with the elote flavourings - garlicky mayonnaise, crumbled cotija or feta, scallions, cilantro, jalapeno, lime juice and chile powder - so the dressing clings to each kernel. It is good hot or at room temperature, which makes it a picnic dish.

What readers report: The highest-voted comments are about serving rather than method: the top one treats it as an appetiser with sturdy tortilla chips, and the next premixes everything but the corn, grills oiled and seasoned cobs, then cuts the kernels straight into the bowl at service. The most common correction is timing, with reviewers reporting the charring takes closer to twice the stated ten minutes and that stirring too often prevents it. Substitutions people report working: frozen corn, which caramelises less but is fine and even makes a decent uncooked cold salad; flat-leaf parsley for cilantro; feta for cotija; minced tinned chipotle in place of chile powder for smoke; and two cans of black beans replacing two ears to make it a main. Sour cream stood in for mayonnaise but did not bind to the hot corn as well. One reader suggests the steps should be reordered so the dressing is made first.

Note on the source: Comments truncated at 'Read More'. Many reviews carry 2026 dates. The recipe gives no quantity for the chile powder, which one reviewer flags.

name: Migas (Scrambled Eggs with Crispy Tortillas)
ingredients:
3 tablespoons (41 g) vegetable oil
2 corn tortillas cut into strips or squares
1 jalapeno pepper diced
1 small red bell pepper diced
1 small onion white or yellow, diced
4-5 eggs lightly scrambled
1 medium tomato diced
Salt and pepper to taste
½ cup (56 g) shredded pepperjack or Monterrey Jack cheese
For Serving: spicy chili flakes extra sliced peppers, avocado, hot sauce
directions:
Heat the vegetable oil in a large pan and add the corn tortillas. Fry them lightly in the hot oil until they crisp up, flipping a bit, about 4-5 minutes. Remove them from the pan and set them into paper towels to drain. Sprinkle them with a bit of salt while they are hot.

Next, add the peppers and onion to the hot pan and cook them down about 5 minutes.

Stir in the tomato, then pour in the scrambled eggs. Sprinkle with salt and pepper and stir.

Cook the eggs, stirring here and there, about 2-3 minutes, or until the eggs just begin to set.

Remove from heat and stir in the reserved crispy tortillas and shredded cheese.

Top with spicy chili flakes, extra sliced peppers and avocado. And hot sauce if desired!
notes:
Heat Factor: Mild-Medium. You can up the heat by adding extra jalapeno peppers, and using a spicy hot sauce to finish. Reduce the heat by coring the jalapenos before cooking, or using bell peppers instead.

Make it a Bigger Meal. Migas is a great dish on its own, but as a variation, consider adding spicy Mexican chorizo for some added kick and flavor. You can even add in other crumbled sausage, ground chicken or refried beans to make it more of a meal.

Add Some Salsa. Salsa is also a popular addition. Scoop a few spoonfuls of Salsa Roja or your favorite Salsa Verde as a finisher. You'll love the added flavor pop.

Tortilla Chips. If you'd like to skip the steps for frying the tortillas, use crispy tortilla chips instead. They work great for quick and easy migas!

Web summary (chilipeppermadness.com, 5 out of 5 stars, 16 ratings). Mike Hultquist's Tex-Mex breakfast of scrambled eggs shot through with fried corn tortilla strips, peppers, onion, tomato and melted cheese. He frames it partly as a use for stale tortillas, which fry up crisper than fresh ones. The important bit of timing is that the crisp tortilla goes in only after the eggs have begun to set, so it keeps some crunch instead of softening completely into the curds.

What readers report: The substitution that comes up most is skipping the frying step entirely and stirring in crushed tortilla chips, which several cooks say saves time and gives a comparable crunch, though it runs saltier. One reader adds bacon and garlic at the pepper stage and uses salsa in place of the fresh diced tomato, which avoids the wateriness fresh tomato can introduce into the eggs. Another practical note from the thread is to serve the jalapeno on the side rather than cooking it in, so heat can be adjusted per person when feeding a mixed table.

name: Migliaccio (Italian Ricotta and Semolina Cake)
ingredients:
1 cup (165g) fine or medium semolina flour, plus more for the pan
1/2 teaspoon (1.4 g) kosher salt
2 1/2 cups (610 g) whole milk
1/4 cup (57g) unsalted butter, plus more for greasing the pan
1 cup (200g) granulated sugar
4 large eggs
1 1/2 cups (350g) whole milk ricotta, well-drained (see recipe note)
1 tablespoon (6.0 g) freshly grated lemon zest, from 2 lemons
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) vanilla extract
1/4 teaspoon (0.7 g) ground cinnamon
directions:
Preheat the oven to 375°F.

Grease the bottom and sides of a 9-inch springform pan with butter. Line the bottom of the pan with parchment paper and butter the parchment. Coat the pan with semolina flour and tap out the excess.

Add the semolina, salt, and milk to a medium saucepan and whisk to combine. Set the pan over medium heat, and cook, stirring, until the mixture thickens into a porridge, 5 to 8 minutes. It should be similar to the consistency of cream of wheat. 

Take the pan off the heat. Add the butter and sugar, and stir until combined and smooth.

Before adding the eggs, let the semolina cool slightly until warm but not scalding hot, 10 to 15 minutes.

Once the semolina has cooled a bit, add the eggs, one at a time, whisking to combine after each. Beat in the ricotta until fully combined and smooth. Stir in the lemon zest, vanilla extract, and cinnamon. 

Pour the batter into the prepared pan. Bake until the outermost edge of the cake has turned golden brown and the cake has puffed and cracked a bit in places, about 50 minutes. The cake will jiggle slightly, but the center should be no more wobbly than the rest of the cake.
description: 4/26 Ok but perhaps too solid/cheesecakey. Made according to recipe. Nice lemon flavor. But we wanted a drier, cakier crumb.
notes:
I like to make it ahead of time and chill it overnight before serving it the next day with a dusting of powdered sugar and maybe some berries on the side. Especially in summer, I like it fridge cold, but the overnight chill also gives time for the flavors to meld. On a cold day, though, I might just have a messy slice while it’s still warm and pudding-like.

Web summary (simplyrecipes.com, 5.0 (4) shown, but 0 written reviews). Mark Beahm, a former professional baker who says he prefers rustic home desserts to finicky, decoration-heavy ones, introduces migliaccio, a ricotta-and-semolina cake from Campania traditionally eaten at Carnevale, describing its texture as landing between a plain cake and a cheesecake. He explains the technique goal: cooking semolina into a milk porridge on the stove before folding in cooled eggs and ricotta gives richness and creaminess without needing a water bath or extra dairy, and the same pan is used throughout to save on dishes. He flavors it with lemon zest, vanilla and a pinch of cinnamon (rather than the traditional Fiori di Sicilia extract), and recommends chilling it overnight so the flavors meld, though it can also be eaten warm and pudding-like straight from the oven. What readers report: none -- despite a 5.0 rating shown from 4 ratings at the top of the page, the reviews section itself reads 'Be the first to review!', meaning no written comments, corrections, or substitutions have actually been posted.
