name: Moros Y Cristianos (Black Beans and Rice)
ingredients:
4 lean bacon slices, chopped
Extra-virgin olive oil, as needed
1 white onion, diced
2 garlic cloves, smashed
1 green bell pepper, seeded and deveined, then diced
1 teaspoon (2.6 g) Rancho Gordo New Mexican Red Chile Powder
1 teaspoon (1.1 g) dried Mexican oregano, preferably Rancho Gordo Oregano Indio
2 cups (344 g) cooked Rancho Gordo Midnight Black beans in their broth
Salt
1½ cups (278 g) warm cooked white rice
Lime wedges and hot sauce, for serving
directions:
In a large saucepan over medium-low heat, gently cook the bacon until the fat is rendered and bacon is cooked through, about 10 minutes. You should have about 2 tablespoons fat. If there is less, add oil as needed.

Add the onion, garlic, and bell pepper; cook gently, stirring occasionally, until the bell pepper is soft, about 8 minutes. Add the red chile powder and oregano; stir until incorporated. Add the beans and their broth; stir gently until combined. Reduce heat to low; cook, stirring occasionally, for about 10 minutes to allow flavors to mingle. Taste and adjust seasoning, as desired.

Spoon some of the rice and the beans alongside each other on individual plates. Serve immediately with limes and hot sauce.
description:
4/24 Delicious! Used one cup dried beans, or at least 2½ cups cooked. 5 slices Oscar Mayer. Had no green pepper or celery. Cooked beans according to Rancho Gordo basic recipe with sofrito and garlic. 

10/24 Really good again. Used the green pepper this time. Noticeable. Used ½ tsp of Himalayan chile powder. Noticeable but could have done ⅔ tap
notes:
Web summary (ranchogordo.com). Steve Sando of Rancho Gordo makes the case for the older Cuban practice of cooking the rice and the black beans separately and only bringing them together on the plate. Cooking them in one pot, as many modern recipes do, blurs both; kept apart, each keeps its own definition and the dish tastes sharper. The sofrito of bacon, onion, garlic and green pepper with New Mexican red chile powder and Mexican oregano is built first, then the cooked beans go in with their broth.

Note on the source: no comments section on page

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Your 4/24 and 10/24 notes already dialed in the chile powder amount and confirmed the green pepper; cooking beans and rice separately is already Sando's recommended technique.

name: Mushroom & Leek Bread Pudding
ingredients:
6 cups (270 g) (½-inch-diced) bread cubes from a rustic country loaf, crusts removed
2 tablespoons (27 g) good olive oil
1 tablespoon (14 g) unsalted butter
2 ounces (57 g) pancetta, small-diced
4 cups (356 g) sliced leeks, white and light green parts (4 leeks)
1½ pounds (680 g) cremini mushrooms, stems trimmed and ¼-inch-sliced
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) chopped fresh tarragon leaves
1/4 cup (59 g) medium or dry sherry
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
1/3 cup (20 g) minced fresh flat-leaf parsley
4 extra-large eggs
1½ cups (357 g) heavy cream
1 cup (240 g) chicken stock, preferably homemade
1½ cups (170 g) grated Gruyère cheese (6 ounces), divided
directions:
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Spread the bread cubes on a sheet pan and bake for 15 to 20 minutes, until lightly browned. Set aside.

Meanwhile, heat the oil and butter in a large (12-inch) sauté pan over medium heat. Add the pancetta and cook for 5 minutes, until starting to brown. Stir in the leeks and cook over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, until the leeks are tender. Stir in the mushrooms, tarragon, sherry, 1 tablespoon salt, and 1½ teaspoons pepper and cook for 10 to 12 minutes, until most of the liquid evaporates, stirring occasionally. Off the heat, stir in the parsley.

In a large mixing bowl, whisk together the eggs, cream, chicken stock, and 1 cup of the Gruyère. Add the bread cubes and mushroom mixture, stirring well to combine. Set aside at room temperature for 30 minutes to allow the bread to absorb the liquid. Stir well and pour into a 2½ to 3-quart gratin dish (13 x 9 x 2 inches). Sprinkle with the remaining ½ cup of Gruyère and bake for 45 to 50 minutes, until the top is browned and the custard is set. Serve hot.
notes:
Web summary (barefootcontessa.com). A savoury bread pudding from Ina Garten's Barefoot Contessa Foolproof. Diced country bread is toasted first so the cubes can absorb the custard without collapsing, and the mushroom-leek-pancetta mixture is deglazed with sherry to concentrate it. The custard is eggs and heavy cream cut with chicken stock, which keeps it from being as heavy as a straight cream custard, and Gruyere goes both through the mixture and on top. Garten presents it as an assemble-ahead dish for holidays, baked just before serving.

Note on the source: barefootcontessa.com has no comments section

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Method already matches best practice: bread is toasted first, mushroom liquid is reduced before assembly, and it rests to absorb custard. Food Network's review section wouldn't load to check further.

name: Mushroom Quiche
ingredients:
1 fully baked 9" pie shell
2 T. (28 g) butter
2 T. (20 g) shallots, finely chopped
3/4 lb. (340 g) mushrooms, thinly sliced
3 large eggs
1 3/4 c. (416 g) heavy cream
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
1/4 t. (0.6 g) freshly ground pepper [recipe says T.]
2 T. (11 g) parmesan cheese ground
2 T. (7.5 g) parsley
2 T. (28 g) butter
directions:
Preheat oven to 375.
1. Melt 2 T. butter in large saucepan. Add shallots and cook until they are transparent. 
2. Add mushrooms, cover pan and cook for 8 mins. Remove cover, raise heat and cook until liquid has evaporated. Remove mixture to plate to cool.
3. Scatter cooked mushroom mixture on bottom of cool, pre-baked pie shell. Place shell in freezer making sure it is level.
4. Beat eggs, cream, salt and pepper together in large bowl. Ladle egg mixture into the shell and sprinkle with the cheese, parsley, and small pieces of butter. If you want to freeze the quiche, wrap well.
5. Bake 45-55 minutes or until the custard has set and turned a light golden color. Internal temperature should be 170 to 175. If baking frozen quiche, do not thaw first.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing to change. Baking to 170-175F internal and chilling the filled shell before baking already match current quiche technique for a silky set and crisp bottom.

name: Mustard Chicken Salad with Tarragon Ina
source: Ina Garten - How Easy is That? Cookbook p. 104
ingredients:
2 whole (4 split) chicken breasts, bone-in, skin-on
Good olive oil
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 cups (182 g) broccoli florets
1 1/2 cups (330 g) good mayonnaise
2 tablespoons (30 g) dry white wine
1/4 cup (62 g) Dijon mustard
3 tablespoons (47 g) whole-grain mustard
2 tablespoons (6.9 g) minced fresh tarragon leaves
1 cup (149 g) cherry or grape tomatoes, halved
directions:
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F.

Place the chicken breasts on a sheet pan and rub the skin with olive oil. Sprinkle liberally with salt and pepper. Roast for 35 to 40 minutes, until the chicken is just cooked. Set aside until cool enough to handle. Remove the meat from the bones, discard the skin, and dice the chicken in large bite-size pieces.

Meanwhile, add the broccoli florets to a large pot of salted boiling water. Cook for 1 minute, until crisp tender, drain, and place into a bowl of ice water until cool. This will stop the cooking and set the bright green color.

For the dressing, whisk together the mayonnaise, wine, mustards, 1/2 teaspoon of salt (more to taste if desired - see description above) and 1/2 teaspoon pepper. Add enough sauce to the warm chicken to moisten well. Add the tarragon, broccoli, and tomatoes and mix gently to combine. Refrigerate for a few hours to allow the flavors to blend. Serve at room temperature.
description:
10/2015 Ina's original recipe calls for 1 T salt in the dressing. This is way too much! Use 1/2 to 1 teaspoon instead and taste. Also, consider making only 2/3 of the dressing quantity, since there is usually extra dressing. On the other hand, any extra dressing is yummy on sandwiches! 
4/2024 You can use rotisserie chicken for this recipe even if it is cold. Fresh tarragon makes it special!
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten's chicken salad from How Easy Is That?, built on bone-in skin-on breasts roasted rather than poached, which keeps the meat moister and gives it more flavour than boiled chicken. The dressing is mayonnaise loosened with a little dry white wine and sharpened with both Dijon and whole-grain mustard, with fresh tarragon as the defining herb. Blanched broccoli and halved cherry tomatoes make it a full lunch dish rather than a sandwich filling. She has it chilled before serving so the mustard and tarragon have time to work through.

Note on the source: no comments retrieved from page

claude_opt.changes: Recipe already sound. Your 10/2015 note fixed the two real issues (1 T salt is too much; make 2/3 batch of dressing). Dressing added while chicken is still warm matches best-reviewed chicken salads.

name: My Favorite Challah
ingredients:
1 1/2 packages active dry yeast (about 3 1/2 teaspoons)
1 tablespoon (13 g) plus 1/2 cup sugar
1/2 cup (109 g) vegetable oil, more for greasing bowl
5 large eggs
1 tablespoon (18 g) salt
8 to 8 1/2 cups (1-1 kg) all-purpose flour
Poppy or sesame seeds for sprinkling
directions:
In a large bowl, dissolve yeast and 1 tablespoon sugar in 1 3/4 cups lukewarm water.

Whisk oil into yeast, then beat in 4 eggs, one at a time, with remaining sugar and salt. Gradually add flour. When dough holds together, it is ready for kneading. (You can also use a mixer with a dough hook for both mixing and kneading.)

Turn dough onto a floured surface and knead until smooth. Clean out bowl and grease it, then return dough to bowl. Cover with plastic wrap, and let rise in a warm place for 1 hour, until almost doubled in size. Dough may also rise in an oven that has been warmed to 150 degrees then turned off. Punch down dough, cover and let rise again in a warm place for another half-hour.

To make a 6-braid challah, either straight or circular, take half the dough and form it into 6 balls. With your hands, roll each ball into a strand about 12 inches long and 1 1/2 inches wide. Place the 6 in a row, parallel to one another. Pinch the tops of the strands together. Move the outside right strand over 2 strands. Then take the second strand from the left and move it to the far right. Take the outside left strand and move it over 2. Move second strand from the right over to the far left. Start over with the outside right strand. Continue this until all strands are braided. For a straight loaf, tuck ends underneath. For a circular loaf, twist into a circle, pinching ends together. Make a second loaf the same way. Place braided loaves on a greased cookie sheet with at least 2 inches in between.

Beat remaining egg and brush it on loaves. Either freeze breads or let rise another hour.

If baking immediately, preheat oven to 375 degrees and brush loaves again. If freezing, remove from freezer 5 hours before baking. Then dip your index finger in the egg wash, then into poppy or sesame seeds and then onto a mound of bread. Continue until bread is decorated with seeds.

Bake in middle of oven for 35 to 40 minutes, or until golden. Cool loaves on a rack.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (5,193)). Joan Nathan opens with the word's origin, the small portion of dough set aside when baking bread as a remembrance of the destruction of the Temple, and traces how it became the sweet, brioche-like braided loaf brought to America from Central and Eastern Europe. Braided loaves are year-round; round ones, often with raisins, belong to Rosh Hashana, Yom Kippur and Sukkot. Her accumulated tips from bakers in the US, Europe and Israel: multiple risings improve the loaf, one slow rise in the refrigerator gives a more brioche-like crumb, and two coats of egg wash produce the gloss.

What readers report: Two notes matter most. The highest-voted (994) supplies the gram weights the recipe lacks: 3 1/2 teaspoons active dry yeast at 9.9g, 1 tablespoon sugar at 12.6g, 1/2 cup sugar at 100g, 1/2 cup vegetable oil at 120g, 1 tablespoon salt at 17.07g, and 8 to 8 1/2 cups all-purpose flour at 960 to 1020g; a separate 449-vote comment is the request that prompted it, asking the Times to publish weights. The other significant correction (560 votes) states the six-strand braiding instructions are written incorrectly. A 466-vote baker adds a sponge step, using part of the flour and liquid first, for better brioche flavour and texture. A 245-vote note swaps in 1/2 cup plus 1 tablespoon honey for the sugar and steeps a pinch of saffron in boiling water. A 757-vote comment explains the pale bands in the photograph come from oven spring exposing new surface after the wash.

Note on the source: comments report the six-braid instructions are wrong; top comment supplies gram weights useful for the collection

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

makeahead: If freezing, remove from freezer 5 hours before baking.

claude_opt.changes: The six-strand braid instructions are garbled per readers (560 votes); follow a standard six-strand video tutorial instead of the text. Weights are already in the ingredient list.

name: My Thai Chicken Wraps
ingredients:
1 rotisserie chicken, skinned and boned, meat pulled into large chunks
1 (12 ounce) package coleslaw mix with carrots
2 tablespoons (25 g) white sugar
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) minced garlic
1 tablespoon (6.0 g) minced fresh ginger
1 tablespoon (1.5 g) chopped fresh basil
black pepper to taste
½ cup (135 g) hoisin sauce
¼ cup (64 g) soy sauce
2 tablespoons (30 g) white vinegar
1 head green leaf lettuce, leaves separated, rinsed, and patted dry
1 cup (240 g) Thai-style peanut sauce
directions:
Heat a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add chicken, coleslaw mix, sugar, garlic, ginger, basil, and pepper to the hot skillet. Pour in hoisin sauce, soy sauce, and vinegar; bring to a simmer. Cook and stir until chicken is hot and liquid has been absorbed, about 10 minutes.

To serve, line a platter with lettuce leaves and pour chicken mixture into the center of the platter. Each diner assembles their own wrap by placing some of the chicken mixture onto a lettuce leaf, adding a little peanut sauce, and then rolling it into a cylinder.
description: 5/25 Excellent flavors, great with a salad or in a wrap. Used 12 oz bag of cabbage, carrot, broccoli pre-sliced fr wegmans. Wegmans rotisserie chicken. Used rice wine vinegar. Used wegmans thai peanut. Good made ahead and reheated, even better fresh cooked.
notes:
Web summary (Allrecipes, 4.3 (67) / 38 reviews). A one-line headnote from submitter gztg44: these lettuce wraps are her home version of a restaurant appetizer she loves, and her family asks for them weekly. The site's own blurb adds that rotisserie chicken is re-sauteed with garlic, ginger, basil, hoisin and soy for extra flavour, and that store-bought Thai peanut sauce finishes each wrap. No technique explanation is given beyond simmering until the liquid is absorbed.

What readers report: The most helpful review (24 votes, Lori) says the dish is too sweet as written and recommends dropping the sugar or cutting the hoisin; this is by far the most repeated correction, with others halving the sugar and one reducing hoisin to 1/4 cup with good results. A few instead want more hoisin. The step people get wrong is the slaw timing: several report it turning to mush and advise stirring the coleslaw mix in at the very end. Common additions are water chestnuts, red pepper flakes, scallions, extra basil and crisp fried rice noodles. Substitutions that work include ground chicken, poached breast, chicken thighs, broccoli slaw, rice vinegar or lime juice for the white vinegar, and honey for hoisin. Butter or Bibb lettuce is preferred; tortillas and rice bowls also get good reports. Other complaints: soupy, messy, high in sodium.

claude_opt.changes: Add the coleslaw mix in the last minute, not the full 10; simmering it the whole time turns it to mush per multiple reports. Your 5/25 note found the recipe good as-is on sweetness, so keep the sugar.

name: Nancy Silverton’s Basic Focaccia
ingredients:
1/2 cup (60 g) plus 3 tablespoons (3.04 ounces) bread flour
1 1/4 cups (296 g) plus 2 tablespoons (11.04 ounces) water
1/2 cup (108 g) plus scant 1 tablespoon (.39 ounce) olive oil, divided
Focaccia sponge
2 packed tablespoons plus ¼ packed teaspoon (.39 ounce) fresh cake yeast or 1¾ teaspoons (5.4 g) (.195 ounce) active dry yeast
2 tablespoons (15 g) plus ¾ teaspoon (.56 ounce) rye flour
3 1/3 to 3 2/3 cups (400-440 g) (15 to 16.45 ounces) bread flour, more if needed
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) (.39 ounce) kosher salt
directions:
1. In a small mixing bowl (preferably plastic or ceramic), sprinkle the yeast over the water. Set the bowl aside for a few minutes to give the water time to absorb the yeast. Using a wooden spoon, stir in the bread flour until all of the ingredients are thoroughly combined.

2. Cover the bowl tightly with a sheet of plastic wrap, then tightly wrap another piece of plastic wrap or twine around the perimeter of the bowl to further seal the bowl.

3. Set the bowl aside at room temperature (ideally 68 to 70 degrees) until the sponge becomes bubbly and thick, like the consistency of wallpaper paste (thicker than a pancake batter but thinner than dough), 12 to 24 hours.

Focaccia dough

1. About 3½ hours before you are ready to bake the focaccia, place the water, scant tablespoon olive oil and sponge in the bowl of a stand mixer. Fit the mixer with a dough hook and, over low speed, add the yeast, rye flour and 15 ounces (3 1/3 cups) bread flour. Mix the ingredients over low speed for 2 minutes to thoroughly combine and form the dough.

2. With the mixer running, slowly add the salt, then increase the speed to medium. Continue mixing the dough until it is smooth and well-formed, and starts to pull away from the bowl, 6 to 8 minutes. Note that the dough will not pull so much that it “cleans” the bowl, but if the dough is too sticky and is not pulling away from the sides of the bowl at all, add a little more bread flour (a spoonful as needed at a time) to achieve the right consistency.

3. While the dough is mixing, lightly grease a bowl large enough to hold the dough when it doubles in size with olive oil. When the dough is ready, turn it out of the mixer into the oiled bowl. Wrap the dough tightly in plastic wrap and tightly wrap the perimeter of the bowl with kitchen twine or another piece of plastic wrap to further seal the bowl. Set the dough aside at room temperature (ideally 68 to 70 degrees) until doubled, about 1½ hours.

4. Dust the work surface lightly with flour and turn the dough out onto the floured surface. Acting as if the round has four sides, fold the edges of the dough toward the center. Turn the dough over and return it, folded side down, to the bowl. Cover the bowl again with plastic wrap and set it aside at room temperature until it has doubled in volume, 50 minutes to 1 hour. (The dough will be puffy and will feel alive, springy and resistant. It will not collapse under the touch of your fingertips.)

5. Pour ¼ cup olive oil into each of the cake pans, and tilt the pans so the oil coats the bottom evenly. Dust the work surface again lightly with flour and carefully turn the dough out onto the floured surface, taking care not to deflate the dough in the process. Divide the dough into two equal segments, each weighing approximately 18 ounces. Place the dough segments in the prepared cake pans and very gently pull the edges just to obtain a roughly round shape. Cover the pans with a clean dishcloth and set aside at room temperature until relaxed and spread to cover about half of the surface of the pans, about 30 minutes.
notes:
Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

Web summary (latimes.com, no rating or review count shown). This is a 2014 Los Angeles Times Test Kitchen feature presenting Nancy Silverton's professional bakery method for basic focaccia dough, built around a slow pre-ferment: a wallpaper-paste-consistency sponge made with a tiny amount of cake yeast, water and bread flour, left at 68-70F for 12 to 24 hours before being mixed into the final dough. The final dough adds rye flour, more yeast, olive oil and salt, is mixed in a stand mixer to a specific pull-away-from-the-bowl consistency, and undergoes a bulk rise, a fold, a second rise, then division into two 18-ounce rounds pressed into oiled cake pans -- all specified by weight in ounces on a digital scale, reflecting Silverton's bakery-trained precision. The piece is framed as one installment of a Nancy Silverton recipe series the paper's Test Kitchen ran, inviting readers to submit photos of their results for the food blog. What readers report: this page as captured shows no comment or review section at all -- there is no reader feedback to summarize, positive or corrective.

ahead: Set the bowl aside at room temperature (ideally 68 to 70 degrees) until the sponge becomes bubbly and…

claude_opt.changes: Stored directions are truncated mid-sentence after the second rise — no dimpling, no oil/salt topping, no baking temp or time survive in this entry. Recover the missing steps before using; do not bake from what's stored.

name: New Mexico Green Chile Sauce
ingredients:
1 tablespoon (14 g) butter or lard
⅔ cup (107 g) chopped onion
2 tablespoons (15 g) flour
1½ cups (360 g) chicken or vegetable broth
1 cup (140 g) (or more) chopped green chiles
1 large clove garlic, finely minced
¾ teaspoon (4.5 g) salt
Dash of ground cumin
directions: Melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Sauté the onion until soft. Stir in the flour. Add the broth. Then add chiles, garlic, salt and cumin. Simmer for 20 minutes.
description: Chile is a sauce made from red or green chiles and served hot over many New Mexican dishes. Chile does not use vinegar, unlike most salsas, picantes and other hot sauces. This basic yet versatile sauce can be used to create enchiladas or poured over chimichangas, tacos or burritos.
notes:
Web summary (visitalbuquerque.org). Visit Albuquerque frames New Mexican cooking around corn, beans, squash and above all chile, describing red or green chile sauce as the element that defines the cuisine and distinguishes it from Mexican cooking. The green sauce is a simple roux: butter or lard with softened onion, flour stirred in, then broth whisked to smooth before the chopped green chiles, garlic, salt and a little cumin go in. The flour is what carries the sauce so it naps enchiladas or burritos rather than running off.

Note on the source: tourism-board page, no comments or ratings; page is a roundup of several New Mexican entree recipes, and the Green Chile Sauce is one section on it rather than a dedicated page - a New Mexico Red Chile Sauce sits alongside it

Merged September 2026: this entry absorbed a duplicate previously filed as "Green Chile Sauce". Every cook's note from both copies is kept above.

claude_opt.changes: Bloom the cumin with the onion in the fat before adding the broth, rather than dropping it in with the liquid; releases more of its flavor.

name: New York-Style Pizza Sauce
servings: Enough for 2 to 4 (12-inch) pies, depending on how much sauce you like
ingredients:
1 (28-ounce) can whole peeled tomatoes
1 tablespoon (14 g) extra-virgin olive oil
1 tablespoon (14 g) unsalted butter
2 medium cloves garlic, grated on microplane grater (about 2 teaspoons)
1 teaspoon (1.0 g) dried oregano
Pinch red pepper flakes
Kosher salt
2 (6-inch) sprigs fresh basil with leaves attached
1 medium yellow onion, peeled and split in half
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) sugar
directions:
1. Process tomatoes and their juice through food mill, pulse in food processor until pureed, or puree with hand blender. Puree should not be completely smooth, but should have no chunks larger than 1/16 of an inch. Set tomatoes aside.

2. Combine butter and oil in medium saucepan and heat over medium-low heat until butter is melted. Add garlic, oregano, pepper flakes, and large pinch salt and cook, stirring frequently, until fragrant but not browned, about 3 minutes. Add tomatoes, basil sprigs, onion halves, and sugar. Bring to a simmer, reduce heat to lowest setting (bubbles should barely be breaking the surface), and cook, stirring occasionally, until reduced by 1/2, about 1 hour. Discard onions and basil stems. Season to taste with salt. Allow to cool and store in covered container in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.3 (42) / 167 reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt is after a cooked, heavily seasoned sauce for by-the-slice New York pies, balancing sweetness, acidity and heat over a herbal backbone, and thin enough to spread but thick enough that the slice survives being folded. He swaps one of the two tablespoons of olive oil for butter, borrowing from Marcella Hazan, for a rounder mouthfeel, and keeps her trick of simmering halved onion in the pot and discarding it; side-by-side tests also showed dried oregano matched fresh, which he explains by noting that herbs from hot, dry climates hold their flavour through drying, though basil has to go in as fresh sprigs. He walks through the five canned tomato products and settles on whole peeled tomatoes packed in juice, pureed at home, because diced are firmed with calcium chloride, crushed are unregulated, and puree and paste already taste cooked. The sauce then reduces by half over very low heat for about an hour, since high heat would add unwanted roasted notes.

What readers report: The long-running argument is whether a cooked sauce can be called New York style at all. Several readers, including one who worked in a Manhattan pizzeria in the 1980s, insist the real thing is an uncooked puree of canned tomato seasoned with salt, oregano and garlic or onion powder that cooks on the pie; others who also worked in pizzerias say theirs was always cooked and that simmering melds the flavours. Sweetness is the other complaint: one reviewer found the sugar plus the simmered onion halves too sweet to repeat, while another suggests whole carrots in place of the sugar. Reported umami additions include a single dash of Worcestershire and a Parmesan rind dropped in the pot. One cook needed about 90 minutes rather than 60 to reduce by half, and several say not to throw the cooked onion away.

Note on the source: Comments truncated at 'Read More'. Much of the review section is an argument about authenticity rather than usable feedback, and several readers appear to misread the method (one asks how to remove onion that is in fact left in halves). Vote counts are all zero.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. This is Kenji's tested, side-by-side-compared formula; the loudest comments are an authenticity argument about cooked vs. raw sauce, not a fixable error.

name: No-Knead Bread
ingredients:
3 ⅓ cups/430 grams all-purpose or bread flour, plus more for dusting
¼ teaspoon (0.8 g) instant yeast
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) kosher salt
Cornmeal or wheat bran, as needed
directions:
In a large bowl combine flour, yeast and salt. Add 1 1/2 cups plus 2 tablespoons/390 milliliters water, and stir until blended; dough will be shaggy and sticky. Cover bowl with plastic wrap. Let dough rest at least 12 hours, preferably about 18, at warm room temperature, about 70 degrees.

Dough is ready when its surface is dotted with bubbles. Lightly flour a work surface and place dough on it; sprinkle it with a little more flour and fold it over on itself once or twice. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let rest about 15 minutes.

Using just enough flour to keep dough from sticking to work surface or to your fingers, gently and quickly shape dough into a ball. Generously coat a cotton towel (not terry cloth) with flour, wheat bran or cornmeal; put dough seam side down on towel and dust with more flour, bran or cornmeal. Cover with another cotton towel and let rise for about 2 hours. When it is ready, dough will be more than double in size and will not readily spring back when poked with a finger.

At least a half-hour before dough is ready, heat oven to 450 degrees. Put a 6- to 8-quart heavy covered pot (cast iron, enamel, Pyrex or ceramic) in oven as it heats. When dough is ready, carefully remove pot from oven. Slide your hand under towel and turn dough over into pot, seam side up; it may look like a mess, but that is O.K. Shake pan once or twice if dough is unevenly distributed; it will straighten out as it bakes. Cover with lid and bake 30 minutes, then remove lid and bake another 15 to 30 minutes, until loaf is beautifully browned. Cool on a rack.
description:
RM 2/13: I find that it takes less overall cooking time than he suggests.
RM 4/20: The overnight white bread version is the one now used, not the original 2013 formula.
notes:
See Overnight White Bread (Ken Forkish) for the version Robert bakes now; this entry is the original 2013 Lahey formula.

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

ahead: Let dough rest at least 12 hours, preferably about 18, at warm room temperature, about 70 degrees.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing here — your 4/20 note already retired this in favor of the Forkish overnight white bread, kept only for reference.

name: Oatmeal Cookies
ingredients:
3/4 c. (170 g) butter or margarine (Land O Lakes real margarine works best)
1 c. (213 g) light brown sugar
1/2 c. (100 g) granulated sugar
1 egg
1/4 c. (59 g) water
1 t. (4.2 g) vanilla
3 c. (267 g) oats (old-fashioned)
1 c. (120 g) flour
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
1/2 t. (2.3 g) baking soda
1 c. (145 g) raisins
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.
Beat together shortening, sugars egg, water, and vanilla until creamy. Add combined remaining ingredients except raisins; mix well. Fold in raisins. Bake for 12-15 minutes.
description: Our favorite.
notes:
Web summary (food.com, 31 reviews, Community Pick (no star count displayed)). A food.com member (spatchcock) posts this as the oatmeal cookie she settled on after testing many others, preferring it because it bakes up crisp rather than cloyingly sweet. It is the older Quaker Oats canister formula, built on shortening or margarine rather than all butter, with a quarter cup of water added to the creamed sugars. That water thins the dough just enough for the three cups of oats to hydrate and spread, which is what gives the crisp edge and chewy center.

What readers report: The added water is the main argument: one baker regretted it and compensated with extra flour. Several insist the 'optional' salt should be treated as required. Cinnamon, nutmeg, raisins and chocolate chips are all reported as good additions. Pressed into a 9x13 pan for 35-40 minutes it works as a bar cookie. Substituting oil for the shortening gives a crunchier cookie; pulling them at 9-10 minutes instead of the full time gives a chewier one.

Note on the source: Ingredient list matches the family text exactly, including the telltale 3/4 c shortening/margarine, 1/2 c granulated + 1 c brown sugar, 1 egg, and the unusual 1/4 cup water -- this is the pre-1990s Quaker package recipe, consistent with the recorded source 'Quaker Oats 1983'. Marked medium only because this is a member repost on food.com rather than a Quaker-published page; Quaker's current site carries the reformulated all-butter 'Vanishing Oatmeal Raisin Cookies' (1 c butter, 2 eggs, no water), which is NOT the family's version. Runner-up: https://www.justapinch.com/recipes/quakers-best-oatmeal-cookies.html

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. The family already rates this their favorite; it's the pre-1990s Quaker formula with the water that gives the crisp edge, not the reformulated all-butter version.

name: Oklahoma Onion Burgers
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) ground beef, preferably 20 to 30 percent fat
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 medium or 1 large yellow or white onion, sliced as thinly as possible, and on a mandoline for best results (8 to 10 ounces of sliced onion)
4 slices American cheese
4 soft, sturdy hamburger buns, such as King’s Hawaiian rolls
Dill pickle chips and condiments, as desired
directions:
Divide the beef: Line a 13-by-18-inch rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper. Divide the ground beef into 4 even balls. Working one ball at a time and using your hands, massage the meat until it is cohesive and tacky, about 15 seconds. Next, using clean hands, roll each into a smooth ball. Place the balls on the baking sheet, with 1 ball in the center of each quadrant. Refrigerate until ready to cook.

Shape the patties: Gently press each ball into a disk-shaped patty about 3 inches wide. Place the patties on a sheet pan or large plate, and season the tops with salt and pepper. Flip the patties, and top each with a large pile of sliced onions — as many as you can balance on top; they should resemble a large haystack. (It is important to not add salt to the onions at this point, as it will draw out excess moisture, which will inhibit searing.)

Heat the skillet or griddle: Heat a large (12-inch) cast-iron or carbon-steel skillet or griddle (see Tips) over an indoor burner set to high heat or on the grates of a hot outdoor grill for a few minutes until very hot; a drop of water should skitter around the surface. (If you don’t have a pan skillet or griddle big enough, you can cook the burgers in batches.) Place 1 patty of beef in the center of one quadrant of the pan, with the onions on top (do not add any oil).

Smash the burgers: Using a very stiff spatula, press on the onions and beef to form a patty 4½- to 5-inches wide. As you smash, focus on the patty’s edges so that the finished patty is slightly thicker in the center and smashed out as thinly as possible along the edges. Repeat with the remaining patties. Use the spatula to place any stray onions back on top of the burgers. Season the onions lightly with salt and pepper.

Cook the burgers: Allow patties to cook without moving until the edges are dark brown and crusty, 1 to 2 minutes. Holding the spatula upside down (so that the head of the spatula is angled down to increase leverage), scrape the edges of each patty off the pan, working around each patty to ensure that you don’t leave any crispy edges behind. When the edges have all been loosened, turn the spatula back over (so you are holding it the standard way) and flip the patties onion side down. Use the spatula and tongs or a fork to tuck any stray onion slices mostly under the patties.

Steam the cheese and buns: Add a slice of cheese to each patty. Place the top half of each burger bun on top of the cheese, and place the bottom half of each bun on top of the top bun, split-side down. Cover the pan or griddle with a large domed lid, a large overturned saucepan or a clean folded dish towel. (To avoid a fire, make sure the edges of the dish towel do not hang over the skillet or griddle. If cooking on an outdoor grill, just close the lid.) Continue cooking until the onions are browned along the edges and the buns are steamed through, 1 to 2 minutes longer.

To serve, open the cover or lid. Remove the bottom burger bun halves to a serving platter. Add pickles and condiments as desired. (These burgers don’t typically need condiments.) Lift each burger from the skillet with the spatula and transfer to the bottom bun. Serve immediately.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (2,059)). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt traces this to Homer Davis and his son Ross at the Hamburger Inn in El Reno, Oklahoma, where it began as a Depression-era way of bulking out a burger cheaply with onion. The patties are smashed under a heap of very thinly shaved onions, and the buns are steamed in the onion vapour rather than toasted. He notes you can move the whole operation outdoors by setting the skillet or griddle over a hot grill, which also keeps the onion smell out of the house.

What readers report: The comments are unusually consensual: almost nobody argues with the method. A 74-vote note says El Reno has done it this way for eighty years and they know best. The most concrete cooking advice (106 votes) endorses the recipe's own suggestion of putting the cast-iron pan on an outdoor grill to avoid filling the house with onion smoke, and a 58-vote comment recommends a portable induction cooktop for the same reason. A 255-vote commenter whose former partner's grandfather ran an Oklahoma diner reports the family version used diced rather than sliced onion and no cheese. Bun choice gets real attention: Martin's potato rolls (62 votes) for softness without sweetness, or Trader Joe's brioche buns (50) as a sturdier brioche. One note stresses the details that matter: when to salt, and scraping the pan hard so all the browned crust ends up in the burger.

claude_opt.changes: Cook this on the Weber griddle outdoors instead of an indoor skillet — readers (106+58 votes) confirm it avoids filling the house with onion smoke, with zero change to the method.

name: Old-Fashioned Pecan Pie
ingredients:
your favorite 9" single pie crust prepared
8 tablespoons (113g) unsalted butter
1/4 cup (30g) King Arthur Unbleached All-Purpose Flour
2 1/8 cups (454g) light brown sugar packed
1/2 teaspoon (3.0 g) table salt
6 tablespoons (85g) milk
3 large eggs whisked briefly to combine
2 teaspoons (10.0 g) cider vinegar or white vinegar
2 teaspoons (8.4 g) King Arthur Pure Vanilla Extract
1/4 teaspoon (1.1 g) vanilla-butternut flavor optional
1/2 cup (57g) pecans diced
1 cup (113g) pecan halves for topping
directions: Preheat the oven to 375°F. , Roll out the pastry and place it in a greased 9" pie pan. Crimp the edges as desired., Melt the butter and set it aside to cool. , In a large bowl, mix together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the milk and eggs and beat well., Stir in the vinegar, vanilla, and flavoring, then the butter and diced pecans., Pour the mixture into the crust and scatter the pecan halves on top., Bake the pie for 47 to 50 minutes. When done, the top will be puffed up and set, and the center should just barely wobble when you jiggle the pan., Remove the pie from the oven (the pie will finish setting up as it sits) and cool completely before slicing., Store any leftover pie in the refrigerator for a day or so; freeze for longer storage.

Liz Pearl, an employee-owner at King Arthur, contributes a family pecan pie that leaves out corn syrup entirely; light brown sugar with butter, milk and a little flour carries the filling instead, giving a silkier set than the usual syrup version. name: Omelet for Two
ingredients:
1/4 pound (113 g) good thick-cut bacon
1 tablespoon (14 g) unsalted butter
1 cup (150 g) medium-diced Yukon gold potato
1/2 cup (80 g) chopped yellow onion
1 tablespoon (6.9 g) minced jalapeno pepper
5 extra-large eggs
2 tablespoons (30 g) milk or cream
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt
1/2 teaspoon (1.1 g) freshly ground black pepper
1/4 cup (25 g) chopped scallions, white and green parts
4 ounces (113 g) extra-sharp Cheddar, diced, plus extra grated cheese, for garnish
directions:
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F.

Cut the bacon crosswise in 1-inch slices. Cook the bacon in an 8-inch ovenproof saute pan over medium-low heat for 5 to 7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until browned. Drain the bacon on paper towels and discard the fat from the pan. Add the butter to the pan, and then add the potato and yellow onion. Cook over medium-low heat for about 10 minutes, tossing occasionally, until the onion starts to brown and the potato is tender but firm. Add the jalapeno pepper and cook for 30 seconds.

Meanwhile, in a medium bowl, beat the eggs, milk, salt, and pepper together with a fork. Stir in the scallions and diced Cheddar. When the potato is cooked, add the bacon to the pan and pour over the egg mixture. Place the pan in the oven for 15 to 20 minutes, until the omelet puffs and the eggs are almost cooked in the center. Sprinkle with a handful of grated Cheddar and bake for another minute. Serve hot directly from the pan.
description: 11/22 Excellent. Cover the potatoes and onions to cook them quicker. Bake in the oven for 30 minutes total.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten's omelet for two is finished in the oven rather than folded on the stovetop, which lets a heavy load of filling - bacon, diced Yukon gold potato, onion, jalapeno, scallion and extra-sharp cheddar - cook through without tearing the eggs. Baking sets the five eggs evenly all the way across instead of setting the base before the centre. It is scaled and cut for two people, closer to a shallow frittata than a classic French omelet.

Note on the source: no comments retrieved

claude_opt.changes: Your 11/22 note already fixed the timing (cover potatoes, 30 min total). One more: reserve 1 tbsp bacon fat instead of fresh butter for the potatoes, as comparable Country French Omelet versions do, for more flavor at no cost.

name: One-Pot Spaghetti with Cherry Tomatoes and Kale
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) spaghetti
1 pound (454 g) cherry tomatoes, halved (about 2 pints)
2 lemons, zested
1/4 cup (54 g) plus 3 tablespoons olive oil
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) kosher salt, plus more to taste
1 bunch kale or spinach, leaves only, washed and chopped
Black pepper
Parmesan, for serving
directions:
Bring just over a quart of water to a boil. Meanwhile, place spaghetti, tomatoes, lemon zest, oil and 2 teaspoons kosher salt in a large, dry, shallow pan. (The pan should be large enough that the dry spaghetti can lie flat.)

Carefully add the boiling water to the pan with the spaghetti. Cover pan, and bring up to a boil. Remove lid and simmer for about 6 minutes, using tongs to move the spaghetti around now and then so it doesn’t stick. Add kale or spinach and continue cooking until remaining liquid has reduced to a sauce and the pasta is cooked through. Taste, season with salt and pepper, and top with Parmesan.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (8,579)). Tejal Rao presents the internet-famous one-pan method, raw pasta simmered together with cherry tomatoes so the starch thickens into its own sauce, in the vegetarian version by British author Anna Jones, adapted from A Modern Way to Cook. The headnote pushes the adaptability: anchovies and a good pinch of red-pepper flakes can go in with the kale, and chopped mint, basil or oregano can be piled on with the cheese at the end.

What readers report: The big disagreement is whether cooking pasta this way is worth doing at all. A 522-vote comment defends it firmly, arguing the unconventional cooking is the entire point and that making it the normal way produces a different dish; a 382-vote note takes the opposite line, saying conventional pasta cooking is better and that the recipe is fine mainly as a base for whatever greens you have, arugula or Swiss chard included. A 285-vote reply deflates the one-pot claim, pointing out you can boil water in an electric kettle. On seasoning, the most-repeated advice is to be generous: plenty of garlic and red chili flakes (695 votes), with a 312-vote cook sauteing onion and garlic first and adding a splash of wine. A 1,059-vote comment is a joke about pasta purism.

name: Orange Phyllo Dough Cake (Portokalopita)
ingredients:
For the syrup
700 g granulated sugar
500 g water
100 g orange juice
Orange peels, from 2-3 oranges
1 stick cinnamon

For the orange pie
200 g strained yogurt
100 g orange juice
200 g sunflower oil
200 g granulated sugar
1 g vanilla powder
4 eggs, medium
Orange zest, from 2 oranges
20 g baking powder
1 pinch salt
450 g phyllo dough sheets
Sunflower oil for the pan
directions:
Preheat the oven to 170C set to fan. In a bowl add the yogurt, the orange
juice and whisk. Add the sunflower oil, the sugar, the vanilla powder, the
eggs, the orange zest, the baking powder, salt and whisk. Cut the phyllo into
thin strips and open them up with your hands, so that they won’t stick
together. Add 1/5 of the phyllo strips into the bowl with the rest of the
ingredients and mix with a serving spoon. Follow the same process for all the
phyllo strips. Grease an about 25x30 cm baking pan and transfer the whole
mixture inside. Bake for 40 minutes. Remove and pour the cold syrup over the
pie, using a ladle. Let it cool and absorb the whole syrup.
description:
8/26 Made at home. Great again. Followed Claudes instructions to makee the syrup, using the amounts from our recipe. Used Valencia oranges, juicy and delicious. Used 1 t ov vanilla extract instead of powder. 

4/26 Made in our cooking class in Nafplio. Delicious and different.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing to change. Cooks' notes already record two successful tests, the second with syrup amounts already tuned; the recipe is proven and shouldn't be altered further.

name: Orange Whip
source: Lizzie MacArthur, Adele Davis Let's Cook Right
ingredients:
1/4 c. (62 g) orange juice
1 T. (9.6 g) unflavored gelatin (1 pkg.)
1/2 c. (100 g) sugar
2 T. (30 g) lemon juice
1 1/4 c. (310 g) orange juice
grated orange zest, if desired
3/4 c. (189 g) chilled evaporated milk (1/2 can)
directions:
Put into saucepan:
1/c. orange juice
1 T. unflavored gelatin (1 pkg.)

Soak 5 minutes, dissolve by heating slowly, cool slightly and add:
1/2 c. sugar
2 T. lemon juice
1 1/4 c. orange juice
grated orange zest, if desired

Chill until gelatin starts to congeal. 

Beat until stiff 3/4 c. CHILLED evaporated milk (1/2 can). It helps if the bowl is chilled as well.

Fold milk into gelatin mixture, pour into bowl or mold, and chill until firm.
notes: Data fix (Sept 2026): the ingredients were listed only inside the directions; extracted into an ingredients list. The card reads '1/c. orange juice' for the first quantity, taken as 1/4 cup.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing to change. Chilling the bowl and evaporated milk before whipping, and blooming the gelatin before dissolving, are exactly the steps modern versions of this technique still specify.

name: Original Green Bean Casserole
ingredients:
1 can (10 3/4 oz.) Campbell's Cream of Mushroom Soup
1/2 c. (122 g) milk
1 t. (5.3 g) soy sauce (optional)
dash pepper
4 c. (500 g) cooked cut green beans
1 1/3 c. (53 g) French's French Fried Onions (divided)
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.
1. In 1 1/2 c. casserole, mix soup, milk, soy, pepper, beans, and 2/3 c. of onions.
2. Bake 25 minutes or until hot.
3. Stir. Sprinkle remaining 2/3 c. onions over bean mixture. Bake 5 minutes or until onions are golden.
notes:
Web summary (campbells.com). Campbell's own page for the casserole its test kitchen developed in 1955, still presented as the canonical holiday version. The appeal is the short ingredient list -- condensed cream of mushroom soup, milk, soy sauce, cooked green beans and French fried onions -- assembled in one dish with almost no prep. Holding back two-thirds of the onions and adding them only for the last five minutes is what keeps the topping crisp and golden instead of soggy.

What readers report: No reader comments on the page. Campbell's own notes cover using fresh blanched, frozen or canned beans interchangeably, and variations with almonds, pancetta or red pepper.

Note on the source: Family text is the Campbell's original verbatim, naming both Campbell's Cream of Mushroom Soup and French's French Fried Onions, with the same 4 c beans / 1-1/3 c onions / 1/2 c milk / 1 t soy sauce proportions and the same two-stage bake (25 min, stir, 5 min). Only drift is the can size (10-3/4 oz in the old printing vs 10.5 oz now).

claude_opt.changes: Use fresh or frozen blanched green beans, not canned — canned goes mushy under the bake, a common complaint versus this exact recipe. Don't skip the soy sauce; every upgraded version (Kenji included) keeps it for umami.

name: Original Plum Torte
ingredients:
3/4 to 1 cup (150-200 g) sugar
1/2 cup (114 g) unsalted butter, softened
1 cup (120 g) unbleached flour, sifted
1 teaspoon (4.0 g) baking powder
Pinch of salt (optional)
2 eggs
24 halves pitted purple plums
Sugar, lemon juice and cinnamon, for topping
directions:
Heat oven to 350 degrees.

Cream the sugar and butter in a bowl. Add the flour, baking powder, salt and eggs and beat well.

Spoon the batter into a springform pan of 8, 9 or 10 inches. Place the plum halves skin side up on top of the batter. Sprinkle lightly with sugar and lemon juice, depending on the sweetness of the fruit. Sprinkle with about 1 teaspoon of cinnamon, depending on how much you like cinnamon.

Bake 1 hour, approximately. Remove and cool; refrigerate or freeze if desired. Or cool to lukewarm and serve plain or with whipped cream. (To serve a torte that was frozen, defrost and reheat it briefly at 300 degrees.)
description: 9/25 Delicious. Fruit forward and not too sweet. 15 small, sweet plums with the 10 inch springform pan. A scant 1 cup of sugar. 1/2 tsp cinnamon and 2 tsp sugar for topping. Baked a full hour. Seemed fine. Parchment on the base.
notes:
To freeze, double-wrap the torte in foil, place in a plastic bag and seal.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (23,505)). Marian Burros's plum torte ran in The Times every September from 1983 to 1989, when editors tried to retire it and were met with a flood of protest letters from readers who treated its yearly appearance as the marker of summer turning to fall. The paper relented and now keeps it permanently available. The original 1983 version used 1 cup of sugar; the 1989 revision cut that to three-quarters of a cup, and both amounts are offered.

What readers report: The single most-voted thread (4,607 votes, answered at 4,106) is a measuring question that changes the outcome: "sifted flour" means sift first then measure, while "flour, sifted" means measure then sift, so the cup here should be measured after sifting. Many bakers report the torte works with other fruit - raspberries and blackberries in place of plums (1,955 votes), with a third of the flour swapped for cornmeal. A 1,397-vote note prefers slicing the plums and fanning them over the batter rather than pressing in halves: prettier and more evenly distributed, and suggests lemon zest and sliced almonds. Several comments are affectionate anecdotes rather than technique.

Note on the source: this is the second of two entries in the collection under this name; the summary is from the same source page as its twin.

Merged September 2026: this entry absorbed a duplicate previously filed as "Original Plum Torte". Every cook's note from both copies is kept above.

name: Outdoor Burgers
ingredients:
1 lb. (454 g) ground beef
1/4 c. (40 g) chopped onion
2 T. (14 g) finely chopped green pepper (optional)
3 T. (51 g) ketchup
1 T. (15 g) prepared horseradish
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
2 t. (10 g) prepared mustard
dash pepper
directions: Combine all ingredients; mix lightly Shape into 4+ patties. Broil over hot coals.

claude_opt.changes: Add a 160F internal-temp target for the patties; ground beef mixed raw with vegetables has no visual doneness cue, and 'broil over coals' alone risks undercooking.

name: Oven-Roasted Rosemary Potatoes
ingredients:
5 lbs. (2.3 kg) potatoes, unpeeled, cut into 2" chunks
2/3 c. (145 g) salad oil
1 T. (3.6 g) dried rosemary leaves, crushed
2 t. (12 g) salt
1/2 t. (1.1 g) pepper
directions:
About 1 1/2 hours before serving:
1. In 5 qt. Dutch oven or saucepot over high heat, heat potatoes and enough water to cover them to boiling. Reduce heat to low, cover and simmer 5 minutes or until potatoes are almost tender; drain. Place potatoes in roasting pan or jelly-roll pan.
2. Preheat oven to 425. Toss potatoes with salad oil, rosemary, salt and pepper to coat evenly. Bake 50-60 minutes, turning potatoes occasionally, until tender and golden.

claude_opt.changes: Boil potatoes with 1/2 tsp baking soda and shake them roughly in the colander before roasting -- raises surface pH and roughens starch for a much crispier crust.

name: Pace Six-Layer Dip
ingredients:
3 avocados
2 tbsp. (30 g) lemon juice
Salt and pepper
2 cans bean dip
1 c. (100 g) green onions with tops
1 pkg. sharp Cheddar cheese (grated) 
1 c. (230 g) sour cream
1/2 c. (110 g) mayonnaise  
3 chopped tomatoes
2 cans black olives
1 c. (250 g) Pace Picante Sauce
directions: Mash avocados in a bowl with lemon juice, salt and pepper. Then combine sour cream and mayonnaise in another bowl. To assemble: spread bean dip in an oblong dish; top with avocado mixture, layer with sour cream mixture. Sprinkle with onions, tomatoes and olives and cover with cheese. Top with Pace Picante Sauce. Serve with chips.
notes:
Web summary (food.com). A member transcription of the Pace Foods promotional recipe, posted to food.com by user kadidel as an easy party dip. It is the layered Tex-Mex dip in its branded form: a bean-dip base, mashed avocado sharpened with lemon juice, a sour cream and mayonnaise layer, then green onions, tomatoes, olives and cheddar, with Pace Picante Sauce spooned over the top. Keeping the avocado under the dairy layer slows browning, and the picante sauce goes on last so it does not soak the base.

Note on the source: Title matches the family entry exactly and the ingredient list is the same recipe, consistent with the recorded source '1985 Pace Foods, Inc.' The family clipping uses can counts (2 cans bean dip, 2 cans olives, 3 tomatoes) where food.com converts to weights (9 oz bean dip, 4 oz olives, 2 tomatoes); otherwise identical. No Pace/Campbell's page for this specific 1985 promo remains online.

claude_opt.changes: 2 tbsp lemon juice for 3 avocados is thin acid versus standard guacamole ratios (~1 tbsp/avocado); bump to 3 tbsp to slow browning. If assembling ahead, press plastic directly on the avocado layer before adding sour cream.

name: Pan-Seared Tilefish with Garlic, Herbs and Lemon
ingredients:
2 skinless tilefish or other sturdy, thick white fish fillets (about 7 to 8 ounces each), skins removed
Kosher salt, to taste
Black pepper, to taste
2 ½ tablespoons (35 g) unsalted butter
3 green garlic shoots or scallions, thinly sliced
1 ½ tablespoons (4.5 g) finely chopped chives, mint, lovage and/or sorrel
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) minced lemon thyme or regular leaves
2 teaspoons (2.0 g) finely chopped tarragon, basil or marjoram
Juice of 1/2 lemon
directions:
Remove any remaining pin bones in the fish, pat dry, and season both sides with salt and pepper.

In a large sauté pan over medium heat, melt butter. Once butter has begun to foam, lay fish in pan. Add green garlic or scallions and a pinch of salt. Without disturbing the fish, tilt the pan toward you; using a spoon, ladle green garlic butter over fish. Continue basting fish for 2 to 3 minutes.

Using a spatula, gently flip fish. Reduce heat to low, cover pan and cook for 2 minutes.

Uncover pan, add herbs and continue basting fish with butter until it is just cooked through, another minute or two longer.

Transfer fish to a serving platter or individual plates, pour pan sauce over the top, and pour lemon juice over everything. Season with more salt and black pepper if needed. Serve immediately.
description: 7/2019 Fish nicely cooked, used flounder. Tarragon flavor was strong. Steph thought too much salt. Could use thyme instead of tarragon.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (343)). A basic sauteed fish fillet that the headnote argues every cook should know. The one step that looks harder than it is: spooning the pan fat back over the fish as it cooks, which cooks it evenly and keeps it moist. The fat here is butter, which browns and turns nutty as the fish cooks. Tilefish is named but any firm fillet - sea bass, grouper - substitutes.

What readers report: Very few comments, but they agree on the method more than the fish. The top note (45 votes) cooked it with tilefish straight off the Outer Banks and swapped shallots for scallions and dried basil for fresh with no loss. A dissent worth noting (19 votes) warns that tilefish is high in methyl mercury and points to the Monterey Bay Aquarium guide, suggesting another species. Others confirm the basting technique transfers: one used it on halibut cheeks, another on supermarket cod, both successfully. Repeated advice is to use a generous amount of butter, roughly a tablespoon per person, and to get the pan properly hot before the fish goes in. Fresh garden herbs are what several credit for the dish.

Note on the source: only 9 comments

name: Panettone (Great Italian Chefs)
ingredients:
FIRST REFRESH:
20g of strong white flour
20g of natural yeast
9g of water
SECOND REFRESH:
40g of strong white flour
40g of natural yeast
17g of water
THIRD REFRESH:
80g of strong white flour
80g of natural yeast
34g of water
FIRST PANETTONE DOUGH:
400g of strong white flour
170g of butter, soft
190g of natural yeast, from the third refresh
200g of egg yolk
150g of water, at 28C
175g of caster sugar
SECOND PANETTONE DOUGH:
100g of strong white flour
35g of caster sugar
60g of egg yolks
60g of butter, soft
16g of honey
12g of salt
1/2 vanilla pod, Tahitian, seeds scraped
1/2 orange, freshly zested
1/2 lemon, freshly zested
200g of candied orange zest, 1cmx1cm
200g of raisins
ICING:
40g of white almond flour
40g of hazelnut flour
120g of caster sugar
9g of soft flour
2g of cocoa powder
3g of cornflour
50g of egg white
almonds, to garnish
pearl sugar, to garnish
directions:
To begin, start making a mother dough - it’s best to do this at 6am the day before serving. Mix all of the ingredients for ‘natural yeast, first refresh’ in a stand mixer fitted with a dough hook and stir for 7 minutes, making sure the temperature of the dough does not exceed 27°C. Allow to rise for 3 hours at 27°C until tripled in volume

At approximately 10am, mix all of the ingredients for the ‘second refresh’ in the stand mixer with the first set of dough, stirring for 7 minutes. The final dough should reach a max temperature of 27°C. Leave to rise for 3 hours at 27°C until tripled in volume

At approximately 2pm, repeat the process with the mixture of ingredients for the third refresh, stirring for 7 minutes with the final dough reaching 27°C. Leave to rise for 3 hours at 27°C until tripled in volume. The resulting dough is the 'mother dough' for your panettone

That night (at around 6pm) make the first panettone dough. Melt the caster sugar in the water over a low heat, then add the flour and half of the egg yolks

Combine in a stand mixer and mix thoroughly to obtain a smooth and elastic dough. Add the mother dough from the third refresh and the remaining egg yolks, mixing until combined. Finish by adding the soft butter a little at a time. The final dough should be at a temperature of 26°C

Leave to rest and triple in volume for 12 hours at 27°C

At 7am the next day, make the second panettone dough by mixing the first dough with the flour in a stand mixer. Knead for about 15 minutes. If the dough is very thin, you may need to add a little more flour

Add the sugar and egg yolks in 3 additions, allowing to combine before the next addition each time

Add the honey, vanilla seeds, orange and lemon zests. Once combined, add the salt and mix for another 3 minutes

Gradually add the soft butter a knob at a time and mix until smooth, shiny and elastic. Mix together the candied oranges and raisins and add to the dough. Allow to rest for one hour at 27°C

At approximately 8.30am, divide the dough in half – each piece should weigh about 1050g. Roll each piece twice and place in the panettone moulds. Leave to rise for another 6 hours at 27°C

At around 3.30pm, preheat the oven to 170°C/gas mark 3.5

To make the icing, blend all of the ingredients with a hand blender and use to glaze the panettone. Sprinkle with almonds and pearl sugar

Bake until the inner part of the panettone reaches 94°C, then remove from the oven and leave to hang upside down by inserting a knitting needle or long piece of dowling through the bottom of the panettone and suspending it. Leave for 12 hours before serving
notes:
Web summary (wildyeastblog.com). Susan of Wild Yeast has been refining this panettone since 2006 and is frank that it demands patience and exact technique across several fermentation stages. Her sweet starter is kept warm between feeds specifically to hold acidity down, since a sour starter shows badly in a bread this sweet. The mixing order matters as much as the schedule: gluten is developed before the butter, sugar and liquids go in, because a dough that has not built structure first cannot carry that much fat and fruit and will collapse.

What readers report: The dominant complaint is that the final dough comes out batter-like and far too slack even when the formula is followed exactly; several experienced bakers fixed it by adding 60 to 80 grams of extra flour, and suspect the specified 12 percent protein flour is too weak or that regional flour varies. Related to that, people who mix by hand report never reaching gluten development at all, and Susan confirms a stand mixer is effectively required. Collapse is the other recurring failure, from overproofing or weak gluten: one baker succeeded by proofing only to about 2cm below the rim rather than to the top, and several found that cooling the loaves on their sides on a folded towel, per Carol Field, beat hanging them upside down, which caused tops to separate. Where diastatic malt is unavailable, one baker ground malted barley from a home-brew shop. Susan posted one correction five years on: the initial sweet starter feed takes 10g water, not 20g.

Note on the source: duplicate of the 'Panettone Wild Yeast' entry - same page

Note on the source: this is the second of two entries in the collection under this name; the summary is from the same source page as its twin.

Renamed September 2026 from "Panettone": another, different recipe in the collection shares that title, so both were given distinguishing names.

ahead: To begin, start making a mother dough - it’s best to do this at 6am the day before serving.
Leave to rest and triple in volume for 12 hours at 27°C

claude_opt.changes: Keep 60-80 g extra flour ready if the dough won't clear the bowl, a known failure point. Proof only to ~2 cm below the rim and cool loaves on their side, not hanging — hanging splits the tops.

name: Panettone Iginio Massari
ingredients:
Day 1- Primo Impasto (1st dough)
90 g Lievito Madre Italian sourdough starter
360 g unbleached bread flour 14% protein or higher, sifted
135 g filtered water
114 g granulated sugar
90 g egg yolks at room temperature
129 g unsalted butter softened
Day 2 - Secondo Impasto (2nd dough)
90 g unbleached bread flour 14% protein or higher, sifted
117 g egg yolks
90 g granulated sugar
120 g unsalted butter softened
63 g filtered water
7 g fine sea salt
18 g melted unsalted butter
180 g sultana raisins
135 g candied orange peel
45 g candied lemon peel
Aromatic Mix
23 g acacia honey
1/2 vanilla bean seeds scraped
1 organic lemon zest
1 organic orange zest
directions:
9:00 pm; Day 1- Primo Impasto

Into the bowl of a stand mixer add flour, sugar, soft butter, 1/3 of egg yolks and water. Mix at medium speed (#4 on Ankarsrum mixer) until the elastic dough is formed, about 18 minutes.

Add lievito madre and remaining 2/3 of egg yolks to the bowl, continue working the dough until it is almost smooth, but making sure it doesn't become too shiny (overworked). That is about another 5 minutes of mixing. Note: The whole dough mixing operation should not last more than 22-25 minutes.

Place the dough into covered container and keep in dough proofer for 10-12 hours at temperature of 24/25°C (75/77°F) or until dough triples by volume. Note: The dough not leavened sufficiently will delay the next leavening cycle (second dough) by triple the time missed in the first leavening cycle.

Into the bowl of a stand mixer add first dough, flour and aromatic mix, mix at medium low speed (#3 on Ankarsrum mixer) for about 15 minutes.

Add sugar with 1/3 of egg yolks and keep mixing until dough is homogenous and smooth.

Add another 1/3 of egg yolks and salt, mix until the dough is homogenous and smooth.

Add and incorporate the last 1/3 of egg yolks and softened butter. Mix everything well, forming a silky-like dough.

Add and incorporate water as needed (up to 63g) in order to adjust the dough consistency.

Pour in and incorporate melted butter.

Add raisins, candied orange, and lemon peel, mix for 4-5 minutes until everything is distributed evenly in the dough. Note: The whole mixing operation should not last longer than 45 minutes, ideally 35 minutes.

Remove the dough from mixer, place in a covered container and let rest for 30 minutes at room temperature.

Weigh and divide the dough into two equal parts. Shape each part into a ball, place on a large parchment paper lined baking pan. Let rest for 35/40 minutes in the oven at about 28°C (82°F). Note: You can prewarm the oven or use oven light to maintain approximate temperature during rest time.

Round each ball tightly and place into a separate panettone paper mold, suited for a 750g panettone.

Cover the molds and keep in a dough proofer for 6-7 hours at 28/30°C (82/86°F) or until the top of raised dough dome is roughly the same height as the mold edge. Note: Remove cover from the molds when the dough reaches 1.5" below the mold edge. This way the dough will create a crust which will make it easier to score.

Score each panettone with a cross shape, place a knob of butter in the center of the cross.

Bake at 177°C(350°F) in prewarmed oven, rack in the lower 1/3 of the oven for 45-50 minutes or until internal temperature reaches 94°C (201°F).

Insert two sharp skewers through the very bottom of each mold, carefully flip upside down and and let rest on prepared supports. Let cool for about 10 hours. Note: Due to their delicate structure, panettones have to be cooled off in this way in order to preserve their shape.

Store each panettone in a separate cellophane bag. Spray lightly inside the bag with 70% ethyl alcohol before inserting panettone and sealing the bag.

Let panettone rest for minimum of 3-4 days to let the flavours mature. Cut with sharp serrated knife. Due to its tender structure it is advisable to cut panettone in half first and then into separate smaller slices.

Keep panettones in a dry and cool place 12-18°C (54-65°F). If left whole and stored properly, the panettone will stay fresh and moist for about 4 weeks.
description:
12/25 Followed this recipe. Supposed to be the best from a real panettone pro. I did not succed finally, but came close. I used the lievito madre and topping recipes from Wild Yeast, and candied orange and lemon recipes from Max Makes Munch. Used panettone flour from Molino Pasini (it took 1 small bag). 

For first dough I used the kitchenaid paddle, not the dough hook and mixed at slow speed. It seemed to be the right choice. 

The first rise took 20 hours in the oven with the light on, not 8-10. But after 20 hours the dough looked excellent. 

Switched to the doughhook for the second dough and mixed everything in in about 40 minutes at low speed. Looked perfect, and went into 3 500 g molds. 

Unfortunately it went back in the oven for the second rise at around 9 pm. It probably was ready to top and bake by 2 or 3 am. But i didnt get it into the oven until about 8 am, by which time it had overrisen and blurped over out of the molds. 

Baked anyway, perhaps a bit too long. Tasted perfect. A bit dry. Very ugly.
notes:
Web summary (sweetthought.ca). Gordan of Sweet Thought works through the master pastry chef Iginio Massari's panettone formula after several successful batches. The departure from convention is that softened butter goes into the primo impasto at the start rather than being worked in at the end, and candied orange and lemon peel do the aromatic work alongside acacia honey, vanilla and fresh zest. He notes his own starter was sluggish, which stretched the fermentation times well past the stated ones, and that careful temperature management plus properly prepared ingredients still carried the loaf to a good crumb.

Note on the source: no comments on page

ahead: Let cool for about 10 hours.
Let panettone rest for minimum of 3-4 days to let the flavours mature.
