Recovered technique for the exact failure your 12/25 note hit (overproofed, blurped over): bake to 199F/93C internal, then skewer and hang upside down 8-11 hrs — prevents collapse regardless of proof time drift.

name: Panettone Wild Yeast
cook_time: build the sweet starter: at least 12 hours, tended to at 4-hour intervals (see below)
ingredients:
First Dough Ingredients:
346 grams flour
190 grams water
1 gram (1/3 teaspoon) osmotolerant yeast, or 1.3 grams (1/2 teaspoon) instant yeast
83 grams sugar
55 grams egg yolk
7 grams (1.5 teaspoons) diastatic malt powder
83 grams unsalted butter, at room temperature
86 grams sweet starter (instructions below)
Final Dough Ingredients:
all of the first dough
82 grams flour
5 grams (7/8 teaspoon) salt
25 grams egg yolk
scraped seeds from 4/5 of a vanilla bean (use the other 1/5 for the glaze)
zest of half a medium orange
114 grams water, divided
82 grams sugar
126 grams unsalted butter, at room temperature (pliable)
19 grams honey
126 grams raisins
44 grams candied lemon peel
126 grams candied orange peel
Glaze Ingredients (optional; this makes enough for three loaves):
83 grams granulated sugar
4.5 grams (2 teaspoons) ground almonds (or almond flour)
6 grams (1.5 teaspoons) vegetable oil
6 grams (1 tablespoon) corn flour
6 grams (1 1/8 teaspoon) cocoa powder
30 g egg whites
scraped seeds from 1/5 of a vanilla bean
Topping (optional):
powdered sugar
Swedish pearl sugar
whole blanched almonds
Special Supplies:
three 5-1/4-inch paper panettone molds
six bamboo skewers
Sweet Starter Ingredients:
20 grams mature stiff (50%-hydration) sourdough starter
flour
water
directions:
Method: (sweet starter method below)

Prepare the sweet starter over a period of one to several days. Its final feeding should be given 4 hours before mixing the first dough.

Prepare the first dough the evening before baking: In the bowl of a stand mixer, mix all of the first dough ingredients just until combined. Cover the bowl and ferment for 12 hours at warm room temperature (about 72F), or longer for a cooler room. The dough should more than triple in volume.

To start mixing the final dough: To the first dough in the mixer bowl, add the flour, salt, egg yolks, orange zest, vanilla seeds, and 40 grams of the water. Mix in low speed until the ingredients are just combined, about 3 minutes.

Turn the mixer to medium speed, mix for a minute or two, then continue to mix while slowly adding the sugar, in about 5 or 6 increments. Mix for one to two minutes between additions.

Continue to mix until the dough pulls away from the sides of the bowl and the gluten is almost fully developed.

Turn the mixer back to low speed and add the butter. Mix for a minute in low speed, then in medium speed until the butter is completely incorporated into the dough and the gluten has reached full development.

In low speed, add the honey, and about half of the remaining water. Mix until the water is fully incorporated.

Add the remaining water and mix until it is fully incorporated.

In low speed, add the raisins and candied peels, mixing just until they are evenly distributed.

Place the dough in a lightly oiled container (preferably a low, wide one, to facilitate folding).

Ferment at warm room temperature for about one hour, folding the dough after the first 30 minutes. If the dough seems very loose, fold it at 20-minute intervals instead.

Turn the dough onto a buttered surface. Divide the dough into three pieces, and form each piece into a light ball.

Allow the balls to rest (may be left uncovered) for 20 minutes. Meanwhile, skewer the molds.

Shape the dough into tight balls and place into the skewered molds.

Proof at 80F for 4 – 6 hours (or about 12 hours at room temperature), until the tops of the dough domes are even with the top of the molds and the sides are an inch or so below the tops.

When the dough is nearly fully proofed, preheat the oven to 350F, with the rack in the lower third of the oven.

Optional step: To mix the glaze, whisk all ingredients together. Pour, brush, or pipe the glaze evenly onto the top of the loaves. Sift powdered sugar generously over the tops, then sprinkle with pearl sugar and garnish with whole blanched almonds.

If you leave the panettone unglazed, use scissors to snip an X into the top of the loaf and tuck a pat of butter inside.

Place the loaves directly on the oven rack and bake for about 35 – 40 minutes, until the tops are dark brown and the internal temperature is 185F. If the tops are already quite dark after 25 – 30 minutes, turn the heat down to 325F.

While the panettone is baking, set up your hanging apparatus (See above). When the bread is done, hang them as quickly as possible.

Allow the panettone to hang for at least four hours, up to overnight.

Sweet Starter method:

Mix 20 grams of stiff starter with 20 grams of flour and 10 grams of water. Ferment at 85F for 4 hours.

Repeat feedings at 4-hour intervals, each time discarding all but 20 grams of starter, and feeding it with 20 grams of flour and 10 grams of water.

For the nightly feeding before you go to bed, use only 10 grams of starter with the 20 of flour and 10 of water.

Keep the feedings up for at least 12 hours, and up to several days.

For the last feeding (4 hours before you will mix the final dough), start with 40 grams of starter and add 40 grams of flour and 20 grams of water.

Scale out the amount of starter you need for the final dough 4 hours after the final feeding.
description: 12/25 Followed this recipe for the lievito madre and topping glaze, while using the Massari recipe for the main bread. Check the corn flour: its hard to find.
notes:
Web summary (wildyeastblog.com). Susan of Wild Yeast has been refining this panettone since 2006 and is frank that it demands patience and exact technique across several fermentation stages. Her sweet starter is kept warm between feeds specifically to hold acidity down, since a sour starter shows badly in a bread this sweet. The mixing order matters as much as the schedule: gluten is developed before the butter, sugar and liquids go in, because a dough that has not built structure first cannot carry that much fat and fruit and will collapse.

What readers report: The dominant complaint is that the final dough comes out batter-like and far too slack even when the formula is followed exactly; several experienced bakers fixed it by adding 60 to 80 grams of extra flour, and suspect the specified 12 percent protein flour is too weak or that regional flour varies. Related to that, people who mix by hand report never reaching gluten development at all, and Susan confirms a stand mixer is effectively required. Collapse is the other recurring failure, from overproofing or weak gluten: one baker succeeded by proofing only to about 2cm below the rim rather than to the top, and several found that cooling the loaves on their sides on a folded towel, per Carol Field, beat hanging them upside down, which caused tops to separate. Where diastatic malt is unavailable, one baker ground malted barley from a home-brew shop. Susan posted one correction five years on: the initial sweet starter feed takes 10g water, not 20g.

Note on the source: duplicate of the earlier 'Panettone' wildyeastblog entry - same page, http vs https

Time (assumes you are starting with a mature stiff starter):

Build the sweet starter: at least 12 hours, tended to at 4-hour intervals (see below)
Mix and ferment first dough: 12.5 hours
Mix final dough: 30 minutes or longer
First fermentation of final dough: 1 to 1.5 hours, with folds every 20 – 30 minutes
Divide, rest, and shape: 25 minutes
Proof: 4 – 6 hours at 80F, or about 12 hours at room temperature
Bake: about 40 minutes
Hang/cool: several hours

Note on the source: duplicate of the 'Panettone Wild Yeast' entry - same page

Merged September 2026: this entry absorbed a duplicate previously filed as "Panettone". Every cook's note from both copies is kept above.

ahead: build the sweet starter: at least 12 hours, tended to at 4-hour intervals (see below)
Its final feeding should be given 4 hours before mixing the first dough.

claude_opt.changes: Your 12/25 note already worked around this formula's notoriously slack dough by using Massari's dough recipe — keep doing that. The glaze's 'corn flour' means cornstarch (UK term), not corn flour; use cornstarch, no special sourcing needed.

name: Pappardelle with Greens and Ricotta
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) greens, such as chard, kale or broccoli rabe, stemmed and washed well, or half of a 1-pound bag prepared greens
Salt
2 tablespoons (27 g) extra virgin olive oil
1 to 2 garlic cloves, to taste, minced
¾ cup (184 g) fresh ricotta cheese
½ to ¾ cup (45-68 g) freshly grated Parmesan, or a mixture of Parmesan and Romano Pecorino (to taste)
¾ pound (340 g) pappardelle
directions:
Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Fill a bowl with ice water. When the water comes to a boil, salt generously and add the greens (you may have to do this in two batches). After the water returns to a boil, boil two to four minutes until the greens are tender. Using a deep-fry skimmer or slotted spoon, transfer them to the ice water. Do not drain the hot water in the pot, as you’ll use it to cook the pasta. Drain the greens, squeeze dry and chop.

Heat the oil over medium heat in a large, heavy nonstick skillet. Add the garlic, cook for about a minute just until fragrant, and stir in the greens. Toss in the hot pan for about a minute, just until the greens are lightly coated with oil and fragrant with garlic. Season with salt and pepper, and remove from the heat.

Place the ricotta in a large pasta bowl. Bring the water for the pasta back to a boil, and add the pappardelle. Cook al dente. Ladle 1/2 cup of the cooking water from the pasta into the ricotta and stir together. Drain the pasta, and toss with the ricotta, greens and cheeses. Serve at once.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (634)). A fast pasta pitched at dinner-party cooking when there is no time to prep ahead. The headnote's one real instruction is to hunt down fresh ricotta from an Italian market rather than the supermarket tub.

What readers report: The top note (78 votes) rewrites the workflow: chop the greens raw and throw them into the pasta water for the last minute instead of cooking them separately, then drain both together - one pot, less time. Close behind (76 votes), a cook substituted Bulgarian sheep's-milk feta for the ricotta and reports it worked better, being softer and sharper. That points at the recipe's main complaint: as written it reads bland, and people fix it with anchovies, cherry tomatoes sauteed with the garlic, lemon, or red pepper flakes. Counter to the headnote, several say freshly made ricotta melts into the sauce and disappears, and that a firmer store-bought one holds its texture better. Any pasta shape works; spaghetti and penne both reported fine.

name: Parmesan Chive Smashed Potatoes
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) mixed small Yukon Gold and red new potatoes, scrubbed
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
3 tablespoons (40 g) good olive oil
1/2 cup (45 g) freshly grated Parmesan cheese
2 tablespoons (6.0 g) minced fresh chives
Fleur de sel or sea salt
directions:
Preheat the oven to 400 degrees.

Place the potatoes and 1 tablespoon salt in a large saucepan and add enough water to cover the potatoes. Bring to a boil, reduce the heat, and simmer for 17 to 20 minutes, until the potatoes are tender when pierced with a skewer. Drain the potatoes and place on a sheet pan. With a potato masher or metal measuring cup, press each potato until it's about 1/2 inch thick (they will be messy). Toss the potatoes with the olive oil, 1 teaspoon salt, and 3/4 teaspoon pepper.

Roast the potatoes for 25 to 30 minutes, turning once, until the skins have become nicely browned. Sprinkle the potatoes with the Parmesan cheese and roast for another 2 to 3 minutes, just until the cheese melts. Sprinkle the potatoes with the chives and fleur de sel and serve hot.
description: 6/17 Excellent!
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten boils small Yukon Gold and red new potatoes whole, then flattens them thin on a sheet pan and roasts them in olive oil. Pressing them out increases the surface area in contact with the hot pan, so the edges crisp and brown while the inside stays creamy from the boiling. Parmesan is scattered on at the end so it melts over the crisp surface rather than being stirred in, and chives and fleur de sel finish it.

Note on the source: no comments retrieved

Web summary (barefootcontessa.com). Ina Garten's own-site version of the smashed potatoes: small potatoes boiled whole until soft, then flattened and roasted in olive oil so the increased surface area against the hot pan gives crisp golden edges while the interior stays tender from the boil. Parmesan melts over the top at the end and chives and a finishing salt go on last. She notes it can be taken most of the way ahead of time, which is the practical argument for the two-stage method.

Note on the source: same recipe as the Food Network entry; barefootcontessa.com has no comments section

name: Parmesan Soup From Elva
ingredients:
1 scallion, finely chopped
 25 g butter
150 g parmesan
½ L chicken stock
1 L cream
1 L milk
30 g bacon
1 small bundle chives, chopped.
2 slices of bread for croutons
Salt and pepper to taste. (Mostly pepper, since the stock and cheese is salty)
(I used less cream and more stock)
directions:
Slice crust of bread, cut in small cubes and sauté in olive oil until golden brown let cool on kitchen towel.
Sauté onion in butter few minutes. Add all liquid as well as 100g of grated parmesan cheese. Cook at low temp. for 45 minutes. Stir regularly, to prevent the cheese from burning.
Meanwhile fry the bacon, until brittle, set aside to cool on kitchen towel. Chop.
Add the rest of cheese to soup and cook further for 10 minutes. Put in mixer or better yet use hand-blender. Sieve soup into clean pot. (optional)
Pour soup into small bowls, and sprinkle a little of bacon, croutons and chives on to before serving.
Bon appetite!
description: 6/2023 We loved this soup when we had it with Elva and Skeggi in Iceland.

claude_opt.changes: Blend with the immersion blender right in the pot rather than a sealed countertop jar -- hot liquid can force the lid off and scald; the low-heat method already prevents the cheese scorching.

name: Parmesan-Crusted Rack of Lamb
ingredients:
1 rack of lamb, approximately 1¼ pounds (567 g), frenched
2 tablespoons (27 g) extra-virgin olive oil
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
½ cup (54 g) fresh bread crumbs
¼ cup (22 g) grated Parmesan
1 tablespoon (3.8 g) chopped flat-leaf parsley.
directions:
Preheat oven to 450. Put a large frying pan over high heat until very hot. Rub lamb with 1 tablespoon of the oil, season aggressively with salt and pepper and then sear the meat in the pan until it is golden brown all over, approximately 4 minutes a side. Place on a rimmed baking sheet, and let rest for 20 or 30 minutes, until cool.

In a bowl, combine the bread crumbs, cheese and parsley. Rub the cooled-off lamb with the remaining olive oil, then pat the seasoned bread crumbs all over the meat in an even layer.

Put the lamb back on the baking sheet, and roast until a thermometer inserted into the thickest part of the meat registers 120 degrees, approximately 20 to 30 minutes. (Tent the lamb with foil if the crust threatens to get too dark at the end.) Remove the lamb from the oven, and allow to stand, covered loosely in foil, for 10 minutes or so. (The internal temperature will rise to 125 degrees, or medium-rare, while the lamb sits.) Carve into chops, and serve on a warmed platter.
description:
4/25 We had a 1.7 lb rack. Cooked to 144° in the heart of the meat. Good temp, but give it enough time to rest. Could add slivers of garlic, knifed into lamb. We were happy as cooked. 

4/23 Roasted 25 minutes for a smaller rack. Registered 130 in fat part. Perfect. 

12/22 30 minutes at 450 with a meaty lamb roast. Internal was 150 near the bone and 130 at the surface. Perfect. The topping was delicious. 

1/22 Delicious again. Roasted 28 minutes to 140 degrees, then rested for 10 minutes. Slightly pink and pretty much spot on for us.

7/2020 second time making this! Excellent! Alan cooked in cast iron fry pan on grill side burner and then finished on grill indirect.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (1,103)). A rack of lamb adapted from an old Escoffier recipe, coated so the outside turns salty and crunchy against the sweet roasted meat. It is pitched as a dinner-party showpiece served alongside Macaroni Milanaise, with the headnote noting how little work it actually takes.

What readers report: The two highest-voted notes are both about timing: 20 minutes in the oven is too long for rare or medium-rare, so use a thermometer rather than the clock (32 votes); another got a perfect medium-rare at 400F for about 25 minutes (31 votes), searing and roasting in the same cast-iron skillet to save a pan. The loudest recurring correction is the missing garlic - multiple cooks (30 and 26 votes) add two or more crushed cloves during the sear or into the crumb mix, and call it essential. Rosemary in the dry mix is the other common addition. A well-liked variation brushes the seared rack with Dijon before the cheese and breadcrumbs go on, which helps the crust adhere and adds sharpness.

name: Party Mix
ingredients:
6 T. (85 g) butter 
4 t. (20 g) Worcestershire
1  1/2 t. (9.0 g) seasoned or savor salt
1/2 t. (3.0 g) garlic salt
2 c. (60 g) Wheat Chex or substitute with Crispix for all 6 cups of Chex
2 c. (308 g) Corn Chex
2 c. (370 g) Rice Chex 
3/4 c. (98 g) unsalted nuts
Cherrios & thin pretzels
directions:
Heat oven 250° Melt butter in shallow pan over low heat. Stir in Worcest. sauce & salt. Add chex, etc. mix over low heat till all pieces are covered. Heat in oven 1 hr. Stir every 15 mins. Spread on absorbent paper to cool.
Yield 6 3/4 cups.
notes:
Web summary (chex.com). Chex's own page for the snack mix that made the cereal famous, also known historically as Nuts and Bolts. Three Chex varieties are tossed with melted butter, Worcestershire and seasonings so every piece is coated before baking, which is what dries the cereal to a crisp rather than leaving it greasy. The page gives a fast microwave method and keeps the traditional oven version -- 250F for an hour, stirred every fifteen minutes -- as the alternative.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS on the brand page. On the food.com transcription of the same recipe (39 reviews) the recurring arguments are that bagel chips and Corn Chex are later additions to what older bakers remember, that the seasonings want doubling, and that cayenne or cheese crackers are worthwhile changes; several recall a 1950s printing that used Cheerios.

Note on the source: Dish identity is certain -- the family text is unmistakably Chex Party Mix (same 6 T butter, 1 1/2 t seasoned salt, 250F for 1 hour stirring every 15 min, spread on absorbent paper to cool). But the family version is an older, smaller printing: 2 cups each of the three Chex rather than 3, 4 t Worcestershire rather than 2 T, garlic SALT rather than garlic powder, no onion powder, no bagel chips, and it adds Cheerios and thin pretzels. No source was recorded in the collection, so this is the canonical brand recipe rather than provably the exact clipping. Runner-up with the oven method foregrounded: https://www.landolakes.com/recipe/9853/the-original-chex-party-mix/

claude_opt.changes: Double the seasoned salt and garlic salt — both food.com's 39 reviews and a tested Kitchn rebuild of this same recipe independently land on doubling the seasoning as the fix for a bland original.

name: Pasta Alla Genovese
ingredients:
4 ¼ pounds (1.9 kg) red onions
⅓ cup (72 g) extra-virgin olive oil
2 carrots, peeled and roughly chopped
1 celery rib, trimmed and roughly chopped
¼ pound (113 g) bacon or pancetta, chopped
2 ¼ pounds (1 kg) beef chuck, cut into 2-inch cubes
Salt and freshly ground black pepper
¼ cup (59 g) dry white wine, plus more if desired
1 pound (454 g) dried pasta, like ziti, tortiglioni or rigatoni
Finely grated Parmesan cheese
directions:
Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Place the onions in the boiling water, and cook, covered, 15 minutes. Drain the onions, and let cool a bit, then slice very thinly.

Heat half the oil in a large heavy pot over medium-high heat; stir in the carrots, celery and bacon, and cook for 4 minutes. Add the beef, then cover with the onions. Pour the remaining oil over the onions, then sprinkle with 1 1/2 teaspoons salt and 3/4 teaspoon pepper. Cover, bring to a simmer and cook gently until the beef is tender, about 2 hours; the onions will release a good deal of liquid.

Uncover the pot and bring to a boil. Cook, stirring more frequently as the liquid reduces and lowering the heat as necessary to prevent scorching, until the meat has fallen apart and the sauce is creamy, about 45 minutes. Stir in the wine and taste, adding more wine if desired. Reduce the heat to low, and continue to cook, stirring frequently, until the sauce is glossy and quite thick, about 15 minutes more.

Cook the pasta in a large pot of boiling salted water until al dente, then drain and toss with the sauce. Stir in Parmesan to taste, then serve.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (1,862)). La Genovese is a Neapolitan beef sauce that many in the city regard as the center of its cooking, despite being almost nothing but a huge quantity of onions and beef simmered until both collapse. The recipe boils the onions first as a time-saving departure from tradition, though the headnote concedes the saving is modest. Slicing them raw and simply cooking longer is the more orthodox route.

What readers report: The top comment (287 votes), from a cook in Naples, says the recipe is missing white wine - it belongs in with the meat - and that the cut matters: use rump, as for pot roast. Onion handling is the other big thread. A widely endorsed technique (160 votes) layers sliced onions with salt under water and a weighted plate to press them before cooking; several others (82, 97 votes) simply skip the boiling step entirely, calling it a scald that adds little, and sweat the raw sliced onions instead. Time is the real ingredient: one Neapolitan chef reportedly runs his for 16 hours on the lowest possible flame. Expect a rich, glossy, almost creamy sauce. Halving the recipe works for two.

name: Pasta Alla Gricia
ingredients:
8 ounces (225g) guanciale (cured pork jowl), in one piece
1 tablespoon (15ml) extra-virgin olive oil
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
12 ounces (340g) rigatoni
2 ounces (60g) finely grated Pecorino Romano cheese, plus more for serving
directions:
1. Freeze guanciale for at least 15 minutes, and up to 45 minutes (partially freezing the guanciale makes it easier to slice). Using a sharp chef's knife, cut into 1/4-inch-thick planks, then cut planks into 1/4-inch-thick batons (lardons).

2. In a large 12-inch stainless steel skillet, heat oil over medium-low heat until shimmering. Add guanciale and cook, stirring occasionally, until fat has rendered and guanciale is golden brown and crisp, about 15 minutes. Using slotted spoon, transfer guanciale to a plate; set aside. Reduce heat to low, and bloom about 1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper in rendered guanciale fat until pepper foams and is aromatic, about 1 minute. Remove skillet from heat.

3. Meanwhile, in a Dutch oven or medium pot, bring 3 quarts of water and 2 teaspoons kosher salt to a boil over high heat. Set a colander inside a large heatproof bowl in the sink. Add rigatoni to water and cook, stirring frequently during the first minute to prevent pasta from sticking.

4. Once pasta has cooked for 4 minutes 30 seconds, transfer 2 cups (475ml) of starchy pasta water to skillet. Return skillet to high heat and bring to a boil, swirling to emulsify pasta water with guanciale fat.

5. When pasta has cooked for a total of 5 minutes, drain in prepared colander, then transfer pasta to skillet (the pasta will be very undercooked at this point, but it will continue cooking in the skillet); reserve drained pasta water.

6. Cook rigatoni, swirling skillet constantly and gently stirring with a spoon or rubber spatula, to ensure even cooking and that the sauce remains emulsified, until pasta is al dente and sauce is thickened and reduced, 6 to 8 minutes; if sauce reduces too much before pasta has finished cooking, add more reserved pasta water to skillet in 1/4-cup increments. Add guanciale to skillet and carefully toss to combine.

7. Remove from heat, add half of the grated Pecorino Romano, and toss or stir rapidly to combine. Once cheese is fully emulsified in the sauce, add remaining Pecorino Romano, and toss or stir rapidly once more to combine. Adjust sauce consistency as needed with more pasta water. Season with salt and pepper, if needed. Serve right away, passing more cheese at the table.
description: 4/1/21 delicious. But we thought the sauce really didn’t emusify perhaps because we used fresh pasta so not enough starch. Made with 250 flour g of fresh egg pasta. Could use less guanciale for that amount of pasta maybe ⅔ recipe.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.6 (9) / 28 reviews). Sasha Marx, who grew up in Rome, writes this as a defence of the least famous of the city's four classic pastas, which is usually dismissed as a white amatriciana or an eggless carbonara. With only pork, pepper, pasta and cheese in play, he insists on guanciale rather than pancetta for its funk, and on bronze-die pasta, which leaches more starch and holds sauce better than Teflon-extruded supermarket brands; the guanciale is cut into lardons, rendered slowly over medium-low heat so the fat comes out before the meat burns, then lifted out so it stays crisp, and the pepper is bloomed in the rendered fat. The pasta boils in only three quarts of water for a starchier broth and comes out at five minutes, badly undercooked, to finish in the skillet with two cups of that water, constantly swirled so it keeps shedding starch, builds the emulsion and glazes itself. The pecorino goes in off the heat in two additions so it does not clump or break the sauce.

What readers report: The most detailed critique comes from a cook who found the dish far too salty and over-porked: he says two cups of pasta water was too much, that he had to lift the par-cooked rigatoni out and reduce the sauce separately to stop it overcooking, that his sauce turned an unappealing tan despite rendering slowly, and that he would cut the guanciale, the water and the cheese. Cooks scaling up report the opposite ratio, needing roughly 2.5 to 3 cups of pasta water for a full pound of rigatoni, with one saying he would go lower next time for a drier result. One skips salting the pasta water entirely here and seasons at the table, and substitutes diced pancetta where jowl is unavailable, reporting both fresh and dried pasta work. Guanciale's cost is a recurring objection, and one reviewer felt the skillet finish added no depth for the extra active time.

Note on the source: Thinner comment section than the other pages: 28 reviews, only nine of which carried a star rating, and no 'Featured Tweaks' block. Comments truncated at 'Read More'.

claude_opt.changes: Your 4/1/21 note found this: with fresh pasta, cut guanciale to about 2/3 (150 g) and add pasta water more gradually — fresh pasta's lower starch is why the sauce didn't emulsify, not the technique.

name: Pasta with Bacon, Cheese, Lemon and Pine Nuts
ingredients:
Coarse salt, such as Maldon
1 to 1 1/2 cups (90-135 g) freshly grated Parmesan, in a small serving bowl
About 1/3 cup (20 g) chopped parsley, scallions or mint, in a small serving bowl
Hot red pepper flakes, in a small serving bowl
1 large lemon
8 ounces (227 g) thickly sliced bacon, cut across into pieces about 3/4-inch wide
1 1/2 to 2 pounds (680-907 g) pasta
4 to 8 tablespoons (57-114 g) unsalted butter (1/2 to 1 stick)
1/3 cup (45 g) pine nuts
directions:
Put a large pot of salted water on to boil. Put the cheese, herbs and red pepper flakes on the table. Zest the lemon and put the zest on the table in a small serving bowl. Cut the lemon in half.

Put bacon in a medium-size heavy pot and turn the heat on low. Cook, turning occasionally, until fat has rendered and bacon is chewy-crisp, about 10 minutes. Lift out bacon pieces and drain on a plate lined with paper towels. Keep warm on top of the stove.

When the water boils, add pasta, stir well and cover. When the water comes back to the boil, uncover and stir again.

Put 4 tablespoons butter in a small saucepan and melt it over medium-low heat. When it foams, throw in the pine nuts and cook, shaking the pan, until they turn brown and toasty. Turn off heat and squeeze the lemon into the pan, cupping your hand underneath to catch any pits. Stir and set aside. Transfer bacon to a serving bowl and place on the table.

As soon as the pasta is tender (it will cook a bit more later on), drain it, reserving a cup of the cooking water. Immediately return the pasta to the pan over low heat. Toss in a chunk of butter. Add a splash of cooking water and a pinch of salt, stir well, cover and let rest 1 minute. Taste and adjust the seasonings until the pasta is completely cooked and tasty (but plain).

For those who like plain pasta or pasta with just butter and cheese, set aside a good amount in serving bowls. For others, pour the pine nuts and butter into the pasta remaining in the pot, add another splash of cooking water, and toss to combine. Serve from the pot or in a serving bowl, passing the various toppings.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (1,848)). The pitch is a modular family dinner: start with a plain base of pasta, butter and cheese that picky eaters will accept, then set out pine nuts, lemon zest, brown butter, bacon and herbs so everyone builds their own bowl. The framing comes from a piece on feeding a table with incompatible tastes.

What readers report: The most-voted note (324) is a set of upgrades: pancetta instead of bacon, half butter and half olive oil, dry-toast the pine nuts in a skillet first, and grate the lemon zest in for brightness. The clearest correction (129 votes) is that four tablespoons of butter is far too much for the amount of cheese - cut it well back; a scaled-for-two version (248 votes) uses about three-quarters of a tablespoon. Because the sauce comes together fast, several warn to have it ready before the pasta drains, or the noodles sit and turn sticky. One cook oven-baked whole bacon strips on a foil-lined sheet to make doubling easy. Bucatini gets a specific endorsement.

name: Peanut Butter Blossoms
ingredients:
1 3/4 c. (210 g) flour
1 t. (4.6 g) soda
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
1/2 c. (102 g) shortening
1/2 c. (129 g) peanut butter
1/2 c. (100 g) sugar
1/2 c. (106 g) brown sugar
1 egg
2 T. (30 g) milk
1 t. (4.2 g) vanilla
Hershey's Kisses
directions:
Preheat oven to 375.
Sift together flour, soda, and salt. In mixer, cream shortening, peanut butter, sugar, brown sugar. Cream well. Add egg, milk, and vanilla. Beat well. Blend in dry ingredients. Mix thoroughly. Shape rounded teaspoons of dough into balls. Roll in sugar. Bake on ungreased cookie sheets for 8 minutes. Remove from oven and place a milk chocolate candy kiss on top of each cookie, pressing gently into cookie. Return to oven for 2-5 mins until chocolate just starts to glisten. Don't leave too long or the chocolate will get chalky.
notes:
Web summary (pillsbury.com). Pillsbury's page for the cookie as Freda Smith of Gibsonburg, Ohio entered it in the 1957 Bake-Off, where it became one of the contest's most durable recipes. The dough is a soft peanut butter cookie rolled in sugar, and the chocolate kiss goes on only after the cookies come out of the oven so it holds its shape while softening into the still-hot center. That order is the whole trick -- baking the kiss with the cookie melts it flat.

Note on the source: Verified against the family text ingredient by ingredient: 1 3/4 c flour, 1/2 c sugar, 1/2 c brown sugar, 1 t soda, 1/2 t salt, 1/2 c shortening, 1/2 c peanut butter, 2 T milk, 1 t vanilla, 1 egg, roll in sugar, kisses. This is the Pillsbury original, NOT the Hershey's version, which differs materially (3/4 c peanut butter, 1/3 + 1/3 c sugars, 1 1/2 c flour) -- I checked hersheyland.com and rejected it. Family text's return-to-oven step for the kiss is a house addition.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Most well-reviewed versions chill the dough 30-60 min before shaping to curb spread. Unwrap kisses ahead so they're room-temp, not fridge-cold, to prevent cracking when pressed in.

name: Pear Crisp with Oatmeal Topping
ingredients:
6 large pears
2 tablespoons (30 g) lemon juice
1 1/2 cups (320 g) light brown sugar
1 cup (120 g) all-purpose flour, divided
1/2 teaspoon (1.3 g) cinnamon
1/2 teaspoon (2.1 g) vanilla extract
3/4 cup (67 g) quick-cooking oats
1/4 teaspoon (1.0 g) baking powder
6 tablespoons (85 g) (3 ounces) unsalted butter, melted
Ice cream, or heavy whipping cream, for serving
directions:
Steps to Make It

Gather the ingredients.

Heat the oven to 350 F. Generously butter an 8-inch square baking pan.

Peel the pears, cut out the stems, and scoop out the seeds and the fibers.

﻿Slice the fruit thinly and put in a bowl with the lemon juice. Toss to coat with the lemon juice. The lemon juice will keep them from turning brown.

Add 3/4 cup of the brown sugar to the pears, along with 1/4 cup of flour, cinnamon, and vanilla. Mix well and transfer to the prepared baking pan.

In a medium bowl, combine the oats, the remaining 3/4 cup flour, the remaining 3/4 cup brown sugar, baking powder, and the melted butter. Mix with a fork until the crumbs are blended.

Sprinkle the oat crumb topping evenly over the pear mixture.

Bake for 35 to 45 minutes until the ​oat ​topping is browned and the pears are tender.

Serve the crisp warm with a generous scoop of vanilla or butter-pecan ice cream or a drizzling of heavy or light cream.

Recipe Variations

Peach crisp with oat topping: Replace the fresh pears with the same number of fresh peaches. Peel and dice the peaches before adding them to the recipe.

Apple crisp with oat topping: Replace the pears with the same amount of peeled and sliced apples.

Pear crisp without oats: To make a crisp without oats, increase the flour in the topping to one cup. Add 1/2 cup chopped nuts, such as walnuts or pecans, for a crunchy texture.
description:
12/22 Just too bland and sweet. And using oatmeal is odd. 

Susan says: We tried this recipe (twice so far).  pretty good. add enough sugar and butter and anything is good.  used 4 of the 'large' pears from Greg & Jill instead of '6 medium' pears.

Also found that draining off any excess pear/lemon juice from bowl of cut pears just before adding the brown sugar, 1/4 cup flour, cinnamon  &  vanilla helped keep the crisp crisp.
notes:
The best pears for baking are the Bosc (golden brown, long neck) and Anjou (oval, greenish yellow skin). They are both firm and hold their shape well in pies and baked desserts.

Plan to buy pears several days before you plan to eat them or bake with them. Pears are picked before they've ripened, so they will likely be firm when you buy them. The best way to ripen pears is to keep them at room temperature. You'll find the stem end is slightly soft when they are ripe. Once they are ripe, refrigerate them and eat or use them in recipes within three to five days.

Try mixing together a bunch of different types of sliced fruit to make a crisp. Combine stone fruit such as peaches or cherries with berries like blueberries or strawberries. Just plan to have about one cup of fruit for every person you are serving.

Note: the page pasted in for this recipe was The Spruce Eats' "Asian Pear Crisp", a different recipe from the "Warm Spiced Pear Crisp" this entry links to, so it was not used.

name: Pepper Steak
ingredients:
4 shell or filet steaks (1/2 lb. each)
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
3 T. (21 g) pepper corns coarsely crushed
3 T. (43 g) butter
1 T. (14 g) oil

directions: Preheat oven to 225, and warm an ovenproof platter. Rub steaks with salt. Sprinkle with pepper and use a meat pounder to pound the pepper into the steak. Turn meat over, and repeat seasoning on other side. Heat butter and oil in heavy skillet and saute steaks for a bout 4 minutes on each side. Transfer to warm platter. name: Perfect Buttermilk Pancakes
ingredients:
2 cups (240 g) all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons (38 g) sugar
1 ½ teaspoons (6.0 g) baking powder
1 ½ teaspoons (6.9 g) baking soda
1 ¼ teaspoons (3.5 g) kosher salt
2 ½ cups (605 g) buttermilk
2 large eggs
3 tablespoons (43 g) unsalted butter, melted
Vegetable, canola or coconut oil for the pan
directions:
Heat the oven to 325 degrees. Whisk flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda and kosher salt together in a bowl. Using the whisk, make a well in the center. Pour the buttermilk into the well and crack eggs into buttermilk. Pour the melted butter into the mixture. Starting in the center, whisk everything together, moving towards the outside of the bowl, until all ingredients are incorporated. Do not overbeat (lumps are fine). The batter can be refrigerated for up to one hour.

Heat a large nonstick griddle or skillet, preferably cast-iron, over low heat for about 5 minutes. Add 1 tablespoon oil to the skillet. Turn heat up to medium–low and using a measuring cup, ladle 1/3 cup batter into the skillet. If you are using a large skillet or a griddle, repeat once or twice, taking care not to crowd the cooking surface.

Flip pancakes after bubbles rise to surface and bottoms brown, about 2 to 4 minutes. Cook until the other sides are lightly browned. Remove pancakes to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet, and keep in heated oven until all the batter is cooked and you are ready to serve.
description:
6/21 Very fluffy and nice. Waited 15 minutes after mixing to get more fluffy. Added blueberries into the mix beforehand.

1/22 Very good again. Some were not fully cooked.
notes: Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

claude_opt.changes: Cooks' notes flag undercooked centers; hold the griddle at a steady medium-low, not medium, for the whole cook, and finish any doubtful pancake 2-3 min in the 325F holding oven.

name: Perfect Pad Thai
ingredients:
6 ounces (170 g) Chantaboon rice noodles
⅓ cup (73 g) peanut or vegetable oil
3 large eggs, lightly beaten
8 ounces (227 g) medium shrimp, shelled and deveined (or 6 ounces of chicken, pork, etc., sliced thinly)
3 garlic cloves, minced
½ cup (120 g) Pad Thai Sauce (recipe follows)
¼ cup (38 g) thinly sliced sweet preserved radish (optional)
½ cup (80 g) thinly sliced green onion
1 ½ cups (156 g) mung bean sprouts, rinsed thoroughly, divided
¼ cup (36 g) roasted peanuts, unsalted, finely chopped, plus more for garnish
1 lime, cut into wedges, for garnish

Pad Thai Sauce (makes 1 ½ cups):
⅓ cup (87 g) tamarind concentrate (Thai brands only)
⅓ cup (80 g) white vinegar
2 T. (32 g) soy sauce
2 T. (32 g) fish sauce
½ teaspoon (2.8 g) sea salt
½ cup (106 g) grated palm sugar or light brown sugar
2 t. (5.6 g) garlic powder
2 - 3 T. (34-52 g) Sriracha chili sauce, depending on preference
directions:
1. Soften Chantaboon rice noodles: Place noodles in a large bowl and cover with boiling water. Soak for 30 minutes or until tender and soft. Drain in a colander and set aside, covered with a clean dish towel.

2. Make the sauce: Place all ingredients in a medium saucepan and bring to a boil over medium heat. Cook sauce at a high simmer until it thickens and coats the back of a spoon, about 10-15 minutes. Set aside. This makes more than enough sauce for one recipe of Pad Thai. Store leftovers in the fridge for up to 2 weeks or freeze in ⅔-cup batches.

3. Marinate protein in 2 T. Pad Thai sauce for 5 minutes or so. 

4. Prepare Pad Thai: Prepare and measure each ingredient before starting the wok as things move quickly.

5. Heat a wok over high heat, add 3 T. oil, and swirl to coat the sides. Add the protein and cook lightly since it will be cooked more later. Remove protein. Add 2 T. oil to the hot wok, then the eggs and stir fry for 30 seconds. Stir in garlic and noodles followed by 1/2 c. Pad Thai Sauce. Simmer noodles in the sauce until cooked through, 1 to 2 minutes. Stir in the protein and radish.

6. Check the noodles; they should be easy to pinch in half with your fingers. If they are not tender, add ¼ cup water. When the noodles are tender, stir in green onions, 1 cup of bean sprouts, and half of the peanuts; remove the wok from the stove. Be careful not to overcook the noodles or they will stick together. If this happens, add small amounts of water to separate them. When the water is absorbed, remove the wok immediately from the heat.

7. To serve: Place Pad Thai in a large serving bowl and garnish with remaining bean sprouts, lime wedges, and peanuts.
description:
Delicious. Made in our online cooking class, 2/4/2021.
Sauce can be made ahead - see step 2.
notes:
Chantaboon rice noodles (available at H Mart) do not seem to differ from rice stick noodles which are easier to find. 
Palm sugar is pretty easy to find at Asian groceries. It comes very hard and we used a mortar and pestle to break it up. 
Thai tamarind concentrate comes in a small plastic jar, unrefrigerated. I found it at H Mart.  
Thai sweet radish comes shredded in a bag in the refrigerator section. I found it at 99Ranch. Could use fresh radish as a substitute.

Web summary (surlatable.com). The Sur La Table kitchen's home version of pad thai, written to get the dish off the takeout menu. The sauce is made from scratch - tamarind concentrate, vinegar, soy and fish sauce, palm sugar and Sriracha - so it can be balanced to taste rather than accepted as bottled. Rice noodles are softened in advance, and the method stresses having every component measured and within reach before the pan gets hot, since the actual stir-fry moves too fast to prepare anything mid-cook.

Note on the source: page is titled 'Perfect Tofu Pad Thai' - tofu version of the named recipe, minor drift only; no comments section

claude_opt.changes: No wok in this kitchen -- a 12in+ flat skillet or Lodge cast iron on the high-output burner works fine, shape matters less than heat. Soak noodles in hot tap water, not boiling, to avoid mush.

name: Perfect Peach Pie
ingredients:
FOR THE PIE DOUGH:
2 ½ cups or 300 grams all-purpose flour
12 tablespoons or 169 grams unsalted butter, cold, cut into 1/2-inch cubes
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt
Yolk of 1 egg, beaten
1 teaspoon (5.0 g) cider vinegar
¼ cup (59 g) water, from 3/4 cup ice water
White of 1 egg, beaten
Pinch granulated sugar
FOR THE FILLING:
6 or 7 ripe peaches, peeled and sliced, approximately 5 cups
2 tablespoons (30 g) lemon juice
1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar
¼ cup or 30 grams all-purpose flour
Pinch of ground nutmeg
directions:
Make the pie dough. Using your fingertips or the pulse function of a food processor, blend together the flour, butter and salt until the mixture resembles a coarse meal. There should be pebbles of butter throughout the mixture.

Add egg yolk and vinegar to 1/4 cup ice water, and stir to combine. Drizzle 4 tablespoons of this mixture over the dough, and gently stir or pulse to combine. Gather a golf-ball-size bit of dough, and squeeze to combine. If it does not hold together, add a little more of the liquid, and stir or pulse, then check again. Repeat as necessary.

Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface, and gather together into a rough ball. Divide the ball in half with a knife or a pastry scraper, then divide each portion in half again, and again, to create 8 portions. Using the heel of your hand, flatten each portion of dough once or twice to expand the pebbles of butter, then gather the dough together again in one ball. Divide this ball in half.

Flatten each ball into a 5- or 6-inch disc, one slightly larger than the other. Wrap the discs in plastic wrap, and place in the refrigerator for at least 60 minutes.

Preheat oven to 425. Make the pie filling: Combine sliced peaches, lemon juice, sugar and flour in a large bowl, and gently mix to combine. Set aside.

Take the larger of the pastry discs out of the refrigerator, roll it out on a lightly floured surface and place in a 9-inch pie plate. Add the peaches. Sprinkle them with the ground nutmeg.

Roll out second disc of pastry. Place on top of filling. Wet edges of the bottom pastry disc with some cold water. Trim pastry, pinch bottom and top edges together and cut a few slits to allow steam to escape from the pie. Brush the egg white on the top, particularly around the edges, and sprinkle with a pinch of granulated sugar.

Bake the pie for 15 minutes, then reduce heat to 375. Cook until peaches bubble and pastry is golden, approximately 45 minutes to an hour.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (3,220)). The argument is that a truly great fresh peach is rare - one or two a season - but a pie reliably lifts merely good fruit, and works even with frozen peaches. Sugar does the heavy lifting, with lemon juice and a little nutmeg added for a touch of bitterness against the sweetness. Vanilla ice cream is suggested for a diner-style finish.

What readers report: A runny filling is the recurring failure, and the top note (866 votes) fixes it by macerating the sliced peaches in the sugar first and draining off the released juice before filling the shell; a corroborating comment (262) cites Cook's Illustrated doing the same and then thickening with cornstarch slaked in a little of the reserved juice. Peeling is contested: a well-voted note (328) argues skins on give the filling more body and color, and another (287) confirms leaving them on works fine, while others recommend a soft-fruit peeler over blanching. Thickener choice affects appearance - tapioca sets clear, flour cloudy. Bake on a low rack (220 votes) to crisp the bottom crust; blind baking is also endorsed.

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

name: Perfect Roast Chicken
ingredients:
1 (5 to 6 pound) roasting chicken
Kosher salt
Freshly ground black pepper
1 large bunch fresh thyme, plus 20 sprigs
1 lemon, halved
1 head garlic, cut in half crosswise
2 tablespoons (28 g) (1/4 stick) butter, melted
1 large yellow onion, thickly sliced
4 carrots cut into 2-inch chunks
1 bulb of fennel, tops removed, and cut into wedges
Olive oil
directions:
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees F.

Remove the chicken giblets. Rinse the chicken inside and out. Remove any excess fat and leftover pin feathers and pat the outside dry. Liberally salt and pepper the inside of the chicken. Stuff the cavity with the bunch of thyme, both halves of lemon, and all the garlic. Brush the outside of the chicken with the butter and sprinkle again with salt and pepper. Tie the legs together with kitchen string and tuck the wing tips under the body of the chicken. Place the onions, carrots, and fennel in a roasting pan. Toss with salt, pepper, 20 sprigs of thyme, and olive oil. Spread around the bottom of the roasting pan and place the chicken on top.

Roast the chicken for 1 1/2 hours, or until the juices run clear when you cut between a leg and thigh. Remove the chicken and vegetables to a platter and cover with aluminum foil for about 20 minutes. Slice the chicken onto a platter and serve it with the vegetables.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten's signature roast chicken. The cavity is packed with a halved lemon, a head of garlic cut crosswise and a large bunch of thyme, which scent the meat from inside as they steam during roasting, while melted butter on the skin and high heat handle the browning outside. Onion, carrot and fennel go under and around the bird so they cook in the rendered fat and drippings and come out as the side dish.

What readers report: Cooks repeatedly report the vegetables catching and burning before the chicken is done, and the common fix is to pour a little chicken broth or white wine into the pan, which keeps the bottom moist and turns the drippings into something closer to a pan sauce. Fennel is the most substituted ingredient: those who dislike its anise character swap in potatoes or celery and say the dish loses nothing essential. The lemon-garlic-thyme cavity combination is the part nobody quarrels with, and is credited for both the crisp skin and the juiciness. It comes up often as a Thanksgiving and Christmas main as well as a Sunday dinner.

Note on the source: no vote counts shown

claude_opt.changes: Pour 1/2 cup broth or wine into the pan before roasting; the vegetables otherwise scorch before the chicken finishes at 425°F. Swap potatoes for fennel if anise isn't wanted — loses nothing per reviewers.

name: Perfect Roasted Pork Tenderloin with Apples
ingredients:
YOU WILL NEED
2 pork tenderloins (about 1 1/2-pounds each)
2 tablespoons (27 g) vegetable oil, plus more as needed
1 1/2 teaspoons (9.0 g) salt, plus more as needed
1 tablespoon (16 g) Dijon mustard
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) chopped fresh thyme leaves
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) ground black pepper
2 apples, cored and sliced (we like Granny Smith, Golden Delicious or Braeburn)
2 onions, sliced
1 cup (240 g) chicken stock, see our homemade chicken stock recipe
1 tablespoon (14 g) butter
directions:
PREPARE PORK

Heat oven to 425 degrees F. Trim each tenderloin of any silver skin (this can be tough when cooked). To do this, use a small sharp knife and slide the blade under and outward to remove it.

Pat pork dry with paper towels and then rub with one tablespoon of the oil and 1 1/2 teaspoons of salt. Heat a tablespoon of oil in a heavy-bottomed oven-safe skillet over medium heat. When the oil is hot and shimmers, add the pork tenderloins and cook, occasionally turning, until evenly browned all over; about 12 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or cutting board. (The pork will not be cooked through).

PREPARE APPLES AND ONIONS

Keep the pan used to sear the pork on the stove over medium heat. Check the pan, if it looks dry, add two to three teaspoons of additional oil. (If there is fat left in the pan from cooking the pork, there is no need to add extra oil).

Add the apples and onions then cook, occasionally stirring, until lightly browned around edges, about 5 minutes. Stir in 1 teaspoon of thyme.

TO FINISH:

Use a pastry brush (or use your fingers) to rub the seared pork all over with the mustard, 2 teaspoons of thyme, and the black pepper. Place the seared pork tenderloins on top of the apples and onions, and then slide into the oven.

Roast 10 to 15 minutes or until an internal thermometer inserted into the thickest part registers between 145 and 150 degrees F. Transfer the pork to a large plate and cover with aluminum foil. Let rest about 10 minutes.

While the pork rests, place the pan with apples and onions back onto the stove and turn heat to medium. Add chicken stock and use a wooden spoon to scrape the pan, lifting any brown bits from the bottom. Bring to a simmer and cook until reduced by half. Add butter and stir until melted.

To serve, slice pork into 1-inch slices then serve on a bed of the apples and onions with pan sauce drizzled on top.
description:
10/2020 Pretty tasty! Used 1 tenderloin and whole recipe of apples and onions. Could add apples a little later to keep them not too mushy.

12/2022 enjoyed it quite a bit. Again one tenderloin with full sauce. Stamens with thick slice. Fine even after a long fridge. Cooked pork 23 minutes. Perhaps a couple minutes too long.  145-150 internal is probably right.
notes:
Web summary (inspiredtaste.net, 4.9 stars, 236 reviews). Joanne Gallagher sears the tenderloins first and only then applies the Dijon-and-thyme coating before roasting. The order matters: the sear builds the crust at a heat that would scorch mustard and herbs, so putting the rub on afterwards protects it. The pork then roasts on a bed of sliced apples and onions, which caramelise underneath while the meat's juices run into them, so the pan produces its own sauce with stock and a knob of butter rather than needing one made separately.

What readers report: The most common report is that the apples break down to mush at the stated timing; the fix people agree on is a firmer variety - Honeycrisp, Fuji or Granny Smith - or cooking the apples separately and adding them near the end. Second, a good number of cooks found the 15 to 20 minute roast too short to reach temperature and simply extended it, which suggests checking with a thermometer rather than trusting the clock. Successful variations include finishing the pan sauce with heavy cream, using white wine in place of the chicken stock, adding rosemary alongside the thyme, and one each of cognac and beef stock. Several also flag that the silver skin is awkward to remove and want a sharper knife for it.

claude_opt.changes: Your 10/2020 note already found this: add the apples partway through their sauté (or use firmer Honeycrisp/Fuji) so they don't turn to mush by the time the pork finishes roasting. No time change.

name: Petite Cheesecakes
ingredients:
2 8-oz. (227 g) pkgs. cream cheese
2 eggs
1 T. (15 g) lemon juice
1 t. (4.2 g) vanilla
1 c. (200 g) sugar
15 vanilla wafers
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.

Combine cream cheese, eggs, juice, vanilla and sugar. Beat until smooth. Put vanilla wafers on bottom of foil cupcake liners. Fill each half-full with cream cheese mixture or divide evenly into 15 cupcakes. Bake for 15-18 minutes.

claude_opt.changes: Use room-temperature cream cheese and eggs and mix on low -- minis crack and sink easily if overbeaten. Bake at 325F instead of 350F for a gentler set, same 15-18 min.

name: Pickled Mushrooms
ingredients:
Boil:
2 lbs. (907 g) button mushrooms
1 c. (239 g) vinegar
1/2 t. (0.6 g) tarragon (optional)
1 T. (13 g) sugar
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
directions:
Sterilize 4 8-oz. jars. Cut mushrooms in slices or quarters or whole. Drop in solution of 1 qt. water mixed with 1 T. salt. This keep mushrooms light. 

Cook vinegar, etc., to a boil. Drain mushrooms and add about 1/2 the boiling mixture. Reduce heat and cook slowly for 3 minutes. Pack mushrooms into jars tightly. Pack second batch in the same manner. Cap securely and let stand at least 4 days before using. They will keep for months if you use a mason jar and keep refrigerated.

At least 1 day before using, take them out of the vinegar mixture and add oregano, small clove of garlic, and olive oi and marinate overnight.

name: Pizza with Caramelized Onions, Ricotta and Chard
ingredients:
2 tablespoons (27 g) extra virgin olive oil
1 ¼ pounds (567 g) onions, sliced
1 teaspoon (1.1 g) chopped fresh thyme leaves
2 garlic cloves, minced
Salt
freshly ground pepper
½ pound (227 g) chard, stemmed, leaves washed
1 14-inch pizza crust (1/2 batch pizza dough)
¾ cup (184 g) ricotta (6 ounces)
2 ounces Parmesan, grated 1/2 cup, tightly packed
1 egg yolk
directions:
Thirty minutes before baking the pizza, preheat the oven to 500 degrees. Heat the olive oil over medium heat in a large, heavy skillet. Add the onions. Cook, stirring often, until tender and just beginning to color, about 10 minutes. Add the thyme, garlic and a generous pinch of salt. Turn the heat to low, cover and cook another 10 to 20 minutes, stirring often, until the onions are golden brown and very sweet and soft. Remove from the heat.

While the onions are cooking, stem and wash the chard leaves, and bring a medium pot of water to a boil. Fill a medium bowl with ice water. When the water comes to a boil, salt generously and add the chard. Blanch for one to two minutes, just until the leaves are tender, and transfer to the ice water. Drain and squeeze out excess water. Alternatively, steam the chard for two to three minutes until wilted, and rinse with cold water. Chop the chard medium-fine.

Roll out the dough, oil a 14-inch pizza pan and dust with cornmeal or semolina. Place the dough on the pan.

In a medium bowl, combine the ricotta, egg yolk, Parmesan and chard. Spread over the pizza dough in an even layer, leaving a 1-inch border around the rim. Spread the onions over the ricotta mixture.

Place in the hot oven, and bake 10 to 15 minutes until the crust and bits of the onion are nicely browned. Remove from the heat, and serve hot or warm.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (714)). A rich vegetable pizza: caramelized onions spread over a base of ricotta, Parmesan and chopped Swiss chard. It came out of a piece on cooking chard in a cold spring. The headnote is brief and offers no technique notes.

What readers report: Two practical themes dominate a thin comment set. First, it needs acid or heat - cooks add red pepper flakes, a balsamic drizzle, or green olives for salt, and the top note (38 votes) reports arugula in place of the greens working well. Second, the recipe dirties too many pans (14 votes): one cook caramelized the onions, then wilted the chopped chard with garlic in the same skillet and assembled from there. Chard swaps freely with spinach or kale. Baking time runs short of what the recipe implies - one finished in about six minutes - so watch it. A cast-iron pan bottom stands in for a pizza pan and gives a crisper crust.

name: Plain Pastry for Pie Crust
ingredients:
2 c. (240 g) flour
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
2/3 c. (137 g) shortening
5-8 T. (74-118 g) ice water
directions:
Preheat oven.
Sift flour and salt together; cut in shortening with pastry blender untill pieces are the size of small peas. For extra-tender pastry, cut in the shortening until like cornmeal. Cut in remaining shortening until like small peas. Sprinkle 1 T. water over part of mixture. Gently toss with fork; push to side of bowl. Repeat with additional T's of water until all flour is moistened. Form into a ball, or two balls for double crust pie.
description: For one 8, 9, or 10" double-crust pie, one lattice top pie, or two single crust pie shells including quiches. Scale by half for one single-crust pie.
notes:
Web summary (food.com). A member transcription, credited to Better Homes and Gardens, of the standard all-shortening double-crust pastry. Flour and salt are cut with shortening to pea-size pieces, then ice water is sprinkled a tablespoon at a time over one section of the mixture, tossed with a fork and pushed aside before the next addition. Adding the water in that piecemeal way is what keeps the dough from being overworked in any one spot, which is where toughness comes from.

Note on the source: LOW CONFIDENCE, flagged for human review. The family entry records no source at all, but its directions are near-verbatim Better Homes and Gardens New Cook Book 'Plain Pastry' wording ('For extra-tender pastry, cut in the shortening until like cornmeal. Cut in remaining shortening until like small peas'), and the cook's note ('For one 8, 9, or 10 inch double-crust pie, one lattice top pie, or two single crust pie shells') is BH&G's own yield line. So the recipe identity is almost certainly BH&G Plain Pastry. What is weaker is this particular page: it lists 1/2 t salt and a flat 6 T water, where the family text has 1 t salt and 5-8 T water, so it is an imperfect transcription of the same recipe. No official BH&G page for Plain Pastry is online. Promote or replace at will.

Link confidence: LOW — this URL is a plausible version of the dish but was not verified as the family's exact recipe. Treat the link as a lead, not a citation.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Universal step missing: chill the formed dough 30-60 min before rolling -- every ATK/King Arthur version does this to prevent shrinkage and toughness. The 'preheat oven' first step is orphaned; this recipe has no bake step.

directions:

name: Popeye Drops (Spinach Balls)

directions: Do not cook stuffing mix. Mix everything together (stuffing mix, seasoning & all) and shape into walnut size balls. Place on ungreased cookie sheet and freeze. When ready to use, remove as many as needed and bake for 10 minutes at 350°. Makes approximately 50 "drops."

name: Porchetta Pork Chops
ingredients:
2 bone-in pork chops, 1 1/4 to 1 1/2 inches thick
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) coarse kosher salt, plus a pinch
1 lemon
2 garlic cloves, minced
2 tablespoons (6.9 g) chopped rosemary
Large pinch red pepper flakes
½ teaspoon (1.0 g) fennel seeds, lightly crushed
2 tablespoons (11 g) chopped fennel fronds, more for garnish
2 tablespoons (27 g) olive oil
directions:
Heat oven to 350 degrees. Pat pork chops dry and, using a very sharp paring knife, cut a large pocket into the fat-covered edge of each chop. Season chops all over with 1 teaspoon salt, including inside pockets.

Finely grate zest from lemon and put in a small bowl. Cut lemon lengthwise in quarters for serving.

Using a mortar and pestle or the flat side of a knife, mash garlic with a pinch of salt until you get a paste. Add to the bowl with the lemon zest and stir in rosemary, red pepper flakes, fennel seeds, 2 tablespoons fennel fronds and 1 tablespoon olive oil.

Divide filling between pork chops, stuffing some inside pockets and rubbing the rest on the outside.

Heat a large ovenproof skillet over high heat and add 1 tablespoon olive oil. Sear pork chops on one side for 5 minutes, or until golden brown. Gently turn over chops and cook for another minute, then transfer skillet to oven. Cook until meat is just done, about 5 to 10 minutes longer (internal temperature should read 135 degrees on a meat thermometer). Transfer pork chops to a plate, tent with foil, and let rest for 10 minutes before serving. Garnish with fennel fronds and lemon wedges.
description: 11/30 Good flavor, but a bit tough. Maybe overcooked.  Went to about 165 degrees. Take out sooner next time
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (4,167)). Melissa Clark's shortcut on porchetta: the garlic, rosemary and fennel seasoning of the whole roast pig, applied to pork chops instead. The pitch is that it comes together fast enough to be a spur-of-the-moment weeknight dinner rather than a project.

What readers report: Overcooking is the trap. Multiple high-voted notes (158, 101) warn to follow the stated times rather than instinct - cooks who added a minute at each stage ended up with dry chops, and anyone working with thinner chops than Clark's needs to cut the time further. A thermometer is the standard advice. The top note (374 votes) enriches the herb filling with a teaspoon of Dijon and two diced anchovies. A well-liked adaptation (318 votes) scales the same garlic-herb paste to a butterflied pork loin for a bigger meal. Others prefer thyme to half the rosemary, and finish with a white-wine pan sauce. One dissent (105 votes) finds the flavors harsh and calls the 20-minute time estimate unrealistic.

name: Pork Ragù Al Maialino
ingredients:
1 pork shoulder, bone in, roughly 4 pounds (1.8 kg)
Kosher salt
3 tablespoons (40 g) olive oil
1 medium white onion, peeled and cut into large pieces
1 rib celery, cut into large pieces
1 small fennel bulb, trimmed and cut into large pieces
1 quart (960 g) chicken stock (or enough to almost cover the pork)
3 sprigs fresh thyme
Freshly ground black pepper
4 tablespoons (57 g) unsalted butter
2 9-ounce (255 g) boxes dry lasagna, broken into 3-inch shards
2 tablespoons (30 g) fresh lemon juice
2 tablespoons (11 g) grated grana Padano cheese
1 tablespoon (3.8 g) chopped parsley
Small handful arugula leaves, cleaned
directions:
Using a sharp knife, remove the thick skin from the pork, leaving a sheen of fat on top of the meat. Season aggressively with salt and place in the refrigerator until ready to use, as long as overnight.

Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Place a deep saucepan or Dutch oven over medium-high heat and add 2 tablespoons olive oil. When it shimmers, gently cook the onion, celery and fennel until they begin to soften, about 10 minutes. Add the stock and thyme and bring to a simmer, then season to taste with salt and pepper. Rinse pork to remove excess salt, dry with a paper towel and add to seasoned broth. Cover and place in the oven for 90 minutes or more, until the meat just begins to pull away from the bone.

Allow both meat and broth to cool on the stove top for 30 minutes, or until you can touch the meat with your hands. Remove the pork and gently pull the meat from the bone, then tear the chunks into bite-size shreds. Place these in a large bowl.

Strain the liquid into a separate bowl and then pour enough of it over the meat to barely cover. (Use the rest for soup.) Cover and store in the refrigerator until ready to use.

Put a large pot of salted water over high heat and bring to a boil.

Place a large pan over medium-high heat and add the pork and braising liquid. Bring to a boil, then lower heat to medium and cook until the liquid is reduced by half. Add the butter and stir to emulsify.

Meanwhile, cook the pasta in salted water according to the directions on the package, 10 to 12 minutes. When it is finished, drain and add to the sauce along with a splash of pasta water. Simmer for 1 minute, then add the lemon juice, half of the cheese, a tablespoon of olive oil and the parsley. Stir to incorporate.

Serve immediately, topped with arugula and the remaining cheese.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (452)). Sam Sifton's home adaptation of a restaurant ragu that began as a way to use up leftovers, stripped of the suckling pig, fresh pasta and veal stock the original relied on. Cheap pork shoulder and extra butter stand in, and the result is meant to taste like restaurant cooking anyway.

What readers report: Make it a day ahead - the top-rated practical note (42 votes) tears the meat while still warm, refrigerates, and says it improves overnight; it also converts pork skeptics. Browning the pork before softening the aromatics is the most common addition (several notes) for deeper flavor, though the recipe does not call for it. Expect roughly 2.5 hours of cooking. Boneless pork butt or cubed shoulder both work, and red wine plus water substitutes acceptably for stock. An Instant Pot version is reported as reliable and easy to scale up or down. Pappardelle is the preferred pasta. The comment set is small, with no real disagreement about the method.

ahead: Season aggressively with salt and place in the refrigerator until ready to use, as long as overnight.

claude_opt.changes: Braise the pork a day ahead: tear it while still warm and refrigerate in the strained broth overnight — the top-voted fix (42 votes), and it noticeably improves flavor. Otherwise nothing to change; the reduction already builds the sauce.

name: Pork Sausage Jim Lahey
ingredients:
3 grams (1 heaping teaspoon) fennel seeds
500 grams (about 1 pound) ground pork butt
1½ garlic cloves, finely chopped
8 grams (1¼ teaspoons) grated fresh ginger
2 dried chili peppers, crumbled, or ½ teaspoon (0.9 g) chili flakes
6 grams (¾ teaspoon) fine sea salt
directions:
Toast the fennel seeds in a dry saucepan over medium heat, shaking the pan continuously, until they just start to color and turn fragrant, 1 to 2 minutes; be careful not to burn them. Transfer to a plate to cool.

In a medium bowl, with your hands, mix the pork, fennel seeds, garlic, ginger, chili flakes, and salt. Set aside if you're going to prepare a pizza immediately. If not, cover and refrigerate for up to 3 days; bring back to room temperature before using.

makeahead: If not, cover and refrigerate for up to 3 days; bring back to room temperature before using.

claude_opt.changes: No changes; toasting the fennel, hand-mixing, and roughly 1.2% salt match modern fennel-sausage technique. Salt is lighter than a standalone sausage's usual 1.5-2% but appropriate since this is a pizza topping.

name: Pork Tenderloin Roll-Up
ingredients:
1 pork tenderloin, butterflied to about 2/3 inch thick
2 cloves garlic
lemon zest from half a lemon
3 branches of rosemary
1 branch of sage
Grate and chop these, then saute for a couple of minutes in a bit of olive oil to make the flavors less harsh

3 strips bacon, cut in pieces
1/2 tsp (0.8 g) fennel pollen
2 oz (57 g) feta
directions:
In cuisinart, chop bacon, add cooked herb mixture, fennel pollen and feta and pulse til nearly a paste

Salt and pepper the pork, then spread filling mixture evenly, roll up the pork and tie it to make the log even thickness. Coat with a thin layer of olive oil, add a bit of salt and pepper, and bake at 400-450 F for 30-40 minutes, until it reaches160-165 internal.
description: This recipe can be endlessly adjusted. Add cooked, drained spinach. Use cheddar and apples. No bacon. Different herbs.

claude_opt.changes: Pull at 145F internal (USDA's standard since 2011) plus a 3-min rest, not 160-165F; the old target overcooks lean tenderloin and dries out the cheese-herb filling.

name: Potato Rosti
ingredients:
3 medium potatoes such as russet or Kennebec (about 1 3/4 lb. or 875 g total)
1 Tbs. (8.4 g) kosher salt
1/2 cup (4 oz./125 g) clarified butter, melted
Snipped fresh chives for garnish
directions:
Preheat an oven to 350°F (180°C).

Peel the potatoes, then quickly grate them using the coarse holes of a grater, holding the potatoes vertically and using long strokes to keep the potato shreds as long as possible. In a bowl, toss the potatoes with the salt and set aside for 5 minutes while the potato shreds wilt and release some of their liquid. Using your hands, squeeze the potatoes to release any remaining moisture, then pour off as much of the liquid as possible. Repeat the squeezing and pouring a few times; you want the potatoes to be quite dry.

Add 2 Tbs. of the clarified butter to the bowl with the potatoes and toss to evenly coat. Heat an 8-inch (20-cm) fry pan over medium-high heat. Add 3 Tbs. of the clarified butter to the pan. When the butter just begins to smoke, start placing the grated potatoes in the pan. Use a flat spatula to compact the potatoes tightly in the pan and flatten them into an even layer about 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick. When the rösti begins to brown around the edges, use the spatula to gently lift the edge of the potatoes and take a peek at the bottom. Adjust the heat up or down as necessary so that the potatoes brown but do not scorch or stick to the pan.

When the bottom layer is a rich, golden brown, use a wide spatula to quickly but carefully turn the rösti over. Pour the remaining 3 Tbs. clarified butter around the edges of the rösti and continue to cook until the second side begins to brown.

Transfer the rösti to the center of the oven and bake for 20 minutes. Remove from the oven and check to see that the bottom is well browned and crisp. Test for tenderness, too, by piercing the rösti with the tip of a paring knife; the potatoes should offer no resistance other than the crust. If the top or the bottom isn’t quite crisp the potatoes may be placed back on the stove over medium heat until crisp; watch carefully to avoid burning the potatoes.

Remove the pan from the heat and loosen the edges of the rösti from the pan with a spatula. Tilt the pan and coax the rösti out of the pan and onto a serving dish or cutting board. As soon as the rösti is cool enough to handle, sprinkle with chives and use a serrated knife to cut it into wedges. Serve immediately. Serves 4.
notes: Web summary (williams-sonoma.com, 3.0 (2)). The recipe is credited to Thomas Keller of The French Laundry; the framing treats rösti as a basic template — grated, salted, squeezed-dry potatoes pressed and browned in clarified butter, then finished in a 350°F oven — that a cook can embellish with bacon, minced onion or other add-ins. What readers report: only two reviews exist, both mixed-to-critical. One reviewer (2 helpful votes vs. 10 unhelpful) calls the dish 'completely inedible' because of the salt: 1 Tbs. kosher salt for 3 medium potatoes was excessive in her and her husband's judgment, and she notes they scaled the recipe up proportionally rather than deviating from its ratio, so this reads as a genuine complaint about the recipe's salt level rather than a cook's error. She adds the effort of grating is as expected and not itself a problem. The other reviewer (1 helpful vote, 0 unhelpful) rated it 5 stars but flagged it as a lot of work for a small yield, noting it can be made ahead and reheated. No technique fixes or substitutions are offered beyond these two points.

claude_opt.changes: The 'too salty' complaint (1 Tbs. for 3 potatoes) carries a 2-helpful/10-unhelpful vote split — readers largely reject it, so leave the salt as written. The one useful tip: rösti can be made ahead and reheated.

name: Potato Salad
ingredients:
3 pounds (1.4 kg) small white potatoes
Kosher salt
1 cup (220 g) mayonnaise
1/4 cup (60 g) buttermilk
2 tablespoons (31 g) Dijon mustard
2 tablespoons (31 g) whole-grain mustard
1/2 cup (22 g) chopped fresh dill
Freshly ground black pepper
1/2 cup (50 g) chopped celery
1/2 cup (80 g) chopped red onion
directions:
Place the potatoes and 2 tablespoons of salt in a large pot of water. Bring the water to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer for 10 to 15 minutes, until the potatoes are barely tender when pierced with a knife. Drain the potatoes in a colander, then place the colander with the potatoes over the empty pot and cover with a clean, dry kitchen towel. Allow the potatoes to steam for 15 to 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, in a small bowl, whisk together the mayonnaise, buttermilk, Dijon mustard, whole grain mustard, dill, 1 teaspoon of salt, and 1 teaspoon of pepper. Set aside.

When the potatoes are cool enough to handle, cut them in quarters or in half, depending on their size. Place the cut potatoes in a large bowl. While the potatoes are still warm, pour enough dressing over them to moisten. Add the celery and red onion, 2 teaspoons of salt and 1 teaspoon of pepper. Toss well, cover, and refrigerate for a few hours to allow the flavors to blend. Serve cold or at room temperature.
description:
6/12 Made this recipe substituting 1/4 c. red wine vinegar for buttermilk. Tossed vinegar and salt and pepper w/warm potatoes. Then substituted 1/2 c. of mayo for 1 c. and added herbs, mustard, celery, and onion to potatoes. Could try less dill.
7/12 Excellent. Followed the above adjustments with less dill. Will would like more mayo than the half amount we used.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten dresses small white potatoes while they are still warm, which is the point of the recipe: warm potato absorbs the dressing instead of just being coated by it. The potatoes are boiled and then left to steam dry so they stay tender rather than waterlogged. The dressing is mayonnaise thinned with buttermilk, sharpened with both Dijon and whole-grain mustard, and carried by a generous half cup of fresh dill, with celery and red onion for crunch. It then chills for several hours before serving.

What readers report: The potato itself is the most-adjusted element: many cooks prefer red or Yukon Gold to the specified small white potatoes, saying they hold their shape better once cut and dressed. Buttermilk is the other frequent swap, replaced by sour cream or Greek yogurt both for availability and for a thicker dressing. Beyond that the changes are matters of proportion - dialling the half cup of dill down, or the mustard up or down - and some cooks drop the celery, or the whole-grain mustard, without trouble. It is described over and over as a potluck and summer-gathering recipe that travels well.

Note on the source: no vote counts shown

claude_opt.changes: Nothing to fix in the method. Per your 7/12 note, use closer to the full 1 cup mayo rather than the half-cup you tried, which that note found under-dressed; keep the red-wine-vinegar swap for buttermilk.

name: Potatoes Anna
ingredients:
2 T. (28 g) butter
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
3 lg. potatoes, peeled
directions:
1. In 1 qt. saucepan over low heat, melt butter with salt. Preheat oven to 425.
2. With knife slice potatoes about 1/4 inch thick.
3. In greased 8" pie plate, arrange potato slices, overlapping them; drizzle butter mixture on top. Cover plate tightly with foil. Bake 20 minutes.
4. Uncover and bake about 55 minutes more until potatoes are very tender and crusty.
5. Let stand at room temp 5 minutes. With metal spatula, carefully loosen potatoes. Place inverted plate over potatoes. Invert and unmold. Cut in wedges.

name: Pumpkin Pie
ingredients:
1 9" pie shell unbaked
1 16-oz. (454 g) can Libby pumpkin
1 14-oz. (397 g) can sweetened condensed milk (not evaporated milk)
2 eggs
1 t. (2.6 g) cinnamon
1/2 t. (1.0 g) ginger
