directions:
Preheat oven to 425.

In a large bowl, combine all ingredients except pastry shell; mix well. Pour into pastry shell. Bake 15 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350; bake 35 minutes longer or until knife inserted near edge comes out clean. Cool. Refrigerate leftovers.
description: This is an older Libby's recipe. Their current recipe uses 1 12-oz. can of evaporated milk plus 3/4 c. sugar, in place of the condensed milk used here.
notes: Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: No changes beyond the milk swap already flagged in cooks_note; testing for a clean knife near the edge, not the center, already matches current guidance to leave the center jiggly.

name: Quick & Easy Creamy Spinach Orzo
ingredients:
2 cups (480 g) vegetable broth
1 cup (244 g) whole milk
1 cup (200 g) orzo pasta
1 cup (90 g) Parmesan cheese
4 oz. (113 g) roughly chopped baby spinach
½ tsp. (3.0 g) salt or to taste
½ tsp. (1.1 g) pepper or to taste
directions:
Combine the vegetable broth and milk in a medium saucepan and bring to a boil.

Add the orzo and cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally.

Reduce the heat to medium-low and add the Parmesan and spinach. Keep cooking for about 3 minutes, until the spinach wilts down.

Taste the orzo. Add salt and pepper to taste. Stir, and remove from heat. Serve.

HOW TO STORE AND REHEAT THIS SPINACH ORZO

Store this pasta in an airtight container, refrigerated, for up to 4 days. When reheating, you’ll want to do so in a skillet with a little water, milk, or veggie broth to prevent the pasta from drying out or becoming gummy.
description: 4/23 What’s not to like? Recommended by Susan. Added a nice ⅛ c of dill for a half recipe, at the same time as the spinach. Doubled spinach. Use bouillon for the broth, and some creme fraiche along with 2 percent milk.
notes:
HELPFUL TIPS AND TRICKS

Use a non-stick pot. Because this recipe requires milk, orzo pasta may stick to the bottom of the pan if it’s not stirred frequently.

Adjust seasonings to taste. Because I don’t know how salty your vegetable broth is, I recommend adding salt in the final step, after you have tasted the dish. This way, you won’t end up with over-salted orzo.

Add extra vegetables. You can also add some peas, carrots, asparagus, broccoli, cauliflower, or mushrooms to this dish.

Use fresh herbs. Fresh parsley, dill, or cilantro would add a nice flavor and extra nutrients to the dish.

Web summary (cooktoria.com, 4.65 stars, 150 ratings). Tania Sheff cooks the orzo directly in a mix of vegetable broth and whole milk in one pan, so the starch the pasta gives off thickens the liquid into a sauce and no heavy cream is needed. Parmesan stirred in at the end does the rest of the enriching, and chopped baby spinach wilts into the hot orzo. She pitches it as a roughly fifteen-minute weeknight dish that children will eat.

What readers report: Dairy-free adaptations come up most: oat milk in place of the whole milk and a vegan Parmesan both work, with readers reporting the sauce still thickens because the orzo starch is doing the work. The best flavour tweak in the thread is toasting the dry orzo in butter with garlic, thyme and onion powder before the liquid goes in, which gives it a nuttier base. On additions, frozen peas should go in at the same time as the orzo so they cook through rather than being stirred in at the end. Nobody in the thread disputes the timings or the liquid ratio.

name: Rack of Lamb Persillade
ingredients:
3 small or 2 large racks of lamb, frenched
Good olive oil
1 1/2 teaspoons (4.2 g) kosher salt
1/2 teaspoon (1.1 g) freshly ground black pepper
2 cups (120 g) loosely packed fresh parsley leaves
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) chopped garlic cloves (3 cloves)
1 cup (45 g) fresh white bread crumbs
2 teaspoons (4.0 g) grated lemon zest (2 lemons)
4 tablespoons (57 g) (1/2 stick) unsalted butter, melted
directions:
Preheat the oven to 450 degrees F.

Place the racks in a roasting pan, fat side up. Rub the tops with olive oil and sprinkle with the salt and pepper. Roast the lamb for 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, place the parsley and garlic in the bowl of a food processor fitted with the steel blade and process until they're both finely minced. Add the bread crumbs and lemon zest and process for a second until combined.

Take the lamb out of the oven and quickly press the parsley mixture on top of the meat. Drizzle with the melted butter and return immediately to the oven and roast for another 15 minutes.

Take the lamb out of the oven and cover with aluminum foil. Allow it to rest for 15 minutes, cut in double chops, and serve.
description: Enjoyed this. Roast 25-30 minutes. Internal temp 155°.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten's take on a classic French roast: racks of lamb given a short blast in a hot oven, then finished under a green crust of parsley, garlic, fresh breadcrumbs, lemon zest and melted butter. The two-stage approach lets the meat take colour first and keeps the crumb topping from scorching, so you end up with a crisp herbal shell over pink meat. It is an entertaining-scale dish that still only asks for a food processor and a roasting pan.

Note on the source: no reader comments surfaced on page

claude_opt.changes: Your note already fixed timing/temp. Brush lamb with a thin Dijon layer before pressing crumbs -- nearly every other persillade version does, since it's what keeps the crust from sliding off when carved.

name: Raspberry Sauce
ingredients:
1/2 pt. fresh raspberries
1/2 c. (100 g) sugar
1/4 c. (59 g) water
1 c. (320 g) seedless raspberry jam
1 T. (15 g) framboise liqueur
directions: In a small saucepan bring raspberries, sugar, water to a boil. Lower heat and simmer for 4 minutes. Pour cooked raspberries, jam, and liqueur into a food processor. Blend until smooth.

claude_opt.changes: Strain the cooked raspberry mixture through a fine-mesh sieve before blending in the jam to remove seeds; standard in modern versions of this sauce for a silkier result, a couple minutes' extra work.

name: Really Good Hummus
ingredients:
2 1/2 cups (500g, drained weight) jarred chickpeas (plus their liquid, for cooking)
3/4 cup (200g) good-quality tahini, well-stirred before measuring
1 to 1 1/2 teaspoons (2.8-4.2 g) kosher or flaky sea salt
4 medium garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced
1/4 cup (60ml) freshly squeezed lemon juice
Ice cubes and water
directions:
Put the chickpeas and their liquid in a medium saucepan. Add a little water if necessary to make sure they’re completely submerged. Cook over medium heat, at a low boil until the chickpeas practically disintegrate when you smoosh one with your fingers. There should be no firmness when you press one.

Optional: Once cooked, if a lot of chickpea skins have floated to the top of the liquid when cooking, give the chickpeas a brisk stir to loosen any other skins, then skim them off and discard them. You can also remove them in the next step if you want your hummus especially smooth.

Drain the chickpeas, reserving 1 tablespoon of the liquid. Add the warm chickpeas to the bowl of a food processor along with the tablespoon of cooking liquid, the tahini, and 1 teaspoon of salt. Process the chickpeas and tahini until the mixture is a stiff, relatively smooth paste. Stop the food processor midway and scrape down the sides of the work bowl to make sure everything is getting incorporated.

Add the garlic and lemon juice, and continue to process until the mixture is very smooth. Once again, stop the processor and scrape down the sides of the bowl midway through.

Put two ice cubes in a measuring cup and fill the cup until the water reaches the 1/2-cup (120ml) mark. With the food processor running, drop the two ice cubes into the feed tube of the food processor, then add the ice water in a slow, steady stream. Continue to process for a few minutes, until the ice cubes are completely melted and the mixture is as smooth as possible. Taste, and add the remaining 1/2 teaspoon of salt if desired. Scrape into a bowl, cover, and let rest for an hour.

Storage: Store the hummus in the refrigerator if not eating it soon after making it. Let it come to room temperature before serving. Hummus will last 2-3 days in the refrigerator.
description: 6/24 Terrific. Used Soom tahini which has a fresh unburnt flavor. Used 1 cup dried chickpeas from Ranch Mirage. Soaked for almost 2 hours and cooked for 5. Still probably not enough as some peas were still a bit hard. Peeled the skins, which took ½ hour. Had 310g of peas and scaled back to tahini to 120g. The mixture was very stiff at first but the ice cubes worked like a charm. Very smooth and airy. Yield 2-3 cups
notes:
Web summary (davidlebovitz.substack.com). David Lebovitz writes about forty years of chasing a hummus he actually liked, starting from a coarse meat-grinder version and ending at something silky. His conclusion is that tahini quality and the doneness of the chickpeas matter far more than the garlic or lemon, which he treats as background notes rather than the point. He also leans on ice water beaten in during processing, which lightens the texture and takes the paste from dense to fluffy.

What readers report: Only a couple of short reader notes appear, and neither corrects the method. One reader mentions the difference in chickpeas available in the United States compared with what Lebovitz uses; another simply offers a friendly aside. There is no substantive disagreement, no reported quantity or timing fix, and no discussion of substitutions, so the comment thread adds nothing practical to the recipe as written.

Note on the source: comments present but contentless

claude_opt.changes: Your 6/24 note found it: dried chickpeas undercooked, skins took 30 min to peel. Add 1/2 tsp baking soda to the soak and cook water — it softens beans faster and loosens skins so peeling is nearly unnecessary.

name: Red Beans and Rice
ingredients:
1 1/2 pound (680 g) dried red beans (preferably New Orleans Camelia brand)
1 pound (454 g) andouille sausage, sliced 1/2-inch thick (smoked sausage can also be used)
4 tablespoons (54 g) olive oil
6 garlic cloves, minced
2 medium onions, finely diced
1 large rib celery, finely diced
1 medium green bell pepper, chopped
1 1/2 teaspoons (3.4 g) black pepper
1/8 teaspoon (0.2 g) cayenne pepper
2 teaspoons (12 g) salt
3 bay leaves
2 teaspoons (2.0 g) dried basil
3/4 teaspoon (0.9 g) rubbed sage
1 cup (60 g) chopped fresh parsley
1 bunch fresh green onions, chopped
Cooked white long-grain rice, for serving
directions:
In a large bowl, cover beans in water and soak for at least 4 hours or overnight. (Water should cover beans by at least an inch.)

In a large, heavy pot, brown sausage in 1 tablespoon of oil until slightly crisp. Add remaining oil, then the garlic and onions. Sauté over medium heat until onions become transparent and limp. Add celery and bell pepper and sauté for 5 minutes.

Pour soaked beans and water into the pot and bring to a simmer. Add black pepper, cayenne, salt and all herbs except parsley.

Cook until beans are softened, about 1 1/2 to 2 hours. Taste and adjust seasonings.

Fifteen minutes before serving, remove 1 cup of beans to a bowl and, using a fork, mash them and stir back into the pot to enhance the creamy texture of the dish. Add parsley and green onions. Simmer about 15 minutes, taste and adjust seasoning, and add up to 1 cup more water if beans seem too thick. Remove bay leaves. Serve over white long-grain rice.
description: 3/13 Excellent thought Alan, Steph at least tooks seconds and said “it’s better than white beans.” Used Domingo Rojo beans from Rancho Gordo, kielbasa, plus a ham hock for 1 hour of the cooking.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (5,350)). Kim Severson's version of the Monday-night New Orleans staple, as made by the late food writer Pableaux Johnson, who fed a rotating table of writers and musicians on it. The dish dates from when Monday was laundry day and the beans were built on the leftover pork bone from Sunday. Louisiana andouille is the sausage to look for; smoked sausage is the fallback.

What readers report: The dominant note (1,801 votes) comes from a native New Orleans family: soak the beans only about 10 minutes, boil 20, then let them sit off the heat until cooking time; mash some of the beans near the end for creaminess and finish with a little butter. That creaminess is the point most commenters insist on. The second-most-voted note (1,120) says the dish is nearly impossible to ruin and treats the recipe as a template. Practical additions with strong support: a couple of splashes of vinegar at the end for acid (325 votes), and an Instant Pot conversion that skips soaking entirely (464 votes). Local voices note white beans, limas and field peas are equally traditional. Ham hock is the common enrichment.

name: Red Lentil Soup with Lemon
ingredients:
3 tablespoons (40 g) olive oil, more for drizzling
1 large onion, chopped
2 garlic cloves, minced
1 tablespoon (16 g) tomato paste
1 teaspoon (2.1 g) ground cumin
¼ teaspoon (0.7 g) kosher salt, more to taste
¼ teaspoon (0.6 g) ground black pepper
Pinch of ground chile powder or cayenne, more to taste
1 quart (960 g) chicken or vegetable broth
2 cups (474 g) water
1 cup (192 g) red lentils
1 large carrot, peeled and diced
Juice of 1/2 lemon, more to taste
3 tablespoons (8.6 g) chopped fresh cilantro
directions:
In a large pot, heat 3 tablespoons oil over high heat until hot and shimmering. Add onion and garlic, and sauté until golden, about 4 minutes.

Stir in tomato paste, cumin, salt, black pepper and chili powder or cayenne, and sauté for 2 minutes longer.

Add broth, 2 cups water (1 cup if you want the soup to be thicker), lentils, and carrot. Bring to a simmer, then partially cover pot and turn heat to medium-low. Simmer until lentils are soft, about 30 minutes. Taste and add salt if necessary.

Using an immersion or regular blender or a food processor, purée half the soup then add it back to pot. Soup should be somewhat chunky.

Reheat soup if necessary, then stir in lemon juice and cilantro. Serve soup drizzled with good olive oil and dusted lightly with chili powder if desired.
description:
A classic. We generally use only 1 cup of water.

RM 1/24: Laura's read — may be too involved for a weeknight. Fallback that night was sausages and mashed potatoes.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (42,038)). Melissa Clark's take on mercimek corbasi, the Turkish red lentil soup - light, spicy and distinctly red rather than the usual brown, and done in under an hour. Onion and garlic are sauteed, then tomato paste, cumin and chile powder are cooked in to deepen them before broth, water, red lentils and carrot go in for a 30-minute simmer. Half the pot gets pureed so the texture lands between chunky and smooth, and lemon juice at the end lifts the cumin and chile.

What readers report: The highest-voted comment (3,440) calls this essentially daal missing its seasonings, and rebuilds it with ginger-garlic paste and fresh chopped tomatoes in place of tomato paste. Just behind it (3,422 votes), a cook uses chicken stock and a 14-ounce can of diced tomatoes instead of the water. The most actionable correction (2,196 votes) is that there is too much liquid for the lentils - either cut the water or add a diced potato or two for body; another popular ratio (1,299 votes) is 1.5 cups lentils to 5 cups chicken broth and no water, with grated carrot sauteed in with the garlic. Note the yield (1,265 votes): it makes four small bowls, so double it to serve four to six. More lemon than called for is near-universal.

Note on the source: NYT has renamed the page 'Red Lentil Soup' (URL redirects to /1016062-red-lentil-soup); same recipe

name: Rhubarb-Raspberry Pie (or Strawberry)
ingredients:
Double pie crust

1 1/3 c. (267 g) sugar
1/4 c. quick-cooking tapioca
4 c. (488 g) 1/2-inch pieces rhubarb (if using large stalks, cut lengthwise before chopping to make smaller pieces)
1 c. (123 g) fresh or frozen raspberries (or strawberries)
2 T. (30 g) lemon juice
directions:
Preheat oven to 400.

In a large bowl, stir together sugar and tapioca. Add rhubarb, berries, and lemon juice; mix gently but thoroughly. Let stand 15 minutes or up to 1 hour to soften tapioca; mix gently several times. 

Roll out 1/2 of pastry and place in 9" pie pan. Fill with rhubarb mixture. On a floured board, roll remaining pastry into 10" square. With a pastry wheel or knife, cut into 8 equal strips. Arrange strips on top of pie in a lattice pattern. Trim ends and seal crusts.

Set pie in a foil-lined 10x15 inch pan to contain drips. Bake on lowest rack until pastry is golden brown and filling is bubbly, 40-50 minutes. If rim begins to darken excessively before filling bubbles, drape with strips of foil. 

Serve warm or at room temperature.

claude_opt.changes: Cool the pie fully on a rack, about 4 hours, before cutting rather than serving warm; rhubarb releases a lot of liquid and needs that time to set or the filling runs.

name: Rib Roast Beef Recipe--from The Prime Choice--the one we use
ingredients: 5-8 pound (2.3-3.6 kg) rib roast
directions: Place your roast fat side up in a DRY roasting pan. Generously sprinkle garlic powder on the fat cap. With a long fork pierce top of roast several times, forcing garlic into the meat. Follow this with several dashes of worcestershire sauce and rub into fat. Pre-heat oven to 550 degrees. Sear roast for 10 minutes, then turn oven down to 250 degrees. Cook at this temperature until the inside temperature of the meat reaches 130-135 degrees for medium rare, a little higher for medium. Cooking time will be approximately 25 min/lb. The heavier the roast the less time per pound.
description:
12/2020 Excellent at 127 degrees internal. Could have been 1-2 degrees more.
12/2017 126 degrees; consider doing 128.

claude_opt.changes: Reverse the sequence: roast low at 250F to just under target, rest 20 min tented, then sear at 500-550F a few minutes for crust; avoids the gray, overcooked ring that searing first leaves near the edges.

name: Rice Krispie Treats
ingredients:
3 T. (43 g) butter
10 oz. (284 g) marshmallows (40 lg. or 4 c. mini)
6 c. (1.1 kg) Rice Krispies
directions: Melt butter and marshmallows over low heat. Add rice krispies. Stir until well coated. Spread out over 13x9x2 pan using wax paper or butter spatula. Let cool 15 minutes before cutting.
description: Sue Hoag always said Mom made the best rice krispie treats. Is that a compliment?
notes:
Web summary (ricekrispies.us). Kellogg's own page for the treats, presented as the three-ingredient original that has been on the box for generations. Butter and marshmallows are melted together over low heat before the cereal goes in, so every grain gets coated while the marshmallow is still fluid; the mixture is then pressed into a buttered 13x9 pan with a buttered spatula or wax paper, which is what keeps it from sticking to everything.

What readers report: No reader comments. Kellogg's own guidance: use fresh marshmallows for the best texture, serve the same day, and store airtight for up to two days at room temperature or up to six weeks frozen with wax paper between layers.

Note on the source: Matches the family text exactly -- 3 T butter, 10 oz marshmallows (40 large or the mini equivalent), 6 cups Rice Krispies, melt over low heat, press into a 13x9x2 pan with wax paper or a buttered spatula. Recorded source is 'Rice Krispie Box', and this is that box recipe on the brand's site. Only drift: the box now says 5 1/2 cups minis where the family card says 4 cups.

claude_opt.changes: Cook's note is just praise, no problem to fix. Top-rated versions (vs. this bare Kellogg's original) reserve ~1 cup marshmallows unmelted to fold in, and press gently rather than compact, for a gooier result.

name: Rice Noodles with Spicy Pork and Herbs
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) thin, round rice noodles
2 tablespoons (30 g) rice vinegar
1 tablespoon (16 g) soy sauce
1 tablespoon (15 g) black vinegar
1 tablespoon (14 g) chile oil (like Lao Gan Ma brand)
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) sugar
1 tablespoon (14 g) canola or other neutral oil
1/2 pound (227 g) ground pork
1 teaspoon (6.0 g) salt
2 garlic cloves, sliced
1 1-inch piece ginger, chopped
2 scallions, light parts chopped, green parts reserved for garnish
1 tablespoon yacai (Sichuan preserved vegetables, optional)
Handful of herbs like mint, basil and cilantro leaves, washed
1/4 cup (36 g) salted, roasted peanuts, chopped
4 breakfast radishes, sliced (optional)
directions:
Bring a large pot of water to boil, and cook noodles according to instructions. Drain noodles while running under cold water, until they are cool to the touch. Set aside. Mix dressing by whisking rice vinegar, soy sauce, black vinegar, chile oil and sugar until sugar dissolves. Set aside.

Cook the pork topping: Heat oil in saucepan over medium heat, and add ground pork and salt. Pan-fry, breaking meat into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until no pink parts and no liquid remain in the pan, about 5 minutes. Add garlic, ginger and scallion whites, and stir occasionally until the raw smell has disappeared and the meat is starting to brown in places, about 5 minutes. Add the vegetables, if using, along with a tablespoon of water, and cook for 2 or 3 minutes more, or until mixture is darkened and thick. Set aside.

When you’re ready to serve, divide cool, drained noodles into four individual bowls, and top each with a tablespoon of vinegar dressing followed by a pile of ground pork, herbs, peanuts and radishes, to taste. Serve with any remaining garnish, and additional chile oil and chile-oil solids, on the side.
description: 3/25 Great! Used 1 lb of pork, 8 oz Thai Kitchen thin rice noodles. (Other ingredient amounts by recipe.) Planters peanuts. Omitted yacai. Used 1 inch piece of ginger, chopped. Red radish instead of breakfast raddish. Sriracha instead of chile oil. Fun, different.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (1,736)). Tejal Rao writes up a cold rice-noodle bowl with Yunnan roots: noodles dressed in vinegar and chile oil under spicy ground pork, fresh herbs and peanuts, with the garnishes changing by kitchen and season. It goes together quickly but is meant to be eaten slowly, either plated or spread out so people build their own. The chef Simone Tong, whose Manhattan restaurant inspired it, adds raw breakfast radishes and lacto-fermented pickles for crunch, and the headnote invites you to improvise.

What readers report: Black vinegar is the sticking point, and the top comment (476 votes) gives a workable substitute: one part rice vinegar, one part balsamic, one to three parts water. Others identify the real thing as Chinkiang fermented black rice vinegar, available online or in Chinese groceries; a separate note (104 votes) relays Nina Simonds's suggestion of Worcestershire as a stand-in. The most useful cooking correction (191 votes) is to double the sauce, since the pork seasoned only with garlic, ginger and scallions tastes plain on its own - stir some sauce and herbs into the meat rather than leaving them all as garnish. Enthusiasm runs high (307 votes calling it a top-three recipe), and the herb quantity is meant to be generous, not a sprinkle.

name: Rigatoni with Sausage & Fennel
ingredients:
3 tablespoons (40 g) good olive oil
3 cups (261 g) chopped fennel (1 large bulb)
1 1/2 cups (240 g) chopped yellow onion
1 1/4 pounds (567 g) sweet Italian sausages, casings removed
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) minced garlic (2 cloves)
1/2 teaspoon (1.0 g) whole fennel seeds, crushed with a mortar and pestle
1/2 teaspoon (0.9 g) crushed red pepper flakes
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 cup (237 g) dry white wine
1 cup (238 g) heavy cream
2/3 cup (161 g) half-and-half
2 tablespoons (33 g) tomato paste
1 pound (454 g) rigatoni
1/2 cup (30 g) chopped fresh parsley leaves
1 cup (90 g) freshly grated Italian Parmesan cheese, divided
directions:
Heat the olive oil in a large heavy pot or Dutch oven, such as Le Creuset, over medium heat. Add the fennel and onion and saute for 7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until tender. Add the sausage and cook for 7 to 8 minutes, crumbling it with a fork, until nicely browned. Add the garlic, crushed fennel seeds, red pepper flakes, 2 teaspoons salt, and 1 teaspoon black pepper and cook for one minute. Pour in the wine, bring to a boil, and add the heavy cream, half-and-half, and tomato paste. Bring back to a boil, lower the heat, and simmer for 20 minutes, until the sauce has thickened.

Meanwhile, bring a large pot of water to a boil, add 2 tablespoons salt, and cook the rigatoni according to the directions on the package. Drain and add to the sauce, stirring to coat the pasta. Cook over low heat for 5 minutes to allow the pasta to absorb the sauce. Off the heat, stir in the parsley and 1/2 cup of the Parmesan. Serve hot in shallow bowls with the remaining 1/2 cup Parmesan on the side.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten pairs sweet Italian sausage with a large bulb of fennel plus crushed fennel seed, doubling down on the anise note that suits pork. The sauce is deglazed with white wine and enriched with heavy cream, half-and-half and tomato paste, then the drained rigatoni finishes cooking in it over low heat so the pasta drinks up the sauce instead of sitting in it. Parmesan and parsley go in at the end, with more cheese at the table.

What readers report: Reader feedback centres on swaps rather than corrections. Several cooks report good results with plant-based sausage and non-dairy cream substitutes, and chicken broth stands in acceptably for the white wine when alcohol is unwanted. Others bulk the dish out with spinach, mushrooms or tomatoes without upsetting the sauce. The general verdict is that it scales and travels well, showing up at potlucks and dinner parties as often as at family weeknight meals. No one flags a timing or quantity problem in the written method.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. No cooks note flags a problem, and reader comments are only about substitutions (plant sausage, broth for wine) that don't touch the base technique.

name: Rigatoni with White Bolognese
ingredients:
Extra virgin olive oil
½ sweet onion, peeled and finely chopped
2 medium carrots, peeled and finely chopped
1 stalk celery, finely chopped
Sea salt
Freshly ground black pepper
1 pound (454 g) mild Italian pork sausage meat, removed from casings
1 pound (454 g) ground beef (not lean)
1 ½ cups (356 g) dry Italian white wine
1 cube beef bouillon dissolved in 2 cups (474 g) simmering water
1 ½ ounces dried porcini mushrooms rehydrated in 3 cups (711 g) lukewarm water
⅓ cup (79 g) heavy cream
1 pound (454 g) rigatoni
¾ cup (68 g) freshly grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese
directions:
Add enough oil to a large, deep sauté pan to coat the base and place over medium-high heat. When the oil shimmers, add the onion, carrots and celery and sauté until glassy and just tender, about 5 minutes. Season lightly with salt and pepper. Add the sausage and beef to the pan, breaking it into walnut-size pieces, and brown well.

Pour in the wine and keep at a rapid simmer until the pan is almost dry. Then pour in 1 1/2 cups beef bouillon and lower the heat to medium. Simmer gently, uncovered, until the bouillon is nearly gone, stirring now and then. Meanwhile, chop the rehydrated porcini into small pieces, reserving the liquid.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add mushroom liquid to the sauce to cover the meat halfway (about 1 cup) along with the porcini and continue simmering until the sauce is loose but not soupy, about 10 minutes. Taste and adjust salt and pepper; it should be highly seasoned. When the consistency is right, fold the cream in. Remove from the heat and cover.

When the pasta water is at a full boil, add the rigatoni and cook until still firm, but not hard, in the center. When the pasta is almost done, scoop out 1 cup of pasta water and reserve. Drain the pasta and then return it to the pot. Pour the pasta sauce on top and fold in with a wooden spoon. The pasta should not be dry. Add a little pasta water or mushroom liquid to loosen it. (It will continue to soak up sauce on the way to the table.) Serve in one large bowl or in individual bowls, passing the cheese at the table.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (5,781)). Amanda Hesser's version of a meat sauce built without tomato - a variation she notes is seldom encountered in the United States. The headnote is a single line and offers no technique guidance.

What readers report: The best practical tip (503 votes) is to use your widest-bottomed pot, which cuts the long reduction of wine, broth and mushroom liquid substantially. Another well-voted note (415) says to stagger the soffritto rather than dumping it in together, though commenters argue about the order - a reply (198 votes) points out carrots need far longer than onion, so carrot first makes more sense. Nutmeg is widely considered non-negotiable for a real bolognese (352 votes). The top comment (585 votes) reports a vegetarian version, swapping a pound of sliced mushrooms for the beef and skipping the cream entirely, with good results. One recurring gripe questions cooking in extra-virgin olive oil given its low smoke point.

claude_opt.changes: Add a pinch of grated nutmeg with the cream — missing from the ingredient list but called non-negotiable by readers (352 votes). Use your widest pot for the wine/broth reduction; it cuts that simmer time noticeably.

name: Rishia Zimmern’s Chicken with Shallots
ingredients:
8 bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs
2 tablespoons (15 g) all-purpose flour
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) kosher salt
1 tablespoon (6.9 g) black pepper
2 tablespoons (28 g) unsalted butter
12 to 15 whole medium shallots, peeled
2 cups (474 g) white wine
2 tablespoons (31 g) Dijon mustard
2 tarragon sprigs
2 cups (298 g) cherry tomatoes, halved
directions:
Pat the chicken thighs very dry with paper towels. Sprinkle the flour, salt and pepper over the chicken.

Melt the butter in a large, heavy-bottomed pot or skillet set over medium-high heat. When the butter foams, cook the chicken, in batches if necessary, until well browned and crisp on all sides. Set aside.

Add the whole shallots to the pot and sauté them in the butter and chicken fat until they begin to soften and caramelize, about 10 to 12 minutes. Add the wine to deglaze the pot, stir with a large spoon, then add the mustard and tarragon, then the chicken thighs. Cover the pot, turn the heat to low and simmer for 30 minutes.

Remove the lid, and allow the sauce to reduce and thicken, 15 to 20 minutes.

Add the cherry tomatoes to the pot, stir lightly to combine and serve immediately.
description: 8/22 Very good. Made half. Nice tarragon flavor. Used large short all-clad pan. Still got a lot of spatter. Use large tall next time?
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (13,839)). A one-pot midweek braise that reached The Times in 2014 through Andrew Zimmern's Twitter account, where he posted his then wife Rishia's compressed adaptation of a Martha Stewart recipe: brown thighs and shallots, add wine, tarragon and Dijon, simmer, reduce, finish with cherry tomatoes. Sam Sifton says the kitchen has been tinkering with it since. Serve bread alongside for the sauce.

What readers report: The single most-endorsed change (1,384 votes) is to finish the dish uncovered in the oven, because the covered simmer leaves the chicken skin soft; a detailed no-splatter variant (603 votes) sautes the shallots in butter in an oven-proof pan, nestles in bone-in thighs and bakes at 400F. A long-standing ambiguity (1,268 votes) is what counts as a shallot: one lobe or both halves of a double shallot, which changes the quantity significantly. Several cooks find the full wine measure too sour and cut it, replacing part with broth (909 votes). Substitutions reported as successful: thyme and bay for tarragon, a splash of cognac with the wine, skinless thighs. Leftovers are said to improve.

name: Riso Al Forno with Crab and Shrimp
ingredients:
2 tablespoons (28 g) salted butter, plus more for greasing the pan
2 tablespoons (27 g) extra-virgin olive oil
1 large onion, finely diced
Salt and black pepper
1 1/2 cups (300 g) carnaroli or arborio rice
Pinch of crumbled saffron threads
2 tablespoons (33 g) tomato paste
1/4 cup (59 g) dry white wine
4 cups (960 g) unsalted fish, chicken or vegetable stock, plus more as needed
1 pound (454 g) crab meat (fresh or canned, drained if needed)
1 pound medium unpeeled shrimp, drizzled with 1 tablespoon (18 g) olive oil and seasoned with salt and pepper
1/4 cup (27 g) bread crumbs, preferably coarse homemade
1 cup (230 g) crème fraîche
1 teaspoon (5.2 g) Dijon mustard
1 tablespoon (3.0 g) finely sliced chives, plus more for serving
1 small lemon, zested, plus more zest for serving
directions:
Heat oven at 375 degrees and butter a 9-by-13-inch baking dish.

Put butter and olive oil in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat. Add onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, about 5 minutes. Season with salt and pepper.

Add rice and continue to cook, stirring, until well coated. Add saffron and tomato paste, and stir well, then add wine and cook until evaporated, about 2 minutes.

Add 2 cups stock and adjust heat to a brisk simmer. Cook for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring every minute or so. When broth is absorbed, add 1 cup more and continue cooking for another 5 minutes. Stir in the last cup of stock, and cook for another 5 minutes, until the rice is done but the grains are still firm. Add more stock if the rice looks dry. Taste rice mixture and adjust seasoning. Turn off heat.

Fold crab meat into rice mixture, and transfer contents of pot to the baking dish. Lay shrimp on top and sprinkle with bread crumbs. Bake for about 30 minutes, until golden. Meanwhile, combine crème fraîche, mustard, chives and lemon zest in a small bowl. Taste and adjust seasoning, as necessary.

To serve, spoon rice and shrimp into warm soup plates. Top each serving with a tablespoon of the crème fraîche mixture. If desired, sprinkle more chives and lemon zest over everything.
description: 2/23 Quite fancy and good. But perhaps the flavors didn't really shine enough to justify the cost. Made half recipe for 2, and we had plenty of leftovers. Unpeeled shrimp made for some work at the dinner table, but they were cooked perfectly. Perhaps add some more lemon juice to the dish before serving or at least to drizzle. The creme freche sauce was good. Could the rice and crab part use some cheese?
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (128)). A rice casserole pitched as a relaxed dinner-party main: it takes any shellfish you like, from shrimp to lobster, and forgives timing because it is not served straight from the pot. The rice can be cooked and the shellfish folded in up to two hours ahead, then topped with shrimp and crumbs and baked before serving.

What readers report: Nearly the whole comment set is one argument: the recipe leaves the shrimp in their shells, and guests do not want to peel shrimp at the table. The three highest-voted notes (69, 50, 40) all object, adding that breadcrumbs scattered over unpeeled shrimp are wasted since the coating comes off with the shell. The constructive version (53 votes) peels the shrimp and simmers the shells into a quick stock to cook the rice in, which puts the shell flavor into the dish instead of on the plate. A cook who peeled ahead and used slightly over a pound reports the shrimp did not dry out (19 votes), so the shells are not needed as protection. A minority defends eating them shell-on with a discard bowl.

name: RO-TEL Cheese Dip and Spread
ingredients:
1/2 can Ro-Tel Tomatoes and Green Chilies
1/2 lb. (227 g) pasteurized cheese
directions: To 1/2 can Ro-Tel Tomatoes and Green Chilies, add 1/2 lb. Pasteurized Cheese which has been melted in double boiler. Mix together. Serve as a dip for potato or corn chips or use as a spread on toast, crackers, sandwiches, hamburger buns. May be used as a filling for hard-boiled eggs or celery hearts. May be poured over any corn chips or broken toasted tortillas and served while warm. Try it as a flavoring ingredient in your own recipes.
notes:
Web summary (ro-tel.com). The brand's page for the two-ingredient queso that made Ro-Tel a pantry staple: undrained Ro-Tel tomatoes and green chiles melted into cubed Velveeta over medium heat, about five minutes, or microwaved for the same time with a stir partway. Cubing the cheese and leaving the tomato liquid in is what lets it come together smooth instead of breaking or seizing. It is pitched as party and Tex-Mex food, served warm with chips, crackers or vegetables.

Note on the source: Same dip, but the family text is the OLDER can-label version credited to Elsa Canning Co. (Ro-Tel's original Elsa, Texas canner), written at half scale -- 1/2 can Ro-Tel to 1/2 lb pasteurized cheese melted in a double boiler -- and it carries a long list of uses the brand no longer prints (spread on toast or hamburger buns, filling for hard-boiled eggs or celery, poured over corn chips). The linked page is the modern brand descendant at exactly double the quantities (10 oz can to 16 oz Velveeta). Marked medium because the specific Elsa Canning Co. label text is not online. Runner-up with the vintage history written up: https://www.deepsouthdish.com/2008/12/original-ro-tel-famous-queso-dip.html

name: Roast Chicken Herbed Faux-Tisserie Chicken and Potatoes
ingredients:
2 teaspoons (4.0 g) fennel seeds
1 teaspoon (1.8 g) crushed red pepper flakes
2 tablespoons (6.0 g) finely chopped fresh marjoram; plus 4 sprigs, divided
2 tablespoons (6.9 g) finely chopped fresh thyme; plus 4 sprigs, divided
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) kosher salt, plus more
½ teaspoon (1.1 g) freshly ground black pepper, plus more
6 tablespoons (81 g) olive oil, divided
1 3½–4 pound (1.6-1.8 kg) chicken
1 lemon, quartered
1 head of garlic, halved crosswise
2 pounds (907 g) Yukon Gold potatoes, scrubbed, halved, or quartered if large
directions:
Preheat oven to 300°. Coarsely grind fennel seeds and red pepper flakes in a spice mill or with a mortar and pestle. Combine spice mixture, chopped marjoram, chopped thyme, 1 Tbsp. salt, ½ tsp. pepper, and 3 Tbsp. oil in a small bowl. Rub chicken inside and out with spice mixture. Stuff chicken with lemon, garlic, 2 marjoram sprigs, and 2 thyme sprigs. Tie legs together with kitchen twine.

Toss potatoes with remaining 3 Tbsp. oil on a rimmed baking sheet; season with salt and pepper. Push potatoes to edges of baking sheet and scatter remaining 2 marjoram and 2 thyme sprigs in center; place chicken on herbs. Roast, turning potatoes and basting chicken every hour, until skin is browned, meat is extremely tender, and potatoes are golden brown and very soft, about 3 hours. Let chicken rest at least 10 minutes before carving.
description:
4/24 Followed the slow cooking technique with different herbs—Steph’s Provence picnic recipe. Baked 3 hours for 4½ pound chicken. Temped frequently and went to 165+ in white meat. Moist and tender, delicious. 

12/23 First test. Very promising. Delicious flavor. Followed recipe as written with a sheet pan and fresh marjoram. 4½ pound chicken. 3 hours is too long for the white meat, but dark meat was great. Temp it next time. Maybe put the spices under the skin and turn upside down. Potatoes great even with 3 hours cooking. We added fennel and it dessicated to almost nonexistence. Could make gravy with drippings.
notes: Web summary (bonappetit.com, 4.1 (342)). Carla Lalli Music's 2014 recipe rubs a whole chicken with a fennel-seed and chile-flake spice paste, stuffs it with lemon, garlic and herbs, and slow-roasts it at 300°F on a bed of Yukon Golds for about 3 hours to produce shreddable, tender meat rather than the texture of a faster high-heat roast. What readers report (25 notes): the most substantive fix is on timing — several cooks, including one who hit 180°F (15 degrees past done) after only 1.5 hours and another whose 5-lb. bird was already dry at 3 hours in a calibrated oven, warn the stated time is a ceiling, not a guarantee, and the bird should be temped well before the 3-hour mark. Multiple commenters independently confirm the oven must not be run on convection, which several blame for dry results. One clears up a point of confusion in the recipe: the 'basting liquid' isn't anything added — it's the chicken's own rendered fat, so a lid works as well as basting. A typo is flagged ('pepper flakes,' not 'paper flakes'). Reader-tested substitutions that hold up: dried herbs (including herbes de Provence) at half the fresh quantity work well; rubbing paste under the breast skin as well as over it is called an improvement; one suggests trussing with a needle rather than string for better results.

name: Roast Chicken With Mustard Vinaigrette
ingredients:
1 6- to 7-pound (2.7-3.2 kg) roasting chicken
1 large shallot, quartered
2 fresh rosemary sprigs
2 fresh sage sprigs
1 cup (249 g) Mustard Vinaigrette (see recipe)
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) chopped fresh rosemary
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) chopped fresh sage
Fresh rosemary and sage sprigs
directions:
Preheat oven to 450°F. Pat chicken dry.
Season cavity with salt and pepper. Place shallot, 2 rosemary sprigs and 2 sage sprigs in cavity. Slide hand between chicken skin and meat over breast to form pockets. Spread 2 tablespoons vinaigrette under skin over breast meat.
Tie legs together to hold shape; tuck wings under body. Place chicken in roasting pan. Brush 2 tablespoons vinaigrette over chicken. Sprinkle with chopped rosemary and sage. Season with salt and pepper.
Roast chicken 20 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 375°F. Continue roasting until juices run clear when chicken is pierced in thickest part of thigh, basting occasionally with pan juices, about 1 hour 20 minutes. Remove from oven and let cool 1 hour. (Can be
made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.)
Place chicken and herb sprigs on platter. Serve with remaining vinaigrette. 

MUSTARD VINAIGRETTE
This multipurpose dressing is used for the chicken and the potato salad.
MAKES ABOUT 1½ CUPS
¼ cup Dijon mustard
3 tablespoons white wine vinegar
¾ cup olive oil
3 tablespoons chopped shallots
2 tablespoons chopped fresh rosemary
2 teaspoons chopped fresh sage

Mix mustard and vinegar in bowl. Gradually whisk in oil. Mix in shallots and herbs. Season with salt and pepper. (Can be made 1 day ahead. Cover; chill. Bring to room temperature; mix before using.)
notes:
Web summary (bigoven.com). A transcription of the Bon Appetit recipe, which the page itself credits to the May 1994 issue. A whole roasting chicken is stuffed with shallot and whole rosemary and sage sprigs, and mustard vinaigrette is worked under the breast skin as well as brushed over the outside. Starting at 450F for twenty minutes sets the skin, then dropping to 375F for the remaining hour and twenty lets the bird cook through without the herb-and-mustard coating burning; the reserved vinaigrette is served alongside.

Note on the source: Page states the source as Bon Appetit, May 1994, which matches the collection's recorded source exactly, and the method and temperatures match the family text step for step (450F/20 min, 375F/1 hr 20, vinaigrette under the skin, cool 1 hour, can be made a day ahead). BigOven is an aggregator rather than the publisher, and it omits the accompanying Mustard Vinaigrette sub-recipe that the family text preserves. Runner-up: https://www.marga.org/foodblog/2011/01/roast-chicken-with-mustard-vinaigrette/

Data fix (Sept 2026): the mustard vinaigrette read '3 cup chopped shallots' against a stated yield of about 1 1/2 cups, which is impossible - the other ingredients already come to roughly 1 1/8 cups. Read as 3 tablespoons.

ahead: made 1 day ahead.
makeahead: Can be made 1 day ahead.

claude_opt.changes: Vinaigrette's '3 cup chopped shallots' is implausible for a dressing yielding 1.5 cups total — likely a transcription error for 3 tablespoons; verify before using. Also swap 'juices run clear' for a thermometer, 165°F breast.

Asparagus bunch

salt and pepper

name: Roasted Brussels Sprouts
ingredients:
1 1/2 pounds (680 g) Brussels sprouts
3 tablespoons (40 g) good olive oil
3/4 teaspoon (2.1 g) kosher salt
1/2 teaspoon (1.1 g) freshly ground black pepper
directions:
Preheat oven to 400 degrees F.

Cut off the brown ends of the Brussels sprouts and pull off any yellow outer leaves. Mix them in a bowl with the olive oil, salt and pepper. Pour them on a sheet pan and roast for 35 to 40 minutes, until crisp on the outside and tender on the inside. Shake the pan from time to time to brown the sprouts evenly. Sprinkle with more kosher salt ( I like these salty like French fries), and serve immediately.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten's version is deliberately bare: trimmed sprouts, olive oil, kosher salt and pepper, roasted hot. The point of the high heat plus periodic shaking of the pan is even browning, so the outer leaves crisp while the cores stay tender rather than steaming into mush. She describes the result as closer to a french fry than to a boiled vegetable.

What readers report: The dominant reader habit is enrichment. Many swap bacon fat for the olive oil or scatter chopped bacon over the pan; others add minced garlic, a finishing splash of balsamic, or grated parmesan for the last few minutes. Small onions roasted alongside come up repeatedly. A few cooks substitute sea salt for the kosher salt without trouble. The one technique note people stress is to actually shake the pan partway through, since that is what delivers the crisp, fry-like texture the recipe is known for. It shows up most often as a Thanksgiving side but readers treat it as a weeknight staple too.

name: Roasted Brussels Sprouts with Garlic
ingredients:
1 pint brussels sprouts (the recipe says "about a pound", so ~450 g)
4 to 6 tablespoons (54-81 g) extra virgin olive oil, to coat bottom of pan
5 cloves garlic, peeled
Salt and pepper to taste
1 tablespoon (16 g) balsamic vinegar
directions:
Heat oven to 400 degrees. Trim bottom of brussels sprouts, and slice each in half top to bottom. Heat oil in cast-iron pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers; put sprouts cut side down in one layer in pan. Put in garlic, and sprinkle with salt and pepper.

Cook, undisturbed, until sprouts begin to brown on bottom, and transfer to oven. Roast, shaking pan every 5 minutes, until sprouts are quite brown and tender, about 10 to 20 minutes.

Taste, and add more salt and pepper if necessary. Stir in balsamic vinegar, and serve hot or warm.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (14,356)). Mark Bittman's roasted brussels sprouts, which NYT calls its most popular version and positions as a default Thanksgiving side. The claim is that this plain treatment caramelizes the sprouts sweet enough to convert skeptics. It comes from a Minimalist column about cast iron.

What readers report: Burning is the recurring problem: a much-voted account (539) followed the directions and got sprouts burnt to a crisp at 20 minutes, and NYT itself replied in a highly rated note (1,143 votes) that the recipe was revised downward to 10-20 minutes at 400F with a few shakes of the pan. Commenters also mock the instruction to cook 'undisturbed' until the bottoms brown (930 votes) as unverifiable without looking. The most-voted comment (2,763) is a make-ahead question for Thanksgiving, echoed by others (429) - a strong signal people want a reheat plan the recipe does not give. A popular alternative (1,707 votes) is Ina Garten's method: halve, toss in about 1.5 tablespoons of oil, roast at 450F, using far less oil than here. Dried cranberries and walnuts stirred in at the end are a favorite addition.

Data fix (Sept 2026): the line read '1 pint (176 g) brussels sprouts (about a pound)'. A pint of sprouts is roughly 340 g and a pound is 454 g, so our 176 g figure was wrong and the source contradicts itself. Gram figure removed; weigh to about 450 g if following 'about a pound'.

name: Roasted Cauliflower with Garlic
ingredients:
6 lbs. (2.7 kg) cauliflower (3 heads), cut into 2" wide florets
1/2 c. (108 g) olive oil
4 garlic cloves, minced
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt (or more, usually more)

Preheat oven to 425.
Toss cauliflower with oil, garlic, salt and pepper in large bowl. Spread in shallow pan and roast 25-30 minutes, stirring occasionally until golden.

name: Roasted Cauliflower with Pancetta, Olives and Crisp Parmesan
ingredients:
1 large head cauliflower (about 1 3/4 pounds), trimmed and cut into bite-size florets (about 8 cups)
½ cup (108 g) extra-virgin olive oil
½ teaspoon (1.4 g) kosher salt, plus more as needed
⅓ cup (45 g) olives, crushed, pitted and chopped
1 fat garlic clove, finely grated or minced
1 ½ tablespoons (23 g) fresh lemon juice, plus more to taste
⅛ teaspoon (0.2 g) red-pepper flakes, plus more as needed
4 ounces (113 g) pancetta or bacon, cut into 1/8-inch cubes
¾ teaspoon (1.6 g) cumin or caraway seeds
½ cup (45 g) shredded (not ground) Parmesan
¼ cup (15 g) chopped fresh parsley or mint leaves and tender stems, for serving
directions:
Heat oven to 425 degrees. Place cauliflower on a rimmed baking sheet and toss with 1/4 cup olive oil and 1/2 teaspoon salt until well coated. Roast for 15 minutes.

In a small bowl, whisk together olives, garlic, lemon juice, 1/8 teaspoon red-pepper flakes and a large pinch of salt. Drizzle in the remaining 1/4 cup olive oil, whisking well.

After the cauliflower has roasted for 15 minutes, add pancetta and cumin seeds to pan and gently mix to combine. Sprinkle Parmesan on top and roast for another 15 to 20 minutes, until cauliflower is tender, the pancetta rendered, and cheese is golden brown and crunchy.

Spoon olive dressing all over roasted cauliflower while still hot and toss to combine. Taste, and add more salt, red-pepper flakes or lemon juice, if needed. Scatter parsley over the top before serving.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (5,523)). Melissa Clark's roasted cauliflower loaded with olives, pancetta and Parmesan that crisps and browns at the edges, offered either as a vegetarian-leaning main or a side to meat, fish or pasta. The recipe assumes finely diced packaged pancetta that dissolves into the sauce; dicing it yourself into half-inch cubes and adding it with the cauliflower gives a chunkier result, and it can be left out entirely to make the dish vegetarian.

What readers report: The substantive criticism (208 votes) is that the finished dish is too oily, and points at the quarter cup of olive oil in the dressing as the culprit - cut it back. Bacon substitutes for pancetta but should be pre-rendered and added to the partly roasted cauliflower rather than raw (120 votes), otherwise it steams. On olives, a helpful note (152 votes) recommends mild, meaty Castelvetrano over saltier varieties. A well-liked variation (191 votes) adds a can of rinsed chickpeas before roasting - they crisp up - and swaps Aleppo pepper and lime for the flakes and lemon. The top two comments are unanswered questions about a non-meat substitute (anchovies suggested) and a milder seasoning than red pepper flakes, plus confusion over what 'grated' Parmesan means.

Note on the source: top-voted comments are questions rather than tested advice

claude_opt.changes: The 208-vote consensus says the dish is too oily; cut the dressing oil from 1/4 cup to 2-3 tablespoons. Use mild Castelvetrano olives rather than saltier ones, per the well-liked reader tip.

name: Roasted Italian Meatballs--Ina
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) ground sirloin
1/2 pound (227 g) ground pork
1/2 pound (227 g) ground veal
1 3/4 cups (189 g) dry seasoned bread crumbs
1/2 cup (45 g) freshly ground Italian Pecorino cheese (2 ounces)
1/2 cup (45 g) freshly ground Italian Parmesan cheese (2 ounces), plus extra for serving
2 garlic cloves, minced
2 tablespoons (7.5 g) chopped fresh parsley leaves
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 extra-large eggs, lightly beaten
3/4 cup (178 g) dry red wine, such as Chianti
1/4 cup (54 g) good olive oil
2 (32-ounce) jars good marinara sauce, such as Rao's
Creamy Parmesan Polenta (recipe follows) or cooked spaghetti, for serving
directions:
Preheat the oven to 400 degrees F. Line two sheet pans with parchment paper.

Place the sirloin, pork, and veal in a large mixing bowl and lightly break up the meats with a fork and your fingertips. Add the bread crumbs, Pecorino, Parmesan, garlic, parsley, 2 teaspoons salt, and 1/2 teaspoon black pepper. Add the eggs, wine, and 3/4 cup water and combine lightly but thoroughly.

Measure out 2-ounce portions of the mixture (I use a rounded 1 3/4-inch ice cream scoop) and roll each lightly into a ball. Place one inch apart on the prepared sheet pans. Brush the meatballs with the olive oil.

Bake the meatballs for 25 to 30 minutes, until lightly browned. Pour the marinara into a large pot and bring to a simmer. Carefully add the meatballs and simmer for 10 minutes, until heated through.
description: 11/21 Made with chuck and short ribs ground beef only. Made 1/2 recipe and formed 13 meatballs--so a bit bigger than Ina's. Cooked for 30 minutes. Next time try 25. They got fairly dark on the outside and reached about 190 degrees internal.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten builds these on the classic three-meat mix of sirloin, pork and veal, bound with seasoned breadcrumbs, Pecorino, Parmesan and egg and loosened with red wine. Rather than frying them in batches on the stove, she roasts them, which browns all sides at once, keeps the kitchen clean, and lets you make a big tray at a time for entertaining. They then simmer in jarred marinara and go out over polenta or spaghetti.

Note on the source: no reader comments surfaced on page

claude_opt.changes: Your 11/21 note already caught the overcook (190°F, dark exterior); target 160-165°F instead of visual doneness. Convection ovens run hot — drop to 375°F if using that setting.

name: Roasted Potatoes with Sage and Garlic
ingredients:
1 ½ pounds (680 g) small creamer potatoes, halved
⅓ cup (47 g) flour
1 ½ tablespoons (20 g) vegetable oil
4 cloves garlic, minced
¼ cup (14 g) chopped sage leaves
1 tablespoon (14 g) unsalted butter
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper to taste
directions:
Preheat oven to 450 degrees and place a large, heavy skillet or roasting pan in the oven to heat up. Place the potatoes in a large saucepan and cover with cold salted water. Place over high heat and bring to a boil. Lower the heat and simmer 5 minutes.

Drain the potatoes well and place them on paper towels. Place the flour on a plate and when the potatoes are dry, roll them in the flour to coat, shaking off any excess. Remove the hot skillet from the oven and add the oil and potatoes. Roast, shaking the pan occasionally until the potatoes are golden brown all over, about 30 minutes. Remove from the oven and add the garlic, sage and butter. Return the pan to the oven for one minute. Season generously with salt and pepper and serve.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (1,191)). The headnote is mostly a short history of sage, whose Latin name salvia means safe or whole, and which served as a medieval cure-all for everything from digestion to headaches. Its argument is that sage suits earthy peasant cooking rather than refined dishes, which is why it works with potatoes and holds up against garlic. Suggested alongside roasted or grilled meat.

What readers report: The most-voted note (327) says the recipe is more work than it needs to be - the flour dredge does not stick well and adds little. A cook of 30 years' habit (55 votes) simply drains, shakes, and dumps onto an oiled sheet pan. The parboiling can be done hours ahead (97 votes), which makes it practical for a dinner. Sweet potatoes substitute well. Comment volume is low and the enthusiasm is mostly for the sage-garlic pairing.

name: Rosemary Focaccia Sheet
ingredients:
2 ¾ cups/ 13.6 ounces/ 390 grams unbleached all purpose flour (use only Gold Medal, King Arthur, or Pillsbury)
3/8 teaspoon/ 1.2 grams instant yeast
2 liquid cups minus 2 tablespoons/ 15.5 ounces/442 grams water, at room temperature (70°F to 90°F)
¾ teaspoon/ 3 grams sugar
¾ teaspoon/ 5.2 grams salt
2 tablespoons plus 2 teaspoons, divided/ 5.2 grams extra virgin olive oil
2 teaspoons (2.4 g) fresh rosemary needles or dried rosemary (1/2 teaspoon for dried)
¼ teaspoon (1.4 g) fleur de sel or sea salt
A heavy-duty stand mixer with paddle attachment
A half sheet pan (12 inches by 17 inches)
A baking stone OR baking sheet
1 large head of garlic (about 2 ½ inches wide)
About 1 cup (216 g) extra virgin olive oil
directions:
Oven Temperature: 475 degees F

Mix the dough. In the mixer bowl, with the paddle attachment on low speed (#2 if using a KitchenAid), combine the flour and the yeast. With the mixer running, gradually add the water, mixing just until the dough comes together, about 3 minutes. It will be very soupy. Increase the speed to medium (#4 KitchenAid) and beat until the dough is transformed into a smooth, shiny ball, about 20 minutes.

Add the sugar and salt and beat until they are well incorporated, about 3 minutes.

Let the dough rise. Using an oiled spatula or dough scraper, scrape the dough into a 1 ½ -quart dough-rising container or bowl, lightly greased with cooking spray or oil. The dough will look like melted mozzarella. Lightly spray or oil the top of the dough. Cover the container with a lid or plastic wrap. With a piece of tape, mark the side of the container at approximately where double the height of the dough would be. Allow the dough to rise (ideally at 75 degrees F to 80 degrees F) for about 4 hours or until it has at least doubled.

Shape the dough and let it rise. Coat the sheet pan with a heaping tablespoon of the olive oil. Pour the dough onto it—it will be thin enough to pour but very stretchy. Coat your hands with a little of the remaining olive oil and spread the dough as thin as possible without tearing it. Let it relax for 10 minutes, then spread it to almost fill the entire sheet, trying to maintain the bubbles in the dough. (If the dough is still very elastic and resists stretching, allow it to rest for another 10 minutes.)

Cover the pan with a large plastic box or greased plastic wrap and allow to rise until double its original volume, about 1 ½ to 2 hours.

Preheat the oven. Preheat the oven to 475 degrees F 1 hour before baking. Have an oven shelf at the lowest level and place a baking stone or baking sheet on it before preheating.

Sprinkle on the toppings and bake the focaccia. Uncover the dough and drizzle the remaining olive oil evenly over it. With oiled or wet fingertips, deeply dimple the dough. Sprinkle evenly with the rosemary and salt. Place the pan directly on the hot stone or hot baking sheet and bake for 12 to 13 minutes or until the top is golden. Remove from the oven and drizzle on a little extra virgin olive oil, if desired. Serve immediately.

* Peel the garlic cloves: you should have about 2/3 cup. Place them in a small saucepan and cover them with the olive oil, adding more if the oil does not cover the garlic completely.

* Cover the pan and leave it partially uncovered if the oil starts to bubble. Bring the oil just to a boil over low heat. Turn down the heat as low as possible (use a heat diffuser if necessary) and poach the garlic at a bare simmer (if the oil starts to bubble too much, partially uncover the pan) for about 20 to 30 minutes, until a cake tester or metal skewer inserted in it goes in fairly easily but not so soft that it turns to mush. Smaller cloves may take only 15 minutes, so remove them as they are softened. (You can also poach garlic by placing the partially covered [ovenproof] pan in a preheated 250°F oven for the same amount of time.)

* Lift the garlic from the oil with a slotted spoon, and let the oil cool. Use the garlic-infused oil in place of the olive oil to prepare the focaccia, if desired, and refrigerate the remainder for other uses.

* Slice any large garlic cloves lengthwise in half or in thirds. After pouring the dough onto the sheet pan, make about 32 evenly spaced depressions in the dough with your fingertip (8 rows of 4 across), and gently press a garlic clove into each one. As the dough rises, it will partially enclose the garlic and protect it from becoming any darker than golden during baking.

name: Rugbrod Danish Rye Bread
ingredients:
sourdough starter
rye flour
AP wheat flour
malt syrup
kosher salt
cracked rye
sunflower seeds
pumpkin seeds
flax seed
directions:
In the evening:

Make the "starter":
50 g of sourdough starter from this morning
350 g of rye flour
350 g of water

Pre soak the seeds:
250 g cracked rye
~250 g water
perhaps a handful of flax seed

Next morning (or even better 1-3 days later if starter dough was in refrigerator):
Mix the starter and wet seeds in a large bowl
Starter was well risen and wet
Did not need more water

Added
~ 100 g rye flour
~ 1 cup AP wheat flour (probably more than I would have if I hadn’t run out of rye flour)
2 spoons of malt syrup
1-2 handfuls of sunflower and or pumpkin seeds
1 heaping tbsp diamond kosher salt

Mix and check that the consistency is like pretty dry cement mix

Rise 3 1/2 hours (winter)
Poke many holes with a skewer
Bake at 350 for 1 hour 15 minutes
Check that temp is above 205
Remove from pan and bake another 15
Cool for one hour then put in bag for six hours to moisten crust
description: From Anders on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P7eLOtMzaGI
notes:
Web summary (youtube.com). The family card records this as coming from Anders on YouTube and reproduces the URL in its cook's note, so the link is the recorded source rather than a found match. The method is a two-stage overnight build: a loose 50g starter / 350g rye flour / 350g water preferment alongside a separate soak of 250g cracked rye with about 250g water and a handful of flax, then both combined next morning with roughly 100g more rye flour, a cup of AP flour, two spoons of malt syrup, sunflower and pumpkin seeds and a heaping tablespoon of Diamond kosher salt. The dough is deliberately stiff - the note says the consistency should be like dry cement mix - which is what lets an all-rye loaf hold its shape without gluten. Baking is 350F for 1 hr 15 min in the pan to above 205F internal, then 15 minutes out of the pan, and the cooled loaf is bagged for six hours so the crust softens.

name: Rugbrod Rye Bread—Food Geek
ingredients:
For the levain
125 g sourdough starter (100 pct hydration)
150 g rye flour
350 g water

Presoak

170 g pumpkin seeds, mostly, sunflower seeds, flax seeds, etc
500 g water

For the dough
400 g levain

pre-soaked seeds
directions:
Mix levain and leave overnight. Also soak cracked rye, pumpkin seeds, sunflower seeds, flax overnight. Leave both on the counter. 

Mix dough ingredients until combined. Butter bread pan well. Pour mix into pan and cover with plastic wrap. Proof to rise 30-50 percent. Look for 6 or 7 pinholes on the top when fully risen. Perhaps 3 hours. 

Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Bake for 75 minutes. Remove from pan and bake another 15 minutes. Allow to cool. Wrap in plastic bag overnight. Slice!
notes:
Web summary (foodgeek.io). Sune Trudslev (Foodgeek) makes a true Danish rugbrod from 100 percent rye rather than the wheat-and-rye blends sold as rye bread elsewhere. It is a sourdough loaf packed with soaked cracked rye kernels and pumpkin seeds, and that heavy soaker is what produces the dense, moist, thinly sliceable crumb Danes expect for smorrebrod. Because rye has almost no gluten to develop, the loaf is simply mixed, poured into a tin and proofed rather than shaped. He gives two levain options depending on whether you keep a 100 percent hydration wheat starter or a 166 percent hydration rye starter.

name: Rugbrod Rye Bread — Food Geek (second transcription)
ingredients:
Levain (using 100% hydration wheat starter)
80 g sourdough starter 100% hydration
140 g dark rye flour
260 g water

Levain (using 166% hydration rye starter)
80 gram sourdough rye starter 166% hydration
150 gram dark rye flour
250 gram water

Seeds
330 g rye kernels, cracked if you can't get these, use whole rye kernels but soak them even longer
170 g pumpkin seeds
500 g water

Dough
400 g levain
20 g fine salt
50 g barley malt syrup
400 g dark rye flour
200 g water
soaked seeds
directions:
Make the levain and prepare the seeds – the night before

Mix all the ingredients for the levain; if you use a 100% hydration wheat sourdough, you should use those ingredients. Use the other ingredients; if you've keep a 166% rye sourdough from your last bake.

There will be enough levain to save for the next bread.

Mix the seeds with the water and leave to soak overnight.

Mix the dough

Put 400 grams of levain, 20 grams of salt, 50 grams of malt syrup, 400 grams of rye flour, and 200 grams of water in a bowl.

Whatever of the levain is left over is your new mother rye starter. Put it in the fridge until the next time you need it.

Strain whatever water hasn't been soaked by the seeds and add the seeds to the bowl.

Mix the dough by hand until everything is well incorporated.

Butter a large bread pan liberally.

Add the dough and level it using a wetted spatula.

Leave to proof covered with a wet dish towel or cling film.

Proofing the bread

A rye bread needs to rise about 30%-50% before it's put in the oven. If you put it in too early, the bread will crack on top because of too much oven spring; if you put it in too late, the bread will deflate in the oven.

The proofing can take anywhere from 2 to 6 hours depending on a lot of factors, like the ambient temperature, the strength of your starter, the temperature of the dough, and the consistency of the dough

A good rule of thumb for when it is ready to put in the oven is when there are 6-7 pinhead-sized holes on top of the dough.

Baking the bread

Heat the oven to 240°C/465°F/Gas Mark 9.

When the bread is ready to bake, put it in the oven and close the door. Bake for 10 minutes, then reduce the temperature to 180°C/355°F/Gas Mark 4.

Bake for another 40-70 minutes until the bread's internal temperature is 98°C/208°F. Leave the bread to cool on a wire rack.

Once it's cooled to room temperature, put it in zip lock bags and let it rest for a day before slicing into it.
notes:
Web summary (foodgeek.io). Sune Trudslev sets out a genuine Danish rugbrød made with one hundred percent rye rather than the wheat-and-rye blends sold as rye bread elsewhere. The loaf is a sourdough, loaded with soaked cracked rye kernels and pumpkin seeds, which is what gives it the dense, moist, sliceable crumb Danes expect. He frames it as the everyday base for smørrebrød, and gives levain options for either a wheat starter or a rye starter.

name: Saffron Risotto with Butternut Squash
ingredients:
1 butternut squash (2 pounds)
2 tablespoons (27 g) olive oil
Kosher salt
Freshly ground black pepper
6 cups (1.4 kg) chicken stock, preferably homemade
6 tablespoons (85 g) (3/4 stick) unsalted butter
2 ounces (57 g) pancetta, diced
1/2 cup (80 g) minced shallots (2 large)
1-1/2 cups (200-100 g) Arborio rice (10 ounces)
1/2 cup (118 g) dry white wine
1 teaspoon (0.7 g) saffron threads
1 cup (90 g) freshly grated Parmesan cheese
directions:
Preheat the oven to 400 degrees.

Peel the butternut squash, remove the seeds, and cut it into 3/4-inch cubes. You should have about 6 cups. Place the squash on a sheet pan and toss it with the olive oil, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, tossing once, until very tender. Set aside.

Meanwhile, heat the chicken stock in a small covered saucepan. Leave it on low heat to simmer.

In a heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven, melt the butter and sauté the pancetta and shallots on medium-low heat for 10 minutes, until the shallots are translucent but not browned. Add the rice and stir to coat the grains with butter. Add the wine and cook for 2 minutes. Add 2 full ladles of stock to the rice plus the saffron, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper. Stir, and simmer until the stock is absorbed, 5 to 10 minutes. Continue to add the stock, 2 ladles at a time, stirring every few minutes. Each time, cook until the mixture seems a little dry, then add more stock. Continue until the rice is cooked through, but still al dente, about 30 minutes total. Off the heat, add the roasted squash cubes and Parmesan cheese. Mix well and serve.

name: Sausage and Cheese Stuffed Anaheim Peppers
ingredients:
6 Anaheim peppers
1 tablespoon (14 g) olive oil
1 onion chopped
1 jalapeno pepper chopped (or use a serrrano for a spicier version)
3 cloves garlic chopped
12 ounces (340 g) Italian sausage (I used hot Italian sausage)

directions:
Stem the peppers and remove the innards with a knife. Slice them in half lengthwise.

Heat the oil in a pan to medium heat and add the onion and peppers. Cook them down about 5 minutes to soften.

Add the garlic and cook another minute, until fragrant.

Add the Italian sausage and break it apart. Add the basil, salt and pepper. Cook the sausage about 5 minutes, stirring, until it is cooked through. Let it cool slightly.

While the sausage is cooking, bring a small pot of water to boil and boil the Anaheim pepper halves for 2-3 minutes to soften. NOTE: You can skip this step if you prefer firmer stuffed peppers.

Set the peppers onto a baking sheet. Stuff each pepper with layers of your seasoned cooked sausage mixture, then top with shredded cheese. The amount will vary depending on the size of the pepper, so plan accordingly. Be sure to stuff the mixture in good and tight with your thumb.

Heat a grill to medium heat and grill for 15 minutes. Or, you can broil the stuffed peppers not too close to the heat source about 15 minutes, until the skins begin to char.

Mike Hultquist pitches these as an easy weeknight stuffed pepper using Anaheims, which sit at roughly 500 to 2,500 Scoville and so stay mild enough for people who do not want heat. The peppers are halved and softened briefly before being filled, which means the filling and the pepper finish at the same time. name: Sautéed Scallops
ingredients:
3 tablespoons (43 g) unsalted butter
1 pound (454 g) sea scallops, patted dry
Kosher salt, to taste
1 tablespoon (15 g) dry white vermouth or white wine
1 tablespoon (3.8 g) finely chopped parsley, for garnish
directions:
Place a large sauté pan or skillet over medium-high heat, and add to it 3 tablespoons of the butter. When it has melted and started to foam, place the scallops in the pan in a single layer, and season with a pinch or two of salt.

Cook scallops without moving until the bottoms are golden brown, approximately 2 to 3 minutes, then turn them over, add the wine and cook an additional 1 to 2 minutes.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (2,968)). Sam Sifton distinguishes the two scallops: sea scallops want a hard sear and a crust, finished with a splash of wine in the butter for acidity against their sweetness, while small bay scallops are better off gently poached in butter. The warning he repeats is against overcooking - he argues an undercooked scallop is essentially not a thing. It comes from a holiday feature.

What readers report: Dryness is the whole game, and the top three notes (655, 357, 286 votes) all say so. The best refinement: after patting the scallops dry, leave them uncovered in the refrigerator for up to half an hour, which draws out more moisture and gives a noticeably better sear. Equally important is pan space - scallops must not touch each other or they steam instead of browning, so work in batches. Several cooks bring them to room temperature first, and one from the Bay of Fundy prefers a little olive oil with the butter to raise the smoke point. A frequently repeated step the recipe omits: pull off the small tough side muscle before cooking. Wet-packed scallops will not sear; buy dry-packed if you can.
