name: Scalloped Potatoes with Leeks and Cream
ingredients:
1/4 c. (57 g) (1/2 stick) butter
4 c. (356 g) sliced leeks (white and pale green parts only) (about 2 lbs.)
salt and pepper

1 T. (14 g) butter
2 c. (476 g) whipping cream
3 large garlic cloves, peeled
4 lbs. (1.8 kg) russet potatoes, peeled, thinly sliced
2 c. (226 g) grated white cheddar or gruyere cheese, about 8 oz.
1/3 c. (30 g) freshly grated Parmesan cheese
directions:
Melt 1/4 c. butter in heavy large skillet over medium heat. Add leeks and stir to coat. Reduce heat to medium-low. Cover and cook until leeks are tender, stirring occasionally, about 8 minutes. Uncover and cook until almost all liquid is absorbed, about 3 minutes. Season leeks with salt and pepper.

Preheat oven to 375 degrees. Rub 9x12x2 inch baking dish with 1 T. butter. Mix cream and garlic in small bowl. Arrange half of potatoes in prepared dish. Season generously with salt and pepper. Cover with leeks. Sprinkle with half of cheddar cheese. Ladle half of cream mixture over. Repeat layering with remaining potatoes, cheddar cheese, and cream mixture. Sprinkle with Parmesan. (Can be prepared 6 hours ahead. Cover and refrigerate. Let stand 1 hour at room temperature before baking.) Bake until potatoes are tender and top is golden brown, about 1 hour 15 minutes. Let stand 15 minutes at room temperature before serving.
description:
4/23 Excellent as always. Used the mandolin thick slice. 

Slice the potatoes into salt water to prevent them from turning gray while preparing the recipe. For this, mix 4 t. table salt in one quart of lukewarm water.
notes:
Web summary (food.com, No star rating displayed). Posted by a food.com member writing as Miss V of Snellville, Georgia, this is the classic leek-and-cream potato gratin. The leeks are softened in butter first and their liquid cooked off, so they season the dish rather than water it down, and only the white and pale green parts are used to keep the flavor sweet rather than grassy. Cream infused with whole garlic cloves is ladled between the layers, and white cheddar goes inside while Parmesan finishes the top for browning.

What readers report: Reviewers agree it is rich but easy, and it comes up repeatedly as a potluck and dinner-party dish. The one practical warning is that cleaning the leeks is the fiddliest part of the job. The family's own cook's note adds two useful pieces: slice the potatoes straight into salt water (4 tsp table salt per quart of lukewarm water) to stop them graying while you work, and a mandoline on the thick setting gives the right slice.

Note on the source: MEDIUM because the phrasing of the family's card ('Can be prepared 6 hours ahead. Cover and refrigerate. Let stand 1 hour at room temperature before baking.') is unmistakable Bon Appetit house style, so the true original is almost certainly a Bon Appetit recipe - and bonappetit/epicurious are both on the hard-blocked list, so it cannot be reached or confirmed. The food.com page is a member repost of what is evidently the same recipe: quantities match the family card line for line (1/4 c butter, leeks, 1 T butter, 2 c whipping cream, 3 garlic cloves, 4 lbs potatoes, 2 c grated white cheddar, Parmesan). Only two differences - the repost says yukon gold where the family says russet, and 1/2 c Parmesan where the family says 1/3 c. Card's own source is 'Jan Symmes Gourmet Club', i.e. the family got it secondhand. A human may prefer to demote this to notfound and hunt the Bon Appetit original instead.

makeahead: Can be prepared 6 hours ahead.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing beyond what your 4/23 note already applies - slicing the potatoes into salted water and using the mandoline's thick setting. Reviewers' only caution, that cleaning leeks is fiddly, is already assumed.

name: Scotch Eggs, Baked
ingredients:
1 lb (454 g) ground lean Pork or ground Turkey
1/2 teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
1 teaspoon (1.1 g) rubbed sage
1/2 teaspoon (1.1 g) pepper
1/2 teaspoon (0.6 g) thyme
1/8 teaspoon (0.3 g) cloves
4 large eggs, hard boiled (not too large)
flour
1 large egg
2 cups (216 g) fine dry breadcrumbs
directions:
Mix the meat thoroughly with the seasonings and divide into four equal portions.
Have the four eggs hard boiled, for about 12 minutes.
Peel them, dip them in water and coat them in flour.
Wrap each egg evenly in a portion of meat, being sure they are covered completely.
Beat the remaining egg.
Dip each egg in the beaten egg then coat thoroughly in breadcrumbs.
Chill for one hour.
Bake until golden brown on a cookie sheet at 400 °F; about 30 minutes.
description: Scotch eggs are typically fried. However, these are just as good baked and a great deal less greasy.
notes:
Scotch eggs are typically fried. However, these are just as good baked and a great deal less greasy.

Web summary (food.com, Community Pick, 32 reviews (no star figure shown)). Jenny Sanders offers the baked rather than deep-fried treatment of the Scottish pub staple, on the argument that you lose nothing in flavor and shed a great deal of grease. The sausage casing is built from scratch out of lean ground pork (or turkey) seasoned with sage, thyme, pepper and a pinch of clove, which is what supplies the banger character without buying bulk sausage. Dipping the peeled hard-boiled egg in water and then flour gives the meat something to grip, so the coat does not slide off in the oven.

What readers report: Across 32 reviews the dominant note is to under- rather than over-boil the eggs: people who cooked them the full time got rubbery whites and a grey ring, so pull them earlier. Second most common is that the baked version browns pale, and reviewers fix it by spraying the coated eggs with olive oil or finishing under the broiler. Several say to double the batch because they vanish. Successful substitutions reported: bulk sausage in place of the seasoned ground pork, fresh breadcrumbs for dry, and almond meal for a gluten-free coating.

Note on the source: Exact ingredient-for-ingredient match with the family card, including the unusual 1/8 tsp cloves and the 2 cups fine dry breadcrumbs. The family card's headnote ('typically fried... just as good baked and a great deal less greasy') is a paraphrase of this author's own intro. Rejected along the way: https://www.food.com/recipe/scotch-eggs-baked-not-fried-76904 , which is a different recipe entirely (bread-and-milk panade, bacon wrap, nutmeg).

claude_opt.changes: The 32-review consensus says pull the eggs earlier than 12 minutes; the full boil leaves rubbery whites and a grey ring, so try 9-10 minutes. Mist the coated eggs with oil before baking so they brown.

name: Sean Brock's Buttermilk Biscuits
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) White Lily self-rising flour
1 1/2 cups (363 g) real buttermilk
1/4 pound (113 g) cold butter taken from the freeze
salt and black pepper
all-purpose, non-self-rising flour (for dusting)
melted butter (for the pan and finished biscuits)
directions:
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Pour the flour into a large mixing bowl. Chop the butter into small pieces. Add the butter into the flour, breaking it into smaller pieces with your fingers as you distribute it throughout the flour. Grab a different piece every time and break until the pieces of butter are about the size of peas. As you break down the butter, add a big pinch of salt and a big pinch of black pepper. Once there are no big pieces of butter, make a well in the center. Add buttermilk. Work one hand around the edge of the pan to mix the flour into the buttermilk. Depending on how thick the buttermilk is, you may have to add more buttermilk or flour. (Watch the video above to learn more.)

Once the dough stops sticking to your hands, powder a cutting board with flour and dump out the dough. It should fall out in one mass. Wash your hands and rub flour on them. Knead the dough, adding all-purpose flour to the board and folding as needed. Pat down the biscuits for cutting. Brush a pan with melted butter. Punch out the biscuits by dipping a biscuit cutter in the flour. Tap it on the board, push it into the dough, twist, pull it out, and place the biscuit on the pan. The biscuits should barely touch on the pan. Spread a tiny bit of melted butter on top of the biscuits. Cook in the oven on 425 degrees for 15 minutes. Take the biscuits out of the oven and spread a small amount of butter on top.
description: Thanksgiving 2015 from Robert.
notes:
Web summary (outsideonline.com). Sean Brock, of McCrady's and Husk, passes on his grandmother's biscuit method. His emphasis is less on the short ingredient list than on handling: how the frozen butter is worked into the self-rising White Lily flour determines the texture, and he is candid that getting it right takes repetition. Real buttermilk and a buttered pan do the rest.

Note on the source: magazine article, no comments section

claude_opt.changes: Directions say to twist the cutter when punching biscuits — nearly every well-reviewed biscuit recipe (Kitchn, Sally's Baking) warns twisting seals the edges and blunts the rise. Press straight down.

name: Seven Layer Fiesta Dip
ingredients:
24 ounces (680 g) of refried beans or bean dip
6 ripe California avocados
2 tablespoons (30 g) of lemon juice
1 cup (230 g) sour cream
4 tablespoons (55 g) of mayonnaise
1 package of taco seasoning mix (1 1/4 ounces)
1 bunch green onions
2 to 3 medium tomatoes
1 small can of sliced black olives (about 2 ounces)
1 package of shredded cheddar cheese (8 ounces)
directions: On a round pizza pan or large round plate: spread bean dip; layer mashed California avocados over the bean dip and sprinkle with lemon juice. Mix sour cream, mayonnaise and taco seasoning mix, then spread over avocados. Chop green onions and tomatoes for the fourth and fifth layers. Spread olives on top, sprinkle with cheddar cheese and garnish with sliced avocados. All you need are Chips to Dip...

claude_opt.changes: No recipe changes needed; the layers match modern versions closely. It holds mayo, sour cream, and avocado, so keep chilled and don't leave it out past 2 hours.

name: Shakshuka with Feta
ingredients:
3 tablespoons (40 g) extra-virgin olive oil
1 large onion, halved and thinly sliced
1 large red bell pepper, seeded and thinly sliced
3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1 teaspoon (2.1 g) ground cumin
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) sweet paprika
1/8 teaspoon (0.2 g) ground cayenne, or to taste
1 (28-ounce) can whole plum tomatoes with their juices, coarsely chopped
3/4 teaspoon (2.1 g) kosher salt, plus more as needed
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) black pepper, plus more as needed
5 ounces (142 g) feta, crumbled (about 1 1/4 cups)
6 large eggs
Chopped cilantro, for serving
Hot sauce, for serving
directions:
Heat oven to 375 degrees. Heat oil in a large skillet over medium-low. Add onion and bell pepper. Cook gently until very soft, about 20 minutes. Add garlic and cook until tender, 1 to 2 minutes; stir in cumin, paprika and cayenne, and cook 1 minute. Pour in tomatoes and season with 3/4 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper; simmer until tomatoes have thickened, about 10 minutes. Taste and add more salt and pepper if needed. Stir in crumbled feta.

Gently crack eggs into skillet over tomatoes. Season eggs with salt and pepper. Transfer skillet to oven and bake until eggs are just set, 7 to 10 minutes. Sprinkle with cilantro and serve with hot sauce.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (22,594)). Melissa Clark's one-skillet eggs baked in a tomato and red-pepper sauce seasoned with cumin, paprika and cayenne - dinner food here, breakfast food in Israel, eaten with pita or challah. The sauce goes together on the stovetop, the eggs are nestled into it, and the pan finishes in the oven. The dish comes from North Africa and has countless versions; this one departs from tradition by adding crumbled feta, which softens into creamy pockets.

What readers report: The most-voted note (2,039) says the oven overcooks the eggs - by the time the whites set, the yolks are hard - and recommends dropping to a stovetop simmer with the lid on instead, which also skips heating the oven; a Tuscan cook (1,157 votes) independently confirms the covered-pan stovetop method as standard. The same top note adds chickpeas or lentils to make it a fuller dinner. A detailed comment from an Algerian cook (1,680 votes) offers family variations: small meatballs for substance, and grilling and peeling the peppers before they go in. Spinach stirred in and thicker diced tomatoes instead of watery ones are common (760 votes). One popular comment (859) defends the recipe exactly as written, conceding only a little anchovy paste.

name: Shrimp Creole
ingredients:
1 med. onion, minced (1/2 c.)
2 T. (28 g) butter
1/2 c. (74 g) chopped green pepper
1/4 c. (25 g) diced celery
1 bay leaf, crushed
1 t. (1.2 g) chopped parsley
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
1/8 t. (0.2 g) cayenne
1 6 oz. (170 g) can tomato paste
2 c. (474 g) water
2 c. (300 g) cleaned, cooked shrimp (1 1/2 lb. fresh or frozen)
directions: Cook onion in butter until tender. Stir in remaining ingredients except shrimp. Cook over low heat stirring occasionally for about 30 minutes. Stir in shrimp. Heat through. Serve over rice.

claude_opt.changes: Add raw shrimp, not pre-cooked, directly to the simmering sauce for the last 3-5 minutes; modern versions avoid double-cooking, which turns already-cooked shrimp rubbery.

name: Shrimp Scampi with Orzo - NYT
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) large shrimp, peeled and deveined
3 tablespoons (40 g) extra-virgin olive oil
1 tablespoon (6.0 g) lemon zest, plus 1 tablespoon juice (from 1 lemon)
1/2 teaspoon (0.9 g) red-pepper flakes
Kosher salt (such as Diamond Crystal) and black pepper
4 garlic cloves, minced
2 tablespoons (28 g) unsalted butter
1 cup (200 g) orzo
1/3 cup (79 g) dry white wine
2 cups (480 g) boiling water, seafood stock or chicken stock
3 tablespoons (11 g) finely chopped parsley
directions:
In a medium bowl, stir together shrimp, 1 tablespoon olive oil, lemon zest, red-pepper flakes, 1/2 teaspoon salt, 1/4 teaspoon pepper and half of the garlic. Set aside to marinate. (This step can be done up to 1 hour in advance.)

Add butter, remaining olive oil and remaining garlic to a medium skillet set over medium heat. When the butter starts to bubble, add the orzo and 1/2 teaspoon salt and cook, stirring often, until the orzo is toasted, about 2 minutes, adjusting the heat as necessary to prevent the garlic from burning. Carefully add the wine — it will bubble — and stir until absorbed, about 1 minute. Stir in water, reduce heat to low, cover, and cook until orzo is al dente, about 12 minutes.

Add the shrimp in a snug, even layer on top of the orzo, cover, and cook until all the shrimp is pink and cooked through, 2 to 4 minutes. Remove from heat and let sit, covered, 2 minutes.

Sprinkle with parsley and lemon juice, season with salt and pepper, and serve immediately.
notes:
2/22/25 Delicious! Very garlicky. Starch from Orzo thickened the sauce nicely. Used ¾ lb raw shrimp from Camerons. Had to peel and devein. Cooked orzo in Better than Bullion chicken broth. Used 12” fry pan. Served with salad. Alan liked eventhough he isn’t a shrimp fan.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (23,222)). The argument is that scampi is really about the pan sauce - garlicky butter cut with white wine, lemon, parsley and red-pepper flakes - so instead of pasta or bread this version simmers orzo directly in it, which glosses the sauce with starch and absorbs the garlic. The shrimp marinate in garlic, lemon zest and pepper flakes while the orzo cooks, then steam on top. Suggested with Caesar salad, broccoli or arugula.

What readers report: Liquid and timing are where people adjust. The top comment (931 votes) cuts to 1.5 cups of liquid, halves the salt, uses only a quarter teaspoon of pepper flakes and starts tasting the orzo at nine minutes; a second high-voted note (796) independently reports two cups left the shrimp swimming. Timing runs both ways - some find 12 minutes too long (410 votes), others needed 14-plus (375) - so taste rather than trust the clock. Toasting the orzo to a deeper brown before liquid goes in is widely endorsed (926, 560 votes), with the caveat to add the garlic later so it does not burn. One well-voted objection (454) is that simply steaming the marinated shrimp on top leaves a raw-garlic taste; lightly sauteing them first fixes it.

name: Simmered Smoked Links
ingredients:
2 pkgs (16 oz each) miniature smoked sausage links 
1 cup (213 g) packed brown sugar 
1/2 cup (135 g) ketchup 
1/4 cup (60 g) prepared horseradish
directions: Place sausages in slow cooker. Combine brown sugar, ketchup and horseradish, pour over sausages. Cover and cook on low for 4 hours.
notes:
Web summary (tasteofhome.com, 6 reviews (no star figure rendered)). Maxine Cenker's slow-cooker party appetizer: cocktail sausages left to simmer for hours in a three-ingredient glaze of brown sugar, ketchup and prepared horseradish. The horseradish is the whole point - it cuts the sweetness of a cup of brown sugar so the links read as sweet-and-sharp rather than candied, and because it is raw horseradish rather than a hot sauce the heat fades over the long cook into a background warmth. Nothing needs browning first; the sausages are already smoked and cooked, so the four hours on low is purely about the glaze reducing onto them. Taste of Home suggests serving them speared on decorative toothpicks.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS - the page shows a review count but no readable review text was returned.

Note on the source: Exact match to the family card, which already names 'Taste of Home Quick Cooking 2002' as its source: 2 pkgs (16 oz each) miniature smoked sausage links, 1 cup packed brown sugar, 1/2 cup ketchup, 1/4 cup prepared horseradish, low 4 hours. Gram conversions for Robert: 1 cup packed brown sugar = 220 g, 1/2 cup ketchup = 120 g, 1/4 cup prepared horseradish = 60 g, 2 x 16 oz sausage = 907 g.

ahead: Cover and cook on low for 4 hours.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing — comparable slow-cooker cocktail-sausage recipes confirm the same no-brown, glaze-and-hold method; sausages are precooked so 4 hrs low is standard, not excessive.

name: Simple Braised Pork Chops
ingredients:
4 (1 1/2-inch thick) bone-in, center-cut pork chops
Kosher salt, to taste
Freshly ground pepper, to taste
1/2 cup (120 g) chicken broth
3 tablespoons (40 g) brown sugar
1 tablespoon (16 g) Dijon mustard
1 tablespoon (15 g) apple cider vinegar
1 tablespoon (15 g) Worcestershire sauce
2 tablespoons (27 g) vegetable oil
1 cup (160 g) diced onions
2 cloves garlic, minced
directions:
Steps to Make It

Gather ingredients.

Sprinkle the pork generously with salt and pepper on both sides.

In a small bowl, whisk together the chicken broth, brown sugar, mustard, vinegar, and Worcestershire sauce. Set aside.

Heat the oil in a large, heavy-duty skillet over medium-high heat. When the oil shimmers, add the pork and cook until golden on both sides, flipping half way through cooking time, about 6 minutes total. Remove to a plate.

Lower the heat to medium. Add the onions to the skillet. Cook, stirring frequently, until softened and lightly browned.

Add the garlic and sauté until aromatic, about 30 seconds.

Nestle the pork into the onion-garlic mixture.

Give the chicken broth mixture a swirl. Pour over the pork and lower the heat to low. Cover the pan tightly and cook until the pork chops are tender, 45 to 60 minutes.
description: 10/23 Good! Easy and hearty. Made as directed, using bouillon rather than broth. A bit sweet perhaps, but very nice.
notes:
If you prefer to use the oven, use an oven-safe skillet or transfer the pork chops to a baking pan; cover with a lid or tightly with foil. Braise the pork chops in a preheated 325 F oven for about 45 to 55 minutes, or until tender.

If you are looking for a faster dish, take a look at these quick and easy oven roasted pork chops.

Web summary (thespruceeats.com, 4.0 (141), 13 Reviews). Diana Rattray's recipe (tested by Carrie Parente, updated Aug. 2025) sears bone-in pork chops, then braises them low and covered in a pan sauce of chicken broth, Dijon, brown sugar, cider vinegar and Worcestershire with softened onion and garlic, aiming for tender chops with minimal fuss. What readers report: the most developed correction (with 4 replies) comes from a reviewer who followed the recipe exactly and got dry meat — she diagnoses the cause as the instructed medium heat, which suits the onions but is too low to properly sear the pork, and recommends searing the chops in a hot pan first, removing them, then building the onion mixture afterward. This matches two separate short complaints that the meat came out tough or chewy despite following the Dijon method, and a blunter review calling these 'the worst pork cooking instructions,' though allowing the sauce has potential. A step-numbering question ('how did seared pork chops become raw again' in Step 7) points to a possible discontinuity in the written steps. Common substitutions: one cook cut brown sugar from 3 Tbs. to 1 Tbs. for a low-sugar version, doubled the sauce, and added a small sliced apple, calling the Worcestershire the key flavor addition; another asked, unanswered, about swapping rice wine vinegar for cider vinegar; others added sherry, extra Worcestershire, and suggested a touch of anchovy for depth.

name: Simple Steak Au Poivre
ingredients:
4 beef tenderloin steaks, 6 ounces (170 g) each, cut 1 inch thick
Salt
1 tablespoon (6.9 g) coarsely crushed black pepper
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) coarsely crushed Sichuan pepper
2 tablespoons (28 g) unsalted butter
2 large shallots, finely diced
1 ½ cups (360 g) rich beef or chicken broth
1 tablespoon (14 g) Cognac or bourbon
¼ cup (58 g) crème fraîche
1 bunch watercress, for garnish
directions:
Put steaks in a shallow dish and season well on both sides with salt. Sprinkle black pepper and Sichuan pepper evenly over steaks. Press pepper into both sides with hands and leave for 10 minutes.

Put a large cast iron skillet over high heat. When surface is nearly smoking, swirl 1 tablespoon butter in the pan and add steaks. Adjust heat as necessary to keep steaks sizzling briskly.

Cook for 2 minutes on first side; seared side should be nicely browned. Flip and cook for 2 minutes more. Transfer steaks to a warm platter.

Make the sauce: Add 1 tablespoon butter to the pan. Add shallots and sauté for a minute or so, stirring, until they begin to brown. Add broth and bring to a brisk simmer. Add Cognac and continue to simmer until reduced by half, 3 to 4 minutes. Stir in crème fraîche and cook until sauce is lightly thickened.

Return steaks to pan to warm, spooning sauce over them and turning once. Arrange steaks on platter or individual plates and top with more sauce. Garnish with bouquets of watercress and serve immediately.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (1,594)). NYT Cooking presents steak au poivre as far less daunting than its reputation: a sauteed steak finished with a fast pan sauce. This version leans on both black peppercorns and Sichuan pepper, which keeps it bright rather than aggressively hot or boozy. Scallion mashed potatoes are suggested alongside.

What readers report: The two highest-voted notes are both about the pan. One (180 votes) warns to sear in light-coloured stainless steel rather than a dark pan so you can watch the fond: burn it and the sauce is ruined. A follow-up (55 votes) cautions against preheating cast iron on the highest burner setting and suggests preheating the pan in a 350F oven instead to avoid setting off smoke alarms. A 268-vote comment describes keeping jars of mixed peppercorns steeped in brandy for a couple of months as a standing substitution. Others adjust the sauce toward heavy cream with more butter and only a little beef broth, and several with thick 8 oz filets sear both sides then finish in the oven, since the stovetop-only timing leaves them raw in the centre.

name: Skillet-Roasted Chicken & Potatoes
ingredients:
4 large bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs (2 1/2 to 3 pounds total)
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 1/2 cups (605 g) buttermilk, shaken
Good olive oil
2 tablespoons (31 g) Dijon mustard
1 tablespoon (15 g) dry white wine, such as Chablis
1 1/2 teaspoons (1.7 g) fresh thyme leaves
1/8 teaspoon (0.3 g) sweet Hungarian paprika
1 pound (454 g) medium Yukon Gold potatoes, unpeeled, sliced 1/4 inch thick
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) minced garlic (3 cloves)
2 tablespoons (7.5 g) minced fresh parsley
1 tablespoon (3.0 g) chopped fresh chives
directions:
At least 4 hours (but not more than 12 hours) before you plan to serve, sprinkle the chicken all over with 1 teaspoon salt and 1/2 teaspoon pepper. Place in a 1-gallon sealable plastic bag and pour in the buttermilk. Seal the bag and massage it lightly to be sure the chicken is coated with the buttermilk. Place in the refrigerator to marinate.

Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Pour 2 tablespoons olive oil in an unheated 12-inch cast-iron skillet and tilt the pan so the oil covers the bottom. Lift the thighs out of the buttermilk, letting any excess buttermilk drip off, and place them in the skillet, skin side up, in one layer. Discard the marinade. In a small bowl, combine the mustard and wine and brush it on the top of the chicken. Sprinkle with the thyme, paprika, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper. Place the skillet in the oven and roast the chicken for 30 minutes.

Using tongs, transfer the chicken to a plate and put the potatoes, garlic, 1 teaspoon salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper into the skillet. Toss to coat with the pan juices then spread the potatoes out. Return the chicken to the skillet, placing it on the potatoes. Roast 30 minutes longer, until the chicken registers 155 degrees F on an instant-read thermometer. Transfer just the chicken to a plate and cover loosely with aluminum foil to keep warm. Return the skillet to the oven, raise the temperature to 425 degrees F, and roast the potatoes for 15 minutes, until they’re tender and starting to brown. Return the chicken to the pan and sprinkle with the parsley, chives, and extra salt. Serve hot from the skillet.
description: 4/22 Delicious. Pototoes maybe a bit overcooked? Shorten second cook time?
notes:

Ina Garten marinates bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs in buttermilk, which both seasons and tenderises the meat through gentle acidity without turning it mushy the way a sharper marinade can. The thighs then roast in a cast-iron skillet over sliced Yukon Golds, so the potatoes cook in the rendering fat and juices. Dijon, white wine, thyme and paprika season the coating, and it all comes out of one pan.

name: Slow-Roasted Beef Tenderloin
ingredients:
1 center-cut trimmed beef tenderloin, 2 to 3 pounds (900g to 1.4kg; see note)
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
4 tablespoons (57g) unsalted butter
4 sprigs thyme
1 shallot, roughly sliced
Finely minced chives, for serving
Coarse sea salt, such as fleur de sel or Maldon, for serving
1 recipe Horseradish Cream Sauce, for serving
directions:
The Day Before: Using butcher's twine, tie tenderloin at 1-inch intervals using butcher's knots. Season generously with salt and pepper. Transfer to a wire rack set in a foil-lined rimmed baking sheet and refrigerate uncovered at least overnight and up to 2 nights.

When Ready to Cook: Adjust oven rack to center position and preheat oven to 225°F (107°C). Place baking sheet with rack and tenderloin in oven and roast until internal temperature registers 120 to 125°F (49 to 52°C) on an instant-read thermometer, 2 to 3 hours. Remove from oven and set aside at room temperature for 10 minutes. Cut and remove twine.

To Finish Under the Broiler: Adjust rack to 6 inches from broiler element and preheat broiler to high. Heat butter, swirling, in a medium skillet over high heat until foaming subsides and butter turns a light nutty brown. Add thyme and shallots and stir until crackling stops. Pour butter mixture over tenderloin and spread with a spoon until all surfaces are coated. Remove shallots from top surface of meat. Place pan with tenderloin under broiler and broil, turning every 30 seconds, until meat is well browned on all sides and internal temperature registers 125°F (52°C) for rare or 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare, about 2 minutes total. Proceed to step 5.

To Finish on the Stovetop: Heat butter, swirling, in a medium skillet over high heat until foaming subsides and butter turns a light nutty brown. Add tenderloin, shallots, and thyme and cook, turning occasionally and spooning hot butter and aromatics over roast, until meat is well browned on all sides and internal temperature registers 125°F (52°C) for rare or 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare, about 1 1/2 minutes.

Transfer tenderloin to a cutting board and allow to rest for 5 minutes. Slice into 1/2-inch slices, sprinkle with chives and coarse sea salt, and serve with Horseradish Cream Sauce.
description: Christmas 2023 Salted two days ahead and wrapped. Cooked the whole tenderloin, tied and folded, to 132 degrees. Finished under broiler. Really excellent. Pink all through and very tender.
notes:
For best results, season and trim the meat and allow it to rest at least overnight uncovered in the refrigerator to improve seasoning, browning, and texture. A center-cut beef tenderloin is also called a chateaubriand. Ask your butcher for it, or buy a whole tenderloin and trim it yourself, reserving the ends for another use. Plan on 1/2 pound of meat per person.

Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.8 (25) / 102 reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt argues that tenderloin's problem is its leanness: with no marbling to insulate it, it cooks fast and develops a wide band of overcooked grey meat before the centre is ready, and overcooked lean meat goes cottony. His answer is the reverse sear, roasting the tied roast at 225F until the centre is just under the serving temperature so the meat is nearly uniform edge to edge, then browning it at the very end. He also pretreats: salting heavily and resting the roast uncovered in the fridge overnight dissolves myosin so the meat shrinks and expels less liquid, and dries the surface into a pellicle that browns fast, which is the one advantage this method holds over sous vide's wet exterior. The finish is brown butter with shallot and thyme poured over the roast, then about two minutes under a broiler with a turn every 30 seconds.

What readers report: The dominant correction, repeated by nearly every reviewer, is that the stated two-to-three-hour roast is far too long: three- to four-pound roasts routinely hit 120 to 125F in 60 to 100 minutes, and one reviewer complains the wide range is useless for timing a dinner party. Several describe holding the roast successfully, pulling it early and wrapping it in foil or a towel-lined cooler for an hour or two, then returning it briefly to a 200 to 225F oven to recover temperature before searing. Use a leave-in probe and insert it straight rather than diagonally; one cook found a slanted probe reading ten degrees low. On the finish, roughly 30 seconds per turn for about two minutes total is the consensus, and going longer starts a grey rim; one suggests leaving the ends tied so the roast does not flop under the broiler. A minority found the overnight salting much too salty.

Note on the source: Helpfulness counts exist but top out at 1, so ranking by votes is weak. Several near-duplicate reviews are posted by the same accounts (one cook posted essentially the same review three times, another posted 'too salty' twice), which slightly inflates those signals. Comments truncated at 'Read More'.

name: Slow-Roasted Turkey
ingredients:
1 (14-pound) whole turkey
4 ounce (113 g) (1 stick) softened butter (preferably something with high butter fat, like Plugrá or Kerrygold)
5 lemons, halved
4 sprig rosemary
4 sprig sage
4 sprig thyme
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 cup (237 g) white wine
directions:
OPTIONAL FIRST STEP: One of the keys to miraculously crispy skin is a VERY dry turkey. The best way to accomplish this is to air-dry your turkey (in the refrigerator) for 1 to 2 days before you roast. I know this sounds a little crazy, and I do have the luxury of a second fridge at home, but I do it with my chickens too—and it makes a huge difference. Unwrap the turkey, rinse it, and pat it dry inside and out with paper towels. Place the turkey onto a tray or in a roasting pan and refrigerate, uncovered, for 24 to 48 hours.

Heat the oven to 250°F. Remove the wing tips or tuck them behind the turkey by bending them backward and securing them near the neck. Tie the legs tightly together. Place the turkey on a roasting rack inside a roasting pan.

Using your hands, evenly cover the outside of the turkey with the butter. Make sure to get the sides.

Stuff the inside of the turkey with the lemon, rosemary, sage, and thyme. Season well with salt and pepper (inside and out). Pour the wine into the roasting pan.

Roast the turkey, basting every hour or so (you can go 2 to 3 hours safely without basting, but every hour is best), for about 10 hours, until the skin is crisp and evenly golden. (Basting often is the best way to ensure a crisp skin and a moist interior. You could not baste it as often, but the more you baste it, the crisper the skin, the more even the browning, and the juicier the interior.) At this point, the turkey can be safely cooled until you're ready to reheat and serve.

Increase the oven temperature to 375°F. Continue to roast the turkey for about 40 minutes, until the skin is even crisper and more golden and the meat is fully cooked through. Let cool for at least 15 to 30 minutes before carving.
description: 11/25 We did a 14 pound turkey very successfully with this method. Took 8 hours. A whole stick of butter on top, and lemon and herbs in caviity. Added 1 cup better-than-bouillon in the pan at the start. Had to turn the bird after 6 ½ hours later into a large stainless bowl to slow the breast and put more heat on the dark meat. Moist and tender.  Used a frozen Shady Brook Farms pre-brined turkey, 27 cents per pound. Took it cold to Williamsburg and reheated very large chunks wrapped in tin foil in the oven.
notes:
Web summary (food52.com, 5 ratings (star value not shown)). Erin Jeanne McDowell roasts a fourteen-pound bird at a very low oven temperature for a long stretch, on the logic that gentle heat keeps the muscle fibres from seizing and squeezing out juice. Regular basting with butter and the pan juices, plus a final blast of high heat, is what restores the crisp skin that low roasting alone would not give. She is upfront that it is a long process better suited to cooks with a second oven or willingness to start early. Lemons and a bundle of rosemary, thyme and sage go in the cavity, with white wine in the pan.

name: Small Batch Strawberry Jam
ingredients:
1 lb (454 g) fresh strawberries
1 1/2 cups (300 g) sugar
2 Tbs (30 g) lemon juice
½ tsp (1.0 g) lemon zest optional
directions:
Wash and slice the strawberries, removing the hulls and green tops.

Add them to a saucepan, and mix the sugar in well.

Stir continually over medium heat, and bring the strawberries to boil.

Once boiling, add the lemon juice and zest (if using).

Boil for about 15 minutes, or until the jam reaches 220F.

Stir often, to make sure the jam doesn’t burn.

Pour into a jar and allow to cool.

name: Snickerdoodles
ingredients:
1 c. (227 g) margarine
1 1/2 c. (300 g) sugar
2 eggs
2 3/4 c. (330 g) flour
2 t. (6.2 g) cream of tartar
1 t. (4.6 g) baking soda
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
2 T. (25 g) sugar
2 t. (5.2 g) cinnamon
directions:
Preheat oven to 375.
Mix margarine, sugar, and eggs together thoroughly. Sift flour, cream of tartar, baking soda, and salt. Combine with wet mixture, stirring well. Chill dough for 2 hours. Shape dough into balls the size of walnuts. Roll each ball in a mixture of sugar and cinnamon. Place 2" apart on ungreased cookie sheet. Bake for 12 minutes or until lightly browned but still soft.
notes:
Web summary (bettycrocker.com, No star rating or review count shown on the page). Betty Crocker's canonical snickerdoodle. The published version splits the fat between butter and shortening on purpose: shortening keeps the crumb tender and pillowy while butter supplies flavor and edges that crisp. Cream of tartar is what makes a snickerdoodle a snickerdoodle rather than a cinnamon sugar cookie - it gives the tang and, working with the baking soda, the characteristic crackled top. The dough is rolled in cinnamon sugar before baking, not after, so the coating bakes into the surface.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS - the Betty Crocker page carries recipe tips and variations but no reader comment section. The family's own card adds the practical steps the published page leaves loose: chill the dough two hours, shape into walnut-sized balls, space 2 inches apart on an ungreased sheet, and pull at 12 minutes at 375F while still soft.

Note on the source: MEDIUM. The card is attributed to Julie Horsley, a personal source, so this is not provably where she got it - but the dry skeleton is identical to Betty Crocker's and unmistakably descended from it: 1 1/2 c sugar, 2 eggs, 2 3/4 c flour, 2 tsp cream of tartar, 1 tsp baking soda, cinnamon-sugar roll. The differences are exactly what a home cook's copy looks like: 1 cup margarine standing in for Betty Crocker's 1/2 c butter + 1/2 c shortening, salt raised from 1/4 to 1/2 tsp, and 2 Tbsp coating sugar instead of 1/4 cup. Robert may prefer to treat this as 'adapted from' rather than a source link. Gram conversions for the family card: 1 c margarine = 227 g, 1 1/2 c sugar = 300 g, 2 3/4 c all-purpose flour = 344 g, 2 Tbsp sugar = 25 g.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

Data fix (Sept 2026): the research notes above describe Betty Crocker's published version, which uses a butter and shortening split. The family card itself calls for margarine; that has been left as written.

claude_opt.changes: Existing summary describes a butter/shortening split that isn't in this card — it lists margarine only. Well-reviewed versions (Sally's Baking) use all butter, not margarine, for real snickerdoodle flavor; swap 1:1.

name: Soubrette
ingredients:
4 oz. lasagna noodles, about 10, or 125 g flour homemade pasta recipe rolled to 6
1 c. (160 g) chopped onions
4 T. (57 g) butter, divided
10 oz. (284 g) frozen chopped spinach

paprika
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.
Cook noodles. Saute onions in 2 T. butter until transparent. Cook spinach until thawed, drain, squeeze dry. Add to onions and set aside.
Combine Monterey jack cheese, cottage cheese, and eggs. Divide cheese mixture equally into two bowls. Add spinach mixture to one bowl, blending well. name: Sourdough Naan
ingredients:
17.5oz (500g) all purpose flour
4.4oz (125g) full fat yoghurt
3.5oz (100g) coconut milk
1.75 oz (50g) sugar
1 tbsp (18 g) salt
7oz (200g) mature sourdough starter/ 1tsp instant dried yeast
1.75oz (50g) melted garlic butter
2.6oz (75g) water
directions:
For this recipe you’ll need to prepare your dough ahead of time, starting 18 hours before you’re ready to cook.

In a large bowl, combine the yoghurt, coconut milk, water and sourdough starter and whisk together until combined.

In a separate bowl, mix the flour, sugar, and salt together. Add the dry ingredients into your wet mix and begin to combine with your hands. Once a dough starts to form, turn onto a lightly floured work surface and knead until smooth and round. The dough should be a little sticky.

Place your dough back in the bowl, cover, and leave to ferment at room temperature. After 4 hours, place the dough in the refrigerator for a further 12 hours to prove. This provides plenty of time for the dough to develop a rich flavor and texture.

After 12 hours, remove the dough from the refrigerator and allow it to come back to room temperature for 2 hours.

Fire up your Ooni pizza oven. Aim for 725°F (400°C) on the stone baking board inside. You can check the temperature of your oven quickly and easily using the Ooni Infrared Thermometer.

Turn your dough onto a lightly floured work surface and divide into small, 40g balls. With your rolling pin, roll each ball into small 2cm thick circles, then brush with a thin layer of melted garlic butter or ghee. Using a small amount of flour, dust your Ooni pizza peel and lay your naans on top.

Slide the naans off your peel and into your Ooni pizza oven. Cook for 1 minute, turning every 15 seconds or so. If you see any large air bubbles, pinch them down with your peel.

Once the edges turn golden brown, remove the naan and carefully flip it over. Slide the naan back in your oven and let the other side cook for a further minute.

Once you see a nice color all round, remove the naans from the oven and slide onto a wooden peel or serving board. Serve hot and fresh!
notes:
Web summary (ooni.com). Ooni's kitchen team adapts naan to a sourdough starter, so the flatbread gains the tang and extended fermentation of a levain while keeping the soft, pillowy chew naan is meant to have. The recipe is endorsed by Ooni ambassador Artisan Bryan and finishes with a garlic butter brush. It is built for a very hot pizza oven, which blisters the surface fast the way a tandoor would.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

After 4 hours, place the dough in the refrigerator for a further 12 hours to prove.

name: Sourdough No-Knead Bread
ingredients:
3 ½ cups/475 grams bread flour, plus more for dusting
1 teaspoon/6 grams kosher salt
¾ cup/180 grams sourdough starter, “fed”
2 tablespoons/20 grams sesame seeds
directions:
In a large mixing bowl, combine the flour and salt.

In a small mixing bowl, stir together 300 grams (about 1 1/4 cups) lukewarm tap water with the sourdough starter, then pour the mixture into the bowl with the flour mixture. Mix until just combined. Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and a tea towel and leave it to rise overnight, about 10 to 24 hours.

The next day, generously dust a clean kitchen surface with flour. The dough should have risen considerably and you should see visible bubbling along the sides. The dough will be spongy and wet. Scoop the dough directly onto the surface, then dust with more flour. With lightly floured hands, gently fold the edges of the dough from the outside in, to form a round loaf. Dust a clean towel with yet more flour, sprinkle sesame seeds in a small area about the size of your loaf and place the dough on top of the seeds, seam side down. Lightly dust with additional flour, cover and allow to double in size, about 2 hours.

Meanwhile, heat oven to 450. Place a covered enamel Dutch oven or heavy pot with a lid into the oven and allow it to heat for 30 minutes or so. Remove the pot from the oven, take off its top, and carefully invert the risen dough into it, so that the seam side is now facing up. (Alternately you can invert the risen dough onto a flour-dusted sheet of parchment paper and lower your loaf into your pot that way.). Put the top back on the pot and return it to the oven.

Bake for about 25 to 30 minutes, then take the top off the pot and allow it to continue to cook until it is brown and crusty all over, an additional 20 minutes or so. Put the loaf on a rack to cool for at least 30 minutes before serving.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (2,791)). Sam Sifton's adaptation of Jim Lahey's no-knead loaf for people who have a live sourdough starter and want something to do with it. Commercial yeast is replaced by just under three-quarters of a cup of well-fed starter, the dough gets a very long rise, and it bakes covered in a preheated enameled cast-iron pot.

What readers report: The top note (764 votes) is a handling fix: line the rising vessel with parchment and lift the dough into the hot pot by the paper, which ends the mess of flour-dusted towels. The single biggest point of confusion (613 votes) is what "fed" starter means in practice; the best-voted answers say to build the starter up so it is at peak activity, and to use the float test - a spoonful dropped in water should float before you mix (165 votes). A 320-vote comment questions why this bakes at 550F when standard no-knead bakes at 450F; an experienced baker (237 votes) preheats a cast-iron Dutch oven to 500F and drops to 450F once the loaf goes in. Rating is 4 stars, lower than most, consistent with the timing ambiguity.

name: Sourdough Pancake or Waffle Batter
ingredients:
FOR THE OVERNIGHT SPONGE, OR BASE:
1 cup/240 grams sourdough starter “unfed”
1 cup/224 grams buttermilk
1 cup/120 grams all-purpose flour
1 tablespoon/about 13 grams light brown sugar
FOR THE BATTER:
1 large egg
¼ cup (57 g) melted unsalted butter or neutral oil
½ teaspoon (2.1 g) vanilla extract
½ teaspoon/3 grams kosher salt
1 teaspoon/6 grams baking soda
directions:
Put the sourdough starter in a large bowl and add the buttermilk, flour and sugar, then stir to combine. Cover the bowl and allow it to rest overnight at room temperature.

When you are ready to cook, whisk the egg, melted butter or oil and the vanilla extract together in a small bowl, then add the rested sponge. Add the salt and the baking soda to the batter and mix to combine.

Pour some of the batter onto a preheated greased waffle iron and cook until the waffle is brown and crisp, then repeat. Or use a small ladle to create pancakes on a preheated oiled pan or griddle, flipping them when they are well browned on the bottom. Serve immediately.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (3,407)). A use for the starter discard that would otherwise go in the bin when you feed a sourdough culture. The discard becomes the base of a batter that ferments overnight and is cooked as pancakes or waffles the next morning, giving a lot of tangy flavour for very little active work. Part of Sam Sifton's sourdough coverage.

What readers report: The most-voted thread is a running argument about weight versus volume that matters directly for gram conversion. One note (369 votes) points out that a cup of a liquid and a cup of a solid do not weigh the same - a cup of water is 8 oz or about 230 grams, and flour, being less dense, weighs appreciably less - so a single gram figure cannot be applied to every cup in a recipe. A 281-vote comment thanks the Times for printing grams at all and argues cups and teaspoons are the unreliable measure; a 301-vote reply pushes back that scales vary too. On technique, plain yogurt substitutes cleanly for buttermilk (232 votes), and a 135-vote note replaces all or part of the all-purpose flour with wholewheat, oat or other flours without trouble.

name: Sous Vide Barbecue Pulled Pork Shoulder Kenji
ingredients:
For the Spice Rub:
1/4 cup (50g) paprika
1/4 cup (50g) dark brown sugar
3 tablespoons (35g) kosher salt
1/2 teaspoon (2g) Prague Powder #1 (optional; see note)
1 tablespoon (12g) whole yellow mustard seed
1 teaspoon (4g) freshly ground black pepper
2 tablespoons (20g) granulated garlic powder
1 tablespoon (8g) dried oregano
1 tablespoon (12g) whole coriander seed
1 teaspoon (4g) red pepper flakes
For the Pork:
1 whole boneless or bone-in pork butt (shoulder), 5 to 7 pounds total (2.25 to 3.25kg)
1/2 teaspoon (3ml) liquid smoke, such as Wright's Liquid Smoke (optional; see note)
Kosher salt
directions:
1. For the Spice Rub: Working in batches, combine paprika, brown sugar, salt, Prague Powder (if using), mustard seed, black pepper, garlic powder, oregano, coriander seed, and red pepper flakes in a spice grinder and reduce to a fine powder.

2. Divide mixture in half. Rub half of mixture evenly all over pork shoulder, pressing it in until it adheres. Place pork shoulder in a sous vide–safe vacuum-sealer bag. Add liquid smoke (if using) and seal bag.

3. To Cook: Set your precision cooker to 165°F (74°C) for more traditionally textured pulled pork, or 145°F (63°C) for sliceable but tender pork. When the bath is at temperature, add sealed bag with pork and cover with foil or plastic wrap. Allow to cook for 18 to 24 hours. After this stage, pork can be refrigerated for up to 1 week before continuing.

4. To Finish in the Oven: Adjust oven rack to lower-middle position and preheat oven to 300°F. Remove pork from sous vide bag and carefully blot dry with paper towels. (The liquid from the bag can be added to your favorite barbecue sauce and simmered down to provide extra flavor.) Rub reserved spice mixture into the surface of the pork. Place pork on a wire rack set in a rimmed baking sheet and place in oven. Roast until a deep, dark bark has formed, about 1 1/2 hours. Continue with step 7.

5. To Finish on the Grill: Light 1/2 chimney full of charcoal. When all the charcoal is lit and covered with gray ash, pour out and arrange coals on one side of the charcoal grate. Set cooking grate in place, cover grill, and allow to preheat for 5 minutes. Alternatively, set half the burners on a gas grill to medium-high heat, cover, and preheat for 10 minutes. Clean and oil the grilling grate.

6. Remove pork from bag and carefully blot dry with paper towels. (The liquid from the bag can be added to your favorite barbecue sauce and simmered down to provide extra flavor.) Rub reserved spice mixture into the surface of the pork. Place pork on the cooler side of grill. Add 4 to 5 hardwood chunks to the hotter side of grill. Cover and allow pork to smoke, adjusting vents to maintain a temperature between 275 and 300°F and adding 2 to 3 wood chunks twice during cooking. Smoke until a deep, dark bark has formed, about 1 1/2 hours. Continue with step 7.

7. Transfer pork to a large bowl or cutting board. Using a couple of forks, shred meat into bite-size pieces (or, if you cooked it at 145°F, use a knife to slice the pork). Season pulled pork to taste with salt and serve immediately, passing your favorite barbecue sauce at the table.
description:
5/26 7 lbs yielded 3½ lbs. Soak wood in water before baking step. 
8/22 Used a 5.3 Lb butt and it yielded about half. 3 Lb is too small for all that work!
10/22 8 lbs yielded 3½ lbs finished.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.5 (21) / 69 reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt makes the case for cooking pork shoulder sous vide on two grounds: it is hands-off compared with babysitting a smoker all day, and it reaches textures traditional methods cannot. Collagen breaks down with both heat and time, but hotter meat squeezes out more moisture, so a low, stable bath buys tenderness without the loss; he tested a range and landed on 165F for 18 to 24 hours for shreddable-but-moist pork, with 145F for the same span giving a firmer, sliceable roast, while 200F shreds instantly but goes dry. Smoke can come from liquid smoke or smoked salt in the bag, or from a real session over wood afterwards, which he prefers for convenience even though smoke adheres better to raw meat. A pinch of pink curing salt in the rub fakes the cosmetic smoke ring, and the shoulder still needs 90 minutes in a 300F oven or on the grill to build bark.

What readers report: The strongest thread is what the post-bath finish costs you. One cook found the pork superb straight from the bag but noticeably drier and less supple after 90 minutes in the oven and says he will stop at the bath next time; another crisps individual portions in a pan instead, and a third skips bark entirely, trading caramelised bits for tenderness. One reviewer goes further and says not to sous vide before grilling at all, because his 22-hour 165F shoulder fell apart before it reached the grate, cutting against the author's preference for smoking afterwards. Successful reports stay close to the recipe: 24 hours at 165F, ice bath, overnight in the fridge, then about two hours over apple wood. Two useful tweaks: trim the fat cap and bag it alongside the meat for a crisper, less greasy bark, and chill the bag juices, skim the fat, and stir the gelatin back into the shredded pork.

Note on the source: Comments truncated at 'Read More'. One reviewer's reheating instructions are internally inconsistent about the oven time, so his numbers were not reported. The recipe was not tested by commenters at the 145F sliceable setting in any visible review.

ahead: Allow to cook for 18 to 24 hours.
makeahead: After this stage, pork can be refrigerated for up to 1 week before continuing.

claude_opt.changes: Your 5/26-10/22 notes already established ~50% yield; buy 7-8+ lb shoulder, not 5.3 lb. Skip the 90-min oven bark step entirely — commenters report it dries out meat already tender from the bath; sear portions in the Lodge instead.

name: Sous Vide Pork Chops
ingredients:
4 bone-in pork rib chops, 1 1/2 inches thick each (about 2 1/2 pounds; 1.1kg total)
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
4 sprigs thyme or rosemary (optional)
2 garlic cloves (optional)
2 shallots, thinly sliced (optional)
2 tablespoons (30ml) vegetable, canola, or rice bran oil (optional)
2 tablespoons (30ml) butter (optional)
directions:
1. Preheat a sous vide cooker to the desired final temperature according to the chart below. Season pork chops generously with salt and pepper. Place in sous vide bags along with herbs, garlic, and shallots (if using) and distribute evenly. Seal bags and place in water bath for time recommended in chart below.

2. To Finish in a Pan: Turn on your vents and open your windows. Remove pork from water bath and bag and carefully pat dry with paper towels. Add vegetable, canola, or rice bran oil to a heavy cast iron or stainless steel skillet, place it over the hottest burner you have, and preheat skillet until it starts to smoke. Working in batches if necessary, gently lay pork chops in skillet, using your fingers or a set of tongs. If desired, add 1 tablespoon butter; for a cleaner-tasting sear, omit butter at this stage. Carefully lift and peek under pork as it cooks to gauge how quickly it is browning. Let it continue to cook until the crust is deep brown and very crisp, about 45 seconds.

3. Flip pork chops. If desired, add 1 more tablespoon butter, along with thyme, rosemary, garlic, and/or shallots. Spoon butter over pork chops as they cook. Continue cooking until second side is browned, about 45 seconds longer.

4. When pork is browned, pick it up with a pair of tongs, rotate it sideways, and make sure to brown the edges as well. Transfer cooked pork chops to a wire rack set over a rimmed baking sheet and repeat with remaining pork chops as necessary.

5. Just before serving, reheat the drippings in the pan until sizzling-hot, then pour them over pork chops in order to re-crisp their exteriors. Serve immediately.

6. To Finish on the Grill: Light one chimney full of charcoal. When all the charcoal is lit and covered with gray ash, pour out and arrange the coals on one side of the charcoal grate. Set cooking grate in place, cover grill, and allow to preheat for 5 minutes. Alternatively, set half the burners on a gas grill to the highest heat setting, cover, and preheat for 10 minutes. Clean and oil the grilling grate. Remove pork chops from water bath and bag and carefully pat dry with paper towels. Place pork chops directly over the hot side of the grill and cook, turning every 15 to 30 seconds, until a deep, rich crust has formed, about 1 1/2 minutes total. If the fire threatens to flare up as pork chops drip fat into it, suffocate the fire by closing the grill lid until the flames die out. Alternatively, transfer pork chops to the cooler side of the grill using a set of long tongs until the flames subside. Do not allow pork chops to become engulfed in flames. Transfer cooked pork chops to a cutting board or serving platter and serve immediately.

1/21 Great with rosemary. Cooked at 145 degrees for 1 hour 20. Excellent. Cpuld go a bit longer for the meat near the bone. 
5/21 Made with Ina’s pork tenderloin with herbs marinade—good! Cooked over three hours. Tender but a bit dry. Try 2½ hours next time. Used Wegmans regular chops and they were quite good.

RM 11/14: I followed this pork chop recipe, and it came out great (but not as pretty). My mom's pork chops growing up were always tough and dry. This was the juiciest one I've ever had.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.7 (13) / 45 reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt presents this as a complete guide rather than a single recipe, aimed at the reader who grew up on dry, overcooked chops. Because the water bath sits at the temperature you actually want to serve, the chop cooks evenly from edge to edge and timing becomes forgiving, so the choice of temperature does all the work: he walks through the texture at 130F, 140F, 150F and 160F and picks 140F as his own favourite for meat that is juicy but still has a meaty bite. Time still matters at the margins, and he caps the bath at about four hours before the muscle fibres go mushy. Brining is unnecessary, bone-in chops gain flavour that spreads through the meat in a sealed bag, and because sous vide cannot brown anything, the chop has to be finished fast in a smoking-hot skillet or over a hot grill.

What readers report: The most repeated safety note warns against putting fresh garlic in the bag at bath temperatures below 140F, citing the anaerobic environment and C. botulinum. Results at 140F split sharply: one cook calls 140F for 90 minutes on a two-inch bone-in chop perfect, while another found a one-inch-plus chop at the same setting practically inedible. A detailed troubleshooting comment aimed at those failures blames the finish rather than the bath, advising thick bone-in chops, a smoking pan with avocado rather than olive oil, a sear measured in seconds not minutes, and no resting at all, which contradicts the recipe's three-to-five-minute rest. One reader flags an apparent conflict between the fifteen-minutes-per-half-inch rule of thumb and the chart's flat one-to-four-hour range. Several readers ask whether chops chilled in an ice bath can simply be seared the next day; none of those questions are answered in the visible text.

Note on the source: Comments are heavily truncated at 'Read More'. A large share of the review section is unanswered reader questions rather than feedback. The star rating is based on 13 ratings while 45 reviews are listed.

claude_opt.changes: Below 140F, skip raw garlic in the bag — a sealed anaerobic pouch at that temperature is a real C. botulinum risk per reader safety warnings, not just flavor advice. Add garlic to the pan sear instead.

ingredients:

Salt and pepper

1/4 cup (12 g) finely chopped fresh cilantro
directions:
1. MAKE DRESSING Combine scallions, chipotle, honey, lime juice, ½ teaspoon salt, and ½ teaspoon pepper in large bowl. Slowly whisk in 2 tablespoons
2. TOAST CORN Heat remaining oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Cook corn untl spotty brown, about 5 minutes. 
3. TOSS SALAD Add beans, avocados, tomatoes, cilantro, and toasted corn to bowl with dressing and toss to combine. Season with salt and pepper.
Serve. (Salad can be refrigerated in airtight container for 2 days. Bring to room temperature and toss before serving.)
BOOST BEAN FLAVOR
When making salads such as Black Bean Salad, we prefer to use canned beans processed with salt. Why? Easy-they taste better. Many "natural" or
"Organic" brands containing little or no salt can be quite bland, especially in recipes where the canned beans are not cooked. If all you've got in your
pantry are unsalted beans, here's a neat trick for improving their flavor: Marinate them in the dressing for your salad for about 10 minutes
America's Test Kitchen is a 2,500-square-foot kitchen located just outside of Boston. It is the home of Cook's Country and Cook's Illustrated
1/2
ww.cookscountry.com/recipes/print/20159/
description:
8/25 Made without beans. Nice and light. Corn starred. Added some adobo marinade from wegmans. Not good! Maybe just use Sriracha. 


WHY THIS RECIPE WORKS: We quickly edited out the dull bell pepper and harsh onion found in traditional recipes for Southwestern black bean salad. Instead, we used scallions, which were mellow and light. Creamy avocados gave the salad richness, tomatoes lent juicy freshness, and corn added welcome sweetness. Sautéing the corn (both fresh and frozen worked well) in a skillet until it was toasty and just starting to brown added a pleasant nuttiness to the kernels.
In order to give our salad the wake-up call it needed, we turned the typical dressing ratio of 1 part acid to 3 parts oil nearly upside down, using much more lime juice than olive oil. A teaspoon of honey balanced the citrus kick, and throwing the scallions into the dressing mellowed them nicely.
Serves 6
notes:
Web summary (americastestkitchen.com, 4 out of 5 stars, 291 ratings). Cook's Country rebuilt the standard black bean salad by throwing out the two ingredients that usually flatten it - raw bell pepper and raw onion - and using scallions instead, which stay mellow. The real move is toasting the corn in a hot skillet until it is spotty brown, which gives the kernels a nutty depth raw or thawed corn never has. They also invert the usual dressing ratio, running far more lime juice than oil, with a teaspoon of honey to keep the acid in check; the scallions go into the dressing so the lime tames them. Avocado supplies the richness that the reduced oil gave up.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS returned from the page. The recipe's own sidebar carries the one tip worth keeping: use canned beans packed with salt rather than no-salt 'natural' or 'organic' brands, which taste flat in an uncooked salad - and if you only have unsalted beans, marinate them in the dressing for ten minutes before assembling. Robert's own cook's note (8/25) records making it without beans, where the toasted corn carried the dish, and warns off one substitution: adding Wegmans adobo marinade was a failure, use Sriracha instead if you want the heat.

Note on the source: Exact match to the family card, which already names 'Cooks Country 2009'. Ingredient list matches item for item; the only differences are the can size (family wrote 16-ounce, site says 15-ounce) and Parmesan-free trivia. The family card even preserves the magazine's 'WHY THIS RECIPE WORKS' block verbatim, confirming it was copied from the Cook's Country print/online page. claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. The recipe's own chipotle-in-adobo already supplies the heat; your 8/25 note found adding extra Wegmans adobo marinade fails — use Sriracha instead if more heat is wanted, as you noted.

name: Spaghetti Al Limone with Asparagus
ingredients:
1 lb. (454 g) spaghetti
⅔ cup (144 g) extra-virgin olive oil
1 large bunch asparagus, trimmed, thinly sliced on a deep diagonal
4 garlic cloves, smashed
4 3"-long strips lemon zest
½ tsp. (0.9 g) crushed red pepper flakes
8 large basil leaves
2 lemons, halved
2 oz. (57 g) Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup), plus more for serving
directions:
Cook pasta in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente. Drain pasta, reserving 1½ cups pasta cooking liquid.

Meanwhile, heat oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high until shimmering. Add asparagus, season with salt, and cook, stirring often, until just beginning to take on color, about 1 minute. Add garlic, lemon zest, and red pepper flakes and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Remove from heat and let sit until pasta is done.

Add pasta and basil to pot with asparagus mixture and return to medium-high heat. Squeeze juice from both lemons into pot and add 2 oz. Parmesan and 1 cup reserved pasta cooking liquid. Cook, tossing vigorously and adding more pasta cooking liquid if needed, until sauce is creamy and emulsified and pasta is coated, about 1 minute. Taste and season with more salt if needed. Remove and discard garlic.

Divide pasta among bowls, placing a lemon strip in each, and top with more Parmesan.
description: 4/22 Delicious! Lemony, garlicky. Needs good oil. Didn’t get too much emulsion. Perhaps because used fresh pasta. But still great!
notes: Web summary (bonappetit.com, 4.6 (126), 44 notes). Evan Funke's asparagus pasta (first printed 2020), framed by BA editors as a quick, craftsmanship-forward dish where thinly sliced asparagus and an emulsified Parmesan-lemon-olive oil sauce, finished with starchy pasta water, are meant to complement the noodles rather than overwhelm them. What readers report: the clearest recurring correction is that the recipe under-specifies lemon quantity — it calls for '2 lemons' rather than a juice volume, and because lemon size and juiciness vary widely, multiple independent readers report batches that turned out too sour or overpoweringly lemony; one explicitly asks the site to give a juice measurement instead, and another cautions to add zest and juice gradually to avoid an overpowering result. A second cluster says the dish runs oily as written and suggests cutting back the oil, with one reviewer also calling the vegetable-to-pasta ratio off and the result bland. A separate commenter flags a mismatch between the written recipe and the site's test-kitchen video, which shows heavy cream, butter and no asparagus at all. Reader-tested tweaks that held up: cooking the asparagus separately for about 2 minutes just before the pasta finishes to preserve its color, and mixing everything directly in the pasta pot rather than transferring to a skillet; pressing rather than smashing the garlic; and dialing back the red pepper flakes to taste.

claude_opt.changes: Your 4/22 note found the emulsion never came together; readers separately call it oily too — cut the 2/3 cup oil slightly. Add lemon juice gradually and taste; readers report '2 lemons' swings from balanced to overpowering.

name: Spiced Chickpea Stew with Coconut and Turmeric
ingredients:
¼ cup (54 g) olive oil, plus more for serving
4 garlic cloves, chopped
1 large yellow onion, chopped
1 (2-inch) piece ginger, finely chopped
Kosher salt and black pepper
1 ½ teaspoons (4.5 g) ground turmeric, plus more for serving
1 teaspoon (1.8 g) red-pepper flakes, plus more for serving (we use 1/2 tsp)
2 (15-ounce) cans chickpeas, drained and rinsed
2 (15-ounce) cans full-fat coconut milk
2 cups (480 g) vegetable or chicken stock
1 bunch Swiss chard, kale or collard greens, stems removed, torn into bite-size pieces
1 cup (45 g) mint leaves, for serving
Yogurt, for serving (optional)
Toasted pita, lavash or other flatbread, for serving (optional)
directions:
Heat 1/4 cup oil in a large pot over medium. Add garlic, onion and ginger. Season with salt and pepper, and cook, stirring occasionally until onion is translucent and starts to brown a little at the edges, 3 to 5 minutes.

Add 1 1/2 teaspoons turmeric, 1 teaspoon red-pepper flakes, and the chickpeas, and season with salt and pepper. Cook, stirring frequently, so the chickpeas sizzle and fry a bit in the spices and oil, until they’ve started to break down and get a little browned and crisp, 8 to 10 minutes. Remove about a cup of chickpeas and set aside for garnish.

Using a wooden spoon or spatula, further crush the remaining chickpeas slightly to release their starchy insides. (This will help thicken the stew.) Add coconut milk and stock, and season with salt and pepper.

Bring to a simmer, scraping up any bits that have formed on the bottom of the pot. Cook, stirring occasionally, until stew has thickened, 30 to 35 minutes. (Taste a chickpea or two, not just the liquid, to make sure they have simmered long enough to be as delicious as possible.) If after 30 to 35 minutes, you want the stew a bit thicker, keep simmering until you've reached your desired consistency. Determining perfect stew thickness is a personal journey!

Add greens and stir, making sure they’re submerged in the liquid. Cook until they wilt and soften, 3 to 7 minutes, depending on what you’re using. (Swiss chard and spinach will wilt and soften much faster than kale or collard greens.) Season again with salt and pepper.

Divide among bowls and top with mint, reserved chickpeas, a sprinkle of red-pepper flakes and a good drizzle of olive oil. Serve alongside yogurt and toasted pita if using; dust the yogurt with turmeric if you'd like.
