name: Spinach and Artichoke in Puff Pastry
ingredients:
1 (10 oz) package frozen chopped spinach, thawed
1 (14 oz) can artichoke hearts, drained, chopped
1/2 c mayonnaise 
1/2 c grated Parmesan cheese
1 tsp (3.3 g) onion power
1 tsp (2.8 g) garlic powder
1/2 tsp (1.1 g) pepper
1 (17.3 oz) pkg frozen puff  pastry
directions:
Drain spinach well, press between layer of paper towels. 

Stir together spinach, artichoke hearts, and next 5 ingredients. 

Thaw puff pastry at room temperature for 30 minutes. Unfold pastry and place on a lightly floured surface on heavy-duty plastic wrap. Spread 1/4 spinach mixture evenly over pastry sheet, leaving a 1/2 inch border. 

Pull up pastry jelly roll fashion, Pressing seal seam; wrap in heavy duty plastic wrap. Repeat procedure with remaining pastry and spinach mixture. Freeze 30 min. 

Cut into 1/2 inch thick slices (roll may be frozen up to 3 months. 

Bake 400 F for 20 minutes. Yields 4 dozen.
notes:
Web summary (food.com, 1 review, no star figure shown). A make-ahead pinwheel appetizer: the familiar spinach-artichoke dip mixture, bound with mayonnaise and Parmesan and seasoned only with onion powder, garlic powder and pepper, is spread thin over sheets of frozen puff pastry, rolled jelly-roll style, firmed in the freezer and then sliced into rounds. Freezing before slicing is the step that makes it work - a soft roll smears when you cut it, a firm one gives clean spirals. The logs keep up to three months frozen, so the whole thing can be built weeks ahead and baked straight from the freezer for a party. The food.com poster, Debbwl, credits the Complete Southern Cookbook as the original.

What readers report: One review only, and it carries a real warning worth keeping: after about a week in the freezer the rolls wept a greenish oil while thawing, so the baked slices tasted fine but looked unappealing. The practical reading is to freeze just long enough to firm the logs for slicing rather than storing them for weeks, or to slice and bake from a shorter freeze.

Note on the source: Ingredient-for-ingredient match with the family card including the oddly specific 17.3 oz puff pastry package; only the garlic powder differs trivially (family 1 tsp, page 3/4-1 tsp). Note the true original is cited on the page as the Complete Southern Cookbook, so a human may prefer to record that book rather than the food.com repost. Gram conversions: 10 oz frozen chopped spinach = 283 g, 14 oz can artichoke hearts = 397 g, 1/2 cup mayonnaise = 110 g, 1/2 cup grated Parmesan = 50 g, 17.3 oz puff pastry = 490 g.

claude_opt.changes: If freezing logs longer than about a week, expect a harmless greenish oil to weep out on thawing — bake anyway, only appearance is affected, taste and texture are unchanged. No prep change needed.

name: Spinach Lasagna with Fennel Sausage
ingredients:
FOR THE PASTA:
3 ounces (85 g) raw washed and stemmed spinach leaves, shredded (2 cups packed)
2 eggs
½ teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
2 tablespoons (27 g) olive oil
3 cups (360 g) all-purpose flour
FOR THE FILLING:
2 pounds (907 g) washed and stemmed spinach leaves
12 ounces (340 g) fresh ricotta cheese
1 teaspoon (2.0 g) freshly grated lemon zest
1 teaspoon (2.0 g) fennel seed, crushed
Salt and pepper
1 ¼ pounds (567 g) Italian fennel sausage, sweet or hot, removed from casings
2 ½ cups (225 g) grated Parmesan cheese
FOR THE BÉCHAMEL:
4 tablespoons (57 g) unsalted butter, plus more for pan
¼ cup (30 g) all-purpose flour
5 cups (1.2 kg) whole milk or half-and-half, plus more as needed
1 bay leaf
Pinch of cayenne
Pinch of grated nutmeg
FOR THE TOMATO SAUCE:
1 tablespoon (14 g) olive oil
2 small garlic cloves, grated
A small handful fresh basil leaves or sprigs, more for garnish
3 cups (750 g) tomato purée, preferably Italian
4 tablespoons (57 g) unsalted butter, diced in small pieces
directions:
Make the pasta: Combine spinach, eggs, salt and olive oil in a blender or food processor and purée until smooth. Transfer to a mixing bowl and stir in flour. Knead mixture into a soft dough. If sticky, add a little more flour. Form into a ball, wrap in plastic, and set aside to rest while you prepare the other elements.

Make the filling: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add spinach and let wilt for a few seconds. Drain spinach in a colander and rinse well with cold water. Squeeze spinach dry and chop roughly.

Put ricotta in a mixing bowl and stir in chopped spinach. Stir in lemon zest and crushed fennel seed. Season to taste with salt and pepper.

Set a large skillet over medium-high heat and add sausage meat. Cook, breaking up with a spatula, until crumbled. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until just cooked through. Transfer to a bowl and let cool.

For the béchamel, melt butter in a large saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in flour and let cook for about 1 minute, stirring; do not let mixture brown.

Whisk in milk 1/2 cup at a time, letting sauce thicken after each addition. Add bay leaf, cayenne and nutmeg and continue cooking over low heat, whisking frequently, for about 10 minutes, to create a smooth sauce. Season to taste with salt and pepper. Thin with a little more milk if necessary; consistency should be that of a not-too-thick milkshake. If needed, strain sauce to remove lumps. Keep warm in a double boiler to prevent thickening.

Make the tomato sauce: In a saucepan, heat the olive oil over medium heat. Add garlic and basil and let sizzle without browning, 1 minute or less. Add tomato purée and bring to a simmer. Season to taste with salt and pepper. Cook for about 5 minutes, until slightly thickened. Remove from heat, pull out the basil leaves, and whisk in butter. Set aside.

Roll out the pasta: Set up a pasta machine and divide the dough into 5 roughly equal pieces. Roll each piece into a thin sheet of pasta about 12 inches long. Rolling twice at the second-to-last setting on the machine should give you the right thickness. Set aside on baking sheets, dust lightly with flour and keep covered with a slightly damp kitchen towel to prevent them from drying out.

Butter a medium-large baking dish, not larger than 9 by 13 inches. Heat oven to 375 degrees.

Cook the pasta: Have a large pot of salted boiling water on the stove and a large bowl of ice water nearby. One by one, place pasta sheets in boiling water to par-cook for about 1 minute, leaving pasta quite firm. Using tongs or a spider, lift pasta out and plunge into ice water. Lift out and lay on a clean kitchen towel to blot. Cut into two pieces.

As the pasta is cooked, assemble the lasagna: Place 2 sheets cooked pasta side by side, in the bottom of the baking dish. Spread pasta with 1/2 cup béchamel and dot with one-quarter of the ricotta mixture. Sprinkle over one fourth of crumbled sausage and 1/2 cup grated Parmesan. Repeat process for each layer. You will have 4 layers. Finish with 2 sheets of pasta. Spread top with 1/2 cup béchamel and sprinkle with remaining Parmesan. (The lasagna can be made up to this point up to 1 day in advance, covered and refrigerated.)

Cover with foil and bake about 30 minutes, until lasagna is bubbling. (If baking a refrigerated lasagna, this will take longer, up to 60 minutes.) Remove foil and bake uncovered for about 15 minutes, until lightly browned on top. Let lasagna rest for 10 to 15 minutes before cutting.

Just before serving, reheat tomato sauce. To serve, cut lasagna into 3- or 4-inch squares. With a spatula, transfer each serving to individual plates. Spoon about ½ cup tomato sauce around each serving. Garnish with basil leaves.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (158)). A from-scratch holiday lasagna, pasta included, that the headnote openly calls a time-consuming project worth doing - ideally with a helper or spread across two days. Store-bought fresh or dried noodles and your own tomato sauce are sanctioned shortcuts. The result is described as delicate and rich enough that small portions are right.

What readers report: Comment volume is low, so vote counts are small. The most-voted note (14) says the fresh pasta sheets do not need pre-cooking - they cook through in the sauce - though a 10-vote comment from someone who has made it two Christmases running recommends cooking them and, more usefully, says the bechamel needs only 4 cups of milk rather than 5, as 5 is too loose. An 8-vote note suggests crushed fennel seeds added to the filling to echo the sausage, plus sauteed mushrooms or carrots. Another swaps broccoli rabe into the filling, blanching chopped stems first and the leaves a minute later. Several cooks confirm the time commitment is real.

Note on the source: only 39 comments, so vote counts are in single/low double digits

makeahead: The lasagna can be made up to this point up to 1 day in advance, covered and refrigerated.)

claude_opt.changes: Cut the bechamel milk to 4 cups (976 g) instead of 5 — a cook who made this two Christmases running found 5 cups too loose; easy to thin further later if needed.

name: Split Pea Soup with Crispy Kielbasa
ingredients:
Good olive oil
2 cups (178 g) chopped leeks, white and light green parts, spun-dried (2 leeks)
1 1/2 cups (240 g) chopped yellow onion (1 large)
2 cups (256 g) (1/2-inch) diced, scrubbed carrots (3 large)
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) minced garlic (3 cloves)
1 pound (454 g) dry green split peas
8 cups (1.9 kg) good chicken stock, preferably homemade
1 smoked ham hock
8 fresh thyme sprigs, tied with kitchen twine
2 large fresh bay leaves
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
12 ounces (340 g) smoked kielbasa, halved lengthwise and sliced diagonally in 1/4-inch-thick pieces
Minced fresh parsley, for serving
directions:
Heat 1/4 cup olive oil in a large (11 to 12-inch) pot or Dutch oven, such as Le Creuset, over medium-high heat. Add the leeks, onion, and carrots and cook for 7 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until tender and starting to brown. Stir in the garlic and cook for one minute. Stir in the peas to coat with oil and cook for one minute. Add 8 cups of the chicken stock, 2 cups water, the ham hock, thyme bundle, bay leaves, 2 teaspoons salt, and 1 teaspoon pepper. Bring to a boil, lower the heat, and simmer, partially covered, for 1 1/4 hours, stirring occasionally, until the peas are very tender and falling apart. After 45 minutes, stir more frequently, scraping the bottom of the pot to be sure the soup doesn’t burn.

Discard the thyme bundle, bay leaves, and ham hock. Transfer 2 cups of the soup to the bowl of a food processor fitted with the steel blade and purée. Return the purée to the pot, adding more chicken stock or water if the soup is too thick.

To serve, heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a medium (10 to 11-inch) sauté pan over medium heat. Add the kielbasa and sauté for 5 to 6 minutes, tossing occasionally, until the kielbasa is browned. Serve the soup hot with the kielbasa and parsley sprinkled on top.

Make ahead: Reheat the soup over low heat, adding chicken stock or water to thin.
description: 2/23 Followed the recipe pretty exactly. Added a touch of Worcestershire and perhaps were heavy on the onions. Came out really nice. Very comfort-foody, especially with the kielbasa.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten's grown-up version of the canned split pea soup with cut-up hot dogs she ate as a child. Green split peas simmer with leeks, onion, carrot, garlic, a smoked ham hock, thyme and bay until they collapse into a creamy base, and sliced kielbasa is crisped separately so it stays browned rather than going soft in the pot. The contrast of smooth soup and crisp sausage is the whole point of the dish.

Note on the source: AMP URL; duplicate of the Parade entry; no comments

Web summary (parade.com). Ina Garten rebuilds a childhood favourite that used to come out of a can, replacing it with a from-scratch pot of green split peas simmered with leeks, carrots, onion and a smoked ham hock. The hock does the seasoning work that canned soup gets from additives, giving smoke and body as the peas break down. Crisped kielbasa goes on top so there is something with bite against the creamy base. She notes it freezes well and that you thin it with extra stock on reheating, since it thickens as it sits.

Note on the source: Parade reprint of the Food Network recipe; no comments

Merged September 2026: this entry absorbed a duplicate previously filed as "Split Pea Soup". Every cook's note from both copies is kept above.

name: Spring Green Spaghetti Carbonara
ingredients:
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
12 ounces (340 g) spaghetti, such as De Cecco
½ pound (227 g) snow peas, julienned lengthwise
1 cup (145 g) shelled fresh peas (1 pound in the pod), or frozen peas
12 to 14 thin asparagus, bottom third discarded and tips sliced in 2-inch pieces
2 tablespoons (27 g) good olive oil
8 ounces (227 g) small-diced pancetta
½ cup (119 g) heavy cream
2 extra-large eggs
2 extra-large egg yolks
¾ cup (68 g) freshly grated Italian Parmesan cheese, plus extra for serving
5 scallions, white and green parts, thinly sliced diagonally
¼ cup (12 g) minced fresh chives, plus extra for serving
Zest and juice of 1 lemon
directions:
Bring a large pot of water with 2 tablespoons salt to a boil. Add the spaghetti and cook for 8 minutes, stirring occasionally. Reserve a cup of the pasta water, then add the snow peas, fresh peas, and asparagus to the spaghetti and cook for 2 minutes longer. Drain the pasta and vegetables together.

Meanwhile, heat the oil in a medium (10 to 11-inch) sauté pan over medium heat, add the pancetta, and cook for 7 to 9 minutes, stirring occasionally, until browned. Transfer the pancetta to a plate lined with paper towels and set aside.

While the pancetta cooks, fill a large bowl with the hottest tap water and set aside to heat the bowl. Just before you drain the pasta, pour the water out of the bowl. Put the cream, eggs, egg yolks, and ¼ cup of the reserved pasta water into the bowl and whisk to combine. Immediately, add the hot pasta and vegetables and toss with tongs for a full minute or two, until the pasta absorbs the sauce. Add enough reserved hot pasta water to keep the sauce creamy. Add the ¾ cup Parmesan, the scallions, chives, lemon zest and juice, 1 tablespoon salt, and 1 teaspoon pepper and toss well. Add the pancetta, sprinkle with salt, and serve hot sprinkled with extra chives and Parmesan.
description: 5/21. Springy. Tried sugar snap peas for both. Too tough. Do snow peas alone if you cant get shelling peas.  Or just asparagus which is great. Needed to cook it on the stove to make the eggs set. Pancetta delish.
notes:
Web summary (barefootcontessa.com). From Ina Garten's Modern Comfort Food, this is carbonara loaded with spring vegetables: julienned snow peas, shelled fresh peas and thin asparagus blanched with the pasta. Pancetta, whole eggs plus extra yolks, cream and Parmesan make the sauce, with lemon zest and juice, scallions and chives cutting the richness. The page itself carries no explanatory headnote.

Note on the source: barefootcontessa.com pages carry no headnote or comments section

claude_opt.changes: Your 5/21 note already found both fixes: finish on the stove (matches the standard carbonara trick of gentle reheat, not bowl heat alone) and skip sugar snaps for snow peas or asparagus.

name: Sticky Buns
ingredients:
For the dough:
1 pkg dry yeast
1/4 c. (59 g) warm water
1 c. (244 g) scalded milk
1/4 c. (51 g) shortening
1/4 c. (50 g) sugar
1 t. (6.0 g) salt
3 1/4 - 3 1/2 c. (390-420 g) flour
1 beaten egg

For the filling:
2 T. (28 g) melted butter
1/2 c. (100 g) sugar
2 t. (5.2 g) cinnamon

For the topping:
1 c. (213 g) brown sugar, divided
1/2 c. (114 g) butter, divided
2 T. (41 g) corn syrup, divided
2/3 c. (87 g) nuts, divided
directions:
For the dough:
Soften yeast in water. Set aside. Combine hot milk, shortening, sugar, and salt. Cool till lukewarm. Add 1 c. flour. Beat well. Beat in yeast and egg. Gradually add remaining flour to form soft dough beating well. Brush top lightly with soft shortening. Cover dough and let rise until doubled, 1 1/2 - 2 hours. Punch down. Divide in half. Roll each piece into a 12 x 8 inch rectangle.

For the filling:
Brush each rectangle with 2 T. melted butter. Combine 1/2 c. sugar, 2 t. cinnamon. Sprinkle over each half. Start with long side, and roll up, jelly roll style. Cut each log into 8 slices to make 16 rolls total. 

Preheat oven to 375 degrees.

For the topping:
In each of 2 loaf pans (9 x 5") mix 1/2 c. brown sugar, 1/4 c. butter, 1 T. corn syrup. Heat slowly, stirring frequently until blended. Remove from heat, sprinkle 1/3 c. nuts over each pan. Top with rolls, cut side down. Cover and let rise until doubled, 35-45 mins. 

Bake at 375 for about 25 minutes. Cool 2-3 mins. Invert, remove pans.
notes: Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Yeast is proofed in unspecified-temp water; specify 105-110°F so it activates without killing it. Otherwise dough and caramel-topping technique already match King Arthur's modern method.

name: Strawberry Eton Mess
ingredients:
5 ounces (142 g) vanilla meringue cookies
1 1/2 pounds (680 g) fresh strawberries
2 teaspoons (4.0 g) lime zest plus 1 tablespoon lime juice
2 to 4 tablespoons (14-29 g) confectioners’ sugar
2 cups (476 g) cold heavy cream
directions:
Transfer the meringue cookies to a large, resealable plastic bag. Use a rolling pin to lightly crush the cookies. (You should have pieces of varying sizes.)

Trim the berries, discarding the greens. Halve or quarter 1 pound of the strawberries; add to a medium bowl. Blend or mash the remaining 1/2 pound strawberries until you have a chunky purée. Add the strawberry purée, lime zest, lime juice and 2 to 3 tablespoons confectioners’ sugar to the chopped strawberries and toss to coat. (The better the strawberries, the less sugar you’ll need.)

In a large bowl, beat the cream with 1 tablespoon confectioners’ sugar with an electric mixer on medium-high until whipped cream holds stiff peaks. Fold the crumbled meringue into the whipped cream.

Starting and ending with the strawberry mixture, layer it with the cream mixture in individual serving dishes (preferably clear cups, bowls or jars), creating as many layers as you like. Serve immediately.
description: 7/24 Delicious. Used homemade meringues instead of cookies.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (930)). The traditional British assembly of fresh fruit, whipped cream and crushed meringue, pitched here as a hot-weather dessert with almost no cooking. Store-bought meringue cookies are explicitly fine, which reduces it to a mixing job. Lime zest and juice are added for a sweet-tart edge, with lemon offered as an alternative.

What readers report: The highest-voted comments (229 and 81 votes) are a pointed objection to other readers who substitute cookies or cake for the meringue: without meringue it is a trifle, not an Eton mess, and they urge anyone wanting that to use a different recipe. A 135-vote note confirms the classic form is meringue, whipped cream and strawberries. On execution, a 122-vote comment halved the recipe for two but accidentally used the full tablespoon of lime juice and found the extra acid a marked improvement, implying the stated amount is conservative. Fruit swaps that work: raspberries, peaches, and blueberries heated until they pop for the syrup with more raw berries folded in. Trader Joe's is named as a source for meringue cookies.

name: Strawberry Jam
ingredients:
You will need
5 cups (720 g) crushed strawberries (about 3 lbs)
1/4 cup (61 g) lemon juice
6 Tbsp (60 g) Ball ® RealFruit™ Classic Pectin or 1 box Fruit Jell
7 cups (1.4 kg) granulated sugar
directions:
Prepare boiling water canner. Heat jars in simmering water until ready for use. Do not boil. Wash lids in warm soapy water and set bands aside.

Crush strawberries one layer at a time.

Combine strawberries and lemon juice in a 6- or 8-quart saucepan. Gradually stir in pectin. Bring mixture to a full rolling boil that can not be stirred down, over high heat, stirring constantly.

Add entire measure of sugar, stirring to dissolve. Return mixture to a full rolling boil. Boil hard 1 minute, stirring constantly. Remove from heat. Skim foam if necessary.

Ladle hot jam into a hot jar leaving a ¼ inch headspace. Remove air bubbles. Wipe jar rim. Center lid on jar and apply band, adjust to fingertip tight. Place jar in boiling water canner. Repeat until all jars are filled.

Process jars 10 minutes, adjusting for altitude. Turn off heat, remove lid, let jars stand 5 minutes. Remove jars and cool 12-24 hours. Check lids for seal, they should not flex when center is pressed.

Clean exterior of jars and lids. Store jam in a cool, dry, dark area for up to one year.
description:
Yield is about 64 oz of jam. 

Latest Ball recipe has 6 c. sugar, rather than 7 c. as here. We have not had good success scaling this recipe up or down.

Pick the medium box at Larriland. It provides enough berries for more than two of this recipe. We used 3 lb 5 oz of berries for on recipe, slightly more than 2 qts apparently

ahead: Remove jars and cool 12-24 hours.

claude_opt.changes: Your notes already caught the 7c-vs-6c sugar mismatch and no-good-scaling problem — trust the current 6-cup Ball ratio. Add 1/2 tsp butter at the boil to cut foam, per Ball's own tip, skipping the skim step.

name: Strawberry Nut Bread
ingredients:
2 c. (288 g) frozen unsweetened strawberries
3 c. (360 g) + 2 tb. flour
2 c. (400 g) sugar
1 tb. cinnamon
1 tsp. (6.0 g) salt
1 tsp. (4.6 g) baking soda
1 1/4 c. (272 g) oil
4 eggs, beaten
1 1/4 c. (136 g) chopped pecans
directions:
Preheat oven to 350.

Place strawberries in bowl and sprinkle with a few spoonfuls of sugar. Butter and flour 2 9x5 inch loaf pans. Combine flour, sugar, cinnamon, salt and baking soda in bowl. Mix well.

Blend oil and eggs into strawberry mixture. Add this to four mixture and stir in nuts. Mix until just moist.

Divide batter into pans. Bake until tester inserted in center comes out clean, 50-60 minutes.
notes:
Web summary (bettycrocker.com, No star rating or review count shown on the page). Betty Crocker pitches this as the quick bread that beats banana bread at its own game. It is an oil-and-egg batter rather than a creamed one, with a full tablespoon of cinnamon and no leavening but baking soda - the soda works against the acid of the strawberries, which is why the fruit has to go in juice and all rather than being patted dry. Two cups of sugar for two loaves makes it firmly a sweet bread, close to cake, and the nuts are what keep it from reading as one-note.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS - the Betty Crocker page shows no reader comment section. The family's card supplies the technique the published version leaves out: sprinkle the frozen berries with a few spoonfuls of sugar and let them sit while you assemble, blend the oil and eggs into the strawberry mixture rather than the other way around, and stir the wet into the dry only until just moist. Butter and flour two 9x5 pans; 50-60 minutes at 350F.

Note on the source: MEDIUM. The family card carries no source, and this recipe circulates widely in church and community cookbooks, so this cannot be proved to be where Robert's copy came from. But the fingerprint matches Betty Crocker's exactly on every distinctive line: 2 cups sugar, 1 1/4 cups oil, 4 eggs, 3 teaspoons (= 1 tablespoon) cinnamon, 1 teaspoon baking soda as the only leavening, 1 teaspoon salt, frozen strawberries. The two differences are trivial home-baker drift - the card writes 3 cups plus 2 tablespoons flour against Betty Crocker's flat 3 cups, and 1 1/4 cups pecans against 1 cup nuts. Gram conversions: 2 c sugar = 400 g, 1 1/4 c vegetable oil = 273 g, 3 c + 2 Tbsp all-purpose flour = 391 g, 1 Tbsp cinnamon = 8 g, 1 1/4 c chopped pecans = 138 g, 16 oz frozen strawberries = 454 g.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. The family card already carries the technique Betty Crocker's own page omits — sugar the berries, blend wet into the fruit, mix dry in only until just moist — and no note or comment flags a problem.

name: Stuffed Mushrooms
ingredients:
1 lb. (454 g) Jimmy Dean's spicy sausage
8 oz. (227 g) cream cheese
1 large container stuffing mushrooms (cleaned)
directions: Brown sausage. Drain well on paper towels. Mix with cream cheese using hands. Remove stems of mushrooms. Stuff. Bake at 350 for 12-15 minutes. Put under broiler for 2-3 minutes. Can freeze left over mixture.

claude_opt.changes: Raw sausage is browned only by eye ('drain well'); check with a thermometer to 160°F before mixing with cream cheese, since the filling gets just 12-15 min more baking.

name: Summer Italian Pasta Salad
ingredients:
1 16-oz. (454 g) pkg. Trio rotini pasta (about 5 1/2 c. dry)
1/3-1/2 c. (30-45 g) grated parmesan cheese
1-2 8-oz. (227 g) bottles Seven Seas Viva Italian Dressing
3 c. (273 g) broccoli florets

4-6 oz. (113-170 g) cubed mozzarella cheese, optional
4-6 oz. (113-170 g) pepperoni slices, optional
directions: Cook pasta according to package directions; drain. Rinse with cold water to cool quickly; drain. Mix all ingredients in a large bowl. Refrigerate several hours before serving.

claude_opt.changes: Dress in two stages: toss pasta with half the Viva dressing before chilling, add the rest just before serving. Pasta absorbs dressing over hours and dries out otherwise.

name: Summer Pasta with Zucchini, Ricotta and Basil
ingredients:
Extra-virgin olive oil
1 small onion, finely diced
2 pounds (907 g) zucchini, sliced into 1/4-inch-thick pieces (for larger zucchini, cut in half lengthwise before slicing)
Salt and pepper
2 garlic cloves, minced, or 2 tablespoons (17 g) chopped green garlic
1 ounce basil, about 2 cups loose leaves
1 pound (454 g) ziti or other dry pasta
8 ounces ricotta, about 1 cup (see recipe)
Pinch of crushed red pepper
Zest of 1 lemon
2 ounces grated Parmesan, pecorino or a mixture, about 1 cup, plus more for serving
directions:
Put a pot of water on to boil. In a large skillet over medium-high heat, cook the onions in 3 tablespoons olive oil until softened, 5 to 8 minutes. Reduce heat as necessary to keep onions from browning. Add zucchini, season generously with salt and pepper, and continue cooking, stirring occasionally until rather soft, about 10 minutes. Turn off heat.

Meanwhile, use a mortar and pestle to pound garlic, basil and a little salt into a rough paste (or use a mini food processor). Stir in 3 tablespoons olive oil.

Salt the pasta water well and put in the pasta, stirring. Boil per package instructions but make sure to keep pasta quite al dente. Drain pasta, reserving 1 cup of cooking water.

Add cooked pasta to zucchini in skillet and turn heat to medium-high. Add 1/2 cup cooking water, then the ricotta, crushed red pepper and lemon zest, stirring to distribute. Check seasoning and adjust. Cook for 1 minute more. Mixture should look creamy. Add a little more pasta water if necessary. Add the basil paste and half the grated cheese and quickly stir to incorporate. Spoon pasta into warm soup plates and sprinkle with additional cheese. Serve immediately.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (15,393)). A deliberately plain summer pasta built on garden or market zucchini, fresh ricotta and basil. The headnote's main instruction is about shopping rather than technique: seek out good artisanal ricotta, because with this few components the quality of each one shows.

What readers report: The top note (1,349 votes) changes the method: combine the ricotta, red pepper flakes and lemon zest in a large bowl with enough pasta water to loosen them into a sauce before the pasta goes in, rather than adding them to the pan. A 1,144-vote comment says to cook the garlic together with the onions - it will not burn since everything is sweating - and treats the dish as a template open to variation. Two independent notes (643 and 456 votes) push for more browning and more seasoning: let some onion and zucchini go past soft to genuinely caramelized, do not skimp on the red pepper flakes, and double the lemon zest. A 404-vote comment complains the written steps are fussier than the dish warrants and needs constant re-reading.

name: Summer Shrimp Scampi with Tomatoes and Corn
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) large shrimp, peeled and deveined
Kosher salt and black pepper
2 tablespoons (27 g) extra-virgin olive oil
1 pint (298 g) cherry or grape tomatoes
2 cups (308 g) fresh or frozen corn kernels (from 4 ears)
5 garlic cloves, minced
½ teaspoon (0.9 g) red-pepper flakes
¼ cup (59 g) dry white wine
2 tablespoons (30 g) fresh lemon juice (from 1 lemon), plus wedges for serving (optional)
5 tablespoons (71 g) unsalted butter, cut into 5 pieces
3 tablespoons (11 g) chopped parsley or chives, or torn basil leaves
directions:
Pat the shrimp very dry and season with salt and pepper. In a large (12-inch) skillet, heat the olive oil over medium-high. Add the shrimp and cook until pink and lightly golden in spots, 1 to 2 minutes per side. Use a slotted spoon to transfer the shrimp to a plate.

Add the tomatoes to the skillet, season with salt and pepper, and cook, stirring just once or twice, until they start to blister in spots, 3 to 4 minutes. Add the corn, season with salt and pepper, and cook, stirring just once or twice, until the tomatoes burst and the corn is golden in spots, 3 to 4 minutes.

Add the garlic and red-pepper flakes and cook, stirring, until you smell garlic, about 1 minute.

Reduce heat to medium, and add the wine and lemon juice, scraping any brown bits from the bottom of the pan. Cook until nearly evaporated, then add the butter and stir until melted. Add the shrimp and its juices and stir until warmed through. (If the sauce breaks and looks greasy, add 1 or 2 teaspoons of water and stir until emulsified.)

Remove from heat, add the herbs, season to taste with salt and pepper, and serve with extra lemon for squeezing over, if you like.
description: 7/21 Really delicious with fresh corn.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (6,136)). A one-skillet scampi that swaps the usual pasta context for peak-summer corn and tomatoes. A very hot pan is the point: the tomatoes blister and the corn caramelizes before everything gets coated in garlic-lemon butter. It is meant to stand alone as a meal, with pasta or bread optional.

What readers report: The highest-voted practical note (271 votes) restructures the sequence to cut prep fuss: start the tomatoes in olive oil, push them aside once blistered, add the corn to the cleared space, and carry on from there in the one pan. Protein swaps are well attested - scallops sauteed in butter instead of olive oil, with only another 2 tablespoons of butter at the end (138 votes), and lobster meat (100 votes) - all reported as working. A 158-vote comment cut the butter back for a lighter weeknight version and was happy with it, while conceding the full amount would taste better. A 114-vote variant skips cooking the vegetables entirely: marinate raw corn and tomatoes in a lemon, garlic and basil vinaigrette and fold in seared shrimp.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Shrimp already gets seared first and returned only at the end, which is the fix others need; your 7/21 note confirms the dish already works well as written.

name: Sun-Dried Tomato Pesto (Pesto Rosso)
ingredients:
1 cup (110 g) sun-dried tomatoes (see note below)
1/3 cup (48 g) almonds (unsalted, dry roasted)
2-3 cloves garlic
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) fresh rosemary leaves
1/2 teaspoon (1.4 g) kosher salt
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) cracked black pepper
1/2 teaspoon (0.9 g) crushed red pepper flakes , optional
3/4 to 1 cup (162-216 g) extra virgin olive oil
directions:
Place all ingredients in the bowl of a food processor and process until all ingredients are finely chopped. Stop the food processor and scrape the sides of the bowl once or twice.

Store, covered, in the refrigerator, for 5-7 days.

Serve tossed with pasta, spread onto crostini, as a sandwich spread, or with your favorite meats and seafood. If refrigerated and not heating for a recipe, let the Pesto Rosso return to room temperature before serving.
description: From Ruby Lai. June 2019. Enjoyed while camping at Big Sur.
notes:
I've tested batches of this recipe using both dry-packed and drained, oil-packed sun-dried tomatoes. When using oil-packed, I find I only need 3/4 cup olive oil to reach the thick, yet spreadable consistency we like best; when using dry-packed, I add a full cup.

Web summary (stripedspatula.com, 5 out of 5 from 31 ratings). Amanda Biddle writes this up as a Sicilian-style red pesto, where sun-dried tomatoes and almonds replace the basil and pine nuts of the Genoese original. She notes that Sicilian cooks vary it freely with different herbs or olives, and her own version is pared back to about five core ingredients blitzed in a food processor. The result is thick enough to spread rather than pour, which is what makes it work on bread and grilled meat as well as pasta.

What readers report: Readers report the recipe is highly tolerant of swaps. Cashews or pumpkin seeds stand in for the almonds without trouble, and fresh basil, sage or a generic Italian seasoning blend replace the rosemary depending on what is to hand. Several batch it and freeze portions for later, which appears to work well. Beyond pasta, the most common uses mentioned are as a spread for grilled proteins and as an appetiser on naan. One reviewer specifically valued it as a pantry recipe for when fresh herbs are not available. No one disputes the quantities or the olive oil range.

name: Surprise Meringues
ingredients:
2 egg whites
1/8 t. (0.8 g) salt
1/8 t. (0.4 g) cream of tartar
1 t. (4.2 g) vanilla
1/2 c. (100 g) sugar
1 6 oz. (170 g) package of semi-sweet chocolate chips
1/4 c. (29 g) chopped nuts
directions:
Preheat oven to 300.
Beat egg whites, salt, cream of tartar, and vanilla until soft peaks form. Add sugar gradually. Beat until peaks are stiff. Fold in bits and nuts. Line cookie sheet with parchment paper. Drop teaspoonfuls on paper. Bake in oven for 25 minutes. Dry on rack.
notes: Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: 300°F/25min risks browning outside before center sets. Drop to 275°F, bake about 35 min, then cool in the closed, turned-off oven to prevent weeping and get a fully crisp shell.

name: Swedish Nuts
ingredients:
1 lb. (454 g) shelled pecans (4 cups)
1/4 lb. (113 g) butter (8 Tablespoons)
3 egg whites at room temperature
dash of salt
1/2 c. (100 g) sugar
directions: 1 lb. shelled pecans (4 cups). Toast pecans in 325 degree oven until light brown (12-15 minutes). Cool on foil. In jelly roll pan (still warm) melt 1/4 lb. butter. Beat 3 egg whites at room temperature and dash of salt till foamy. Add 1/2 c. sugar gradually and beat to stiff peaks are formed. Fold in cooled nuts. Spread nut mixture over butter. Bake 30 minutes in oven at 325 stirring carefully about every 10 minutes or until light brown. Cool. Break into pieces. Store in an airtight container.

name: Swiss Chard Ravioli
ingredients:
FOR THE FILLING:
2 pounds (907 g) Swiss chard (more if the white stalks are large)
Kosher salt
4 tablespoons (57 g) (1/2 stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces
1/4 cup (40 g) finely chopped yellow onion
2 ounces (57 g) prosciutto, finely diced
1 cup (246 g) (8 ounces) whole-milk ricotta
1/2 cup (45 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese, plus more for serving
1/8 teaspoon (0.3 g) freshly grated nutmeg
1 large egg yolk
FOR THE PASTA:
1 1/2 cups (180 g) (about 7 1/2 ounces) flour
2 large eggs
directions:
For the filling: Discard the chard stems (or reserve them for another use). Rinse the leaves in several changes of cool water, making sure they are grit-free. Transfer the wet leaves to a large pot over medium-high heat; season lightly with salt. Cover and cook for about 5 minutes or until the leaves have softened and are somewhat wilted. Drain; when cool enough to handle, squeeze as much water out of the leaves as possible, then finely chop them.

Combine the butter and onion in a saute pan over medium heat; cook for about 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onion takes on a little color. Add the prosciutto and cook for about another minute, then add the chopped chard and cook for 3 minutes. Transfer the vegetable mixture to a mixing bowl; let it cool to room temperature, then add the ricotta, cheese and nutmeg. Mix well until the mixture is thoroughly combined. Taste, and add salt, as needed, then stir in the egg yolk until well incorporated.

For the pasta: Make a mound with the flour at the center of a clean work surface; Hazan prefers a wooden surface. Use your fingers to push the flour from the inside out to form a well in which the eggs will fit comfortably, making it wide enough to avoid a possible egg overflow.

Break the eggs into the center of the well. Use a fork to scramble the eggs until well blended, then introduce a little flour into the eggs by taking it from the bottom of the inside walls of the well. Continue until the mixture thickens enough to cling to the fork when you raise it up a bit. Use your fingers to squeeze the dough attached to the fork back into the well; set the fork down. Push a little less than 3 tablespoons of flour to the side, then use your hands to bring the rest into the center of the well. Mix together with your hands to begin forming a dough. If the dough feels sticky when you plunge a finger into it, add a little more flour. The dough should feel moist but not sticky. You might not have to work in all the flour, depending on how the dough feels and the climate of your kitchen.

Wrap the dough in plastic wrap; let it sit while you scrape off any bits of dough that have stuck to the counter. Reserve any remaining flour off to the side. Wash your hands thoroughly.

Unwrap the dough; knead it on the cleared surface until homogeneous and smooth. If it seems to stick to your hand or to the counter, add a little of the reserved flour. Conversely, if it feels too hard to knead, you might have added too much flour; try wetting your hands and kneading in that moisture. (If that does not seem to help, it’s probably easier and faster to start over.) If you don’t need to add flour while kneading, the process should take 5 to 6 minutes. Wrap the dough in plastic again and let it rest for at least 20 minutes or up to 3 hours at room temperature.

Unwrap the pasta dough and knead it a few times to incorporate the moisture that inevitably rises to the surface. The surface of the dough at this point should feel silky-smooth.

Cut the dough in half. Rewrap one of the pieces in the plastic wrap.

Flatten the remaining piece of dough as best you can with your hands, then put it through the rollers of the machine set at the widest setting. Fold the dough like a letter (in thirds), and put it through the rollers again, with the folds perpendicular to the rollers. Fold the dough in half and put it through one more time, again with the folds perpendicular to the rollers.

Adjust the rollers one notch closer together and put the piece of dough through once. Repeat, going down one notch at a time, until you reach the next-to-last setting. Cut the sheet of pasta dough crosswise in half, then put each half through the machine at the thinnest setting. By this point, each long sheet should be 4 to 5 inches wide. Place one sheet of dough on a clean dish towel and cover it with plastic wrap.

To form the ravioli, lay the uncovered sheet of pasta dough on your work surface, parallel to the edge. Use a spoon or pastry bag to portion 1-tablespoon dollops of the filling along the bottom half of the pasta sheet, spacing them about 1 inch apart. Fold the top half of the pasta sheet over the filling, then use your fingers to gently smooth the dough to get rid of any excess air in the pockets.

Use a pastry cutting wheel to cut along the bottom edge, the sides and in between each dollop of stuffing, so that you form about 8 square ravioli. The edges should be sealed by the cutting action of the pastry wheel; make sure they are, and pinch shut any loose edges with your fingers.

Place the ravioli on a clean, dry cloth, spacing them apart so they won't stick to each other.

Repeat using the covered sheet of pasta dough, adding the next batch of ravioli to the first one without letting them touch each other.

Unwrap the remaining portion of dough. Proceed with the rolling, filling and cutting to create a total of 30 to 32 ravioli.

For the best results, cook the ravioli within an hour of when they were made.

Bring a large pot of generously salted water to a boil over high heat. Working in batches as needed, add the ravioli and cover the pot to quickly bring it back up to a boil, stirring occasionally to keep the ravioli from separating. Once the water is boiling again, remove the lid, stirring periodically until the ravioli are done, about 5 minutes. To check, pinch the corner of one raviolo; it should feel soft but not mushy.

Use a Chinese skimmer or wide slotted spoon to transfer the cooked ravioli to a colander to drain; pouring them into a colander would be too rough on the pasta. Gently shake the colander to remove any excess water.

Transfer the ravioli to a platter, top with freshly grated Parmigiano-Reggiano cheese and serve warm.
notes:
Web summary (washingtonpost.com). Giuliano Hazan's ravioli, filled with Swiss chard, ricotta and prosciutto in a tender handmade pasta. The Washington Post drew it from his online Homemade Italian Pasta class and tested it with a plain sage-butter sauce, noting that a tomato sauce also works if used sparingly. They close with Hazan quoting his mother Marcella on keeping the sauce subordinate to the pasta.

name: Symmes Chocolate Cake
ingredients:
For the cake:
1/2 c. (102 g) Crisco
1 1/4 c. (250 g) sugar
2 eggs
1/2 t. (3.0 g) salt
1 t. (4.2 g) vanilla
2 oz. (57 g) baking chocolate

For the frosting:

1/3 c. (81 g) milk

1/8 t. (0.8 g) salt

directions:
Preheat oven to 350. 

For the cake:

name: Taco Salad
ingredients:
2 packages softened Philly cream cheese 
1 16 oz. (454 g) jar of Pace picante sauce (I usually use mild) 
3/4 fresh grated cheddar cheese - 3/4 lb. (340 g) or less
lettuce, cut into thin strips

directions:

name: Takeout-Style Sesame Noodles
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) noodles, frozen or (preferably) fresh
2 tablespoons (27 g) sesame oil, plus a splash
3 1/2 tablespoons (56 g) soy sauce
2 tablespoons (30 g) Chinese rice vinegar
2 tablespoons (30 g) Chinese sesame paste
1 tablespoon (16 g) smooth peanut butter
1 tablespoon (13 g) granulated sugar
1 tablespoon (6.0 g) finely grated ginger
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) minced garlic
2 teaspoons (9.1 g) chile-garlic paste, chile crisp or chile oil, or to taste
Half a cucumber, peeled, seeded and cut into 1/8-inch by 1/8-inch by 2-inch sticks
1/4 cup (36 g) chopped roasted peanuts
directions:
Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Add noodles and cook until barely tender, about 5 minutes. They should retain a hint of chewiness. Drain, rinse with cold water, drain again and toss with a splash of sesame oil.

In a medium bowl, whisk together the remaining 2 tablespoons sesame oil, the soy sauce, rice vinegar, sesame paste, peanut butter, sugar, ginger, garlic and chili-garlic paste.

Pour the sauce over the noodles and toss. Transfer to a serving bowl, and garnish with cucumber and peanuts.
notes:
Recommend as NYT most requested 2023. The Chinese sesame paste called for here is made of toasted sesame seeds; it is not the same as tahini, the Middle Eastern paste made of plain, untoasted sesame. But you could use tahini in a pinch. You need only add a little toasted sesame oil to compensate for flavor, and perhaps some peanut butter to keep the sauce emulsified.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (12,651)). Sam Sifton's version of the cold peanut-butter-based sesame noodles that became a Chinese-American standard in 1970s New York. The headnote credits the dish to Shorty Tang, who came from Sichuan via Taipei and opened Hwa Yuan in Chinatown in 1967; his family still serves it and has never released the recipe, so this is the Times' own reconstruction.

What readers report: The step people get wrong is the noodle quantity (1,121 votes): the pound called for is fresh or frozen noodles, not dried, so anyone reaching for a dried pound is badly overshooting the sauce. The most-voted note overall (2,086) says thick supermarket noodles give a close approximation when proper Chinese noodles are unavailable. A 1,541-vote comment from someone who has made it many times for crowds multiplies the sauce with a stick blender and uses only a minimal amount of the hottest element. An 868-vote note treats it as a picnic dish with condiments served alongside - shredded duck or chicken, tofu, cucumber, sweet pepper, scallion, jicama. For gram conversion: a 674-vote comment makes sesame paste from scratch with 200g toasted sesame seeds blended with 5-6 tablespoons olive oil.

Note on the source: gram datapoint: homemade sesame paste = 200 g toasted sesame seeds + 5-6 tbsp olive oil (674 votes)

name: Tarte Tatin
ingredients:
For the Tart Dough:
3/4 cups (90 g) flour
1/4 cup (28 g) cake flour
2 tablespoons (25 g) sugar
6 tablespoons (85 g) chilled butter, diced
2 tablespoons (26 g) chilled vegetable shortening
1/4 cup (59 g) ice water, or as needed
For the Tart Tatin:
6 Golden Delicious apples, cored, peeled and halved
1 lemon, zested and juiced
1 1/2 cups (300 g) sugar
6 tablespoons (85 g) unsalted butter
Whipped cream or vanilla ice cream, as accompaniment
directions:
In the bowl of a food processor fitted with a steel blade, place the flours, sugar and butter. Pulse 5 or 6 times in 1/2-second bursts to break up the butter. Add the shortening, turn on the machine and immediately add the ice water, pulsing 2 or 3 times. The dough should look like a mass of smallish lumps and should just hold together in a mass when a handful is pressed together. If the mixture is too dry, pulse in more water by droplets.

Turn the dough out onto the work surface and with the heel of your hand, rapidly and roughly push egg-size blobs into a 6-inch smear. Gather the dough into a relatively smooth cake, wrap in plastic and refrigerate at least 2 hours (or up to 2 days).

Slice the halved apples into 4 lengthwise wedges each, and toss in a large bowl with the lemon juice and zest and 1/2 cup sugar. Drain the apples after macerating 20 minutes.

In a 9-inch skillet melt the butter over high heat. Stir in the remaining sugar and cook until the syrup bubbles and caramelizes, and turns a brown color. Remove the pan from the heat and arrange a layer of apple slices in a neat pattern on the caramel in the skillet, then arrange the remaining apples neatly on top.

Return the pan to moderately high heat and cook for about 25 minutes, covering the pan after 10 minutes. Every few minutes press down on the apples and baste them with the exuded juices. When the juices are thick and syrupy, remove the pan from the heat.

On a lightly floured surface, roll the chilled dough into a circle, 3/16-inch thick and 1-inch larger than the top of the pan. Drape the dough over the apples, pressing the edge of the dough between the apples and the inside of the pan. Cut 4 small steam holes on the top of the dough. Bake until the pastry has browned and crisped, about 20 minutes.

Unmold the tart onto a serving dish (so the pastry is on the bottom), and serve warm or cold with whipped cream or vanilla ice cream, as desired.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Julia Child's upside-down apple tart: halved Golden Delicious apples caramelise in sugar and butter in a skillet, pastry goes over the top, and the whole thing is inverted after baking so the glossy caramelised fruit becomes the surface. Cooking the apples under the crust rather than over it means the pastry stays dry and crisp while the fruit sits in its own syrup. The dough is a mix of plain and cake flour with both butter and shortening.

Note on the source: no reader comments surfaced on page

claude_opt.changes: Cook the caramel to deep mahogany, not just brown — pale, under-caramelised sugar is tarte tatin's commonest failure and the one thing that separates a good one from a sweet one.

name: Tartine’s Country Bread
ingredients:
200 grams leaven
900 grams white-bread flour
100 grams whole-wheat flour, plus more for dusting
20 grams fine sea salt
100 grams rice flour
directions:
Make the starter: Combine 1,000 grams white-bread flour with 1,000 grams whole-wheat flour. Put 100 grams of warm water (about 80 degrees) in a small jar or container and add 100 grams of the flour mix. Use your fingers to mix until thoroughly combined and the mixture is the consistency of thick batter. Cover with a towel and let sit at room temperature until mixture begins to bubble and puff, 2 to 3 days.

When starter begins to show signs of activity, begin regular feedings. Keep the starter at room temperature, and at the same time each day discard 80 percent of the starter and feed remaining starter with equal parts warm water and white-wheat flour mix (50 grams of each is fine). When starter begins to rise and fall predictably and takes on a slightly sour smell, it’s ready; this should take about 1 week.(Reserve remaining flour mix for leaven.)

Make the leaven: The night before baking, discard all but 1 tablespoon of the mature starter. Mix the remaining starter with 200 grams of warm water and stir with your hand to disperse. Add 200 grams of the white-wheat flour mix and combine well. Cover with a towel and let rest at room temperature for 12 hours or until aerated and puffed in appearance. To test for readiness, drop a tablespoon of leaven into a bowl of room-temperature water; if it floats it’s ready to use. If it doesn’t, allow more time to ferment.

Make the dough: In a large bowl, combine 200 grams of leaven with 700 grams of warm water and stir to disperse. (Reserve remaining leaven for future loaves; see note below.)

Add 900 grams of white-bread flour and 100 grams of whole-wheat flour to bowl and use your hands to mix until no traces of dry flour remain. The dough will be sticky and ragged. Cover bowl with a towel and let dough rest for 25 to 40 minutes at room temperature.

Add 20 grams fine sea salt and 50 grams warm water. Use hands to integrate salt and water into dough thoroughly. The dough will begin to pull apart, but continue mixing; it will come back together.

Cover dough with a towel and transfer to a warm environment, 75 to 80 degrees ideally (like near a window in a sunny room, or inside a turned-off oven). Let dough rise for 30 minutes. Fold dough by dipping hand in water, taking hold of the underside of the dough at one quadrant and stretching it up over the rest of the dough. Repeat this action 3 more times, rotating bowl a quarter turn for each fold. Do this every half-hour for 2 1/2 hours more (3 hours total). The dough should be billowy and increase in volume 20 to 30 percent. If not, continue to let rise and fold for up to an hour more.

Transfer dough to a work surface and dust top with flour. Use a dough scraper to cut dough into 2 equal pieces and flip them over so floured sides are face down. Fold the cut side of each piece up onto itself so the flour on the surface remains entirely on the outside of the loaf; this will become the crust. Work dough into taut rounds. Place the dough rounds on a work surface, cover with a towel, and let rest 30 minutes.

Mix 100 grams whole-wheat flour and 100 grams rice flours. Line two 10- to 12-inch bread-proofing baskets or mixing bowls with towels. Use some of the flour mixture to generously flour towels (reserve remaining mixture).

Dust rounds with whole-wheat flour. Use a dough scraper to flip them over onto a work surface so floured sides are facing down. Take one round, and starting at the side closest to you, pull the bottom 2 corners of the dough down toward you, then fold them up into the middle third of the dough. Repeat this action on the right and left sides, pulling the edges out and folding them in over the center. Finally, lift the top corners up and fold down over previous folds. (Imagine folding a piece of paper in on itself from all 4 sides.) Roll dough over so the folded side becomes the bottom of the loaf. Shape into a smooth, taut ball. Repeat with other round.

Transfer rounds, seam-side up, to prepared baskets. Cover with a towel and return dough to the 75- to 80-degree environment for 3 to 4 hours. (Or let dough rise for 10 to 12 hours in the refrigerator. Bring back to room temperature before baking.)

About 30 minutes before baking, place a Dutch oven or lidded cast-iron pot in the oven and heat it to 500 degrees. Dust tops of dough, still in their baskets, with whole-wheat/rice-flour mixture. Very carefully remove heated pot from oven and gently turn 1 loaf into pan seam-side down. Use a lame (a baker’s blade) or razor blade to score the top of the bread a few times to allow for expansion, cover and transfer to oven. Reduce temperature to 450 degrees and cook for 20 minutes. Carefully remove lid (steam may release) and cook for 20 more minutes or until crust is a rich, golden brown color.

Transfer bread to a wire rack to cool for at least 15 minutes before slicing. The bottom of the loaf should sound hollow when tapped. Increase oven temperature to 500 degrees, clean out pot and repeat this process with the second loaf.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (2,129)). Chad Robertson's cult loaf from Tartine Bakery in San Francisco, adapted by the Times for a home kitchen: a tangy open crumb inside a blistered dark crust, raised entirely on a starter you build yourself. Allow roughly two weeks from nothing, or two days if your starter is already active. The headnote is candid that the outcome is not fully controllable - starter vigour, kitchen humidity, rise temperature and your own timing all shift the result.

What readers report: The most-voted note (599) is a source for a free starter by mail from the Oregon Trail Sourdough Preservation Society, sidestepping the two-week build. The recurring complaint (318 votes) is how much starter the method discards - most of it during the build, then all but a tablespoon for the bake - and a 235-vote comment says step 3's wording is what confuses people: the night before baking you keep only 1 tablespoon of mature starter and build the leaven from that. A 166-vote comment reports the loaves come out just as well without the three-plus hours of turn-and-fold, which is the most substantive disagreement with the method. A 255-vote reader put the whole schedule into a spreadsheet with date/time formulas to track the stages.

name: Tender and Easy Buttermilk Waffles
ingredients:
2 cups (240 g) all-purpose flour
2 tablespoons (25 g) white sugar
2 teaspoons (8.0 g) baking powder
1 teaspoon (4.6 g) baking soda
½ teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
2 cups (484 g) low-fat buttermilk
⅓ cup (76 g) melted butter
2 large eggs, lightly beaten
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) vanilla extract
directions:
Whisk flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and salt together in a bowl until evenly combined.

Whisk buttermilk and melted butter together in a separate bowl; whisk in eggs. Stir buttermilk mixture into flour mixture until just combined and batter is slightly lumpy; stir in vanilla extract.

Preheat a waffle iron according to manufacturer's instructions.

To cook each waffle, pour enough batter into the preheated waffle iron to reach 1/2 inch from the edge. Cook according to manufacturer's instructions.
description:
7/22 Delish!
12/23 Great again on new Cuisinart double waffle maker
4/24 yield is 6 waffles; used darkness indicator set ¾ way to max on double waffle maker; warmed buttermilk so that melted butter didn’t chunk up
notes:
You can heat the oven to about 250 degrees F (120 degrees C) to 275 degrees F (135 degrees C), and place a rack on a baking sheet to keep waffles warm as you make the whole batch.

Web summary (Allrecipes, 4.7 (528) / 404 reviews). Diana Perry's note is brief: she wanted waffles that come out crisp outside and tender inside without the fuss of separating eggs and beating the whites, and she points out they reheat well in a toaster for weekday mornings. The site adds that the batter comes together fast and that members like how quickly the waffles crisp back up in a toaster oven. There is no real technique discussion beyond stirring the wet into the dry only until the batter is still slightly lumpy.

What readers report: The top review (84 helpful, Sarah Jo) found the batter too thin when doubled and added an extra cup of all-purpose flour; she also used half whole wheat, which made the waffles sturdier. Thin batter is the recurring complaint, and others likewise add about half a cup more flour, sometimes with cream of tartar and cinnamon; a few go the other way and thin it further for upright irons. Half whole wheat flour is the most-reported substitution and works well, as does a 1-to-1 gluten-free flour blend (one reviewer used 280 g) with no added gum. Without buttermilk, people substitute 1/3 cup Greek yogurt or sour cream plus 2/3 cup milk per cup. Doubling the vanilla, or adding almond extract or cinnamon, is a common flavour tweak. On doneness, one reviewer warns to pull the waffles at medium brown, since going darker dries them out and toughens them; another reported them going dark before crisping.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Pull waffles at medium brown, not dark — several readers report darker waffles dry out and toughen. Your notes already solved the butter-clumping and yield issues; this doneness cue is the one gap.

name: Thai Green Curry
ingredients:
CURRY - USE ONE:
4 - 6 tbsp (64-96 g) Thai Green Curry Paste (Maesri best) OR (Note 1)
1 quantity homemade green curry paste (Note 1)
2 large garlic cloves , minced
2 tsp (4.0 g) fresh ginger , finely grated
1 tbsp (16 g) lemongrass paste (Note 2)
GREEN CURRY:
2 tbsp (27 g) vegetable oil
1 cup (250ml) chicken or vegetable broth, low sodium
400 g/14oz coconut milk , full fat (Note 4)
1 - 3 tsp (5.3-16 g) fish sauce *
1 - 3 tsp (4.2-13 g) white sugar *
1/8 tsp (0.8 g) salt *
6 kaffir lime leaves , torn in half (Note 5)
350 g/12 oz chicken thigh , skinless boneless, sliced (Note 6)
2 Japanese eggplants, , small, 1cm / 2/5" slices (Note 7)
1 1/2 cups (218 g) snow peas , small, trimmed
16 Thai basil leaves (Note 8)
Juice of 1/2 lime , to taste
GARNISHES:
Crispy fried Asian shallots , high recommended (Note 9)
Thai basil or cilantro/coriander , recommended
Green or red chillies slices , optional
Steamed jasmine rice
directions:
Heat oil in a heavy based skillet or pot over medium high heat.

Add curry paste (and garlic, ginger and lemongrass Extras, if using) and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until it mostly "dries out" - see video. Don't breath in the fumes!!

Add chicken broth and coconut milk, mix to dissolve paste.

Curry in a jar seasonings: Add 1 tsp fish sauce, 1 tsp sugar, no salt.

Homemade curry paste seasonings: Add 3 tsp fish sauce, 3 tsp sugar, 1/8 tsp salt.

Add kaffir lime leaves. Mix then bring to simmer.

Add chicken, stir then lower heat to medium so it's bubbling gently. Cook 7 minutes.

Add eggplants, cook 5 minutes until soft.

Taste sauce. Add fish sauce or salt for more saltiness, sugar for sweetness.

Add snow peas, cook 2 minutes until a bit softened, then stir through basil and lime juice. Sauce should have reduced but will still be a be on the thin side, not thick - that's how it's should be. DO NOT keep simmering - sauce will darken.

Serve curry over jasmine rice with garnishes of choice.
notes:
Web summary (recipetineats.com, 4.95 stars from 280 votes). Nagi Maehashi gets a thirty-minute green curry by either making the paste from scratch or, more commonly, taking a jarred paste such as Maesri and boosting it with fresh garlic, ginger and lemongrass. The step she insists on is frying the paste in oil before any liquid goes in: it blooms the aromatics and is the difference between a curry with depth and one that tastes flat. Coconut milk, a little broth, fish sauce, sugar and kaffir lime leaves finish it.

What readers report: The most repeated point is that the paste-boosting trick genuinely works, taking supermarket paste to something close to restaurant standard. Cooks report the recipe scales well for a crowd, and that chicken can be swapped for tofu, salmon, white fish or frozen mixed vegetables without changing the method. Several note the sauce is deliberately thinner than a red curry or a massaman, so do not expect it to reduce to a cling. A run of newer cooks found the full paste quantity too hot and cut it back; Maehashi's response is that green curry is meant to be the spiciest of the three, but that making the paste yourself gives you control over heat.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. Frying the paste before adding liquid is already the method here, and the 4-6 tbsp range already lets you dial heat down if the full amount runs too spicy.

name: The Best Italian-American Tomato Sauce
ingredients:
4 (28-ounce) cans whole peeled tomatoes, preferably imported D.O.P. San Marzano tomatoes (see notes)
1/4 cup (54 g) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for finishing
4 tablespoons (57 g) butter
8 cloves garlic, minced (about 3 tablespoons)
1 teaspoon (1.8 g) red pepper flakes
1 tablespoon (3.0 g) dried oregano
1 medium carrot, cut into large chunks
1 medium onion, split in half
1 large stem fresh basil
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
1 tablespoon (16 g) fish sauce, such as Red Boat (optional)
1/2 cup (30 g) minced fresh parsley or basil leaves (or a mix of the two)
directions:
Adjust oven rack to lower position and preheat oven to 300°F (165°C). Place tomatoes in a large bowl. Using your hands, crush the tomatoes by squeezing them in your fingers until pieces no larger than 1/2-inch remain. Transfer 3 cups of crushed tomatoes to a sealed container and reserve in the refrigerator until step 4.

Heat olive oil and butter over medium heat in a large Dutch oven until butter is melted. Add garlic and cook, stirring, until softened and fragrant but not browned, about 2 minutes. Add pepper flakes and oregano and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add tomatoes, carrot, onion, and basil, and stir to combine. Season lightly with salt and pepper. Bring to a simmer over high heat.

Cover Dutch oven with lid slightly ajar and transfer to oven. Cook, stirring once every 1 to 2 hours, until reduced by about half and darkened to a deep red, 5 to 6 hours (reduce oven temperature if the sauce is bubbling too rapidly or the browned bits begin to turn too dark).

Remove from oven. Using tongs, discard onion halves, carrots, and basil stems. Add reserved tomatoes to sauce and stir to combine. Add fish sauce, if using. Season generously with salt and pepper and stir in minced herbs along with additional olive oil as desired. Serve immediately, or allow to cool at room temperature, transfer to airtight containers, and refrigerate for up to 1 week. Sauce can also be frozen in sealed containers for up to 6 months. To reheat, warm very gently in a saucepan with 1/2 cup water, stirring until it all melts and heats through.
description: 8/24 Used with 6 lbs costo meatball pack and served at 90th birthday party. Didnt need to add water. Used 4 cans Cento San Marzano and didnt remove seeds. The meatballs and sauce were delicious. Perhaps a bit hotter than needed. Cut cayenne in half.
notes:
Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.7 (56) / 233 reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt set out to build the long-cooked Italian-American red sauce that restaurants used to stake their reputations on, and spent dozens of tests getting there. He starts with good canned whole peeled plum tomatoes crushed by hand for a chunky body, and blooms knife-chopped garlic, dried oregano and pepper flakes in a mix of olive oil and butter, arguing that the butter emulsifies more readily and makes the sauce creamier while hand-chopped garlic is coarse enough not to scorch. Sweetness comes from a whole carrot and a halved onion simmered in the pot and fished out later rather than from sugar. His key move is finishing the pot in a 300F oven with the lid cracked for five to six hours, which lets the surface caramelize gently and evenly with little stirring; a few cups of reserved raw crushed tomato stirred in at the end restores fresh flavor, and a splash of fish sauce adds savoriness.

What readers report: Several cooks report the reduction running faster than the recipe implies. One found his sauce nearly at paste stage after only three hours and had to add canned sauce to stretch it; another advises watching it closely and lowering the oven temperature as the liquid drops rather than trusting the full five-to-six-hour window, and notes that little visible bubbling early on is normal. One reviewer would hold back less raw tomato at the end, about two cups instead of three, because the full amount diluted the richness he had cooked all day for. The fish sauce draws the most substitution traffic: readers report soy sauce, soy plus Marmite, minced shiitake or MSG as alternatives, and one asks about miso. Other reported variations include an eight-hour sealed slow cooker, adding reduced red wine and sweet Italian sausage, and swapping small white peaches for the carrot.

Note on the source: Most featured comments are cut off at 'Read More', so only the visible text was used. Several reviews carry 2026 dates. Vote counts are all zero, so nothing could be ranked by helpfulness.

name: The Best Rolled Sugar Cookies
ingredients:
2 cups (400 g) white sugar
1 ½ cups (340 g) butter, softened
4 large eggs
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) vanilla extract
5 cups (600 g) all-purpose flour
2 teaspoons (8.0 g) baking powder
1 teaspoon (6.0 g) salt
directions:
Gather all ingredients.

Beat sugar and softened butter together in a large bowl with an electric mixer until smooth.

Beat in eggs and vanilla. Stir in flour, baking powder, and salt. Cover, and chill dough for at least 1 hour (or overnight).

Preheat the oven to 400 degrees F (200 degrees C).

Lightly dust a work surface with flour. Roll out dough to 1/4 to 1/2 inch thickness.

Cut into shapes with any cookie cutter. Place cookies 1 inch apart on ungreased baking sheets.

Bake in the preheated oven until cookies are lightly browned, 6 to 8 minutes. Carefully transfer cookies to a wire rack and cool completely before decorating.

Enjoy!
notes:
Web summary (Allrecipes, 4.5 (11,177) / 9,193 reviews). Submitter J Saunders presents this as the only rolled sugar cookie recipe she uses, and warns that anyone who tastes them will ask for a copy. She adds that she ices them with a confectioners' sugar and milk mixture thinned just enough to brush on with a pastry brush without running off the cookie. Allrecipes' editors (contributions by Vanessa Greaves) append a long technique section: cream the butter and sugar four to five minutes until pale and airy, keep the butter cool but pliable, whisk the dry ingredients separately, mix only until no dry streaks remain, and chill at least an hour so the cookies hold their shape. They also stress measuring flour by fluffing and spooning rather than packing, rolling to an even thickness, using parchment, spacing cutouts an inch apart, and loading only a fully cooled sheet.

What readers report: The most-voted review (7,789 helpful, Shannon Dailey) calls the dough reliable for cutouts but adds an extra cup of sugar and a teaspoon of vanilla, plus 1/4 to 1/2 cup more flour in humid climates, and dusts with powdered sugar rather than flour when it turns sticky. That extra sugar and vanilla is the most repeated fix; reviewers with 1,930 and 1,266 helpful votes also chill overnight, keep most of the dough refrigerated while working a quarter at a time, and freeze the cut shapes briefly so they hold their edges. One with 823 votes instead dropped an egg and a cup of flour for a more buttery cookie. Almond extract and citrus zest are common additions. Bake time is the usual mistake: it suits roughly 2-inch cutters, so larger ones need 12 to 13 minutes and thin ones only 8 to 9. Dissenters report dough too soft to roll even after overnight chilling.

Note on the source: Headnote is a mix of the submitter's short note and a long Allrecipes editorial section; both paraphrased. Several reviews are truncated with 'Read More' in the paste, so only visible text was used.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

ahead: Cover, and chill dough for at least 1 hour (or overnight).

claude_opt.changes: Bake time depends on cutter size: the written 6-8 minutes only suits ~2-inch cutters — large cutters need 12-13 minutes, thin ones 8-9. Also spoon-and-level the flour rather than packing to avoid tough dough.

name: The Silver Palate’s Chicken Marbella
ingredients:
1/2 cup (108 g) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 g) red wine vinegar
1 cup (174 g) pitted prunes
1/2 cup (68 g) pitted Spanish green olives
1/2 cup (71 g) capers, with a bit of juice
6 bay leaves
1 head of garlic, peeled and puréed
1/2 cup (28 g) fresh oregano, chopped, or 1/4 cup dried oregano
2 teaspoons (12 g) of salt
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) freshly ground pepper
2 chickens, 3 1/2 to 4 pounds (1.6-1.8 kg) each, quartered
1 cup (237 g) dry white wine
1 cup (213 g) brown sugar
2 tablespoons (7.5 g) finely chopped flat-leaf parsley
directions:
In a large bowl, combine the olive oil, vinegar, prunes, olives, capers and juice, bay leaves, garlic, oregano, salt and pepper. Add the chicken pieces and turn to coat. Refrigerate overnight.

Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Arrange the chicken in a single layer in a shallow roasting pan; spoon the marinade over it evenly. Pour in the wine and sprinkle the chicken with the brown sugar.

Bake until the thigh pieces yield clear yellow juice when pricked with a fork, 50 to 60 minutes, basting two or three times with the pan juices once the chicken begins to brown. (When basting, do not brush off the sugar. If the chicken browns too quickly, cover lightly with foil.)

Transfer the chicken pieces to a warm serving platter and top with the prunes, olives and capers; keep warm. Place the roasting pan over medium heat and bring the pan juices to a boil. Reduce to about 1/2 cup. Strain into a heatproof bowl, add the parsley and pour over the chicken. (Silver Palate skips this reduction step, and just pours some pan juice over the chicken and the rest in a bowl for those who want to add it at the table.)

To serve Chicken Marbella cold, cool to room temperature in cooking juices before tranfeering to a serving platter. If chicken has been covered and refrigerated, allow it to return to room temperature before serving. Spoon some if the reserved juice over chicken. 

When prepared with small drumstcks and wings, this recipe makes a delicious hors d’oeuvre. Travels well and makes excellent picnic fare.
description:
10/22 Delicious. Used a bit less sugar (maybe half) but otherwise followed the recipe as written. 

4/23 Used 2 4⅓ lb chickens. Had to cut breasts in half. Just barely fit in the large roasting pan. Cooked for 1 hour 15 minutes, seemed perfect. Added extra olives, Goya cocktail pitted manzanilla. Goya capers great. 

1/25 6 boneless skin-on breasts and six legs. Full amount of sauce. Mostly fresh oregano. 1 whole bag of prunes, somewhat extra. Cooked for 1 hour. No need to reduce sauce—there wasn’t very much. Really great. The breasts were tender and excellent!

Claude recommends: Couscous is a classic pairing and soaks up the sauce beautifully. Roasted baby potatoes, orzo, or a simple rice pilaf also work well. For something a bit more rustic, crusty bread to mop up the pan juices is hard to beat.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (5,957)). Christine Muhlke's framing of the Sheila Lukins and Julee Rosso dish from "The Silver Palate Cookbook" (1982), which reached the Times in a 2007 piece marking the book's 25th anniversary. The chicken marinates with prunes, olives, capers and oregano - a sweet-briny pairing that read as daring in the eighties and now reads as a standard.

What readers report: The most useful correction (1,328 votes) is a scaling error: this NYT version halves the original cookbook's ingredients except for the wine and the brown sugar, which stayed at full quantity - so the sugar on top is roughly double what it should be. A former Silver Palate kitchen cook confirms it (861 votes), saying the brown sugar was only ever a light dusting, and adds a technique note: crisp the skin a little before dusting. Two well-voted substitutions: dried apricots for the prunes with much less sugar, served with couscous and roast butternut (1,115 votes), and boneless thighs instead of bone-in pieces, which guests find easier and which shortens the roasting time (997 votes). The single highest-voted comment (2,447) is a request for a site feature, not recipe content.

Note on the source: top-voted comment by votes is a site feature request, not recipe content; real technique lead is the brown-sugar scaling error

name: Thomas Keller’s Butternut Squash Soup with Brown Butter
ingredients:
1 3-to-3 1/2-pound (1.6 kg) butternut squash
2 tablespoons (27 g) canola oil
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
2 sprigs sage
1 cup (89 g) thinly sliced leeks
1/2 cup (64 g) thinly sliced carrots
1/2 cup (80 g) thinly sliced shallots
1/2 cup (80 g) thinly sliced onions
6 garlic cloves, smashed
2 tablespoons (42 g) honey
6 cups (1.4 kg) vegetable stock, more if needed
Bouquet Garni made of 8 sprigs thyme, 2 sprigs Italian parsley, 2 bay leaves and 1/2 teaspoon (1.4 g) black peppercorns, all wrapped in a packet made of 2 green leek leaves
1/4 cup (58 g) crème fraîche
Freshly grated nutmeg
4 tablespoons (57 g) unsalted butter
1 tablespoon (3.0 g) minced chives
Extra-virgin olive oil
directions:
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Line a small baking sheet with aluminum foil. Cut the neck off the squash and set it aside. Cut the bulb in half and scoop out and discard seeds. Brush each half inside and out with about 1 1/2 teaspoons of the canola oil. Sprinkle the cavities with salt and pepper and tuck a sprig of sage into each. Place cut-side-down on the baking sheet and roast until completely tender, about 1 hour. Remove the squash from the oven and let cool, then scoop out and reserve the flesh (discard sage).

Meanwhile, using a paring knife, peel away the skin from the neck of the squash until you reach the bright orange flesh. Cut the flesh into 1/2-inch pieces (you should have about 4 cups).

Put the remaining canola oil in a stockpot over medium-high heat, add the leeks, carrots, shallots and onions and cook, stirring often, for about 6 minutes. Add the diced squash, garlic, 1 1/2 teaspoons salt, and 1/2 teaspoon pepper and cook gently for 3 minutes, reducing the heat as necessary to keep the garlic and squash from coloring. Stir in the honey and cook, stirring, for 2 to 3 minutes. Add the stock and bouquet garni, bring to a simmer and cook for 10 to 15 minutes or until the squash is tender.

Add the roasted squash and simmer gently for about 30 minutes for the flavors to blend. Remove from the heat and discard the bouquet garni. Transfer the soup to a blender, in batches, and purée. Strain the soup through a fine sieve into a bowl. Taste the soup and adjust the seasoning. Let the soup cool, then refrigerate until ready to serve.

Place the crème fraîche in a small chilled bowl and stir in nutmeg to taste. Whisk until the crème fraîche holds a shape. Cover and refrigerate.

Gently reheat the soup until just hot. If it is too thick, add a little more vegetable stock. Heat a medium skillet over high heat. When it is very hot, add the butter and rotate the skillet over the heat as necessary to brown the butter evenly, scraping up any bits that settle in the bottom. As soon as the butter is a hazelnut brown, pour it into the pot of soup -- keep a safe distance, it may sputter -- then stir.

Ladle the soup into six serving bowls. Top each with a dollop of crème fraîche. Grind some black pepper over the top and sprinkle on the chives. Drizzle a little olive oil over the top.
description: 1/24 Made according to recipe but without brown butter. Used chicken stock. It took 2½ hours. We strained it and the result was amazingly silky. Steph liked it, but Alan was not a fan because of that squashy flavor. Possibly making the soup with a just-picked squash would help?
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (5,973)). An adaptation of the butternut squash soup in Thomas Keller's "Bouchon," presented frankly as a four-hour undertaking that includes making your own vegetable stock. The payoff is a soup of unusual depth, finished by swirling in sizzling brown butter just before serving.

What readers report: The step that trips people up is the squash prep (541 votes): the recipe has you cut the neck off and roast only the bulb, then work with the raw neck in the next step, which reads as contradictory until you notice it. Two well-voted comments propose simplifying it - poke and roast the squash whole (670 votes), or split it lengthwise and roast both halves for more caramelization (400 votes), with the 400-vote commenter noting 25 years of making it this way despite the recipe's instruction. A 522-vote tip: do not throw away the thick paste left in the strainer; chill it and mix with Parmesan as ravioli filling. A 202-vote note keeps a freezer bag of vegetable scraps going so the stock step is not a separate shopping trip.
