name: Toasted Almond Biscotti
ingredients:
1 cup (143 g) whole blanched almonds
2 ¾ cups (330 g) flour, plus flour for work surface
Pinch of salt
½ teaspoon (2.3 g) baking soda
¾ teaspoon (3.0 g) baking powder
4 large eggs
1 cup (200 g) sugar
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) almond extract
directions:
Preheat oven to 350 degrees. Spread the almonds on a baking sheet, place in the oven and toast for about 15 minutes.

Meanwhile, sift the flour, salt, baking soda and baking powder together and set aside.

Beat the eggs lightly, just until they are blended in a mixing bowl with a whisk or in an electric mixer. Remove two tablespoons of the egg mixture to a small dish and set aside. Beat the sugar and almond extract into the remaining eggs until blended. Stir in the flour mixture to form a soft dough.

When the almonds are toasted, remove them from the oven and transfer them to a bowl. Line the baking sheet with parchment paper.

Divide dough in half and place one portion on well-floured work surface. With floured hands, pat into a six-inch square. Scatter half of almonds on dough and press them into surface. Roll dough into cylinder about 2 inches in diameter and 12 to 15 inches long. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet. Repeat with remaining dough. Brush the tops of both cylinders with the reserved egg.

Place in the oven and bake about 15 minutes, until golden and firm to the touch. Transfer to a cutting board and cut on an angle into slices one-half-inch thick. Return the slices to the baking sheet, standing them up, and return them to the oven. Bake another 20 minutes, until they are crisp and dry. Allow to cool completely before storing or serving.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (141)). 

What readers report: With only nine comments the votes are tiny, but they converge on one clear fault: the first bake is too short. Multiple cooks (5 votes, 2 votes and an unvoted note) found raw dough in the centre when they went to slice the log at the stated 15 minutes; one cites Jacques Pepin's biscotti as baking 25 minutes at 350F for the first bake and 30 to 40 for the second, and another added 10 minutes to the sliced cookies and found the flavour improved as well. A 4-vote comment credits the recipe with two genuine advantages over others: the almond-toasting method, and a dough that slices without crumbling, possibly because the oven temperature is lower. One cook doubled it using 1 1/2 cups almond flour plus 1 cup self-rising flour for a more tender result. A further objection is that the recipe never specifies which flour to use.

name: Toll House Cookies
ingredients:
1 c. (227 g) butter or margarine
3/4 c. (150 g) sugar
3/4 c. (160 g) light brown sugar
2 eggs
2 1/4 c. (270 g) flour
1 t. (4.6 g) soda
1t. (6.0 g) salt
2 T. (30 g) hot water
1 t. (4.2 g) vanilla
1 c. (130 g) nuts chopped
1 12 oz. (340 g) package chocolate bits
directions:
Preheat oven to 375.
Cream together butter and sugars. Add eggs and beat until light and fluffy. Sift together flour, soda, and salt. Add to wet mixture, together with water and vanilla. Mix until well blended and smooth. Then add nuts and chocolate bits. Drop by spoonfuls on greased baking sheets. Bake 10-12 minutes.
description: Mom's standard. Usually make 1/2 recipe.
notes:
Web summary (newengland.com, No star rating or review count shown). Yankee Magazine's transcription of Ruth Wakefield's original 1930s Toll House cookie from the inn in Whitman, Massachusetts - the recipe that started the chocolate chip cookie. The step that marks the original, and that modern printings dropped, is dissolving the baking soda in hot water before it goes into the dough: it disperses the leavening evenly and produces a thinner, crisper, better-browned cookie than stirring dry soda into the flour does. Everything else is the familiar skeleton - equal white and light brown sugar, a full pound of butter's worth of fat per 2 1/4 cups of flour, two eggs, 12 ounces of chips and a cup of nuts.

What readers report: The loudest recurring argument is fat: readers who use all butter complain the cookies spread too thin, and a large contingent goes to all shortening or half butter and half Crisco for a crisper, taller cookie. A second group confirms the hot-water soda trick does exactly what it claims - thinner and crispier with more browning - so treat it as a choice rather than a formality. Chilling the dough is repeatedly urged even though the recipe does not require it. Readers also note the original circulated in several forms, with chopped chocolate rather than chips, shifted sugar ratios, and sometimes oatmeal.

Note on the source: The family card is unmistakably the ORIGINAL Toll House rather than the modern Nestle back-of-bag version, because it keeps the hot-water step that Nestle later dropped. Line for line: 1 c butter or margarine, 3/4 c sugar, 3/4 c light brown sugar, 2 eggs, 2 1/4 c flour, 1 tsp soda, 1 tsp salt, hot water, 1 tsp vanilla, 1 c chopped nuts, one 12 oz package chips. The single discrepancy is the water quantity - the family card says 2 tablespoons where this transcription says 1 teaspoon; older printings of the original vary on exactly this line, so it is period drift, not a different recipe. Robert's cook's note calls it 'Mom's standard' and says they usually make a half recipe. Gram conversions: 1 c butter = 227 g, 3/4 c granulated sugar = 150 g, 3/4 c packed light brown sugar = 165 g, 2 1/4 c all-purpose flour = 281 g, 12 oz chocolate chips = 340 g, 1 c chopped nuts = 113 g.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. It's already the original hot-water-soda version, not the modern Nestle recipe, and it's Mom's tested standard. The all-butter-vs-shortening spread debate is a taste preference, not an error.

name: Tomato Feta Cheese Canapes
ingredients:
4 oz (113 g) cream cheese
2 T chopped basil
2 T chopped chives
 1/4 c Feta cheese (or more)
1 T low fat Hellman's mayo
4 Italian pear tomatoes
1 baguette of French bread or French rounds
directions:
Mix together cheese, mayo herbs. Thinly slice french bread. Brush lightly with olive oil and toast until lightly brown. Cool. 

Place 1 tsp cheese mixture on bread slice. Place a slice of thinly sliced tomato on top. Brush again w/ olive oil. Decorate with a basil leaf or dried basil.

claude_opt.changes: Salt the sliced tomatoes and let them drain on paper towels 10 minutes before topping the toasts, standard bruschetta practice, so the bread doesn't go soggy under the tomato.

name: Tomato Sauce--Symmes family
ingredients:
2 6-oz. (170 g) cans Italian style tomato paste
1 no. 2 1/2 can Italian or American style tomatoes, or 3 1/2 cups fresh peeled tomatoes
2 T. (27 g) olive oil
1/4 c. (40 g) finely chopped onion
1 small clove garlic finely chopped
1/4 c. (25 g) celery finely chopped
1 1/2 t. (9.0 g) salt
1 t. (4.2 g) sugar
1/4 t. (0.6 g) nutmeg
1/2 t. (0.6 g) oregano
1/8 t. (0.3 g) pepper
1/4 c. (22 g) grated parmesan
1/4-1/2 t. (1.1-2.3 g) baking soda
1/2 lb. (227 g) meat or meatballs
mushrooms optional
directions: Fry onion, garlic, celery slowly in the olive oil for about 5 minutes. Put tomatoes through food strainer and discard seeds or blend in blender. Add tomatoes with tomato paste to the onion, garlic and celery. Add all the ingredients except baking soda and simmer in a covered saucepan for about 1 hour. Then add meatballs that have been browned nicely on all sides and simmer covered about 30 minutes longer, or until meatballs are tender. Mushrooms that have been sliced and sauteed for about 5 minutes may be added in the last 15 minutes. Baking soda should be added in the last 10 minutes. Baking soda helps to neutralize acid  making tomato sauce more palatable. Add soda, a very little at a time, and cook sauce several minutes. Taste and add more soda if needed. If sauce becomes too thick a little water may be added toward end of cooking. If too thin cook uncovered 15 minutes. Makes 6 medium servings.

claude_opt.changes: Baking soda for acidity is validated by modern testing, not an outdated trick — keep it. Bloom the tomato paste with the sauteed onion/garlic/celery for 1-2 minutes before adding tomatoes to deepen flavor.

name: Tortilla Pie

name: Toscakage -- Elva Adelsteinsdottir
ingredients:
For the dough:
3 eggs
215 g sugar (1 scant cup)
150 g flour (⅔ cup)
1 cube melted butter (8 tbs.)
3/4 tsp (3.0 g) baking powder

For the topping:
4 tbs. (57 g) butter
2 oz. (57 g) sliced almonds
2 oz. (57 g) sugar (4 tbs.)
1 tbs. (7.5 g) flour 
1-2 tbs. (15-30 g) heavy cream

Strawberries
Whipping cream
directions:
For the dough:
Preheat oven 350 degrees. 
Whip eggs and sugar. Add flour, baking powder, and melted butter. Beat 2-3 minutes. Put in floured, greased springform pan. Bake 25 mins. Then pour on cooked topping and bake for a further 10 mins.

For the topping:
Blend together topping ingredients, except almonds, in a saucepan. Cook, stirring until sugar is dissolved. (I bring to a boil and cook, stirring, for 2 minutes.) Do not brown. Add sliced almonds. Pour on top of cake as directed above.

Strawberry preparation.
Slice fresh strawberries. Add 2 tb sugar and some liqueur if desired, to make juice. Slice cake in two layers. Pour juice on the "sore" sides. Arrange the strawberries on the lower, then whipped cream, then upper layer.
description: 7/21 Tried 8 inch springform. Probably too small. Cooked 10-15 mins extra and it was good. But better in the 9” pan

claude_opt.changes: Line the springform's bottom and sides with parchment before baking; the hot caramel-almond topping commonly leaks through springform seams, a recurring failure point in modern Toscakaka recipes. Pan-size issue already covered by cooks_note.

name: Trifle
ingredients:
1 8-oz. (227 g) container whipped cream cheese
1/2 c. (122 g) low fat milk 1 percent
1/4 c. (28 g) confectioners sugar
2 t. (8.4 g) vanilla extract
1 8 oz. (227 g) container thawed frozen light  whipped topping
2 3 oz. (85 g) pkg. sponge-type lady fingers
3/4 c. (186 g) orange juice
1/4 c. (60 g) orange liqueur
2 pints (576 g) strawberries, hulled and sliced
1/2 pint (123 g) raspberries
directions:
1. In large bowl, with wire whisk or fork, mix whipped cream cheese, low-fat milk, confectioners sugar and vanilla extract until smooth. With rubber spatula, fold in 1 1/2 c. whipped topping until well blended.

2. In bottom of 2 qt. glass bowl or souffle dish, spread 1 c. cream cheese mixture. Separate lady fingers, and arrange half in a layer over cream cheese mixture. In 1 c. measure, mix orange juice and orange liqueur. Drizzle half of this mixture over lady fingers to moisten.

3. Top moistened ladyfingers with half of sliced strawberries; spread with half of remaining cream cheese mixture, then top with remaining ladyfingers. Moisten ladyfingers with remaining orange juice mixture; top with remaining strawberries, then with remaining cream cheese mixture.

4. Spoon remaining whipped topping into decorating bag with large star tube; pipe whipped topping around edge of bowl to make pretty design. Arrange raspberries over top of trifle.

5 Refrigerate at least 3 hours before serving to blend flavors and allow ladyfingers to soften. To serve, spoon servings into dessert plates.
description: Jan makes 1 1/2 times this recipe for her large bowl.

claude_opt.changes: Whipped cream cheese plus whipped topping instead of custard is a legitimate, currently popular trifle style (cheesecake trifle), not a dated shortcut. Nothing here needs correcting.

name: Tuna-Salad Sandwich, Julia Child Style
ingredients:
FOR THE TUNA SALAD:
1 (5-ounce) can tuna packed in oil, drained
3 to 4 tablespoons (41-55 g) mayonnaise, preferably Hellmann’s, plus more for spreading
3 tablespoons (19 g) finely chopped celery
2 to 3 tablespoons (20-30 g) finely chopped onion, preferably Vidalia
3 to 4 cornichons, finely chopped
1 tablespoon (8.9 g) capers, rinsed, patted dry and chopped if large, or 5 olives, pitted and chopped
Fresh lemon juice
Salt
Freshly ground pepper, preferably white
1 to 2 tablespoons (3.0-6.0 g) minced fresh chives or parsley (optional)
FOR ASSEMBLY:
2 toasted English muffins (preferably Bays) or 4 untoasted white bread slices
4 soft lettuce leaves, such as Boston
4 tomato slices
4 thin slices onion (optional)
directions:
Prepare the tuna salad: Using a fork, mash the tuna with 3 tablespoons mayonnaise. Add the celery, as much onion and chopped cornichons as you’d like, and the capers or olives, and toss to combine. Add a squirt of lemon juice, some salt (go easy at first) and pepper. Taste and see if you'd like more mayo, onion or cornichons. Add more lemon juice, salt and pepper to taste. Stir in the chives or parsley, if you’re using either. (Makes 1 1/2 cups.) The tuna salad is good to go as soon as it’s made, but it’s even better after a couple of hours in the fridge.

When you’re ready to serve, spread the muffins or bread with a little mayonnaise. If you’re using English muffins, do what Julia did: Make open-face sandwiches. Put a leaf of lettuce on each muffin half, top with tuna salad and finish with tomato and onion. If you’re using sliced bread, prepare traditional sandwiches: Top each of 2 slices of bread with 1 piece lettuce, tomato and onion, then spread over the tuna and finish with remaining onion, tomato, lettuce and bread.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (1,383)). Dorie Greenspan's account of what Julia Child ate for a working lunch when she was home between trips. Per her longtime assistant Stephanie Hersh, only two things were fixed - oil-packed tuna and Hellmann's mayonnaise - and everything else was negotiable. The suggested build adds capers, cornichons, chopped onion, lemon juice and herbs, served open-face on an English muffin or on white bread.

What readers report: This thread is dominated by reminiscence rather than technique, so the vote counts reward anecdote: the top comment (503 votes) is a joke about Duke's mayonnaise being better than Hellmann's, and the next several (420, 342, 264, 218 votes) are personal stories about Julia Child and about tuna sandwiches generally, with no cooking content. The one substantive technique note (109 votes) recommends peeling the celery before chopping it - it removes the stringy outer layer and markedly improves the texture, which the commenter concedes sounds like French fussiness but considers worth doing. Little disagreement with the recipe itself appears; the 4-star rating seems to reflect that it is barely a recipe.

Note on the source: comments are mostly anecdote; only one real technique point (peel the celery)

claude_opt.changes: Peel the celery before chopping (the one substantive tip, 109 votes) - removes the stringy fibers and improves texture noticeably for almost no extra effort.

name: Turmeric Rice--Franey
ingredients:
2 tablespoons (28 g) butter
¼ cup (40 g) chopped onion
½ teaspoon (1.4 g) chopped garlic
1 cup (185 g) converted rice
½ teaspoon (1.5 g) turmeric
3 sprigs parsley
2 sprigs fresh thyme or 1/4 teaspoon dried
4 drops Tabasco sauce
1 bay leaf
1 ½ cups (356 g) water
½ teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
Freshly ground black pepper to taste
directions:
Heat 1 tablespoon of the butter in a saucepan and add the onion and garlic. Cook, stirring, until the onion is wilted. Add the rice, turmeric, parsley, thyme, Tabasco, bay leaf, water, salt and pepper. Bring to a boil, stirring. Cover and simmer 17 minutes.

Discard the parsley and thyme sprigs and bay leaf. Add the remaining butter and toss the rice with a fork.
description: Excellent! Use basmati rice.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (51)). 

What readers report: Only two comments. The more useful one (3 votes) warns that the site carries two different Pierre Franey turmeric rice recipes and argues this one is the better side dish, using considerably less turmeric and water rather than stock - worth knowing if a differently-proportioned version turns up elsewhere in the collection. The other reports it works fine with jasmine rice in place of the specified rice, came together easily, and pairs well with the site's roasted shrimp cocktail with aioli.

Note on the source: no headnote, only a 'Featured in: 60-Minute Gourmet' line; byline confirmed as Pierre Franey, matching the batch name; page title is 'Turmeric Rice' without the Franey suffix; only 2 comments; a second distinct Franey turmeric rice exists on the site

name: Tuscan Grilled Cornish Hens
ingredients:
2 Cornish hens, flattened
Kosher salt
1/3 cup (72 g) good olive oil
2 teaspoons (4.0 g) grated lemon zest (2 lemons)
1/3 cup (81 g) freshly squeezed lemon juice
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) minced garlic (3 cloves)
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) minced fresh rosemary leaves
Freshly ground black pepper
1 lemon, halved
Fleur de sel, for serving
directions:
Sprinkle the Cornish hens with 1 teaspoon salt on each side.

Combine the olive oil, lemon zest, lemon juice, garlic, rosemary, and 1 teaspoon pepper in a ceramic or glass dish just large enough to hold the flattened hens. Add the hens, and turn to coat. Cover the dish with plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight, turning once or twice.

When ready to grill, prepare a hot charcoal fire on one side of a grill (or turn a gas grill on low heat). Spread 1/4 of the coals across the other side of the grill. Place the hens on the cooler side skin-side up and weigh them down with a gratin dish with a foil-wrapped brick inside.

Cook for 12 minutes, until the underside is golden brown. Turn the hens skin-side down, weigh them down again, and cook for another 12 minutes until the skin is golden brown and the hens are cooked through.

Place the lemon halves on the cool side of the grill, cut-side down, for the last 10 minutes of cooking. Remove the Cornish hens and lemons to a plate or cutting board, cover with aluminum foil, and allow to rest for 5 minutes. Cut the hens in half, sprinkle with fleur de sel, and serve with the grilled lemon halves.
description: 8/23 Ok but not amazing. The time on the grill was right. The bird was a bit tougher than expected. With 4 hours of marinade, the flavor was not noticeable.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten spatchcocks Cornish hens and grills them under a weight, which presses the whole bird flat against the grate so it browns evenly and cooks quickly instead of leaving thick and thin parts at different doneness. A marinade of olive oil, lemon zest and juice, garlic and rosemary carries the Tuscan character and stands up to the char. Fleur de sel and a halved grilled lemon finish it at the table.

name: Tuscan White Bean Soup—Ina
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) dried white cannellini beans (for canned beans, see note)
Good olive oil
4 ounces (113 g) pancetta, ¼-inch diced (see note)
2 cups (178 g) chopped leeks, white and light green parts (2 leeks)
2 cups (320 g) chopped yellow onion (2 onions)
2 cups (256 g) (½-inch) diced carrots, scrubbed (5 carrots)
2 cups (202 g) (½-inch) diced celery (4 ribs)
2 tablespoons (17 g) minced garlic (6 cloves)
2 teaspoons (2.3 g) minced fresh rosemary
8 to 10 cups (1.9-2.4 kg) chicken stock, preferably homemade
2 bay leaves
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
Freshly grated Parmesan cheese
directions:
At least 8 hours or the night before you make the soup, place the beans in a large bowl and add enough cold water to cover the beans by 2 inches. Refrigerate for at least 8 hours or overnight. Drain the beans, rinse under cold running water, and drain again. Set aside.

In a large (10-inch) pot or Dutch oven such as Le Creuset, heat ¼ cup of olive oil over medium heat, add the pancetta, and sauté for 4 to 5 minutes, until browned. Add the leeks, onions, carrots, celery, garlic, and rosemary and cook over medium-low for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables are tender. Add the beans, 8 cups of the chicken stock, bay leaves, 1 tablespoon salt, and 1 teaspoon pepper and bring to a boil. Lower the heat and simmer, partially covered, for 1 hour and 30 minutes, until the beans are tender. Stir occasionally, scraping the bottom of the pot. Discard the bay leaves, cover the pot, and allow the soup to sit off the heat for 15 minutes. Add up to 2 more cups of chicken stock if the soup is too thick.

Reheat slowly, ladle into large shallow soup bowls, sprinkle with Parmesan cheese, drizzle with olive oil, and serve hot.

FOR CANNED BEANS:

First, use 2 (14-ounce) cans of white cannellini beans. Drain the beans, reserving the liquid. Place 1 cup of the beans and ½ cup of the liquid into the bowl of a food processor fitted with the steel blade and puree. When ready to add the beans in the recipe, stir in the puree and add the remaining drained beans (discard the remaining liquid).

Second, use only 6 cups of chicken stock.

Third, simmer the soup for 45 minutes, rather than 1 hour and 30 minutes.
description:
2/25 Excellent again. Added chicken again. Used Rancho Gordo small white beans, leeks, and pancetta. 

7/24 Excellent! Rancho Gordo Marcella beans. Used bacon, no leeks. Didn’t presoak beans, took about 2½ hours to cook. Used 4 c of homemade stock and about 4 c of water, plus a bit of better than bouillon. Didn’t add parm—didn’t seem to need it! Added about a half a rotisserie chicken. Very nice
notes:
Notes: To reheat a second day, you’ll need to add some water, salt, and pepper.

Use bacon if you don't have pancetta.

Web summary (barefootcontessa.com). Ina Garten's rustic Italian soup for six to eight, built on a pound of dried cannellini beans that must be soaked overnight before they go anywhere near the pot. Pancetta renders first, then leeks, onion, carrot and celery soften in the fat before the beans and chicken stock go in with rosemary and bay. Grated Parmesan finishes each bowl. The page offers no further authorial commentary.

Note on the source: barefootcontessa.com pages carry no headnote or comments section

ahead: At least 8 hours or the night before you make the soup, place the beans in a large bowl and add enough…
Refrigerate for at least 8 hours or overnight.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing — your 2/25 and 7/24 notes both call it excellent with different beans, bacon vs. pancetta, leeks or not, proving the recipe is forgiving and sound as written.

name: Umbrian-Style Chicken Alla Cacciatora
ingredients:
1 tablespoon (14 g) plus 1 teaspoon olive oil
1 small chicken (about 2 1/2 pounds), cut into serving pieces, or use bone-in, skin-on thighs and drumsticks
1 onion, sliced
2 to 3 cloves garlic, very finely minced
1 tablespoon (8.9 g) capers
¼ cup (34 g) good-quality brine-cured olives, black or green, with pits
1 sprig rosemary
1 handful sage leaves
Salt and black pepper
1 cup (237 g) dry white wine
Zest and juice of 1/2 lemon
1 tablespoon (16 g) balsamic vinegar
directions:
Heat 1 tablespoon olive oil in a large non-stick pan. Add chicken pieces and sear over medium heat until golden on all sides, about 15 minutes. Transfer to a plate and wipe the pan clean before proceeding.

Turn heat to low, add remaining 1 teaspoon oil, and return the chicken to the pan. Add onions and stir frequently until caramelized, about 18 minutes. Add minced garlic, capers, olives, rosemary sprig and sage leaves. Season with just a sprinkle of salt and black pepper.

After a couple of minutes, when everything smells fragrant, add wine. Cover and simmer very slowly until the chicken is tender and cooked through (165 degrees). Start checking the temperature of the chicken after 15 minutes to avoid overcooking. Add some water if the sauce gets too dry while simmering.

When ready to serve, reheat if necessary, then add lemon juice and zest and balsamic vinegar. Taste and add more lemon if desired. Remove the rosemary sprig and serve.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (1,241)). Julia Moskin's write-up of the central-Italian version of hunter's chicken, which predates the arrival of tomatoes and therefore has none. Lemon, vinegar, olives and rosemary carry the dish instead of the southern tomato sauce Americans expect. She suggests serving it over mashed potatoes or polenta with steamed greens dressed in fruity olive oil.

What readers report: The whole thread turns on one disputed step. A 202-vote comment questions step 2, which returns the seared chicken to the pan with raw onions rather than waiting for them to soften, and a 33-vote reply argues that cooking the onions to caramelized would overcook the chicken given the later simmer. The recipe's own author answers (106 votes) and settles it: adding the raw onions to the chicken is intentional, the onions will collapse into the wine anyway, and the perceived timing problem comes from searing the chicken in batches, which takes longer than people expect. She adds two things the recipe does not say - never pit the olives, since the pits flavour the braise, and organic chicken will take a long simmer without drying out. A 42-vote commenter who cooked it with the author in Assisi says change nothing. Roasting it in the oven also works (33 votes).

name: Vanillekipferl (German Vanilla Crescent Cookies)
ingredients:
For the cookie dough:
250 g all-purpose flour, spoon and level
1 pinch of salt
230 g unsalted butter, cold, cut into small cubes
90 g powdered sugar
100 g finely ground almonds, or hazelnuts or walnuts
1/2 vanilla pod, seeds scraped out or 2 tsp (8.4 g) vanilla extract
For the sugar mixture:
85 g powdered sugar
1 Tbsp (13 g) vanilla pod
directions:
In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment combine flour, salt, cubed butter, powdered sugar, nuts, and vanilla seeds. Mix at medium speed until a crumbly dough forms, about 1-2 minutes. If the dough is too crumbly add 1-2 Tbsp milk.

Use your hands to press the dough together and wrap it in plastic wrap. Chill the dough for one hour in the fridge.

Preheat the oven to 350°F (177°C) and line one or two baking sheets with parchment paper.

Roll the chilled dough into a log approximately 1/2 inch thick. Cut the log into 1 1/2-inch pieces, form the pieces into small cylinders and taper the ends into dull points. Bend each one into a crescent shape. Place the Vanillekipferl on the baking sheet about 1 inch apart.

Bake the Vanillekipferl one cookie sheet at a time for 12 to 15 min (depending on the size of the cookies) until the edges are golden. They should not brown.

Scrape out vanilla pod and combine with powered sugar. This works great in a small food processor. Sift the mixture over the hot Vanillekipferl. Let them cool completely then give them a second dusting.

These cookies keep fresh for about 3 weeks in an airtight container stored in a cool place.
description: Made cookies like this on our Rhine River cruise in December 2024; followed metric measures excellent results!
notes:
Web summary (platedcravings.com, 4.90 stars from 65 ratings). Julia Foerster writes these up as the German Christmas cookie of her family's baking tradition. There is no egg and no leavening at all: butter and finely ground nuts alone hold the dough together, which is precisely why the baked crescent crumbles and melts rather than snapping. She warns that the raw dough looks worryingly crumbly and simply needs gentle handling, and that the cookies must come out pale, since overbaking destroys the tender texture.

What readers report: The comments are mostly confirmations rather than corrections. The most useful practical note comes from a baker who weighed the portions and found ten to twelve grams per cookie worked well, with a larger twenty-gram crescent also succeeding. Another reader said the recipe matched a family grandmother's version closely. Nobody in the visible thread disputes the flour, butter or sugar quantities, or reports a problem with the baking time, so the main risk flagged remains the author's own warning about taking them too far in the oven.

Data fix (Sept 2026): '1 Tbsp vanilla pod' measures a pod by volume, which is unusual; it may mean vanilla sugar. Left as written.

name: Vomit Cake (aka Magic Cookie Bars)
ingredients:
1 stick butter or margarine
1 c. (100 g) graham cracker crumbs
1 c. (85 g) flake coconut
1 c. (170 g) semi-sweet chocolate bits
1 c. (117 g) chopped walnuts
1 15 oz. (425 g) can sweetened condensed milk
directions:
Preheat oven to to 350.
Combine melted butter, graham cracker crumbs and coconut in ungreased 9x13" pan. Press lightly so as to cover completely the bottom of the pan with a layer of this mixture. Cover with a layer of chocolate bits. Sprinkle on chopped nuts. Drizzle condensed milk evenly over the surface. Bake for 30 minutes. Cool completely before cutting.

name: Wagshal’s Boeuf Bourguignon
ingredients:
1 tablespoon (14 g) olive oil
2 1/2 pounds (1.1 kg) boneless chuck roast, trimmed of excess fat and cut into 1-inch cubes
Kosher salt
Freshly ground black pepper
1 pound (454 g) carrots (scrubbed well), sliced diagonally into 1-inch chunks
2 yellow onions, sliced
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) chopped garlic, plus a few halved cloves for rubbing the toasted bread
1 tablespoon (16 g) tomato paste
1/2 teaspoon (0.9 g) unsweetened cocoa powder
1 teaspoon (1.1 g) fresh thyme leaves (may substitute 1/2 teaspoon dried thyme leaves)
One 750-milliliter bottle good-quality dry red wine
2 cups (576 g) no-salt-added beef broth, or more as needed
4 tablespoons (57 g) (1/2 stick) unsalted butter, at room temperature
1 pound (454 g) fresh mushrooms (stemmed), cut into thick slices
1 1/2 pounds (680 g) frozen pearl onions
3 tablespoons (22 g) flour
Slices of country or sourdough bread, for serving
1/2 cup (30 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley (optional)
directions:
Preheat the oven to 250 degrees. Have a large plate at hand.

Heat the oil in a large Dutch oven over medium heat. Meanwhile, dry the beef cubes with paper towels, then season them well with salt and pepper.

Working in single-layer batches, sear the beef for 3 to 5 minutes, turning to brown on all sides. Use tongs to transfer the cubes to the plate.

Add the carrots and onions to the pot along with 2 teaspoons of salt and 1 teaspoon of pepper. Stir to coat, then cook for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onions are starting to pick up color. Stir in the garlic; cook for 1 minute, then return all the beef to the pot along with any accumulated juices. Add the tomato paste, unsweetened cocoa powder and thyme, and stir to coat and incorporate.

Pour in the wine and broth, adding more of the latter if the meat and vegetables in the pot are not completely covered. Use a sturdy wooden spoon to dislodge any browned bits from the bottom of the pot. Once the mixture is bubbling at the edges, cover with a tight-fitting lid and transfer to the oven. Cook for 1 1/2 to 2 hours or until the meat is fork-tender; while the pot is in the oven, lift the lid a few times and stir the bourguignon.

Once the meat and vegetables are done, transfer the pot to the stove top, uncovered, off the heat.

Melt half of the butter in a medium skillet over medium-low heat. Stir in the mushrooms and cook for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring a few times, until they’ve browned and released their moisture. Transfer to the pot, then stir in the frozen pearl onions; turn the heat to medium-high.

Meanwhile, whisk together the remaining butter and flour in a medium heatproof bowl until smooth. Borrow a cup of liquid from the pot and whisk it into the butter-flour mixture until smooth, then return the entire mixture to the pot, stirring until well incorporated; once the bourguignon comes to a boil, reduce the heat to medium-low and cook for about 10 minutes or until the bourguignon has thickened. Taste, and adjust the seasoning as needed.

When ready to serve, toast the bread slices, then immediately rub them with the cut sides of the garlic.

Divide the boeuf bourguignon among wide, shallow bowls, sprinkling each portion with parsley. Serve with the garlic-rubbed toast alongside.
notes:
Web summary (washingtonpost.com). The Washington Post's version of the boeuf bourguignon sold at Wagshal's, the long-running market in the District's Spring Valley neighbourhood, where it is among the best-selling prepared dishes. The Post's one serving note is to put garlic-rubbed toast alongside so none of the sauce is wasted.

name: Whole Roasted New York Strip Loin
ingredients:
FOR THE ROAST:
1 tablespoon (8.7 g) black peppercorns
6 allspice berries
2 tablespoons (17 g) kosher salt
5 pound (2.3 kg) New York strip loin roast, tied at 2-inch intervals (ask your butcher to do this)
4 cloves garlic, grated
2 bunches rosemary, thyme or savory
3 pounds (1.4 kg) medium Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled
3 pounds (1.4 kg) medium parsnips, peeled, cut in 3-inch lengths
¼ pound (113 g) unsalted butter, melted
1 large bunch watercress, for garnish (optional)
FOR THE HORSERADISH SAUCE:
1 cup (230 g) (8 ounces) crème fraîche
1 tablespoon (16 g) Dijon mustard
3 tablespoons (45 g) grated horseradish, preferably freshly grated
Small pinch cayenne
Salt and pepper
directions:
Coarsely grind peppercorns and allspice together in a spice mill. Combine with salt in a small bowl. Sprinkle mixture evenly over exterior of roast. Add the grated garlic and rub in all over.

Line a roasting pan with herb branches and set roast on top. Leave to absorb seasonings for at least 1 hour at room temperature, or refrigerate overnight (bring back to room temperature before proceeding). Heat oven to 400 degrees.

In a large pot of well-salted boiling water, cook potatoes until just done, about 15 minutes. Remove with a spider or slotted spoon and place in an earthenware baking dish. In the same water, simmer parsnips until just done, about 8 minutes. Remove and add them to potatoes in baking dish. Pour melted butter over the potatoes and parsnips and use a brush to make sure they are well coated.

Make the horseradish sauce: Whisk together crème fraîche, Dijon mustard, horseradish and cayenne in a small bowl. Season with salt and pepper and refrigerate.

Roast the beef, uncovered, for about 1 hour. Check with an instant-read thermometer after 45 minutes. For medium-rare, take the roast out of the oven when thermometer registers 120 degrees (residual heat will cause roast to continue cooking as it rests). Remove the roast, tent it with foil, and let it rest for 15 minutes; the temperature should rise to 125 degrees. About 15 minutes after the roast goes into the oven, put in the baking dish of potatoes and parsnips, uncovered, and roast until beautifully golden brown, about 30 minutes.

Slice the beef into 1/4-inch-thick pieces and arrange on a warmed platter, garnished with a big bunch of watercress. Pass the roasted vegetables and horseradish sauce separately.
notes:
Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 4 (689)). An argument for roasting a whole strip loin - the cut normally sliced into New York or Kansas City strip steaks - as a holiday centrepiece, positioned as cheaper than tenderloin or standing rib while still impressive. Served with roasted potatoes and parsnips and horseradish sauce.

What readers report: The comments largely argue against the recipe's method, which is why the rating sits at 4. The top note (135 votes) advocates the reverse sear: start the room-temperature roast at 180-200F with a probe in it, cook until it reaches target, then blast it to finish. A 42-vote comment says roasting an expensive cut at a flat 400F produces a mediocre result and urges searing each side first. A 99-vote reply defends the recipe's logic on Maillard grounds, arguing the browning flavours need sustained high heat that low-and-slow alone will not give. Useful doneness reference from a 28-vote professional chef: bleu is 115-120F, rare (saignant) 125-130F, medium rare above that. A cook who followed it exactly on a 10 lb prime loin pulled at 127F and rested under foil with good results.

Note on the source: top comments dispute the recipe's roasting method rather than endorse it

name: Whole-Wheat Buttermilk Pancakes
ingredients:
2 large eggs
2 tablespoons (25 g) granulated sugar
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt (such as Diamond Crystal)
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) vanilla extract
2 cups (484 g)/480 milliliters buttermilk (see Tip)
2 tablespoons (28 g) unsalted butter, melted, plus more for cooking and serving
2 1/2 cups/270 grams whole-wheat flour
1 1/2 teaspoons (6.0 g) baking powder
1/2 teaspoon (2.3 g) baking soda
Maple syrup, jam, and/or nut butter, for serving
directions:
In a large bowl, whisk together the eggs, sugar, salt and vanilla to combine, then whisk in the buttermilk and butter. Sprinkle the flour, baking powder and baking soda on top; stir with a rubber spatula just until combined. (Avoid overmixing; some lumps are OK.) Let sit for 5 minutes. Meanwhile, heat a griddle or large (12-inch) cast-iron or nonstick skillet over medium.

Give the batter one more stir to dissolve any lingering lumps. Reduce heat to medium-low, grease the griddle with butter, then drop 1/3-cup portions of batter onto the griddle, leaving about 1 inch in between for the batter to expand. Cook until the bottoms are golden-brown and the top edges are bubbling, 2 to 4 minutes. Flip and cook until golden-brown and cooked through, about 2 minutes more. Repeat with more butter and the remaining batter, reducing the heat as necessary for subsequent batches. Serve right away with butter, maple syrup, jam or nut butter as you like.
description: 3/23 Fluffy and good. Used 1/4 c farro flour with 1 c whole wheat. Batter seemed very thick and we added a bit more buttermilk. Still thick.
notes:
If you don’t have buttermilk, combine 2 cups whole milk with 2 tablespoons white vinegar; let sit for 5 to 10 minutes until curdled.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (939)). A 100 percent whole-wheat pancake that sets out to avoid the density that reputation attaches to them. The trick is resting the batter for the five minutes the pan takes to heat, which lets the bran and germ hydrate and soften so the pancakes stay tender while keeping the nutty whole-wheat flavour.

What readers report: The most valuable thread for anyone working in weights is a flour discrepancy. Commenters (44 and 30 votes) reported that 270 grams of whole-wheat flour is well over the 1 1/2 cups the recipe then stated, and that measuring by volume gave a soupy batter - one habitual weigher confirmed it after measuring by cup for once. NYT has since corrected the listing, which now reads 2 1/2 cups/270 grams, so anyone working from an older copy should use the gram figure. Several cooks who followed it as written, including the rest, call the pancakes light and fluffy and among the best whole-wheat pancakes they have had (55 and 24 votes). A 59-vote note calculates roughly 160 calories per pancake before oil or toppings.

Note on the source: gram datapoint: whole-wheat flour 2 1/2 cups = 270 g (recipe was corrected after comments flagged 1 1/2 cups as wrong; also buttermilk 2 cups = 480 ml per the ingredient list)

name: Wild Mushroom Risotto
ingredients:
1-ounce (28 g) dried morel mushrooms
1/2 pound (227 g) fresh porcini or cremini mushrooms
4 cups (960 g) chicken stock, preferably homemade
6 tablespoons (85 g) (3/4 stick) unsalted butter
2 ounces (57 g) pancetta, diced
1/2 cup (80 g) chopped shallots (3 shallots)
1 1/2 cups (300 g) Arborio rice
1/2 cup (118 g) dry white wine
1/2 teaspoon (0.3 g) saffron threads
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt
1/2 teaspoon (1.1 g) freshly ground black pepper
2/3 cup (60 g) freshly grated Parmesan cheese, plus extra for serving
directions:
Place the dried morels in a bowl and pour 2 cups boiling water over them. Set aside for 30 minutes. Scoop the morels from the water with a slotted spoon, reserving the liquid. You should have 2 cups; if not, add water to make 2 cups. Drain the morels and rinse once more. If some of the mushrooms are large, cut into 2 or 3 pieces. Pour the mushroom liquid through a coffee filter or paper towel, discarding the gritty solids. Set the mushrooms and the liquid aside separately.

Meanwhile, remove and discard the stems of the porcini and rub any dirt off the caps with a damp paper towel. Dont rinse them! Slice thickly and set aside.

In a small saucepan, heat the chicken stock with the 2 cups of reserved mushroom liquid and bring to a simmer.

In a heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven, melt the butter and saute the pancetta and shallots over medium-low heat for 5 minutes. Add the morels and porcini and saute for another 5 minutes. Add the rice and stir to coat the grains with butter. Add the wine and cook for 2 minutes. Add 2 full ladles of the chicken stock mixture to the rice plus the saffron, salt, and pepper. Stir and simmer over low heat until the stock is absorbed, 5 to 10 minutes. Continue to add the stock mixture, 2 ladles at a time, stirring every few minutes. Each time, cook until the mixture seems a little dry before adding more of the stock mixture. Continue until the rice is cooked through, but still al dente, about 25 to 30 minutes total. When done, the risotto should be thick and creamy and not at all dry. Off the heat, stir in the Parmesan cheese. Serve hot in bowls with extra cheese.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Ina Garten uses two kinds of mushroom here, dried morels rehydrated for their concentrated perfume and fresh porcini or cremini for body, with saffron adding another layer. The dried mushroom soaking liquid and the patient ladle-by-ladle addition of warm stock are what coax starch out of the Arborio and give the dish its creaminess without any cream. Pancetta and shallots build the base, Parmesan finishes it.

Note on the source: no reader comments surfaced on page

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing — the ladle-and-stir-every-few-minutes pacing already matches current best practice (constant stirring is a debunked myth); no reader complaints found on this or comparable mushroom risottos.

name: Zucchini Gratin—Ina
ingredients:
6 tablespoons (85 g) (3/4 stick) unsalted butter, plus extra for topping
1 pound (454 g) yellow onions, cut in 1/2 and sliced (3 large)
2 pounds (907 g) zucchini, sliced 1/4-inch thick (4 zucchini)
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) kosher salt
1 teaspoon (2.3 g) freshly ground black pepper
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) ground nutmeg
2 tablespoons (15 g) all-purpose flour
1 cup (244 g) hot milk
3/4 cup (81 g) fresh bread crumbs
3/4 cup (85 g) grated Gruyere
directions:
Preheat the oven to 400 degrees F.

Melt the butter in a very large (12-inch) saute pan and cook the onions over low heat for 20 minutes, or until tender but not browned. Add the zucchini and cook, covered, for 10 minutes, or until tender. Add the salt, pepper, and nutmeg and cook uncovered for 5 more minutes. Stir in the flour. Add the hot milk and cook over low heat for a few minutes, until it makes a sauce. Pour the mixture into an 8 by 10-inch baking dish.

Combine the bread crumbs and Gruyere and sprinkle on top of the zucchini mixture. Dot with 1 tablespoon of butter cut into small bits and bake for 20 minutes, or until bubbly and browned.
notes:
Web summary (foodnetwork.com). From Barefoot in Paris, Ina Garten's gratin cooks a pound of sliced yellow onions down slowly before the zucchini joins them, so the aromatics are sweet and concentrated rather than raw. Flour and hot milk turn the vegetable liquid into a light sauce, seasoned with nutmeg, and a topping of fresh breadcrumbs and Gruyere bakes to a crust. Slow-cooking the onions first is what keeps the dish from going watery.

name: Butterscotch Pudding
ingredients:
4 large egg yolks
3 tablespoons (23 g) cornstarch
1/2 teaspoon (3.0 g) fine sea salt
3/4 packed cup/165 grams dark brown sugar
1 tablespoon (14 g) unsalted butter
2 cups (488 g)/480 milliliters whole milk
1 cup (238 g)/240 milliliters heavy cream
1 tablespoon (14 g) bourbon or Scotch whisky (optional)
2 teaspoons (8.4 g) vanilla extract
Whipped cream, sour cream or creme fraiche, for serving
Chopped candied ginger, sliced almonds, Demerara sugar, shaved chocolate, cocoa nibs or flaky sea salt (or a combination), for garnish (optional)
directions:
Put egg yolks, cornstarch and salt into a large heatproof bowl, and whisk until the mixture is smooth and there are no lumps.

In a medium pot over medium heat, combine brown sugar and butter, whisking, until the brown sugar melts, 1 to 2 minutes. Let cook, whisking constantly, until the mixture starts to smell like hot caramel and darkens slightly, about 1 minute longer. (Don't walk away, or the mixture may burn.)

Immediately pour the milk and cream into the pot. (It will bubble fiercely and seize up.) Continue to cook, whisking constantly, until the clumps melt, 2 to 4 minutes.

Slowly whisk about 1/2 cup of the hot cream mixture into the bowl with the egg yolks, whisking yolks until smooth, then whisk in the remaining hot cream mixture. Pour the egg-cream mixture back into the saucepan and place it over medium heat.

Cook pudding, whisking constantly especially around the bottom and edges of the pot, until it comes to a full boil. (Don't worry about the eggs curdling. You're going to strain the mixture later.) Reduce heat to medium-low and cook, stirring the mixture constantly, until it thickens enough to mound thickly on the spoon, 4 to 7 minutes. If at any point the pudding looks curdled, whisk to help smooth it out.

Strain mixture through a fine sieve into a heatproof container or bowl, then stir in the Scotch or bourbon, if using, and vanilla. To prevent a skin from forming, press plastic wrap directly onto the surface of the pudding. (If you like the skin, don't cover pudding until it cools.) Chill for at least 2 hours and up to 2 days.

When serving, spoon pudding into dishes. Top with dollops of whipped cream, sour cream or creme fraiche, and any of the optional garnishes.

Tip: Make sure to bring the pudding to a full, vigorous boil to activate the cornstarch. Otherwise, it may not set. If you've ever ended up with thin, runny pudding, undercooking may have been the issue.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Thread has a single message, sent to Robert by Laura (laura.lantrip@gmail.com) on 1/25/2021; no replies and no annotation by Robert.

makeahead: If you like the skin, don't cover pudding until it cools.) Chill for at least 2 hours and up to 2 days.

claude_opt.changes: This already is a modern, well-tested recipe (full boil to set cornstarch, tempering, straining, resting) matching current best practice from major food sites. Nothing to improve.

name: Cauliflower Soup
ingredients:
2 lb (907 g) head of cauliflower
8 tbsp (114 g) unsalted butter
1 leek, white and light green parts only, halved, sliced thin, washed
1 small onion, halved and sliced thin
4-5 cups (0.9-1.2 kg) water
0.5 tsp (2.5 g) sherry vinegar
3 tbsp (9.0 g) minced fresh chives
directions:
Begin 50-60 minutes ahead.

1. Remove stems and leaves. Set aside 1 cup of half in florets. Cut remaining cauliflower crosswise into half in thick slices.

2. Melt 3 tbsp butter in large saucepan over medium-low heat. Add leek, onion, 1.5 tsp salt. Sweat for seven minutes.

3. Increase heat to medium-high, add 4 cups water, sliced cauliflower, and bring to summer. Reduce heat and simmer for 15 mins. Add remaining cauliflower, return to simmer, and cook for 15-20 minutes until cauliflower is tender and crumbles easily.

4. Melt remaining 5 tbsp butter in eight inch skillet over medium heat until bubbling. Add reserved florets and cook until golden brown and butter has browned with a nutty aroma, 6-8 minutes. Remove florets to small bowl, and toss with vinegar and salt. Reserve browned butter for garnish.

5. Blend soup. While on medium heat, adjust soup so it is thick, but settles with a flat surface after stirring. Adjust salt.

6. Ladle into bowls, add florets, drizzle brown butter, and add chives. Season with pepper.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (2014-08-08, Robert to himself); no replies or forwards, so no cook's note.

Web summary (americastestkitchen.com, 4 out of 5 stars (459 ratings)). Dan Souza for Cook's Illustrated / America's Test Kitchen. The trick is staggering the cauliflower: part of the head goes into the pot early and part late, so the finished soup carries both the sweet, deeply cooked flavour and the fresher, grassier note of briefly cooked florets. Cauliflower has enough body of its own that pureeing it with water alone gives a velvety texture, so no cream is needed. A separate handful of florets is browned in butter and used, with the resulting brown butter, as the garnish.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS returned on the recipe page.

Family copy carried no source line; ATK/Cook's Illustrated confirmed. Companion article: https://www.americastestkitchen.com/cooksillustrated/articles/6643-creamy-cauliflower-soup

name: Chicago Single-Crust Deep Dish Pizza
servings: For each 9 inch by two inch round cake pan pizza. Serves two hungry men as an only course.
ingredients:
Crust:
Flour Blend (100%): 206.59 g | 7.29 oz (80% King Arthur AP, 20% semolina, or just KAAP if you don't have semolina)
Water (45%): 92.96 g | 3.28 oz
ADY (.8%): 1.65 g | 0.06 oz | 0.44 tsp (says he normally uses less)
Salt (1%): 2.07 g | 0.07 oz | 0.37 tsp
Olive Oil (6%): 12.4 g | 0.44 oz | 2.75 tsp
Corn Oil (12%): 24.79 g | 0.87 oz | 1.84 tbsp
Butter (6%): 12.4 g | 0.44 oz | 0.87 tbsp (softened, not melted)
Sugar (1.5%): 3.1 g | 0.11 oz | 0.78 tsp
Total (172.3%): 355.95 g | 12.56 oz | 0.78 lbs
Everything else:
~8 oz (227 g) of sliced aged mozzarella (Whole milk, Polly-O brand blocks are ideal)
~6 oz (170 g) italian sausage, uncooked (hot or mild)
~12 oz (340 g) chunky tomato sauce (I haven't yet found a perfect one. Consider not cooking it since it will cook on the pie.)
~1 TBS (9.6 g) Corn or other high smoke point oil
Parmesan cheese to top (optional)
directions:
Combine dry ingredients in one bowl, wet ingredients in another, and mix until butter is in small dots. Cover and let rest overnight on counter or use more yeast for a shorter rest.

The next day, preheat oven to 440F for at least an hour with at rack near the bottom.

Spread one tablespoon of oil on the cake pan using a paper towel.

Press down the dough into the pan until it's uniform on just the bottom of the pan. Then take dough from the outside inch or two and press some of it up the edges of the pan at least an inch and a half. The final crust should be thinner on the sides and at the corners as it will expand. Avoid pushing oil up over the edge of the crust as this will cause burn marks.

Add 8 oz of whole milk mozzarella cheese (ideally sliced Polly-O blocks), 6 oz of sausage pressed down, and around 12 oz? of chunky pizza sauce of your choice. Make sure there's at least a quarter of an inch of space.

Put near the bottom of a preheated 440 degree oven for ~35 minutes. If the exposed crust browns well before 30 mins, consider covering the top with aluminum foil and starting the next pizza on the range for a few minutes. Internal temperatures on mine are often around 190 when I take them out. Add grated parmesan cheese on top.

Wait 5-10 mins, then remove the whole pizza using a spatula and a coordinated swooping motion.
description:
RM 2/13: No satisfactory chunky sauce found yet — consider not cooking the sauce at all, since it cooks on the pie. Do not push oil up over the crust edge; it causes burn marks. Internal temp ~190F at the pull.
RM 2/18: Use 50% more cheese than the 8 oz written. Bottom burns with the rack near the bottom — but this was observed in a previous kitchen, and the recipe's own instruction is a low rack, so the two conflict. Untested in the current oven.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Recipe from Robert's original message of 2/4/2013; the cook's note is his reply to himself in the same thread on 2/12/2018.

Web summary (pizzamaking.com). A long-running pizzamaking.com thread started by the poster BTB, working out a Chicago deep dish with semolina blended into the flour. His central argument is that Italian sausage should go on raw, because the long bake in a deep pan cooks it through while keeping it tender, whereas pre-cooked sausage dries out. On sauce he is a minimalist: good canned tomatoes, briefly drained, with very little added.

What readers report: The strongest consensus in the replies is on raw sausage, which multiple posters confirm works and saves a step. Tomato brand matters a lot to this crowd: Escalon 6 in 1 and Muir Glen crushed are recommended while Hunts and Contadina are dismissed as inferior. The clearest disagreement is over sauce seasoning, with Clive At Five adding honey, Italian seasoning, salt and fresh basil for a sweeter profile against BTB's minimal approach, and Hdale85 wanting sweetness but objecting to plain tomato. Posters also report that pan material changes the result, with stoneware and metal giving noticeably different crispness. A side thread clarifies that fennel and anise are not the same spice, with most preferring a light hand in deep dish.
