name: Chicken Thighs With Anchovy, Caper And Garlic
ingredients:
1 1/4 pounds (567 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs (4 to 5 thighs)
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) coarse kosher salt
Freshly ground black pepper
6 garlic cloves, smashed and peeled
1/4 cup (54 g) extra-virgin olive oil
5 anchovy fillets
2 tablespoons (18 g) drained capers, patted dry
1 large pinch chile flakes
1 lemon, halved
Fresh chopped parsley, for serving
directions:
1. Heat oven to 400 degrees. Season the chicken thighs with salt and pepper and let rest while you prepare the anchovy-garlic oil. Mince one of the garlic cloves and set it aside for later. In a large, ovenproof skillet over medium-high heat, add the oil. When the oil is hot, add the 5 smashed whole garlic cloves, the anchovies, capers and chile. Let cook, stirring with a wooden spoon to break up the anchovies, until the garlic browns around the edges and the anchovies dissolve, 3 to 5 minutes.

2. Add the chicken thighs and cook until nicely browned on one side, 5 to 7 minutes. Flip the thighs, place the pan in the oven and cook another 5 to 10 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through.

3. When chicken is done, transfer thighs to a plate (be careful, as the pan handle will be hot). Place skillet back on the heat and add minced garlic and the juice of one lemon half. Cook for about 30 seconds, scraping up the browned bits on the bottom of the pan. Return chicken to the pan and cook it in the sauce for another 15 to 30 seconds.

4. Transfer everything to a serving platter. Squeeze the remaining lemon half over the chicken and garnish with chopped parsley. Serve.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (Robert to himself, 2013-10-30); no reply or forward carrying an annotation.

claude_opt.changes: Replace 'cooked through' with checking chicken to 165°F on an instant-read thermometer; boneless thighs are forgiving but a target removes guesswork. Otherwise matches modern lemon-anchovy chicken recipes closely.

name: Chinese Smashed Cucumbers With Sesame Oil And Garlic
ingredients:
About 2 pounds (907 g) thin-skinned cucumbers like English or Persian (8 to 10 mini cucumbers, 4 medium-size or 2 large greenhouse)
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt, plus more for cucumbers
2 teaspoons (8.4 g) granulated sugar, plus more for cucumbers
1 ½ tablespoons (22 g) rice vinegar
2 teaspoons (9.1 g) sesame oil
2 teaspoons (11 g) soy sauce
1 tablespoon (14 g) grapeseed or extra-virgin olive oil
2 large garlic cloves, minced or put through a press
Red pepper flakes, to taste
Small handful whole cilantro leaves, for garnish
2 teaspoons (6.0 g) toasted white sesame seeds, for garnish (optional)
directions:
1. Rinse cucumbers and pat dry. Cut crosswise into pieces about 4 inches long. Cut each piece in half lengthwise.
2. On a work surface, place a piece of cucumber (or several) cut side down. Lay the blade of a large knife flat on top the cucumber and smash down lightly with your other hand. The skin will begin to crack, the flesh will break down and the seeds will separate. Repeat until the whole piece is smashed. Break or slice diagonally into bite-size pieces, leaving the seeds behind.
3. Place the cucumber pieces in a strainer and toss with a big pinch of salt and a big pinch of sugar. Place a plastic bag filled with ice on top of the cucumbers to serve as a weight and place the strainer over a bowl. Let drain 15 to 30 minutes on the counter, or in the refrigerator until ready to serve, up to 4 hours.
4. Make the dressing: In a small bowl, combine salt, sugar and rice vinegar. Stir until salt and sugar are dissolved. Stir in sesame oil and soy sauce.
5. When ready to serve, shake cucumbers well to drain off any remaining liquid and transfer to a serving bowl. Drizzle with grapeseed or olive oil and toss. Add half the dressing, half the garlic and the red pepper flakes to taste, and toss. Keep adding dressing until cucumbers are well coated but not drowned. Taste and add more pepper flakes and garlic if needed. Serve immediately, garnished with cilantro and sesame seeds.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread sent by Laura (llantrip@carrallison.com) to herself and Robert, 2020-05-26; body is the NYT Cooking text only, with no annotation from either of them.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (5,497)). Julia Moskin on pai huang gua, the smashed cucumber salad eaten across China as a counter to hot weather and hot food, sometimes with dried chiles and Sichuan peppercorns. Smashing is the point: it cracks the skin, loosens the seeds and breaks the flesh into rough pieces that hold dressing. Salting and chilling afterwards draws out water and delivers the cold, crunchy texture the dish depends on.

What readers report: Two well-voted comments argue the recipe is missing an authentic component. A reader who ate this regularly in Sichuan (413 votes) says to toast Sichuan peppercorns until fragrant, crush them and add them to the dressing; a 319-vote comment repeats the Sichuan pepper point and additionally swaps the rice wine vinegar for Chinkiang-style aged dark vinegar, whose sorghum base suits the dish better. On method, a 624-vote note offers a shortcut: scoop the seeds first, smash lightly, then spread the pieces on a plate to dry rather than salting and draining. A 303-vote comment reassures cooks anxious about smashing technique that precision does not matter much. The highest-voted note overall (1,621) is a joke about using the drained cucumber water for a gin martini.

ahead: Let drain 15 to 30 minutes on the counter, or in the refrigerator until ready to serve, up to 4 hours.

claude_opt.changes: Skip the salt-and-ice-weight drain: the top-voted tip (624 votes) says to scoop out seeds first, smash lightly, then air-dry on a plate instead - faster, less fuss, same crunch.

name: Croque Monsieur
ingredients:
BÉCHAMEL
2 tablespoons (28 g) (¼ stick) unsalted butter
1 ounce (28 g) all-purpose flour
8 ounces (227 g) whole milk
1 teaspoon (1.1 g) fresh thyme leaves
½ teaspoon (1.4 g) kosher salt
½ teaspoon (1.2 g) ground white pepper
¼ teaspoon (0.6 g) freshly grated nutmeg

SANDWICHES
4 slices sourdough bread, cut ½ inch thick
1 tablespoon (16 g) whole grain mustard
8 ounces (227 g) thinly sliced black forest ham
8 ounces (227 g) grated Gruyère cheese
2 teaspoons (2.0 g) herbes de Provence blend
directions:
1. Melt the butter in a small saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook for 2 minutes, whisking occasionally, until the roux smells nutty. Whisk in the milk, thyme, salt, white pepper and nutmeg. Cook the milk mixture, whisking to smooth, until thickened. Set the sauce aside to cool and thicken slightly more while preparing the sandwiches.

2. Set the top rack 6 inches under the broiler and heat the broiler to high. Line a half sheet pan with aluminum foil, spray with a little nonstick cooking spray, and set the bread slices on the pan. Spread the mustard on the bread slices.

3. Top the bread slices with 2 ounces each of the ham. Cover the ham evenly with the béchamel and top each with 2 ounces Gruyère. Sprinkle each sandwich with ½ teaspoon herbes de Provence. Broil these open-face sandwiches for 2 to 3 minutes, or until the cheese is melted and lightly browned.

4. Serve with a knife and fork and plenty of napkins.

Note: If you add a fried egg to the top of the sandwich, it becomes a croque madame.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (Robert to himself, 2016-11-02); no reply or forward carrying an annotation.

Web summary (altonbrown.com). Alton Brown's take on the French ham-and-cheese, published on his own site as 'Mr. Crunchy.' The sandwich is built open-faced so the broiler can do two jobs at once: melt the Gruyere and crisp the bread's surface. A roux-based bechamel seasoned with thyme, white pepper and nutmeg is spread over the ham so the sandwich stays moist under high heat, and a homemade herbes de Provence blend goes on top. Add a fried egg and it becomes a croque madame.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS on the page.

Note on the source: Bechamel matches the family copy exactly - 2 Tbsp butter, 1 oz flour, 8 oz whole milk, 1 tsp fresh thyme, 1/2 tsp kosher salt, 1/2 tsp white pepper, 1/4 tsp grated nutmeg - as do the 4 half-inch sourdough slices and 1 Tbsp whole grain mustard. Only difference is the fillings: the site version says 6 oz Gruyere / 4 oz ham / 1 tsp herbes, the family copy 8 oz each and 2 tsp herbes; that is the cookbook-vs-website variance, same author, same recipe. The site also gives the full herbes de Provence blend the family copy assumes you have: 1 Tbsp each dried thyme, rosemary, tarragon, basil; 2 tsp each fennel seed and marjoram; 1 tsp each oregano, dill, chervil.

claude_opt.changes: Alton's version skips toasting the bread before topping, unlike ATK's croque monsieur, which pre-bakes it; broil the bread alone 1-2 min first so it doesn't go soggy under the béchamel.

name: Deviled Eggs
ingredients:
1 dozen HB eggs
1/2 cup (110 g) Mayonaise
2 tsp. (10 g) yellow deli mustard
1 tsp. (3.3 g) toasted ground mustard seed
1.5 tsp. (9.0 g) salt
1 Tbs. (15 g) Durkee sauce
2 Tbs. (19 g) Wickles relish
1 Tbs. (15 g) Cider vinegar
several grinds of pepper
directions: Mash the yolks, then incorporate the other ingredients. The best way to get the mixture into the halves is to put it into a ziploc, squeeze it all to one corner, then cut about 0.5" off the corner.
description: RM 10/13: Now the beauty and pain of deviled eggs is that they are always slightly different. There is enough yolk mixture to taste several times and fine tune. Mayo just about perfect. Mustard is a bit more flexible, can use powdered yellow mustard, but I like to toast whole seeds the grind them in coffee grinder. The real flex ingredients are the salt, pepper, and relish. Some people like more some less. but anyway you mash the yolks then incorporate other ingredients. best way to get mixture into haves is to put it in to ziploc and squeeze all to one corner then cut about .5" of the corner off. I have tried several garnishes, Olives look nice, but they don't really add much and they don't look as good with paprika. There is just the traditional paprika which I always use. My favorite though might be to quarter Wickles pickles and then use paprika. adds a bit more of the sweet/spicy and the yellow, green, and red look really neat.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Robert's own first-person commentary in the 'Deviled Eggs recipez' message (2013-10-09), moved out of the recipe body into the cook's note; the mashing/ziploc method stays in directions.

claude_opt.changes: Cook's note already dials in seasoning; only add is steaming eggs 12-13 min then ice-bathing, which peels cleaner than boiling and doesn't change flavor.

name: Everyday Turmeric Chicken Drumsticks
ingredients:
10 skinless chicken drumsticks (about3 pounds)
1 teaspoon (3.0 g) ground turmeric
2½ teaspoons (7.0 g) kosher salt (plus more as needed)
¼ teaspoon (0.6 g) ground black pepper (plus more as needed)
3 tablespoons (40 g) olive oil
1 medium yellow onion, diced
2 cloves garlic, chopped
Splash of white wine (optional, if you happen to have some open)
2 tablespoons (30 g) fresh lemon juice (about ½ lemon plus more as needed)
Parsley, as a garnish (optional)
directions:
Make a couple of slits in the flesh of each drumstick. This allows the drumsticks to cook faster and for all the flavors to seep in. In a bowl, season the drumsticks with the turmeric, salt, and pepper. Set aside.

In a large pan with a lid (12-inch works well), heat the oil over medium heat. Add the onion, sprinkle with a little salt, and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 2 minutes. Splash with the wine (if using).

Add the drumsticks to the pan. It's okay if they overlap a little, just scoot them around once in a while. Cook until the chicken takes on a little color, about 3 minutes on each side. Add the lemon juice and a scant ¼ cup hot water. Turn the chicken pieces in the sauce to coat all sides, and scrape up all the crispy bits. Reduce the heat to medium-low, partially cover, and simmer, turning once in a while, until the chicken is cooked through and tender, about 35 minutes. Taste as it cooks and make delicious. More salt, pepper, lemon juice? Garnish with parsley, if using, and serve.

MAKE AHEAD: A few hours in advance, but leave the chicken in its juice in the pot. You might need to drizzle in a little more water when reheating.

PLAN AHEAD: Can be stored in the fridge for up to 3 days or in the freezer for up to 3 months.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (Robert to himself, 2020-11-12). Two earlier copies exist (thread 173df61755c7a554, 2020-08-11, to himself; thread 173b54dc4b8d74cd, 2020-08-03, to Laura) and neither carries an annotation from Robert; the 2020-08-03 copy's long lead-in is the cookbook author's headnote, so it was not promoted.

Web summary (kosher.com, 5.0 out of 5 stars (4 ratings)). Naz Deravian, from Bottom of the Pot: Persian Recipes and Stories - the dish is morgh ba zardchoobeh, her family's weeknight standby. Slitting the drumsticks is the working part of the technique: it shortens the cooking and lets the turmeric, salt and lemon reach the meat rather than sitting on the skin-less surface. The onion is cooked down to gold first so its sweetness balances turmeric's earthiness, and the sauce is finished with lemon juice and a scant quarter cup of hot water rather than stock, which keeps it bright.

What readers report: Readers questioned whether the full 2 1/2 tsp kosher salt is right if the chicken was already koshered (i.e. pre-salted) - worth halving in that case. Several cooked the drumsticks noticeably longer than the stated 35 minutes.

Note on the source: Identical to the family copy, quantity for quantity: 10 skinless drumsticks (about 3 lb), 1 tsp ground turmeric, 2 1/2 tsp kosher salt, 1/4 tsp black pepper, 3 Tbsp olive oil, 1 medium yellow onion diced, 2 cloves garlic, optional splash of white wine, 2 Tbsp lemon juice, parsley. The family copy's MAKE AHEAD / PLAN AHEAD blocks and the line 'taste as it cooks and make delicious' are Deravian's own. kosher.com is a licensed reprint of the cookbook, not the author's site; the author's own site is https://bottomofthepot.com/ but does not host this recipe.

makeahead: PLAN AHEAD: Can be stored in the fridge for up to 3 days or in the freezer for up to 3 months.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing — slit-and-sear technique, golden-onion base, and partial-cover simmer match every reputable version of this dish; it's the author's own method with no evident gap.

name: Flour Bakery Chocolate Chip Cookies
ingredients:
1 cup (2 sticks; 224 grams) unsalted butter
3/4 cup (150 grams) granulated sugar
3/4 cup (175 grams) light brown sugar
2 eggs
1 1/4 cup (175 grams) all-purpose flour
1 cup (160 grams) bread flour
1 teaspoon (4.6 g) baking soda
1/2 teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
1 1/2 cups (9 ounces; 250 grams) chopped semisweet chocolate
1/2 cup (2.5 ounces; 70 grams) finely chopped milk chocolate
directions:
Using a stand mixer fitted with a paddle attachment (or mixing by hand with a wooden spoon), beat the butter, granulated sugar, and brown sugar on medium speed until mixture is light and fluffy, about five minutes. Stop the mixer and use a rubber spatula to scrape down the sides and bottom of the bowl and the paddle itself a few times; the sugar and butter love to collect here and stay unmixed. Beat in the eggs and vanilla extract on medium speed until thoroughly combined, two to three minutes. Again scrape the bowl and the paddle to make sure the eggs are thoroughly incorporated.

Mix together the all-purpose flour, bread flour, baking soda and salt. Add both chocolates to the flour mix and toss to combine. Turn the mixer to low speed (or continue to use a wooden spoon if mixing by hand) and slowly blend the flour-chocolate mixture into the butter-sugar mixture. Mix until the flour and chocolate are totally incorporated and the dough is completely mixed.

For best results, scrape dough into a container and let rest in the refrigerator for a day before baking.

The next day, let cookies come up to room temperature a bit to help with scooping. Scoop 1/4 cup cookies on to round sheet pans. About eight is the max number that will fit on a half sheet pan. Cook at 350 for about 11 minutes? until edges are starting to brown but middles are not at all browned and still puffy. Remove and let cool on the pan for 5 minutes before transferring to a rack.
description:
RM 2/13: the 72% cacao was too dark and the 45% cacao from Aldi was not dark enough.
RM 2/13: Use 1/2 tsp vanilla extract per full recipe, 1/4 per half recipe.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Cacao note is the closing 'Note:' line of Robert's own original message of 2/4/2013; the vanilla note is his reply to himself on 2/15/2013 (re-forwarded unchanged to Laura on 8/28/2018, adding nothing new).

Web summary (masterclass.com, 5 stars (105 ratings)). Joanne Chang of Flour Bakery, Boston. She hand-chops bar chocolate instead of using chips, both so you can pick the chocolate and so the shards give bigger, more irregular pockets than uniform chips do. The dough is built on a mix of bread flour and all-purpose - the bread flour's extra protein gives the chew - and she insists on chilling it overnight, which hydrates the flour and deepens the flavour before baking.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS shown on the page.

Note on the source: Confirmed as Joanne Chang's Flour chocolate chunk cookie. The distinctive chocolate split matches the family copy to the gram: 9 oz / 250-255 g semisweet chopped (about 1 1/2 cups) plus 2 1/2 oz / 70 g milk chocolate (about 1/2 cup), as do 3/4 cup/150 g granulated, 3/4 cup/165-175 g light brown, 1 cup/224-228 g butter, 2 eggs, 1 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp salt. One variance across printings: MasterClass gives 1 cup/150 g bread flour + 1 cup/140 g AP, the family copy 1 cup/160 g bread + 1 1/4 cups/175 g AP - i.e. the family copy runs about 45 g more flour. Gram weights on the published page are usable for the conversion project. Robert's own notes (72 percent cacao too dark, 45 percent not dark enough; 1/2 tsp vanilla per full recipe) are his, not the author's - note the family ingredient list omits vanilla although the method calls for it, while MasterClass lists 1 tsp.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

Data fix (Sept 2026): this shares a source link with Chocolate Chunk Cookies, but the two ingredient lists differ (flour ratios, chip vs chunk). Treat the link as a lead rather than a citation.

makeahead: For best results, scrape dough into a container and let rest in the refrigerator for 1 day before baking.

claude_opt.changes: Well-documented reprints of this exact recipe bake 14-17 min at 350°F; your copy's own '11 minutes?' is likely underbaked. Extend it and pull when edges are golden but centers still soft.

name: Fresh Pasta For Two
ingredients:
One large egg + one large egg yolk
125g flour
1/8 tps salt
directions:
Bring mixture together to the point where you can stick in your thumb deep without anything coming off on you.

When correct ratio is achieved, knead for eight minutes by hand. Then let rest for 30-60 minutes covered in the fridge.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (2013-05-28, Robert to himself); no replies or forwards, so no cook's note.

claude_opt.changes: Ratio and hand-knead time match modern fresh-pasta standards. Let dough sit 15-20 min at room temperature after the fridge rest before rolling; cold dough cracks in the roller.

name: General Tso's Chicken
source: Fuchsia Dunlop, Revolutionary Chinese Cookbook: Recipes from Hunan Province
ingredients:
For the sauce:
1 tablespoon (16 g) double-concentrate tomato paste, mixed with 1 tablespoon water
1/2 teaspoon (1.6 g) potato starch (corn starch can be substituted)
1/2 teaspoon (2.7 g) dark soy sauce
1 1/2 teaspoons (8.0 g) light soy sauce
1 tablespoon (15 g) rice vinegar
3 tablespoons (45 g) chicken stock or water

For the chicken:
12 ounces (340 g) (about 4 to 5) boneless, skinless chicken thighs
1/2 teaspoon (2.7 g) dark soy sauce
2 teaspoons (11 g) light soy sauce
1 egg yolk
2 tablespoons (19 g) potato starch (corn starch can be substituted)
1 quart (864 g) peanut oil, more as needed, for frying
6 to 10 dried red chile peppers
2 teaspoons (4.0 g) finely chopped ginger
2 teaspoons (5.6 g) minced garlic
2 teaspoons (9.1 g) sesame oil
Scallions, sliced thinly, for garnish.
Rice, for serving
directions:
1. Make the sauce: Combine all the ingredients in a small bowl, and set aside.

2. Make the chicken: Unfold the chicken thighs; lay on a cutting board. Remove as much of the sinew as possible. (If some parts are very thick, cut in half horizontally.) Slice a few shallow crosshatches into the meat; cut each thigh into roughly 1/4-inch slices, and place in a large bowl. Add the soy sauces and egg yolk; mix well. Stir in the potato starch and 2 teaspoons peanut oil; set aside.

3. Using scissors, snip the chile peppers into 1/4-inch pieces, discarding seeds. Set aside.

4. Pour 3 1/2 cups peanut oil into a large wok or deep saucepan or enough oil to rise 1 1/2 inches from the bottom. Set over high heat until oil reaches 350 to 400 degrees. Add half the chicken; fry until crisp and deep golden brown, 3 to 4 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer chicken to a plate. Repeat with second batch of chicken. Pour oil into a heatproof container, and wipe the wok or saucepan clean.

5. Place wok or saucepan over high heat. Add 2 tablespoons peanut oil. When hot, add chile peppers and stir-fry for a few seconds, until they just begin to change color. Add the ginger and garlic; stir-fry for a few seconds longer, until fragrant. Add the sauce, stirring as it thickens. Return chicken to wok, and stir vigorously to coat. Remove from heat; stir in the sesame oil, and top with scallions. Serve with rice.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (Robert to himself, 2013-02-15); no reply or forward carrying an annotation.

claude_opt.changes: Recipe already substitutes 'deep saucepan' for the wok, fine for this kitchen. Rest fried chicken 3-5 min then re-fry both batches ~1 min at 400°F for a crust that survives saucing.

name: Giada's Mushroom Ragù
servings: Makes about 3 cups; serves 4 over a pound of pasta as a first course
ingredients:
¼ cup (54 g) extra-virgin olive oil
1 large onion, chopped
2 garlic cloves, minced
1 pound (454 g) mixed wild mushrooms (such as cremini, oyster, stemmed shiitake), chopped
½ teaspoon (3.0 g) salt, plus more to taste
¼ teaspoon (0.6 g) freshly ground black pepper, plus more to taste
1 cup (237 g) Marsala
2 cups (480 g) reduced-sodium chicken broth
⅔ cup (60 g) grated Parmesan cheese
5 fresh basil leaves
¼ cup (15 g) chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
directions:
In a large skillet, heat the oil over a medium flame. When almost smoking, add the onion and garlic and sauté until the onion is tender, about 8 minutes. Add the mushrooms, ½ teaspoon of salt, and ¼ teaspoon of pepper. Increase the heat to high and sauté until the mushrooms are tender and all the liquid has evaporated, about 8 minutes. Remove the pan from the heat and add the Marsala. Return the pan to the heat and simmer until the Marsala evaporates, about 5 minutes. Add the chicken broth and simmer until the sauce has reduced by half, about 30 minutes. Remove the pan from the heat and stir in the cheese, basil, and parsley. Season the ragù with more salt and pepper to taste.

(The sauce can be made up to 2 days ahead. Cool, then cover and refrigerate. Rewarm before using.)
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (2013-05-28, Robert to himself); no replies or forwards, so no cook's note.

Web summary (foodnetwork.com). Giada De Laurentiis, from Everyday Italian. The mushrooms are cooked over high heat until every bit of their liquid has gone, which is what concentrates their flavour instead of stewing them; only then does the Marsala go in, off the heat, and reduce away. A long half-hour reduction of chicken broth builds the body a meat ragu would get from bones, and the Parmesan, basil and parsley go in off the heat at the end. She warns against plain white button mushrooms, which carry too much water and too little flavour.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS available - Food Network's review panel did not load.

Note on the source: Same recipe family, not provably the exact printing the family copy came from. Family copy: 1 cup Marsala, no cream, 2/3 cup Parmesan, 1/2 tsp salt and 1/4 tsp pepper stated explicitly. Food Network (Everyday Italian): 1/2 cup Marsala plus 1/3 cup heavy cream, 1/2 to 3/4 cup Parmesan. Giadzy, her own site (https://giadzy.com/blogs/recipes/giadas-mushroom-ragu), instead uses 3/4 cup red wine, 2/3 cup Parmesan and 1 Tbsp butter. Everything else - 1/4 cup EVOO, 1 large onion, 2 garlic cloves, 1 lb mixed wild mushrooms, 5 basil leaves, 1/4 cup parsley, 2 cups chicken broth - is identical across all three. Chose the Food Network page because Marsala is the family copy's distinctive ingredient; a human might prefer the Giadzy page as the author's own site. Duplicate FN posting: https://www.foodnetwork.com/recipes/mushroom-ragu-recipe-1956251

makeahead: The sauce can be made up to 2 days ahead.

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing — Giada's own current site (Giadzy) republishes this near-identically; searing mushrooms fully dry and avoiding button mushrooms already matches every well-reviewed version of this dish.

name: Heston's Slow-Roasted Brined Chicken
source: Heston Blumenthal, How to Cook Like Heston
cook_time: 3-4 hours roasting, plus 45 minutes resting and about 10 minutes browning
ingredients:
6% brine (300g salt dissolved in 5 litres of water)
1.5-2kg chicken
1 lemon
1 bunch of thyme
125g unsalted butter, at room temperature, plus extra for rubbing into the skin
30ml dry white wine

For the gravy (optional)
20ml dry white wine
250ml chicken stock
1 tsp (5.2 g) Dijon mustard
1 sprig of tarragon
1 sprig of parsley
directions:
Warning: Whilst Heston cooks his chicken to an internal temperature of 60°C, if you want to stick to safety guidelines your chicken should reach 75°C in the thickest part of the breast.

1. Remove the trussing from the chicken then place it in a clean container. Pour over the brine ensuring that the chicken is submerged then cover the container with clingfilm and place in the fridge overnight.

2. Remove the chicken from the liquid and dry well with kitchen paper. Remove the wishbone and place on a cooling rack over a tray.

3. Preheat the oven to 90ºC (about fan 70°C, gas mark ¼ **PLEASE NOTE** ovens vary so use an oven thermometer to get an accurate temperature).

4. Roll and pierce the lemon then place it in the cavity of the bird with half the thyme. Rub some butter on top of the skin.

5. Place the chicken on the rack in a roasting tray and place in the oven. Roast the chicken until the internal temperature in the thickest part of the breast is 60ºC (this should take 3-4 hours).

6. Remove the chicken from the oven and allow to rest for 45 minutes. Turn the oven temperature as high as it will go.

7. In the meantime, melt the butter in a pan and add 30ml wine and a few sprigs of thyme. Bring to the boil then remove the pan from the heat and use the melted butter to baste the chicken before and during browning.

8. Once the resting time has elapsed, put the chicken back in the roasting tray and return it to the oven for approximately 10 minutes or until golden brown, taking care that it doesn't burn.

9. Once coloured, remove the chicken from the oven and place on a cooling rack.

10. To carve the chicken, remove the legs by slicing down where they meet the breast and splaying them outwards to expose the joint, which you can then sever.

11. Remove the breast by running a sharp knife deeply into the flesh along one side of the centre bone that extends the length of the bird, making a deep vertical cut. Then cut horizontally through the flesh at the bottom of the breast until the horizontal cut meets the vertical, separating the breast from the ribcage. Repeat the procedure on the other side of the centre bone. The breasts can then be laid cut-side down on the chopping board and sliced.

12. Season with salt and freshly ground black pepper.

If making the gravy...

13. When the chicken has been browned and removed from the roasting tray, place the tray containing the juices on the hob over a medium-high heat. Add the white wine and scrape and stir to deglaze the pan. Add the chicken stock and cook until reduced to a sauce. Strain into a small saucepan.

14. Before serving, stir in the mustard and warm through. Finish with freshly chopped tarragon and parsley and season with salt and freshly ground black pepper.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (Robert to himself, 2013-02-04). The quoted paragraph in the body is Heston Blumenthal's own blurb, not Robert's.

Web summary (sbs.com.au). Heston Blumenthal's roast chicken as broadcast in How to Cook Like Heston. Two things carry it: an overnight 6 percent brine, which seasons the bird throughout and helps the muscle hold water, and then a very low 90C oven that takes three to four hours to bring the breast to 60C, so the meat never contracts and squeezes its juices out. The bird rests a full 45 minutes, then goes back into an oven turned as high as it will go for about ten minutes purely to colour the skin - browning is separated from cooking.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS on the page.

Note on the source: Exact match to the family copy, including the quantities and the safety caveat: 6 percent brine of 300 g salt in 5 litres water; 1.5-2 kg chicken; 1 lemon; 1 bunch thyme; 125 g unsalted butter at room temperature plus extra for the skin; 30 ml dry white wine; optional gravy of 20 ml wine, 250 ml chicken stock, 1 tsp Dijon, a sprig each of tarragon and parsley. Oven 90C (about 70C fan, gas 1/4), roast to 60C internal over 3-4 hours, rest 45 minutes, blast at maximum about 10 minutes; the page carries the same warning that food-safety guidance wants 75C in the thickest part of the breast, which is the line Robert's copy opens with. Note a widely circulated fan version at https://bigspud.co.uk/heston-blumenthals-roast-chicken/ uses a smaller 1.4 kg bird and 240 g salt in 4 litres - not the family's version.

name: Kung Pao Chicken With Peanuts (Gong Bao Ji Ding)
servings: Serves 2 as a main dish with rice and one stir-fried vegetable dish, 4 with three other dishes
ingredients:
2 boneless chicken breasts (about 300g or 3/4 pound in total)
3 cloves of garlic and an equivalent amount of ginger
5 spring onions, white parts only
2 tbsp (27 g) groundnut oil
a handful of dried red chillies (at least 10)
1 tsp (2.3 g) whole Sichuan pepper
75g (2/3 cup) roasted peanuts

For the marinade:
1/2 tsp (3.0 g) salt
2 tsp (11 g) light soy sauce
1 tsp (4.9 g) Shaoxing wine
1 1/2 tsp (3.8 g) potato flour
1 tbsp (15 g) water

For the sauce:
3 tsp (13 g) sugar
3/4 tsp (1.9 g) potato flour
1 tsp (5.3 g) dark soy sauce
1 tsp (5.3 g) light soy sauce
3 tsp (15 g) Chinkiang vinegar
1 tsp (4.5 g) sesame oil
1 tbsp (15 g) chicken stock or water
directions:
1. Cut the chicken as evenly as possible into 1cm strips and then into small cubes. Mix with the marinade ingredients.
2. Peel and thinly slice the garlic and ginger, and chop the spring onions into Icm (1/2 inch) chunks. Snip the chillies into 1.5cm (3/4 inch) sections, discarding seeds as far as possible. Combine the sauce ingredients in a small bowl.
3. Pour a little groundnut oil into the wok and heat until it smokes, swirling the oil around to cover the entire base of the wok. Pour off into a heatproof container. Add 3 tbsp fresh oil and heat over a high flame. When the oil is hot but not smoking, add the chillies and Sichuan pepper and stir-fry for a few seconds until they are fragrant (take care not to burn them).
4. Add the chicken and continue to stir-fry. When the chicken cubes have separated, add the ginger, garlic and spring onions and stir-fry until they are fragrant and the meat is just cooked.
5. Give the sauce a stir and add to the wok, continuing to stir and toss. As soon as the sauce has become thick and lustrous, add the peanuts, mix them in, and serve immediately.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (Robert to himself, 2013-02-13); no annotation in the thread. A separate SMS-backup email of 2014-11-14 reads 'The kung pao was really hot. Just had it,' but it does not state he cooked this recipe, so it was not used.

Web summary (leitesculinaria.com, 5 out of 5 stars (12 votes)). Fuchsia Dunlop's Sichuan gong bao, reprinted by Leite's Culinaria. The chicken is marinated in potato flour, soy and Shaoxing so it stays tender through the brief, very hot stir-fry - the coating is the whole point. The sauce is mixed in advance because once the wok is going there is no time; its balance of sugar, Chinkiang black vinegar and two soy sauces is what separates the real dish from takeout. Whole dried chillies and Sichuan pepper are fried first, for fragrance rather than raw heat.

What readers report: Cut the chillies back if you want it mild - leaving them whole lets heat-averse eaters pick them out, and heat varies a lot by chilli type. Arrowroot works as a substitute for the potato flour. A nonstick pan keeps the sauce from catching better than stainless. One cook finished it with angel hair pasta and liked it.

Note on the source: Marinade and sauce match the family copy ingredient for ingredient: marinade 1/2 tsp salt, 2 tsp light soy, 1 tsp Shaoxing, 1 1/2 tsp potato flour, 1 Tbsp water; sauce 1 Tbsp (family: 3 tsp) sugar, 3/4 tsp potato flour, 1 tsp dark soy, 1 tsp light soy, 1 Tbsp (family: 3 tsp) Chinkiang vinegar, 1 tsp sesame oil, 1 Tbsp stock. Chicken 2/3 lb vs family's 300 g / 3/4 lb; 10+ dried chillies, 1 tsp Sichuan pepper, 2/3 cup (family: 75 g) roasted peanuts, 3 garlic, equal ginger, 5 spring onions - all the same. Gram anchors usable for conversion: roasted peanuts 2/3 cup = 75 g; chicken breast 300 g = 2 breasts.

claude_opt.changes: No wok here; Kenji's well-reviewed version, like this one, is written wok-specific for max heat retention. Use the Lodge cast iron or Weber griddle's hottest zone, cooking chicken in small batches so it sears, not steams.

name: Lahey Stecca
source: Jim Lahey, My Bread: The Revolutionary No-Work, No-Knead Method
ingredients:
3 cups (400 grams) bread flour
1/2 teaspoon (3.0 g) table salt
3/4 teaspoon (3.2 g) sugar
1/4 teaspoon (0.8 g) instant or other active dry yeast
1 1/2 cups (350 grams) cool 55-65F water
additional flour for dusting
20 pieces of the any combination of following: whole garlic cloves, whole olives, halved cherry tomatoes
1/4 cup (54 g) extra virgin olive oil
3/4 teaspoon (2.1 g) coarse sea salt or kosher salt
directions:
1. In a medium bowl, stir together the flour, table salt, sugar and yeast. Add the water and, using a wooden spoon, mix until you have a wet, sticky dough, about 30 seconds. Cover the bowl and let sit at room temperature until the surface is dotted with bubbles and the dough is more than doubled in size, 10 to 18 hours (24 hours if you have a cold cold home.)

2. When the first rise is complete, generously dust a work surface with flour. Use a bowl scraper or rubber spatula to scrape the dough out of the bowl in one piece. Fold the dough over itself to her three times and gently shape it into a somewhat flattened ball. Brush the surface of the dough with some of the olive oil and sprinkle with 1/4 teaspoon of the coarse salt (which will gradually dissolve on the surface).

3. Grab a large bowl (large enough to hold the dough when it doubles in size. you could also use a large pot) and brush the insides of the bowl with olive oil. Gently place the dough, seam side down into the bowl. Cover bowl with a towel. Place in a warm draft free spot to rise for 1 to 2 hours. The dough is ready when it is almost doubled. If you gently poke it with your finger, it should hold the impression. If it springs back, let it rise for another 15 minutes.

4. Half an hour before the end of the second rise, pre-heat the oven to 500F, with a rack in the center. Oil a 13" x 18" x 1" baking sheet.

5. Cut the dough into quarters. Gently stretch each piece evenly into a long, thin, baguette shape approximately the length of the pan. Place on the pan, leaving about 1 inch between the loaves. Embed the garlic cloves, olives or cherry tomatoes into the loaves, about five pieces per loaf. Drizzle, tab or brush olive oil on each loaf. Sprinkle sea salt or kosher salt over each loaf, remember to go light on the olive loaf since the olives are salty.

6. Bake for 15 to 25 minutes, until the crust is golden brown. Cool on a pan for five minutes, then use a spatula to transfer the baguette to a rack to cool thoroughly.

Note: The baguette may become a bit soggy in just a few hours because of the salt on the surface. If that happens, reheat the loaves in a hot oven until crisp.
description: RM 5/13: I almost never include the garlic, olives, or tomatoes that the recipe says you can put on top.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Ingredients and steps 1-5 from Robert's 2/4/2013 recipez message (thread 13ca6e14edc99f6b, single message, no replies); step 6, the soggy-crust note and the cook's note come from Robert's own identical copy of this recipe sent 5/14/2013 in thread 13ea37422df3331e ('Bread recipe'), which the recipez thread is missing.

Web summary (leitesculinaria.com, 5 out of 5 stars (vote count not shown)). Jim Lahey's stick loaves from My Bread, run by Leite's Culinaria as a licensed excerpt. The no-knead method does the work: a 10-to-18-hour room-temperature ferment with a quarter teaspoon of yeast develops the flavour and gluten that kneading would otherwise have to build. Because the loaves are stretched thin, they bake through in 15 to 25 minutes at 500F rather than needing a covered pot, and the olive oil and coarse salt brushed on before the second rise give the crust its snap.

What readers report: Testers warn the tips brown fast, so watch the last few minutes. Plan roughly 20 hours from start to table. Double the batch for six or more - it goes quickly. Several preferred the loaves plain with just olive oil and coarse salt rather than topped, which matches Robert's own cook's note that he almost never adds the garlic, olives or tomatoes.

Note on the source: Exact match to the family copy: 3 cups bread flour, 1/2 tsp table salt, 3/4 tsp sugar, 1/4 tsp instant or active dry yeast, 1 1/2 cups cool 55-65F water, 1/4 cup EVOO, 3/4 tsp coarse salt, about 20 topping pieces (5 per loaf), 4 loaves. Gram note: the family copy already carries weights the published page lacks - 400 g bread flour and 350 g water, i.e. an 87.5 percent hydration by the family's own reckoning (350/400). Alternate full text: https://steamykitchen.com/6795-no-knead-baguette-stecca.html

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

ahead: Cover the bowl and let sit at room temperature until the surface is dotted with bubbles and the dough is…

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing beyond what your 5/13 note already fixed (skip the toppings); hydration, fermentation window, and bake match Leite's reprint of Lahey's own recipe exactly.

name: Leek And Potato Soup Or Vichyssoise
ingredients:
3 medium sized leeks: white part only
1 medium sized onion
2 tablespoons (28 g) butter
4 medium potatoes
4 cups (960 g) poultry stock
1 to 2 cups (238-476 g) cream
1/4 tsp (0.4 g) mace (optional)
Salt and white pepper
Chipped watercress or chives
directions:
This leek soup may be served hot or very cold. Be sure to serve the soup reduced to a velvety smoothness.

Mince the leeks (white part only) and the onion.

Stir and saute them 3 minutes in the butter.

Pare, slice very fine, and add the potatoes.

Add the poultry stock.

Simmer the vegetables, covered, 15 minutes or until tender. Put them through a very fine sieve, food mill or blender. Add the cream, mace (optional), salt and white pepper, and chipped watercress or chives.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message recipez thread (2013-02-04). An earlier thread 1388cc93f3db16c7 (2012-07-15) carries the same text from Robert's parents plus his own forward with only the word 'Recipe.'; neither contains a cooking annotation.

claude_opt.changes: Use a food mill or fine sieve, not a blender, for the potatoes; over-processing starchy potatoes in a blender turns the soup gluey rather than velvety.

name: Mexican Shredded Pork In Ancho-Orange Sauce (Chilorio)
source: Pati Jinich, Pati's Mexican Table, via Serious Eats
ingredients:
3 pounds (1.4 kg) boneless pork butt (shoulder) or loin, preferably with some fat, cut into 2-inch chunks
1 1/4 cups (310 g) freshly squeezed orange juice
1 1/4 cups (296 g) water
1 1/4 teaspoons (3.5 g) kosher or coarse sea salt, or more to taste
4 ancho chiles (2 ounces), rinsed, stemmed, and seeded
1/2 cup (80 g) coarsely chopped white onion
4 garlic cloves
1/2 cup (30 g) chopped fresh Italian parsley
1 teaspoon (1.0 g) dried oregano, preferably Mexican
1/4 teaspoon (0.5 g) ground cumin
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) freshly ground black pepper, or to taste
2/3 cup (160 g) apple cider vinegar
3 tablespoons (41 g) vegetable oil
16 flour tortillas, warmed
directions:
1. Place the pork in a heavy 12-inch skillet or Dutch oven. Add the orange juice, water, and 1 teaspoon of the salt and bring to a boil over high heat. Reduce the heat to medium and simmer for 40 to 45 minutes, or until most of the liquid has cooked away and the meat is lightly browned and has rendered most of its fat. Set aside to cool.

2. Meanwhile, place the chiles in a bowl, cover with hot water, and soak for 10 to 15 minutes, until softened.

3. Place the chiles, along with 1 1/2 cups of their soaking liquid, in a blender or food processor, along with the onion, garlic, parsley, oregano, cumin, the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt, the pepper, and vinegar and puree until completely smooth.

4. When it is cool enough to handle, shred the pork with your hands or two forks and place it and any juices in a large bowl.

5. In the pot in which the meat was cooked, heat the oil over medium heat. Pour in the chile puree, bring to a simmer, and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until thickened and darkened. Toss in the shredded meat and juices and cook until the meat has absorbed most of the chile sauce, 20 to 25 minutes. Taste for salt.

6. Serve the meat rolled up in the warm flour tortillas or with the tortillas on the side.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (Robert to himself, 2013-04-03). The 'What worked / What didn't / Suggested tweaks' block in the body is the Serious Eats Cook the Book reviewer's text, not Robert's, so it was not promoted to a cook's note. The source URL comes from Robert's companion email of the same day, thread 13dd17bfbe5698b0.

Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.5 (4) / 14 Reviews). Kate Williams writes up a recipe from Pati Jinich's cookbook Pati's Mexican Table as a dressed-up cousin of carnitas. Instead of plain slow-braised pork, the shoulder simmers in orange juice and water until the liquid cooks off and the meat browns in its own rendered fat, and it is then folded into a pureed ancho chile sauce sharpened with a lot of cider vinegar. Williams notes the combination reads almost like a Mexican take on pulled pork, and that the anchos and citrus work particularly well together. In her own testing she needed closer to an hour of simmering than the stated 40 to 45 minutes and topped the pot up with roughly another third of a cup of water and juice, and she stresses leaving the rendered fat and browned bits in the pot to flavor the sauce. Jinich also suggests swapping in bone-in, skin-on dark-meat chicken.

What readers report: Substitutions get the most attention. One cook made it with chicken thighs and said his wife assumed it was pork; another used lard in place of the vegetable oil. Several report the dish reads sweet rather than hot, so do not scale the chiles back: one reviewer who reduced them wished she hadn't, and another left seeds in for heat and served it over creamy polenta. One cook swapped the stovetop reduction for the oven, boiling off the orange juice and browning the meat hands-off, slower but easier. Another used Kenji's chile prep, toasting the dried chiles and softening them in simmering chicken stock rather than plain hot water. Serving notes: shredded lettuce lightens a rich taco, and queso fresco with raw onion suits it. Two questions went unanswered: whether it freezes, and how to adapt the sauce to already-cooked leftover pork.

Note on the source: Ratings display is odd: page shows 4.5 (4) as the star average but lists 14 reviews. Page shows a 'Load More reviews' button, so only the first 9 of 14 reviews are in this paste. One comment ends with 'Read More' and may be truncated.

claude_opt.changes: Simmer the pork closer to an hour, not 40-45 minutes, per the Serious Eats tester's own retest; top up with extra orange juice/water if it dries out first.

name: Model Bakery English Muffins
ingredients:
BIGA
1/2 cup/75 g bread flour
1/4 cup/60 ml water
1/4 tsp (0.8 g) instant (also called quick-rising or bread machine) yeast
DOUGH
1 1/3 cups/315 ml water
3/4 tsp (2.3 g) instant (also called quick-rising or bread machine) yeast
1 Tbsp (14 g) plus 1 tsp extra-virgin olive oil
1 1/2 tsp (9.0 g) fine sea salt
3 1/2 cups/510 g unbleached all-purpose flour, as needed
1/4 cup/35g yellow cornmeal, preferably stone-ground
6 Tbsp/90 ml melted Clarified Butter (page 37), as needed
directions:
You will need a heavy skillet or griddle (preferably cast-iron) to make these. And be sure to make the biga at least 12 hours before making the dough. Since you will probably be toasting the muffins, they don't have to be fresh from the griddle; so make them a day or two ahead (or freeze them) if you wish.

1. TO MAKE THE BIGA: At least 1 day before cooking the muffins, combine the flour, water, and yeast in a small bowl to make a sticky dough. Cover tightly with plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least 12 hours or up to 24 hours. The biga will rise slightly.

2. TO MAKE THE DOUGH: Combine the biga, water, yeast, olive oil, and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer. Affix the bowl to the mixer and fit with the paddle attachment. Mix on low speed until the mixture looks creamy, about 1 minute. Mix in 3 cups/435 g of the flour to make a soft, sticky dough. Turn off the mixer, cover the bowl with plastic wrap, and let stand for 20 minutes. (To make by hand, combine the water, biga, yeast, oil, and salt in a large bowl and break up the biga with a wooden spoon. Stir until the biga dissolves. Mix in enough flour to make a cohesive but tacky dough. Cover and let stand for 20 minutes.)

3. Mix in enough of the remaining flour to make a soft dough that barely cleans the mixer bowl. Replace the paddle with the dough hook. Knead on medium-low speed (if the dough climbs up the hook, just pull it down) until the dough is smooth and elastic, about 8 minutes. Turn out the dough onto a lightly floured work surface to check its texture. It should feel tacky but not stick to the work surface. (To make by hand, knead on a floured work surface, adding more flour as necessary, until the dough is smooth and feels tacky, about 10 minutes.)

4. Shape the dough into a ball. Oil a medium bowl. Put the dough in the bowl and turn to coat with oil, leaving the dough smooth-side up. Cover with plastic wrap. Let stand in a warm place until almost doubled in volume, about 2 hours. (The dough can also be refrigerated for 8 to 12 hours. Let stand at room temperature for 1 hour before proceeding to the next step.)

5. Using a bowl scraper, scrape the dough out of the bowl onto a lightly floured work surface. Cut into twelve equal pieces. Shape each into a 4-in/10-cm round. Sprinkle an even layer of cornmeal over a half-sheet pan. Place the rounds on the cornmeal about 1 in/2.5 cm apart. Turn the rounds to coat both sides with cornmeal. Loosely cover the pan with plastic wrap. Let stand in a warm place until the rounds have increased in volume by half and a finger pressed into a round leaves an impression for a few seconds before filling up, about 1 hour.

6. Melt 2 Tbsp of the clarified butter in a large, heavy skillet (preferably cast-iron) over medium heat until melted and hot, but not smoking. In batches, add the dough rounds to the skillet. Cook, adjusting the heat as needed so the muffins brown without scorching, adding more clarified butter as needed. The undersides should be nicely browned, about 6 minutes. Turn and cook until the other sides are browned and the muffins are puffed, about 6 minutes more. Transfer to a paper towel-lined half-sheet pan and let cool. (It will be tempting to eat these hot off the griddle, but let them stand for at least 20 minutes to complete the cooking with carry-over heat.) Repeat with the remaining muffins, wiping the cornmeal out of the skillet with paper towels and adding more clarified butter as needed.

7. Split each muffin in half horizontally with a serrated knife. Toast in a broiler or toaster oven (they may be too thick for a standard toaster) until lightly browned. Serve hot. (The muffins can be stored in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days.)
description: RM 1/16: Yes, corn meal on both sides. Cooked on each side in a cast iron pan in clarified butter.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. From Robert's 2016-01-23 message describing his bake (thread 1526fb01b3c4fe85), three days after the recipez email; not in the recipe thread itself.

Web summary (bakepedia.com). From The Model Bakery Cookbook (Chronicle, 2013) by Karen and Sarah Mitchell with Rick Rodgers, reprinted on Bakepedia. Hand-shaping the muffins instead of baking them in ring molds turned out to give bigger, airier muffins - better for sandwiches - so the book abandoned the bakery's own original method. A biga made 12 to 24 hours ahead supplies the flavour and structure, and the muffins are cooked on a cast-iron griddle in clarified butter rather than baked.

What readers report: Dense muffins trace to under-proofing, the wrong flour, or tired yeast. Griddle heat is the step people get wrong - keep it to medium, around 275F. Two tablespoons of clarified butter per batch is enough despite the 6 Tbsp the recipe allows. The 1/4 tsp yeast in the biga looks too low but is correct as printed. High-altitude bakers need adjustments.

Note on the source: Exact match to the family copy including the published gram/millilitre weights: biga 1/2 cup/75 g bread flour + 1/4 cup/60 ml water + 1/4 tsp instant yeast; dough 1 1/3 cups/315 ml water, 3/4 tsp instant yeast, 1 Tbsp plus 1 tsp EVOO, 1 1/2 tsp fine sea salt, 3 1/2 cups/510 g unbleached AP flour; plus 1/4 cup/35 g yellow cornmeal and 6 Tbsp/90 ml clarified butter. The family copy's step-2 sub-weight (3 cups/435 g of the flour) also matches. Robert's cook's note - cornmeal on both sides, cast iron, clarified butter - is consistent with the published method.

ahead: And be sure to make the biga at least 12 hours before making the dough.
TO MAKE THE BIGA: At least 1 day before cooking the muffins, combine the flour, water, and yeast in a…

claude_opt.changes: Weigh 435 g flour into the mixer and add only ~25 g more in step 3, for a wetter, more open crumb. Refrigerate the shaped, covered rounds 10-16 h; griddle from cold at 300°F, lidded on the second side.
log: RM 9/25/26: added all 510 g flour in step 1 by mistake. Rescue: 20-min rest, knead with no more flour, add water 1 Tbsp (15 g) at a time only if stiff. Prompted the hold-back-75 g change.

RM 9/25/26: chose the overnight cold proof of shaped rounds and ~70% hydration (about 460 g of the flour). Covering the griddle for part of the cook is his idea, to finish centers without running the oven too; untested.
RM 9/26/26: griddle raised to 300°F for more browning, since the lid now cooks the centers. Drop to 275°F if the first side is dark before 5 min.

name: Mushroom Stroganoff
ingredients:
10 ounces (284 g) extra wide egg noodles
2 tablespoons (28 g) (¼ stick) unsalted butter
5 portobello mushrooms, stems and gills removed, thinly sliced
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt
10 scallions, thinly sliced on the bias, white bottoms and green tops separated
1 tablespoon (7.5 g) all-purpose flour
14 ounces (397 g) beef broth
1 cup (230 g) sour cream
4 ounces (113 g) goat cheese
½ teaspoon (1.1 g) freshly ground black pepper, plus more for serving
directions:
1. Add the noodles to 4 quarts cold water in a large pot, cover, and place over high heat. Cook to al dente, 18 to 22 minutes, stirring occasionally (Cold Water Pasta, see M).
2. Melt 1 tablespoon of the butter in a 10-inch straight-sided sauté pan over medium-high heat.
3. Increase the heat to high, add half of the mushrooms and sprinkle with ½ teaspoon of the salt. Sauté for 5 to 6 minutes, until the mushrooms darken and reduce in volume by half. Remove to a bowl.
4. Repeat with the remaining 1 tablespoon butter, the remaining mushrooms and the remaining ½ teaspoon salt, along with the white bottoms of the scallions.
5. Return the first batch of mushrooms to the pan, sprinkle in the flour and stir to combine, cooking for 1 minute, or until the flour disappears and a dark "fond" appears on the bottom of the pan.
6. Deglaze the pan with the beef broth and as soon as it simmers (almost immediately), decrease the heat to low and cook for 10 to 12 minutes to reduce the liquid.
7. Add the sour cream, goat cheese and pepper and stir to combine. Bring to a bare simmer and cook, covered, for 2 to 4 minutes.
8. Drain the noodles and stir gently into the mushroom mixture. Turn onto a platter and garnish with the scallion tops and additional pepper.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (2016-11-02, Robert to himself); no replies or forwards, so no cook's note.

Web summary (tastecooking.com). Alton Brown, excerpted from Alton Brown: EveryDayCook. His argument is that beef was never essential to stroganoff - noodles and sour cream are the Russian part, and mushrooms belong there at least as much as beef does. Searing the portobellos in two batches rather than crowding the pan is what builds the dark fond the flour and broth later deglaze, and goat cheese stirred in with the sour cream adds the tang and body that beef fat would otherwise supply.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS on the page.

Note on the source: Exact ingredient match to the family copy, quantity for quantity: 10 oz extra wide egg noodles, 2 Tbsp unsalted butter, 5 portobellos (stems and gills removed, thinly sliced), 1 tsp kosher salt, 10 scallions, 1 Tbsp AP flour, 14 oz beef broth, 1 cup sour cream, 4 oz goat cheese, 1/2 tsp black pepper. The family copy's 'Cold Water Pasta, see M' cross-reference confirms the EveryDayCook book text. tastecooking.com is a licensed excerpt; note altonbrown.com hosts only a different 'Mushroom Stroganoff Toast' (https://altonbrown.com/recipes/mushroom-stroganoff-toast/), which is NOT this recipe.

claude_opt.changes: Sour cream and goat cheese are brought to a simmer, covered, for 2-4 min; stroganoff sources warn this risks curdling. Keep the heat low and warm gently instead, same 2-4 min.

name: Pan-Fried Risotto
total_time: 1 hour, plus time to chill risotto
ingredients:
2 tablespoons (28 g) butter
2 tablespoons (27 g) olive oil, plus more for frying
1 medium onion, diced fine
2 cups (248 g) butternut squash, about 2/3 pound, cut in 1/2-inch dice
Salt and pepper
1 cup (200 g) Carnaroli or Arborio rice
1 tablespoon (3.4 g) chopped fresh sage
1/4 cup (59 g) dry white wine
4 to 5 cups (1-1.2 kg) vegetable broth (see recipe)
1 ounce (28 g) grated Parmesan, plus more for garnish
4 ounces (113 g) grated Fontina
Zest and juice of 1 lemon
2 tablespoons (6.0 g) finely sliced chives, plus more for garnish
1 cup (120 g) all-purpose flour
2 large eggs, lightly beaten
directions:
1. Put butter and 2 tablespoons olive oil in a wide heavy-bottom saucepan or deep skillet over medium-high heat. Add onion and cook until softened and lightly colored, about 5 minutes. Add squash and season generously with salt and pepper. Cook, stirring occasionally, until squash is cooked but not soft, about 5 minutes. Add rice and sage and stir to combine, then add wine and cook for 1 minute more.

2. Add 2 cups vegetable broth and bring to a brisk simmer. Cook until liquid is nearly evaporated, about 5 minutes. Continue adding broth 1 cup at a time and cook in the same fashion until rice is just done and all liquid is absorbed (it should take 4 to 5 cups broth), about 10 minutes. Turn off heat and stir in Parmesan, Fontina and lemon zest and juice. Taste and adjust seasoning (rice should be well seasoned). Stir in chives, then spread mixture on a baking sheet or platter to cool. Cool for at least 2 hours (or refrigerate overnight, covered).

3. With a spoon, divide mixture into 12 pieces. Shape each piece into an oval patty. Roll patties lightly in flour to coat. Pour olive oil to a depth of 1/2 inch into a cast-iron skillet and place over medium heat. Dip floured rice patties briefly into beaten egg, then fry gently on both sides until browned. Drain on paper towels. Serve hot, sprinkled with more Parmesan and chives if desired.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (2013-11-08, Robert to himself); no replies or forwards, so no cook's note.

ahead: Cool for at least 2 hours (or refrigerate overnight, covered).

claude_opt.changes: Technique already matches modern risotto-cake methods (chill, shape, fry). Specify oil at 350°F when pan-frying patties so the crust browns before the centers overheat or the coating turns greasy.

name: Penne Alla Vodka
ingredients:
¼ cup (54 g) good olive oil
2½ cups (400 g) chopped Spanish onion (1 large)
1 tablespoon (8.4 g) minced garlic (3 cloves)
½ teaspoon (0.9 g) crushed red pepper flakes
1½ teaspoons (1.5 g) dried oregano
1 cup (221 g) vodka
2 (28-ounce) cans whole peeled plum tomatoes, drained (see note)
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
¾ pound (340 g) penne, such as De Cecco
2 tablespoons (6.9 g) chopped fresh oregano leaves, plus extra for serving
1 cup (238 g) heavy cream
½ cup (45 g) freshly grated Parmesan cheese, plus extra for serving
directions:
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees.

Heat the oil in a large (12-inch) ovenproof sauté pan over medium heat. Add the onions and garlic and cook for about 5 minutes, until the onions are translucent. Add the red pepper flakes and dried oregano and cook for 1 more minute. Add the vodka and simmer for 5 to 7 minutes, until the mixture is reduced by half. Using clean hands, crush each tomato into the pan. Add 2 teaspoons of salt and ½ teaspoon of black pepper. Cover the pan with a tight-fitting lid, place in the oven, and bake for 1½ hours.

Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Add 2 tablespoons of salt and the pasta and cook according to the directions on the package. Drain and set aside.

Two cups at a time, carefully pour the tomato mixture into a blender and purée until smooth. Return the tomato mixture to the sauté pan (be careful; the handle is hot!). Add the fresh oregano, cream, 1 teaspoon salt, and ½ teaspoon pepper and simmer partially covered for 10 minutes. Add the pasta to the sauce and cook for 2 more minutes. Stir in ½ cup of the Parmesan cheese and serve hot sprinkled with extra Parmesan and fresh oregano.

Note: If you don't have a twelve-inch ovenproof sauté pan with a tight-fitting lid, you can use a Dutch oven or large pot.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (2013-11-12, Robert to himself); no replies or forwards, so no cook's note.

Web summary (barefootcontessa.com). Ina Garten's version, on her own Barefoot Contessa site. The unusual move is that the sauce is not simmered on the stove but covered and baked at 375F for an hour and a half, which concentrates the tomatoes without scorching them and needs no attention. The vodka goes in early and is reduced by half before the tomatoes are crushed in by hand, so its bite cooks off and only the aroma it carries remains. The sauce is pureed smooth after baking, then finished with cream, fresh oregano and Parmesan.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS on the page.

Note on the source: Matches the family copy ingredient for ingredient and step for step: 1/4 cup good olive oil, 2 1/2 cups chopped onion, 1 Tbsp minced garlic (3 cloves), 1 1/2 tsp dried oregano, 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes, 1 cup vodka, 2 (28 oz) cans whole peeled plum tomatoes drained, 3/4 lb penne, 2 Tbsp fresh oregano, 1 cup heavy cream, 1/2 cup Parmesan, plus 2 tsp salt / 1/2 tsp pepper into the pot and 2 Tbsp salt in the pasta water. The only wording difference is the onion - family copy says 'Spanish onion (1 large)', the site 'yellow onions (2 onions)' - a printing variance between her cookbooks, not a different recipe. Printable version: https://barefootcontessa.com/recipes/print/63194

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing — the oven-braised vodka reduction (cover, bake 375°F for 1.5h) is the exact move other sources single out as what makes Ina's version stand out from stovetop ones.

name: Pork Shoulder Ragu
ingredients:
2 to 2 1/2-pound (0.9-1.1 kg) boneless pork shoulder roast
1 small onion, chopped
1 garlic clove, minced
salt and pepper
2 tablespoons (27 g) olive oil
1 small pat butter
1 large can whole tomatoes, with juice
1 cup (237 g) red wine
5 sprigs fresh thyme
5 sprigs fresh oregano
Small handful of fennel seeds
1 tablespoon (15 g) hot sauce, for smokiness (I used Trader Joe's Hot Chili Sauce)
Pappardelle
Freshly grated Parmesean
directions:
Preheat oven to 325°F. Liberally salt and pepper the pork roast. Add olive oil and butter to large Dutch oven and heat over medium-high until butter melts, but does not burn. Add pork roast to pan and brown on all sides, about 8-10 minutes in all.

Add the onion and garlic and saute for 1 minute. Add tomatoes, wine, thyme, oregano, fennel, and hot sauce and bring to a boil. Cover, and put in oven. Braise for 3-4 hours, turning every hour or so. Add more liquid (water, wine, or tomato sauce) if needed. (The liquid should come to about 1/3 of the way up the pork.) Meat is done when it's practically falling apart. Put on a cutting board and pull it apart with two forks, then add back to pot and stir. Cook 1 to 2 pounds pasta according to package directions. When it's is ready, put into individual bowls and top with ragu and lots of Parm.

Scaling note from the source: if you are cooking for more than six, cook another pound of pasta, up the meat to 3 pounds, and add a few more tomatoes, and another 1/2 cup of red wine. If you use 3 pounds of pork and keep the liquid at a third of the way up the meat, that will be enough to feed four parents and four kids, with leftovers.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (Robert to himself, 2013-04-05). The italic lead-in about salad pairings and scaling is the original blog author's headnote, not Robert's.

Web summary (dinneralovestory.com). Andy Ward writing on Jenny Rosenstrach's Dinner: A Love Story, filed under 'Instant Dinner Party.' His point is that the recipe is entertaining strategy as much as cooking: everything happens in the three-to-four-hour braise, so by the time guests arrive the host has nothing left to do. Keeping the braising liquid at about a third of the way up the meat is what lets the shoulder go fork-tender without the sauce turning watery, and the fennel seed and a tablespoon of hot sauce supply the smoky, faintly sausage-like note that makes it read as more work than it was.

What readers report: A pressure cooker does it in about 30 minutes. It freezes well - readers pack leftovers in quart jars for months. Bone-in shoulder works. The sauce thickens a lot once the meat is shredded back in, so add diced tomatoes or a little liquid to loosen it.

Note on the source: Exact match to the family copy: 2 to 2 1/2 lb boneless pork shoulder, 1 small onion, 1 garlic clove, 2 Tbsp olive oil plus a small pat of butter, 1 large can whole tomatoes with juice, 1 cup red wine, 5 sprigs each thyme and oregano, a small handful of fennel seeds, 1 Tbsp hot sauce, pappardelle, Parmesan; 325F, 3-4 hours, turning hourly. The family copy's scaling note (3 lb pork for eight) is the blog's own. Also reprinted with a review at https://food52.com/recipes/39733-andy-ward-jenny-rosenstrach-s-pork-shoulder-ragu and https://www.thekitchn.com/dinner-a-love-story-slow-braised-pork-ragu-recipe-23115729

ahead: Braise for 3-4 hours, turning every hour or so.

claude_opt.changes: Comparable braises skim rendered fat from the pork liquid before stirring the meat back in, for a cleaner sauce; this recipe skips that step and risks a greasy ragù.

name: Red-Braised Pork (Dunlop)
ingredients:
1-1.25 lbs (454-567 g) pork belly with skin
2 inches ginger
2 scallions
3 tbsp (40 g) peanut oil
2 cups (480 g) stock
1 tbsp (16 g) dark soy sauce
2 tbsp (23 g) Shaoxing rice wine
3/4 tsp (4.5 g) salt
3 tbsp (40 g) brown sugar
1/2 star anise
directions:
Blanch the pork in boiling water, then rinse in cold water. Cut into 2-3 inch chunks.

Crush ginger and segment scallions into 3-4 chunks.

Heat oil in Dutch oven until smoking, then stir fry pork for a few minutes. Then add stock and other ingredients.

Bring to a boil, then simmer half-covered or uncovered for 2 hours, stirring occasionally until liquid is much reduced and meat is fork tender.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (Robert to himself, 2017-06-26); no reply or forward carrying an annotation. Transcription check: the emailed ingredient list reads "3.4 tsp salt", almost certainly 3/4 tsp. Left verbatim.

Data fix (Sept 2026): '3.4 tsp (20 g) salt' was a misread of 3/4 tsp, and our gram figure was computed from it. Corrected; the dish takes most of its salt from the soy sauce.

claude_opt.changes: Cut added salt from 3.4 tsp (20g) toward 1 tsp; dark and light soy already salt the braise, and published Dunlop-style hong shao rou recipes use little or no added salt.

name: Red-Cooked Pork Belly (Hongshao Rou)
source: Fuchsia Dunlop, Revolutionary Chinese Cookbook: Recipes from Hunan Province
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) pork belly
2 tablespoons (27 g) peanut oil
2 tablespoons (25 g) white sugar
1 tablespoon (15 g) Shaoxing wine
1-inch piece ginger, peeled and sliced
2 pieces star anise
2 dried red chilies
1 piece cinnamon stick or cassia bark
2 tablespoons (32 g) light soy sauce
Salt and sugar to taste
Scallion greens, thinly sliced, for garnish
directions:
1. Dunk pork belly into a pot of boiling water and simmer for 3 to 4 minutes until partially cooked. Remove and set aside until cool enough to handle. Slice into 1-inch cubes.
2. In a wok, heat sugar and oil over low heat until the sugar melts and turns golden brown. Add pork and Shaoxing wine.
3. Add enough water to cover the pork, along with ginger, star anise, chilis, and cinnamon/cassia. Bring liquid to boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 40 to 50 minutes. Keep extra water nearby in case too much water evaporates.
4. With 5 minutes left of cooking to go, turn up heat if liquid needs to reduce further to sauce-like consistency. Stir in soy sauce. Season to taste with salt and sugar. Transfer to serving dishes and garnish with scallion greens.

Notes on the skin: you can remove the skin before cooking, but I hardly ever do. The skin and the fat is 80% of what makes hongshao rou so darn good.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (Robert to himself, 2013-02-13). The long blurb in the body is the original blogger's headnote, not Robert's, so it was not promoted to a cook's note.

Web summary (cinnamonsociety.com). Diana Kuan, adapting Fuchsia Dunlop's Revolutionary Chinese Cookbook. The sugar is caramelised in oil before the pork goes in - that is what gives hongshao rou its mahogany colour and its faint bitterness against the soy. Blanching the belly first firms it enough to cube neatly and rids it of scum. Kuan argues the dish is underrated abroad and points out it is one of the mildest things in the Hunan repertoire, Mao Zedong's favourite; she is emphatic that the skin and fat are most of what makes it good.

What readers report: The page shows roughly 27 comments but their text did not render on fetch, so no themes could be extracted. Worth a human revisit.

Note on the source: This is the exact source of the family copy. Ingredient list matches item for item (1 lb pork belly, 2 Tbsp peanut oil, 2 Tbsp white sugar, 1 Tbsp Shaoxing, 1-inch ginger sliced, 2 star anise, 2 dried red chilies, 1 cinnamon stick or cassia, 2 Tbsp light soy, salt and sugar to taste, scallion greens) and the family copy's closing line about the skin and fat being 80 percent of what makes hongshao rou good is verbatim from this page - which is why the library's 'Further notes' says the long blurb in the body is the original blogger's headnote.

claude_opt.changes: No wok on hand — braise in the enameled Dutch oven instead; it holds heat more evenly for this simmer. Well-reviewed hongshao rou versions (Woks of Life) add dark soy for deeper color; this one relies on sugar alone.

name: Roux
source: Thomas Keller, Ad Hoc at Home
ingredients:
8 tablespoons (114 g) (1 stick; 4 ounces) unsalted butter
.5 cup (60 g) plus 3 tablespoons all-purpose flour
directions:
We use roux, the traditional thickener made by cooking equal parts by weight butter and flour, for sauces and other dishes. For the smoothest sauces, add room-temperature or cold roux to a simmering liquid, or add cold liquid to a hot roux, to prevent the roux from seizing up.

Put the butter in a small skillet or saucepan and set it over medium heat. When it is almost melted, whisk in the flour and cook, whisking constantly and adjusting the heat as necessary so the roux bubbles but does not brown, 3-4 minutes. Transfer to a bowl of other container to cool, then store in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread (2013-03-18, Robert to himself); no replies or forwards, so no cook's note.

claude_opt.changes: No changes; equal-weight butter-to-flour roux cooked to bubbling without browning matches America's Test Kitchen and standard culinary-school technique exactly. Keller's method is already the accepted modern approach.

name: Saffron Chicken Thighs
ingredients:
3 tablespoons (40 g) olive oil
1 medium yellow onion, sliced into ¼-inch-thick half-moons
4 cloves garlic, chopped
8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (about2 pounds), cleaned and cut in half
2½ teaspoons (7.0 g) kosher salt (plus more as needed)
¼ teaspoon (0.6 g) ground black pepper (plus more as needed)
¼ cup (61 g) fresh lemon juice (plus more as needed)
¼ teaspoon (0.2 g) ground saffron, steeped in 1 tablespoon hot water
directions:
In a large pan with a lid, heat the oil over medium heat. Add the onion and cook, stirring occasionally, until soft and golden, about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and cook for 2 minutes.

In a small bowl, season the chicken well with the salt and pepper. Add it to the pan, a little overlap is okay, and cook until the chicken takes on a little color, about 3 minutes on each side. Drizzle on the lemon juice and the saffron water, making sure you get every last drop of the saffron water. Add a few more drops of water to the glass or bowl, swirl it around, and use. Turn the chicken pieces well in the brilliant sauce to coat all sides, reduce the heat to medium-low, partially cover, and cook, turning once in a while, until the chicken is cooked through and tender, about 30 minutes.

If the chicken makes too much juice, remove the lid and reduce the sauce. Taste and make delicious.

MAKE AHEAD: A few hours in advance, but leave the chicken in its juice in the pot. You might need to drizzle in a little more water when reheating.

PLAN AHEAD: Can be stored in the fridge up to 3 days or in the freezer up to 3 months.
description: RM 6/21: This works out really nicely for a weeknight meal. The saffron and lemon are both essential.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Recipe body from the single-message 'Saffron Chicken recipez' thread (Robert to himself, 2020-11-12), which carries no note. The cook's note is Robert's own opening line in a separate forward of the same recipe, subject 'Persian chicken thighs', thread 179d86be4bf3287b, sent 2021-06-04 to his parents and brothers.

makeahead: PLAN AHEAD: Can be stored in the fridge up to 3 days or in the freezer up to 3 months.

name: Triple-Cooked Chips
ingredients:
1kg Maris Piper potatoes, peeled and cut into chips (approx. 2 × 2 × 6cm)
Groundnut or grapeseed oil
Salt
directions:
1. Put the cut chips into a bowl under running water for 5 minutes to wash the starch off.

2. Place 2 litres of cold tap water in a large saucepan and add the potatoes. Place the pan over a medium heat and simmer until the chips are almost falling apart (approximately 20–30 minutes, depending on the potato).

3. Carefully remove the cooked chips and place them on a cooling rack to dry out. Then place the rack in the freezer for at least 1 hour to remove more moisture.

4. Heat a deep-fat fryer or a deep pan no more than half filled with oil (to a depth of around 10cm) to 130ºC. Fry the chips in small batches until a light crust forms (approximately 5 minutes), remove from the oil and drain on kitchen paper.

5. Put the potatoes on a cooling rack and place in the freezer for at least 1 hour. (At this stage, if you don't want to cook and serve immediately, the chips can be kept in the fridge for 3 days.)

6. Heat the oil in the deep-fat fryer or deep pan to 180ºC and fry the chips until golden (approximately 7 minutes). Drain and sprinkle with salt.
description:
RM 11/12: Better than almost all restaurant fries I have had but a lot of work.
RM 11/12: It is definitely a lot of work. Groundnut oil is peanut oil which was on sale at aldi. Maris piper is close to russet which I used. I'm not sure it's more work that pizza, but it's only for a side dish.
RM 2/13: Note, the simmering step takes much longer than he says in the recipe.

The two 11/12 notes come from Robert's messages in a separate earlier thread, 13ade029d35bc9b5 'I made these tonight' (2012-11-08), which links the same Channel 4 recipe.

name: Roasted Butternut Squash Soup
ingredients:
4 pounds (1.8 kg) whole butternut squash (about 2 medium), halved lengthwise and seeds removed
2 tablespoons (28 g) unsalted butter (1/4 stick)
1 medium Granny Smith apple (about 8 ounces)
1/2 medium yellow onion
8 fresh sage leaves
2 1/2 cups (600 g) low-sodium vegetable or chicken broth
2 1/2 cups (592 g) water
1 1/2 teaspoons (4.2 g) kosher salt, plus more as needed
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) freshly ground black pepper, plus more as needed
1/3 cup (79 g) heavy cream
1/2 cup (64 g) toasted pumpkin seeds, for garnish (optional)
directions:
Heat the oven to 425 degrees F and arrange a rack in the middle.

Line a baking sheet with aluminum foil. Place the squash pieces cut-side up on the baking sheet. Melt 1 tablespoon of the butter and brush all of it over the tops and insides of the squash halves (alternatively, you can rub it on evenly with your fingers). Season generously with salt and pepper. Roast until knife tender, about 50 minutes to 1 hour.

Meanwhile, peel, core, and cut the apple into medium dice. Cut the onion into medium dice. Melt the remaining tablespoon of butter in a large saucepan or Dutch oven over medium heat. Add the apple, onion, and sage, season with salt and pepper, and cook, stirring occasionally, until softened, about 7 minutes. Remove the pan from the heat and set aside.

When the squash is ready, set the baking sheet on a wire rack until the squash is cool enough to handle. Using a large spoon, scoop the flesh into the saucepan with the sauteed apples and onions; discard the skins.

Add the broth, water, and measured salt and pepper, stir to combine, and bring to a boil over medium-high heat. Reduce the heat to medium low and simmer, stirring occasionally and breaking up any large pieces of squash, until the flavors meld, about 15 minutes. Remove the pan from the heat and stir in the cream.

Using a blender, puree the soup in batches until smooth, removing the small cap from the blender lid (the pour lid) and covering the space with a kitchen towel (this allows steam to escape and prevents the lid from popping off). Alternatively, use an immersion blender. Taste and season with salt and pepper as needed. Serve garnished with the pumpkin seeds, if using.

If you're making the soup in advance, cool it to room temperature, cover, and refrigerate for up to 3 days, or freeze it for up to 1 month.
description: RM 9/15: Season with both salt and cider vinegar. Dry sage is fine if you bloom it.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Thomas Keller's Butternut Squash Soup with Brown Butter": Keller's soup roasts only the bulb, sweats leeks, carrots, shallots, onions and garlic, sweetens with honey, simmers with a bouquet garni in 6 cups of vegetable stock and finishes with creme fraiche and brown butter over about 2 1/4 hours. This one roasts both squash halves whole and scrapes out the flesh, then simmers it with sauteed Granny Smith apple, onion and sage in broth and water and finishes with heavy cream - no honey, leeks, carrots, bouquet garni or brown butter. Roasted Butternut Squash-Ina is a plain roasted side, and the WSJ Creamy Winter Squash Soup boils cubed raw squash and adds maple, ginger and a streusel, so neither matches either. Thread 1423404b48680529: the recipe was mailed to himself 11/7/2013 and the annotation is the covering line of his 9/28/2015 forward of that same thread to Laura ('Don't forget to season with both salt and cider vinegar. Dry sage is ok if you bloom it when you cook your onions.').
