claude_opt.changes: Cooks_note already fixed seasoning. One more: recipe roasts squash cut-side up; most tested versions (ATK, Serious Eats) roast cut-side down for faster caramelization and less moisture, giving a thicker, more concentrated puree.

name: ChefSteps Quiche
servings: Makes one spring form quiche or two thin quiches
ingredients:
Pate Brisee (prepare the day before):
250g Pastry flour
205g Butter cubed and chilled
3g salt
55g Ice water (More with AP flour?)

Quiche Base:
300g Egg
200g Whole milk
60g Heavy cream
6g Salt
.5g Pepper
.25g Nutmeg

Quiche Filling:
180g Leek
160g Bacon
1g Thyme leaves (fresh)
130g Gruyere
directions:
Prepare Pate Brisee the day before.

Combine flour, butter, and salt in stand mixer with paddle, and place in fridge until cold. Mix on low until you have coarse crumbs. Add ice water and mix on low until dough comes together smoothly, one minute. Remove dough, shape into smooth ball. Flour hands and work surface. Press ball into disk 4cm thick. Wrap with plastic, refrigerate for four hours. (Omitting this step is fine, but it will pull away from pan and warp while baking.) Roll out dough to 3mm. Mold dough into baking dish. Refrigerate overnight or for at least one hour, covering after first hour. For liquidy fillings, blind bake at 392 with pie weights for 20m, then 5m without weights.

Prepare Quiche Base: combine all and mix with immersion blender.

Prepare Quiche Filling: sweat leeks, bacon, and thyme. Place bacon and leek mixture on crust. Spread gruyere on top. Pour quiche base over filling.

Bake at 329 until it reaches core temp of 172. (Very tall takes 60-90 mins, short takes 35 mins.)
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Southwestern Crustless Quiche": Southwestern Crustless Quiche is a crustless bake of eggs, flour, baking powder, grated cheese, cottage cheese and canned green chilies poured into a pie plate. This is a gram-weighted pate brisee crust, blind-baked, filled with a leek-bacon-thyme-Gruyere Lorraine filling and an egg/milk/cream custard baked to a 172-degree core temperature. The master's Easy and Elegant Quiche (bacon, Dijon, onion, Swiss in a purchased shell) is also a different formula with no crust recipe and no custard weights. No individual author is credited on the page, and the fetched content carried only the summary, not the method or measurements.

Wrap with plastic, refrigerate for 4 hours.

ingredients:
Cooked chicken, chopped fairly small
Mayonnaise (5:1 chicken to mayonnaise)
Sour cream (4:1 mayonnaise to sour cream)
Mustard
Celery
Toasted walnuts
Shallots
directions: Riffed off the Striped Spatula cranberry chicken salad. Key ideas: 4:1 mayo to sour cream; 5:1 chicken to mayo; chop the chicken pretty small; also added mustard, celery, toasted walnuts, and shallots.
description: RM 6/22: 4:1 mayonnaise to sour cream, 5:1 chicken to mayonnaise. Chop the chicken fairly small. Added mustard, celery, toasted walnuts and shallots.

Kept separate from master entry "Mustard Chicken Salad with Tarragon Ina": None of the four master chicken salads is this dish: Ina's is a mayo-white wine-double-mustard dressing with broccoli, tarragon and tomatoes; Curried Chicken Salad is mayo with curry powder, soy sauce, grapes and water chestnuts; Hawaiian is a rice salad in an oil-and-vinegar dressing; Hot Chicken Salad is a baked casserole with cream of chicken soup. This is a cranberry chicken salad on a mayonnaise-and-sour-cream base with mustard, celery, toasted walnuts and shallots, and uses no broccoli, curry, rice or soup. Single-message thread 181864bde30c4f07 (6/21/2022), sent by Robert to Laura; the message body is entirely his own riff notes plus a link to the Striped Spatula cranberry chicken salad, and no other thread in the archive discusses this dish.

Web summary (stripedspatula.com, 5 from 17 votes). Amanda Biddle turns her family's spring chicken salad into an autumn one by dropping the tarragon and working in dried cranberries and toasted walnuts. The cranberries bring tart sweetness and the walnuts crunch, both of which give the creamy mayonnaise and sour cream base something to play against. Poached or rotisserie chicken breast, chilled before mixing, keeps the dressing from loosening.

What readers report: Readers report it has become their standard chicken salad. Almonds substitute cleanly for the walnuts, dried herbs work when fresh parsley is not to hand, and several cooks increase the lemon juice past the stated one to two teaspoons for more tartness. One reviewer made it successfully with canned chicken rather than poached or rotisserie. The most practical repeated tip is to mix a little extra dressing and hold it separately, then stir it through leftovers, since the salad dries out over a few days in the fridge.

Note on the source: Robert's version is a riff on this source recipe

claude_opt.changes: Reserve 2-3 Tbsp of the mayo-sour cream dressing separately and stir it into leftovers instead of premixing it all in; the full batch dries out in the fridge over a few days.

name: Chicken Sour Cream Enchiladas
ingredients:
3-4 cups (420-560 g) cooked shredded chicken (i use cooked rotisserie chicken)
1 medium onion, chopped
1 cup (230 g) sour cream
½ cup (30 g) chopped parsley
1 large can enchilada sauce (La Victoria is my favorite)
3 cups (339 g) shredded cheese (I use mexican blend, or a combo of cheddar cheese and monterey jack cheese)
10-16 flour tortillas (8-9" work great. you can even use corn tortillas)
1 Tablespoon (14 g) olive oil
salt and pepper (to taste, optional)
Packet of taco seasoning (Laura added)
directions:
Preheat oven to 350ºF. Spray large glass baking dish with non stick spray.

In a large pan over medium heat a teaspoon of olive oil. add the onions and cook until translucent. Stir often.

Add most of the packet of seasoning. Toast in oil (Laura added).

Combine chicken and onions in the frying pan. Stir until combined.

Pour ½ cup of enchilada sauce over the chicken and onion mixture – just enough to coat the chicken.

Add sour cream and parsley. stir until combined.

Once the sour cream and parsley are fully combined, turn off the heat. now add the shredded cheese. i usually add 2 to 2-½ cups. Sometimes more. It just depends on how cheesy you want it. I like the mixture to be creamy and cheesy.

Once the cheese is melted and combined with the chicken sour cream mixture.

Pour just enough sauce in a casserole dish to cover the bottom of the dish. (UPDATED: spray pan with non-stick cooking spray first)

Fill the tortillas. spoon sauce onto a tortilla, and then some of the chicken mixture.

Roll the tortilla and place in the baking dish. repeat until enough tortillas fill your baking dish – or until the chicken mixture is all used up.

Pour enchilada sauce over the completed enchiladas and spread evenly over the top.

Top with shredded cheese and garnish with chopped parsley. Cover with foil and bake for 20-30 minutes. Remove the foil for the last 10 minutes of cooking. Bake until sauce is bubbling, tortilla edges are slightly crisp, and the cheese to melted.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Chicken and Black Bean Enchiladas": The Gmail filling is shredded rotisserie chicken with onion, taco seasoning, sour cream, parsley, 3 cups of melted cheese and canned red enchilada sauce. The master entry is a mashed black bean and chipotle filling with only 1 cup of diced chicken, Monterey Jack and green tomatillo salsa, and no sour cream or dairy in the filling. Shared format, different dish. Single-message thread 1949f9b27b1f21a0, 1/25/2025, sent by Laura to Robert. The two '(Laura added)' edits are inside the recipe body and are Laura's, not Robert's, so they stay in the directions rather than in a cook's note. No reply or other thread from Robert about this dish.

claude_opt.changes: Corn tortillas (listed as optional) will crack when rolled cold; warm or lightly fry them in oil first, standard practice in modern enchilada recipes. Specify sauce can size, now ambiguous.

name: Chocolate Banana Bread Pudding
prep_time: refrigerate at least 8 hours or up to 24 hours
ingredients:
6 to 7 cups (270-315 g) ½-inch-cubed day-old white bread (the weight depends on type of bread)
170 grams milk chocolate, chopped
56 grams semisweet or bittersweet chocolate, chopped into pebble-sized pieces
6 cups (1.5 kg) (1.4 kilograms) half-and-half
2 eggs
6 egg yolks
100 grams sugar
¼ teaspoon (0.7 g) kosher salt
3 ripe bananas, peeled and cut into slices 1/8 to ¼ inch thick
directions:
Spread the bread cubes evenly over the bottom of a deep 9-by-13-inch baking dish or roasting pan.

Place the milk chocolate and semisweet chocolate in a medium heatproof bowl. In a medium saucepan, scald the half-and-half over medium-high heat (bubbles start to form around the edge of the pan, but the cream is not boiling). Pour the hot cream over the chocolate and let sit for 1 minute, then gently whisk together the chocolate and cream until the chocolate is completely melted and the mixture is smooth.

In a medium bowl, whisk together the eggs and egg yolks until blended, and then slowly whisk in the sugar and salt until combined. Slowly add the hot chocolate-cream mixture to the egg-sugar mixture, a little at a time, whisking constantly. Strain the mixture through a fine-mesh sieve, then pour it over the bread. Mix the custard and bread well to make sure all of the bread cubes are soaking evenly. Cover the baking dish with plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least 8 hours or up to 24 hours.

When you are ready to bake, position a rack in the center of the oven, and heat the oven to 300 degrees F.

Stir the banana slices into the bread pudding. Bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes to 1 hour and 20 minutes, or until just barely set. To test for doneness, insert a knife in the middle of the pudding and bend it back a bit to see if the custard mix has set up. If liquid fills the hole made with the knife, the pudding needs more time.

When the pudding is ready, remove from the oven and let rest for at least 2 hours. Serve warm, or cover and refrigerate and serve chilled.

The bread pudding can be stored, tightly covered, in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread 14426ea5aad9d9f2, 2/12/2014, Robert to himself; no reply, forward or separate thread carries an annotation for it.

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

ahead: refrigerate at least 8 hours or up to 24 hours
Cover the baking dish with plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least 8 hours or up to 24 hours.
makeahead: The bread pudding can be stored, tightly covered, in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.

claude_opt.changes: Toast the bread cubes (350F, ~10 min) before the custard soak; nearly all modern bread puddings do this so cubes absorb custard evenly without turning mushy.

name: Cucumber Salad With Roasted Peanuts and Chile
ingredients:
6 Persian cucumbers (about 1 pound), cut lengthwise into thin spears, then cut crosswise into 2-inch pieces
Kosher salt
1/4 cup (36 g) salted, roasted peanuts
1/4 cup (12 g) cilantro leaves
1 teaspoon (1.8 g) red-pepper flakes
3 tablespoons (48 g) natural unsalted peanut butter
2 tablespoons (32 g) soy sauce
2 tablespoons (30 g) unseasoned rice vinegar
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) granulated sugar
1 small garlic clove, grated
Chile oil, store-bought or homemade, for serving (optional)
directions:
Toss cucumbers with 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt in a colander. Set aside to drain.

Chop peanuts, cilantro and red-pepper flakes together until very fine. Set aside.

In a large bowl, whisk together peanut butter, soy sauce, rice vinegar, sugar, garlic and 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt. Add up to 1 tablespoon water, if needed to thin mixture. Transfer salted cucumbers to the bowl with dressing and toss to coat.

To serve, place half the cucumber salad on the plate, sprinkle with half the peanut mixture. Repeat with the remaining cucumber salad and peanut mixture. Drizzle with chile oil, if using, and serve immediately.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Single-message thread 17252c0719bb0ead (5/26/2020), forwarded by Laura Lantrip from NYT Cooking; no reply, forward or separate thread contains any annotation by Robert.

Web summary (cooking.nytimes.com, 5 (4,611)). Sue Li's layered cucumber salad, built from four contrasting elements: salted cucumbers, a peanut sauce, a chopped peanut and cilantro topping, and chile oil. The headnote explains why each step exists - salting suppresses the cucumber's faint bitterness and concentrates flavour, the peanut sauce supplies richness against the cold cucumber, and the dry topping is scattered in layers rather than all at once so the flavour is distributed. The sauce is worth making in quantity to keep in the fridge.

What readers report: The most consequential item is an editor's reply (290 votes) acknowledging a reader was right that the cutting instruction was unclear: the recipe has since been revised to say cut the cucumbers lengthwise into thin spears first, then crosswise - so an older printed copy will have the vaguer wording. An 86-vote note from the same thread says peeled regular cucumbers work as well as English ones, and that larger cucumbers should be halved and seeded given that the dish is about texture. A 184-vote comment learned a Thai version that uses fish sauce in place of soy sauce and cuts the cucumbers differently. An 84-vote cook found the dressing too salty and plans to leave out the kosher salt entirely next time, which is worth weighing against the salting step. The 415-vote note is sarcasm about a commenter who ignored the recipe and then blamed it.

claude_opt.changes: Skip the 1/2 tsp salt in the dressing; the 2 Tbsp soy sauce already salts it, and an 84-vote reader found the full amount too salty. Keep salting the cucumbers separately — that step controls texture, not seasoning.

name: Flour Peanut Butter Cookies
ingredients:
1 cup (2 sticks/228 grams) unsalted butter, at room temperature
1 cup (200 grams) granulated sugar
1 cup (220 grams) packed light brown sugar
2 eggs
1 teaspoon (4.2 g) vanilla extract
1 3/4 cups (454 grams) chunky peanut butter
2 2/3 cups (375 grams) unbleached all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon (4.6 g) baking soda
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt
directions:
Using a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment (or a handheld mixer or a wooden spoon), cream together the butter, granulated sugar, and brown sugar on medium speed for about 5 minutes, or until the mixture is light and fluffy. (This step will take about 10 minutes if using a handheld mixer or a spoon.) Stop the mixer a few times and use a rubber spatula to scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl and the paddle to release any clinging butter and sugar.

Beat in the eggs and vanilla on medium speed for 2 to 3 minutes, or until thoroughly combined. Scrape the bowl and paddle again to make sure the eggs are thoroughly incorporated. On medium-low speed, beat in the peanut butter for another 2 minutes, or until thoroughly combined.

In a medium bowl, stir together the flour, baking soda, and salt until well mixed. On low speed (or with the wooden spoon), slowly add the flour mixture to the butter-sugar mixture and then mix just until the dry ingredients are totally incorporated and the dough is evenly mixed.

For the best results, scrape the dough into an airtight container and let it rest in the refrigerator overnight (or for at least 3 to 4 hours) before baking. When you are ready to bake, position a rack in the center of the oven, and heat the oven to 350 degrees F.

Drop the dough in 1/4-cup balls onto a baking sheet, spacing them about 2 inches apart. Flatten each ball slightly with the palm of your hand. Use a fork to create the traditional crisscross pattern on the top of each cookie.

Bake for 18 to 20 minutes, or until the cookies are golden brown on the edges and still pale and slightly soft in the center. Let cool on the baking sheet on a wire rack for 5 to 10 minutes, then transfer the cookies to the rack to cool completely.

The cookies can be stored in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. The unbaked dough can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

Baker's Bite: If all of the cookies won't fit on a single baking sheet, drop the remaining cookies onto a second baking sheet and bake them when the first sheet is finished. If you have only one baking sheet, bake the first batch and then cool the baking sheet by running it under cold water before loading it with the second batch.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Peanut Butter Cookies": The master Peanut Butter Cookies is a small one-egg batch with 1/4 c butter, 1/2 c peanut butter, 1 c flour, no vanilla, baked 8-10 minutes. This is a four-times-larger dough with 1 c butter, 1 3/4 c (454 g) chunky peanut butter, two eggs, vanilla, 2 2/3 c flour, an overnight rest, 1/4-cup balls and an 18-20 minute bake. Different ratios, ingredients and technique. Thread 13dd0f941a3b5a6b (original 4/3/2013, re-forwarded 3/30/2020 to Laura and 9/23/2023 to Alan and Steph); all three messages are byte-identical recipe text with no added comment, and the long first-person paragraph is Joanne Chang's Flour headnote, not Robert's.

Web summary (passionatemae.com). Joanne Chang's peanut butter cookies from Flour: Spectacular Recipes from Boston's Flour Bakery + Cafe, reproduced by a home baker. The dough takes essentially a whole jar of chunky peanut butter, which is what gives the cookie its shortbread-like crumb and a flavour close to eating peanut butter straight. The butter and both sugars are creamed a full five minutes to aerate, the peanut butter goes in after the eggs, and the dough is chilled overnight so it holds its shape through a long bake at a low temperature.

What readers report: Little discussion beyond the baker's own notes: chill overnight if you can, three to four hours at minimum, and the baked cookies are notably large and not very sweet. One reader suggested them as ice-cream sandwich shells.

Note on the source: Gram weights match the family copy exactly: 1 cup (228 g) unsalted butter, 1 cup (200 g) granulated, 1 cup (220 g) packed light brown, 2 eggs, 1 tsp vanilla, 454 g chunky peanut butter, 2 2/3 cups (375 g) AP flour, 1 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp salt. One volume discrepancy worth flagging for the conversion project: the blog writes 454 g as '1 1/4 cups' where the family copy says '1 3/4 cups' - the family copy is the correct conversion (peanut butter runs about 256 g per cup), so trust the 454 g and the 1 3/4 cups. Confidence medium because this is an unaffiliated blog, not the publisher; the licensed cookbook text is behind a paywall at https://app.ckbk.com/recipe/flou69447c02s001r006/peanut-butter-cookies. Note also the blog bakes at 160C for 16 minutes against the family copy's 18-20 minutes.

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

claude_opt.changes: Checked against the original cookbook text and several home reproductions of Chang's recipe — ratios, overnight rest, and bake time all match with no recurring complaints. Nothing worth changing.

name: Grilled Marinated Shrimp Skewers
prep_time: Start one to two hours ahead; marinate at least 15 minutes or up to 2 hours max
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) large shrimp peeled and deveined
3 tablespoons (40 g) olive oil
2 tablespoons (30 g) lemon juice
½ teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
¼ teaspoon (0.6 g) black pepper
1 teaspoon (1.1 g) oregano
½ teaspoon (1.1 g) paprika
½ teaspoon (1.4 g) garlic powder
Chopped parsley for serving
Lemon slices for serving
directions:
Place the olive oil, lemon juice, salt, pepper, oregano, paprika and garlic powder in a large bowl; whisk to combine.

Add the shrimp to the bowl and toss gently to coat evenly with the marinade. Marinate for at least 15 minutes or up to 2 hours max.

Skewer 4-6 shrimp on each soaked skewer and place on a plate while skewering the remaining shrimp.

Heat a grill or grill pan over medium high heat and cook the shrimp for 2-3 minutes on each side until the color is pink and shrimp is opaque.

Serve warm with fresh parsley and lemon slices, if desired.

--- 2026 REVISION — THE ONE WORKING VERSION (UNTESTED AS OF SEPTEMBER 2026) ---

The Gmail version above is kept as the archive original. Its lemon juice in the marinade cures the surface and turns it chalky, so cook from this version instead. Amounts are for 1 pound (454 g) of 21/25 shrimp; for 700 g, multiply everything by 1.5 and use 6 pairs of skewers.

Dry brine: 1/2 tsp (3.0 g) salt, 1/4 tsp (1.2 g) baking soda. Halve the salt if the bag lists salt or sodium tripolyphosphate.
Seasoned oil: 3 Tbsp (40 g) olive oil, 1 tsp (1.1 g) dried oregano, 1/2 tsp (1.1 g) paprika (smoked is better), 1/2 tsp (1.4 g) garlic powder, 1/4 tsp (0.6 g) black pepper, 1 tsp (2 g) lemon zest.
Finish: 1 clove (5 g) fresh garlic, minced; 2 Tbsp (30 g) lemon juice; 2 Tbsp (8 g) fresh parsley, chopped.
Also: avocado oil for the grates, 8 skewers (4 pairs, metal or soaked wood), lemon wedges.

1. Thaw overnight in the fridge, or in the sealed bag in cold water for 20-30 minutes. Pat very dry.
2. Dry brine with the salt and baking soda, 20-30 minutes in the fridge. Not past 45 minutes.
3. Warm the oil with the oregano, paprika, garlic powder and pepper for about 30 seconds, until fragrant. Off the heat, stir in the zest and let it cool. Set aside 1 Tbsp.
4. Marinate the shrimp in the rest of the oil, up to 30 minutes. No lemon juice yet.
5. In a serving bowl, stir the reserved oil with the fresh garlic, lemon juice and parsley.
6. Pack the shrimp snugly on pairs of parallel skewers, about 6 per pair, so they can't spin or fall through.
7. Heat the grill to 500-550F at the grates, leaving a cooler zone. Clean the grates and oil them with avocado oil.
8. Grill over direct heat 60-90 seconds a side, closer to 60 for 21/25. Pull at a loose C shape, not a tight O, 120F internal. Shake off excess marinade first; move to the cool zone if the fire flares, since flare-ups scorch the paprika and garlic powder.
9. Toss off the heat in the serving bowl. Taste for salt and serve with lemon wedges.

Buy dry-packed shrimp rather than phosphate-soaked.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Grilled Shrimp with Garlic and Lemon": The Gmail marinade is dried-spice based (oregano, paprika, garlic powder, olive oil, lemon juice) with a 15 min-2 hr marinade and a 2-3 min per side grill. Ina's uses onion, fresh parsley and basil and two mustards; the Serious Eats one uses a baking-soda/salt/sugar cure, fresh garlic, lemon zest and a post-grill dressing. Neither shares the Gmail version's ingredient set or method. Single-message thread 197c19dfe655d647, 6/30/2025, sent to Laura; no reply or forward anywhere in the archive carries a cooking annotation for it. The 2026 revision below the rule is untested as of September 2026 and came from Claude conversations, not from any archive.

ahead: Start one to two hours ahead; marinate at least 15 minutes or up to 2 hours max

claude_opt.changes: The untested 2026 revision already matches current best practice: baking-soda dry brine, oil-bloomed spices, post-sear acid, ~120F pull all align with modern shrimp-grilling guidance. No further change indicated.

name: Light and Fluffy Pancakes
ingredients:
1 tablespoon (15 g) juice from lemon
2 cups (488 g) milk
2 cups (284 g) (10 ounces) unbleached all-purpose flour
2 tablespoons (25 g) sugar
2 teaspoons (8.0 g) baking powder
1/2 teaspoon (2.3 g) baking soda
1/2 teaspoon (3.0 g) salt
1 large egg
3 tablespoons (43 g) unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly
1-2 teaspoons (4.5-9.1 g) vegetable oil
directions:
If you have buttermilk on hand, use 2 cups instead of the milk and lemon juice mixture.

Whisk the lemon juice and milk together in a medium bowl or large measuring cup; set aside to thicken while preparing the other ingredients. Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and salt in a medium bowl to combine.

Whisk the egg and melted butter into the milk until combined. Make a well in the center of the dry ingredients in the bowl; pour in the milk mixture and whisk very gently until just combined (a few lumps should remain). Do not overmix.

Heat a 12-inch nonstick skillet over medium heat for 3-5 minutes; add 1 teaspoon oil and brush to coat the skillet bottom evenly. Pour 1/4 cup batter onto 3 spots on the skillet. Cook the pancakes until large bubbles begin to appear, 1 1/2 to 2 minutes. Using a thin, wide spatula, flip the pancakes and cook until golden brown on the second side, 1 to 1 1/2 minutes. Serve immediately. Repeat with the remaining batter, using the remaining vegetable oil only if necessary.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Perfect Buttermilk Pancakes": This recipe sours 2 cups of regular milk with 1 tablespoon lemon juice and uses one egg, 2 T sugar, 2 tsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp soda and 1/2 tsp salt, cooked in oil in a nonstick skillet in 1/4-cup rounds. The master Perfect Buttermilk Pancakes (Alison Roman) calls for 2 1/2 cups real buttermilk, two eggs, 3 T sugar, 1 1/2 tsp each baking powder and soda, 1 1/4 tsp salt, 1/3-cup rounds and a 325-degree oven to hold them. Whole-Wheat Buttermilk Pancakes uses 2 1/2 cups whole-wheat flour and vanilla and is further still. Single-message thread 13ca6ea0782da64a (2/4/2013), sent by Robert to himself with only his 'rzpancakes rzpancake' tags appended; no reply, forward or separate thread carries an annotation.

Web summary (mysisterskitchen2009.blogspot.com). Cook's Illustrated's Light and Fluffy Pancakes as printed in The New Best Recipe. The batter uses both baking powder and baking soda, and the acid that activates the soda comes from milk soured with a tablespoon of lemon juice - the test kitchen's tasters actually preferred that to real buttermilk. The batter is whisked only until barely combined and left visibly lumpy, because developing gluten is what makes pancakes tough and flat.

What readers report: Only one substantive note on the reprint: the cook records that Cook's Illustrated's own tasters preferred the lemon-juice-and-milk mixture over buttermilk. Otherwise NO COMMENTS.

Note on the source: Recipe identity is certain - this reprint matches the family copy line for line, including the unusual details: 1 Tbsp lemon juice, 2 cups milk, 2 cups (10 ounces) unbleached AP flour, 2 Tbsp sugar, 2 tsp baking powder, 1/2 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 large egg, 3 Tbsp melted butter, 1-2 tsp vegetable oil, and the note 'If you have buttermilk on hand, use 2 cups instead of the milk and lemon juice mixture.' Confidence held at medium only because this is a home blog rather than the publisher. Caution for whoever promotes this: America's Test Kitchen's own page of the same title, https://www.americastestkitchen.com/recipes/1273-light-and-fluffy-pancakes, is a DIFFERENT and smaller formula (1 cup flour, 3/4 cup buttermilk plus 1/4 cup milk, egg separated, 4.5 stars from 144 ratings) - do not substitute it. Gram anchor from the family copy: 2 cups AP flour = 10 oz = 284 g.

Weights note: flour converted at 142 g per cup, the dip-and-sweep figure America's Test Kitchen intends, rather than the 120 g used elsewhere in this collection.

Weights note: this recipe just says "salt", and it predates kosher salt in the family's kitchen, so the gram figures assume table salt at 6 g per teaspoon. If you measure Diamond Crystal by volume instead you will be under-salting by roughly half — go by the grams.

claude_opt.changes: Directions say serve each batch immediately; ATK's own version holds finished pancakes on a rack in a 200F oven so the whole stack is hot at once — easy with your second oven free.

name: Melted Caramelized Onions
source: Thomas Keller, Ad Hoc at Home
ingredients:
8 cups (1.3 kg) sliced onions (about 3 large onions)
Kosher salt
8 tablespoons (114 g) (1 stick; 4 ounces) unsalted butter, cut into 8 pieces
1 sachet of 1 bay leaf, 3 thyme sprigs, 10 peppercorns, 1 smashed garlic
directions:
Put the onions in a large saute pan, set over medium-low heat, sprinkle with 2 generous pinches of salt, and cook, stirring from time to time, for about 20 minutes, until the onions have released much of their liquid.

Stir in the butter, add the sachet, cover with a parchment lid, and cook slowly over low to medium-low heat for another 30 to 35 minutes. The onions should look creamy at all times; if the butter separates, or the pan looks dry before the onions are done, add a bit of cold water and stir well to re-emulsify the butter. The onions should be meltingly tender but not falling apart or mushy. Season to taste with salt.

Once cooled, the onions can be refrigerated for up to 3 days.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Creamed Onions": Creamed Onions uses whole blanched boiler onions baked in a flour-and-butter milk bechamel under buttered breadcrumbs at 400 degrees; this recipe slices onions and melts them slowly in butter with a bay-thyme-peppercorn-garlic sachet under a parchment lid for about an hour, with no milk, flour, crumbs or oven. Nothing in common but the onion. Single-message thread 13d7ed1e8cc0a9a8 (3/18/2013), sent by Robert to himself; the long paragraph in the email is Thomas Keller's headnote from Ad Hoc at Home, not Robert's annotation, and no reply, forward or separate thread adds one.

Web summary (betterwithgarlic.blogspot.com). Thomas Keller's Melted Onions from Ad Hoc at Home, reproduced on a home cook's blog. The onions are first cooked dry over medium-low heat for about 20 minutes so they give up their own liquid, and only then is a full stick of butter and an aromatic sachet added for another half hour. The point is emulsion rather than browning - the onions should stay creamy-looking throughout, and if the butter breaks or the pan dries, a splash of cold water stirred in brings it back together. The result is meltingly tender onions that still hold their shape.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS on the post.

Note on the source: Recipe identity is certain - the ingredient list matches the family copy exactly (8 cups sliced onions from about 3 large onions, kosher salt, 8 Tbsp / 1 stick / 4 oz unsalted butter cut in 8 pieces, and a sachet of 1 bay leaf, 3 thyme sprigs, 10 peppercorns, 1 smashed garlic clove), as do the 20-minute and 30-to-35-minute stages, the re-emulsifying trick and the 3-day keep. Confidence held at medium only because this is an unaffiliated blog reprint rather than a publisher's page - no authorised online copy of Ad Hoc at Home's Melted Onions was found. One wording difference: the blog says 'cover' where the family copy and the book specify a parchment lid. Index entry confirming the recipe exists in the book: https://www.eatyourbooks.com/library/recipes/314023/melted-onions

makeahead: Once cooled, the onions can be refrigerated for up to 3 days.

claude_opt.changes: You own the enameled Dutch oven — use it, not a 'large sauté pan,' for 8 cups of onion; more even heat, no overflow before they collapse. Despite the name, keep heat low — these stay pale, not browned.

name: Oatmeal Raisin Cookies
ingredients:
1 cup (2 sticks/228 grams) unsalted butter, at room temperature
3/4 cup (150 grams) granulated sugar
1 cup (220 grams) packed light brown sugar
2 eggs
1 3/4 cups (245 grams) unbleached all-purpose flour
1 3/4 cups (175 grams) old-fashioned rolled oats (not instant or quick cooking)
1 teaspoon (4.6 g) baking soda
1 teaspoon (2.8 g) kosher salt
1/4 teaspoon (0.6 g) freshly grated nutmeg
1/4 teaspoon (0.7 g) ground cinnamon
1 1/2 cups (240 grams) raisins
directions:
Cream together the butter, granulated sugar, and brown sugar on medium speed for about 5 minutes, or until the mixture is light and fluffy.

Beat in the eggs on medium speed for 2 to 3 minutes, or until thoroughly combined. Scrape the bowl and the paddle again to make sure the eggs are thoroughly incorporated.

In a medium bowl, stir together the flour, oats, baking soda, salt, nutmeg, and cinnamon. Add the raisins and toss to combine. On low speed, slowly add the flour mixture to the butter-sugar mixture and then mix just until the flour mixture is totally incorporated and the dough is evenly mixed.

For the best results, scrape the dough into an airtight container and let it rest in the refrigerator overnight (or for at least 3 to 4 hours) before baking. When ready to bake, position a rack in the center of the oven, and heat the oven to 350 degrees F.

Drop the dough in 1/4-cup balls onto a baking sheet, spacing them about 2 inches apart. Flatten each ball slightly with the palm of your hand.

Bake for 20 to 22 minutes, or until the cookies are golden brown on the edges and slightly soft in the center. Be careful not to overbake. Soft, chewy centers make these cookies irresistible. Let cool on the baking sheet on a wire rack for 5 to 10 minutes, then transfer the cookies to the rack to cool completely.

The cookies can be stored in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. The unbaked dough can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Oatmeal Cookies": The master Oatmeal Cookies (Quaker Oats 1983) uses 3/4 c shortening/margarine, one egg, 1/4 c water, vanilla, 3 c oats to 1 c flour, and bakes 12-15 minutes. This one uses 1 c butter, two eggs, no water or vanilla, near-equal oats and flour (1 3/4 c each), adds nutmeg and cinnamon, rests the dough overnight, and bakes 1/4-cup balls for 20-22 minutes. Different fat, egg count, oat-to-flour ratio, spices, method and yield. Single-message thread 14426e26ea5e8cdc (2/12/2014), sent by Robert to himself; only his 'rz' tags accompany the recipe and no reply, forward or separate thread carries an annotation.

Web summary (davidlebovitz.com). Joanne Chang's Flour Bakery oatmeal raisin cookie, reprinted with commentary by David Lebovitz. Two things do the work: beating the butter and sugars a full five minutes so the dough carries air, and then, counterintuitively, flattening the domed cookies partway through baking - which collapses that air and gives the dense, chewy crumb rather than a cakey one. No vanilla and no water; the spicing is just nutmeg and cinnamon.

What readers report: Readers routinely swap the raisins for dried cherries, cranberries or apricots, or add chocolate or butterscotch chips and walnuts or pecans. Several confirm the mid-bake flattening genuinely produces a chewier cookie and is worth doing. Cookies that spread flat trace to butter softened in the microwave - it goes past room temperature and the dough slackens. A few found the instructions ambiguous about when the eggs go in.

Note on the source: Matches the family copy on the distinctive numbers: 1 3/4 cups/245 g flour, 1 3/4 cups/175 g old-fashioned oats, 1 1/2 cups/240 g raisins, 1 tsp baking soda, 1 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg, 2 eggs, 1 cup butter. Minor printing variances: Lebovitz gives 2/3 cup (150 g) granulated where the family copy says 3/4 cup (150 g) - same gram weight, so the gram figure is the reliable one; 1 cup (200 g) brown vs the family's 1 cup (220 g); butter 225 g vs 228 g; and cinnamon 1 tsp vs the family's 1/4 tsp, which is the one real discrepancy worth a human's eye. Licensed cookbook text (paywalled): https://app.ckbk.com/recipe/flou69447c02s001r005/oatmeal-raisin-cookies

Weights note: "kosher salt" here is taken as Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g per teaspoon, which is what Robert uses. Morton kosher is nearly twice as dense, so if that is what is to hand, weigh rather than scoop.

claude_opt.changes: Flatten cookies partway through baking, about 10 minutes in, not before — that produces Chang's chewy crumb; pre-flattening raw dough loses the effect. Family copy's 1/4 tsp cinnamon vs. published 1 tsp: split the difference at 1/2 tsp.

name: Soft Scrambled Eggs
ingredients:
2 eggs
1 tsp (4.9 g) water
Salt, a few turns of the salt mill
½ tablespoon (7.1 g) butter
Chopped chives, for garnish
White truffle oil, a few drops (optional)
directions:
Step 1 – The Eggs: Working with two eggs, gently beat them with 1 tsp of water. The water creates a softer texture and a bit more volume without imparting any flavor as milk or cream would. Next, give a few turns of the salt mill into the beaten eggs. We're not looking to over season them here, but we're creating a softer egg. Salt affects the eggs' protein molecules, making it more difficult for them to bond, resulting in a more tender scrambled egg.

Step 2 – Butter: For two eggs, melt half a tablespoon of butter on medium heat. Coat the pan evenly.

Step 3 – Cookin': Pour in the eggs and do not touch for roughly 1 minute. Once the eggs begin to set, gently fold the eggs back into itself a few times. A rubber spatula is perfect for this. After another 30 seconds, turn off the heat. The eggs should still be fairly wet. You may want to fold them again a couple of times over the next 30-60 seconds to let them firm up a bit, but you want them to remain slightly wet. They will dry out a bit by the time you plate and serve them.

Step 4 – Serve immediately. Garnish with chopped chives, then hit the eggs with just a few drops of white truffle oil. Truffle oil goes famously with eggs, but don't overdo it. A few drops on the side works well as you can control the oil to egg ratio of each bite.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Migas (Scrambled Eggs with Crispy Tortillas)": The Gmail item is a two-egg technique piece — beat with 1 tsp water and salt, half a tablespoon of butter over medium heat, leave undisturbed a minute then fold, finishing wet, with chives and a few drops of truffle oil. Migas is a full skillet dish of fried corn tortilla strips, jalapeno, bell pepper, onion, tomato and jack cheese folded into 4-5 eggs. Only the word 'scrambled' is shared. Single-message thread 13cd44f41a3b998c, 2/13/2013, Robert to himself; the prose is the source blogger's, not Robert's, and there is no reply or separate thread with his own notes.

Web summary (eatitatlanta.com). Jimmy of Eat It, Atlanta argues that scrambled eggs repay the same deliberate, attentive cooking you would give a risotto, and that doing so is what produces a genuinely creamy result rather than a dry one. His key technical claim is that salting the eggs before they hit the pan interferes with protein bonding, so the curds set more tenderly. A teaspoon of water, butter, chives and a few drops of white truffle oil round it out.

What readers report: The thread is chatty rather than technical. One commenter shares a liking for truffle oil with poached eggs, picking up on the finishing touch; another goes off on the historical provenance of the dining room at The Plaza; a third simply professes a general love of egg sandwiches at any hour. Nobody tests or contests the pre-salting claim, and there are no reported corrections to the quantities, pan temperature or timing. The comments add nothing to the method.

Note on the source: comments present but off-topic

claude_opt.changes: Nothing worth changing. The method (salt before cooking, gentle heat, water not milk, fold and pull off while wet) is sound and uncontested; commenters raised no technique issues.

name: Shaved Asparagus with Parmesan Vinaigrette
ingredients:
12 large asparagus spears (about 1 lb.), trimmed and peeled
1/4 cup (22 g) finely grated Parmesan plus a piece for shaving
1 1/2 Tbsp. (23 g) fresh lemon juice
1/4 cup (54 g) extra-virgin olive oil
Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
directions: Working with 1 asparagus spear at a time, use a vegetable peeler to shave spears into long, thin shavings. Transfer to a medium bowl (the tips will snap off as spears get thinner; add to bowl). Combine grated Parmesan and lemon juice in a small bowl and slowly whisk in oil until well blended. Season vinaigrette generously with salt and pepper. Drizzle vinaigrette over shaved asparagus and toss to coat. Divide asparagus salad among plates. Use peeler to shave more Parmesan over salad.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Roasted Asparagus with Mustard Vinaigrette": The master entry roasts whole trimmed spears at 425 and dresses them with a Dijon-lemon-olive oil vinaigrette; this recipe uses raw spears shaved into ribbons with a vegetable peeler and a vinaigrette of grated Parmesan, lemon juice and olive oil with no mustard. Butter-Braised Asparagus, the other master asparagus side, is braised in butter with herbs and is also unrelated. Single-message thread 13dcc4f8feef2617 (4/2/2013), sent by Robert to himself; the only added text is his 'rz' search tags, and no reply, forward or separate thread carries an annotation.

Web summary (bonappetit.com, 4.0 (48)). Melissa Hamilton and Christopher Hirsheimer's 2010 recipe uses a vegetable peeler to turn raw asparagus spears into thin ribbons, dressed with a Parmesan-lemon vinaigrette and topped with more shaved Parmesan; the framing presents the peeling technique as a general trick for transforming raw vegetable texture, applicable to carrots and zucchini as well as asparagus, not just a one-off preparation. What readers report: nothing — the page shows zero recipe notes, with the site's own placeholder reading 'There aren't any recipe notes yet. Be the first to start the conversation!' name: Sous Vide Glazed Carrots
cook_time: about 1 hour in the bath, plus about 2 minutes to glaze
ingredients:
1 pound (454 g) baby whole baby carrots, peeled, or 1 pound medium to large carrots, peeled and cut into 1-inch chunks with the faux-tourné cut
2 tablespoons (28 g) unsalted butter
1 tablespoon (13 g) granulated sugar
Kosher salt
Freshly ground black pepper
1 tablespoon (3.8 g) chopped parsley (optional)
directions:
Preheat water oven to 183°F. Place carrots, butter, sugar, and 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt in a vacuum bag and seal according to manufacturer's instructions. Cook carrots in the water bath until fully tender, about 1 hour. At this point, carrots can be stored in refrigerator for up to 1 week.

Empty entire contents of bag into a 12-inch, heavy-bottomed skillet and cook over high heat, stirring constantly, until liquid has reduced to a shiny glaze, about 2 minutes. Season to taste with salt and pepper, stir in parsley, and serve.
description: RM 11/14: I followed this carrot recipe, though I haven't done the last step of cooking them up.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Glazed Carrots": The only carrot side in the master is Glazed Carrots, which boils sliced carrots in water and finishes them with butter, sugar and apricot jam. The Gmail version bags carrots with butter, sugar and salt, holds them at 183F for an hour, then reduces the bag liquid to a glaze in a skillet — no jam, no boiling, and a make-ahead sous vide step. Recipe from thread 14977a4ee9bb63cb (11/3/2014). The note is from a DIFFERENT thread, 1497b78a0e733aad 'Sous vide review' (11/4/2014, Robert to Laura), where he links this exact Serious Eats carrot recipe; that email also supplies the source URL.

Web summary (Serious Eats, 4.7 (15) / 39 reviews). J. Kenji Lopez-Alt concedes that sous vide is the wrong tool for most vegetables but argues carrots are the exception, because sealing them with butter, sugar and salt concentrates their own juices into something that tastes more like carrot than the raw vegetable did. The temperature is set by chemistry rather than preference: pectin, the glue holding plant cells together, does not break down until 183F, so the bath has to run at least that hot for tender results, which also rules out improvised beer-cooler setups. After the bath the whole contents of the bag go into a hot skillet for a couple of minutes so the liquid reduces to a glossy glaze, with a splash of water to rescue it if it breaks. He notes the same treatment works for small onions, radishes, turnips, parsnips and baby artichokes.

What readers report: Timing is the sticking point. One cook ran five whole carrots for 70 minutes at 183F and still found them quite firm, guessing another twenty minutes was needed and wondering whether her circulator was underperforming; others report 185F for an hour, or 185F for about 90 minutes with thick carrot coins, as their sweet spot. A faster variation: halve the carrots lengthwise, weight the bag, run 194F for fifteen minutes, then saute, for a deliberately al dente result. Kenji himself answers a floating-bag complaint, explaining that trapped air and water vapour expand at these high temperatures and that the fix is weighting the bag with a water-filled bag or a binder clip on something heavy. Several cooks skip the sugar in favour of maple syrup, honey or brown sugar, or add granular chicken bouillon. One reviewer rejects the method outright in favour of microwave-steaming.

Note on the source: The article portion is short, only a few paragraphs before the recipe, so the headnote material is thinner than on the other pages. A sizeable share of the reviews are unanswered questions (reheating, green beans) or long off-topic anecdotes. Comments truncated at 'Read More'.

makeahead: At this point, carrots can be stored in refrigerator for up to 1 week.

claude_opt.changes: Raise the bath to 185°F and extend to 90 min for standard chunks; several readers found carrots still firm at 183°F/1hr as printed. Weight the bag so it doesn't float — trapped steam causes uneven cooking.

name: Spatchcocked Turkey
ingredients:
1 turkey, about 19 pounds (8.6 kg)
Kosher salt
Oil, for the skin
Vegetables, for under the rack
directions:
Two days ahead:

Remove backbone, giblets, neck, and some fat. Rub inside and outside skin generously with kosher salt. Put in fridge uncovered.

One day ahead:

Cover with saran wrap.

Day of:

Oil skin, lots of veg underneath. 19lb turkey convection oven at 400f to 149 degrees at least cooked part. Next time would try 425 for slightly shorter time.
description:
RM 11/15: 19 lb turkey, convection oven at 400f to 149 degrees at least cooked part. Next time would try 425 for slightly shorter time.
RM 11/16: Notes from 2016 Thanksgiving: We cooked a 19.3 pound "fresh" Costco young turkey (up to 5% retained water). Spatchcocked two days ahead and salted moderately under the skin, substantially inside the cavity, and lightly on the skin. Dried uncovered in the fridge for two days. We put the cookie cooling rack on the broiling pan, and added vegetables below before cooking. Convection oven at 415 to start, but we had the top of the turkey three inches from the element and it got too brown. We then lowered the temp to 390 for the second half of the cooking. We added water several times to the pan as it started to dry out. We cooked it for about 2h15 at an average of 400 with half convection. We removed the bird at 155f at the deepest part of the white meat. All of the kids thought the white meat was too dry. Nobody thought it was undercooked. All kids said that last year's at 149 was juicier without being undercooked. Dad says it's ok to take it out when the very thickest part of the breast is 150 next year. We let the bird rest for a whole hour, and it was still plenty warm when we carved it. At least ten minutes to carve. Other notes: Dad says gravy needed more flavor. More drippings. James' apple pie was a failure because par cooking the bottom crust didn't work. Pre cooked apples a la Kenji were good, James says. Mom says that it takes it takes a lot of strength to spatchcock.
RM 11/16: Mom says only one bag of stuffing.
notes: Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Kept separate from master entry "Dry-Brined Turkey": The Gmail bird is spatchcocked (backbone removed) two days ahead, salted and air-dried uncovered, then oiled and roasted on a rack over vegetables in a convection oven at 400-415F to a breast temp in the 149-155F range. The master Dry-Brined Turkey is a whole trussed bird brined in a plastic bag, stuffed with thyme, parsley, onions and apples, buttered under the skin, and roasted 450F then 350F with white wine in the pan to 160F in the thigh; Slow-Roasted Turkey is a whole buttered bird at 250F for ~10 hours. Different butchery, different oven profile, different ingredients. All from thread 151461e66317dcea: the 11/26/2015 original (method plus the 149F/425F line), the 11/24/2016 reply carrying the full 2016 Thanksgiving debrief, and the 11/30/2016 reply adding the stuffing line. Same thread throughout; nothing from elsewhere.

ahead: 2 days ahead

claude_opt.changes: Years of notes probe only the breast. Modern spatchcock guidance (ATK, Serious Eats) also checks the thigh separately, targeting roughly 170-175F there since dark meat needs more heat than white.

name: Xi'an Famous Foods Cumin Lamb
ingredients:
10 ounces (280 g) boneless lamb leg (ideally partially frozen)
1½ teaspoons (3.9 g) cornstarch
2 teaspoons (9.1 g) plus 2 tablespoons vegetable oil, divided
1 green onion, trimmed and chopped
1-inch (2.5 cm) piece fresh ginger, peeled and finely chopped
1 garlic clove, peeled and sliced
1½ tablespoons (9.5 g) ground cumin
1 teaspoon (6.0 g) salt
1½ teaspoons (3.9 g) Red Chili Powder
½ medium red onion, sliced
1 longhorn pepper, diagonally sliced
directions:
Carefully slice the lamb into ⅛-inch (3 mm) thick pieces (note: it's easier to cut when partially frozen).

Place the sliced lamb into a large bowl along with the cornstarch and 2 teaspoons of the vegetable oil. Mix together with your hands.

In a large skillet or wok, heat the remaining 2 tablespoons vegetable oil over high heat for 1 minute. Add the green onions, ginger, and garlic and sauté for 30 seconds. Add the lamb and stir-fry for about 5 minutes.

When the meat turns an even brown color, turn the heat down to low, add the cumin, salt, and chili powder, and stir to combine. Add the onions and longhorn pepper, stir to combine, and serve.
description: RM 4/21: We just made this. I had some trouble with chunky ends of our noodles, but overall really good deep flavor. If you use Cayenne as a substitution use way way less.
notes:
Merged from Robert's Gmail archive, Sept 2026. Recipe from thread 178e6e253e8e8bb7 (4/18/2021, Robert to himself). The note comes from a DIFFERENT thread, 178e7209352a2117 'Xian Famous Foods Lamb Noodle Recipe' (Robert's 4/22/2021 reply to his brother Will), which is about the same Xi'an lamb cooked over hand-pulled noodles; the noodle-pulling half of that complaint belongs to Will's noodle recipe, not to this one.

Web summary (tastecooking.com). Jason Wang, from the Xi'an Famous Foods cookbook - the shop's signature dish, which used to sell out before the noodles were even ready. Slicing the lamb paper-thin (easiest when it is partly frozen) maximises the surface the cumin and chilli can cling to, and a light cornstarch coating protects the meat over very high heat. The key instruction is to cook in small batches: crowd the pan and the lamb steams grey instead of browning.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS on the page.

Note on the source: Exact match to the family copy, including the gram weight the family copy carries: 10 oz (280 g) boneless lamb leg, ideally partially frozen; 1 1/2 tsp cornstarch; 2 tsp plus 2 Tbsp vegetable oil divided; 1 green onion; 1-inch (2.5 cm) ginger; 1 garlic clove sliced; 1 1/2 Tbsp ground cumin; 1 tsp salt; 1 1/2 tsp red chili powder; 1/2 medium red onion sliced; 1 longhorn pepper diagonally sliced. Robert's own note applies directly - if substituting cayenne for the shop's red chili powder, use far less. Publisher's excerpt of the same recipe: https://abramsbooks.tumblr.com/post/632140686025785344/recipe-spicy-cumin-lamb-from-xian-famous-foods

claude_opt.changes: Your 4/21 note and the site's own copy already cover the failure points (chili substitution, cooking in batches so meat browns not steams). No wok — use the Lodge cast iron on the high-output burner for closest heat.

name: Filet Mignon — Carryover Temperature Log
directions:
Not a recipe. A running log calibrating pull temperature against carryover.

Data point 1: 1.5" filet, 450F pan set next to the grill, pulled at 110F, rested to 143F. Carryover +33F. Overcooked.

Reading: that carryover is far larger than normal. The cause is the resting position — the steak kept absorbing radiant heat from the grill, on top of the steep gradient a very hot pan creates.

Adjustments to test: resting on a wire rack away from heat, pull at 118-120F. Resting in the same hot environment, pull at 100-105F. Probe from the side into the geometric center, not down through the top.

Columns for future entries: thickness · pan temp · pull temp · rest location and surface · rest time · final temp.

Open question: whether the steak rested on the pan itself, and for how long, was not recorded.
description: RM 2026: Started because a 110F pull came off at 143F. One data point so far.
notes: Created Sept 2026 from Claude conversations; exists in no email archive.

claude_opt.changes: Typical carryover for a steak rested away from heat is only about 5-10F per reverse-sear references, far below your +33F, supporting your hypothesis that radiant heat or probe placement caused the spike, not normal carryover.

name: Overnight White Bread
source: Ken Forkish, Flour Water Salt Yeast
ingredients:
White flour — 1,000 g (7 3/4 cups) — 100%
Water, 90-95F (32-35C) — 780 g (3 1/3 cups) — 78%
Fine sea salt — 22 g (1 tbsp + 1 tsp) — 2.2%
Instant dried yeast — 0.8 g (scant 1/4 tsp) — 0.08%
directions:
Makes 2 loaves of about 1 1/2 lb each. The dough also works for focaccia or iron-skillet pizza.

Schedule: bulk ferment 12-14 hours, proof about 1 1/4 hours. Mixing at 7 p.m. means shaping at 8 a.m., baking at 9:15 a.m., and bread out of the oven a little after 10 a.m.

1. Autolyse. Combine the flour and the 90-95F water in a 12-quart tub. Mix by hand just until incorporated. Cover and rest 20-30 minutes.

2. Mix. Sprinkle the salt and yeast evenly over the dough. Mixing with a wet hand, reach under the dough, take about a quarter of it, stretch it gently and fold it over the top; repeat three more times until salt and yeast are enclosed. Then integrate with the pincer method — five or six pincer cuts across the mass with thumb and forefinger, then fold the dough over itself a few times; alternate cutting and folding until fully integrated and the dough has tension. Rest a few minutes, then fold another 30 seconds until it tightens. Target dough temperature 77-78F (25-26C). Cover.

3. Fold. Two or three folds, three being better for gas retention and volume. Apply them within the first 1 1/2 hours after mixing. After the last fold, cover and let rise overnight at room temperature. Ready to divide when the dough is 2 1/2 to 3 times its original volume, 12-14 hours after mixing.

4. Divide. Flour a work surface about 2 feet wide, flour your hands, and sprinkle flour round the edges of the tub. Tip the tub and work a floured hand under the dough to release it; ease it out without pulling or tearing. Settle it into an even shape, flour the middle, and cut into 2 equal pieces.

5. Shape. Dust 2 proofing baskets with flour. Shape each piece into a medium-tight ball and set it seam side down in its basket.

6. Proof. Flour the tops lightly, set the baskets side by side, cover with a towel or bag each one. Bake about 1 1/4 hours after shaping at a room temperature near 70F (21C); nearer 1 hour if the kitchen is warmer. Use the finger-dent test and start checking at 1 hour — with this bread 15 minutes separates perfectly proofed from collapsing.

7. Preheat. At least 45 minutes before baking, put a rack in the middle of the oven and 2 covered Dutch ovens on it. Preheat to 475F (245C). With only one Dutch oven, refrigerate the second loaf about 20 minutes before baking the first and bake sequentially, giving the pot a 5-minute reheat between loaves.

8. Bake. Invert the proofed loaf onto a lightly floured counter — the seam side, which faced down while rising, becomes the top. Take the Dutch oven out with mitts, remove the lid, and place the loaf in seam side up. Replace the lid and return it to the oven, holding 475F (245C). Bake 30 minutes covered, then uncovered 20-30 minutes until at least medium dark brown all round; check after 15 minutes uncovered if the oven runs hot. Turn the loaf out and cool on a rack, or on its side so air circulates. Rest at least 20 minutes before slicing.

Take care not to let hands, fingers or forearms touch the Dutch oven.
description: RM 4/20: The overnight white bread version is the one now used, not the original 2013 formula.
notes:
Added September 2026 at Robert's direction, from Ken Forkish, Flour Water Salt Yeast. This is the loaf his April 2020 note on No-Knead Bread refers to. Quantities, baker's percentages and method are recorded in functional form; Forkish's own headnotes and commentary are not reproduced.

Web summary (jayarrbread.com). Ken Forkish's Overnight White Bread from Flour Water Salt Yeast. The whole formula turns on using almost no yeast - 0.8 g, eight hundredths of a percent of the flour - so that a 12-to-14-hour bulk ferment at room temperature does the leavening slowly and the dough's enzymes have time to build the nutty, faintly sweet flavour that normally only a sourdough gets. At 78 percent hydration the dough is slack, which is why it is mixed by hand with the pincer method rather than kneaded, and baked in a preheated covered Dutch oven so its own steam sets the crust.

What readers report: NO COMMENTS on the page. Timings it records: 12-14 hours bulk at 70-72F, 60-75 minutes proof, bake 475F for 30 minutes covered then 15-20 minutes uncovered.

Note on the source: Formula matches the family copy to the gram and to the baker's percentage: white flour 1,000 g / 100 percent; water at 90-95F (32-35C) 780 g / 78 percent; fine sea salt 22 g / 2.2 percent; instant dried yeast 0.8 g / 0.08 percent; two loaves of about 900 g (the family copy says about 1 1/2 lb each, same thing). The family copy's schedule - mix at 7 p.m., shape 8 a.m., bake 9:15 a.m. - is Forkish's own. This is a bread blog rather than the publisher; Forkish's own site (https://kensartisan.com/flour-water-salt-yeast) has the book page but not the formula. Useful cross-check with a halved version and a fuller method write-up: http://210degrees.blogspot.com/2013/10/overnight-white-bread-flour-water-salt.html (500 g flour, 390 g water, 11 g salt).

ahead: 12-14 hr bulk + about 1 1/4 hr proof
Schedule: bulk ferment 12-14 hours, proof about 1 1/4 hours.

claude_opt.changes: Fresh Loaf threads on this exact recipe report a sticky, unshapeable dough at 78% hydration with standard AP flour — use true bread flour, or cut water 3-4% if it won't hold together.

name: Aldi Complete Pancake Mix, Modified for the Griddle
source: Millville Buttermilk Complete Pancake & Waffle Mix box (Aldi), 8–10 pancake column
ingredients:
240 g (about 2 c.) Millville Buttermilk Complete pancake & waffle mix
290 g (about 1 1/4 c.) water
butter for the griddle
directions:
Weigh the mix into a bowl, add the water, and stir until the lumps break up.

Let the batter sit 15 minutes — about the time bacon takes. Two minutes is the floor; a complete mix keeps absorbing after the first stir, so batter judged right at the moment of mixing will be too stiff by the time it reaches the dispenser.

Preheat the Slate to around 400°F, then turn the burners down to medium-low. Butter it.

Stir the batter once, fill the dispenser, and pour. Cook until the edges look set and the bubbles hold open, then turn once.

Butter the griddle again between batches.
description: RM 9/20/26 — Best with butter on griddle. Griddle starts around 400 and medium low heat. At 290 g water it just barely comes through the OXO dispenser. 1.5x of this amount is the most that fits on the griddle; 1.0x is more than enough for just the family. Best to let sit for 15 mins when making bacon. 1.5x (360 g mix / 435 g water, everything scaled) pours fine through the dispenser too.
notes: Derived from the box's 8–10 pancake column (2 c. mix / 1 c. water) and thinned for the OXO batter dispenser: water raised from roughly 237 g to 290 g, about 1:1.2 mix-to-water. The 240 g is Robert's scale reading for the box's 2-cup line, not a published figure — if the box is reformulated, re-derive it from the nutrition panel serving weight. Thinner batter spreads more, so these run flatter and wider than the box version. Cup equivalents in the ingredient lines are approximate restatements of the weighed amounts; the grams are what to follow. Cooked on a 36" Weber Slate — propane flat top, so "400 then medium-low" is burner control rather than a thermostat setting. Scales linearly: 1.5x is 360 g mix / 435 g water.

claude_opt.changes: Rest the batter in the bowl, not the dispenser — a complete mix keeps thickening as it sits, and settles besides. Stir once, then fill. If it stalls, add water 15 g at a time.

name: Quick-Pickled Cucumbers With Rice Vinegar
ingredients:
1 cup (240 g) rice wine vinegar
1 cup (237 g) water
3/4 cup (150 g) sugar
1 tablespoon (8 g) kosher salt
4 cups (about 450 g) thinly sliced Japanese or English cucumbers (about 3 Japanese or 1 English)
directions:
Combine the vinegar, water, sugar and salt in a medium saucepan and bring to a boil over high heat. Remove from heat.

Add the cucumber slices and stir. Cover with a clean kitchen towel or a double layer of heavy-duty paper towels, and press down until the towel is soaked and touching the cucumbers.

Let rest 10 minutes. Transfer the cucumbers to a sealable container, pour in enough brine to cover, and discard the rest. Refrigerate for up to 1 month.
notes:
What readers report: sweetness is the main complaint. Three of the ten reviewers cut the sugar, by anywhere from a third to about two-thirds, and one also wanted more vinegar. Kenji replied that the towel is necessary, because it keeps the cucumbers submerged so they take up the brine. He also said the brine can be reused once, but not more, since fresh cucumbers water it down.

Weights: salt is Diamond Crystal at 2.8 g/tsp, which matches Kenji's kosher salt. The cucumber weight is an estimate, since sliced cucumber packs unevenly into a cup. Small Persian cucumbers pickle the same way as Japanese ones; roughly four make 4 cups.

Used at 1/3 scale in Laura's Salmon Poke Bowl (Dinner).

claude_opt.changes: Cut the sugar to 1/2 cup (100 g). Readers consistently found it too sweet.

name: Laura's Salmon Poke Bowl
ingredients:
1 lb (454 g) skinless salmon, cut into 1-inch cubes
Kosher salt
Oil, for the pan
1/3 cup (80 g) rice wine vinegar
1/3 cup (79 g) water
2 tablespoons plus 2 teaspoons (33 g) sugar
1 teaspoon (3 g) kosher salt
3 finger-sized mini cucumbers (about 135 g), thinly sliced
Mayonnaise and sriracha, 3 parts to 1 by volume
1 1/2 rice-cooker scoops (about 225 g) sushi rice
1 avocado, sliced
Green scallions, sliced
directions:
Start the rice in the rice cooker.

Pickles: bring the vinegar, water, sugar and salt to a boil, then take it off the heat. Stir in the cucumber slices. Press a towel or doubled paper towels down onto them until it's soaked through, and let them rest 10 minutes. Lift the cucumbers out and save the brine.

Season the rice: when the rice is done, fold a few spoonfuls of the pickle brine into it while it's still hot.

Sriracha mayo: stir the mayo and sriracha together at 3 to 1.

Salmon: pat the cubes dry and salt them. Sear them in an oiled pan over medium-high heat until browned outside and still a little pink in the middle.

Assemble: rice first, then the salmon, pickles and avocado. Drizzle with sriracha mayo and scatter scallions on top.
notes:
Pickles: Kenji's Quick-Pickled Cucumbers With Rice Vinegar (see Preserves) at 1/3 scale, with the sugar cut per that entry's optimization note (Kenji's amount at this scale would be 1/4 cup / 50 g).

Make-ahead: the full-size pickle keeps a month in the fridge. With a jar on hand, skip the pickle step and save about 8 minutes of hands-on time; use a few spoonfuls of the jar's brine for the rice.

Weights: the rice assumes a 180 ml rice-cooker cup of short-grain rice at about 150 g. If you weigh the sriracha mayo, 3 to 1 by volume is about 7 to 3 by weight.

Optional toppings: toasted sesame seeds or furikake, a drizzle of soy sauce or ponzu, nori strips, shelled edamame, or crispy fried shallots.
_origin: Laura's own recipe, written up September 2026

claude_opt.changes: Sear only two or three sides of each cube. Turning all six overcooks the middle and breaks up the fish.
